# Political and Public International Law

## Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA

**LOTRIM CONSTRUCTION, INC., REPRESENTED BY ITS PRESIDENT, ENGINEER ODILON MARLON L. GAVIOLA, AND ENGINEER ODILON MARLON L. GAVIOLA, PETITIONERS, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 270295 | 2026-04-29 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction  
**Specific topics:** COA Proper is not limited to the auditor's grounds (Yap v. COA); Administrative due process in COA proceedings; TechITS inspection reports; Quantum meruit also allows the Government to recover overpayments; Rule 64 period: 30 days, and not less than five days after denial of reconsideration; Estoppel against belatedly invoking CIAC jurisdiction
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (II. Jurisdiction > B. Subject Matter Jurisdiction > 2. Effect of Estoppel)

### Doctrine
**COA Proper is not limited to the grounds relied upon by the auditor** (*Yap v. COA*, reiterated). In the exercise of its constitutional audit power (Const., Art. IX-D, Sec. 2(2)), it must make its own assessment of a disallowance. It may adjust the amount, identify additional persons liable, or modify their participation without a separate audit observation memorandum, notice of suspension or notice of disallowance, provided the parties have a fair opportunity to be heard. Due process is satisfied where the party could explain its side or seek reconsideration. COA's Technical and Information Technology Services (TechITS) is an internal office answerable only to COA, so it need not notify the contractor of its inspection or furnish it its report.

**Quantum meruit cuts both ways.** It lets a contractor recover the reasonable value of work done under a void government contract. But it "cannot be distorted into a shield for contractors to retain payments in excess of what is legally or contractually due": the Government may recover payments that exceed the actual accomplishment. COA's factual findings on the amount due, if supported by substantial evidence, are respected.

Procedurally, under **Rule 64, Sec. 3**, the petition must be filed within 30 days from notice. A motion for reconsideration interrupts the period, and after its denial only the remaining period, but not less than five days, is left. A late petition makes the COA ruling final and immutable. Also, **a party who actively participated in the COA proceedings and sought affirmative relief is estopped from belatedly invoking CIAC jurisdiction** under an arbitration clause (*Tijam v. Sibonghanoy*; *Amoguis v. Ballado*).

### Facts
In a December 20, 2012 public bidding for the expansion of the Administration Building of the Bureau of Customs (BOC) Port of Davao, Lotrim Construction, Inc. was declared the bidder with the lowest calculated and responsive bid, PHP 17,203,203.18. The approved budget for the contract was PHP 20,000,000.00. The contract was signed on March 15, 2013, and the notice to proceed was received on April 2, 2013. The BOC paid Lotrim a 15% advance payment of PHP 2,419,200.45 on April 12, 2013 and a first partial payment of PHP 3,828,184.10 on June 17, 2013.

COA disallowed the advance payment (ND dated July 12, 2013) and the partial payment (ND dated January 22, 2014). Its grounds were that maintenance and other operating expenses (MOOE) funds were diverted to new construction, contrary to PD 1445 and PD 1777. Funds had also been obligated on December 27, 2012 to a nonexistent creditor before any award, contrary to Book VI, Sec. 40 of EO 292, and FY 2011 savings had been spent beyond FY 2012. Lotrim was held liable as payee. The BOC ordered Lotrim to stop work, and Lotrim reported 80.67% accomplishment worth PHP 13,878,362.71. On the BOC's request, COA TechITS inspected the project. Its report dated April 7, 2014 found only 36.90% accomplishment, worth PHP 6,347,826.73.

The COA Cluster Director (October 7, 2015) lifted both NDs and allowed payment on *quantum meruit* up to the TechITS figure. On automatic review, COA Proper (Decision No. 2018-204, January 30, 2018) affirmed the NDs and held the contract void for lack of a valid appropriation. It held all persons named liable for PHP 6,247,384.55, but it limited Lotrim's liability to PHP 408,859.16: recomputing on *quantum meruit*, it found that Lotrim had been overpaid by that amount. It also ordered a supplemental ND against the BAC chairman and referred the matter to the Ombudsman.

Lotrim received the COA Proper decision on October 16, 2018 and moved for reconsideration on November 12, 2018. It attached a third-party report putting its accomplishment at 64.15% (PHP 12,131,455.56). COA denied the motion by Resolution No. 2022-010 dated January 28, 2022, which Lotrim received on August 31, 2023. Lotrim filed a Rule 64 petition on October 2, 2023. It claimed it was denied due process because the inspection was made without notice to it, and because the extent of its accomplishment should have been the subject of a separate audit observation memorandum, notice of suspension and notice of disallowance. It also claimed that the dispute belonged to the Construction Industry Arbitration Commission (CIAC).

### Issues
1. Whether the Rule 64 petition was filed on time.
2. Whether petitioners were denied due process when COA relied on the TechITS inspection, made without notice to them, and determined their accomplishment without a separate notice of disallowance.
3. Whether petitioners may invoke the jurisdiction of the CIAC at this stage.
4. Whether COA gravely abused its discretion in ordering petitioners to refund PHP 408,859.16 as an overpayment under quantum meruit.

### Ruling
**1. No, the petition was filed out of time.** Lotrim moved for reconsideration 27 days after receiving the COA Proper decision, leaving three days. Under Rule 64, Sec. 3, it therefore had five days from notice of the denial (August 31, 2023), or until September 5, 2023. It filed on October 2, 2023. **The COA rulings thus became final and immutable** and "may no longer be modified in any respect, even if the modification is meant to correct erroneous conclusions of fact and law." Lotrim neither sought an extension nor offered any compelling reason to relax the rules. The petition would fail on the merits anyway.

**2. No denial of due process.** Due process is simply the opportunity to be heard or to seek reconsideration (*Saligumba v. COA*). Art. IX-D, Sec. 2(2) gives COA exclusive authority to define the scope of its audit and its techniques. Under *Yap v. COA*, COA on appeal "is not required to limit its review only to the grounds relied upon by a government agency's auditor" and is "duty-bound to make its own assessment." It may identify additional persons liable, adjust the amount, or modify participation. **No separate audit was needed to fix Lotrim's percentage of accomplishment, because that issue was "part and parcel of the subject audit."** Lotrim's appeal and motion were resolved on the merits, and its *quantum meruit* claim was granted. COA also reviewed the site and Lotrim's own accomplishment reports and billings. **TechITS, an internal office providing technical support (COA Memorandum No. 2009-083), "is answerable only to COA, and not to any private party."** No COA rule requires it to notify the contractor or furnish its report. In any case, Lotrim was able to refute the findings before COA Proper.

**3. No, petitioners are estopped from invoking CIAC jurisdiction.** The CIAC may have had jurisdiction through the contract's arbitration clause, but the issue was raised for the first time on appeal. A party cannot change its theory on appeal (*Chinatrust v. Turner*). Belated objections to jurisdiction are barred after a party has actively participated and sought affirmative relief (*Tijam v. Sibonghanoy*; *Megan Sugar*; *Spouses Rebamonte*). Under *Amoguis v. Ballado*, the bar arises when six circumstances concur:

- the claimant had a statutory right;
- the claimant did not invoke it;
- an unreasonable length of time passed before the claimant raised jurisdiction;
- the claimant actively participated in the case and sought affirmative relief from the court without jurisdiction;
- the claimant knew or had constructive knowledge of which forum had subject matter jurisdiction; and
- irreparable damage would be caused to the other party, who relied on the forum and on the claimant's implicit waiver.

All six were present. Lotrim appealed to the Cluster Director for *quantum meruit* payment and moved for reconsideration before COA Proper. It first raised CIAC jurisdiction on September 29, 2023, nearly eight years after the Cluster Director's decision. **CIAC jurisdiction "is not absolute and may be waived by the party's conduct."**

**4. No grave abuse of discretion.** *Quantum meruit* prevents unjust enrichment of the State (*Torreta v. COA*). But "[i]ts equitable nature cuts both ways: while it obliges the government to pay for benefits actually received, it likewise safeguards public funds by allowing the recovery of overpayments." COA's expertise-based findings, supported by substantial evidence, deserve respect and even finality. **Lotrim must return the PHP 408,859.16 overpayment.**

### Disposition
Petition DISMISSED. COA Decision No. 2018-204 dated January 30, 2018 and Resolution No. 2022-010 dated January 28, 2022 were AFFIRMED. COA was DIRECTED to implement them and to collect the amounts overpaid to Lotrim Construction, Inc., consistent with *quantum meruit* and subject to applicable laws, rules and regulations.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** BuildCo's contract with a government agency was declared void for lack of a valid appropriation, and the payments made to it were disallowed. On appeal, the COA Cluster Director allowed BuildCo to be paid on quantum meruit. On automatic review, COA Proper relied on an inspection report of its Technical and Information Technology Services (TechITS), which put BuildCo's actual accomplishment far below what it had billed. COA Proper found that BuildCo had been overpaid and ordered it to refund the excess. BuildCo was never notified of the inspection, but it attacked the inspection report in its motion for reconsideration, which COA Proper resolved on the merits. BuildCo argues that (i) it was denied due process, since the extent of its accomplishment should have been the subject of a separate notice of disallowance, and (ii) quantum meruit exists to protect contractors and cannot be used to make them refund. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. BuildCo was not denied due process, and quantum meruit may be the basis for ordering a contractor to refund an overpayment.
- **Legal basis:** Under Art. IX-D, Sec. 2(2) of the Constitution, COA has exclusive authority to define the scope of its audit and to disallow irregular or excessive expenditures. On appeal, COA Proper is not limited to the grounds relied upon by the auditor; it must make its own assessment and may adjust the amount disallowed or the persons liable, so long as the parties are given an opportunity to be heard (Yap v. COA). COA TechITS is an internal office that need not notify the contractor of its inspection or furnish it its report. Quantum meruit cuts both ways: it obliges the government to pay for benefits received but also allows recovery of overpayments. (Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA, G.R. No. 270295, April 29, 2026)
- **Application:** (i) The extent of BuildCo's accomplishment was part and parcel of the audit of the disallowed payments, so no separate notice of disallowance was needed. The TechITS inspection was an internal technical aid to COA. BuildCo was heard: it attacked the report in its motion for reconsideration, and COA Proper ruled on it. That is all due process requires. (ii) BuildCo invoked quantum meruit to be paid for the reasonable value of its work. The same principle limits it to that value. Keeping payments beyond its actual accomplishment would unjustly enrich BuildCo at the public's expense.
- **Conclusion:** COA Proper did not gravely abuse its discretion in ordering BuildCo to refund the overpayment.

**Q2.** Contractor Delta received a COA Proper decision on March 1. It moved for reconsideration on March 28. It received the resolution denying the motion on June 2 and filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 with the Supreme Court on July 2, without asking for an extension. (a) Was the petition filed on time? (b) If not, may the Supreme Court still correct a clear error in the computation of Delta's liability?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No, the petition was late. (b) No. The COA ruling has become final and immutable, absent a compelling reason to relax the rules.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 64, Sec. 3 of the Rules of Court, a petition for certiorari against a COA judgment must be filed within 30 days from notice. A motion for reconsideration, if allowed by the COA rules, interrupts the period. If it is denied, the petitioner may file within the remaining period, which shall not be less than five days from notice of the denial. A late petition is fatal: the COA ruling becomes final, and under the doctrine of immutability it may no longer be modified, even to correct erroneous conclusions of fact or law. (Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA, G.R. No. 270295, April 29, 2026)
- **Application:** (a) From March 1 to March 28, 27 of Delta's 30 days had run, leaving 3 days. Because the remaining period may not be less than five days, Delta had until June 7, five days from its June 2 receipt of the denial. Filing on July 2 was late. (b) Delta did not seek an extension, and no compelling reason to relax the rules appears. The COA decision therefore became final and immutable, and the Supreme Court can no longer modify it, even to correct an alleged error.
- **Conclusion:** Delta's petition was filed out of time and should be dismissed, leaving the COA ruling final and unalterable.

**Q3.** Gamma's construction contract with a government agency provides that disputes shall be submitted to arbitration before the Construction Industry Arbitration Commission (CIAC). COA disallowed payments to Gamma and later found that Gamma had been overpaid. Gamma appealed to the COA Cluster Director and asked to be paid on quantum meruit. It then moved for reconsideration before COA Proper. It never mentioned arbitration in either proceeding. Only in its Rule 64 petition, nearly eight years after the Cluster Director's decision, did Gamma argue that COA had no jurisdiction to determine the extent of its accomplishment because that is a construction dispute cognizable by the CIAC. Will the argument prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Gamma is estopped from invoking CIAC jurisdiction at this late stage.
- **Legal basis:** Issues not raised below cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, and a party may not change its theory on appeal. Under Tijam v. Sibonghanoy and Amoguis v. Ballado, a belated jurisdictional challenge is barred when six circumstances concur: the claimant had a statutory right; it did not invoke it; an unreasonable time passed before it raised jurisdiction; it actively participated and sought affirmative relief from the forum; it knew or should have known which forum had jurisdiction; and the other party would suffer irreparable damage after relying on the forum. CIAC jurisdiction, though generally available under an arbitration clause, is not absolute and may be waived by conduct. (Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA, G.R. No. 270295, April 29, 2026)
- **Application:** Gamma had a contractual and statutory basis to seek CIAC arbitration but never invoked it. Instead, it actively litigated before COA and sought affirmative relief, namely quantum meruit payment and reconsideration. Gamma was a party to the arbitration clause, so it knew of the CIAC option. It raised the issue only after adverse rulings and after an unreasonable delay of almost eight years. Its conduct amounts to a waiver of CIAC jurisdiction and an implied submission to COA's.
- **Conclusion:** Gamma's belated invocation of CIAC jurisdiction will not prosper.

> Note: Promulgated April 29, 2026, within the June 30, 2026 cutoff. The main opinion adopts points raised by Associate Justices Lazaro-Javier (immutability) and Singh (the eight-year delay); both concurred, and these points are part of the main opinion. The body gives the disallowed payments as PHP 2,419,200.45 and PHP 3,828,184.10, totaling the PHP 6,247,384.55 liability. COA's overpayment computation, reproduced in footnote 36, uses gross figures (PHP 2,580,480.48 and PHP 5,568,341.04) less recoupment and retention. The decision says CIAC jurisdiction was first raised on September 29, 2023, although it records the petition as filed on October 2, 2023.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70508)

## Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras

**RE: DROPPING FROM THE ROLLS OF MS. MAILYN E. MIRAS, STENOGRAPHER III, BRANCH 65, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, INFANTA, QUEZON.**  
A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC | 2025-11-05 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Resolution

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** XI. Law on Public Officers > B. Public Office > 9. Termination of Official Relation  
**Specific topics:** Dropping from the rolls for AWOL of at least 30 working days (2025 RACCS, Rule 20, Section 132); No prior notice required; notice of separation and 15-day appeal; Dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary; Mere filing of a leave application does not authorize absence

### Doctrine
Under **Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 Rules on Administrative Cases in the Civil Service (RACCS)** (CSC Resolution No. 2500357), **an official or employee who is continuously absent without official leave (AWOL) for at least 30 working days may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice.** A notice of separation is issued at the employee's last known address, and the employee may appeal within 15 days from receipt. Failure to provide the notice does not invalidate the dropping, but the appeal period then runs from actual receipt of the notice.

**Dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary** (2025 RACCS, Rule 20, Section 135): it does not forfeit any benefit or disqualify the employee from reemployment in the government. Its purpose is to address the disruption caused by continuous and prolonged AWOL by declaring the post vacant so it can be filled. Hence, the dismissal of criminal cases against the employee is irrelevant.

**Approval of a vacation leave is not presumed**; it depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of office, so the mere filing of a leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent. Medical or psychological problems, or a feeling of being bullied by a supervisor, do not excuse an employee who stops reporting without waiting for the leave to be approved. The Court applied these settled rules and denied the appeal with finality.

### Facts
Mailyn E. Miras was Court Stenographer III of RTC Branch 65, Infanta, Quezon. On July 22, 2020, she applied for sick leave, and on July 24, 2020, for 30 days of vacation leave. The Clerk of Court, Atty. Edward Justine R. Orden, recommended disapproval of both, and neither was acted upon by the presiding judge, who had been appointed to another court. Without waiting for action, Miras stopped reporting on July 27, 2020 and ignored a Return to Work Order sent on July 30, 2020. She came back only on September 23, 2020, after 43 working days, to accomplish her DTRs for July to December 2020. Atty. Orden refused to accept them and, on September 28, 2020, asked the OCA to drop her from the rolls.

OCA records showed that she had not submitted DTRs from July 2020 onward and had no approved leave for the period. The OCA also noted three pending administrative cases and numerous criminal cases for falsification of public documents, use of falsified documents and perjury against her. It recommended that she be dropped from the rolls for being AWOL for at least 30 days, without prejudice to those cases, and that her position be declared vacant under Rule 20, Section 107(a)(1) of the 2017 RACCS.

On October 9, 2023, the Court's First Division dropped Miras from the rolls effective July 1, 2020, retained the benefits she may be entitled to and her eligibility for reemployment in the government, declared her position vacant, and directed that she be notified. On March 27, 2024, she filed an untitled pleading seeking reconsideration, which the Court treated as an appeal. She claimed that Atty. Orden harassed her and kept recommending disapproval of her leaves although she was bleeding from a uterine myoma; that the criminal and administrative cases he filed, all the criminal cases having been dismissed, caused her an anxiety disorder that led to her long absence; and that being dropped without notice violated her right to due process.

### Issues
1. Whether Ms. Miras was validly dropped from the rolls, without prior notice, for being absent without approved leave.
2. Whether the dismissal of the criminal cases against her, her medical and psychological condition, or her supervisor's alleged harassment justify setting aside her dropping from the rolls.

### Ruling
**1. Yes. Her dropping from the rolls was proper, and no prior notice was required.** Her conduct falls under Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 RACCS, under which an employee continuously AWOL for at least 30 working days "may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice," subject to a notice of separation at the last known address and the right to appeal within 15 days from receipt; failure to provide the notice does not invalidate the dropping. The Court read the provision as clear that "no prior notice is required" to drop such an employee. Her AWOL was proved by the OAS-OCA records of her failure to submit DTRs and bundy cards, the absence of any approved leave for the period, and the undisputed fact that she ignored a written order to return to work.

**2. No.** **Dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary** under Rule 20, Section 135 of the 2025 RACCS; it does not forfeit benefits or disqualify from reemployment. It addresses the disruption caused by continuous and prolonged AWOL by removing employees who have effectively abandoned their posts, "without the stigma or penalties attendant to disciplinary dismissal." **The dismissal of the criminal cases was therefore irrelevant** to her 43 working days of absence without approved leave. She was also wrong to stop reporting because of her medical and psychological problems or because she felt bullied; she should have waited for the approval of her vacation leave. **"The approval of a vacation leave is not automatically presumed"**; it depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of the agency, and "[t]he mere filing of a vacation leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent." Her refusal to return when ordered, and her 43-working-day absence although she applied for only 30 days of leave, showed a "recalcitrant attitude and willful intention to be absent." Her AWOL prejudiced the public service: public office is a public trust, and those in the administration of justice must uphold public accountability.

### Disposition
Ms. Miras's appeal from the October 9, 2023 Resolution, which dropped her from the rolls effective July 1, 2020, declared her position of Court Stenographer III, RTC Branch 65, Infanta, Quezon vacant, and informed her of her separation from the service, was DENIED with finality.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Liza, a Clerk III in a municipal trial court, stopped reporting for work and did not file any leave application. After she had been continuously absent for 35 working days, the Supreme Court, on the OCA's recommendation, dropped her from the rolls without first notifying her or asking her to explain. No notice of separation was sent to her last known address; she learned of it only when a co-employee handed her a copy months later. (a) Was Liza denied due process? (b) Did the failure to send her the notice of separation invalidate her dropping from the rolls, and from when may she appeal?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. An employee continuously AWOL for at least 30 working days may be dropped from the rolls without prior notice. (b) No. The failure to send the notice of separation does not invalidate the dropping, but her 15-day period to appeal runs from her actual receipt of the notice.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 RACCS, an official or employee continuously on AWOL for at least 30 working days may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice. A notice of separation is issued at the last known address, and the employee may appeal within 15 days from receipt. Failure to provide a notice of separation does not invalidate the dropping, but the right to appeal is counted from the employee's actual receipt of the notice. In Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras (A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC, November 5, 2025), the Court applied this provision and held that no prior notice is required to drop an employee continuously AWOL for at least 30 working days.
- **Application:** Liza was continuously absent for 35 working days without any leave application, beyond the 30-working-day threshold. The rule allows her to be dropped immediately without prior notice, so the lack of a prior chance to explain does not violate due process; her remedy is to appeal once she is notified of her separation. Since no notice of separation was sent to her, the dropping remains valid, but her 15 days to appeal began only when she actually received the notice from her co-employee.
- **Conclusion:** Liza was validly dropped from the rolls without prior notice, and she may appeal within 15 days from her actual receipt of the notice of separation.

**Q2.** Rico, a court interpreter, filed an application for 30 days of vacation leave. His branch clerk of court recommended disapproval, and the presiding judge never acted on it. Rico stopped reporting the next day, ignored a written order to return to work, and came back after 45 working days. He argues that his leave should be deemed approved because it was never acted upon, and that he was suffering from anxiety caused by his supervisor's harassment. May Rico be dropped from the rolls?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Rico was continuously absent without approved leave for more than 30 working days and may be dropped from the rolls.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 RACCS, an employee continuously on AWOL for at least 30 working days may be dropped from the rolls without prior notice. In Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras (A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC, November 5, 2025), the Court held that the approval of a vacation leave is not automatically presumed but depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of office, so the mere filing of a leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent. It also held that medical or psychological problems, or a feeling of being bullied by a supervisor, did not justify absenting oneself without waiting for the leave to be approved, especially where the employee ignored an order to return to work.
- **Application:** Rico's leave application was never approved, and its mere filing did not authorize him to stop reporting. He also ignored a written order to return and stayed away for 45 working days, longer than the 30 days he applied for, which shows a willful intention to be absent. His anxiety and his complaints against his supervisor did not excuse him from waiting for action on his leave.
- **Conclusion:** Rico may be dropped from the rolls for being continuously absent without approved leave for more than 30 working days.

**Q3.** Nora, a court stenographer, was dropped from the rolls for being absent without approved leave for 40 working days. On appeal, she argues that (a) being dropped from the rolls will forfeit her accrued benefits and bar her from any future government employment, and (b) she should be reinstated because the falsification cases her supervisor filed against her were all dismissed. Rule on her arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Nora is mistaken; dropping from the rolls does not forfeit her benefits or disqualify her from reemployment in the government. (b) The dismissal of the criminal cases does not warrant her reinstatement because it is irrelevant to her absence without leave.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 20, Section 135 of the 2025 RACCS, dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary in nature and does not result in the forfeiture of any benefit or in disqualification from reemployment in the government. In Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras (A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC, November 5, 2025), the Court explained that its purpose is to address the disruption caused by an employee's continuous and prolonged AWOL by declaring the position vacant so it can be filled, "without the stigma or penalties attendant to disciplinary dismissal"; hence, the dismissal of criminal cases against the employee was irrelevant to her continuous absence without approved leave.
- **Application:** Nora's separation is not a penalty but a measure to fill a post she effectively abandoned, so she keeps the benefits she is entitled to under existing laws and may be reemployed in the government. The ground for her separation is her 40 working days of absence without approved leave, not the falsification charges, so their dismissal does not affect the validity of her dropping from the rolls.
- **Conclusion:** Nora keeps her benefits and eligibility for reemployment, but her dropping from the rolls stands despite the dismissal of the criminal cases.

> Note: The Court applied the 2025 RACCS (CSC Resolution No. 2500357), although the OCA had recommended dropping under Rule 20, Section 107(a)(1) of the 2017 RACCS. The E-Library text cites "Section 132(A-l)", read here as 132(A-1). The quoted Section 132 also says dropping must be done within 30 days from the time the ground arises, failing which the head of agency is barred; the Resolution did not discuss this point. As printed, the fallo numbers its items (1), (2) and (4), and it does not repeat the retention of benefits stated in the October 9, 2023 Resolution. The dropping took effect July 1, 2020, although the text says she stopped reporting on July 27, 2020; both dates are as printed.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70142)

## Sarigumba v. COMELEC

**PETRONILO SOLOMON SARIGUMBA, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS, REPRESENTED BY CAMPAIGN FINANCE UNIT, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 263615 | 2025-08-19 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** VIII. Constitutional Rights > N. Rights to Speedy Trial and Speedy Disposition of Cases  
**Specific topics:** Inordinate delay in the COMELEC's preliminary investigation of an election offense; Cagang framework: burden shifts to the prosecution when prescribed periods are exceeded; Failure to file a counter-affidavit does not suspend the period to resolve (COMELEC Rules, Rule 34, Secs. 6 and 8); Election overspending (OEC Sec. 100 in relation to Sec. 262, as amended by RA 7166); Exceptions to the prior motion for reconsideration before certiorari
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (XII. Election Law > G. Power to Prosecute Election Offenses (BP 881, Sec. 265, as amended by RA 9369; Exclude penal provisions))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))

### Doctrine
The right to a speedy disposition of cases under **Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution** may be invoked in a preliminary investigation conducted by the COMELEC. Applying *Cagang v. Sandiganbayan*, once the delay goes beyond the prescribed periods, **the burden shifts to the prosecution** to prove that it followed the prescribed procedure, that the complexity of the issues and the volume of evidence made the delay inevitable, and that the respondent suffered no prejudice.

**A respondent's failure to file a counter-affidavit does not give the COMELEC license to delay the preliminary investigation indefinitely.** Rule 34, Sections 6 and 8 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure must be read together: if the respondent does not file a counter-affidavit within the 10-day period, the investigating officer must resolve the complaint on the complainant's evidence, and **the 20-day period to conclude the preliminary investigation (plus five days to resolve) is counted from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit**. A delay of over six years in resolving a simple overspending complaint against one respondent, decided only on his own Statement of Election Contributions and Expenditures (SOCE), is inordinate. The Court applied *Peñas v. COMELEC* and *Peralta v. COMELEC* even though the respondents there filed counter-affidavits and the petitioner here did not.

Reiterating *Peñas* and *Cervantes v. Sandiganbayan*, a respondent is not duty-bound to follow up his case, and he may invoke the right after the adverse resolution, unless the delay is directly attributable to him. Because inordinate delay alone merits dismissal, a prior motion for reconsideration may be dispensed with. The remedy is the **nullification of the resolution finding probable cause and the dismissal of the complaint**.

### Facts
Petitioner Petronilo Solomon Sarigumba ran for mayor of Loboc, Bohol in the May 10, 2010 elections and lost. On June 10, 2010, he filed his SOCE, which reported contributions and expenditures of PHP 143,000.00. On November 3, 2014, he received a letter dated October 1, 2014 from the head of the COMELEC Campaign Finance Unit (CFU) requiring him to explain his alleged overspending. He submitted an Explanation dated November 27, 2014.

Based on the COMELEC's own timeline, the CFU filed a *motu proprio* Complaint on December 20, 2014 for overspending under Section 100 in relation to Section 262 of the Omnibus Election Code (OEC), as amended by RA 7166. The preliminary investigation was set on April 14, 2015, but only the complainant's representative appeared. Petitioner's counsel sought a resetting to May 12, 2015 because petitioner was unfit to travel, which was granted. On May 12, 2015, counsel filed an omnibus motion to cancel the setting and to delegate the investigation to the provincial COMELEC officer. An Order dated June 11, 2015 denied the motion and directed petitioner to subscribe his counter-affidavit before a public prosecutor and send it by registered mail or courier. Petitioner never filed one.

On July 27, 2021, the COMELEC Law Department found probable cause. It reasoned that as a party member, petitioner could spend only PHP 3.00 per voter, or PHP 30,816.00 for Loboc's 10,272 registered voters, yet his SOCE showed PHP 143,000.00 in expenses. On July 28, 2021, the COMELEC En Banc adopted the recommendation in Minute Resolution No. 21-0499-24, which petitioner received on August 18, 2022.

Without moving for reconsideration, petitioner filed a Rule 64 petition for certiorari in relation to Rule 65, claiming inordinate delay and invoking *Peñas*. He also asked for a writ of preliminary injunction. The COMELEC, through the OSG, argued that petitioner failed to file a motion for reconsideration; that the period to resolve never began to run because he filed no counter-affidavit; and that he waived the right by not invoking it on time and by not taking part in the preliminary investigation.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition for certiorari may be entertained even though petitioner did not first move for reconsideration of the COMELEC En Banc Minute Resolution.
2. Whether the COMELEC violated petitioner's right to a speedy disposition of his case, so that the finding of probable cause must be nullified and the complaint dismissed.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, a motion for reconsideration was not required.** As a rule, certiorari will not lie unless a motion for reconsideration is first filed. The exceptions include an urgent necessity for resolution where further delay would prejudice the petitioner, cases where a motion for reconsideration would be useless, and cases where public interest is involved. Because the proceedings were attended by inordinate delay, which "alone merits the dismissal of the *motu proprio* Complaint," a motion for reconsideration would have been futile.

**2. Yes, the right was violated.** Following *Cagang*, the right to speedy disposition may be invoked in the COMELEC's preliminary investigation. The proceedings ran from December 20, 2014 to July 28, 2021, or six years and over seven months, and six years and over one month from the June 11, 2015 Order directing petitioner to file a counter-affidavit. The COMELEC's argument that the period never ran because no counter-affidavit was filed relied on Rule 34, Section 8 alone. **Reading Section 8 with Section 6, failure to file a counter-affidavit does not give the COMELEC "unbridled license to indefinitely toll or delay" the investigation; the 20-day period runs from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit.** The COMELEC never stated when petitioner received the June 11, 2015 Order or when his deadline lapsed, and the Court took that silence against it. Given the length of the delay, the COMELEC plainly failed to observe the 20-day and five-day periods, so it bore the burden of justifying the delay.

It did not discharge that burden. The case involved no complex issues or voluminous records: the Law Department relied only on petitioner's SOCE and a simple computation of the spending limit. As in *Peñas* and *Peralta*, which involved the same kind of *motu proprio* overspending complaints against 2010 mayoral candidates that took the COMELEC about six years or more to resolve, the delay was unjustified. That the petitioners there filed counter-affidavits made no difference, because the COMELEC Rules required the investigating officer to resolve the case even without one. Petitioner's two motions in April and May 2015 did not cause substantial delay; from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit, the delay was the COMELEC's. Nor could petitioner be faulted for invoking the right only after the adverse resolution: it is the duty of the prosecutor to resolve the complaint speedily "regardless of whether the petitioner did not object to the delay or that the delay was with his acquiescence provided that it was not due to causes directly attributable to him" (*Cervantes*, reiterated in *Peñas*). **The Minute Resolution was therefore tainted with grave abuse of discretion; it must be nullified and the complaint dismissed.**

### Disposition
Petition GRANTED. COMELEC En Banc Minute Resolution No. 21-0499-24 dated July 28, 2021 was NULLIFIED for having been rendered with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. The *motu proprio* Complaint against Petronilo Solomon Sarigumba for election overspending under Section 100 in relation to Section 262 of the OEC, as amended by RA 7166, was DISMISSED.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Lorenzo lost the 2019 mayoral elections and filed his Statement of Election Contributions and Expenditures. In January 2020, the COMELEC Law Department filed a motu proprio complaint against him for overspending, based solely on his SOCE. In March 2020, Lorenzo received a subpoena requiring him to file his counter-affidavit within 10 days, but he never filed one. In 2026, the COMELEC En Banc found probable cause and directed the filing of an Information. Lorenzo files a petition for certiorari invoking his right to a speedy disposition of cases. The COMELEC argues that (1) the period to resolve the complaint never began to run because Lorenzo never filed a counter-affidavit, and (2) Lorenzo waived the right because he never followed up on his case or objected to the delay. Rule on the COMELEC's arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. The COMELEC committed inordinate delay, and the finding of probable cause should be nullified and the complaint dismissed.
- **Legal basis:** Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution guarantees the speedy disposition of cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies, including the COMELEC's preliminary investigation. Under Rule 34, Sections 6 and 8 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure, read together, if the respondent does not file a counter-affidavit within 10 days, the investigating officer resolves the case on the complainant's evidence, and the 20-day period to conclude the investigation runs from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit. Once the prescribed periods are exceeded, the prosecution must justify the delay (Cagang v. Sandiganbayan). A respondent is not duty-bound to follow up his case; the prosecutor must resolve it speedily even if the respondent did not object, unless the delay is directly attributable to him. (Sarigumba v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 263615, August 19, 2025)
- **Application:** (1) Lorenzo's 10-day period lapsed in March 2020. From then, the COMELEC had to conclude the investigation within 20 days and resolve it within five days on the evidence it had. Taking about six years violates those periods, so the burden shifted to the COMELEC. The case was simple, involving one respondent and a computation based on his own SOCE, so complexity cannot justify the delay. (2) Lorenzo's silence is not a waiver: the duty to resolve the complaint rests on the COMELEC, and nothing shows that the delay was caused by Lorenzo.
- **Conclusion:** The COMELEC violated Lorenzo's right to a speedy disposition of his case, so its resolution finding probable cause should be nullified and the complaint dismissed.

**Q2.** In a motu proprio overspending complaint filed by the COMELEC in 2021, respondent Dante moved to reset the preliminary investigation nine times over three years, citing his schedule and his counsel's other hearings, and filed two motions to transfer the investigation to another office. He finally filed his counter-affidavit in 2024. The COMELEC concluded the investigation and found probable cause within a month after receiving his counter-affidavit. Dante files certiorari, claiming that the three years from the filing of the complaint violated his right to a speedy disposition of cases, citing Sarigumba v. COMELEC. Will his petition prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The delay is attributable to Dante, not to the COMELEC.
- **Legal basis:** Under Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, as applied in Sarigumba v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 263615, August 19, 2025), the length of delay is never computed mechanically; courts consider the entire context and the causes of the delay, which must be properly laid out, and delay caused by the respondent's own acts is not charged to the prosecution. The prosecutor's duty to resolve the complaint speedily holds regardless of the respondent's silence "provided that it was not due to causes directly attributable to him" (Cervantes v. Sandiganbayan, reiterated in Peñas and Sarigumba). In Sarigumba, the Court counted the delay against the COMELEC only from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit, finding that the respondent's two early motions had not caused substantial delay.
- **Application:** Unlike in Sarigumba, where the COMELEC let the case sit for six years after the counter-affidavit period lapsed, here the three-year delay came from Dante's own repeated requests for resetting and motions to transfer. Once he filed his counter-affidavit, the COMELEC resolved the case within a month, well within its prescribed periods. Dante cannot profit from a delay he caused.
- **Conclusion:** Dante's petition will not prosper because the delay was directly attributable to him.

**Q3.** The COMELEC En Banc issued a minute resolution finding probable cause to charge Mayor Ana with an election offense, more than six years after the complaint was filed against her, with no explanation for the delay. Ana did not move for reconsideration. (a) What remedy should Ana file with the Supreme Court, and may she file it without first moving for reconsideration? (b) If her petition is granted, what relief will the Court give?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) A petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, which she may file without a prior motion for reconsideration. (b) The Court will nullify the resolution finding probable cause and dismiss the complaint.
- **Legal basis:** As a rule, certiorari does not lie unless a motion for reconsideration is first filed, but the requirement is excused where there is an urgent necessity for resolution and further delay would prejudice the petitioner, where a motion for reconsideration would be useless, or where public interest is involved. Inordinate delay in the preliminary investigation is grave abuse of discretion, and the remedy is to nullify the resolution and dismiss the case. (Sarigumba v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 263615, August 19, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Ana is assailing a COMELEC En Banc resolution, so the remedy is Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 on the ground of grave abuse of discretion. Because the proceedings were attended by unexplained delay of over six years, which by itself warrants dismissal, a motion for reconsideration would be futile, and the right to speedy disposition involves public interest and urgency. (b) If the Court finds inordinate delay, the resolution is tainted with grave abuse of discretion; the proper relief is to nullify it and dismiss the complaint, not merely to order the COMELEC to act faster.
- **Conclusion:** Ana may go directly to the Supreme Court on certiorari under Rule 64, and if she proves inordinate delay, the resolution will be nullified and the complaint dismissed.

> Note: The petition alleged that the CFU complaint was filed on February 10, 2015; the Court used December 20, 2014, the filing date in the COMELEC's own timeline. In summarizing the COMELEC's argument, the Decision refers to "Rule 3, Section 8" of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure, but the Court's analysis applies Rule 34, Sections 6 and 8. The Court did not separately rule on the prayer for a writ of preliminary injunction. Kho, Jr., J. took no part (a footnote lists him among the COMELEC Commissioners who signed the assailed Minute Resolution); Singh, J. was on leave.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70155)

## NBI v. Gungob

**NATIONAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION, REGION VII, PETITIONER, VS. AVELINO J. GUNGOB, SR., RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 249916 | 2025-08-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline > a. Grounds  
**Specific topics:** Simple vs. grave misconduct; Good faith is not a defense to simple misconduct; Mayor's extraction of minerals without a permit (Sec. 103, RA 7942); Service on counsel: notice to the party is not notice in law (Rule 13, Sec. 2); Reglementary period runs from the OSG's receipt
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > E. Pleadings > 10. Filing and Service (Rules 13 and 13-A, as amended; AM 10-3-7-SC, 11-9-4-SC, 25-01-13-SC, and 25-09-16-SC))

### Doctrine
**Misconduct is a transgression of an established and definite rule of action, more particularly unlawful behavior or gross negligence by a public officer. It is grave only if it involves corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules, proved by substantial evidence; otherwise it is simple** (*CSC v. Ledesma*). A person charged with grave misconduct may be held liable for simple misconduct. Plain unlawful behavior by a public officer, even without bad faith, malice or corrupt motive, already constitutes simple misconduct, because **good faith is not a defense to simple misconduct** (*Faeldonea v. CSC*). A mayor who directed the extraction and hauling of limestone without the required permits, a prima facie violation of Section 103 of the Philippine Mining Act (RA 7942), is liable for simple misconduct. It does not matter that the materials were used for bona fide municipal projects or that he had repeatedly asked the province to renew the municipality's gratuitous permit.

**When a party is represented by counsel, judgments and other papers must be served on counsel (Rule 13, Sec. 2, 1997 and 2019 Rules). Notice to the party itself is not notice in law and does not start the reglementary period.** A government agency represented by the OSG has 15 days from the OSG's receipt of the decision, not from the agency's own earlier receipt, to move for reconsideration. Reiterated (*Soriano v. Soriano*; *Villalongha v. CA*).

### Facts
On November 26, 2009, the NBI Central Visayas office, together with a lawyer of the Provincial Treasurer's Office, the Cebu Provincial Police Office and Army soldiers, set up checkpoints in Barangays Danglag, Garing and Dagongdong, Consolacion, Cebu to stop illegal extraction and hauling of minerals. They apprehended three ten-wheeler dump trucks loaded with limestone or diorite used as filling material, and seized a backhoe and a bulldozer at the quarry site. All belonged to the Municipality of Consolacion, whose mayor was respondent Avelino Gungob, Sr.

On December 3, 2009, NBI Region VII filed a complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman against Gungob and seven job-order employees (the drivers and operators) for theft of minerals under Section 103 of RA 7942. Gungob explained that the materials were excavated for the municipality's "Mountain Highway Project," whose Environmental Compliance Certificate required their prompt removal, and were used as fill for a new transport terminal and the "Government Center Project." The province had granted the municipality a gratuitous permit on April 29, 2008, which expired when the terminal was completed. The province did not act on the municipality's application for a new permit despite follow-ups. To avoid delaying the projects, the hauling continued until the apprehension.

In a Joint Resolution dated February 9, 2015, the Ombudsman found probable cause for theft of minerals under Section 103, in relation to Section 49, of RA 7942. In the administrative case, it found Gungob guilty of simple misconduct and suspended him without pay for three months, convertible into a fine equal to three months' salary if he had left the service. Reconsideration was denied on April 23, 2015.

On Gungob's petition for review, the CA (March 13, 2019) ruled that it had no jurisdiction over the criminal aspect. It exonerated Gungob administratively: he acted in utmost good faith to implement bona fide municipal projects and had written the governor at least five times between January and October 2009 for renewal of the permit. The NBI received the CA decision on March 29, 2019, and the OSG, its counsel, received it on April 4, 2019. The OSG moved for reconsideration on April 16, 2019. The CA denied the motion as one day late, counting from the NBI's receipt (October 2, 2019 Resolution). The NBI filed a Rule 45 petition.

### Issues
1. Whether the CA erred in denying the NBI's motion for reconsideration as filed out of time, by counting the period from the NBI's receipt of the decision instead of the OSG's.
2. Whether the respondent mayor is administratively liable for simple misconduct despite his good faith.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the CA erred.** Under Rule 13, Section 2 of the 1997 Rules, substantially carried over in the 2019 Rules, service on a party who has appeared by counsel must be made on counsel unless the court orders otherwise. Service on anyone other than the counsel of record "is not legally effective and binding upon the party, nor may it start the corresponding reglementary period" (*Soriano v. Soriano*). The reason is that parties generally do not know the rules of procedure, and courts should deal with only one person in the interest of orderly procedure (*Villalongha v. CA*). The NBI was represented by the OSG, which prepared and filed the motion. **The period ran from the OSG's receipt on April 4, 2019, so the motion was due on April 19, 2019.** The motion filed on April 16, 2019 was timely.

**2. Yes, the mayor is guilty of simple misconduct.** The Ombudsman was correct. It was undisputed that the mayor directed the extraction and transport of earth materials and limestone without the necessary government permits. That act is a prima facie violation of Section 103 of RA 7942, which punishes extracting and disposing of minerals without a mining agreement, lease, permit or license. The CA erred in exonerating him because of good faith: "Good faith is not anathema to a finding of liability for simple misconduct." In *Faeldonea v. CSC*, a postmaster's good intentions negated grave misconduct but did not excuse him from simple misconduct. Like that postmaster, the mayor "ought to remain administratively accountable for his transgression of the law despite his good faith." The Ombudsman's administrative ruling was reinstated.

### Disposition
The Petition was GRANTED. The CA's March 13, 2019 Decision and October 2, 2019 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 09439 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Gungob was found GUILTY of SIMPLE MISCONDUCT and SUSPENDED WITHOUT PAY for three months, with the accessory penalties. If the suspension can no longer be enforced because he has left the service, it is converted into a FINE equal to three months' salary, which may be deducted from his retirement benefits, accrued leave credits or other receivables from his office.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Mayor Delfin ordered municipal dump trucks to haul limestone from a municipal road project to fill the site of a new public market. The municipality's gratuitous permit to extract and haul the limestone had expired, and the provincial governor ignored Delfin's five written requests for its renewal. Delfin acted only to avoid delaying the projects and gained nothing personally. The Ombudsman found him guilty of simple misconduct. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that his good faith negates any misconduct. Is the CA correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Delfin is liable for simple misconduct despite his good faith.
- **Legal basis:** Misconduct is a transgression of an established and definite rule of action, more particularly unlawful behavior or gross negligence by a public officer. It is grave only if attended by corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules; otherwise it is simple. Plain unlawful behavior, even without bad faith, malice or corrupt motive, is simple misconduct, and good faith is not a defense to it. Extracting and disposing of minerals without a permit is punished under Section 103 of RA 7942. (NBI v. Gungob, G.R. No. 249916, August 13, 2025, citing CSC v. Ledesma and Faeldonea v. CSC)
- **Application:** Delfin directed the extraction and hauling of limestone without a valid permit, which is a prima facie violation of Section 103 of RA 7942 and therefore unlawful behavior. His good faith, his public purpose and the governor's inaction may show that there was no corruption or willful intent, so his misconduct is not grave. But they do not erase the transgression itself.
- **Conclusion:** The CA erred; Delfin should be held liable for simple misconduct.

**Q2.** Suppose the Ombudsman had charged Mayor Delfin with grave misconduct for the same hauling. (a) If the evidence shows no corruption and no willful intent to violate the law, but only that he hauled limestone without a permit in good faith, may he be held liable for simple misconduct under a charge of grave misconduct? (b) If the evidence instead shows by substantial evidence that he sold the limestone to a private contractor and kept the proceeds, what offense did he commit?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. He may be held liable for simple misconduct. (b) Grave misconduct, because the element of corruption is present.
- **Legal basis:** Misconduct becomes grave only if it involves any of the additional elements of corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules, which must be established by substantial evidence; otherwise it is simple. A person charged with grave misconduct may be held liable for simple misconduct if the misconduct lacks the elements that qualify it as grave. (NBI v. Gungob, G.R. No. 249916, August 13, 2025, quoting CSC v. Ledesma)
- **Application:** (a) Hauling without a permit is unlawful behavior. Without proof of corruption or willful intent, the qualifying elements are missing, so he may be found guilty of the lesser offense of simple misconduct. (b) Selling public minerals to a private party and pocketing the proceeds shows corruption, an additional element that makes the misconduct grave.
- **Conclusion:** Without the qualifying elements, Delfin is liable only for simple misconduct; if corruption is proved by substantial evidence, he is liable for grave misconduct.

**Q3.** In an administrative appeal, the Court of Appeals decided against a government bureau, which is represented by the Office of the Solicitor General. The bureau's regional office received a copy of the decision on June 3. The OSG, its counsel of record, received its copy on June 10. The OSG filed a motion for reconsideration on June 24. The CA denied the motion as late, counting 15 days from June 3. Is the CA correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The motion was filed on time.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 13, Section 2 of the Rules of Court, when a party has appeared by counsel, service must be made on counsel. Notice to the party itself is not notice in law and does not start the reglementary period for the next procedural step. The 15-day period to move for reconsideration therefore runs from counsel's receipt. (NBI v. Gungob, G.R. No. 249916, August 13, 2025)
- **Application:** The bureau is represented by the OSG, so only the OSG's receipt on June 10 counts. Fifteen days from June 10 is June 25. The motion filed on June 24 was within the period. The bureau's own receipt on June 3 is not notice in law.
- **Conclusion:** The CA erred in denying the motion as late; it was timely filed.

> Note: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred. The CA ruled that it had no jurisdiction over the criminal aspect (the Ombudsman's finding of probable cause for theft of minerals under Section 103, in relation to Section 49, of RA 7942); only the administrative aspect reached the Court. The decision does not discuss whether the complainant NBI had standing to appeal the exoneration. It calls the CA petition simply a "Petition for Review."

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70083)
