## National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC

**NATIONAL PRESS CLUB OF THE PHILIPPINES, AUTOMATED ELECTION SYSTEM WATCH, AND GUARDIANS BROTHERHOOD, INC., PETITIONERS, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 259354 | 2023-06-13 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction  
**Specific topics:** COMELEC's ministerial duty to let designated watchers witness ballot printing (OEC, Sec. 187); Examination and testing of AES equipment and devices, including SD cards (RA 8436, Sec. 14, as amended); Digital signatures on election returns: COMELEC discretion; VCM signature as functional equivalent; Right to information: transmission diagram and network architecture; no right to physical access to data centers; Mandamus requisites, citizen standing, and exceptions to mootness
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > H. Right to Information (See also EO 2, s. 2016; RA 6713, Sec. 5(e)))
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VI. Judicial Department > B. Judicial Review > 3. Exceptions to Mootness)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > E. Certiorari, Prohibition, and Mandamus (Rule 65))

### Doctrine
**Ballot printing.** Under **Section 187 of the Omnibus Election Code**, upon the request of any candidate, political party, or civic, religious, professional, business, service, youth or similar organization collectively designated by the COMELEC, the COMELEC "shall" allow the designated watchers to witness the printing and distribution of ballots and returns and to guard the printer's premises. **This is a ministerial duty that mandamus can compel.** Security zones, schedule pressures and pandemic health protocols do not excuse a refusal. The COMELEC may limit the number of watchers or use other means such as livestreaming, "[t]his is not to say, however, that on-site viewing of the printing process may be dispensed with entirely."

**AES equipment.** Under **Section 14 of RA 8436, as amended by RA 9369**, the COMELEC has no discretion to refuse political parties, candidates, citizens' arms or their representatives the right to **examine and test** the equipment or devices of the AES. This covers not only the vote-counting machines but other devices such as **SD cards**, "even up to the day of the electoral exercise, before voting starts." The right does not depend on compliance with COMELEC guidelines (reiterating *Bagumbayan-VNP*), but the COMELEC may first verify that the requester is a bona fide party, candidate, citizens' arm or authorized representative. **The law does not require the COMELEC to allow witnessing of the configuration and preparation of SD cards and VCMs**; testing presupposes configured devices. On **digital signatures**, the COMELEC's choice to have only electoral boards in highly urbanized cities digitally sign the returns is discretionary and not compellable by mandamus. The VCM's own digital signature is the functional equivalent required by Section 22 of the AES Law.

**Right to information.** The transmission diagram and data/communications network architecture of the VCMs are matters of public concern. Exemptions are construed strictly against confidentiality, and the agency bears the burden of proving an exemption. **Absent mootness, the COMELEC could be compelled by mandamus to disclose them**, but not a vague demand for "all details" of the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room" that could compromise security. The right to information does **not** include **physical access** to the COMELEC's hubs, servers and data centers, which Section 35(c) of RA 8436, as amended, penalizes "whether classified or declassified." A citizen invoking the right to information has standing to seek mandamus (reiterated). The Court resolved these issues despite mootness because the case involved paramount public interest, required controlling principles, and was capable of repetition yet evading review.

### Facts
About 48 days before the May 2022 National and Local Elections (NLE), and 18 days before overseas voting began, petitioners National Press Club of the Philippines, AES Watch, and Guardians Brotherhood, Inc. filed a petition for mandamus with the Supreme Court. They sought to compel the COMELEC to (a) implement the use of digital signatures, and (b) allow political parties, candidates, media and other organizations to access and inspect the "Election Transparency Activities." These were: the printing of ballots at the National Printing Office (NPO); the disposition of some 5.2 million defective ballots; the configuration of SD cards at the Sta. Rosa, Laguna warehouse and the Pre-Logic and Accuracy Test; the preparation and testing of VCMs; the technical support center, hubs and data centers; and the transmission diagram or network architecture, including the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room."

The COMELEC had approved digital signatures in Minute Resolution No. 210021 (January 20, 2021). At the March 9, 2022 Joint Congressional Oversight Committee (JCOC) hearing, however, it was revealed that only electoral boards in the NCR, Cebu City and Davao City would digitally sign. Commissioner Casquejo's March 7, 2022 letter explained that no provider could supply enough cable assemblies for the approximately 300,000 to 350,000 teachers. Political parties had asked in writing, as early as January 2022, to observe the ballot printing. The COMELEC refused, citing restricted security areas at the NPO, possible delays in preparing for overseas voting starting April 10, 2022, and COVID-19 limits on persons in the premises. By the March 9, 2022 hearing, 66.4% of the ballots had been printed without witnesses. Party representatives also testified that they were turned away at the Sta. Rosa warehouse where SD cards were configured, though without any formal denial.

After the hearing, Commissioner Casquejo apologized and said the pandemic was no excuse to bar observers. The COMELEC began livestreaming the printing on March 17, 2022, offered CCTV footage for the earlier period, and conducted random ballot checking with stakeholders. It invited the public to the final testing and sealing of VCMs on May 2–7, 2022 and opened the Sta. Rosa warehouse to public viewing. It also posted its local hubs and dispatch schedules (March 16, 2022), held an end-to-end AES demonstration (March 22, 2022) and a Transparency Media Server walkthrough (April 30, 2022), and disclosed the locations of its data centers. In its July 14, 2022 Comment, the COMELEC argued that the petition was moot after the elections, that it had not neglected any duty, that the law did not require access to SD card configuration or its hubs and data centers, and that the issues were political questions.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition should be dismissed as moot, and whether the Court should nonetheless resolve the issues.
2. Whether petitioners have legal standing to file the petition for mandamus.
3. Whether mandamus lies to compel the COMELEC to implement the use of digital signatures nationwide.
4. Whether the COMELEC may be compelled to allow watchers to witness the printing of ballots.
5. Whether the COMELEC may be compelled to allow the witnessing of the configuration and preparation of SD cards and VCMs, or their examination and testing.
6. Whether the COMELEC may be compelled to disclose the transmission diagram, the data/communications network architecture, and all details of the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room."
7. Whether the COMELEC has a ministerial duty to allow physical access to its technical hubs, servers and data centers.

### Ruling
**1. The petition is moot, but the Court ruled on the issues.** With the 2022 NLE over, no relief could be granted. But three exceptions to mootness were present: the exceptional character of the situation and paramount public interest, the need to formulate controlling principles, and the case being capable of repetition yet evading review. The case presented "novel issues" on the COMELEC's duties regarding SD cards, VCMs, and its hubs, servers and data centers.

**2. Yes, petitioners have standing.** Under *Guingona v. COMELEC*, a mandamus petition anchored on the right to information may be filed by any citizen without showing a special interest. Petitioners' members are registered voters, journalists and concerned citizens. AES Watch's signatory, however, lacked proof of authority to sign the verification and certification against forum shopping. The Court restated the five requisites of mandamus: a clear legal right, a duty mandated by law, unlawful neglect, a ministerial (not discretionary) act, and no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy.

**3. No, mandamus does not lie for digital signatures.** The first paragraph of Section 22 of RA 8436, as amended, which requires signing and thumbmarking, refers to printed election returns. Digital signatures appear only on electronic returns. Since 2010, the digital signatures on returns have come from the machines, and under *Capalla* and *Bagumbayan-VNP* a machine signature is the functional equivalent of a digital signature. How to digitally sign results is subject to the COMELEC's sound judgment (*AES Watch v. COMELEC*), and courts will not interfere with its choice of means unless clearly illegal or a gross abuse of discretion (*Sumulong*). **The VCM-generated signatures outside HUCs were sufficient compliance; "[t]he job of the Court is to say what the law is, not to dictate how another branch, agency, or instrumentality of government should do its job."**

**4. Yes, but the issue is moot.** **By the word "shall" in Section 187 of the OEC, the COMELEC has no discretion. Once a qualified requester designates watchers, allowing them to witness the printing is a ministerial duty.** The COMELEC's reasons failed. Restricted areas did not matter because watchers may even guard the printer's premises. The overseas-voting delay was a "flimsy excuse" given requests made as early as January 2022. Health protocols "did not authorize the COMELEC to disregard the law"; it could have allowed limited watchers or used other methods. The law does not limit the means, and livestreaming strikes a balance, though on-site viewing may not be dispensed with entirely. The COMELEC's later livestreaming, CCTV access and random checks made the issue moot.

**5. Witnessing of configuration, no; examination and testing, yes, but the issue is moot.** RA 9369 replaced "counting machines" with "equipment or device of the AES." Congress thus expanded examination and testing beyond VCMs to devices such as SD cards. **But the law requires only examination and testing, not access to configuration and preparation.** Because the COMELEC must provide test ballots and test forms, testing takes place after configuration; "it would be absurd to allow the examination and testing of unconfigured equipment or devices." Petitioners also failed to prove that watchers of the requesting parties were denied entry to Sta. Rosa or that the lawyers turned away represented any party, candidate or citizens' arm. The right to examine and test does not depend on COMELEC guidelines, but the COMELEC may verify that the requester is a bona fide party, candidate, accredited citizens' arm or authorized representative, since an "unscrupulous individual could feign examination and testing in order to compromise the equipment." The May 2–7, 2022 public testing and sealing and the opening of the Sta. Rosa warehouse made the issue moot.

**6. The transmission diagram, yes; "all details," no; the issue is moot.** RA 9369 protects the secrecy and sanctity of "all election, consolidation and transmission documents" "in order that the process shall be transparent and credible" and elections "informed." Transparency matters more in an AES, which is "inherently less transparent" than manual counting; "the credibility of the system is directly proportional to the transparency of the entire process." Mandamus to enforce the right to information requires (a) a matter of public concern and (b) no exemption by law. Exemptions are construed against confidentiality, and the agency bears the burden of proving one. **The COMELEC failed to discharge that burden as to the transmission diagram and network architecture of the VCMs, so "were it not for the mootness of the issue," it could be compelled to disclose them.** The request for "all details" of the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room" was "too vague and broad." Mandamus will not compel disclosure "for the sake of transparency but at the expense of the security, integrity, and credibility of the AES." Coverage of such documents should be decided case by case, not by a "shotgun approach."

**7. No.** The law does not require the COMELEC to allow physical access to its hubs, servers and data centers. **The right to information does not extend to physical access to facilities.** Section 35(c) of RA 8436, as amended, penalizes "[g]aining or causing access to . . . facilities . . . whether classified or declassified," regardless of authorization. At most, the COMELEC may be compelled to provide information on its hubs and data centers, as it already had. Unlike the watchers' right at the printer's premises, there is no clear legal right to physical access.

### Disposition
The Petition was DISMISSED for being moot and academic.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Two months before a national election, Partido Bago, an accredited political party, wrote the COMELEC asking that its designated watchers be allowed to witness the printing of official ballots at the printing plant. The COMELEC denied the request, citing (1) security-restricted areas inside the plant, (2) the risk of delaying the printing of overseas ballots, and (3) health protocols limiting the number of persons inside. Partido Bago files a petition for mandamus. Will mandamus lie?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Allowing the designated watchers to witness the printing of ballots is a ministerial duty of the COMELEC, and its reasons do not justify the refusal.
- **Legal basis:** Section 187 of the Omnibus Election Code provides that, upon the request of any candidate, political party or organization collectively designated by the COMELEC, the COMELEC "shall" allow its designated watchers to witness the printing and distribution of ballots and returns and to guard the premises of the printer. By the word "shall," the COMELEC has no discretion. Once a request is made and watchers are designated, allowing them to observe the printing is ministerial and may be compelled by mandamus. (National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 259354, June 13, 2023, En Banc)
- **Application:** Partido Bago made a written request and designated watchers, so the COMELEC's duty arose. Restricted areas are no excuse, because the law even allows watchers to guard the printer's premises. Possible delay is a weak excuse where the request was made well ahead of time. Health protocols do not authorize the COMELEC to disregard the law: it could allow a limited number of watchers or use other means such as livestreaming, though on-site viewing cannot be dispensed with entirely. The COMELEC refused outright instead.
- **Conclusion:** Mandamus will lie to compel the COMELEC to allow Partido Bago's designated watchers to witness the printing of the ballots.

**Q2.** Before an automated election, Bantay Halalan, an accredited citizens' arm, demanded that the COMELEC allow its representatives (a) to watch the configuration and loading of contents into the SD cards at the COMELEC warehouse, and (b) to enter the central data center housing the transmission router and inspect the servers. The COMELEC refused both demands but offered to let Bantay Halalan examine and test the configured VCMs and SD cards up to election day, before voting starts. May the COMELEC be compelled by mandamus to grant demands (a) and (b)?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The law does not require the COMELEC to allow witnessing of the configuration of SD cards. (b) No. There is no right to physical access to the COMELEC's data centers.
- **Legal basis:** Section 14 of RA 8436, as amended by RA 9369, requires the COMELEC to allow political parties, candidates, citizens' arms or their representatives to examine and test the equipment or devices of the AES, including SD cards, even up to the day of the electoral exercise, before voting starts. It does not require access to the configuration and preparation of those devices; testing presupposes configured devices. The right to information does not extend to physical access to the COMELEC's hubs, servers and data centers, and Section 35(c) of RA 8436, as amended, penalizes gaining or causing access to such facilities whether classified or declassified. (National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 259354, June 13, 2023, En Banc)
- **Application:** (a) The COMELEC's offer to let Bantay Halalan examine and test the configured VCMs and SD cards is exactly what the law requires. Watching the configuration itself is not a duty the law imposes, so there is no ministerial duty to compel. (b) No law grants a right to enter the data center, and entry would fall within the acts Section 35(c) penalizes. At most, the COMELEC may be compelled to provide information about its data centers, not physical access.
- **Conclusion:** Mandamus will not issue for either demand, although Bantay Halalan is entitled to examine and test the configured equipment and devices.

**Q3.** A group of journalists and registered voters asked the COMELEC for copies of the transmission diagram and data/communications network architecture of the vote-counting machines for the coming elections. They also asked for "all details of all devices and equipment used to transmit election results." The COMELEC refused both requests, stating only that the documents are "sensitive." The group files a petition for mandamus. (a) Does the group have standing? (b) Will mandamus lie as to each request?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, the group has standing as citizens. (b) Mandamus will lie to compel disclosure of the transmission diagram and network architecture, but not the vague request for "all details" of the transmission devices.
- **Legal basis:** When a petition for mandamus is anchored on the right to information on matters of public concern (Const., Art. III, Sec. 7; Art. II, Sec. 28), any citizen is a real party-in-interest without need of a special interest. Mandamus may compel disclosure when the information is of public concern and not exempt by law. Every claim of exemption is construed liberally in favor of disclosure and strictly against confidentiality, must be clearly asserted with its grounds, and must be proved by the agency. In National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 259354, June 13, 2023, En Banc), the Court held that the transmission diagram and network architecture of the VCMs are matters of public concern that the COMELEC could be compelled to disclose. It also held that a prayer for "all details" of the transmission router server is too vague and broad, and that disclosure cannot be compelled at the expense of the security, integrity and credibility of the AES.
- **Application:** (a) The members are journalists and registered voters asserting the people's right to information, so they need not show a personal stake. (b) The transmission diagram and network architecture bear directly on the integrity of election results, which is a matter of public concern. Calling them "sensitive," without specifying a legal ground for exemption, does not discharge the COMELEC's burden, so disclosure may be compelled. The demand for "all details of all devices and equipment" is too broad to identify what must be disclosed and could expose confidential security information, so mandamus will not lie for it.
- **Conclusion:** The group has standing and may compel disclosure of the transmission diagram and network architecture, but not of "all details" of the transmission devices.

> Note: The fallo only dismisses the petition as moot; the rulings on the COMELEC's duties were made under the exceptions to mootness. Votes: Leonen, SAJ. (Acting C.J.) concurred with a separate opinion disagreeing on SD card configuration and access to hubs; Caguioa, J. wrote a separate concurring opinion; Lazaro-Javier, J. concurred. These separate opinions are not examinable and were not used. Several post-filing COMELEC measures (livestreaming from March 17, 2022, public testing and sealing on May 2–7, 2022, opening of the Sta. Rosa warehouse) are taken from the Court's judicial notice of media reports. The 2027 syllabus has no specific Election Law heading on the automated election system; the COMELEC powers heading is the closest.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69168)

## Juan v. COA

**FRANCIS SATURNINO C. JUAN, ISABELO JOSEPH P. TOMAS II, NOEL J. SALVANERA, SHARON O. MONTAÑER, FLORESINDA G. BALDO-DIGAL AND MARIA CORAZON C. GINES, PETITIONERS, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, HON. MICHAEL G. AGUINALDO, IN HIS OFFICIAL CAPACITY AS CHAIRPERSON, AND HON. JOSE A. FABIA AND HON. ISABEL D. AGITO, IN THEIR OFFICIAL CAPACITY AS COMMISSIONERS, OF THE COMMISSION ON AUDIT, RESPONDENTS. [G.R. No. 237860] ELLEN C. EBCAS, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, ET AL., RESPONDENTS. [G.R. No. 237883] LUZVIMINDA N. CABALBAG, PETITIONER, VS. HON. MICHAEL G. AGUINALDO, ET AL., RESPONDENTS. [G.R. No. 237884] MARIANO D. GARCIA, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 237835 | 2023-02-07 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 1. Forms of Accountability  
**Specific topics:** COA disallowance of an across-the-board educational allowance (MC No. 174); Who are approving and certifying officers; liability requires bad faith or gross negligence; Badges of good faith; error on a difficult question of law; Net disallowed amount under the Madera Rules on Return; Payees' liability to return under solutio indebiti
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (X. Quasi-Contracts > B. Kinds > 2. Solutio Indebiti > c. Effect of Good Faith of the Payee)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))

### Doctrine
An allowance granted without legal basis is properly disallowed. Memorandum Circular No. 174 (2009) authorizes only "scholarship programs" for children of government employees "with siblings"; it does not authorize an **across-the-board cash educational allowance** given to every employee regardless of personal circumstances. Such a grant violates Section 17(e), General Provisions, of the 2010 General Appropriations Act (RA 9970) and lacks the presidential approval required by Sections 5 and 6 of PD 1597 and Item 9 of Joint Resolution No. 4, s. 2009. That approval requirement binds even agencies exempt from the Salary Standardization Law, like the ERC.

Every officer whose approval or certification was necessary to release the disallowed amount is "directly responsible" and is an approving or certifying officer under the Madera Rules on Return. This includes one who only certified the payroll list, or who signed in place of an absent superior. But **civil liability attaches only upon proof of bad faith, malice or gross negligence** (Administrative Code, Book I, Secs. 38-39; Book VI, Sec. 43; Madera Rules 2a and 2b). Officers are presumed to have acted in good faith, and bad faith or gross negligence presupposes actual or constructive knowledge of the illegality. An officer whose only duty was to verify the names in the payroll has no duty to inquire into legality. An officer who certified legality but erred on a **doubtful or difficult question of law** acted in good faith. Badges of good faith here were the absence of precedent, the fact that this was the first disallowance of its kind, and the auditors' own request for DBM clarification. A mere mistake is not bad faith.

The solidary liability of officers found liable is limited to the **net disallowed amount**: the total disallowed amount minus amounts excused or allowed to be retained by payees (Madera, applied). Payees must return what they received under *solutio indebiti*, regardless of good faith, unless excused under Madera Rules 2c and 2d. *Madera* abandoned the *Silang* practice of shifting the whole refund to the approving officers. Amounts received by payees who are not parties to the petition cannot be ordered returned and are treated as allowed to be retained. Here the net disallowed amount was reduced from PHP 7,433,834 to PHP 315,000, the sum received by the nine petitioners.

### Facts
The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), whose personnel compensation is exempt from the Salary Standardization Law under Section 39 of RA 9136, granted its personnel in 2010 an educational allowance of PHP 35,000 each, or PHP 7,433,834.00 in total. It was released in three tranches (February, March and May 2010), on top of a PHP 35,000 Collective Negotiation Agreement incentive.

On August 3, 2011, the COA audit team issued Notice of Disallowance (ND) No. 2011-002-101-(10) for lack of legal basis. It cited Section 17 of the 2010 GAA, Item 9 of Joint Resolution No. 4, s. 2009, and a DBM letter stating that there was no legal basis or presidential authorization. Fifteen ERC officials who approved or certified the release were held liable. Before issuing the ND, the audit team leader had asked the DBM whether MC No. 174 or the CNA could justify the allowance.

The COA-NGS Cluster A denied the appeal (Decision No. 2012-013, September 28, 2012). The COA Proper first denied the petition for review as late (Decision No. 2015-387, December 21, 2015). In Resolution No. 2017-452 (December 27, 2017), it found the appeal timely but still affirmed the disallowance. It held the officers who approved, authorized or certified the payment solidarily liable for the entire amount and, applying *Silang v. COA*, exempted the passive recipients.

Nine of the fifteen officers filed four certiorari petitions. Juan, Tomas, Salvanera, Montañer, Baldo-Digal, Gines and Garcia had only certified their offices' payrolls as correct or approved them; Garcia signed in place of his absent superior. Ebcas, OIC of the Finance and Administrative Service, and Cabalbag, a Finance and Management Officer who signed on Ebcas's behalf, signed obligation requests and disbursement vouchers. These certified the charges as "necessary, lawful" and the supporting documents as "valid, proper and legal." The six other officers (Cruz-Ducut et al.) did not file petitions. Each of the nine petitioners had received PHP 35,000.

### Issues
1. Whether the COA gravely abused its discretion in upholding the disallowance of the ERC's educational allowance.
2. Whether petitioners, who signed payrolls, obligation requests or disbursement vouchers, are solidarily liable as approving and certifying officers.
3. Whether the remaining approving and certifying officers are solidarily liable for the entire disallowed amount.
4. Whether petitioners must return the educational allowance they personally received.

### Ruling
**1. No. The disallowance was proper.** MC No. 174 enjoins agencies to provide "scholarships programs for their children with siblings." By its plain text it covers a scholarship benefit only for employees with more than one child. The benefit must be granted under a set of guidelines (a "scholarship program") that identifies the qualified beneficiaries and the amounts. The ERC's allowance was "merely an across-the-board cash endowment given indiscriminately to every personnel of the agency." With no basis in MC No. 174 or any other law, the grant was prohibited by Section 17(e) of the 2010 GAA, which bars allowances "except those specifically authorized by law." It also lacked the presidential approval required by Sections 5 and 6 of PD 1597 and Item 9 of J.R. No. 4, which apply even to agencies exempt from RA 6758.

**2. They are approving and certifying officers, but none of them is liable because the presumption of good faith was not overturned.** Limited participation alone does not absolve an officer. Under Section 43, Book VI of the Administrative Code, every official "authorizing or making such payment, or taking part therein" may be liable. Under Section 39, Book I, a subordinate is liable for negligent acts even if done on a superior's orders. The payroll certifications of Juan et al. and Garcia, and the obligation requests and vouchers signed by Ebcas and Cabalbag, were indispensable to the release, so all were "directly responsible."

But liability also requires bad faith or gross negligence. Juan et al. and Garcia only certified the accuracy of the list of employees. Nothing showed actual knowledge of the illegality, and their task did not require them to inquire into the legal basis, so not even constructive knowledge could be imputed to them. Ebcas and Cabalbag did certify lawfulness and erred, but a mistake is not bad faith (*Lumayna v. COA*). Badges of good faith existed: no case law yet outlawed an educational allowance under MC No. 174, this ND was the COA's first such disallowance, and the auditors themselves first sought DBM clarification. The legality of the allowance was thus "a doubtful or difficult question of law," and their error was made in good faith. **All nine petitioners were absolved as approving and certifying officers.**

**3. No. The remaining officers (Cruz-Ducut et al.) are solidarily liable only for the net disallowed amount of PHP 315,000.** Under *Madera*, the officers' solidary liability is limited to the total disallowed amount minus amounts the payees are excused from returning. The obligation to return ultimately rests on the payees under *solutio indebiti*, and the rule avoids an undue burden on officers and the government's unjust enrichment.

The COA's absolution of all payees under *Silang* was erroneous. *Madera* (September 8, 2020) abandoned that approach, and no Rule 2c or 2d exception applied: the allowance was not paid for services rendered, and no undue prejudice was shown. But the payees other than the nine petitioners are not parties, so their receipts cannot be ordered returned and are effectively "allowed to be retained." The net disallowed amount is therefore the PHP 315,000 received by the nine petitioners. The reduction benefits Cruz-Ducut et al. even though they did not file petitions, because their liability is intricately related to the petitioners'. The Court applied by analogy the rule on the effect of an appellate judgment on parties who did not appeal (*Government v. Tizon*). The ruling is without prejudice to administrative cases against them.

**4. Yes.** As recipients, each of the nine petitioners must return the PHP 35,000 he or she received, under the principle of *solutio indebiti*.

### Disposition
The petitions were PARTIALLY GRANTED. COA Resolution No. 2017-452 dated December 27, 2017 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATIONS. (1) Except for the nine petitioners (Juan, Tomas, Salvanera, Montañer, Baldo-Digal, Gines, Ebcas, Cabalbag and Garcia), all ERC officers and employees who approved and certified the educational allowance, as identified in Annex 1-EA of ND No. 2011-002-101-(10) dated August 3, 2011, are solidarily liable for the net disallowed amount of PHP 315,000.00. (2) Each of the nine petitioners is individually liable to return PHP 35,000.00.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In 2024, the Bureau of Waterways, whose compensation system is exempt from the Salary Standardization Law, paid every employee a PHP 30,000 "education grant" without presidential approval. It relied on a presidential circular enjoining agencies to provide "scholarship programs for children of employees with siblings." The COA disallowed the grant. Division chief Lito had signed his division's payroll, certifying only that the names listed were correct. Finance chief Mila had signed the disbursement vouchers, certifying the expense as "necessary and lawful." There is no evidence that either of them knew the grant was illegal. No court ruling or COA disallowance on such grants existed before, and the auditor herself first asked the DBM whether the circular could support the grant. The COA held Lito and Mila solidarily liable for the entire amount as approving and certifying officers. Is the COA correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The disallowance is proper, and Lito and Mila are approving or certifying officers. But neither is civilly liable, because the presumption of good faith was not overturned.
- **Legal basis:** Officers whose approvals or certifications were necessary to release a disallowed amount are "directly responsible" and are approving and certifying officers. Under Sections 38 and 39, Book I, and Section 43, Book VI of the Administrative Code, as applied in Rules 2a and 2b of the Madera Rules on Return, they are solidarily liable only if clearly shown to have acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence. Bad faith or gross negligence presupposes actual or constructive knowledge of the illegality. An error on a doubtful or difficult question of law, shown by badges of good faith such as the absence of precedent and of prior disallowance, is made in good faith. A circular that authorizes scholarship programs for employees' children does not authorize an across-the-board cash allowance. (Juan v. COA, G.R. No. 237835, February 7, 2023)
- **Application:** The grant was an across-the-board cash payment, not a scholarship program, and had no presidential approval, so the disallowance stands. Lito's payroll certification was necessary for the release, but his only duty was to verify the names. He had no duty to look into the grant's legal basis, so no knowledge of the illegality can be imputed to him. Mila certified the expense as lawful and erred, but a mistake is not bad faith. No precedent or prior disallowance existed, and even the auditor needed DBM clarification, which shows the legal question was doubtful. With no evidence of actual knowledge, the presumption of good faith stands for both of them.
- **Conclusion:** Lito and Mila should be absolved from solidary liability as approving and certifying officers, although each must still return whatever he or she personally received as a payee.

**Q2.** Same agency. A year earlier, the COA had disallowed an identical "education grant," and the DBM had written to the agency's finance chief, Nestor, that the grant had no legal basis. Nestor nonetheless certified the new grant as "necessary and lawful." The total disallowed amount is PHP 5,000,000. The COA excused the rank-and-file payees from returning PHP 2,000,000 under a recognized exception. (a) Is Nestor liable as a certifying officer? (b) If so, up to what amount is he solidarily liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Nestor is liable because he certified the grant knowing it was illegal. (b) His solidary liability is limited to the net disallowed amount of PHP 3,000,000.
- **Legal basis:** Approving and certifying officers clearly shown to have acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence are solidarily liable under Section 43, Book VI of the Administrative Code and Rule 2b of the Madera Rules on Return. Bad faith or gross negligence presupposes actual or constructive knowledge of the illegality; gross negligence includes a palpable or inexcusable breach of duty. The officers' solidary liability is limited to the net disallowed amount: the total disallowed amount minus the amounts the payees are excused from returning or allowed to retain. (Juan v. COA, G.R. No. 237835, February 7, 2023, applying Madera v. COA)
- **Application:** Unlike the officers in Juan, Nestor had actual knowledge: a prior disallowance of the same grant and a DBM letter saying it had no legal basis. The badges of good faith in Juan (no precedent, no prior disallowance) are absent. Certifying as lawful an expense he knew had been disallowed is at least a palpable and inexcusable breach of duty, so the presumption of good faith is overturned. His liability, however, cannot exceed what the government may actually recover. Of the PHP 5,000,000 disallowed, PHP 2,000,000 was excused, leaving a net disallowed amount of PHP 3,000,000.
- **Conclusion:** Nestor is solidarily liable as a certifying officer, but only up to the net disallowed amount of PHP 3,000,000.

**Q3.** Teresa, a rank-and-file employee, received a PHP 30,000 education grant that the COA validly disallowed. She took no part in approving or certifying it. She argues that, as a passive recipient in good faith, she need not refund anything, and that only the approving officers should bear the liability. Is Teresa correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Teresa must return the PHP 30,000 she received.
- **Legal basis:** A payee's obligation to return a disallowed benefit rests on the civil law principle of solutio indebiti (Civil Code, Art. 2154). It arises from the mere receipt of an undue payment, regardless of good faith. Madera v. COA abandoned the Silang practice of absolving passive recipients and shifting the entire refund to the approving officers. Payees are excused only if the amounts were genuinely given in consideration of services rendered, or on grounds of undue prejudice, social justice or other bona fide exceptions (Madera Rules 2c and 2d). (Juan v. COA, G.R. No. 237835, February 7, 2023)
- **Application:** Teresa's good faith does not matter. The grant was a cash allowance paid on top of her compensation, not payment for services rendered, and nothing shows that refunding it would cause her undue prejudice. Her receipt of an amount the agency had no legal basis to pay creates the obligation to return it.
- **Conclusion:** Teresa must refund the PHP 30,000 under the principle of solutio indebiti.

> Note: Consolidated with G.R. Nos. 237860 (Ebcas), 237883 (Cabalbag) and 237884 (Garcia). The petitions were filed under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 (footnote 1). En Banc, unanimous: 14 Justices concurred. The text once refers to "Resolution No. 2017-542", apparently a typo for Resolution No. 2017-452.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68810)

## Gana-Carait v. COMELEC

**MARIZ LINDSEY TAN GANA-CARAIT Y VILLEGAS, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS, ROMMEL MITRA LIM, AND DOMINIC P. NUÑEZ, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 257453 | 2022-08-09 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Citizenship > E. Dual Citizenship and Dual Allegiance  
**Specific topics:** R.A. 9225 applies only to dual citizens by naturalization, not to dual citizens by birth; Material misrepresentation in the CoC (Section 78, OEC) vs. disqualification (Section 40(d), LGC); COMELEC En Banc rulings are only executory, not final, within the 30-day Rule 64 period; Mootness exception: capable of repetition yet evading review; Foreign law is not judicially noticed and must be proved
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))

### Doctrine
**R.A. No. 9225 covers only natural-born Filipinos who became foreign citizens through naturalization.** Its twin requirements for those seeking elective office, the oath of allegiance (Section 3) and the personal and sworn renunciation of any and all foreign citizenship (Section 5(2)), **do not apply to dual citizens by birth**, whose dual citizenship results involuntarily from the concurrent application of the laws of two states. For them, the filing of the certificate of candidacy (CoC) carries an implied renunciation of foreign citizenship (Maquiling; Cordora, reiterated). Presenting documents to a foreign consulate to obtain a Consular Report of Birth Abroad stating that the person "acquired United States Citizenship at birth" only confirms citizenship acquired at birth; it is not naturalization, and positive acts done by a parent do not make the child a naturalized citizen. A dual citizen by birth who declares in her CoC that she is eligible commits no false material representation under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code.

Even for a naturalized dual citizen, **failure to renounce foreign citizenship under Section 5(2) of R.A. 9225 does not affect Filipino citizenship and is not an ineligibility**; it only keeps the person a dual citizen. If at all, it is a disqualification under Section 40(d) of the Local Government Code, the proper subject of a petition for disqualification, not a ground to cancel the CoC.

On procedure, the Court **harmonized** the COMELEC Rules (Rule 37, Section 3 and Rule 23, Section 8, which make decisions in CoC cases final after five days absent a restraining order) with Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution and Rule 64, Section 3 (certiorari within 30 days from notice): a COMELEC En Banc ruling not restrained within five days is **only executory, not final**, so a timely Rule 64 petition may be heard despite a COMELEC certificate of finality and entry of judgment. The Court also decided the case after the term expired because the issue was capable of repetition yet evading review.

### Facts
On October 17, 2018, petitioner Mariz Lindsey Tan Gana-Carait filed her CoC for Member of the Sangguniang Panlungsod of the Lone District of Biñan, Laguna for the May 13, 2019 elections. On October 22, 2018, Rommel Lim filed a petition for disqualification, alleging that she had acquired U.S. citizenship and had not made a personal and sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship. On November 6, 2018, Dominic Nuñez filed a petition to deny due course to or cancel her CoC, claiming that because she used a U.S. passport, her statements that she was a Filipino citizen and eligible were false.

Petitioner was born on June 25, 1991 in Makati City to a Filipino father and an American mother. A Consular Report of Birth Abroad (CRBA) stated that she "acquired United States Citizenship at birth as established by documentary evidence presented to the Consular Service of the United States at Manila, Philippines on August 23, 2004." She obtained a U.S. passport in 2010 and used it to travel until 2018. She had won as barangay kagawad in 2013 and as Sangguniang Panlungsod member in 2016. She answered that she was a dual citizen by birth and not covered by R.A. 9225.

In a Resolution dated February 27, 2019, the COMELEC First Division denied the disqualification petition but granted Nuñez's petition and cancelled her CoC. Relying on provisions of the U.S. Immigration and Nationality Act (cited as Acts 320 and 322), it held that she was a dual citizen by naturalization because a positive act, the presentation of documents to obtain U.S. citizenship, had been done. She therefore had to take the oath and renounce under R.A. 9225, and having failed to do so, she misrepresented her eligibility. The COMELEC En Banc denied her motion for partial reconsideration on September 23, 2021.

The COMELEC then issued a Certificate of Finality and an Entry of Judgment (both dated December 13, 2021) and a Writ of Execution (January 31, 2022). Petitioner filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 within 30 days from notice. Her term of office, which began at noon of June 30, 2019, ended at noon of June 30, 2022, before the Court decided.

### Issues
1. Whether the COMELEC En Banc Resolution had attained finality, given the COMELEC's issuance of a Certificate of Finality, Entry of Judgment and Writ of Execution.
2. Whether the Court should resolve the case even though petitioner's term of office had expired.
3. Whether petitioner is a dual citizen by birth or by naturalization, and whether the twin requirements of Sections 3 and 5(2) of R.A. 9225 apply to her.
4. Whether petitioner made a false material representation in her CoC that justified its cancellation.

### Ruling
**1. No, the COMELEC En Banc Resolution had not become final.** Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution and Rule 64, Section 3 allow an aggrieved party to bring a COMELEC ruling to the Supreme Court on certiorari within 30 days from notice. The COMELEC Rules, in contrast, count the period from promulgation (Rule 37, Section 1) and make decisions in CoC cancellation cases final and executory five days after promulgation unless restrained (Rule 37, Section 3; Rule 23, Section 8, as amended by Resolution No. 9523). Procedural rules must yield to substantive law and cannot shorten the period the Constitution grants (Treyes v. Larlar). Harmonized, COMELEC En Banc rulings not restrained by the Court within five days from receipt are **"rendered only executory — but not final."** Because the petition was timely, the resolution did not attain finality despite the Certificate of Finality and Entry of Judgment.

**2. Yes, the Court resolved the case despite mootness.** The expiration of petitioner's term at noon of June 30, 2022 (Section 43, R.A. 7160) is a supervening event that renders the case moot (Gunsi, Sr. v. COMELEC). But the question of her status, whether she is a U.S. citizen by birth or by naturalization, will come up again whenever she files a CoC. It is capable of repetition yet evading review (IBP v. Atienza), so the Court ruled on it.

**3. She is a dual citizen by birth; R.A. 9225 does not apply to her.** R.A. 9225 covers natural-born Filipinos who lost Philippine citizenship through naturalization abroad and those who, after its effectivity, become foreign citizens. Both categories refer to persons who underwent naturalization (De Guzman v. COMELEC; Tan v. Crisologo). Maquiling distinguishes dual citizens by naturalization, who must take the oath and personally renounce, from dual citizens by birth, who need not, "as the mere filing of the certificate of candidacy already carries with it an implied renunciation of foreign citizenship." The COMELEC's contrary finding was manifestly erroneous for three reasons. *First*, Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign laws; the private respondents had to prove the INA provisions they relied on. *Second*, any positive act under those provisions would have been done by her American parent, and there was no evidence that she applied for U.S. citizenship or went through naturalization. *Third*, naturalization confers citizenship on an alien, so it is superfluous and absurd for one who is already a citizen. The CRBA itself states that she "acquired United States Citizenship at birth"; the documents only established that fact. As in Cordora, the process merely confirmed citizenship acquired at birth. The Court rejected the OSG's theory that R.A. 9225 covers any acquisition of foreign citizenship through a positive act, whoever performed it.

**4. No false material representation; the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion.** Since she was not covered by R.A. 9225, her non-compliance did not affect her declaration of eligibility. Even assuming she violated Section 5(2), the failure to renounce does not affect Filipino citizenship, which is retained or reacquired upon the oath of allegiance (the same oath found in the CoC). Renunciation is only a condition on the exercise of the right to seek elective office. Commonwealth Act No. 63 does not list failure to renounce as a way of losing citizenship. Remaining a dual citizen is, if at all, a disqualification under Section 40 of the LGC and the proper subject of a petition for disqualification; such a petition was filed here, dismissed, and apparently not appealed. **She therefore kept the qualification of Filipino citizenship under Section 39 of the LGC, made no false representation, and the cancellation of her CoC was grave abuse of discretion.**

### Disposition
The petition for certiorari was GRANTED. The COMELEC En Banc Resolution dated September 23, 2021 and the COMELEC First Division Resolution dated February 27, 2019 were ANNULLED and SET ASIDE. The Certificate of Finality and Entry of Judgment (both dated December 13, 2021) and the Writ of Execution dated January 31, 2022 were CANCELLED and SET ASIDE. Nuñez's Petition to Deny Due Course to or Cancel Certificate of Candidacy (SPA Case No. 18-126 (DC)) was DISMISSED. The Court found it unnecessary to act on the prayer for a TRO, status quo ante order or preliminary injunction.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Bianca was born in Quezon City in 1995 to a Filipino mother and a Canadian father. Assume that under Canadian law she became a Canadian citizen at birth because of her father's citizenship. In 2008, her father submitted documents to the Canadian embassy, which issued a certificate stating that Bianca "is a citizen of Canada from birth." She holds a Canadian passport. In October 2024, Bianca filed a certificate of candidacy for city councilor, declaring that she is eligible for the office. She never took an oath of allegiance under R.A. No. 9225 and never executed a sworn renunciation of her Canadian citizenship. Carlo filed a timely petition to deny due course to or cancel her CoC, alleging material misrepresentation because she did not comply with R.A. No. 9225. Will the petition prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Bianca is a dual citizen by birth, so the oath and renunciation requirements of R.A. No. 9225 do not apply to her, and she made no false material representation.
- **Legal basis:** R.A. No. 9225 applies only to natural-born Filipinos who acquired foreign citizenship through naturalization. Its twin requirements, an oath of allegiance (Section 3) and a personal and sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship when the CoC is filed (Section 5(2)), bind only dual citizens by naturalization. Dual citizens by birth need not renounce, because filing a CoC carries an implied renunciation of foreign citizenship. Documents submitted to confirm foreign citizenship acquired at birth are not naturalization, especially when a parent submitted them. (Gana-Carait v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 257453, August 9, 2022, citing Maquiling v. COMELEC and Cordora v. COMELEC)
- **Application:** Bianca was Filipino at birth through her mother and Canadian at birth through her father. Her dual citizenship is involuntary, the result of two states' laws applying to her at the same time. The 2008 embassy certificate, obtained by her father, only confirmed a citizenship she already had, and she never underwent naturalization. R.A. No. 9225 therefore did not require her to take the oath or renounce Canadian citizenship before running. Her declaration that she is eligible is true, so there is no false material representation under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code.
- **Conclusion:** Carlo's petition should be dismissed because Bianca, a dual citizen by birth, made no false material representation in her CoC.

**Q2.** Dante, a natural-born Filipino, moved to the United States and, as an adult, applied for and was granted U.S. citizenship by naturalization in 2012. In 2023 he took the oath of allegiance under R.A. No. 9225 before a Philippine consulate. In October 2024 he filed a CoC for municipal mayor, declaring that he is a Filipino citizen eligible for the office, but he never executed a personal and sworn renunciation of his U.S. citizenship. (a) Was Dante required to renounce his U.S. citizenship? (b) His rival filed a petition under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code to cancel Dante's CoC, arguing that the failure to renounce made his declaration of eligibility false. Is a Section 78 petition the proper remedy?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. As a dual citizen by naturalization, Dante had to take the oath of allegiance and also make a personal and sworn renunciation of his U.S. citizenship. (b) No. His failure to renounce does not make him ineligible. At most it is a ground for disqualification under Section 40(d) of the Local Government Code, which must be raised in a petition for disqualification.
- **Legal basis:** Under Sections 3 and 5(2) of R.A. No. 9225, dual citizens by naturalization must take the oath of allegiance and personally renounce foreign citizenship when they file their CoC in order to qualify for elective office (Maquiling v. COMELEC). In Gana-Carait v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 257453, August 9, 2022), the Court held that failure to renounce under Section 5(2) does not affect the person's Filipino citizenship, which is retained or reacquired upon the oath of allegiance; it only keeps him a dual citizen. Such failure is not an ineligibility. If at all, it is a disqualification under Section 40 of the LGC and the proper subject of a petition for disqualification.
- **Application:** Dante acquired U.S. citizenship through his own application for naturalization, so R.A. No. 9225 covers him, and he had to make a personal and sworn renunciation when he filed his CoC. But because he took the oath of allegiance in 2023, he is a Filipino citizen and has that qualification under Section 39 of the LGC, so his statement that he is a Filipino citizen is true. His failure to renounce leaves him a dual citizen, which bears on disqualification under Section 40(d) of the LGC, not on eligibility. A Section 78 petition, which rests on a false material representation about eligibility, is the wrong remedy; his rival should file a petition for disqualification.
- **Conclusion:** Dante had to renounce his U.S. citizenship, but his failure to do so is a matter for a petition for disqualification, not a ground to cancel his CoC under Section 78.

**Q3.** The COMELEC En Banc affirmed the cancellation of Ellen's certificate of candidacy for city councilor on the ground that she was a foreign citizen by naturalization who had not complied with R.A. No. 9225. Ellen filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 with the Supreme Court within the reglementary period from her receipt of the En Banc resolution. Since no restraining order was issued within five days, the COMELEC issued a certificate of finality, an entry of judgment and a writ of execution. By the time the Court took up the case, the term for which Ellen ran had expired. The COMELEC argues that (a) its resolution has become final and can no longer be reviewed, and (b) the case is moot. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The argument fails. The resolution was only executory, not final, so the Court may still review it. (b) The case is moot, but the Court may still decide it because the issue is capable of repetition yet evading review.
- **Legal basis:** Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution and Rule 64, Section 3 of the Rules of Court give an aggrieved party 30 days from notice to bring a COMELEC ruling to the Supreme Court on certiorari. The COMELEC Rules that make En Banc rulings final five days after promulgation or receipt absent a restraining order (Rule 37, Section 3; Rule 23, Section 8, as amended by Resolution No. 9523) are procedural. They must be harmonized with the Constitution: within the 30-day period, such rulings are executory but not final. The expiration of the term makes a CoC case moot, but the Court may decide it when the issue is capable of repetition yet evading review. (Gana-Carait v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 257453, August 9, 2022)
- **Application:** Ellen filed within the period, so the COMELEC's certificate of finality, entry of judgment and writ of execution did not make the resolution final. At most the resolution could be executed. The Court may review it and, if it finds grave abuse of discretion, set aside even the certificate of finality and the writ of execution. On mootness, the expiration of the term is a supervening event, but the question of Ellen's citizenship status will come up again every time she files a CoC, and the short terms involved make it likely to evade review again. This falls within the exception.
- **Conclusion:** The Court may take cognizance of Ellen's petition despite the COMELEC's certificate of finality and the expiration of the term.

> Note: Leonen, SAJ., Caguioa, J., and Lazaro-Javier, J. wrote separate concurring opinions, which are not examinable. The main opinion adopts some of their points (credited in its footnotes), and those points are part of the ponencia. Inting and Kho, Jr., JJ. took no part; M. Lopez, J. was on official leave. The decision cites the constitutional provision as "Section 7, Article IX"; it is the common provision on the Constitutional Commissions (Article IX-A).

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68545)

## BOCEA v. Biazon

**BUREAU OF CUSTOMS EMPLOYEES ASSOCIATION (BOCEA), REPRESENTED BY ITS NATIONAL PRESIDENT MR. ROMULO A. PAGULAYAN, PETITIONER, VS. HON. ROZZANO RUFINO B. BIAZON (IN HIS CAPACITY AS COMMISSIONER, BUREAU OF CUSTOMS), HON. CESAR V. PURISIMA (IN HIS CAPACITY AS SECRETARY OF FINANCE), HON. MAR A. ROXAS (IN HIS CAPACITY AS FORMER SECRETARY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION AND COMMUNICATIONS), HON. JOSEPH EMILIO A. ABAYA (IN HIS CAPACITY AS INCUMBENT SECRETARY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION AND COMMUNICATIONS), RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 205836 | 2022-07-12 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** X. Administrative Law > C. Powers of Administrative Agencies > 1. Quasi-legislative or Rulemaking Power > b. Requisites for Validity  
**Specific topics:** Expanded certiorari jurisdiction over quasi-legislative acts; Hierarchy of courts and exhaustion of administrative remedies in expanded certiorari; Ordinance-making power of the Executive (shifting schedules); Administrative issuances cannot contravene the statute (Sec. 3506, TCCP); Overtime pay of Customs personnel under Sec. 1508, RA 10863 (CMTA)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > E. Certiorari, Prohibition, and Mandamus (Rule 65))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (I. General Principles > G. Hierarchy of Courts)

### Doctrine
**A petition for certiorari and prohibition under the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction (Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 1, par. 2) is a proper remedy to question quasi-legislative acts** of executive officials, such as administrative orders, memoranda, and circulars. It remains subject to the **hierarchy of courts** (the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction, here the CA, unless the higher court grants an exemption) and to **exhaustion of administrative remedies**, which applies whether the assailed act is quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, or purely regulatory, and which is how ripeness shows itself in the case of administrative acts (reiterating *Association of Medical Clinics for Overseas Workers v. GCC Approved Medical Centers Association*). The Court may relax these rules, as it did here, because the overtime pay of Customs employees had long been debated and repeatedly litigated.

On the merits: (1) requiring Customs personnel to work three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service, to limit overtime, is a **valid exercise of the Executive's ordinance-making power**, which is inherent in executive control (not delegated by Congress) and may be delegated to subordinate executive officials. (2) **An administrative issuance that goes beyond or contradicts the statute it implements is invalid and is issued with grave abuse of discretion.** Before RA No. 10863, Section 3506 of the Tariff and Customs Code required overtime to be paid by "importers, shippers or other persons served" (including airlines, per *Carbonilla v. Board of Airline Representatives*). Memoranda shifting the cost to the national government at government rates were therefore invalid. (3) Section 1508 of RA No. 10863 (CMTA), effective June 16, 2016, adopted that same policy, so the memoranda were invalid only from August 1, 2012 to June 16, 2016.

### Facts
The Bureau of Customs Employees Association (BOCEA) challenged four issuances. (1) Customs Administrative Order No. 7-2011 (July 15, 2011) prescribed official work hours at NAIA and other international airports, set three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service, and stated the policy on night-shift differential. (2) A Memorandum of Finance Secretary Purisima (August 3, 2012) directed that the 24/7 shifting also be implemented at seaports and other areas to avoid charging overtime pay. It required a customs order expressly prohibiting BOC personnel from charging overtime pay against private entities, since overtime would be paid by the national government at government rates, and it barred personnel from accepting any payment, meals, or transportation from private entities for overtime. (3) A Memorandum of Commissioner Biazon (August 10, 2012) stated that the BOC, applying government rates, would pay all overtime work and would stop charging private entities for overtime effective August 1, 2012. (4) Customs Memorandum Circular No. 195-2012 (August 28, 2012) explained that the shifting schedule was meant to avoid overtime work, in response to airline complaints.

The issuances followed a July 31, 2012 Memorandum from the Finance Secretary to the President. After consultation with airlines and various agencies, it reported that payment of government personnel's overtime by airlines and other private entities was "a deterrent to the tourism industry" and an "irregular activity." The issuances were then made upon the President's instructions. They ended the long practice of Customs employees charging overtime pay against private airlines and other entities served.

On March 7, 2013, BOCEA filed directly with the Supreme Court a petition for certiorari, prohibition, and injunction. It claimed that the issuances violated Article VI, Sections 1 and 29(1) of the Constitution, Section 3506 of the Tariff and Customs Code (TCCP), and labor laws, and were issued with grave abuse of discretion and without due process. The OSG countered that the petition was procedurally infirm and that the issuances were valid exercises of administrative authority over BOC personnel.

### Issues
1. Whether direct recourse to the Supreme Court through a petition for certiorari, prohibition, and injunction is proper.
2. Whether respondents committed grave abuse of discretion in issuing the assailed orders and memoranda adopting a 24/7 shifting policy and charging overtime of Customs employees only against the government and not against private entities.

### Ruling
**1. Certiorari was available, but the petition disregarded the hierarchy of courts and exhaustion of administrative remedies; the Court nonetheless resolved it on the merits.** Under the second paragraph of Article VIII, Section 1, judicial power includes the duty to determine grave abuse of discretion by "any branch or instrumentality of the Government" (*Francisco v. House of Representatives*). This expanded jurisdiction differs from traditional certiorari as a supervisory writ over inferior courts and quasi-judicial bodies. **Thus, although respondents exercised quasi-legislative powers, a petition for certiorari, prohibition, and injunction was the appropriate remedy under the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction.** But even then, the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction, the CA, unless the higher court grants an exemption (*Association of Medical Clinics*; *Rosales v. ERC*; *Kalipunan ng Damayang Mahihirap v. Robredo*). The Supreme Court "is a court of last resort, not a court of first instance." Petitioners also had to exhaust administrative remedies first, a requirement that applies to quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, and regulatory acts alike and that goes into ripeness. The proper route was: reconsideration or review by the Commissioner of Customs, appeal to the Secretary of Finance, then the Office of the President, then the CA under Rule 43, and finally the Supreme Court under Rule 45. Still, because the overtime pay of Customs employees "has been the subject of long debate and repeated litigation," the Court set aside procedural rules and decided the merits.

**2. The petition was partly meritorious.**

- **The shifting schedule is valid.** Requiring three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service and limiting overtime to weekends and holidays was a valid and reasonable exercise of the Executive's ordinance-making power. Citing *Province of Pampanga v. Romulo*, that power "is not a delegated authority from the legislature, but is a consequence of executive control over officials of the executive branch," and the President may delegate it to subordinate officials. CAO No. 7-2011 is valid.
- **Exempting private entities from paying overtime was invalid when issued.** Section 3506 of the TCCP allowed Customs employees to be assigned to overtime work "when the service rendered is to be paid for by importers, shippers or other persons served," at rates not less than those paid to employees of private enterprise. *Carbonilla* upheld that provision as complete and held that airline companies, not all taxpayers through national funds, are liable for such overtime. **By exempting airlines and private entities and making the national government pay at government rates, respondents went beyond the law and contravened *Carbonilla*.**
- **RA No. 10863 later adopted the same policy.** RA No. 10863 (Customs Modernization and Tariff Act), approved May 30, 2016 and effective June 16, 2016, repealed Section 3506. Its Section 1508 provides that overtime is paid "by the Bureau, according to service fees fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance." It also drops the floor tied to private-enterprise rates and allows additional service fees when applicable. This policy shift was within Congress's discretion and is not subject to judicial review. It legalized respondents' policy from June 16, 2016. **Respondents therefore committed grave abuse of discretion only in prohibiting the collection of overtime from private entities before June 16, 2016.**
- **Monetary prejudice is for the trial courts.** The national government was prejudiced to the extent of the overtime it paid during that four-year period. Customs employees were prejudiced only by the difference, if any, between private-enterprise overtime rates and the rates actually paid. These are evidentiary matters for the trial courts, because the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts.

### Disposition
The petition was PARTIALLY GRANTED. CAO No. 7-2011 (July 15, 2011), prescribing official work hours at NAIA and other international airports, a shifting schedule of three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service, and the night-shift differential policy, was DECLARED VALID until superseded. For the period from their effectivity on August 1, 2012 until the effectivity of RA No. 10863 on June 16, 2016, the following were DECLARED INVALID: the Finance Secretary's Memorandum dated August 3, 2012; the Customs Commissioner's Memorandum dated August 10, 2012; and CMC No. 195-2012 dated August 28, 2012. Before June 16, 2016, overtime work of BOC personnel should continue to be paid by importers, shippers, or other entities served, including private airlines, under the laws and jurisprudence then in force. Any resulting monetary prejudice to the government or to petitioners must be raised in the proper administrative or judicial proceeding.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In September 2013, the Secretary of Finance and the Commissioner of Customs issued memoranda that (1) required all Customs personnel at international airports to work in three 8-hour shifts to provide continuous 24-hour service and to limit overtime work, and (2) prohibited Customs personnel from charging overtime pay to airline companies, providing instead that all overtime would be paid by the national government at government rates. At the time, Section 3506 of the Tariff and Customs Code provided that Customs employees may be assigned to overtime work "when the service rendered is to be paid for by importers, shippers or other persons served," at rates not lower than those paid by private enterprise. The Customs employees' union challenges both directives. Rule on the validity of each.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** The shifting-schedule directive is valid, but the directive prohibiting the charging of overtime to airlines is invalid for having been issued with grave abuse of discretion.
- **Legal basis:** The Executive's ordinance-making power is not delegated by the legislature but is a consequence of executive control over officials of the executive branch; the President may adopt rules and delegate this power to subordinate executive officials (Province of Pampanga v. Romulo). Administrative issuances, however, cannot go beyond the law they implement. Section 3506 of the TCCP required overtime to be paid by importers, shippers, or other persons served, which include airline companies, and not by all taxpayers through national funds (Carbonilla v. Board of Airline Representatives). (BOCEA v. Biazon, G.R. No. 205836, July 12, 2022)
- **Application:** (1) Organizing work into three 8-hour shifts to provide 24-hour service and limit overtime is a measure to control work within the Bureau. It falls within the Executive's control over its personnel and is a valid and reasonable exercise of ordinance-making power. (2) Section 3506 placed the cost of overtime on the persons served, including airlines. A memorandum exempting airlines and charging overtime to the national government at government rates contradicts that law. In issuing it, the officials went beyond the law and committed grave abuse of discretion.
- **Conclusion:** The shifting schedule is valid, but the prohibition on charging overtime to airlines is invalid.

**Q2.** Suppose the directive prohibiting Customs personnel from collecting overtime pay from airlines, and providing that the Bureau of Customs will pay all overtime work at service fees fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance, was issued only in March 2018. Would your ruling on its validity be the same?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. A directive issued in March 2018 would be valid, because by then the governing law itself provided that the Bureau pays for overtime work.
- **Legal basis:** Section 3506 of the TCCP was repealed by RA No. 10863 (Customs Modernization and Tariff Act), effective June 16, 2016. Section 1508 of RA No. 10863 provides that Customs personnel assigned to overtime work "shall be paid for such services by the Bureau, according to service fees fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance." The Court held that this shift in policy was within Congress's discretion and legalized the policy of charging overtime to the Bureau starting June 16, 2016. (BOCEA v. Biazon, G.R. No. 205836, July 12, 2022)
- **Application:** The 2013 directive was invalid because it contradicted Section 3506, which was then in force. A March 2018 directive would be measured against Section 1508 of RA No. 10863, which makes the Bureau, not the persons served, pay for overtime. It also requires the service fees to be fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance. A directive implementing exactly that scheme conforms to the law.
- **Conclusion:** The 2018 directive would be valid because it conforms to Section 1508 of RA No. 10863.

**Q3.** A Customs employees' union filed directly with the Supreme Court a petition for certiorari and prohibition under Rule 65, assailing customs memoranda on overtime work, without first asking the Commissioner of Customs or the Secretary of Finance to reconsider them. The OSG argues that (i) certiorari does not lie against quasi-legislative acts, and (ii) the union violated the hierarchy of courts and failed to exhaust administrative remedies. (a) Rule on each argument. (b) If the Court reaches the merits and finds the memoranda partly invalid, may it also determine and order payment of the overtime differentials allegedly due the employees?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The first argument is wrong, but the second is correct as a general rule. Certiorari lies against quasi-legislative acts under the Court's expanded jurisdiction, but the union should have filed with the CA after exhausting administrative remedies. The Supreme Court may still relax these rules in exceptional cases. (b) No. Monetary claims require the presentation of evidence and must be raised in the proper administrative or judicial proceeding.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article VIII, Section 1, paragraph 2 of the Constitution, the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction covers grave abuse of discretion by any branch or instrumentality of the government, so certiorari and prohibition may be used to assail quasi-legislative issuances. Even then, the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction (the CA), and administrative remedies must first be exhausted, whether the act is quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, or regulatory; failure to exhaust affects ripeness. The Court may set these rules aside where, as with the overtime pay of Customs employees, the issue has been the subject of long debate and repeated litigation. The resulting monetary prejudice is evidentiary and is for the trial courts, since the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts. (BOCEA v. Biazon, G.R. No. 205836, July 12, 2022)
- **Application:** (a)(i) The memoranda are quasi-legislative, but the union alleges grave abuse of discretion by executive officials, which falls within the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction. (a)(ii) The union skipped the administrative route: reconsideration by the Commissioner, appeal to the Secretary of Finance, then the Office of the President. After that, judicial review would go to the CA under Rule 43 and then to the Supreme Court under Rule 45. Filing directly with the Supreme Court also violated the hierarchy of courts. The petition is dismissible, unless the Court, as it did in BOCEA, relaxes the rules because the issue has long been debated and litigated. (b) Determining whether employees received less than private-enterprise rates, and by how much, requires evidence. The Supreme Court will not make that determination in a certiorari petition; the claim must be pursued in the proper proceeding.
- **Conclusion:** Certiorari is an available remedy, but the direct filing is generally improper absent exceptional reasons, and the overtime differentials cannot be adjudicated in the certiorari case.

> Note: The petition also invoked Article VI, Sections 1 and 29(1) of the Constitution, labor laws, and due process. The main opinion resolved the case on the ordinance-making power and Section 3506 of the TCCP and did not separately rule on those other grounds. The caption names the Commissioner as "Rozzano Rufino B. Biazon", while the fallo refers to "Rufino B. Biazon". The effectivity date of RA No. 10863 (June 16, 2016) is as stated in the decision.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68482)
