## National Housing Authority v. Commission on Audit

**NATIONAL HOUSING AUTHORITY (NHA), REPRESENTED HEREIN BY ITS GENERAL MANAGER, MARCELINO P. ESCALADA, JR., FROILAN R. KAMPITAN, ELVIRA A. SABADO, WILMA D. HERNANDEZ, FE P. VALENZUELA, PRUDENCIA B. GUGOL, RAYMOND N. ABAD, JEANETTE I. BACCAY, DANILO GONZALES, ALEJANDRO A. NUEVAS, EVELYN BALAIS, AVELINA LLEVA, MA. MELANI ABASOLA, AND ALL RANK-AND-FILE EMPLOYEES OF NHA, REPRESENTED HEREIN BY EVANGELINE A. JAVIER, PRESIDENT OF THE CONSOLIDATED UNION OF EMPLOYEES OF NHA (CUE), PETITIONERS, VS. THE COMMISSION ON AUDIT, REPRESENTED BY MICHAEL G. AGUINALDO, IN HIS CAPACITY AS THE CHAIRPERSON; MARY S. ADELINO, IN HER CAPACITY AS DIRECTOR, CLUSTER II-CORPORATE GOVERNMENT SECTOR OF THE COMMISSION ON AUDIT; JANET B. REYES, IN HER CAPACITY AS AUDIT TEAM LEADER; AND REBECCA A. DUMAGUIT, IN HER CAPACITY AS SUPERVISING AUDITOR, RESPONDENTS. [G.R. No. 252584] NATIONAL HOUSING AUTHORITY, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584 | 2022-06-21 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction  
**Specific topics:** RA 6758 repealed GOCC charter powers to fix allowances (NHA Charter, PD 757); Non-negotiable benefits and the CNA Incentive in the public sector; Qualified political agency does not apply to Cabinet members sitting ex officio on a GOCC board; Madera rules on return of disallowed amounts; when good faith cannot be appreciated; Three-year rule of Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA does not apply where recipients signed deeds of undertaking
  
**Also relevant to:** Labor Law and Social Legislation (V. Labor Relations > A. Right to Self-organization > 1. Coverage > a. Government Employees)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))

### Doctrine
**Reiterated:** Section 16 of RA 6758 (Salary Standardization Law) repealed charter provisions that let GOCC boards fix salaries and allowances inconsistent with the Compensation and Position Classification System, including Sections 8 and 9 of the NHA Charter (PD 757). Allowances that the DBM did not exclude from integration (CCC No. 10-99) are deemed included in the standardized salary. Meal, rice and children's allowances may continue only for employees who were incumbents, and actually receiving them, as of June 30, 1989. RATA may be paid only to positions listed in the GAA or declared of equivalent rank by the DBM. A CNA cannot justify benefits that are non-negotiable, or that are not paid as a single CNA Incentive given once after year-end from MOOE savings (DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1). **The doctrine of qualified political agency (alter ego) does not apply to Cabinet members sitting ex officio on a GOCC board, so their approval is not the President's approval.** The non-diminution principle cannot validate unauthorized benefits, however long they have been given.

Good faith cannot be appreciated (a) when a Supreme Court decision on a disallowance of the same nature already existed, or (b) when the approving officers knew facts that made the disbursement illegal. Under the **Madera v. COA** rules (reiterated), approving and certifying officers who acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence are solidarily liable to return the disallowed amounts. Recipients must return what they received unless it was genuinely given for services rendered, or unless the Court excuses the return under Rule 2d (undue prejudice, social justice, or other bona fide exceptions).

**Clarified:** the rule in **Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA**, which excuses passive recipients from refunding when three years pass between receipt and any notice of disallowance, **does not apply where the recipients signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking** acknowledging a possible refund and authorizing salary deductions for it. Those undertakings are notice of the possible illegality, so the recipients must refund even if the Notices of Disallowance came more than three years later.

### Facts
On September 3, 2010, the COA formed a special audit team to examine the allowances and bonuses that the National Housing Authority (NHA), a GOCC, paid its officers, employees and board members for 2008 and 2009. In January and February 2012 the auditors issued seven Notices of Disallowance (NDs) totaling P367,844,754.36:
- cash incentive (SONA) award: P173,832,792.50
- economic subsidy: P54,954,000.00
- Christmas bonus: P71,453,000.00
- citation bonus: P14,530,000.00
- mid-year financial assistance (MYFA): P33,708,957.86
- meal, children's and rice subsidies: P18,295,504.00
- RATA: P1,070,500.00

The NDs cited Section 12 of RA 6758, MO No. 20 (2001), and Section 45 of the 2008 and 2009 GAAs. They named as liable the approving officers, the NHA Board (a majority of whom were Cabinet Secretaries), the certifying officers, and the recipients.

The liable persons relied on LOI No. 97, Sections 9 and 10 of PD 757 (NHA Charter), and Section 35, Chapter 5, Subtitle A, Title I, Book V of EO 292 (incentive awards). They also invoked the President's 1995 approval of the MYFA, non-diminution of benefits, their CNA, the alter ego doctrine (since the Board was made up of the President's alter egos), and good faith. The auditors answered that the charter and LOI had been repealed, and that the employees could not claim good faith because they had signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking.

The COA CGS-Cluster 2 Director (Decision No. 2015-013, August 13, 2015) and the COA Commission Proper (Decision No. 2018-124, January 26, 2018) affirmed the NDs. The NHA and its employees' union filed a Rule 64 petition (G.R. No. 239936). The Court allowed an amended petition after the NHA admitted it had attached the wrong NDs: those it attached covered Program Administration Fees for 2013-2014, which were still pending before the Commission Proper. After the COA issued a Notice of Finality of Decision on March 4, 2020, the NHA filed a petition for injunction (G.R. No. 252584). In a Resolution dated August 25, 2020, the Court denied the prayer for a TRO and writ of preliminary injunction in that petition.

### Issues
1. Whether the COA gravely abused its discretion in affirming the disallowance of the allowances and benefits granted to NHA officers and employees for 2008 and 2009.
2. Whether the approving officers and the recipients acted in good faith and should be excused from returning the disallowed amounts.
3. Whether the passive recipients are excused from refunding under the three-year rule of Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA.

### Ruling
**1. No grave abuse of discretion; the disallowances were proper.** Grave abuse of discretion is a capricious, whimsical or arbitrary exercise of judgment so patent and gross that it amounts to an evasion of duty. The petitioners did not prove it.
- *Charter powers repealed.* Section 16 of RA 6758 repealed laws and charters that authorize allowances inconsistent with the Compensation and Position Classification System, including Sections 8 and 9 of PD 757. The DBM decides which allowances are not integrated (CCC No. 10-99). Except for RATA, none of the benefits was excluded from integration, and meal, rice and children's allowances may continue only for employees who were incumbents, and actually receiving them, as of June 30, 1989.
- *RATA* is paid only to officials whose positions are listed in Section 45 of the 2008 and 2009 GAAs or declared by the DBM to be of equivalent rank. RATA paid to other NHA employees was properly disallowed.
- *CNA.* Under DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, CNA incentives must be combined into one CNA Incentive, paid once after the end of the year and funded solely from MOOE savings. The NHA split them into several allowances paid on different dates, with no proof that they came from savings. Increases in salary and allowances not provided by law, and rice and other subsidies, are not negotiable (Resolution No. 02, s. 2003; PSLMC Resolution No. 02, s. 2004).
- *Alter ego.* The doctrine of qualified political agency cannot be extended to Cabinet members sitting on the NHA Board. Following Manalang-Demigillo v. TIDCORP, it cannot be invoked when Cabinet members act ex officio as members of a board constituted by law.
- *MYFA and Christmas bonus* are year-end benefits governed by MO No. 324 (s. 1990) and DBM Budget Circular No. 2005-06. The President's December 18, 1995 approval of the MYFA did not authorize later grants or increases. Non-diminution cannot justify the MYFA because NHA compensation is governed by laws that "sanction unauthorized or irregular compensation or benefits no matter how long it has been regularly granted."
- *SONA award and citation bonus.* The incentive-award system under Section 35 of the Administrative Code must follow CSC rules, which the NHA did not show it complied with, and it does not authorize across-the-board benefits. The DBM had in fact disallowed the SONA incentive in the NHA's 2008 and 2009 corporate operating budgets.

**2. No good faith; officers and recipients must return the amounts.** Good faith cannot be appreciated where a Supreme Court decision already covers a disallowance of the same nature, or where the approving officers knew facts that made the disbursement illegal. RA 6758 and PD 1597 plainly deny the Board power to grant or increase allowances, the rules require presidential approval, and the DBM had already disallowed some items, yet the NHA kept paying them. The Board members, a majority of them Cabinet Secretaries, are expected to know the compensation rules, so they are solidarily liable under Section 103 of PD 1445. The recipients must refund what they received because they signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking authorizing salary deductions if a refund became necessary, and nothing showed they were forced to sign. The Court also noted that under RA 10149 (GOCC Governance Act of 2011), additional compensation for GOCC employees needs a GCG recommendation and presidential approval, and neither was obtained. Applying the Madera rules, there was no good faith in the release or receipt of the amounts.

**3. No, the three-year rule does not apply.** Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA held under Madera Rule 2d that, absent other circumstances, the lapse of three years between receipt and any notice of irregularity excuses recipients from refunding. The rule does not protect those who actively took part in fraudulent transactions, and it rests on the recipients' lack of notice for a long period. Here the employees "knowingly and willingly executed notarized Deeds of Undertaking" and authorized salary deductions for any refund. **These instruments gave them sufficient notice of the illegality and irregularity of the benefits, which "precludes the application of the 3-year prescriptive period."** Even though the NDs came more than three years after receipt, the passive recipients must still refund.

On the injunction petition, the Court noted that it had already denied the prayer for a TRO and writ of preliminary injunction against the Notice of Finality in its Resolution of August 25, 2020.

### Disposition
The consolidated petitions were DISMISSED for lack of merit, and COA Decision No. 2018-124 dated January 26, 2018 was AFFIRMED in toto. The approving and certifying officers are solidarily liable for the return of the disallowed amounts in accordance with the Notices of Disallowance. The payee-recipients are individually liable for the return of the amounts they each received.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** The 1976 charter of the Philippine Rural Housing Corporation (PRHC), a GOCC, authorizes its Board to fix the allowances of its personnel. In 2023 the Board, a majority of whom are Cabinet Secretaries sitting ex officio, approved a rice subsidy and a "service anniversary bonus" for all employees. The COA disallowed the payments. The PRHC argues that (a) its charter authorizes the Board to grant allowances, and (b) since the Board members are alter egos of the President, their approval amounts to presidential approval. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. The charter power was repealed by RA 6758, and the alter ego doctrine does not apply to Cabinet members sitting ex officio on a GOCC board.
- **Legal basis:** Section 16 of RA 6758 repealed all laws, decrees and corporate charters that authorize or fix salaries, pay rates or allowances inconsistent with the Compensation and Position Classification System. Allowances not excluded from integration by the DBM are deemed included in the standardized salary, and meal and rice subsidies may continue only for employees who were incumbents, and actually receiving them, as of June 30, 1989. The doctrine of qualified political agency does not extend to Cabinet members who sit ex officio on a GOCC board constituted by law (National Housing Authority v. COA, G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584, June 21, 2022, applying Manalang-Demigillo v. TIDCORP).
- **Application:** (a) The 1976 charter provision letting the Board fix allowances is inconsistent with RA 6758 and was repealed by Section 16. A rice subsidy given to all employees, and not only to those who were incumbents and receiving it on June 30, 1989, has no legal basis, and neither does a bonus not authorized by law. (b) The Cabinet Secretaries approved the benefits as Board members acting ex officio, not as the President's alter egos. Their act is not the President's act and does not supply presidential approval.
- **Conclusion:** Both arguments fail, and the COA correctly disallowed the payments.

**Q2.** A regular COA audit found that the rank-and-file employees of a GOCC received an unauthorized "economic subsidy" in 2016. The Notice of Disallowance was issued only in 2020, and nothing shows the employees took part in any fraud. (a) Absent other circumstances, may these passive recipients invoke the lapse of more than three years to be excused from refunding? (b) Would your answer change if, before receiving the subsidy, each employee had signed a notarized Deed of Undertaking agreeing to refund it if disallowed and authorizing salary deductions for that purpose?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Absent other circumstances, the lapse of three years without notice may excuse the passive recipients from refunding. (b) Yes, the answer changes. The Deeds of Undertaking gave them notice, so the three-year rule does not apply and they must refund.
- **Legal basis:** Under Madera v. COA, recipients must return disallowed amounts unless the amounts were genuinely given for services rendered, or the return is excused under Rule 2d (undue prejudice, social justice, or other bona fide exceptions). Applying Rule 2d, Cagayan de Oro City Water District v. COA held that, absent circumstances the Court deems sufficient, the lapse of three years between receipt and any notice of illegality or irregularity excuses recipients from refunding, except those who actively took part in fraudulent transactions. In National Housing Authority v. COA (G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584, June 21, 2022), the Court held that the three-year rule does not apply where the recipients signed notarized Deeds of Undertaking authorizing deductions for a possible refund, because those instruments gave them sufficient notice of the possible illegality.
- **Application:** (a) The employees are passive recipients. They received the subsidy in 2016 and had no notice of any problem until the 2020 ND, more than three years later, and they are not shown to have taken part in fraud. They may be excused. (b) By signing the Deeds of Undertaking, the employees were put on guard that the subsidy might have to be returned. The reason for the three-year rule, a long period without notice, is absent, as in NHA v. COA, so they received and spent the money at their own risk.
- **Conclusion:** Passive recipients may be excused under the three-year rule only if they had no notice; those who signed refund undertakings must return the amounts.

**Q3.** The union of a GOCC's employees concluded a Collective Negotiation Agreement (CNA) with management. The CNA gives each employee a monthly rice subsidy, a mid-year bonus and a quarterly "productivity allowance," all paid from the GOCC's general corporate funds on various dates during the year. When the COA disallowed the payments, the union argued that the CNA is a contract with the force of law between the parties, and that the benefits had been given for many years and so can no longer be withdrawn. Is the union correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The benefits are not valid CNA incentives, and neither the CNA nor long practice can supply a legal basis for them.
- **Legal basis:** Under DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, all cash incentives in CNAs must be combined into a single CNA Incentive, paid once after the end of the year and funded solely from savings in released MOOE (for GOCCs, from savings in their approved corporate operating budget). Increases in salary and allowances not provided by law, and rice or other subsidies, are not negotiable (Resolution No. 02, s. 2003; PSLMC Resolution No. 02, s. 2004). The non-diminution principle cannot justify unauthorized benefits, because government compensation is governed by law (National Housing Authority v. COA, G.R. Nos. 239936 & 252584, June 21, 2022).
- **Application:** The CNA divides the incentives into several allowances paid at different times of the year from general funds, instead of one incentive paid after year-end from savings. The rice subsidy and the other allowances not provided by law are non-negotiable and could not be validly granted through the CNA. That the benefits were paid for years does not make them lawful, because non-diminution does not protect unauthorized compensation.
- **Conclusion:** The union is not correct, and the COA properly disallowed the CNA-based benefits.

> Note: Consolidated cases: G.R. No. 239936 (Rule 64 certiorari) and G.R. No. 252584 (injunction against the COA Notice of Finality). The body says the Board members bear solidary liability "for the total disallowance," while the Madera rule it quotes limits approving and certifying officers' solidary liability to the net disallowed amount; the fallo simply holds them solidarily liable "in accordance with the notices of disallowance." The NDs on Program Administration Fees (2013-2014), which were attached to the original petition by mistake, were not resolved and remained pending before the COA Commission Proper.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68467)

## SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List

**SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION, PETITIONER, VS. 1ACCOUNTANTS PARTY-LIST, INC., REPRESENTED BY ITS PRESIDENT, CHRISTIAN JAY D. LIM, CHRISTIAN JAY D. LIM IN HIS CAPACITY AS CPA, FROILAN G. AMPIL, ALLAN M. BASARTE, VIRGILIO F. AGUNOD, AND JONAS P. MASCARIÑAS, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 246027 | 2022-06-21 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** X. Administrative Law > C. Powers of Administrative Agencies > 1. Quasi-legislative or Rulemaking Power > b. Requisites for Validity  
**Specific topics:** SEC accreditation of external auditors held ultra vires (later reversed); Accreditation as an additional licensing requirement (Airlift Asia); Delegata potestas non potest delegari; A MOA cannot validate a violation of law; Effect of reversal on second motion for reconsideration
  
**Also relevant to:** Commercial and Taxation Laws (VI. Special Commercial Laws > A. Securities Regulation (RA 8799))

> **REVERSED — not the controlling rule.** Reversed on the SEC's second motion for reconsideration by the En Banc Resolution of January 28, 2025, which upheld SRC Rule 68, par. 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009. Study the 2025 Resolution for the controlling rule.

### Doctrine
**Caution: this Decision was reversed.** The SEC filed a second motion for reconsideration. In its Resolution of January 28, 2025, the Court En Banc granted it, reversed and set aside this Decision, and declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the SRC IRR and SEC MC No. 13-2009 valid and not unconstitutional. The holding below is the 2022 ruling, which the Court has since abandoned. For the controlling rule, see *SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (Resolution)*, G.R. No. 246027, January 28, 2025.

In 2022 the Court held that **the SEC had no authority to require accreditation of CPAs acting as external auditors of corporations that issue registered securities and hold secondary licenses. It declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the Amended IRR of the Securities Regulation Code (R.A. No. 8799) and SEC Memorandum Circular No. 13-2009 null and void.** The SEC's powers under SRC Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code cover juridical entities such as corporations. Its other SRC powers must be read together with Sec. 5(a); they flow from its jurisdiction over corporations and do not reach individual CPAs or the practice of accountancy. Applying *Airlift Asia Customs Brokerage v. CA*, the Court held that the accreditation was an additional licensing requirement. It curtailed the practice of a profession whose supervision R.A. No. 9298 (Secs. 9 and 31) gives to the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy.

The Decision also applied two general rules: (1) ***delegata potestas non potest delegari***: the Board cannot redelegate to another body a power that Congress delegated to it; and (2) **a private agreement, such as a MOA, cannot validate a violation of law** (Civil Code, Art. 1306). The 2025 Resolution did not abandon these rules. It held instead that the MOA delegated nothing, because SEC accreditation regulates the activity of statutory audit, not the profession.

### Facts
Respondents were 1Accountants Party-List, Inc. and five CPAs. The organization is a non-stock, non-profit sectoral organization registered with the SEC. It was represented by its President, Christian Jay D. Lim, who also sued in his personal capacity as a CPA. The other CPAs were Froilan G. Ampil, Allan M. Basarte, Virgilio F. Agunod and Jonas P. Mascariñas. They filed a Petition for Declaratory Relief with prayer for preliminary injunction and TRO against the SEC before the RTC of Davao City, Branch 15 (Civil Case No. R-DVO-15-02294-SC). They challenged Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the Amended IRR of the SRC, SEC Memorandum Circular No. 13-2009, and similar circulars. Since 2002, these issuances had required SEC accreditation of CPAs acting as external auditors of corporations issuing registered securities and possessing secondary licenses.

MC No. 13-2009 made the following rules:
- Only an SEC-accredited external auditor (and auditing firm) may be engaged by covered corporations for the statutory audit of their financial statements (Sec. 4.1).
- Applicants pay accreditation filing fees, e.g., P5,000, P3,000 and P2,000 for individual auditors in Groups A, B, and C or D.
- Auditing firms and external auditors who take an engagement without accreditation pay a scale of fines (Sec. 12.4), and so do companies that engage unaccredited auditors.
- An accreditation may be suspended or delisted (Sec. 12.6).

Respondents argued that the issuances were ultra vires, contravened R.A. No. 9298 (Philippine Accountancy Act of 2004), and restricted the right of CPAs to practice their profession. They added that MC No. 13-2009 violated due process and equal protection. The SEC relied on SRC Sec. 5(a), (d), (f), (g) and (n) and Sec. 68, and on Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code. It also invoked a MOA with the BSP, the Insurance Commission and the Board of Accountancy, its police power, and the four-pronged test of reasonable classification.

On March 20, 2018, the RTC declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void for being contrary to R.A. No. 9298, unconstitutional, and ultra vires. In an Order dated February 20, 2019, it denied the SEC's motion for reconsideration. The SEC then filed a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45.

### Issues
1. Whether the SRC and the Corporation Code authorize the SEC to require accreditation of CPAs acting as external auditors of covered corporations.
2. Whether the accreditation requirement is an additional licensing requirement that contravenes R.A. No. 9298, which entrusts the regulation of the accounting profession to the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy.
3. Whether the MOA invoked by the SEC can serve as authority for the assailed issuances.

### Ruling
The Court said the case presented only one principal issue: whether the RTC correctly declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void. It answered yes, on the following grounds.

**1. No, the SRC and the Corporation Code do not authorize the SEC to regulate individual CPAs.** SRC Sec. 5(a) gives the SEC jurisdiction and supervision over "corporations, partnerships or associations." Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code requires "every corporation" to submit an annual report with financial statements certified by an independent CPA. The Court applied the plain-meaning rule (*quoties in verbis nulla est ambiguitas, ibi nulla expositio contra verba fienda est*). Under it, these provisions apply only to juridical entities and nowhere extend to individuals, "moreso CPAs." The other SRC provisions the SEC cited must be read together with Sec. 5(a), because a statute is construed as a whole. All of those powers flow from the SEC's jurisdiction over corporations. In the Court's words, "While petitioner may regulate corporations as well as the securities market, such regulation does not extend to an authority to restrict, even in the slightest degree, the practice of accountancy."

**2. Yes, the accreditation is an additional licensing requirement that contravenes R.A. No. 9298.** *Airlift Asia* defined a license as a "permission to do a particular thing, to exercise a certain privilege or to carry on a particular business or to pursue a certain occupation." A CPA who wants to do a statutory audit of a covered corporation must get SEC accreditation on top of the CPA license, although such audit is already part of the practice of accountancy. The scale of fines in Sec. 12.4 shows the burden. Under Secs. 9(b), (g), (h) and 31 of R.A. No. 9298, the power to supervise the accounting profession and to regulate CPAs is exclusively delegated to the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy. MC No. 13-2009's penal clauses contravene that delegation: the fines under Sec. 12.4 and the suspension or delisting under Sec. 12.6. The SEC argued that nothing stopped CPAs from applying for accreditation. The Court answered that "the accreditation itself is the barrier, however flimsy, which prevents the practice of external auditing of covered entities."

**3. No, the MOA cannot authorize the issuances.** Under *delegata potestas non potest delegari*, the Board cannot redelegate to another body a power that Congress delegated to it. Moreover, "a private agreement such as the MOA cannot operate to validate a transgression of a provision of law" (citing Civil Code, Art. 1306). The MOA was therefore void and could not serve as the SEC's authority for the assailed issuances.

### Disposition
The petition for review on certiorari was DENIED. The Court AFFIRMED the RTC Decision dated March 20, 2018 in Civil Case No. R-DVO-15-02294-SC. It declared Paragraph 3, Rule 68 of the IRR of the SRC and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void. Lazaro-Javier, J. wrote a concurrence, and the other participating Justices concurred.

This disposition was later REVERSED and SET ASIDE by the Court En Banc's Resolution of January 28, 2025, which declared the same issuances valid and not unconstitutional.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In 2023, Gemma, a CPA, was told by her lawyer that she did not need SEC accreditation to audit listed companies. The lawyer cited SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022), which declared null and void Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the SRC IRR and SEC MC No. 13-2009. In 2026, Gemma is still unaccredited. She accepts an engagement for the statutory audit of the annual financial statements of a corporation with registered securities and a secondary license. When the SEC questions the engagement, she invokes the 2022 Decision. Is the 2022 Decision still a valid basis for her position?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The 2022 Decision has been reversed and set aside. The SEC accreditation requirement is now valid.
- **Legal basis:** In SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022), the Court En Banc declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the SRC IRR and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void. It reasoned that the SEC's powers under SRC Sec. 5 and Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code cover only juridical entities, and that R.A. No. 9298 entrusts regulation of the accounting profession to the Board of Accountancy. On the SEC's second motion for reconsideration, however, the Court in its Resolution of January 28, 2025 in the same case reversed and set aside the June 21, 2022 Decision and the June 27, 2023 Resolution. It declared the same issuances valid and not unconstitutional. The Court relied on SRC Secs. 5.1(d), 5.1(n) and 72 and on R.A. No. 11232 (Revised Corporation Code) Secs. 177 and 179.
- **Application:** Gemma relies on a ruling that no longer stands. The Decision she cites was set aside on reconsideration by the same Court En Banc in the same case. The final word in G.R. No. 246027 is the 2025 Resolution. Under it, the SEC may require CPAs who perform the statutory audit of covered entities to be SEC-accredited. Gemma's engagement is a statutory audit of a covered entity, so the accreditation requirement applies to her.
- **Conclusion:** Gemma cannot rely on the 2022 Decision, because the Court reversed it in 2025 and upheld the SEC accreditation requirement.

**Q2.** The Commissioner of Customs issued an order that PRC-licensed customs brokers must first be accredited by the Bureau of Customs before they may practice before it. The order imposes accreditation fees and fines for practicing without accreditation. Most of a customs broker's work is done before the Bureau. The Customs Brokers Act of 2004 (R.A. No. 9280) gives a professional regulatory board power over the profession. It also provides that those who pass the licensure examination may practice in any collection district "without the need of securing another license from the BOC." The Commissioner relies only on his general power to issue rules to enforce the customs laws. Is the order valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The order is invalid because it imposes an additional licensing requirement that the law proscribes.
- **Legal basis:** In Airlift Asia Customs Brokerage v. Court of Appeals, which the Court applied in SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022), the Court defined a license as a "permission to do a particular thing, to exercise a certain privilege or to carry on a particular business or to pursue a certain occupation." It held that a BOC accreditation requirement for customs brokers was a licensing requirement proscribed by law that curtailed their practice. The Court reversed the 2022 Decision in its Resolution of January 28, 2025, but it distinguished Airlift Asia rather than abandoning it. In Airlift Asia, (1) R.A. No. 9280 expressly allows licensed brokers to practice "without the need of securing another license from the BOC"; (2) the Commissioner's mandate to enforce tariff laws does not include power to regulate the profession; and (3) a large part of a customs broker's work is practice before the BOC.
- **Application:** The Commissioner's order has all the features that made the CAO in Airlift Asia invalid. A licensed broker cannot practice before the Bureau, where most of the broker's work is done, without first getting the Bureau's accreditation. That makes the accreditation a second license. It directly contradicts the statute's express command that no other license from the BOC is needed. The Commissioner's general power to enforce customs laws is not a power to regulate the customs broker profession, which the law gave to a professional regulatory board. This case is unlike the SEC accreditation upheld in 2025, where no statute expressly barred another accreditation and the rule covered only the statutory audit of a small class of entities.
- **Conclusion:** The order is void as an additional licensing requirement contrary to R.A. No. 9280.

**Q3.** A statute vests in a professional regulatory board the power to register practitioners of a profession and to promulgate rules on registration requirements, fees, and penalties. To "save on costs," the board signs a Memorandum of Agreement with a government agency, the National Business Office (NBO). Under the MOA, the NBO will issue and renew certificates of registration, set registration fees, and penalize unregistered practitioners. A practitioner fined by the NBO argues that the MOA is void. The NBO answers that the board consented to the arrangement. Who is correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** The practitioner is correct. The MOA is void and cannot give the NBO power to register or penalize practitioners.
- **Legal basis:** Under the maxim delegata potestas non potest delegari, a power that Congress has delegated cannot be further delegated by the original delegate to another. In addition, a private agreement such as a MOA cannot validate a violation of a provision of law (Civil Code, Art. 1306). (SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List, G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022.) In its Resolution of January 28, 2025, the Court reversed that Decision but restated the same maxim. It upheld the SEC's MOA with the Board of Accountancy only because the Board had not delegated its power to regulate the profession: SEC accreditation covers only the activity of statutory audit, and the collaboration did not contravene any statute.
- **Application:** Registration of practitioners and the fees and penalties for violating registration requirements are the very powers the statute entrusted to the board. In the MOA, the board does not merely coordinate with the NBO. It hands those powers over to the NBO. This is a redelegation of delegated power, which the board cannot make. The board's consent cannot cure the defect, because a contract cannot authorize what the law does not allow. The arrangement is unlike the SEC-Board MOA upheld in 2025, where the Board kept its full power over the profession.
- **Conclusion:** The MOA is void, so the NBO has no authority to fine the practitioner.

> Note: REVERSED ON RECONSIDERATION. See SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (Resolution), G.R. No. 246027, January 28, 2025 (case id gr-246027-20250128). In that Resolution, the Court En Banc granted the SEC's second motion for reconsideration (leave was granted on January 30, 2024). It reversed and set aside this Decision and the June 27, 2023 Resolution, which had denied the first motion for reconsideration with finality, and declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009 valid and not unconstitutional. The doctrine of this Decision on the SEC's lack of authority is therefore no longer controlling. The bar questions above test only the current rule and points that survived the reversal. The June 27, 2023 Resolution is known only from the 2025 Resolution's recital and is not in the index. The 2022 Decision did not separately rule on the due process, equal protection, or police power arguments. Lazaro-Javier, J.'s concurrence was not used for the doctrine.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68463)

## Aliping v. Court of Appeals

**REP. NICASIO M. ALIPING, JR., PETITIONER, VS. COURT OF APPEALS (FORMER 4TH DIVISION), BISHOP CARLITO J. CENZON, ARCHBISHOP SOCRATES B. VILLEGAS, SHEREE M. NOLASCO, MARIE A. BALANGUE, NONNETTE C. BENNETT, DR. TERESITA F. DE VENECIA, ANTONIO J. SUPREMIDO, JR., AND PASTOR GENER TANDOC, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 221823 | 2022-06-21 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** VIII. Constitutional Rights > B. Equal Protection  
**Specific topics:** Equal protection: a kalikasan directive aimed only at the impleaded respondent is not discriminatory; Intentional or purposeful discrimination required (People v. Dela Piedra); Due process: opportunity to be heard; restriction not arbitrary or oppressive; Writ of kalikasan: liability for road construction, tree-cutting and earth-moving inside and outside one's claim; Santo Tomas Forest Reserve; Amliang dams and Bued River
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > A. Due Process > 1. Procedural and Substantive Due Process)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VI. Special Proceedings and Writs > J. Environmental Cases (AM 09-6-8-SC) > 3. Writ of Kalikasan)

### Doctrine
**A directive in a writ of kalikasan judgment that permanently enjoins only the impleaded respondent from developing his claim within a forest reserve does not violate the equal protection clause.** This holds even if other residents and garden owners in the reserve are not similarly restrained, where the directive is a specific remedial response to an anthropogenic activity unique to him and proven to be a major contributor to the environmental damage. The others are not similarly situated: they were not impleaded, and they were neither accused nor proven to have engaged in comparable acts. Applying *People v. Dela Piedra* by analogy, unequal application is not a denial of equal protection unless there is an element of **intentional or purposeful discrimination**. A discriminatory purpose is not presumed; there must be a showing of "clear and intentional discrimination."

The same directive does not violate **due process** where it was the product of bona fide proceedings in which the respondent actively participated and had ample opportunity to be heard. It is also not arbitrary or oppressive when it restrains only the acts (bulldozing, leveling, earth-moving, road construction) found to have caused the siltation and degradation of the waterways. It is a "necessary restriction to prevent further damage."

A person established as responsible for the construction of new roads is accountable for the illegal tree-cutting and earth-moving that resulted from it, **whether within or outside his claim**. He may therefore be ordered to mitigate erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas. Bare insistence that the roads were old logging roads cannot overcome evidence that they were newly built.

### Facts
Proclamation No. 581 (July 8, 1940) created the Santo Tomas Forest Reserve in Tuba, Benguet. Its natural springs sustain three Baguio Water District (BWD) dams (the Amliang dams), which supply some 4,176 households in Tuba and Baguio City. The springs are also the headwaters of the Bued River, which supports the San Fabian River Irrigation System serving about 1,144 hectares of Pangasinan farmland. In April–May 2014, acting on a report of tree-cutting and excavation on Mount Santo Tomas, the CENRO found two new roads inside the reserve: 1.5 kilometers from Sitio Amliang to Sitio Pongayan and 1.14 kilometers from Sitio Pongayan to Sitio Bekel. The roads had no Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC), tree-cutting or special land use permit, or road right-of-way or excavation permit. About 306 trees and 455 saplings were cut, causing damage estimated at P10,314,531.40, and the earth-moving silted the tributaries of Amliang Dam 3. The CENRO tagged petitioner Nicasio Aliping, Jr., then Representative of Baguio City, as responsible; the roads originated from land within the reserve that he claimed.

The PENRO filed a criminal complaint under Sections 77 and 78 of PD 705. The EMB issued a Notice of Violation cum Cease and Desist Order on June 2, 2014. At a July 14, 2014 technical conference, petitioner admitted undertaking an excavation project within his claim without an environmental permit, and the EMB fined him P50,000.00 under Section 4 of PD 1586. The BWD attributed the turbidity of Amliang Dam 3 to the road construction around petitioner's claim and to small-scale mining. In a May 21, 2014 letter to the Tuba mayor, petitioner undertook to institute measures "to avoid further damage to plants, trees and the [dam]."

Respondents Bishop Cenzon and others, residents of Baguio City and San Fabian, Pangasinan, filed a petition for writs of kalikasan and continuing mandamus. They named petitioner, DENR officials, Tuba officials and the Tuba police, and complained of four activities: (1) petitioner's road construction with illegal tree-cutting and earth-moving; (2) illegal small-scale mining; (3) expansion of gardens and residences through tax declarations over reserve land; and (4) relay towers on the mountains. On September 30, 2014, the Supreme Court issued the writ and a TEPO and referred the case to the CA. In his return, petitioner admitted excavating within his 2.6885-hectare claim to improve an existing access road. He denied any road construction or tree-cutting outside his claim and said the roads were old logging roads.

On May 6, 2015, the CA found the first three activities proven and the fourth not proven. It granted the writs and made the TEPO permanent. Item 4 of its fallo ordered petitioner to (a) permanently cease and desist from developing or enhancing his claimed property (bulldozing, leveling, any earth-moving, improving the old building, building structures, road opening and concreting), (b) mitigate the soil erosion causing siltation of the Amliang dams, and (c) rehabilitate the 2-kilometer stretch from his claim down to the river by massive tree planting. His motion for reconsideration was denied on October 29, 2015. In his Rule 45 petition, he argued that item 4(a) violated equal protection, since hundreds of other residents with vegetable gardens in the reserve were not restrained, and deprived him of the use of his property without due process. He also argued that items 4(b) and (c) had no evidentiary basis.

### Issues
1. Whether item 4(a) of the CA decision violates petitioner's right to the equal protection of the laws.
2. Whether item 4(a) deprives petitioner of the use of his property without due process of law.
3. Whether items 4(b) and (c) of the CA decision have factual basis.

### Ruling
**1. No violation of equal protection.** The Court conceded that item 4(a) is directed exclusively at petitioner and that no similar restriction was imposed on other residents, even though residences and gardens were recognized as potential contributors to degradation. But petitioner was the only resident impleaded, because the petition imputed to him alone a specific anthropogenic activity: tree-cutting and earth-moving from a road construction project. **Item 4(a) "is nothing more than a specific remedial response"** to earth-moving activities confirmed to be a major contributor to the siltation of the streams leading to Amliang Dam 3 and the Bued River. The others were never impleaded and were not accused of, "much less proven to have engaged in," comparable activities. Citing *People v. Dela Piedra*, the Court held that a violation requires "intentional or purposeful discrimination," which is not presumed. There was "simply no evidence" that the CA intentionally discriminated against petitioner. The directive was designed to remedy an activity unique to him, and the other residents are differently situated.

**2. No violation of due process.** The decision was "the product of bona fide proceedings in which petitioner actively participated"; he filed a return and testified through a judicial affidavit, so he had ample opportunity to be heard. Nor is item 4(a) arbitrary or oppressive. It enjoins only acts such as bulldozing, leveling, earth-moving and road construction, the same acts found to have caused the siltation and continuing degradation of the waterways. It is "a necessary restriction to prevent further damage."

**3. Yes, items 4(b) and (c) have factual basis.** Petitioner conceded causing earth-moving within his claim without an ECC or permits, and his May 21, 2014 letter amounted to an admission of damage. The CENRO memorandum and the judicial affidavit of a resident showed the two roads were new, and petitioner's return admitted that both roads connect to or originate from his claim and that he excavated to improve access to it. **Taken together, these circumstances showed that the roads were built "at the behest of petitioner—and no other"**, for his sole benefit. His claim that they were old logging roads rested only on his "bare insistence." Being responsible for the new roads, he is accountable for the resulting tree-cutting and earth-moving "whether within or without his claim."

### Disposition
The petition was DENIED. The Court of Appeals' May 6, 2015 Decision and October 29, 2015 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 00029 W/K, which granted the writs of kalikasan and continuing mandamus, made the TEPO permanent, and ordered petitioner to cease developing his claim, mitigate the erosion, and rehabilitate the damaged 2-kilometer stretch, were AFFIRMED.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Residents downstream of a watershed reserve filed a petition for a writ of kalikasan against Lito and several government agencies. They alleged that Lito bulldozed two new roads from his claimed lot inside the reserve, cutting hundreds of trees and silting the creeks that feed a city's water dam. Lito filed a return, testified through a judicial affidavit, and joined the hearings. The court granted the writ and permanently enjoined Lito from bulldozing, leveling, any earth-moving, building structures, or opening and concreting roads on his claim. Lito argues that (a) the injunction violates equal protection because hundreds of other settlers with vegetable gardens in the reserve were not similarly enjoined, and (b) it deprives him of the use of his property without due process. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) There is no violation of equal protection. (b) There is no violation of due process. Both arguments fail.
- **Legal basis:** A directive in a kalikasan judgment aimed only at the impleaded respondent is not discriminatory when it is a specific remedial response to an anthropogenic activity unique to him and proven to contribute to the environmental damage. Others who were not impleaded and were not shown to have done comparable acts are not similarly situated. Unequal application violates equal protection only if there is intentional or purposeful discrimination, which is not presumed. Due process is satisfied where the directive results from bona fide proceedings in which the respondent actively participated, and it is not arbitrary or oppressive where it restrains only the acts found to have caused the damage. (Aliping v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 221823, June 21, 2022, En Banc, citing People v. Dela Piedra)
- **Application:** (a) Lito alone was impleaded because the petition imputed to him alone the road construction, tree-cutting and earth-moving that silted the creeks. The other settlers were not accused or proven to have done anything comparable, so they are not similarly situated. Nothing shows the court intended to single him out; the injunction simply addresses his own proven acts. (b) Lito filed a return, testified, and took part in the hearings, so he was heard. The injunction covers only bulldozing, leveling, earth-moving, construction and road-opening, the very acts that degraded the watershed. It is a necessary restriction to prevent further damage, not an arbitrary taking of the use of his property.
- **Conclusion:** The permanent injunction against Lito is valid and violates neither equal protection nor due process.

**Q2.** Forest officers found that dozens of persons had cut trees without permits in a forest reserve. The prosecutor filed charges under the Revised Forestry Code only against Mayor Dante, whose excavation project inside the reserve was documented by a CENRO report and his own admission before the EMB. Dante moves to dismiss, arguing that charging him alone while others equally guilty were not charged denies him the equal protection of the laws. Will the motion prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Prosecuting one person while others equally guilty are not prosecuted is not, by itself, a denial of equal protection.
- **Legal basis:** The unequal application of a law fair on its face is not a denial of equal protection unless there is an element of intentional or purposeful discrimination. A discriminatory purpose is not presumed; there must be a showing of "clear and intentional discrimination." The prosecution of one guilty person while others equally guilty are not prosecuted is not, by itself, a denial of equal protection. (People v. Dela Piedra, as applied in Aliping v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 221823, June 21, 2022, En Banc)
- **Application:** Dante shows only that others were not charged. He offers no evidence that the prosecutor charged him out of a deliberate design to discriminate against him. Like the respondent in Aliping, he was singled out because there was specific evidence against him: the CENRO report and his own admission before the EMB. Without proof of clear and intentional discrimination, his equal protection claim has no basis.
- **Conclusion:** The motion to dismiss will not prosper because Dante has not shown intentional or purposeful discrimination.

**Q3.** In a writ of kalikasan case, Rico admitted excavating within his claimed lot inside a forest reserve "to improve an existing access road." He denied cutting any trees outside his lot and claimed that the two roads running from his lot were old logging roads. A CENRO memorandum and a resident's judicial affidavit showed that both roads were newly opened, and Rico admitted in his return that both roads originate from his lot. Trees were cut along the roads, and the resulting erosion silted a public water dam. May the court order Rico to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas outside his lot?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Rico may be ordered to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas, including those outside his lot.
- **Legal basis:** A person established as responsible for the construction of new roads in a forest reserve is accountable for the illegal tree-cutting and earth-moving that resulted from it, whether within or outside his claim. Responsibility may be inferred from the confluence of circumstances, such as roads that originate from his claim, are designed to connect it to other places, are newly built, and coincide with his own earth-moving. A bare claim that the roads were old logging roads, unsupported by evidence, cannot be given credence. (Aliping v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 221823, June 21, 2022, En Banc)
- **Application:** The roads are new, as shown by the CENRO memorandum and the resident's affidavit. Rico admitted they originate from his lot and that he excavated to improve access, which shows the roads were built for his benefit and at his instance. His claim that they were old logging roads rests only on his word. As the person responsible for the roads, he answers for the tree-cutting and siltation they caused, wherever the damage occurred. Directives to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged stretch are therefore supported by the evidence.
- **Conclusion:** The court may validly order Rico to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas within and outside his claim.

> Note: The CA case is cited as "CA-G.R. SP No. 00029 W/K" in the opening and the fallo, and as "CA-G.R. No. 00029 W/K" elsewhere in the decision. Petitioner's May 21, 2014 letter refers to "Amliang Dam 5" in the source, apparently a typographical error since the reserve has Amliang Dams 1, 2A/2B and 3. The decision does not discuss the procedural rules on writs of kalikasan (A.M. No. 09-6-8-SC); the Remedial Law heading is listed for context only.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68397)

## Fernandez v. Maaliw

**ATTY. RIZA S. FERNANDEZ, PETITIONER, VS. WILLIE FERNANDO MAALIW, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 248852 | 2022-03-09 | Second Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline  
**Specific topics:** CSC decisions are appealable to the CA under Rule 43, including dismissals for lack of a prima facie case; Private complainant's personality to appeal a CSC decision (Dacoycoy line); Administrative due process: no liability without a Formal Charge under the RRACCS; Delay in resolving a case is the institution's responsibility, not that of personnel who came in later
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (X. Administrative Law > C. Powers of Administrative Agencies > 2. Quasi-judicial or Adjudicatory Power > a. Administrative Due Process)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > N. Rights to Speedy Trial and Speedy Disposition of Cases)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > iv. Appeal from Quasi-judicial Agencies to CA (Rule 43))

### Doctrine
**A decision of the Civil Service Commission dismissing an administrative complaint for lack of a prima facie case is appealable to the Court of Appeals by petition for review under Rule 43**, consistent with Section 9(3) of BP 129 and Section 73, Rule 13 of the RRACCS. The non-appealability rules invoked do not apply: Section 47, Book V, Title I of the Administrative Code of 1987 covers decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine not exceeding 30 days' salary, and Section 72 of the RRACCS covers decisions of agencies that would otherwise be appealable to the CSC.

**The private complainant may appeal the CSC decision in appropriate cases.** The RRACCS provisions on elevating decisions of the CSC and its Regional Offices use the generic term "party" (or "either by the complainant or the respondent"), not "party adversely affected," which the RRACCS uses only for motions for reconsideration in disciplinary cases and appeals in non-disciplinary cases. The *Mendez v. CSC* line limiting appeals to the party adversely affected was overruled in *CSC v. Dacoycoy*, and *PNB v. Garcia* and *Constantino-David v. Pangandaman-Gania* recognized the private complainant's standing.

**A court violates administrative due process when it finds a civil servant administratively liable although no Formal Charge was issued and she was never allowed to answer and be investigated under the RRACCS** (*Ang Tibay*; *Salva v. Valle*). At most, the court may find a prima facie case and let the disciplining authority proceed. Finally, **a violation of a complainant's right to speedy disposition of cases does not ipso facto make the personnel in charge liable**, especially those whose employment began long after the case was filed or submitted for resolution; responsibility lies with the agency as an institution, where it sufficiently explains that the delay was not attributable to the individual (applying *Navarro v. COA*).

### Facts
On September 28, 1999, respondent Willie Fernando Maaliw filed an administrative complaint for grave misconduct, oppression, dishonesty, negligence, and violation of RA 6713 and the Civil Service Law against his co-employee Danilo Longasa, a Special Investigator at the Land Bank of the Philippines. The complaint was submitted for decision on January 21, 2000. On June 16, 2014, more than 14 years later, the CSC-National Capital Region (CSC-NCR) dismissed it for being insufficient in form. The decision was signed by Director Lydia Castillo and prepared by petitioner Atty. Riza S. Fernandez.

Because of the delay, Maaliw filed a Complaint-Affidavit dated November 9, 2015 against Fernandez and Dir. Castillo for neglect of duty and violation of RA 6713 before the Office of the Ombudsman, which referred it to the CSC. In their Joint Comment, they said the complaint had been pending long before they took their posts: Dir. Castillo was reassigned to the Legal Services Division (LSD) of the CSC-NCR only on December 6, 2012 precisely to reduce aged cases, and Fernandez was employed only on February 11, 2013. They cited the volume of cases and the LSD's limited personnel, and noted that Maaliw never sought reconsideration of or appealed the 2014 dismissal.

On August 31, 2016, the CSC dismissed Maaliw's complaint. It recognized that the 14-year delay violated Maaliw's right to a speedy disposition of his case, but held that the delay could not be attributed to Fernandez and Dir. Castillo and was justified by the caseload of the LSD's eight personnel. Reconsideration was denied on December 16, 2016.

On Maaliw's Rule 43 petition, the CA (Decision of January 14, 2019) reversed the CSC and found Fernandez and Dir. Castillo guilty of simple neglect of duty, fining each an amount equal to three months' salary in lieu of suspension since both had left the CSC-NCR. It faulted Fernandez for her inaction during the one year and six months after she assumed her post and rejected lack of manpower as an excuse. Dir. Castillo did not timely move for reconsideration. Fernandez's motion was denied on July 26, 2019, and she filed a Rule 45 petition, arguing that the CSC decision was not appealable, that Maaliw had no personality to appeal, that she was found guilty without a Formal Charge, and that she acted on the complaint within days.

### Issues
1. Whether a CSC decision dismissing an administrative complaint for lack of a prima facie case may be appealed to the CA by petition for review under Rule 43.
2. Whether Maaliw, as the private complainant, had personality to appeal the CSC decision.
3. Whether the CA violated Fernandez's right to due process by finding her guilty of simple neglect of duty without a Formal Charge.
4. Whether Fernandez is liable for the 14-year delay in resolving Maaliw's complaint against Longasa.

### Ruling
At the outset, the petition raised questions of law (the proper remedy, due process, and liability on the facts already presented), and in any case fell within the exceptions allowing factual review, since it alleged a denial of due process and the CSC and CA findings conflicted.

**1. Yes.** The complaint against Fernandez was instituted directly with the CSC, so Section 72, Rule 13 of the RRACCS, which refers to non-appealable decisions of agencies that would ordinarily be appealable to the CSC, does not apply. Section 47, Book V, Title I of the Administrative Code makes non-appealable only decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine of not more than 30 days' salary; a CSC dismissal for lack of a prima facie case is not covered. Section 48(2) is silent on whether such a dismissal is appealable. **The CSC decision is appealable to the CA under Rule 43**, consistent with Section 9(3) of BP 129, Section 1 of Rule 43 (which names the CSC), and Section 73, Rule 13 of the RRACCS.

**2. Yes.** Fernandez relied on portions of *Light Rail Transit Authority v. Salvaña* repeating *Mendez v. CSC*, which limited appeals to the "party adversely affected," but those pronouncements were expressly overruled in *CSC v. Dacoycoy*. In *PNB v. Garcia*, the Court held that "the campaign against corruption, malfeasance and misfeasance in government will be undermined if the government or the private offended party is prevented from appealing erroneous administrative decisions"; in *Constantino-David*, that the CSC's right to appeal "does not preclude the private complainant in appropriate cases from similarly elevating the decision for review." The RRACCS uses "party adversely affected" only in Sections 56 and 111; Section 73 provides that "[a] party may elevate" a CSC decision to the CA, and Section 71 allows CSC Regional Office decisions to be elevated "either by the complainant or the respondent." **This was an "appropriate case" for the private complainant to appeal.**

**3. Yes, Fernandez was denied due process.** Under *Ang Tibay*, the first right in administrative proceedings is the right to a hearing. Before being held liable, Fernandez should have been issued a Formal Charge (Rule 5, RRACCS), allowed to file an Answer (Rule 6), and possibly given a formal investigation (Rule 8). The CSC's order to comment was not a Formal Charge. As in *Salva v. Valle*, without a formal charge and proper investigation, the respondent could not defend herself and the truth could not be reasonably ascertained. **"At most, what the CA could have ruled is that there is a prima facie case against Fernandez, thereby allowing the CSC to conduct further proceedings in relation to Maaliw's complaint."**

**4. No.** Nonetheless, given the undisputed facts, the Court agreed with the CSC that there was no prima facie case. **Liability for delay "does not ipso facto attach" to LSD members in charge of the complaint, "more so to members whose employment commenced much later" than its filing or submission for resolution; responsibility for the violation of the right to speedy disposition lies on the CSC as an institution.** Applying *Navarro v. COA* (factors: length of delay, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice), the CSC sufficiently explained that the delay was not attributable to Fernandez: it admitted the violation as an institution and supported the heavy caseload with data on carry-over, ripe and pending cases from 2012 to 2014. The Court also denied Maaliw's request to investigate Fernandez for violating Canons 1 and 12 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, reminding him that allegations against members of the bar must have clear factual and legal basis.

### Disposition
Petition GRANTED. The CA Decision of January 14, 2019 and Resolution of July 26, 2019 in CA-G.R. SP No. 149279 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The CSC Decision of August 31, 2016 and Resolution of December 16, 2016 in CC-D-2015-021, dismissing Maaliw's complaint, were REINSTATED.

### En Banc or Division?
Second Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Carlo filed an administrative complaint for grave misconduct directly with the Civil Service Commission against Dina, an employee of a CSC regional office. The CSC dismissed the complaint for lack of a prima facie case. Carlo filed a petition for review under Rule 43 with the Court of Appeals. Dina moved to dismiss, arguing that (1) a CSC decision dismissing a complaint for lack of a prima facie case is not appealable, and (2) only the "party adversely affected," meaning a respondent found guilty, may appeal, so Carlo, as complainant, has no personality to appeal. Rule on Dina's motion.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** The motion should be denied. The CSC decision is appealable to the CA under Rule 43, and Carlo, as private complainant, has personality to appeal.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 9(3) of BP 129, Section 1 of Rule 43 of the Rules of Court, and Section 73, Rule 13 of the RRACCS, decisions of the CSC are appealable to the CA by petition for review. Section 47, Book V, Title I of the Administrative Code makes non-appealable only decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine not exceeding 30 days' salary; a dismissal for lack of a prima facie case is not covered. The RRACCS allows "a party" to elevate CSC decisions; the Mendez line limiting appeals to the "party adversely affected" was overruled in CSC v. Dacoycoy, and the private complainant may appeal in appropriate cases (PNB v. Garcia; Constantino-David v. Pangandaman-Gania). (Fernandez v. Maaliw, G.R. No. 248852, March 9, 2022)
- **Application:** Carlo's complaint was filed directly with the CSC, and the CSC's dismissal does not fall under the non-appealability rule for minor penalties imposed by department or agency heads. Rule 43 expressly names the CSC among the agencies whose decisions go to the CA. As complainant, Carlo is a "party" under the RRACCS, and barring him from appealing would undermine the campaign against misconduct in government.
- **Conclusion:** Carlo correctly appealed to the CA under Rule 43 and has personality to do so, so Dina's motion should be denied.

**Q2.** In the same case, the Court of Appeals found that Carlo's evidence against Dina was strong. Instead of remanding the case, it reversed the CSC and directly found Dina guilty of simple neglect of duty, fining her three months' salary. The CSC had only required Dina to comment on the complaint; it never issued a Formal Charge or conducted an investigation. Is the CA's ruling valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The CA violated Dina's right to administrative due process.
- **Legal basis:** Under Ang Tibay v. Court of Industrial Relations, the first of the primary rights in administrative proceedings is the right to a hearing, which includes the right to present one's case and submit evidence. Under the RRACCS, a respondent must first be issued a Formal Charge, allowed to file an Answer, and, where warranted, given a formal investigation before being held liable. An order to comment is not a Formal Charge. Where the disciplining authority dismissed the complaint for lack of a prima facie case, the most the appellate court may do is find a prima facie case and allow the CSC to conduct further proceedings. (Fernandez v. Maaliw, G.R. No. 248852, March 9, 2022, citing Salva v. Valle)
- **Application:** Dina was never formally charged, never filed an Answer to a Formal Charge, and was never investigated. A comment on the complaint does not give her the full opportunity to defend herself that the RRACCS requires. However strong the evidence appeared, the CA could at most rule that a prima facie case exists and let the CSC proceed with the Formal Charge and investigation.
- **Conclusion:** The CA's finding of guilt is void for violating due process; it could only have found a prima facie case and allowed the CSC to proceed.

**Q3.** A complaint filed in 2008 sat unresolved in a CSC regional office until 2024, when it was dismissed. Atty. Ella, a hearing officer, joined that office only in 2023 and prepared the 2024 resolution. The CSC admitted that the 16-year delay violated the complainant's right to a speedy disposition of his case, but showed, with data on carry-over and pending cases, that the delay was caused by the office's huge backlog and few lawyers. The complainant charges Atty. Ella with neglect of duty because of the delay. Is Atty. Ella administratively liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Atty. Ella is not liable; responsibility for the delay lies with the CSC as an institution.
- **Legal basis:** Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution guarantees a speedy disposition of cases before administrative bodies. But a violation of this right does not ipso facto make the members of the office in charge of the case liable, more so those whose employment began long after the case was filed or submitted for resolution. Responsibility lies on the agency as an institution where it sufficiently explains that the delay was not attributable to the individual, considering the length of the delay, the reasons for it, the assertion of the right, and the prejudice caused (Navarro v. COA). (Fernandez v. Maaliw, G.R. No. 248852, March 9, 2022)
- **Application:** Almost all of the 16-year delay happened before Atty. Ella joined the office in 2023. The CSC admitted its institutional responsibility and explained, with data, that the delay came from its backlog and lack of personnel, not from Atty. Ella's neglect. As in Fernandez, where the lawyer who joined only in 2013 and prepared the 2014 decision was absolved of a 14-year delay, the facts show no prima facie case of neglect against Atty. Ella.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Ella cannot be held liable for neglect of duty for a delay that is attributable to the CSC as an institution.

> Note: Section numbers of the RRACCS are as cited in the Decision, which refers to both the 2011 RRACCS and the 2017 RACCS (e.g., Section 71, formerly Section 67). Dir. Castillo did not timely move for reconsideration of the CA Decision and was not a party to the petition; the fallo reinstates the CSC Decision without separately addressing her. The Decision's footnotes on the cases cited for the "party adversely affected" discussion contain cross-reference numbering that does not match the notes they point to; the case names in the text were relied on.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68323)
