## Guro v. COMELEC

**SARIPODEN ARIMAN GURO, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS AND SOMERADO MALOMALO GURO, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 234345 | 2021-06-22 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** XII. Election Law > E. Remedies and Jurisdiction > 1. Petition to Deny Due Course or Cancel Certificate of Candidacy  
**Specific topics:** Nature of a petition is determined by its grounds, not its caption; 25-day period to file a Section 78 petition; Strict application of the period for ineligibility grounds (registered voter, age, residence); When the COMELEC Rules may be relaxed
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))

### Doctrine
A petition that seeks to disqualify a candidate on the ground of **ineligibility** (here, that he is not a registered voter of the municipality) is in the nature of a **petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of candidacy under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code**, whatever its caption. It must be filed within the period in Rule 23, Section 2 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure (as amended by COMELEC Resolution No. 9523): within five days from the last day for filing COCs, but **not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC** being challenged.

Where the alleged ineligibility is misrepresentation as to being a registered voter, the period is **applied strictly**, as with age or residence. The Court relaxes it only in exceptional situations, such as the lack of Philippine citizenship (Aznar; Frivaldo), a supervening event that supplies the ground (Hayudini), or peculiar circumstances showing diligence (Caballero; Ocate). Dismissing a late petition on this ground is not grave abuse of discretion.

### Facts
Private respondent Somerado Guro filed his certificate of candidacy (COC) for Municipal Mayor of Lumbaca-Unayan, Lanao del Sur on October 16, 2015 for the May 2016 elections. He stated under oath that he was a registered voter of Barangay Poblacion Dilausan and was eligible for the office.

Petitioner Saripoden Guro, the incumbent mayor running for re-election, filed a "Petition for Disqualification" on April 29, 2016. He alleged that, based on the posted certified voters' list, private respondent was not a registered voter of the municipality and was therefore not qualified to run.

Private respondent answered that the petition was moot: the COMELEC had approved the recommendation of its Election and Barangay Affairs Department to include his name in the supplemental list of voters. He also said he voted on election day and had won and been proclaimed mayor.

The COMELEC First Division dismissed the petition for being filed beyond the 25-day period for a petition under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code. The COMELEC En Banc denied reconsideration, found the petition filed "way beyond" the period, and did not reach the other issues. Petitioner went to the Supreme Court on certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65, claiming the COMELEC should have decided on the merits instead of on "mere technical grounds."

### Issues
1. Whether the petition, captioned as a petition for disqualification but grounded on the candidate's ineligibility, is a Section 78 petition to deny due course to or cancel a COC.
2. Whether the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion in dismissing the petition for having been filed beyond the reglementary period instead of relaxing its rules and ruling on the merits.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, it is a Section 78 petition.** Because the petition was anchored on private respondent's alleged ineligibility, the COMELEC correctly treated it as a petition to deny due course to or cancel his COC under Section 78 of the OEC, governed by Rule 23 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure as amended by Resolution No. 9523. Rule 23, Section 2 requires filing within five days from the last day for filing COCs, but not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC challenged. Private respondent filed his COC on October 16, 2015; the petition came on April 29, 2016, after "a whopping one hundred ninety-six (196) days."

**2. No grave abuse of discretion.** The Court reviewed the cases where it did not insist on the period. In *Aznar* it ruled on the merits despite a late petition because the issue was citizenship. In *Loong* it explained that a misrepresentation as to age is not on the same level as lack of citizenship, and that where disqualification rests on age, residence, or other grounds of ineligibility, "the reglementary period provided by law should be applied strictly." The Court saw no reason to depart from this rule for an alleged misrepresentation as to being a registered voter.

The cases that relaxed the rules were distinguishable: *Hayudini* (a supervening final RTC ruling deleting the candidate from the voters' list armed the petitioner with the ground), *Caballero* (a residency issue imbued with public interest plus peculiar circumstances excusing defective service), and *Ocate* (a one-day delay caused by a typhoon despite due diligence). **No analogous circumstance existed here, so the COMELEC committed no grave abuse of discretion in dismissing the petition on technical grounds.**

### Disposition
The petition was DISMISSED. The COMELEC En Banc Resolution dated September 25, 2017 in SPA No. 16-086 (DC), affirming the COMELEC First Division's Order dated October 19, 2016, was AFFIRMED.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** On October 5, 2024, Pedro filed his certificate of candidacy for municipal mayor, stating under oath that he is a registered voter of the municipality. Five months later, rival candidate Juan filed with the COMELEC a pleading captioned "Petition for Disqualification," alleging only that Pedro is not a registered voter of the municipality and is therefore ineligible. The COMELEC dismissed the petition as filed out of time. Juan argues that his petition is a disqualification case, not a petition to cancel a certificate of candidacy, so the 25-day period does not apply. Is Juan correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No, Juan is not correct. His petition is a Section 78 petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of candidacy, and it was filed out of time.
- **Legal basis:** The nature of a petition is determined by its grounds, not its caption. A petition anchored on a candidate's ineligibility is a petition to deny due course to or cancel a COC under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code. Under Rule 23, Section 2 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure, as amended by COMELEC Resolution No. 9523, it must be filed within five days from the last day for filing COCs, but not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC challenged. Where the ground is misrepresentation as to being a registered voter, the period is applied strictly. (Guro v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 234345, June 22, 2021)
- **Application:** Juan's only ground is that Pedro is not a registered voter, which goes into Pedro's eligibility and the truth of a material representation in his COC. The caption "Petition for Disqualification" does not change its nature; it is a Section 78 petition. It was filed about five months after Pedro filed his COC, far beyond the 25-day limit. Nothing shows an exceptional circumstance, such as a supervening event, that would justify relaxing the rule.
- **Conclusion:** The COMELEC correctly dismissed Juan's petition for having been filed beyond the reglementary period.

**Q2.** Rosa filed her certificate of candidacy for vice mayor on October 3, 2024, declaring that she is a registered voter of the municipality. Teresa filed a timely petition to deny due course to Rosa's COC, but the COMELEC dismissed it because, on that same day, the MTC granted Rosa's petition for inclusion in the list of voters. On appeal, the RTC reversed the MTC, and the order deleting Rosa from the voters' list became final in March 2025. Teresa immediately filed a second petition to deny due course to Rosa's COC, more than 150 days after Rosa filed her COC. Rosa moves to dismiss, citing the 25-day period. May the COMELEC give due course to Teresa's second petition?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. The COMELEC may relax its rules because a supervening event furnished the ground for the second petition.
- **Legal basis:** The 25-day period for a Section 78 petition under Rule 23, Section 2 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure is generally applied strictly when the ground is ineligibility such as not being a registered voter. However, the Court has allowed liberal construction where a supervening event affects the substance of the case, as in Hayudini v. COMELEC, where a final RTC ruling deleting the candidate from the voters' list armed the petitioner with the ground for a petition filed 172 days after the COC. In Guro v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 234345, June 22, 2021), the Court reaffirmed strict application but recognized Hayudini as a valid exception because of the supervening event.
- **Application:** Unlike in Guro, where the petitioner simply filed late with no special circumstance, Teresa was diligent: she filed a timely first petition, which was dismissed only because of the MTC inclusion order. The RTC's later reversal, which became final, is a supervening event. It gave Teresa a ground she did not have before, and enforcing the first dismissal would be inequitable. These facts mirror Hayudini.
- **Conclusion:** The COMELEC may give due course to Teresa's second petition despite the lapse of the 25-day period.

**Q3.** The COMELEC En Banc affirmed its First Division's dismissal of Andres's petition to deny due course to a mayoral candidate's COC because the petition was filed 200 days after the COC. Andres wants to bring the case to the Supreme Court, arguing that the COMELEC should have decided the case on the merits rather than on a technicality. (a) What remedy should Andres file, and on what ground? (b) Will the remedy prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) A petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, on the ground of grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. (b) No, it will not prosper.
- **Legal basis:** Judgments, final orders, and resolutions of the COMELEC En Banc are reviewable by the Supreme Court only through certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65, which requires a showing of grave abuse of discretion. In Guro v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 234345, June 22, 2021), the Court held that the COMELEC did not gravely abuse its discretion in dismissing, on technical grounds, a Section 78 petition filed 196 days after the COC, because the reglementary period is applied strictly for ineligibility grounds and no circumstance justified relaxing it.
- **Application:** Andres must file a Rule 64 petition, alleging grave abuse of discretion by the COMELEC En Banc. But applying a clear reglementary period to a petition filed 200 days late is an exercise of the COMELEC's jurisdiction according to its rules, not a capricious or whimsical act. Absent a supervening event, citizenship issue, or other exceptional circumstance, calling the dismissal a "technicality" does not make it grave abuse of discretion.
- **Conclusion:** Andres should file a Rule 64 certiorari petition, but it will be dismissed because the COMELEC committed no grave abuse of discretion.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67583)

## SSS v. COA

**SOCIAL SECURITY SYSTEM (SSS), PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT (COA), RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 217075 | 2021-06-22 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Political and Public International Law  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction  
**Specific topics:** Period to file a Rule 64 petition against a COA decision; Validity of the COA Notice denying a motion for reconsideration (COA Resolution No. 2013-018); CNA incentives limited to rank-and-file members of the negotiating unit; Liability of approving and certifying officers and recipients to return disallowed amounts (Madera rules)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64))
  
**Also relevant to:** Labor Law and Social Legislation (V. Labor Relations > A. Right to Self-organization > 1. Coverage > a. Government Employees)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (X. Quasi-Contracts > B. Kinds > 2. Solutio Indebiti)

### Doctrine
**A Rule 64 petition against a COA decision must be filed within 30 days from notice. A motion for reconsideration only interrupts the period; if it is denied, the petitioner has only the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of the denial** (Rule 64, Section 3). A petition filed beyond that period leaves the COA decision final and executory. The Notice issued by the Commission Secretary in the form prescribed by COA Resolution No. 2013-018 (amending Section 12, Rule X of the 2009 Revised Rules of Procedure of the COA) validly communicates the Commission Proper's denial of the motion, and the remaining period runs from its receipt, not from a later COA letter answering a request for the minutes.

Reiterated: **only rank-and-file employees who are members of the collective negotiating unit are entitled to CNA incentives; high-level managerial and confidential employees (including coterminous and highly confidential employees, lawyers and executives) are not**, because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit. Their contribution to agency efficiency is immaterial (PD 1597, Section 5; EO 180, Section 3; AO 103, s. 2004, Section 3(b); PSLMC Resolution No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003; AO 135, Section 2; DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, Section 4.2). A predetermined fixed CNA incentive also violates Section 5.6 of DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1.

Applying *Madera v. COA* and *SSS v. COA* (2020): **the presumption of good faith of approving and certifying officers fails when an explicit law, rule or regulation has been violated**, so they must return the disallowed amounts; **the recipient employees must return what they received on the ground of solutio indebiti.**

### Facts
On July 6, 2005, the Social Security Commission issued Resolution No. 259, s. 2005, granting (1) a P20,000.00 CNA incentive to each SSS employee covered by the collective negotiating unit as of December 31, 2004 with at least three months of prior service, and (2) a "counterpart" benefit of the same amount to SSS personnel not covered by the negotiating unit, including confidential, coterminous and contractual employees, lawyers and executives.

On post-audit, the SSS Supervising Auditor issued Notice of Disallowance No. SSS-2007-001 (2005) dated January 9, 2007, disallowing the counterpart benefit, totaling P6,180,000.00, for violating Section 3(b) of AO 103 (2004) and Section 3 of EO 180 (1987). The COA Legal Services Sector denied the SSS appeal in LSS Decision No. 2010-025 dated August 5, 2010. The COA Commission Proper En Banc denied the SSS petition for review in Decision No. 2014-069 dated May 8, 2014, which SSS received on May 15, 2014.

SSS moved for reconsideration on June 11, 2014. The Commission Proper denied it in a Resolution dated November 20, 2014, communicated through a Notice from the Commission Secretary that SSS received on February 4, 2015. On February 13, 2015, SSS asked for a certified copy of the resolution and of the minutes showing how its arguments were resolved. COA replied by letter dated March 12, 2015 that the resolution was copied verbatim in the Notice, whose format COA Resolution No. 2013-018 allows. SSS filed its Rule 64 petition on March 20, 2015, also claiming that the refusal to disclose the resolution and minutes violated due process.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition was timely filed.
2. Whether the COA committed grave abuse of discretion in denying the SSS motion for reconsideration through the Notice.
3. Whether the COA committed grave abuse of discretion in upholding the disallowance of CNA incentives granted to non-members of the negotiating unit.
4. Whether the approving and certifying officers and the recipient employees must return the disallowed amounts.

### Ruling
**1. No. The petition was filed out of time, and the COA Decision had become final and executory.** Under Rule 64, Section 3, the petition must be filed within 30 days from notice; a motion for reconsideration interrupts the period, and upon denial the petitioner may file within the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of denial. SSS received the COA Decision on May 15, 2014, so its 30-day period would have ended on June 14, 2014. Its motion for reconsideration on June 11, 2014 left three days, extended to five by the Rule. Having received the Notice of denial on February 4, 2015, SSS had until February 9, 2015, but it filed on March 20, 2015, "39 days after the last day of filing."

**2. No grave abuse. The Notice validly communicated the denial and started the remaining period.** COA Resolution No. 2013-018 directs the Commission Secretary, when the Commission Proper denies a motion for reconsideration for being filed late or for failing to raise any new matter or sufficient ground, to issue a Notice informing the parties of the resolution, in the form of its Annex "A." The Notice SSS received followed that very format, "hence, there is no doubt as to its validity." SSS's rejection of the officially prescribed Notice while adopting COA's March 12, 2015 letter as its reckoning point showed its awareness that the petition was late. Even counting from March 12, 2015, SSS had only until March 17, 2015, so the March 20, 2015 filing was still late.

**3. Assuming the petition was timely, the COA did not gravely abuse its discretion in upholding the disallowance.** Judicial review of COA decisions is limited to errors of jurisdiction or grave abuse of discretion (*Madera v. COA*), and SSS failed to show that the COA ruling was not based on law and evidence. The COA applied PD 1597, Section 5 (allowances and fringe benefits require presidential approval); EO 180, Section 3 (high-level policy-making, managerial or highly confidential employees cannot join the rank-and-file organization); AO 103, Section 3(b) (new benefits suspended except CNA incentives given in strict compliance with PSLMC Resolutions No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003, which grant CNA benefits only to rank-and-file employees); AO 135, Section 2; and DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, Section 4.2 (rank-and-file employees are those who are not managerial, coterminous or highly confidential). **Taken together, high-level managerial and confidential employees are not entitled to CNA benefits because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit; "[i]t is of no moment" that they also contributed to the agency's efficiency.** The fixed P20,000.00 counterpart incentive also violated Section 5.6 of DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, which bars predetermining the incentive amount in the CNA because it must depend on the cost-cutting measures under the CNA.

**4. Yes. The approving and certifying officers and the recipient employees are all liable to return the disallowed amounts.** The Court reviewed the statutory bases listed in *SSS v. COA* (2020) (Sections 38, 39 and 43 of the 1987 Administrative Code; Section 52, Chapter 9, Title I-B, Book V of the Administrative Code; Sections 102 and 103 of the Government Auditing Code; Section 49 of PD 1177; and Section 19 of the Manual on Certificate of Settlement and Balances) and the *Madera* rules on return. **The presumption of good faith of the approving and certifying officers "fails when an explicit law, rule, or regulation has been violated"**; the six issuances were already in force when the officers granted the benefits, so good faith could not be appreciated. **The recipients must return the payments on the ground of solutio indebiti**, as they were clearly disqualified from the incentives and the government would otherwise be prejudiced.

### Disposition
The petition was DISMISSED. COA Decision No. 2014-069 dated May 8, 2014 and the Resolution dated November 20, 2014 were AFFIRMED, sustaining Notice of Disallowance No. SSS-2007-001 (2005) on the P6,180,000.00 counterpart CNA benefits. The fallo does not separately order the return; the liability of the approving and certifying officers and of the recipients to return the amounts is stated in the body of the decision.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** The COA Commission Proper affirmed a notice of disallowance against the Bayanihan Development Authority (BDA), a GOCC. On the 28th day after receiving the COA decision, BDA filed a motion for reconsideration. The Commission Secretary later sent BDA a one-page Notice, in the form prescribed by the COA rules, stating that the Commission Proper had resolved to deny the motion for failure to raise any new matter. BDA wrote COA asking for the full resolution and the minutes of the meeting, and COA replied by letter that the resolution is copied verbatim in the Notice. BDA filed a Rule 64 petition with the Supreme Court 30 days after receiving the Notice, and 25 days after receiving COA's reply letter. BDA argues that its period began to run only from receipt of the reply letter. (a) Was the petition filed on time? (b) Is BDA's reckoning point correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No, the petition was filed out of time. (b) No, the remaining period ran from receipt of the Notice of denial, not from COA's later reply letter.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 64, Section 3 of the Rules of Court, a petition for certiorari against a COA judgment must be filed within 30 days from notice; a motion for reconsideration, if allowed, interrupts the period, and if it is denied the aggrieved party may file within the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of denial. Under COA Resolution No. 2013-018, amending Section 12, Rule X of the 2009 Revised Rules of Procedure of the COA, when the Commission Proper denies a motion for reconsideration for failure to raise any new matter or sufficient ground, the Commission Secretary issues a Notice in a prescribed form informing the parties of the resolution. In SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 217075, June 22, 2021), the Court held that such a Notice is valid and that the remaining period runs from its receipt; the petitioner cannot reckon the period from a later COA letter answering its request for the minutes.
- **Application:** BDA used 28 of its 30 days before moving for reconsideration, leaving two days, which Rule 64 raises to five. It therefore had five days from receipt of the Notice of denial to file. Filing 30 days after receiving the Notice was far too late. The Notice followed the format prescribed by the COA rules, so it validly informed BDA of the denial. Even if the reply letter were the reckoning point, BDA would still have had only five days from its receipt, and it filed 25 days later.
- **Conclusion:** The petition was filed late under either reckoning, so the COA decision had become final and executory and the petition should be dismissed.

**Q2.** Citing their contribution to the agency's efficiency, the governing board of a GOCC granted a fixed P25,000.00 "counterpart CNA incentive" to its department managers, lawyers and confidential staff, who are not members of the collective negotiating unit. The COA disallowed the payment, and the disallowance has become final. The board members who approved the grant and the officers who certified the vouchers claim good faith because they relied on the board resolution. The managers and lawyers who received the incentive argue that they merely received it and had no part in approving it. Who must return the disallowed amounts?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both the approving and certifying officers and the recipient managers, lawyers and confidential staff must return the disallowed amounts.
- **Legal basis:** Only rank-and-file employees who are members of the collective negotiating unit are entitled to CNA incentives; high-level managerial and confidential employees are excluded under PD 1597, Section 5; EO 180, Section 3; AO 103, s. 2004, Section 3(b); PSLMC Resolution No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003; AO 135; and DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, which also prohibits predetermining the incentive amount (Section 5.6). Under the rules in Madera v. COA, approving and certifying officers who acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence are liable to return, and recipients are liable for what they received unless an exception applies. In SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 217075, June 22, 2021), the Court held that the presumption of good faith of approving and certifying officers fails when an explicit law, rule or regulation has been violated, and that recipient employees must return disallowed CNA incentives on the ground of solutio indebiti.
- **Application:** The incentive went to employees outside the negotiating unit, in violation of the issuances above, all of which were already in force, and it was a predetermined fixed amount. The officers' reliance on their own board resolution cannot sustain good faith because the grant violated explicit laws and regulations, and the recipients' contribution to efficiency is immaterial. The recipients, though passive, were clearly not entitled to the incentive and received it by mistake, so they must return it under solutio indebiti; otherwise the government would be prejudiced.
- **Conclusion:** The approving and certifying officers and all the recipients are liable to return the disallowed counterpart CNA incentives.

**Q3.** Atty. Reyes is a department manager of a government financial institution whose duties are managerial and highly confidential. He applied for membership in the accredited rank-and-file employees' organization so that he could share in the CNA incentive under its collective negotiation agreement. (a) May he join the organization? (b) If the institution instead pays him an amount equal to the CNA incentive, is the payment valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. As a high-level employee, he is not eligible to join the organization of rank-and-file employees. (b) No. The payment is invalid and may be disallowed.
- **Legal basis:** Section 3 of EO 180 provides that high-level employees whose functions are normally considered policy-making or managerial or whose duties are of a highly confidential nature shall not be eligible to join the organization of rank-and-file government employees. Under AO 103, s. 2004, Section 3(b); PSLMC Resolution No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003; AO 135; and DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, Section 4.2, CNA incentives may be granted only to rank-and-file employees, defined as those who are not managerial, coterminous or highly confidential. In SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 217075, June 22, 2021), the Court held that high-level managerial and confidential employees are not entitled to CNA benefits because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit, and upheld the disallowance of "counterpart" CNA benefits paid to them.
- **Application:** Atty. Reyes performs managerial and highly confidential functions, so EO 180 bars him from the rank-and-file organization. Because CNA benefits arise from membership in the negotiating unit, he cannot share in the CNA incentive, and paying him an equivalent "counterpart" amount would do indirectly what the law forbids. As in SSS v. COA, the COA may disallow the payment, and he would have to return what he received.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Reyes may neither join the rank-and-file organization nor validly receive the CNA incentive or its equivalent.

> Note: The petition was dismissed mainly for late filing; the rulings on the merits and on the liability to return were made on the assumption that the petition had been timely filed. The decision relies on Madera v. COA (G.R. No. 244128, September 8, 2020) and SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 244336, October 6, 2020). Leonen, J. was on official leave.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67472)

# Commercial and Taxation Laws

## Lopez v. Lopez

**LILY C. LOPEZ, PETITIONER, VS. LOLITO S. LOPEZ, MA. RACHEL NICOLETTE LOPEZ, BARBARA VILLAS, BENEDICTO VILLAFUERTE, MA. LUISA PARAS, RUEL VILLACORTA, TERESITA C. FERNANDO, AND i SPECIALIST DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION, RESPONDENTS. LOLITO S. LOPEZ, MARIO S. LOPEZ, ANDRESITO S. LOPEZ, BARBARA O. VILLAS, BENEDICTO L. VILLAFUERTE, MA. LUISA I. PARAS, RUEL S. VILLACORTA, TERESITA C. FERNANDO, LC LOPEZ RESOURCES, INC., AND CONQUEROR INTERNATIONAL, INC., RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. Nos. 254957-58 | 2022-06-15 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Commercial and Taxation Laws  
**Syllabus topic:** I. Business Organizations > A. Corporations (RA 11232) > 6. Directors and Trustees > a. Repository of Corporate Powers  
**Specific topics:** Sale of unissued shares requires a board resolution; invalidly acquired shares cannot be voted; Preemptive right of stockholders; Proof of stockholder status: stock and transfer book vs. GIS and other evidence; estoppel; Quorum in a special stockholders' meeting; Presumption of regularity of a court certification of receipt; late petition for review in an intra-corporate case
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > c. Perfection of Appeal)

### Doctrine
**Corporate powers are exercised, all business conducted, and all corporate property controlled by the board of directors** (Section 23, Corporation Code). A corporate president, even one who is a majority stockholder, cannot validly buy the corporation's unissued shares without a board resolution authorizing the sale. **The sale is invalid, and the shares cannot be voted** in electing directors. A sale of unissued shares made without first offering them to the other stockholders also violates their **preemptive right** (Section 39, Corporation Code). A stockholders' meeting where the shares represented are less than one-half plus one of the outstanding shares lacks a quorum and is void, together with the election held at it.

The stock and transfer book (STB) generally controls who are stockholders (Lao v. Lao; F & S Velasco v. Madrid). That rule does not apply squarely where stockholder status is proved by evidence other than the General Information Sheet (GIS), such as admissions of the adverse party and notices of meeting sent to the person as a stockholder. A party who presented a person as a stockholder in his dealings with banks is **estopped** from denying that status. Where the STB entries are of doubtful veracity, the latest GIS may be used to determine the outstanding shares for quorum purposes.

On procedure, a branch clerk of court's certification that counsel, through a messenger, received the decision on a stated date enjoys the **presumption of regularity**, which only clear and convincing evidence can overcome; the burden is on the party disputing receipt. A petition for review filed beyond the 15-day period under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC must be dismissed, because perfecting an appeal within the period is jurisdictional. (Rules reiterated and applied.)

### Facts
Spouses Lily and Lolito Lopez owned the majority shares of i Specialist Development Corporation (i Specialist), which they had run since 2011 with Lolito as president. They were also stockholders of the family corporations LC Lopez Resources, Inc. (LC Lopez) and Conqueror International, Inc. (Conqueror). Without any board resolution authorizing the sale, Lolito bought unissued shares of these corporations: 33,495 unissued shares of i Specialist, whose 2013 GIS showed only 12,500 common shares (5,592 each for the spouses), and, on November 26, 2018, 252,125 unissued shares of LC Lopez and 97,050 of Conqueror. He used these shares to elect new boards.

*Quezon City case.* On February 14, 2019, Lolito, as president, held a special stockholders' meeting of i Specialist at a restaurant in Quezon City, where a new board was elected. Lily and her daughter Christina sued in the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 93, a special commercial court. On July 29, 2019, the RTC declared the meeting and election void ab initio. Lolito had admitted that no board resolution authorized his purchase, so the shares could not be voted, and they were numerous enough to affect the election.

*Marikina case.* At the February 11, 2019 special stockholders' meeting of LC Lopez and Conqueror, the proxies of the couple's children Christina and John Rusty were turned away on the ground that the children were not stockholders. Lily walked out after her lawyer was not allowed to stay, and a new board was elected. The children were listed as stockholders in the GIS but not in the STB. The STB entries, and the stock certificates of Lolito and his co-defendants, had been made only days before the meeting by the accounting head, Edna Victoria, not by the corporate secretary, and the corporate secretary did not know what documents supported them. Lolito and two co-defendants confirmed that the children were stockholders, Lolito had sent them notices of the meeting, and he had recognized them as directors in bank transactions. Under the 2017 GIS, LC Lopez had 162,500 outstanding shares and Conqueror 45,000; only Lolito's 61,750 and 17,100 shares, respectively, were represented. On September 13, 2019, the RTC of Marikina, Branch 273 declared the meeting and the election void. It found the children to be stockholders, held that there was no quorum, nullified Lolito's share purchases (no board resolution and violation of Lily's preemptive right), and held Lolito estopped.

On petitions for review, the CA, in a consolidated Decision dated February 26, 2020, reversed both RTCs and declared the meetings valid. It held the Quezon City petition timely. The RTC-QC branch clerk had certified that respondents' counsel, through a certain Richard Belasco, personally received the decision on August 6, 2019, which would make the August 28, 2019 filing late under the 15-day period of A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC. The CA discounted the certification because there was no proof that Belasco was authorized to receive the decision. It also ruled that Christina was not a stockholder because she was not in the STB, and that Lolito's purchase was merely an ultra vires act, justified by the need for capital and capable of ratification by the board.

### Issues
1. Whether respondents' petition for review in CA-G.R. SP No. 162134 (the Quezon City case) was timely filed.
2. Whether Christina is a stockholder of the subject corporations.
3. Whether Lolito's purchase of the unissued shares was valid, and whether the special stockholders' meetings were valid.

### Ruling
**1. No, it was filed late.** The certification that counsel, through Belasco, personally received the decision on August 6, 2019 was issued by an officer of the court and carries the presumption of regularity. Before that date, the parties had been told in open court that the decision would be promulgated on or about July 30, 2019, and the judge had encouraged them to get their copies personally. With the presumption in petitioner's favor, the burden shifted to respondents to prove, for example, that Belasco was not an employee of their law firm or was not authorized to receive the decision. They did not; their counsel only asked the court whether the firm had sent any letter authorizing him. **The presumption can be overthrown only by clear and convincing evidence** (Yap v. Lagtapon), and the CA erred in requiring petitioner to prove Belasco's authority. Because perfecting an appeal within the reglementary period is jurisdictional (Building Care Corp. v. Macaraeg), the Court held that respondents' petition in CA-G.R. SP No. 162134 must be dismissed on this procedural ground alone, without ruling on its merits, leaving the RTC-QC decision standing.

**2. Yes, Christina is a stockholder.** Lao does not squarely apply because Christina proved her status by evidence other than the GIS. Lolito, Villafuerte and Fernando all confirmed in their testimonies that Christina and John Rusty were stockholders, and Lolito even sent the two notices of the special meeting. **Having presented Christina as a stockholder in his dealings with banks, Lolito is estopped from denying that status** when doing so would serve his interests.

**3. No, the purchase was invalid, and the meetings were void.** Under Section 23 of the Corporation Code, corporate powers are exercised by the board. **Without a board resolution authorizing the sale of the unissued shares, Lolito could not validly buy them, and he could not legally use them to vote for a new set of directors.** The sale also violated petitioner's preemptive right under Section 39. In addition, the special stockholders' meeting was void for lack of quorum. Because the STB entries were of doubtful veracity (made by Edna, who was not the corporate secretary, a few days before the meeting, apparently without supporting documents), the Court used the latest GIS. Only Lolito's 61,750 of LC Lopez's 162,500 outstanding shares, and only his shares out of Conqueror's 45,000, were represented, because the other stockholders and their proxies were prevented from attending. His shares alone could not make up "the one-half plus one of the total outstanding shares required to have a quorum." **The special stockholders' meeting and the sale and voting of the unissued shares were void and produced no legal effect.**

### Disposition
The petition was GRANTED. The CA Decision in CA-G.R. SP Nos. 162134 and 162787 was SET ASIDE. The Decisions of the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 93 (voiding the February 14, 2019 special stockholders' meeting and election of i Specialist) and of the RTC of Marikina City, Branch 273 (voiding the February 11, 2019 special stockholders' meeting of LC Lopez and Conqueror and the election held there) were REINSTATED in toto.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Ramon is the president of Alpha Corp. and owns 45% of its outstanding shares; his estranged wife Sonia owns another 45%. Without any board resolution, Ramon paid for 30,000 of Alpha's unissued shares and had himself recorded as their owner. He never offered any of these shares to Sonia or the other stockholders, and the articles of incorporation do not deny preemptive rights. At a special stockholders' meeting, Ramon voted his original and newly acquired shares to elect a new board that excluded Sonia. Sonia sued to nullify the election. Ramon argues that he acted to infuse urgently needed capital and that the purchase was at most an ultra vires act that the board may ratify. Is the election valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Ramon's purchase of the unissued shares is invalid, so the shares could not be voted, and the election they carried is void.
- **Legal basis:** Corporate powers are exercised, all business conducted, and all corporate property controlled by the board of directors (Section 23, Corporation Code; now Section 22, Revised Corporation Code). Without a board resolution authorizing the sale of unissued shares, a corporate officer cannot validly purchase them, and shares so acquired cannot be voted in electing directors. A sale made without first offering the shares to the other stockholders also violates their preemptive right (Section 39, Corporation Code; now Section 38, Revised Corporation Code). (Lopez v. Lopez, G.R. Nos. 254957-58, June 15, 2022)
- **Application:** The sale of unissued shares is a corporate act that only Alpha's board can authorize. Ramon, though president and a major stockholder, acted without any board resolution, so the sale is invalid. His reasons, the need for capital and the possibility of ratification, do not supply the missing board authority; the Court rejected the same arguments in Lopez. The sale also bypassed Sonia's preemptive right, because the shares were not first offered to existing stockholders in proportion to their holdings. Since the 30,000 shares were invalidly acquired, they could not be voted, and an election decided by them is void.
- **Conclusion:** The election is void because it was carried by unissued shares sold without board authority and in violation of Sonia's preemptive right.

**Q2.** Beta Corp. is a family corporation. Its latest General Information Sheet lists the father (40%), the mother (40%) and their two children (10% each) as stockholders. The stock and transfer book shows only the father; its entries were written by the company accountant, not the corporate secretary, a week before a special stockholders' meeting, with no supporting documents. The father sent the children notices of the meeting as stockholders and had earlier presented them to banks as stockholders and directors. At the meeting, the children's proxies were turned away, the mother walked out, and only the father's shares were represented when a new board was elected. (a) May the father deny that the children are stockholders because they are not in the stock and transfer book? (b) Was there a quorum?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The children proved their status by evidence other than the GIS, and the father is estopped from denying it. (b) No. Only 40% of the outstanding shares was represented, so the meeting and the election are void.
- **Legal basis:** The rule that the stock and transfer book, not the GIS, controls stockholder status (Lao v. Lao) does not apply squarely where status is proved by other evidence, such as the adverse party's admissions and notices of meeting sent to the person as a stockholder. One who held out a person as a stockholder in bank transactions is estopped from denying that status when it would prejudice his interests. Where the STB entries are of doubtful veracity, the latest GIS may be used to determine whether a quorum, one-half plus one of the outstanding shares, was present. (Lopez v. Lopez, G.R. Nos. 254957-58, June 15, 2022)
- **Application:** The children's status rests not only on the GIS but on the father's own notices to them as stockholders and his representation to banks that they were stockholders and directors. He cannot now disown that status to suit his interest. The STB is unreliable because its entries were made by someone other than the corporate secretary, days before the meeting, without supporting documents. Using the GIS, the father's 40% falls short of the majority of outstanding shares needed for a quorum.
- **Conclusion:** The children are stockholders, and the special meeting and the election held at it are void for lack of quorum.

**Q3.** In an intra-corporate election contest, the RTC, acting as a special commercial court, ruled against the newly elected directors of XYZ Corp. The branch clerk of court certified that the directors' counsel, through a messenger named Paolo, personally received a copy of the decision on March 3, 2025. The directors filed a petition for review with the Court of Appeals on March 25, 2025. They argue that the certification deserves no weight because the winning party never proved that Paolo worked for their law firm or was authorized to receive the decision. Their only evidence is that their counsel asked the court whether any letter from the firm had authorized Paolo, and was told there was none. Should the Court of Appeals give due course to the petition?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The petition was filed beyond the 15-day period and must be dismissed.
- **Legal basis:** A certification by an officer of the court that counsel received a copy of a decision carries the presumption of regularity in the performance of official duties, which only clear and convincing evidence can overthrow. The burden is on the party disputing receipt, not on the party relying on the certification. Under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC, a decision in an intra-corporate controversy is reviewed by petition for review filed within 15 days, and perfecting an appeal within the reglementary period is jurisdictional; failure to do so makes the judgment final and executory. (Lopez v. Lopez, G.R. Nos. 254957-58, June 15, 2022, citing Yap v. Lagtapon and Building Care Corp. v. Macaraeg)
- **Application:** The clerk's certification is presumed regular, so it was the directors, not the winning party, who had to prove that Paolo was not their employee or was not authorized. The absence of an authorization letter on file falls far short of clear and convincing evidence. Counted from March 3, 2025, the 15-day period ended on March 18, 2025, so the March 25 filing was late. The RTC decision became final and executory.
- **Conclusion:** The Court of Appeals should dismiss the petition for review for having been filed out of time.

> Note: The decision cites Sections 23 and 39 of the Corporation Code (B.P. Blg. 68), quoting the old Section 23. Footnote 73 quotes the preemptive-right provision under the heading "Section 38." The Revised Corporation Code (R.A. No. 11232) counterparts are Section 22 (board of directors) and Section 38 (preemptive right); the Court did not discuss the RCC. The source text has minor inconsistencies. The facts say respondents' counsel checked with the RTC on "02 October 2022," a date after the decision itself. The quorum discussion gives Lolito's Conqueror shares as "17,000," while the GIS figures quoted earlier give 17,100. The Court's ruling speaks only of Christina's status, although the Marikina RTC also found John Rusty to be a stockholder.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68395)

# Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds

## Soto v. Reyes-Soto

**JUANITO B. SOTO, PETITIONER, VS. CASSANDRA REYES-SOTO AND THE REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 249759 | 2026-04-22 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Family Relations > A. Marriage (Const., Art. II, Sec. 12, and Art. XV) > 4. Void and Voidable Marriages  
**Specific topics:** Psychological incapacity under Article 36 as refined by Tan-Andal, Georfo and Estella; Weight of expert testimony; psychological tests administered by a third person; No rule requiring the expert to interview both spouses; Rule 45: sufficiency and credibility of evidence of psychological incapacity is a question of fact; Article 147 co-ownership; partition not a prerequisite to a declaration of nullity
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 3. Testimonial Evidence > g. Opinion Rule)

### Doctrine
Whether the evidence proves psychological incapacity, including the credibility and weight of expert testimony, is a **question of fact** that is not proper in a Rule 45 petition; the RTC's findings, affirmed by the CA, bind the Supreme Court absent a recognized exception. Ruling on the merits anyway, the Court **reiterated Tan-Andal v. Andal, Georfo v. Republic and Estella v. Perez**: psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code is a legal, not a medical, concept and must be proved by **clear and convincing evidence**. Three requisites must concur: (1) **juridical antecedence**, meaning it existed when the marriage was celebrated even if it showed only later; (2) **incurability in the legal sense**, meaning a condition so enduring and persistent with respect to the specific spouse that the marriage is beyond repair; and (3) **gravity**, meaning a genuinely psychic cause, not mere refusal, neglect, difficulty or ill will. Expert opinion is not required. Ordinary witnesses and the offended spouse may testify to the dysfunctional acts.

**Clarified on expert evidence:** when offered, expert testimony is an aid, not a controlling determinant. It must link observed behavior and life history to antecedence, incurability and gravity, and its weight depends on the expert's qualifications, sound methodology, and whether it rests on hearsay (Halog v. Halog). **No rule requires the expert to personally interview both spouses.** Doing so is ideal but not indispensable. A psychiatrist's testimony does not lose probative value because another person administered the psychological tests, if she interpreted and integrated the results and they only corroborated her own interview-based findings. **"Silent dysfunction"** (emotional distance, withdrawal and resignation) may amount to psychological incapacity even without violence or infidelity, and both spouses may be declared incapacitated.

Property relations in a void marriage are governed by Article 147 or 148 of the Family Code. Under Article 147 the properties are co-owned and may be partitioned by agreement or by judicial proceedings (Civil Code, Art. 496), so **partition is only incidental to the declaration of nullity and is not a prerequisite for it** (Diño v. Diño, reiterated).

### Facts
Juanito Soto and Cassandra Reyes-Soto met in 1979 as students at the University of the Philippines. They became a couple in May 1981 while both worked at BPI, and they married on September 24, 1983 after Reyes-Soto became pregnant. Even before the wedding she sensed that Soto was emotionally unexpressive and showed little concern for her pregnancy, but she kept her doubts to herself.

The couple lived first with her parents in Antipolo and then with his parents in Pasig City. Soto deferred to his mother, on whom he appeared emotionally dependent. He did not intervene when his mother spanked their daughter Carmela, he went along when his mother rejected the couple's plan to sell a lot so they could move out, and he rarely bonded with the child. Reyes-Soto never voiced her frustrations and poured her energy into her career. The spouses had no intimate relations after 1986. In 1987 she told him she was unhappy and wished to live separately, and he answered with silence.

Soto left for the United States in 1988. Reyes-Soto later told him that she and Carmela would not migrate. Their visits there were routine and without intimacy, and on returning she moved back to her parents' house. From 1989 to 2005 Soto sent about USD 200 to 300 for Carmela's schooling. In 1994 he obtained a divorce in the United States; he admitted he filed it out of frustration and in the hope of prompting a reconciliation. When he came home for good in 2007 and tried to rekindle the marriage, she refused.

In 2013 Reyes-Soto filed a petition under Article 36. Psychiatrist Dr. Cecilia Villegas personally interviewed both spouses and used psychological tests administered by another clinical psychologist. She diagnosed Reyes-Soto with Passive-Aggressive Personality Disorder, traced to a strict mother, a sense of rejection and an absent father. She diagnosed Soto with Inadequate Personality Disorder "along masculine strivings, to the degree of oedipal complex," traced to maternal over-protection. She described both conditions as deeply ingrained and permanent. On cross-examination she said her conclusions would have been "basically the same" without the tests.

The RTC (July 18, 2016) declared the marriage void because of the psychological incapacity of both spouses. The CA first reversed (May 29, 2018) but on reconsideration issued an Amended Decision (January 25, 2019) reinstating the RTC ruling. In his Rule 45 petition, Soto argued that the expert's findings were hearsay because a third person conducted the tests, that his wife "merely fell out of love and grew dissatisfied with her marriage," and that the case should have been remanded for liquidation and partition of their properties. The OSG sided with Soto.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition, which attacks the sufficiency and credibility of the evidence of psychological incapacity, raises questions of fact that are improper in a Rule 45 petition.
2. Whether the psychological incapacity of both spouses under Article 36 of the Family Code was proved by clear and convincing evidence, given that the psychological tests the expert relied on were administered by a third person.
3. Whether the CA erred in not ordering the inventory, liquidation and partition of the parties' properties.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the petition raises questions of fact.** Soto framed his challenge as a question of law, but his arguments required the Court "to reweigh the evidence, reassess the credibility of witnesses, and reevaluate the probative value of expert testimony." Under Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., a question of fact exists when the issue calls for a calibration of the evidence, the credibility of witnesses and the probability of factual inferences. Rule 45 allows review of questions of law only. The RTC's findings, affirmed by the CA after reconsideration, bind the Court, and no exception applied. "On this ground alone, the Petition should be dismissed." Because of the importance of the issues and the evolving jurisprudence on Article 36, the Court still ruled on the merits.

**2. Yes, the psychological incapacity of both spouses was proved by clear and convincing evidence.** The Court set out the framework from Tan-Andal (a legal, not medical, concept; the second Molina guideline abandoned; expert opinion not required), Georfo (antecedence, legal incurability, gravity) and Estella (the kinds of lay evidence that may be used). When expert evidence is presented, it complements but does not replace the court's own evaluation. No rule requires a personal interview of both spouses, though one is ideal.

*Credibility of the expert.* Dr. Villegas's qualifications were never seriously controverted, and the trial court found her competent. Her conclusions rested mainly on extensive personal interviews with both spouses. That a third person administered the tests did not reduce the weight of her testimony. As a psychiatrist she could interpret and integrate the results, the tests were "corroborative rather than determinative," and the fact that they matched her interview findings "even further strengthens their reliability."

*Juridical antecedence.* Both incapacities went back to the spouses' formative years. Reyes-Soto's strict, disciplinarian mother, her feeling of rejection and her father's long absence produced emotional passivity and unexpressed anger. Soto's over-protective mother arrested his emotional development "at the infantile level," leaving him unable to separate attachment to his mother from intimacy with his wife.

*Incurability.* Both conditions were deeply ingrained and permanent. The record bore this out: decades of emotional disengagement, no intimacy since the late 1980s, and failed attempts to reconnect.

*Gravity.* Reyes-Soto unconsciously withdrew from and rejected the marital partnership. Soto could not give emotional intimacy, affection and security. Together they showed a "profound psychological incongruity" that made compliance with the essential marital obligations impossible, not merely difficult. The Court noted that there was no violence or infidelity, but held that "[s]ilent dysfunction, manifested in emotional distance, withdrawal, and resignation" is no less within Article 36. Each petition must be judged on the totality of the evidence, not on dramatic signs of marital failure.

**3. No, partition is not a prerequisite.** Article 147 governs because the spouses were capacitated to marry each other, lived exclusively with each other as husband and wife, and their marriage is void (Diño v. Diño). Under Article 496 of the Civil Code, co-owned property may be partitioned by agreement or by judicial proceedings, so a court may declare a marriage void without liquidating the properties in the same case. Partition "is not a precondition but is merely incidental to, and is a consequence of, the nullity of the marriage," and the parties remain free to choose how to divide the properties.

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The CA's January 25, 2019 Amended Decision and September 9, 2019 Resolution in CA-G.R. CV No. 107628 were AFFIRMED. These had reinstated the RTC Decision declaring the marriage void under Article 36 because of the psychological incapacity of both spouses.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Liza filed a petition to declare her marriage to Marco void under Article 36 of the Family Code. Her expert witness, Dr. Cruz, a psychiatrist, personally interviewed both Liza and Marco. She also considered psychological tests that another clinical psychologist administered and scored. Dr. Cruz testified that both spouses have enduring personality structures, formed in childhood, that leave them unable to give each other emotional intimacy and support. She added that her interview findings and the test results "jibed" and that her conclusions would be the same without the tests. Marco argues that Dr. Cruz's opinion is hearsay and worthless because she did not administer the tests herself. Is Marco correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The expert's testimony is not hearsay or unreliable merely because another person administered the psychological tests.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 36 of the Family Code, as construed in Tan-Andal v. Andal, psychological incapacity is a legal concept that must be proved by clear and convincing evidence. Expert opinion is not required, but when offered it aids the court, and its weight depends on the expert's qualifications, sound methodology, and whether it rests on hearsay. In Soto v. Reyes-Soto (G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026), the Court held that a psychiatrist's testimony did not lose probative value because a third person administered the psychological tests. She was competent to interpret and integrate the results, her conclusions rested mainly on personal interviews with both spouses, and the tests were corroborative rather than determinative.
- **Application:** Dr. Cruz personally interviewed Liza and Marco, so her opinion rests on her own observations and not on what others told her. As a psychiatrist she can interpret test results and fold them into her own assessment. She testified that the tests only confirmed her interview findings and that her conclusions would not change without them. The tests therefore support her opinion rather than supply its basis, which makes the opinion more reliable, not less.
- **Conclusion:** Marco is not correct, and the court may give weight to Dr. Cruz's testimony in deciding whether psychological incapacity exists.

**Q2.** In an Article 36 case filed by Ana against her husband Ben, Ben refused to be interviewed. Ana's psychologist assessed Ben through interviews with Ana, Ana's sister, and Ben's childhood friend, who described Ben's behavior before and during the marriage. Ben argues that (a) the psychologist's opinion is worthless because she never personally interviewed him, and (b) without a valid expert opinion, the petition must fail. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Ben is wrong. The lack of a personal interview with him does not, by itself, invalidate the expert's opinion. (b) Ben is wrong. Psychological incapacity may be proved even without expert testimony.
- **Legal basis:** Tan-Andal v. Andal abandoned the second Molina guideline. Psychological incapacity is not a personality disorder that must be proved by expert opinion, and ordinary witnesses who observed the spouse may testify to dysfunctional behavior. In Soto v. Reyes-Soto (G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026), the Court reiterated that no rule requires an expert to personally interview both spouses; doing so is ideal but not indispensable. What controls is whether the expert's conclusions rest on reliable data, such as testimony, personal history and observable patterns of behavior, and whether these are meaningfully linked to juridical antecedence, incurability and gravity.
- **Application:** (a) The psychologist relied on accounts from Ana and from people who knew Ben before and during the marriage. Her opinion may be given weight if these sources are reliable and she ties them to antecedence, incurability and gravity. The missing interview with Ben does not alone defeat it. (b) Even without expert testimony, Ana, her sister and Ben's friend can testify to Ben's behavior. From that evidence the court itself decides whether a true and serious incapacity exists, applying the clear and convincing evidence standard.
- **Conclusion:** Neither argument is a ground to dismiss the petition; the court must evaluate the totality of the evidence.

**Q3.** The RTC declared the marriage of Carlo and Dina void under Article 36 of the Family Code, and the CA affirmed. Carlo filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court. He argues that (a) the evidence did not establish the gravity and incurability of the spouses' condition, and the expert witness was not credible; and (b) the courts erred in declaring the marriage void without first ordering the liquidation and partition of the properties the spouses acquired while living together. Will the petition prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Argument (a) raises questions of fact that cannot be reviewed under Rule 45, and under argument (b), partition is not a prerequisite to a declaration of nullity.
- **Legal basis:** Rule 45 of the Rules of Court allows review of questions of law only. A question of fact exists when the issue calls for a calibration of evidence, the credibility of witnesses and the probability of factual inferences. In Soto v. Reyes-Soto (G.R. No. 249759, April 22, 2026), the Court held that challenges to the sufficiency, credibility and weight of the evidence of psychological incapacity, including expert testimony, are "quintessentially questions of fact." It also held that property relations in a void marriage are governed by Article 147 (or 148) of the Family Code. Because co-owned property may be partitioned by agreement or by judicial proceedings under Article 496 of the Civil Code, partition is only incidental to the declaration of nullity and is not a precondition for it (citing Diño v. Diño).
- **Application:** (a) Carlo does not claim that the courts applied the wrong law. He asks the Supreme Court to reweigh testimony and reassess the expert's credibility. That is a question of fact, and the RTC's findings, affirmed by the CA, bind the Court absent a recognized exception. (b) Assuming Carlo and Dina were capacitated to marry each other and lived exclusively as husband and wife, Article 147 applies and their properties are co-owned. They may divide them by agreement or in a separate judicial proceeding, so the declaration of nullity need not wait for liquidation.
- **Conclusion:** The petition will be denied on both grounds.

> Note: The decision says the spouses had no intimate relations after 1986 (narration and CA), while the expert's judicial affidavit says 1988. The decision mentions Soto's 1994 U.S. divorce but does not discuss its legal effect. The RTC case number appears as both JDRC No. 10317 and JDRC No. 1031. One sentence in the decision says the Court "generally does not review questions of law" under Rule 45, an evident slip for questions of fact; this digest follows the Court's evident meaning.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70372)
