## Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo

**BANCO MAXIMO, INC., PETITIONER, VS. CHRIS ANGELO C. PELAYO, MARY ANN C. PELAYO-CALISURA, AND CATHERINE C. PELAYO-SOCO, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 257251 | 2025-08-18 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Family Relations > B. Family Relations > 5. Family Home  
**Specific topics:** Family home exemption must be timely and properly asserted; Exemption is a personal privilege; heirs who waived their interest lack standing; Family home not exempt from debts secured by a mortgage on the premises (Art. 155(3), Family Code); A judgment on issues not raised in the pleadings is void; Rule 45: conflicting RTC and CA findings as an exception
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45))

### Doctrine
A family home is the dwelling house where the spouses, or an unmarried head of a family, and their family reside, together with the land on which it stands. It is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence, and it is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (Articles 152 and 153, Family Code). **But the exemption is not automatic: it must be timely and properly asserted by the proper party.** The claim must be set up and proved to the sheriff before the public auction (*Honrado v. Court of Appeals*; *Taruc v. Maximo*), or at the latest within a reasonable time, that is, before the one-year redemption period expires (*Spouses Fortaleza v. Spouses Lapitan*). Failure to do so estops the claimant. The Court reiterated these rules.

**The right to claim the exemption is a personal privilege.** Heirs who, through a voluntary extrajudicial settlement, waived all their interest in the property in favor of a co-heir before he mortgaged it have no standing to invoke the family home exemption to annul the mortgage and foreclosure. This is especially so when they raise it only after the auction and after failed attempts to redeem. A mortgagee bank that lent in good faith, relying on a tax declaration in the mortgagor's name and without notice of any adverse claim, is protected.

In any event, **under Article 155(3) of the Family Code, a family home is not exempt from execution for debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether constituted before or after the family home.** A property's character as a family home does not by itself invalidate a mortgage or a foreclosure conducted in accordance with law. On procedure: when a court annuls a deed (here, the extrajudicial settlement) whose nullity no party alleged or prayed for, its judgment goes beyond the pleadings and is "extrajudicial and void."

### Facts
Spouses Edgar and Marlinda Pelayo raised their four children in their house and lot in Barangay Nailon, Bogo City, Cebu. The children are respondents Chris Angelo, Mary Ann and Catherine (Chris et al.) and their brother Ian. Edgar died on January 10, 2004. On March 31, 2008, Marlinda and Chris et al. executed an Extrajudicial Declaration of Heirs with Waiver of Rights (EJS) waiving their interest in the property in favor of Ian, and a tax declaration was issued in Ian's name.

On December 3, 2008, Marlinda, as Ian's attorney-in-fact, obtained a PHP 400,000.00 loan from Banco Maximo, Inc., secured by a real estate mortgage over the property dated December 23, 2008. Ian defaulted, and the bank extrajudicially foreclosed. At the auction on January 24, 2012, the bank was the highest bidder at PHP 353,666.66, the unpaid principal. In October 2012, Chris et al. offered to redeem the property for PHP 500,000.00. The bank counter-offered PHP 800,000.00, and the negotiations failed.

On January 14, 2013, Chris et al. sued to annul the mortgage, the foreclosure sale and the certificate of sale, claiming that the property was a family home exempt from execution. The RTC dismissed the complaint. It held that Chris et al. had no standing because they were neither the owners of the property nor parties to the mortgage. It also held that there was no family home to speak of, because the lot belonged exclusively to Ian, and that the 10-year continuation under Article 159 did not apply because there were no minor beneficiaries.

The CA reversed on October 14, 2020. It held that the property remained a family home for 10 years after Edgar's death under Article 159 of the Family Code, so the 2008 partition through the EJS was invalid. It declared the mortgage, the foreclosure sale and the certificate of sale void. The CA denied reconsideration on April 22, 2021, and the bank filed a Rule 45 petition. Respondents filed no comment despite two directives from the Court.

### Issues
1. Whether the Court may review the factual question of whether the property is a family home in a Rule 45 petition.
2. Whether the CA erred in nullifying the real estate mortgage and the extrajudicial foreclosure on the ground that the property is a family home exempt from execution.

### Ruling
As a preliminary matter, respondents' failure to comment despite repeated directives did not prevent the Court from resolving the case on the pleadings and the evidence on record.

**1. Yes.** Only questions of law may be raised under Rule 45, and the issues here were essentially factual. But a conflict between the findings of the RTC and the CA is a recognized exception. The RTC found that the property ceased to be a family home after Edgar's death and the EJS; the CA held that it remained one. These divergent views required the Court's intervention.

**2. Yes, the CA erred.** A family home is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence, and it is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (Articles 152 and 153, Family Code). **However, "this exemption is not automatic and must be timely and properly asserted."** Under *Honrado v. Court of Appeals*, the claim "should be set up and proved to the Sheriff before the sale of the property at public auction," and failure to do so estops the party from claiming it later. *Taruc v. Maximo* reiterated that the exemption must be asserted before the auction. *Spouses Fortaleza v. Spouses Lapitan* held that it must be asserted within a reasonable time, that is, before the one-year redemption period expires. **The right to claim the exemption "is a personal privilege, and may only be invoked by the proper party."**

Respondents had no standing to invoke it. Through their own voluntary EJS, they waived all their interest in favor of Ian before the mortgage was executed, and they did not assert the exemption before the auction. They first tried to redeem the property, which implicitly recognized the mortgage and the foreclosure. They raised the family home claim only after the negotiations failed and title was consolidated in the bank, which suggests it was "merely an afterthought." Letting them prevail would also be unjust to the bank. It extended credit in good faith on the strength of a tax declaration showing Ian as the owner, with no notice of any adverse claim. A ruling for respondents would "embolden parties to renege on contractual obligations" and erode confidence in secured transactions.

The CA also declared the EJS void even though no one alleged or prayed for its annulment. It thus resolved an issue never raised and disregarded respondents' express waiver in favor of Ian. A judgment that goes beyond the pleadings "is not merely irregular, but extrajudicial and void" (*Bernas v. Court of Appeals*).

**Finally, even if the property remained a family home despite the EJS, the mortgage and the foreclosure stand. Under Article 155 of the Family Code, a family home is not exempt from execution for debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether constituted before or after the family home.** Being a family home does not by itself invalidate a mortgage or a foreclosure conducted in accordance with law.

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated October 14, 2020 and Resolution dated April 22, 2021 in CA-G.R. CEB CV No. 07144 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The Decision dated February 29, 2016 of the RTC, Branch 61, Bogo City, Cebu in Civil Case No. Bogo-02891, which dismissed respondents' complaint, was REINSTATED.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** After their father died, siblings Rina, Sonny and Tess, together with their mother, executed an extrajudicial settlement waiving all their rights over the family's house and lot in favor of their brother Udo. A tax declaration was issued in Udo's name. Udo then mortgaged the property to XYZ Bank to secure a loan. When Udo defaulted, the bank extrajudicially foreclosed and bought the property at the auction. No one claimed any exemption before the sale. After failed negotiations to redeem the property and the consolidation of title in the bank, Rina, Sonny and Tess sued to annul the mortgage and the foreclosure, arguing that the property is their family home and is therefore exempt from forced sale. Will the action prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The siblings cannot invoke the family home exemption to annul the mortgage and the foreclosure.
- **Legal basis:** A family home is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (Articles 152 and 153, Family Code). But the exemption is not automatic. It must be timely and properly asserted, by setting it up and proving it to the sheriff before the auction, or at the latest before the redemption period expires. It is a personal privilege that only the proper party may invoke. Moreover, under Article 155(3) of the Family Code, a family home is not exempt for debts secured by mortgages on the premises. (Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo, G.R. No. 257251, August 18, 2025, citing Honrado v. Court of Appeals and Spouses Fortaleza v. Spouses Lapitan)
- **Application:** The siblings voluntarily waived all their interest in Udo's favor before the mortgage, so they are not the proper parties to claim the exemption. They did not assert it before the auction, and they first tried to redeem the property, which implicitly recognized the mortgage and the foreclosure. Their claim, raised only after title was consolidated, is a belated afterthought. The bank lent in good faith, relying on a tax declaration in Udo's name and without notice of any adverse claim. Finally, the debt was secured by a mortgage on the very property, so even a valid family home would not be exempt from foreclosure.
- **Conclusion:** The action will not prosper, and the mortgage and the foreclosure remain valid.

**Q2.** Vic, a widower, lives with his two minor children in a house and lot he owns, which has been their family residence since 2015. Its value is within the limit allowed by law. In 2022, he borrowed money from Wally without giving any security. Wally obtained a money judgment against Vic, and the sheriff levied on the house and lot. (a) Before the scheduled auction, Vic filed a claim with the sheriff that the property is a family home, with proof that his family has lived there since 2015. Should the claim be recognized? (b) Would your answer be the same if Vic had secured the 2022 loan with a real estate mortgage on the house and lot, and Wally foreclosed the mortgage?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Vic timely and properly asserted the exemption. (b) No. A family home is not exempt from foreclosure for a debt secured by a mortgage on it.
- **Legal basis:** A family home is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence. As long as any of its beneficiaries actually resides there, it is exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment, to the extent of the value allowed by law. The exceptions include debts incurred before its constitution and debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether before or after its constitution (Articles 152, 153 and 155, Family Code). The exemption must be timely and properly asserted by the proper party, that is, set up and proved to the sheriff before the auction. (Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo, G.R. No. 257251, August 18, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The house became a family home in 2015, when Vic and his children began living there, and they still live there. The 2022 debt was incurred after the family home was constituted and is unsecured, so no exception under Article 155 applies. Vic, the owner and head of the family living in the house, is the proper party, and he raised the claim with proof before the auction. Unlike the heirs in Banco Maximo, he did not waive his interest or wait until after the sale. (b) If the loan was secured by a mortgage on the property, Article 155(3) applies. The property's character as a family home would not invalidate the mortgage or the foreclosure.
- **Conclusion:** Vic's timely claim protects the family home against the unsecured judgment debt, but not against foreclosure of a mortgage he constituted on it.

**Q3.** Celia sued to annul a real estate mortgage and the foreclosure sale of a lot, alleging only that the mortgage was void. She did not question the deed of sale by which the mortgagor had earlier acquired the lot from her, and she did not ask for its annulment. The RTC dismissed the complaint. On appeal, the CA, making factual findings contrary to the RTC's, declared void the deed of sale, the mortgage and the foreclosure. The mortgagee bank filed a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 with the Supreme Court. (a) May the Supreme Court review the CA's factual findings? (b) Did the CA validly annul the deed of sale?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. A conflict between the factual findings of the RTC and the CA is a recognized exception to the rule that only questions of law may be raised under Rule 45. (b) No. The CA could not annul a deed whose validity was never put in issue.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 45, only questions of law may be raised, but the Court may review factual issues when the findings of the RTC and the CA conflict. Courts have no jurisdiction or power to decide a question not in issue. A judgment that goes beyond the pleadings and adjudicates matters on which the parties were not heard "is not merely irregular, but extrajudicial and void" (Bernas v. Court of Appeals, applied in Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo, G.R. No. 257251, August 18, 2025).
- **Application:** (a) The RTC and the CA reached opposite conclusions on the facts, so the Supreme Court may examine the evidence to resolve the conflict. (b) Celia's complaint attacked only the mortgage and the foreclosure. She never alleged that the deed of sale was void or asked for its annulment, and the bank was never heard on it. By annulling the deed, the CA decided an issue outside the pleadings, so that part of its judgment is void. Banco Maximo is on point: there, the CA annulled an extrajudicial settlement that no party had challenged.
- **Conclusion:** The Supreme Court may review the conflicting factual findings, and it should set aside the CA's annulment of the unchallenged deed of sale.

> Note: The narrative gives the RTC decision date as February 19, 2016, but the CA fallo, the Supreme Court fallo and footnote 4 give February 29, 2016; the disposition uses February 29, 2016. The Supreme Court did not rule on the CA's reading of Article 159 (the family home continues for 10 years after a spouse's death, and the heirs cannot partition it), nor on the RTC's view that Article 159 requires a minor beneficiary. It held instead that, even if the property remained a family home, Article 155(3) defeats the claim. The text's "SO ORDERED." line carries a stray closing quotation mark.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70081)

## Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa

**SPOUSES NOEL M. AGULLO AND LENY AGULLO, AND JOSEPHINE BERMEJO, PETITIONERS, VS. LEA VICTA – ESPINOSA, REPRESENTED BY AURORA A. VICTA, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 269921 | 2025-04-22 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** V. Property, Ownership, and Its Modifications > G. Actions to Recover Property > 2. Accion Publiciana  
**Specific topics:** When an accion publiciana may be filed (dispossession of one year or less without force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth); Accion publiciana vs. accion reivindicatoria: mere allegation of ownership is not a suit to recover ownership; Meaning of "independently of title" and "without claim of title"; Nature of the action is determined by the allegations of the complaint; Motu proprio dismissal limited to the four grounds in Rule 9, Section 1
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > E. Pleadings > 5. Effect of Failure to Plead (Rule 9, Secs. 1 and 2))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (II. Jurisdiction > A. Concept > 7. How Jurisdiction is Determined and Conferred)

### Doctrine
**An accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, or when the dispossession has lasted for one year or less in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70 of the Rules of Court**, i.e., when there is no allegation of deprivation of possession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. The dispossessed party in such a case need not wait for the one-year period to lapse. The Court En Banc **clarified** *Heirs of Cullado v. Gutierrez* by holding that the action also lies when the dispossession has lasted for exactly one year. It also clarified *Martinez v. Heirs of Lim*: an accion reivindicatoria "can" (not "shall") be filed after one year; no one must wait a year before suing to recover ownership.

The nature of the action, and the court that has jurisdiction, are determined by the **allegations in the complaint**, not by later pleadings or motions. **A complaint that merely alleges the plaintiff's ownership and seeks to recover possession, without praying for recovery of ownership or annulment of title and without alleging that the defendant disputes the plaintiff's title, is an accion publiciana, not an accion reivindicatoria.** Not every encroachment case is an accion reivindicatoria. "Independently of title" means the better right of possession may or may not proceed from title. "Without claim of title" means there is no claim of title hostile to or inconsistent with the plaintiff's, or, if there is one, it is not alleged in the complaint. If ownership is raised only in the answer, the court in an accion publiciana may resolve it provisionally, and only to settle possession, where the two issues are inseparably linked.

Under **Rule 9, Section 1** of the Rules of Court, a court may dismiss a claim motu proprio only for (1) lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, (2) litis pendentia, (3) res judicata, or (4) prescription. Prematurity is not one of them (reiterated).

### Facts
After buying a parcel of land, respondent Lea Victa-Espinosa had it surveyed and found that petitioner spouses Noel and Leny Agullo had encroached on a portion of it. The spouses refused her demand to vacate. She filed a Complaint for Recovery of Possession before the Regional Trial Court of Daet, Camarines Norte. The complaint alleged that she owns the land (assessed at PHP 68,060.00), that the defendants had encroached on it, that they had been illegally occupying it "long before the plaintiff acquired the same" as "mere informal settlers," and that they refused her demands to vacate. It prayed that they be ordered to vacate and to pay attorney's fees, moral damages and exemplary damages. It did not pray for recovery of ownership or annulment of title.

Without issuing summons, the RTC dismissed the complaint on August 5, 2019 as premature: an action for forcible entry could still be filed within one year from the discovery of the dispossession, and only after that may a recovery of possession case be filed. In her motion for reconsideration, respondent argued that her complaint was an accion reivindicatoria because she sought to recover ownership and possession as an attribute of it. The RTC denied the motion on October 4, 2019.

On certiorari, the Court of Appeals (March 17, 2023 Decision; September 25, 2023 Resolution, CA-G.R. SP No. 163854) set aside the RTC orders and ordered a trial on the merits. It held that the complaint was an accion reivindicatoria and that a boundary dispute or encroachment can be settled only in such an action. The spouses Agullo went to the Supreme Court under Rule 45. They argued that the complaint was an accion publiciana, which may be filed only when dispossession has lasted for more than one year, so the case was premature. Citing *Martinez v. Heirs of Lim*, they added that even an accion reivindicatoria may be filed only after more than one year of dispossession.

### Issues
1. Whether the RTC could dismiss the complaint motu proprio, before issuing summons, on the ground of prematurity.
2. Whether the complaint is an accion reivindicatoria or an accion publiciana.
3. Whether an accion publiciana may be filed only when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year.
4. Whether, under Martinez v. Heirs of Lim, an accion reivindicatoria may be filed only when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year.

### Ruling
**1. No.** Rule 9, Section 1 allows a court to dismiss a claim motu proprio in only four instances: lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata, and prescription. "Dismissal on the ground of prematurity is not one of them." The RTC erred procedurally.

**2. It is an accion publiciana; the CA erred in calling it an accion reivindicatoria.** The Court compared the complaint with the one in *Macutay v. Samoy*, captioned "Accion Reivindicatoria with Damages" but held to be an accion publiciana because it had no prayer for recovery of ownership or annulment of title. The present complaint likewise had no such prayer. Respondent's claim, made only in her motion for reconsideration and her CA petition, that she was seeking ownership did not count, because the nature of the action is determined by the allegations in the complaint, "not the allegations in a subsequent pleading or motion." There was no boundary dispute, and respondent did not allege that petitioners disputed her title, so there was no ownership for the court to determine conclusively.

The Court explained the source of the confusion. Accion reivindicatoria has been described as an action to recover possession "as an element of ownership." But a judgment in that action determines ownership and awards possession to the owner; it does not determine possession alone. "Mere averment or allegation of plaintiff's ownership, on its own, is not tantamount to seeking recovery of ownership or alleging dispute as to plaintiff's ownership." Conversely, describing accion publiciana as a suit for the better right of possession "independently of title" or "without claim of title" does not mean that a complaint alleging title cannot be an accion publiciana. "Independently of title" means the better right may or may not proceed from title. "Without claim of title" means no hostile claim of title, or none alleged in the complaint. In *Spouses Cruz v. Spouses Torres*, the defendants' claim of ownership surfaced only in the answer, and the action remained an accion publiciana. The court may still pass on ownership raised in the answer, but only provisionally and to resolve possession.

**3. No.** Both courts and both parties wrongly assumed that an accion publiciana may be filed only after more than one year of dispossession. In *Heirs of Cullado v. Gutierrez*, citing *Gumiran v. Gumiran*, the Court En Banc held that an accion publiciana may be filed even if dispossession has lasted for less than a year "in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70," that is, when there is no allegation of deprivation by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. **The Court clarified *Heirs of Cullado*: the action may also be filed when dispossession has lasted for exactly one year. "In sum, an accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, or when the dispossession has lasted for one year or less in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70 of the Rules of Court."** Since the complaint was an accion publiciana and the assessed value alleged was within the RTC's jurisdiction under Republic Act No. 7691, the law in force when it was filed, it was properly filed with the RTC.

**4. No.** *Martinez* stated that an accion reivindicatoria "can be filed when the dispossession lasted for more than one year." The Court found that *Martinez* may have misquoted *Bongato v. Spouses Malvar*. *Bongato* meant only that once ejectment is no longer available because dispossession has lasted more than a year, the dispossessed party may still file an accion publiciana or reivindicatoria; hence "can be filed" and not "shall be filed." "To say that one must wait for a year to lapse before seeking recovery of ownership is simply absurd and defies logic and reason."

### Disposition
The Petition was DENIED. The Court of Appeals' March 17, 2023 Decision and September 25, 2023 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 163854 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION: the complaint was declared an accion publiciana. The trial court was directed to conduct further proceedings with reasonable dispatch and decide the case on the merits.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Ana bought a titled lot in Camarines Sur. A relocation survey in March 2025 showed that Ben's house encroached on 80 square meters of the lot. Ben ignored Ana's written demand to vacate. In June 2025, Ana filed with the Regional Trial Court (the assessed value is within the RTC's jurisdiction) a "Complaint for Recovery of Possession." She alleged that she is the registered owner, that Ben occupies the encroached portion without right, and that he refused to vacate. She prayed that Ben be ordered to vacate and to pay damages. The complaint does not allege that Ben entered by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth, and it does not allege that Ben disputes her title. (a) What is the nature of Ana's action? (b) Ben moves to dismiss, arguing that the action is premature because less than one year has passed since Ana learned of the encroachment. Should the motion be granted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) It is an accion publiciana, not an accion reivindicatoria. (b) No, the motion should be denied; the action is not premature.
- **Legal basis:** The nature of an action is determined by the allegations in the complaint. A complaint that alleges the plaintiff's ownership and seeks only to recover possession, with no prayer for recovery of ownership or annulment of title and no allegation that the defendant disputes the title, is an accion publiciana. An accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, or when it has lasted for one year or less in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70 of the Rules of Court, i.e., when there is no allegation of deprivation of possession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. (Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa, G.R. No. 269921, April 22, 2025, En Banc)
- **Application:** (a) Ana alleges ownership, but she prays only that Ben vacate and pay damages. She does not seek recovery of ownership or annulment of title and does not allege that Ben disputes her title. Her allegation of ownership alone does not turn the case into an accion reivindicatoria, and encroachment alone does not require one. The action is a plenary action to recover the better right of possession. (b) Her complaint does not allege dispossession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth, so the case is not one of those mentioned in Rule 70. She does not have to wait for one year to lapse before filing an accion publiciana. Since the assessed value is within the RTC's jurisdiction, the RTC may take cognizance of the case.
- **Conclusion:** Ana's complaint is an accion publiciana that was properly and timely filed, so Ben's motion to dismiss should be denied.

**Q2.** Carlos owns a farm lot. In February 2026 he discovered that Dante had secretly entered the lot at night two weeks earlier, fenced off a portion, and planted crops. In April 2026, Carlos filed with the Regional Trial Court a complaint captioned "Accion Publiciana." He alleged that Dante deprived him of possession by stealth and prayed that Dante be ordered to vacate. The assessed value of the lot is within the RTC's jurisdiction. Is the accion publiciana the proper remedy?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Because the complaint alleges dispossession by stealth and the dispossession has not lasted for more than one year, the case falls under Rule 70. The proper remedy is an action for forcible entry in the proper first-level court.
- **Legal basis:** Accion interdictal (forcible entry or unlawful detainer) is the summary action for recovery of physical possession where the dispossession has not lasted for more than one year, and it is brought in the proper inferior court. An accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, but when it has lasted for one year or less only in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70, i.e., when there is no allegation of deprivation of possession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. (Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa, G.R. No. 269921, April 22, 2025, En Banc, applying Heirs of Cullado v. Gutierrez)
- **Application:** Unlike a complaint that is silent on the manner of entry, Carlos's complaint expressly alleges that Dante entered by stealth, a ground mentioned in Rule 70. The dispossession has lasted only a few months. The one-year period for forcible entry, counted in cases of stealth from the time the owner learned of the entry, has not lapsed. The exception allowing an accion publiciana within one year does not apply. The caption "Accion Publiciana" does not control; the allegations do.
- **Conclusion:** Carlos should file a forcible entry case in the proper first-level court, not an accion publiciana in the RTC.

**Q3.** Elena filed with the Regional Trial Court a complaint for recovery of possession of her lot against Fidel. Before summons was issued, the RTC dismissed the complaint motu proprio as "premature," reasoning that Elena should first wait for the one-year period for forcible entry to lapse. (a) Was the motu proprio dismissal proper? (b) On what grounds may a court dismiss a claim on its own initiative?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No, the motu proprio dismissal was improper. (b) Only for lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata, or prescription.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 9, Section 1 of the Rules of Court, a court may dismiss a claim motu proprio only when it appears from the pleadings or the evidence on record that (1) it has no jurisdiction over the subject matter, (2) there is another action pending between the same parties for the same cause (litis pendentia), (3) the action is barred by a prior judgment (res judicata), or (4) the action is barred by the statute of limitations (prescription). In Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa (G.R. No. 269921, April 22, 2025, En Banc), the Court held that an RTC erred in dismissing a complaint for recovery of possession motu proprio, before issuing summons, on the ground of prematurity, because "[d]ismissal on the ground of prematurity is not one of them."
- **Application:** The RTC dismissed Elena's complaint on its own, before summons, solely for prematurity. That is not one of the four grounds in Rule 9, Section 1. The RTC's premise was also wrong, because an accion publiciana may be filed even before one year has lapsed when the complaint does not allege dispossession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth.
- **Conclusion:** The RTC could not dismiss Elena's complaint motu proprio for prematurity, because a court may do so only for lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata, or prescription.

> Note: The decision does not state the date the complaint was filed or exactly when the encroachment was discovered. It says the RTC dismissed the complaint as premature because forcible entry could still be filed within one year from discovery. The Court held the RTC had jurisdiction under RA 7691, "the prevailing law at the time of filing"; it did not discuss the thresholds under RA 11576. Josephine Bermejo is named as a petitioner, but the decision's narration refers only to the spouses Agullo.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69933)

## United Coconut Planters Bank v. Ang (Resolution)

**UNITED COCONUT PLANTERS BANK, SUBSTITUTED BY LAND BANK OF THE PHILIPPINES, PETITIONER, VS. EDITHA F. ANG AND VIOLETA M. FERNANDEZ, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 222448 | 2025-03-03 | Third Division | Rosario, J. | Resolution

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Special Contracts > D. Credit Transactions > 4. Real Estate Mortgage > b. Foreclosure (Rules of Court, Rule 68; Act 3135, as amended by Act 4118; RA 8791, Sec. 47)  
**Specific topics:** Unilaterally imposed interest rates are void (mutuality of contracts, Arts. 1308-1309); No default where the interest stipulations are void; Foreclosure based on void interest rates is itself void; Spouses Andal, Spouses Albos and Vasquez applied instead of the Advocates for Truth in Lending statement; Cause of default and amount paid on the principal are immaterial
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (VIII. Obligations and Contracts > B. Contracts > 1. General Provisions > b. Fundamental Principles > ii. Mutuality)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (IX. Special Contracts > D. Credit Transactions > 1. Loan > b. Mutuum > i. Interest)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (VIII. Obligations and Contracts > A. Obligations > 5. Extinguishment > a. Payment or Performance)

### Doctrine
**When the interest rates on a secured loan are void because the lender imposed them unilaterally (making them potestative and contrary to the mutuality of contracts under Articles 1308 and 1309 of the Civil Code), the foreclosure that follows the borrower's non-payment is also void.** "The unilateral imposition of interests, at such rate that the lender or mortgagee so pleases, cannot and should not be reason to justify a foreclosure sale." The mortgagor must first be given the chance to pay the debt at the correct amount, at an interest rate clearly agreed upon by the parties. As the Court quoted from *Vasquez v. Philippine National Bank*: under **Article 1252 of the Civil Code**, if a debt produces interest, payment of the principal is not deemed made until the interests have been covered; since the void interest is not demandable, the principal is not yet demandable either, so the debtor is not in default and the foreclosure should not proceed. The registration of such a foreclosure sale cannot vest title in the purchaser.

The rule **does not depend on the cause of the borrower's non-payment or on how much of the principal the borrower had paid**: as long as the interest rates were unconscionable or unilaterally imposed by the mortgagee, the foreclosure proceedings that followed should be annulled.

On reconsideration, the Court **vacated its own November 24, 2021 Decision**, which had relied on the statement in *Advocates for Truth in Lending, Inc. v. Bangko Sentral Monetary Board* that the right to foreclose subsists despite the nullity of usurious interest. It held instead that *Spouses Andal v. PNB*, *Spouses Albos v. Spouses Embisan* and *Vasquez v. PNB* (which follow *Heirs of Espiritu v. Landrito*) "should be relied upon for being more attuned to our civil laws and more in keeping with the spirit of fair play and justice," and adopted the view of Justice Zalameda's dissent to the original Decision.

### Facts
Respondents Editha F. Ang and Violeta M. Fernandez obtained a loan from petitioner United Coconut Planters Bank (UCPB), secured by a mortgage. Of their PHP 16,000,000.00 principal obligation, they paid only PHP 2,349,514.95. UCPB extrajudicially foreclosed the mortgage, and an auction sale was held on August 2, 1999. UCPB attributed respondents' default to "dollar shortage, high exchange rate."

Respondents filed a Petition for Declaration of Nullity of Foreclosure, Auction Sale and Promissory Note & Fixing of True Account. The RTC, the CA and later the Supreme Court all found that the interest rates UCPB imposed were unlawful, since it was not shown that respondents could have agreed to them, much less to the rates UCPB would eventually charge. The Credit Agreement and other loan documents were held "null and void for being potestative in character and thus violative of the principle of mutuality of contracts in Articles 1308 and 1309 of the Civil Code." Relying on *Spouses Andal*, the CA (Decision of May 11, 2015 and Resolution of December 4, 2015 in CA-G.R. CV No. 04270) nullified the foreclosure and auction sale.

In a Decision dated November 24, 2021, the Third Division set aside the CA rulings, declared the August 2, 1999 foreclosure and auction sale valid, and dismissed respondents' petition. It relied on *Advocates for Truth in Lending*, which states that the nullity of a usurious interest stipulation does not affect the lender's right to recover the principal or to foreclose. It refused to apply *Spouses Andal* and *Spouses Albos* because the borrowers in *Andal* could not pay solely because of the exorbitant interest and had paid about 68% of their loan, while respondents defaulted because of dollar shortage and paid only PHP 2,349,514.95 of PHP 16,000,000.00. Justice Zalameda dissented.

Respondents moved for reconsideration. They argued that the *Advocates* statement on foreclosure was an *obiter dictum*, since that case concerned the authority of the Monetary Board to enforce Central Bank Circular No. 905, and that *Spouses Andal* and *Spouses Albos* applied. UCPB (later substituted by Land Bank of the Philippines) maintained that the Decision was correct.

### Issues
1. Whether an extrajudicial foreclosure for non-payment of a loan may be held valid even though the interest rates imposed by the lender were void for being unilaterally imposed.
2. Whether Spouses Andal and Spouses Albos may be distinguished on the ground that respondents defaulted for reasons other than the interest rates and paid only a small part of the principal.

### Ruling
**1. No, the foreclosure is void.** The Court acknowledged that the principles in *Advocates* and *Spouses Andal* contradict each other, and that its Decision had chosen *Advocates*. In *Spouses Andal*, the borrowers "cannot be considered in default" for failing to pay arbitrary and unilaterally imposed interest, so the foreclosure was premature and illegal. In *Spouses Albos*, following *Heirs of Espiritu*, the foreclosure was nullified because the debtors were not given the chance to settle the debt at the correct amount without the iniquitous interest. Here, all the courts found that UCPB unilaterally imposed the interest rates, making them potestative and void under Articles 1308 and 1309. **"Being void, the subsequent foreclosure proceedings could not have been held validly."** The Court found *Spouses Andal* and *Spouses Albos* "more attuned to our civil laws and more in keeping with the spirit of fair play and justice," and adopted Justice Zalameda's dissent: the mortgagor must be given a chance to pay at an interest rate clearly agreed upon, "otherwise, they shall be at the mercy of their creditor."

The Court quoted *Vasquez v. PNB* at length: a debtor who was not given an opportunity to settle the debt at the correct amount because of a void interest scheme cannot be subjected to foreclosure; under Article 1252, payment of the principal is not deemed made until the interests are covered, so when the interest obligation is illegal and not demandable, the principal is not yet demandable and the debtor is not in default; and the registration of such a foreclosure sale "cannot vest title over the mortgaged property," because the Torrens system does not create title where one has no rightful claim.

**2. No, the distinctions do not matter.** **"A careful reading of both Spouses Andal and Spouses Albos would reveal that the dispositions therein were not made to depend on the cause of non-payment of the principal loan; nor was the amount paid against the principal loan taken into consideration."** As long as the interest rates were unconscionable or unilaterally imposed by the mortgagee, the foreclosure proceedings that followed should be annulled. That respondents defaulted because of dollar shortage and had paid only about PHP 2.35 million did not make the foreclosure valid.

### Disposition
The Motion for Reconsideration was GRANTED. The Decision dated November 24, 2021 in favor of UCPB was VACATED, and a new one was entered AFFIRMING IN TOTO the CA Decision dated May 11, 2015 in CA-G.R. CV No. 04270, which had nullified the foreclosure and auction sale. Vote: Rosario (ponente), Zalameda and Kho, Jr., JJ.; Leonen, SAJ. dissented; Marquez, J. maintained his vote in the November 24, 2021 Decision.

### En Banc or Division?
Third Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Rosa borrowed PHP 10,000,000.00 from XYZ Bank, secured by a real estate mortgage on her land. The credit agreement allowed the bank to set and reset the interest rate every quarter "at the option of the bank," using reference rates that the bank was free to follow or disregard. The bank repeatedly raised the rate, Rosa failed to pay, and the bank extrajudicially foreclosed the mortgage and bought the land at the auction sale. Rosa sued to annul the foreclosure. The trial court found that the interest provisions were void for violating the mutuality of contracts. The bank argues that the nullity of the interest stipulation does not affect its right to recover the principal and to foreclose. Is the foreclosure valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The foreclosure is void.
- **Legal basis:** Under Articles 1308 and 1309 of the Civil Code, a contract must bind both parties and its validity or compliance cannot be left to the will of one of them; interest rates unilaterally imposed by the lender are potestative and void. When the interest rates are void, the borrower is not in default: under Article 1252 of the Civil Code, payment of the principal is not deemed made until the interests are covered, so when the interest is illegal and not demandable, the principal is not yet demandable either. The foreclosure that follows is void, because the mortgagor must first be given a chance to pay at an interest rate clearly agreed upon. (United Coconut Planters Bank v. Ang, G.R. No. 222448, March 3, 2025 [Resolution], applying Spouses Andal v. PNB, Spouses Albos v. Spouses Embisan and Vasquez v. PNB)
- **Application:** The bank alone could fix and reset the interest rate, so the interest provisions were potestative and void. Rosa was never given the chance to pay her debt at a rate she had agreed to. Since the void interest could not be demanded, the principal was not yet demandable and Rosa was not in default. The bank's argument rests on the Advocates for Truth in Lending statement that the Court declined to follow in UCPB v. Ang. A foreclosure based on the void, unilaterally imposed interest cannot stand.
- **Conclusion:** The extrajudicial foreclosure and the auction sale are void.

**Q2.** Same facts as in the previous question, except that the bank proves that Rosa stopped paying because her export business collapsed during a currency crisis, not because of the interest increases, and that she had paid only about 15% of the principal before the foreclosure. The bank argues that the rule annulling foreclosures applies only when the borrower's default is caused by the void interest and the borrower has paid a substantial part of the loan. Is the bank correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The foreclosure remains void despite the cause of the default and the small amount paid.
- **Legal basis:** The rulings in Spouses Andal and Spouses Albos were not made to depend on the cause of the borrower's non-payment or on the amount paid against the principal. As long as the interest rates were unconscionable or unilaterally imposed by the mortgagee, the foreclosure proceedings that followed should be annulled. (United Coconut Planters Bank v. Ang, G.R. No. 222448, March 3, 2025 [Resolution])
- **Application:** In UCPB v. Ang, the Court first upheld the foreclosure because the borrowers defaulted due to "dollar shortage, high exchange rate" and had paid only PHP 2,349,514.95 of PHP 16,000,000.00. On reconsideration, it rejected precisely these distinctions. Rosa's business losses and her small payments do not change the fact that the bank alone fixed the interest, so she was never given the chance to pay the correct amount at an agreed rate.
- **Conclusion:** The bank is not correct; the foreclosure is still void.

**Q3.** In the same case, after the one-year redemption period, XYZ Bank consolidated its ownership and a new Transfer Certificate of Title was issued in its name. Rosa's foreclosure was later declared void because the interest rates were unilaterally imposed. (a) Is Rosa's obligation to pay the loan extinguished? (b) Can the bank invoke the registration of the foreclosure sale and the new TCT in its name to keep the land?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Rosa still owes the loan, but the bank may foreclose only after the correct amount is determined and she fails to pay it. (b) No. The registration of a void foreclosure sale does not vest title in the bank.
- **Legal basis:** The mortgagor must be given a chance to pay the indebtedness at an interest rate clearly agreed upon; a judgment ordering a foreclosure sale is conditioned on a finding of the correct amount of the unpaid obligation and the debtor's failure to pay that amount. The registration of a foreclosure sale that is declared invalid cannot vest title over the mortgaged property, because the Torrens system does not create or vest title where one has no rightful claim and does not permit one to enrich oneself at the expense of another. (United Coconut Planters Bank v. Ang, G.R. No. 222448, March 3, 2025 [Resolution], quoting Vasquez v. PNB and Heirs of Espiritu v. Landrito)
- **Application:** (a) Only the interest stipulation is void. Rosa's debt is not wiped out; what she is entitled to is the opportunity to pay it at the correct amount, at an interest rate the parties clearly agreed upon. Only if she fails to pay that correct amount may the bank foreclose. (b) Because the foreclosure was void, the consolidation and the new TCT rest on nothing. Registration only confirms and records title that already exists; it cannot give the bank a title it never validly acquired.
- **Conclusion:** Rosa remains liable for the correct amount of her debt, but the bank cannot keep the land on the strength of the registration of a void foreclosure sale.

> Note: Promulgated by the Special Third Division; recorded here as Third Division. The vote was 3-2: Leonen, SAJ. dissented (relying on Spouses Beluso, Advocates and Solid Builders; not examinable), and Marquez, J. maintained his vote in the original Decision. The vacated November 24, 2021 Decision (916 Phil. 482) was penned by J. Carandang; Rosario, J. concurred in it and later penned this Resolution reversing it. The main Resolution does not state that Advocates for Truth in Lending (an En Banc decision) is abandoned; it chose to apply Spouses Andal, Spouses Albos and Vasquez. The terms of the CA fallo that was affirmed in toto (including a remand to compute the total indebtedness) are quoted only in the dissenting opinion, not in the main Resolution. The main Resolution states few facts about the loan itself; the facts above are limited to what it recites.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69919)

## Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido

**MARIA LINA P. QUIRIT-FIGARIDO, PETITIONER, VS. EDWIN L. FIGARIDO, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 259520 | 2024-11-05 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Family Relations > A. Marriage > 4. Void and Voidable Marriages  
**Specific topics:** Who may file a petition to declare a bigamous marriage void (A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, Sec. 2(a)); The guilty spouse in a bigamous marriage has no personality to sue; Effect of a later foreign divorce on the prior spouse's standing; Judicial declaration of nullity is needed only for remarriage (Art. 40, Family Code); Clean hands: no equity relief for the erring spouse
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > C. Parties to Civil Actions (Rule 3))

### Doctrine
**Only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may file a petition to declare a bigamous marriage void. The spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage has no personality to file it.** Bigamous marriages are void ab initio under Article 35(4) of the Family Code. But under Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, a petition for declaration of absolute nullity "may be filed solely by the husband or the wife," and the Rationale of the Rule explains that "[o]nly an aggrieved or injured spouse" may file. Following *Juliano-Llave v. Republic* and *Fujiki v. Marinay*, the "husband or the wife" means the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage are neither husband nor wife in law. The En Banc applied these rules and jurisprudence to deny standing to the guilty spouse. Letting her sue would be a "legal absurdity": the offending spouse could dissolve the marriage at will and treat bigamy "as a matter of convenience."

A foreign divorce later obtained by the prior spouse ends that spouse's standing, since there is no longer a prior subsisting marriage. But it **does not pass the right to sue to the guilty spouse.** When the persons capable of filing are absent or disqualified, other parties do not automatically gain the right to attack the bigamous marriage. The State has no absolute duty to dissolve bigamous marriages, and the Court will not use its equity jurisdiction to free a party who willfully entered the void marriage and does not come with clean hands (*Alcantara v. Alcantara*).

The denial does not legalize the bigamous marriage. Under Article 40 of the Family Code, a judicial declaration of nullity is needed only for purposes of remarriage. For other purposes, such as heirship, legitimacy or illegitimacy of a child, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, or a criminal case, a court may rule on the marriage's validity in any case where the question is essential (*Cariño v. Cariño*). The erring parties also remain civilly and criminally liable for bigamy.

### Facts
Maria Lina married Ho Kar Wai, a Chinese national, on December 13, 1989 in Hong Kong, and again on August 23, 1994 before a Metropolitan Trial Court judge in Parañaque City. In 2000 she met Edwin in Hong Kong. Edwin knew she had problems with her marital status, courted her anyway, and promised to wait until she settled them. While still married to Ho Kar Wai, Maria Lina had an affair with Edwin, became pregnant, and married him on February 22, 2003 in Quezon City. They had two children, born in 2004 and 2007.

On November 28, 2007, Ho Kar Wai obtained a divorce decree (Certificate of Making Decree Nisi Absolute) from the District Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. On Maria Lina's petition, the RTC of Parañaque City, Branch 260 recognized the foreign divorce in a Decision dated February 5, 2009.

Maria Lina and Edwin separated in 2014. On March 6, 2017, Maria Lina filed with a family court a petition to declare her marriage to Edwin void ab initio as bigamous under Article 35(4) of the Family Code, and to declare that she had the capacity to remarry. Edwin was served summons by publication and never appeared. At pre-trial, Edwin admitted that Maria Lina married him while her marriage to Ho Kar Wai was subsisting. Maria Lina admitted that she married Edwin before the RTC decision recognizing her divorce. She was the lone witness.

The family court denied the petition on August 30, 2019 and denied reconsideration. On appeal, the OSG argued that Maria Lina, as the party guilty of contracting the bigamous marriage, had no personality to file, because only the injured or aggrieved spouse may do so. The CA affirmed on June 21, 2021 and denied reconsideration on November 16, 2021. Maria Lina filed a Rule 45 petition. The OSG kept its position, and Edwin filed no comment.

### Issues
1. Whether Maria Lina, the spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage, has the personality to file a petition to declare her marriage to Edwin void ab initio for being bigamous.
2. Whether the Court may declare Maria Lina's marriage to Edwin void so that she may remarry, considering that her first husband has divorced her and that, she claims, no one else can file the petition.

### Ruling
**1. No. Maria Lina has no personality to file the petition.** Article 35(4) of the Family Code declares bigamous marriages void ab initio. Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC provides that the petition "may be filed solely by the husband or the wife." Its Rationale states that "[o]nly an aggrieved or injured spouse may file petitions for annulment of voidable marriages and declaration of absolute nullity of void marriages." In *Juliano-Llave v. Republic*, the Court held that the prior spouse "is clearly the aggrieved party," because the bigamous marriage threatens the financial and property aspects of the prior marriage and places an emotional burden on the prior spouse. In *Fujiki v. Marinay*, it clarified that the "husband or the wife" in Section 2(a) is the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage "are neither the husband nor the wife under the law."

Maria Lina married Edwin in 2003 while her marriage to Ho Kar Wai subsisted. The divorce came only in 2007, and its recognition in 2009. She is guilty of contracting the bigamous marriage, so she cannot be an aggrieved or injured innocent spouse of either marriage. The Court rejected her attempt to distinguish *Juliano-Llave*, noting that the first wife was in fact one of the complainants there. Even if the divorce had ended the emotional and financial harm to the prior spouse, that would not make Maria Lina the aggrieved spouse. If anything, she benefited from the second union: she had two children with Edwin and filed only after 14 years. **Letting the erring spouse invoke the bigamous nature of her own marriage would produce a "legal absurdity": the offending spouse could dissolve the marriage at will and treat bigamy "as a matter of convenience."**

**2. No. The Court will not declare the marriage void at her instance.** Ho Kar Wai, the injured spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, had the right to file the petition. Once he obtained the divorce, however, there was no longer a prior subsisting marriage. He lost his status as the aggrieved spouse and can no longer file it. **The divorce "in no way resulted in the assignment of the right to petition" to Maria Lina.** Nothing in the rules or jurisprudence says that when the persons capable of filing are absent or disqualified, other concerned parties automatically gain the right to sue. The State has no absolute responsibility to dissolve bigamous marriages. The rules aim to preserve marriage, not to give guilty spouses "a convenient means to dissolve their illegitimate union." With no legitimate marriage left to protect, there is "no compelling reason for the State to dissolve her illegitimate marriage."

A judicial declaration of nullity matters only for remarriage. Under Article 40 of the Family Code, the marriage bond of a void marriage subsists only for that purpose. For other purposes (heirship, legitimacy, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, criminal cases), a court may rule on the validity of a marriage even in a suit not filed directly to question it (*Cariño v. Cariño*). Maria Lina's real goal was the capacity to remarry, and the law gives her no remedy for an inability "which she inflicted on herself." Following *Alcantara v. Alcantara*, the Court declined to use its equity jurisdiction for a party who willfully contracted the void marriage and does not come with clean hands.

The denial is not a refusal to declare the bigamous marriage void. It rejects only Maria Lina's personality to file the petition. It does not legalize bigamy: the erring parties may still be held civilly and criminally liable, and heirship, legitimacy, settlement of estate, and dissolution of the property regime may be resolved without a declaration of nullity.

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The CA Decision dated June 21, 2021 and Resolution dated November 16, 2021 in CA-G.R. CV No. 114777, which affirmed the family court's denial of the petition for declaration of nullity, were AFFIRMED.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In 1996, Liza married Kenji, a Japanese national, in Manila. In 2005, while still married to Kenji, Liza married Ramon, who knew of her existing marriage. They had three children. In 2009, Kenji obtained a valid divorce in Japan, which a Philippine RTC recognized in 2011. Liza and Ramon separated in 2016. In 2024, wanting to marry another man, Liza filed a petition to declare her marriage to Ramon void ab initio for being bigamous under Article 35(4) of the Family Code. The OSG opposed, arguing that Liza has no personality to file the petition. Liza replied that the marriage is admittedly bigamous and void, that Kenji can no longer sue because of the divorce, and that she is the only real party in interest left. Should the petition be granted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The petition should be dismissed because Liza, the spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage, has no personality to file it.
- **Legal basis:** Bigamous marriages are void ab initio under Article 35(4) of the Family Code. Under Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, a petition for declaration of absolute nullity may be filed solely by the husband or the wife, which the Rationale of the Rule explains as the aggrieved or injured spouse. Only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may petition to declare a bigamous marriage void; the guilty spouse cannot. A foreign divorce later obtained by the prior spouse ends that spouse's standing but does not transfer the right to the guilty spouse. (Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido, G.R. No. 259520, November 5, 2024, En Banc, applying Juliano-Llave v. Republic and Fujiki v. Marinay)
- **Application:** Liza married Ramon in 2005 while her marriage to Kenji subsisted; the divorce came only in 2009. She is the guilty party, not an aggrieved or injured innocent spouse. Kenji was the injured spouse while the first marriage subsisted. After the divorce there was no longer a prior subsisting marriage, so he lost his standing, but his loss did not pass the right to Liza. That no one else can now file does not give her standing. The court will also not use equity to relieve a party who willfully contracted the bigamous marriage and benefited from it for years. Her real aim, the capacity to remarry, is a disability she brought on herself.
- **Conclusion:** The petition should be dismissed because Liza has no personality to file it.

**Q2.** Liza, a Filipina, married Kenji, a Japanese national, in 1996. In 2005, while still married to Kenji, she married Ramon. In 2007, before any divorce, Kenji learned of the second marriage and filed in the Philippines a petition to declare the Liza-Ramon marriage void for being bigamous. Liza moved to dismiss, arguing that under A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC only "the husband or the wife" may file, and Kenji is not a party to her marriage with Ramon. (a) Does Kenji have personality to file the petition? (b) Would your answer be the same if Kenji filed the petition only in 2012, after his Japanese divorce from Liza had been recognized by a Philippine court?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Kenji, as the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, is the aggrieved party with personality to file. (b) No. After the divorce, Kenji no longer has standing to file the petition.
- **Legal basis:** Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, read with its Rationale, allows only the aggrieved or injured spouse to file. The "husband or the wife" in Section 2(a) refers to the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage are neither husband nor wife in law (Fujiki v. Marinay; Juliano-Llave v. Republic). In Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido (G.R. No. 259520, November 5, 2024, En Banc), the Court held that the injured spouse of the prior subsisting marriage had the right to file the petition. Once he obtained a divorce decree, however, there was no longer a prior subsisting marriage, he lost his status as the aggrieved spouse, and he could no longer file it.
- **Application:** (a) In 2007, Kenji's marriage to Liza was still subsisting. Her bigamous marriage threatened the property side of his marriage and caused him the emotional injury the rule protects against, so he is the aggrieved spouse and the proper party. Liza's reading would unjustly shut out the very spouse the rule is meant to protect. (b) By 2012, his marriage to Liza had been dissolved by a divorce recognized in the Philippines. With no prior subsisting marriage left to protect, he is no longer the aggrieved spouse and has lost the personality to file.
- **Conclusion:** Kenji may file the petition while his marriage to Liza subsists, but not after his divorce from her.

**Q3.** Andrea married Carlos in 2010 while her marriage to Benjie was still subsisting. Benjie never sued. In 2023, Andrea's petition to declare her marriage to Carlos void was dismissed because, as the guilty spouse, she had no personality to file it. In 2025, Carlos died intestate. In the judicial settlement of his estate, Carlos's brother opposed Andrea's claim to inherit as surviving spouse, arguing that the marriage was bigamous and void. Andrea countered that no court has ever declared her marriage to Carlos void, and that the dismissal of her own petition means the marriage must be treated as valid. May the settlement court rule on the validity of Andrea's marriage to Carlos to determine Carlos's heirs?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. The settlement court may rule on the validity of the marriage to determine heirship, even without a prior judicial declaration of nullity.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 40 of the Family Code, a judicial declaration of nullity of a previous marriage is required only for purposes of remarriage. For other purposes, such as heirship, legitimacy or illegitimacy of a child, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, or a criminal case, a court may rule on the validity of a marriage even after the parties' death and even in a suit not filed directly to question it, so long as the question is essential to the case (Cariño v. Cariño). In Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido (G.R. No. 259520, November 5, 2024, En Banc), the Court stressed that denying the guilty spouse's petition for lack of personality is not a refusal to declare the bigamous marriage void and does not legalize it. These incidents may proceed without a declaration of nullity, and the erring parties remain civilly and criminally liable for bigamy.
- **Application:** The dismissal of Andrea's petition rested only on her lack of personality. It did not hold that her marriage to Carlos was valid. Whether Andrea is Carlos's surviving spouse is essential to determining his heirs, so the settlement court may examine whether the marriage was celebrated while her marriage to Benjie subsisted. If it was, the marriage is void under Article 35(4) of the Family Code, and Andrea cannot claim to be Carlos's surviving spouse.
- **Conclusion:** The settlement court may rule on the validity of the marriage to determine Carlos's heirs, despite the absence of a judicial declaration of nullity.

> Note: En Banc vote: Inting, M. Lopez, J. Lopez, Dimaampao, Marquez and Kho, Jr., JJ. concurred. Gesmundo, C.J., Caguioa, J. and Singh, J. wrote concurring opinions. Lazaro-Javier and Zalameda, JJ. dissented; Leonen, SAJ. joined both dissents, and Hernando, J. (on official business) joined Justice Lazaro-Javier's dissent. Gaerlan, J. was on official leave. The separate opinions, which make up most of the cached text, are not examinable and were not used. The children's names are redacted in the decision. The Court did not decide whether the second husband, Edwin, could file the petition; it only noted Maria Lina's claim that he could not.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69745)

## NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation (Judgment on Compromise)

**NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INDIGENOUS PEOPLES (NCIP), ZENAIDA BRIGIDA HAMADA-PAWID, DIONESIA O. BANUA, CONCHITA C. CALZADO, PERCY BRAWNER, COSME LAMBAYON, SANTOS UNSAD, AND BASILIO WANDAG, PETITIONERS, VS. MACROASIA CORPORATION, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 226176 | 2023-08-09 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** VIII. Obligations and Contracts > B. Contracts > 1. General Provisions > b. Fundamental Principles > i. Autonomy  
**Specific topics:** Judgment based on a compromise agreement while a petition is pending before the Supreme Court; Test for approval: not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order; Compromise by a government agency, with the OSG joining the motion; FPIC and Certification Precondition under RA 8371 (background only)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > R. Judgments and Final Orders > 3. How Rendered (Rule 36))
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (IX. National Economy and Patrimony > B. Ancestral Domain and Ancestral Lands (RA 8371, Ch. I–III))

### Doctrine
No new doctrine. **Parties to a case pending before the Supreme Court may settle it through a compromise agreement and jointly move for judgment based on it. The Court will approve and adopt the compromise if it was validly executed and is not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order.** It will then enjoin the parties to comply with its terms in utmost good faith and declare the case closed and terminated. The Court applied this test without reviewing the merits of the CA ruling under appeal.

A government agency may enter into such a compromise. Here the NCIP signed through its Chairperson, and the Office of the Solicitor General joined the motion for judgment. The decision cites no Civil Code provision. The test it applied matches the general limits on contractual stipulations (Civil Code, Art. 1306) and the nature of a compromise as a contract that ends a pending litigation (Civil Code, Art. 2028).

### Facts
Macroasia Corporation held Mineral Production Sharing Agreement (MPSA) No. 220-2005-IVB, issued in December 2005, covering 1,114 hectares in Barangays Ipilan, Mambalot and Maasin, Brooke's Point, Palawan. Its application for mining permits was endorsed to the NCIP for the Free and Prior Informed Consent (FPIC) process, which is required for the issuance of a Certification Precondition. After the FPIC process with the Pala'wan communities, a Joint Resolution of Consent and a Memorandum of Agreement were executed on April 21, 2010, and the FPIC and validation teams recommended issuance of the Certification Precondition. The NCIP En Banc, however, denied it in Resolution No. 001-2012, mainly because a separate field-based investigation (FBI) was required for two indirectly affected barangays, Aribungos and Barong-barong. It denied reconsideration on February 23, 2012.

On Macroasia's petition for review, the CA issued an Amended Decision dated March 14, 2016 directing the NCIP to issue the Certification Precondition, and denied reconsideration on August 9, 2016. The NCIP and its officials filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court.

While the petition was pending, Macroasia assigned its MPSA rights to Macroasia Mining Corporation on June 7, 2019, and the DENR Secretary approved the assignment on February 1, 2021. In August 2022 Macroasia Mining conducted a separate FBI/FPIC process for Aribungos and Barong-barong, which ended in a Memorandum of Agreement with the IP leaders. On February 1, 2023 the NCIP and Macroasia Mining, acting as assignee and authorized representative of Macroasia, signed a Compromise Agreement. In it the parties acknowledged that the FPIC process had been properly conducted and validated and that all five barangays had issued Joint Resolutions of Consent. Macroasia Mining undertook to keep securing all required permits, and the NCIP undertook to keep reviewing its processes. The parties agreed to move for dismissal of the case with prejudice. Macroasia filed a Joint Motion to Render Judgment Based on Compromise Agreement dated February 21, 2023, which the OSG joined on behalf of the NCIP on March 30, 2023.

### Issues
1. Whether the Compromise Agreement may be approved and judgment rendered on it, terminating the petition.

### Ruling
**1. Yes.** The Court reproduced the Compromise Agreement in full and found it "validly executed and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy, and public order." It granted the Joint Motion to Render Judgment Based on Compromise Agreement, approved and adopted the agreement, enjoined the parties to comply with its terms in utmost good faith, and declared the case closed and terminated.

The Court did not rule on whether the CA's Amended Decision was correct or on any issue under RA 8371. The dispute ended on the parties' own settlement. Under that settlement, the FPIC for the two indirectly affected barangays, which was the main reason the NCIP had denied the Certification Precondition, had already been conducted.

### Disposition
The Joint Motion to Render Judgment Based on Compromise Agreement was GRANTED. The Compromise Agreement dated February 1, 2023 was APPROVED and ADOPTED, the parties were ENJOINED to comply with its terms in utmost good faith, and the case was deemed CLOSED and TERMINATED.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** A government agency filed a Rule 45 petition against a mining company in the Supreme Court. While it was pending, the agency, represented by its chairperson, and the company signed a compromise agreement settling the dispute and filed a joint motion for judgment based on it; the Office of the Solicitor General joined the motion. (a) May the Supreme Court render judgment on the compromise instead of deciding the petition on the merits? (b) What must the Court determine before approving it?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. (b) The Court must find that the compromise was validly executed and is not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order.
- **Legal basis:** A compromise is a contract by which the parties, through reciprocal concessions, avoid a litigation or end one already begun (Civil Code, Art. 2028). Contracting parties may agree on terms they consider convenient, provided these are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order or public policy (Civil Code, Art. 1306). In NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation (G.R. No. 226176, August 9, 2023), the Supreme Court acted on a joint motion filed while a Rule 45 petition was pending and joined by the OSG for the government agency. It found the compromise "validly executed and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy, and public order," approved and adopted it, enjoined compliance in utmost good faith, and declared the case closed and terminated.
- **Application:** The case is still pending, so the parties may end it by compromise. The agency acted through its chairperson, and the OSG joined the motion. If the Court finds the agreement validly executed and its terms consistent with law, morals, good customs, public policy and public order, it will approve the agreement, render judgment on it, and close the case without ruling on the merits of the appeal.
- **Conclusion:** The Supreme Court may render judgment on the compromise once it is shown to be valid and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy or public order.

**Q2.** Same facts as in the previous problem, but the compromise provides that the agency will issue the mining company a Certification Precondition over land within an ancestral domain even though the indigenous cultural communities concerned have not given their free and prior informed consent (FPIC). Should the Supreme Court approve the compromise?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. A compromise that dispenses with a requirement of law is contrary to law and public policy and cannot be approved.
- **Legal basis:** The Court approves a compromise only if it is "validly executed and not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public policy, and public order" (NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation, G.R. No. 226176, August 9, 2023; see Civil Code, Art. 1306). Under Section 59 of RA 8371 (IPRA), the NCIP may not issue a Certification Precondition without the free and prior informed and written consent of the ICCs/IPs concerned. The compromise in Macroasia itself described the FPIC process as a requirement for the issuance of the Certification Precondition.
- **Application:** In Macroasia, the parties acknowledged before settling that the FPIC process had been conducted and validated for all the affected barangays. This compromise, by contrast, would have the agency issue the certification without FPIC. That term violates IPRA and the public policy of protecting the rights of indigenous peoples, so the agreement fails the test for approval.
- **Conclusion:** The Supreme Court should refuse to approve the compromise and should resolve the petition on its merits.

**Q3.** The Supreme Court approved a compromise agreement between Agency X and Company Y and declared the case closed and terminated. Under the compromise, the parties had agreed to the dismissal with prejudice of X's pending petition. A year later, X's new chairperson filed a new case against Y raising the same claims that the compromise had settled. Will the new case prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The judicial compromise has the effect of res judicata between the parties, and the case it settled was closed and terminated with prejudice.
- **Legal basis:** A compromise has upon the parties the effect and authority of res judicata (Civil Code, Art. 2037). In NCIP v. Macroasia Corporation (G.R. No. 226176, August 9, 2023), the Court approved and adopted a compromise in which the parties agreed to the dismissal with prejudice of the pending petition. It enjoined them to comply with the agreement in utmost good faith and declared the case closed and terminated.
- **Application:** Agency X, through its chairperson at the time, freely entered into the compromise, and the Supreme Court approved it and rendered judgment on it. The agency is the party bound, regardless of any change in its leadership. The new case involves the same parties and the same claims already settled and closed with prejudice, so it is barred. Reviving those claims would also breach the parties' undertaking to comply with the agreement in utmost good faith.
- **Conclusion:** The new case should be dismissed on the ground of res judicata.

> Note: Decision based on a compromise agreement. It lays down no new doctrine and does not review the merits of the CA's Amended Decision (March 14, 2016) directing the NCIP to issue a Certification Precondition. The Civil Code articles (1306, 2028, 2037) and IPRA Section 59 cited in the doctrine's second paragraph and the suggested answers are basic law supplied for bar purposes; the decision itself does not cite them. The agreement's reference to "Administrative Order No. 03 series of 20212" is reproduced in the source as written (an evident typographical error). The compromise was signed by Macroasia Mining Corporation as assignee and authorized representative of respondent Macroasia Corporation.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69052)
