## Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc.

**KAMERA WORLD INC., PETITIONER, VS. REDDOT IMAGING PHILIPPINES, INC., RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 248256 | 2023-04-17 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** VIII. Obligations and Contracts > A. Obligations > 5. Extinguishment > a. Payment or Performance  
**Specific topics:** Dacion en pago as a special mode of payment that partakes of a sale; Essential requisites of a contract (Art. 1318, Civil Code); Perfection not undone by a later term sheet that is a mere recommended addendum; Estoppel against questioning the consideration after acknowledging it in writing; Rule 45: authority of corporate signatories is a question of fact
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45))

### Doctrine
**Dacion en pago** is the transmission of the ownership of a thing by the debtor to the creditor as an accepted equivalent of the performance of an obligation. It partakes of the nature of a sale: the creditor is really buying the debtor's property, payment for which is charged against the debt. Hence the essential requisites of a contract under **Art. 1318 of the Civil Code** (consent, object certain, and cause) must be present, **except that the consideration or purchase price is deemed to be the existing debt**; in its modern concept it is an objective novation (reiterating *Dacquel v. Spouses Sotelo*). A sale is perfected upon the meeting of minds on the object and the price.

**A memorandum of agreement signed by both parties' representatives, identifying the property and fixing the price to be applied against the debtor's obligations, is a perfected, binding contract.** Later e-mails and a term sheet proposing revisions do not undo perfection where they do not change, amend, revise or deviate from the purpose of the agreement; they are at most a recommended addendum.

A party that acknowledged in writing that the down payment it received included the credits of a related company is **estopped** from later claiming that the consideration was defective for including those credits. Whether the corporate signatories were authorized by board resolutions is a **question of fact** not reviewable under Rule 45, and a party seeking relaxation of that rule must prove an exceptionally meritorious reason.

### Facts
In 2008, I-Digiworld, Inc. delivered imaging equipment and camera products to Kameraworld Inc. for sale in its outlets, with Kameraworld to remit the proceeds less its margin. Kameraworld failed to remit, and its payables reached PHP 12,000,000.00. In 2011, to settle, Kameraworld and I-Digiworld signed a deed of sale over a Kameraworld condominium unit, but I-Digiworld, through its president Dennie T. Dy, instead proposed to buy Kameraworld's properties in España, Sampaloc, Manila (TCT Nos. 131996 and 131997) for PHP 32,500,000.00. Dy said I-Digiworld would assign its right to collect the PHP 12,000,000.00 to Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc., which had the same directors.

The España properties were mortgaged to BPI, as Kameraworld disclosed. With Kameraworld's consent, Reddot entered the premises, introduced improvements, and paid upkeep and realty taxes. In September 2012, Reddot issued three checks to Kameraworld for PHP 7,500,000.00, PHP 1,500,000.00 and PHP 1,000,000.00. Further checks were suspended after a BIR tax lien on the properties surfaced and Chinabank disapproved Reddot's loan.

On July 10, 2013, Kameraworld's chairperson, Ma. Teresa Alba, acknowledged receipt of a PHP 1,500,000.00 check as "additional downpayment" on the España property, to be used to settle the tax lien, and stated a total down payment of PHP 15,289,897.00, consisting of the "[o]utstanding payable to I-Digiworld/Reddot Imaging Philippines" of PHP 13,789,897.70 plus the new check. The same day, Kameraworld (through its president John Pacific Castro) and Reddot (through Dy) signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) under which Kameraworld offered the España properties as payment of its obligation for a total consideration of PHP 32,500,000.00. Reddot would pay the PHP 10,000,000.00 release value of the BPI mortgage and pay the remaining balance of PHP 7,931,345.37 once the BIR lifted the tax lien.

In 2014, Reddot sent a draft deed of sale, to which Castro was noncommittal. In August 2014, Reddot sent Kameraworld checks payable to BPI for PHP 10,000,000.00 and PHP 721,243.07 and undertook to pay the balance within five days after the tax lien was removed. Alba replied that the MOA was only a proposal because she had not signed it, and Kameraworld pointed to a later term sheet with improved terms, which it rejected. Reddot sued for specific performance. The RTC held the MOA binding; the CA affirmed with modifications, characterizing the MOA as a dacion en pago governed by the law on sales.

### Issues
1. Whether the alleged lack of board authority of the signatories to the MOA may be reviewed in a Rule 45 petition.
2. Whether the MOA is a valid contract (a dacion en pago) despite Kameraworld's claims of defective consent and consideration.
3. Whether the later e-mails and term sheet show that there was no meeting of the minds, so that the MOA was never perfected.

### Ruling
**1. No.** Only questions of law may be raised in a Rule 45 petition. Whether board resolutions authorized Dy and Castro to sign for their corporations is a question of fact. Kameraworld cited the recognized exceptions but failed to establish which of them applied. Those who seek exemption from a procedural rule bear the burden of proving an exceptionally meritorious reason (*Waterfront Cebu City Casino Hotel, Inc. v. Ledesma*).

**2. Yes.** A contract requires consent, object certain, and cause (Art. 1318), and a sale is perfected upon the meeting of minds on the thing and the price (*Heirs of Dr. Mario S. Intac v. CA*). The MOA had consent (the signatures of Castro and Dy), an object certain (the España properties), and a cause (the PHP 32,500,000.00 price). Under *Dacquel v. Spouses Sotelo*, dacion en pago is the transmission of ownership of a thing by the debtor to the creditor as an accepted equivalent of performance; it partakes of a sale and requires the elements of a contract of sale, except that the consideration is deemed to be the existing debt. On the alleged defect in consideration because it included I-Digiworld's credits, **Kameraworld was estopped**: in the July 10, 2013 letter, Alba acknowledged the PHP 1,500,000.00 down payment and a total of PHP 15,289,897.00 received, of which PHP 13,789,897.00 represented Kameraworld's payables not only to Reddot but also to I-Digiworld.

**3. No.** The MOA was perfected because all the requisites of a valid contract concurred. The Court agreed with the RTC that the term sheet could be deemed "only as a recommended addendum" to the MOA, since it did not change, amend, revise or deviate from the purpose for which the MOA was created; it could not affect the validity of a complete agreement. The CA committed no reversible error, and the Court adopted the CA's dispositive portion as "spot on" in fixing the parties' obligations and remedies.

### Disposition
The petition was DENIED, and the CA Decision dated February 28, 2019 and Resolution dated July 5, 2019 in CA-G.R. CV No. 109047 were AFFIRMED. As affirmed, the CA judgment: declared the MOA a valid and binding contract; required BPI to accept Reddot's tender of payment of Kameraworld's loan and release the owner's duplicate titles to Reddot; ordered Kameraworld to cause the lifting of the tax lien within 30 days from finality, failing which Reddot may do so at Kameraworld's expense and pay whatever balance of the price remains after deducting the cost; ordered Kameraworld to execute a deed of absolute sale upon delivery of the balance (PHP 7,931,345.37 if Kameraworld settles the tax lien, or the remainder after deducting its cost); dismissed Kameraworld's counterclaims; and deleted the RTC's awards of moral and temperate damages and attorney's fees.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Delta Corp. owed Echo Corp. PHP 20,000,000.00 for unpaid deliveries. Their presidents signed a memorandum of agreement in which Delta offered its warehouse in payment of its debt for a total consideration of PHP 30,000,000.00; the debt would be credited against the price, and Echo would pay the PHP 10,000,000.00 difference once Delta cleared a tax lien on the property. Later, Delta's chairperson refused to execute a deed of sale, claiming that the MOA was a mere proposal because she did not sign it. (a) What is the nature of the MOA? (b) Is it a binding contract?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) It is a dacion en pago. (b) Yes, it is a perfected and binding contract.
- **Legal basis:** Dacion en pago is the transmission of the ownership of a thing by the debtor to the creditor as an accepted equivalent of the performance of an obligation. It partakes of the nature of a sale, so the essential requisites of a contract under Art. 1318 of the Civil Code (consent, object certain, and cause) must be present, with the existing debt deemed the consideration or purchase price. An MOA signed by both parties' representatives that identifies the property and fixes the price is a valid contract of this kind (Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 248256, April 17, 2023, citing Dacquel v. Spouses Sotelo).
- **Application:** Delta, the debtor, offered its warehouse and Echo, the creditor, accepted it as payment of the debt, with the excess of the price payable in cash. This is a dacion en pago. Consent is shown by the signatures of both presidents; the object is the warehouse; the cause is the PHP 30,000,000.00 price, against which the existing debt is credited. The chairperson's failure to sign does not negate consent, because Delta signed through its president; any claim that he lacked authority is a factual matter that Delta must prove at trial.
- **Conclusion:** The MOA is a perfected dacion en pago that binds Delta.

**Q2.** Same facts. Delta further argues that (a) after the MOA was signed, Echo sent a term sheet proposing additional details on the payment schedule and closing documents, which Delta rejected, so the term sheet was a counter-offer showing that there was no meeting of the minds; and (b) the consideration is defective because PHP 5,000,000.00 of the debt credited under the MOA was owed not to Echo but to Foxtrot Corp., Echo's sister company, which is not a party to the MOA. The evidence shows that on the day the MOA was signed, Delta's chairperson signed a receipt acknowledging a down payment and stating that the total credited included the outstanding payable to "Echo/Foxtrot." Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. (a) The term sheet did not undo the perfected MOA. (b) Delta is estopped from questioning the inclusion of Foxtrot's credit in the consideration.
- **Legal basis:** In Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc. (G.R. No. 248256, April 17, 2023), the Court held that a later term sheet that did not change, amend, revise or deviate from the purpose of a complete MOA was only a recommended addendum and could not affect the validity of the perfected contract. It also held the debtor estopped from claiming that the consideration was defective for including the credits of the creditor's affiliate, because its chairperson had acknowledged in writing that the down payment and the total amount received included payables to both companies.
- **Application:** (a) The MOA already contained all the requisites of a valid contract: the parties' consent, the warehouse, and the price. Echo's term sheet only proposed details on payment schedule and documents without altering the object, the price or the purpose of the MOA, so it was a mere recommended addendum and not a counter-offer that prevented perfection. (b) Delta's own chairperson acknowledged, on the day the MOA was signed, that the amounts credited included the payable to "Echo/Foxtrot." Having represented that Foxtrot's credit formed part of the consideration, Delta cannot now deny it to escape the contract.
- **Conclusion:** The MOA remains a perfected and binding dacion en pago, and Delta must comply with it.

**Q3.** After losing in the RTC and the CA, Delta files a Rule 45 petition before the Supreme Court, arguing that the MOA is void for lack of consent because no board resolution authorized its president to sign it. Delta enumerates the recognized exceptions to the rule that only questions of law may be raised, but does not show which exception applies. Will the Supreme Court review this issue?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Whether the signatory was authorized by a board resolution is a question of fact that the Supreme Court will not review under Rule 45, and Delta has not shown that an exception applies.
- **Legal basis:** In a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court, only questions of law may be raised. The presence or absence of board resolutions authorizing the signatories of an agreement is a question of fact. A party that merely cites the exceptions without clearly establishing which one applies is not entitled to relaxation, because those who seek exemption from a procedural rule bear the burden of proving an exceptionally meritorious reason (Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 248256, April 17, 2023, citing Waterfront Cebu City Casino Hotel, Inc. v. Ledesma).
- **Application:** Delta's argument would require the Court to determine from the evidence whether a board resolution existed and whether its president was in fact authorized. That is a factual matter for the trial court, already passed upon below. Listing the exceptions without demonstrating that one fits the case does not discharge Delta's burden to justify a departure from the rule.
- **Conclusion:** The Supreme Court will not review the alleged lack of board authority, and the finding of consent stands.

> Note: The decision quotes the RTC as citing "Article 218" of the Civil Code for the requisites of a contract; the provision is Art. 1318, which the Supreme Court itself quotes. Figures in the quoted documents vary slightly: the MOA states the receivable as PHP 15,289,897.70 in its whereas clause and PHP 15,298,897.70 in its computation, Alba's receipt totals PHP 15,289,897.00, and the check number appears as both 255015 and 225015. The digest uses the figures as the Court states them. The caption reads "Kamera World Inc." while the body uses "Kameraworld." The Supreme Court did not itself discuss Art. 1191; the CA's reliance on it is carried only through the adopted dispositive portion.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68969)

## Equitable PCIBank v. Spouses Lacson

**EQUITABLE PCIBANK, PETITIONER, VS. SPOUSES MAXIMO AND SOLEDAD LACSON AND MARIETTA F. YUCHING, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 256144 | 2023-03-06 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds  
**Syllabus topic:** XII. Damages > B. Actual and Compensatory Damages > 1. Concept  
**Specific topics:** Actual damages must be proved with reasonable certainty (Art. 2199, Civil Code); Check kiting; a bank that dishonors kited checks suffers no loss equal to their face value; Possible measure of loss: interest or time value of amounts credited; Exemplary damages require prior entitlement to compensatory or other damages (Art. 2229); Attorney's fees fall with exemplary damages (Art. 2208)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 1. Standards > b. Preponderance of Evidence)

### Doctrine
Actual or compensatory damages (Art. 2199, Civil Code) compensate for a pecuniary loss actually sustained. They **cannot be presumed**: the claimant must prove (1) the fact of injury or loss and (2) the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty, by competent proof and the best evidence obtainable (reiterated). **A bank that dishonors a depositor's checks drawn against insufficient funds or a closed account suffers no actual loss equal to their face value.** No collection is made and nothing is charged against the bank; the money never leaves its ledger and custody. Even if check kiting is proved, the bank must still prove that it suffered injury as a result.

The Court observed that in a kiting scheme the bank's actual damage could instead take the form of **interest on the amounts credited to the kiting accounts**, from crediting until discovery or reversal. During that time the depositor used the bank's credit, so the amount is treated as borrowed and the depositor answers for its time value. Such interest must be claimed and proved.

**Exemplary damages** (Art. 2229) are awarded only in addition to moral, temperate, liquidated, or compensatory damages. They are not a matter of right. The claimant must first establish a right to one of those damages, and the wrongful act must be accompanied by bad faith, done in a wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive, or malevolent manner. Without compensatory damages, exemplary damages cannot be awarded. Absent a stipulation, **attorney's fees** (Art. 2208) are recoverable only in the cases the law allows, such as when exemplary damages are awarded, so they fall with the exemplary damages (reiterated).

### Facts
Spouses Maximo and Soledad Lacson and their daughter maintained two current accounts with the C.M. Recto branch of Equitable PCIBank (EPCIB), now BDO Unibank. They used both to issue checks for their textile business. EPCIB alleged that, beset by collection problems, the Lacsons engaged in check kiting from November 2002 to January 2003, in connivance with branch manager Marietta Yuching, who allegedly exceeded her authority. They repeatedly drew checks on one account and deposited them in the other without sufficient funds, mostly "on us" or same-branch checks, and issued 214 checks that proved to be drawn against insufficient funds. The scheme ended when two of their checks, each with a face value of PHP 10 million, were dishonored for being drawn against a closed account.

On January 7, 2003, Yuching reported the kiting to her superiors, and the bank immediately stopped all activity in the Lacsons' accounts. The Lacsons promised to sign a real estate mortgage to settle their obligations but did not. On June 4, 2003, EPCIB sued the Lacsons and Yuching for sum of money and damages, with a prayer for preliminary attachment. Yuching denied any connivance and said the Lacsons had turned over eight TCTs and post-dated checks toward settlement. The Lacsons denied any fraud, complained of unexplained deductions without debit memos, and maintained that there was no actual withdrawal of PHP 20 million from either account.

On June 11, 2018, the RTC ordered the Spouses Lacson to pay PHP 20 million as actual damages, representing the dishonored checks, with 6% interest from finality. It held the Spouses Lacson and Yuching solidarily liable for PHP 500,000.00 exemplary damages, PHP 300,000.00 attorney's fees, and costs. On January 25, 2021, the CA reversed, dismissed the complaint, and lifted the writ of attachment on four of the Lacsons' properties. It denied EPCIB's motion for reconsideration on March 10, 2021. EPCIB filed a Rule 45 petition.

### Issues
1. Whether EPCIB proved by preponderance of evidence that it is entitled to PHP 20 million as actual damages.
2. Whether EPCIB is entitled to exemplary damages, attorney's fees, and costs of suit.

### Ruling
**1. No.** The issues were a mere rehash of those the CA had resolved, and the CA committed no reversible error. Actual damages "cannot be presumed" and "cannot be anchored on mere surmises, speculations, or conjectures." The claimant must point to specific facts that afford a basis for measuring the loss. The RTC awarded PHP 20 million, the value of the dishonored checks, without distinctly stating its factual basis. A check is dishonored by non-payment or non-acceptance when payment or acceptance is refused or cannot be obtained (NIL, Secs. 83 and 149). In both cases no actual collection is made and no expense is charged against the bank. **By dishonoring the checks, EPCIB "was able to successfully abate, thwart, or forestall any potential loss." "The money being claimed as actual damages never left EPCIB's ledger and custody,"** and the Lacsons had no obligation to return an amount never disbursed to them. EPCIB itself admitted that in normal checking transactions a bank suffers no harm when checks are dishonored. Its flow charts of the kiting showed how balances were built up, but EPCIB never showed or alleged that PHP 20 million or any other amount left its coffers through collection, withdrawal, or other disbursement. **"Even granting, arguendo, that the Lacsons indeed committed check kiting, the Bank does not automatically become entitled to the award of compensatory damages,"** because it must still prove injury.

The Court added that EPCIB's actual damage could have been interest on the amounts in the Lacsons' accounts attributable to the kiting, from crediting until discovery or reversal. During that time the amounts were under the Lacsons' control and gave them business credit, so they "should be treated as having been borrowed" and the Lacsons would answer for their time value. But the petition said nothing about such interest.

**2. No.** Exemplary damages may be imposed only in addition to compensatory or other damages and are not recoverable as a matter of right. The claimant must first establish a right to moral, temperate, liquidated, or compensatory damages, and the wrongful act must be accompanied by bad faith. **Since EPCIB was not entitled to actual or compensatory damages, the first and second requisites were unavailing, and the RTC's award of exemplary damages was improper.** Absent a stipulation, attorney's fees are recoverable only in particular cases, such as when exemplary damages are awarded (Art. 2208). With the exemplary damages deleted, the attorney's fees were likewise omitted.

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The CA Decision dated January 25, 2021 and Resolution dated March 10, 2021 in CA-G.R. CV No. 114270 were AFFIRMED. This left in place the dismissal of EPCIB's complaint and the lifting of the writ of attachment.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Over two months, depositor Dante issued numerous checks from his current account in Bank X and deposited them in his other current account in the same branch, though neither account had sufficient funds, building up large paper balances. Bank X discovered the scheme, froze both accounts, and dishonored two of Dante's checks of PHP 5 million each for being drawn against a closed account. No cash was ever paid out to Dante on these checks. Bank X sued Dante for PHP 10 million as actual damages, proving the kiting scheme through detailed flow charts. Should the court award PHP 10 million as actual damages?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Bank X is not entitled to PHP 10 million as actual damages because it suffered no loss in that amount.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 2199 of the Civil Code, actual or compensatory damages are recoverable only for pecuniary loss duly proved. The claimant must prove the fact of loss and its actual amount with a reasonable degree of certainty; actual damages cannot be presumed. When a bank dishonors a check, no collection is made and no expense is charged against it. Even if check kiting is proved, the bank must still prove that it suffered injury (Equitable PCIBank v. Spouses Lacson, G.R. No. 256144, March 6, 2023).
- **Application:** Bank X dishonored the two PHP 5 million checks, and no cash was paid out on them. The PHP 10 million never left the bank's ledger and custody, and Dante has no obligation to return money he never received. The flow charts prove the scheme but not a loss. By dishonoring the checks, the bank forestalled any loss in their face amount.
- **Conclusion:** The court should not award PHP 10 million as actual damages.

**Q2.** Same facts as the previous problem, except that before the scheme was discovered, Bank X allowed Dante to withdraw PHP 3 million in cash against the uncollected kited deposits, and Dante never returned it. Bank X proves the withdrawals with withdrawal slips and its ledger. (a) Is Bank X entitled to actual damages? (b) Apart from cash actually paid out, what other loss may a bank claim for the period the kited balances stayed in the depositor's accounts?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, Bank X may recover PHP 3 million as actual damages. (b) The bank may claim interest on the amounts credited through the kiting, for the period they stood in the depositor's accounts until discovery or reversal, if it claims and proves it.
- **Legal basis:** Actual damages require proof of the fact of loss and of its amount with reasonable certainty, by competent proof and the best evidence obtainable (Art. 2199, Civil Code). In Equitable PCIBank v. Spouses Lacson (G.R. No. 256144, March 6, 2023), the Court denied actual damages because the bank failed to show that any amount "left its coffers through collection, withdrawal, or any other form of disbursement." It added that a bank's actual damage from kiting could be interest on the amounts credited to the depositor's accounts, which are treated as borrowed from the bank and answerable for their time value. The bank in that case lost because it did not claim this interest.
- **Application:** (a) Unlike in Equitable PCIBank, money actually left Bank X's coffers: PHP 3 million in cash was withdrawn against uncollected deposits and never returned. The loss and its amount are proved by withdrawal slips and the ledger, so actual damages of PHP 3 million are proper. (b) For the kited balances that were never paid out, Dante enjoyed the bank's credit while they stood in his accounts. Bank X may claim interest on those amounts from crediting until discovery or reversal, but it must plead and prove it.
- **Conclusion:** Bank X may recover the PHP 3 million actually disbursed, and may also claim interest on the kited balances if pleaded and proved.

**Q3.** In a bank's suit against a depositor for check kiting, the trial court found that the depositor acted fraudulently and in bad faith. But it held that the bank suffered no actual loss because all the kited checks were dishonored and nothing was paid out. The bank never claimed moral, temperate, or liquidated damages, and there is no stipulation on attorney's fees. Nonetheless, the trial court awarded the bank PHP 500,000.00 exemplary damages "to deter kiting" and PHP 300,000.00 attorney's fees. Are these awards proper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Both the exemplary damages and the attorney's fees should be deleted.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 2229 of the Civil Code, exemplary damages are imposed by way of example or correction only in addition to moral, temperate, liquidated, or compensatory damages. They are not recoverable as a matter of right. The claimant must first establish a right to one of those damages, and the wrongful act must be accompanied by bad faith. Under Article 2208, absent stipulation, attorney's fees are recoverable only in the cases enumerated, such as when exemplary damages are awarded. In Equitable PCIBank v. Spouses Lacson (G.R. No. 256144, March 6, 2023), the Court upheld the deletion of exemplary damages and attorney's fees because the bank was not entitled to actual damages.
- **Application:** The depositor's fraud and bad faith satisfy only one requisite. The bank has no award of compensatory, moral, temperate, or liquidated damages to which exemplary damages could attach. Deterrence alone cannot support exemplary damages. With the exemplary damages gone, no other ground under Article 2208 is shown, and there is no stipulation, so the attorney's fees must also go.
- **Conclusion:** The awards of exemplary damages and attorney's fees are improper and must be deleted.

> Note: No separate opinions. The daughter's name appears inconsistently in the E-Library text ("Nonnita" and "Normita"), so the digest does not name her. The statement that the bank's actual damage could have been interest on the kited amounts is the Court's observation of what the bank might have claimed; it was not awarded because the bank never asked for it. The decision did not rule on whether Yuching connived in the scheme. The Negotiable Instruments Law is not a separate heading in the 2027 Commercial Law syllabus, so the case is mapped to Civil Law (Damages).

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68853)

# Labor Law and Social Legislation

## Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel (Resolution)

**HACIENDA SAN ISIDRO / SILOS FARMS AND REY SILOS LLAMADO, PETITIONERS, VS. LUCITO VILLARUEL AND HELEN VILLARUEL, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 220087 | 2025-08-11 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Resolution

**Bar subject:** Labor Law and Social Legislation  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Employment Relationship > A. Employer-Employee Relationship > 2. Determination of Employer-Employee Relationship > a. Fourfold Test  
**Specific topics:** Control test: right to control both the end and the manner and means; Burden on the claimant to prove control by substantial evidence; Art. 295 is not a test for the existence of an employment relationship; Gapayao v. Fulo's reading of Mercado and its application of the control test corrected; Requisites for regular seasonal employment maintained
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45))

### Doctrine
On the employer's motion for reconsideration, the Court **maintained** the two requisites for regular seasonal employment laid down in its November 13, 2023 Decision: (1) seasonal work or services; and (2) employment for more than one season. It also kept the rule that pakyaw pay does not negate regular employment if the employer has the right to control. It nonetheless **set aside the Decision and reversed the CA**, because the worker never proved that right.

**Under the control test, the employer must reserve the right to control not only the end achieved but also the manner and means used to reach it. The worker claiming benefits bears the burden of proving that right by substantial evidence, and the control must be of a level that interferes with the means and methods of accomplishing the assigned tasks.** Rules that merely serve as guidelines toward a mutually desired result, without dictating means and methods, do not establish an employment relationship. The fact that a person works on the alleged employer's farm does not automatically mean the farm owner controlled, or reserved the right to control, the means and methods of the work. The Court clarified *Gapayao v. Fulo* on two points:
- *Gapayao* applied the control test incompletely. It presumed control from farm ownership and the right to review the quality of output, which shows control of the end only.
- *Gapayao* misappreciated *Mercado*. Freedom to offer services to other farm owners was merely an added observation of the Labor Arbiter in *Mercado*, not its ratio decidendi. *Mercado* rested on on-and-off hiring.

**Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code is not a criterion for determining whether an employer-employee relationship exists.** It only distinguishes regular from casual employees, and it does not apply where the relationship itself is disputed. The following do not by themselves prove employment: length of service, repeated assignment of tasks, and receipt of wages, which is only one prong of the four-fold test. In a Rule 45 petition, uniform factual findings of the LA, NLRC and CA bind the Court only if supported by substantial evidence. Factual review is allowed in exceptional cases.

### Facts
In its November 13, 2023 Decision, the Court denied petitioners' Rule 45 petition and affirmed the CA's January 9, 2015 Amended Decision, which declared respondent Helen Villaruel a regular seasonal employee of Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms. The Decision held that she met the requisites for regular seasonal employment. It held that her freedom to work elsewhere and her pakyaw pay did not matter. It also held that petitioners "could easily exercise control" over her because she worked on their hacienda.

Petitioners moved for reconsideration. They argued as follows:
- They had no control over the manner by which Helen did her work, and the finding of control rested on an unfounded assumption that they could easily supervise her.
- She was free to contract her services with other employers.
- *Hacienda Fatima* did not distinguish between workers hired on and off for a single phase and workers hired repeatedly for the same phases, so the Court erred in holding *Mercado* inapplicable.

Respondents opposed the motion as pro forma for raising no new matter.

The record of the lower tribunals stood as follows. The NLRC first held (September 30, 2011) that Helen was not an employee, then reversed itself on January 27, 2012. The CA first held (March 27, 2013) that she was not an employee for failure to prove control, then reversed itself in its January 9, 2015 Amended Decision. In their Position Paper, petitioners had disputed the very existence of an employer-employee relationship.

### Issues
1. Whether the Court may review the lower tribunals' factual finding that petitioners had the right to control Helen's work.
2. Whether Hacienda Fatima distinguished workers hired on and off for any single phase from those hired repeatedly for the same phases, and whether freedom to contract with other employers by itself negates regular seasonal employment.
3. Whether Helen proved by substantial evidence that petitioners had the right to control the manner and means of her work.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the factual finding may be reviewed.** Petitioners' claim that they lacked control raises a question of fact, which is generally beyond a Rule 45 petition. The rule has exceptions, however. Examples include findings grounded entirely on speculation, surmises or conjectures; inferences that are manifestly mistaken, absurd or impossible; grave abuse of discretion; and judgments based on a misapprehension of facts. These exceptions were present. The Court rejected petitioners' claim that the LA, NLRC and CA did not uniformly find Helen a regular employee. The NLRC and the CA each reversed themselves, so in the end all three found her regular. But uniform findings bind the Court only if supported by substantial evidence, and here they were not.

**2. Hacienda Fatima did draw the distinction, but freedom to work elsewhere is not decisive.** *Hacienda Fatima* held *Mercado* inapplicable because the *Mercado* workers "were not hired regularly and repeatedly for the same phase/s of agricultural work, but on and off for any single phase thereof." That holding plainly distinguishes the two kinds of workers. *Gapayao*, which petitioners invoked, "misappreciated *Mercado, Sr.*" In *Mercado*, the workers' freedom to offer their services to other farm owners was merely an added observation of the LA, whose findings the Court found supported by evidence. That freedom was not the ratio decidendi. *Mercado* rested on the on-and-off nature of the hiring, and the freedom to work elsewhere was merely the logical result of that hiring.

**3. No, Helen did not prove the right of control, so the CA erred.** The control test requires the right to control both the end achieved and the manner and means of reaching it. It requires the existence of the right, not its exercise. *Gapayao* stated the test correctly, but it "incompletely applied the test." It found only that the farm owner could review the quality of the work, which is control of the result, and made no finding on the manner and means. Even if petitioners could be presumed to have the right to review Helen's output, the right to control the manner and means could not be presumed. Helen had the burden of proving it by substantial evidence, and she failed.

None of the tribunals below found such control:
- The LA relied on the nature of Helen's work and her length of service. But "length of service and the repeated act of assigning tasks do not automatically result in entitlement to the rights and privileges of a regular employee."
- The NLRC relied on her work at the farm since 1978 and her receipt of wages. But receipt of wages "is but one prong in the four-fold test and is not a conclusive factor."
- The CA relied on Art. 280 (now 295). But that article "should not be used as a criterion to determine the existence of an employer-employee relationship," and it does not apply where the relationship is disputed, as it was here. The CA wrongly stated that petitioners never denied that Helen was an employee. They disputed it in their Position Paper, and the LA acknowledged the dispute.

Control must be of a level that interferes with the means and methods of the work. Guidelines toward a mutually desired result do not suffice. The CA therefore "seriously erred" in not finding grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC, whose findings lacked substantial evidence. The Court quoted *Javier v. Fly Ace Corp.*: social justice does not mean "that every labor dispute will be automatically decided in favor of labor," and management's rights are also entitled to respect.

### Disposition
The Motion for Reconsideration was GRANTED. The Court SET ASIDE its November 13, 2023 Decision and rendered a new one GRANTING the Petition for Review on Certiorari. It REVERSED and SET ASIDE the CA's January 9, 2015 Amended Decision and July 20, 2015 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 07025. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Lina filed an illegal dismissal complaint against Finca Verde, a sugarcane farm. She alleged that she had worked on the farm every milling season since 1990, planting and weeding, and was paid per task. Finca Verde denied that she was ever its employee. The Labor Arbiter, the NLRC and the Court of Appeals (on certiorari) all ruled that she was a regular employee. They reasoned that her work was necessary or desirable to the farm's business, that she had worked for many seasons, and that she received wages from the farm. None of them found that Finca Verde had the right to control how she did her tasks, and the record has no evidence on that point. On Finca Verde's Rule 45 petition, should the Supreme Court sustain the finding that Lina was a regular employee?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Lina failed to prove an employer-employee relationship, because she offered no substantial evidence that Finca Verde had the right to control the manner and means of her work.
- **Legal basis:** Under the control test, the employer must reserve the right to control not only the end achieved but also the manner and means of reaching it. The worker claiming the benefits must prove that right by substantial evidence. Art. 295 of the Labor Code is not a criterion for determining whether an employment relationship exists, and it does not apply where the relationship is disputed. Length of service and repeated assignment of tasks do not automatically make one a regular employee. Receipt of wages is only one prong of the four-fold test. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025, Resolution.)
- **Application:** Finca Verde denied the existence of any employment relationship, so the threshold issue is whether Lina was an employee at all. The tribunals relied on Art. 295, which presupposes an employment relationship and so cannot be used to prove one. They also relied on her years of service and her wages, but neither proves control. No tribunal found, and no evidence shows, that Finca Verde could dictate how Lina planted or weeded. That she worked on the farm does not mean the farm controlled her means and methods. Because the uniform findings rest on no substantial evidence of control, they do not bind the Court, and the CA erred in not finding grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC.
- **Conclusion:** The Supreme Court should reverse the finding that Lina was a regular employee, because the right of control was not proved.

**Q2.** Assume instead that Lina presented the farm's written instructions. They fix the depth and spacing of canepoints, the weeding method, and the daily schedule, and they authorize the farm's overseer to reassign or correct workers who deviate. The overseer rarely inspected her work. Lina was paid on a pakyaw basis, was hired every season for the same planting and weeding tasks, and in the off-season worked on neighboring farms. Is Lina a regular employee?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Lina is a regular seasonal employee of Finca Verde.
- **Legal basis:** A seasonal employee is regular if (1) the work or services are seasonal in nature and (2) the employee is employed for that work for more than one season. Pakyaw pay does not negate regular employment if the employer has the right to control. The control test requires only the existence of the right to control the end and the manner and means, not its actual exercise. Freedom to offer services to other farm owners does not by itself negate regular status. In Mercado, that freedom was merely an added observation of the Labor Arbiter, and the ruling rested on on-and-off hiring. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025, Resolution, maintaining the November 13, 2023 Decision on these points.)
- **Application:** The written instructions dictate how the work is done (depth, spacing, method and schedule), and the overseer may correct deviations. This is control over the manner and means, not mere guidelines toward a result, and it is proven by documents. It does not matter that the overseer seldom inspected, because the right need not be exercised. With the employment relationship established, Lina meets both requisites: planting and weeding are seasonal, and she was hired for the same tasks every season. Her pakyaw pay is only a method of computing wages. Her off-season work on other farms does not matter, because she was hired repeatedly for the same tasks, not on and off for single phases.
- **Conclusion:** Lina is a regular seasonal employee because the right of control is proven and both requisites are present.

**Q3.** In a farm worker's case, the Labor Arbiter, the NLRC and the CA all found an employer-employee relationship. The employer filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court. The worker's counsel argues that (a) the uniform factual findings of the three tribunals are binding on the Supreme Court and cannot be reviewed under Rule 45, and (b) under the constitutional policy of social justice and full protection to labor, any doubt must be resolved in the worker's favor, so the employer's petition must fail. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Not necessarily. Uniform findings bind the Court only if supported by substantial evidence, and the Court may review facts in recognized exceptional cases. (b) No. Social justice does not mean that every labor dispute is automatically decided in favor of labor.
- **Legal basis:** Only questions of law are generally raised under Rule 45. This rule admits of exceptions, such as when the conclusion is grounded entirely on speculation, surmises or conjectures; when the inference is manifestly mistaken, absurd or impossible; when there is grave abuse of discretion; or when the judgment is based on a misapprehension of facts. The principle that uniform factual findings of labor tribunals bind the Court applies only if the findings are supported by substantial evidence. Quoting Javier v. Fly Ace Corp., the Court held that the policy of social justice does not mean "that every labor dispute will be automatically decided in favor of labor." Management also has rights entitled to respect, and justice is for the deserving, in light of the established facts and the applicable law. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025, Resolution.)
- **Application:** (a) If the tribunals found an employment relationship without substantial evidence of the right to control, their findings rest on conjecture or a misapprehension of facts. The Court may then review and reverse them despite their uniformity. (b) The worker still bears the burden of proving the employment relationship by substantial evidence. The pro-labor policy does not relieve her of that burden or allow the Court to presume control. If the evidence fails, the employer's petition should be granted.
- **Conclusion:** Neither the uniformity of the findings nor the social justice policy shields the ruling from reversal when the employment relationship was not proven by substantial evidence.

> Note: Cross-reference: this Resolution sets aside Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023 (case id gr-220087-20231113). It keeps that Decision's doctrine on the two requisites for regular seasonal employment and on pakyaw workers, but reverses the result. Doubt: the fallo reverses and sets aside the CA Amended Decision and Resolution in full and does not say what ruling replaces them or expressly dispose of Helen's complaint. The Rule 45 petition had assailed the CA only insofar as it declared Helen a regular employee and awarded her backwages and separation pay. The CA Amended Decision also contained rulings on Lucito (just dismissal, money awards, and attorney's fees for both spouses), which the Resolution does not discuss. The Resolution also does not rule expressly on respondents' objection that the motion was pro forma.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70026)

## Pacific Ocean Manning, Inc. v. Bobiles

**PACIFIC OCEAN MANNING, INC. AND/OR V. SHIPS UK LTD./NORDIC AMERICAN TANKERS LIMITED, PETITIONERS, VS. NICOLAS F. BOBILES, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 259982 | 2024-10-28 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Labor Law and Social Legislation  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Social Legislation > D. Disability and Death Benefits > 2. Seafarers (RA 12021, Secs. 22, 28–29, 32, 57, and its IRR; 2010 POEA Standard Employment Contract)  
**Specific topics:** Attorney's fees under Article 111 of the Labor Code: only for unlawful withholding of wages; Article 2208(2), Civil Code: litigation or expense must be with third persons (wrongful act doctrine); Article 2208(8), Civil Code: only actions under workmen's compensation and employer's liability laws, not POEA-SEC claims; 120/240-day rule; an assessment with a contemporaneous re-evaluation order is not final; Third-doctor referral not required without a valid final assessment
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (XII. Damages > B. Actual and Compensatory Damages > 4. Attorney's Fees and Expenses of Litigation)

### Doctrine
**The Court clarified the rules on attorney's fees in worker disability and death indemnification cases:**

- **Article 111 of the Labor Code** (attorney's fees of 10% of the wages recovered) applies **only to cases of unlawful withholding of wages**. It does not apply to claims involving only disability or death benefits. The statement in Heirs of Aniban v. NLRC that Article 111 is not limited to withheld wages is "inaccurate"; Article 111 sits under the Labor Code chapter on "Payment of Wages."
- **Article 2208(2) of the Civil Code** (defendant's act compelled the plaintiff "to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect [their] interest") applies **only when the litigation or expense is in relation to third persons**, not the defendant itself (the "wrongful act doctrine"). The litigation with third persons may be in the same suit. It must be the natural and proximate consequence of the defendant's wrongful act and be incurred necessarily and in good faith. Being compelled to sue the defendant itself is not enough; otherwise attorney's fees would become the rule rather than the exception, and a premium would be placed on the right to litigate.
- **Article 2208(8)** (actions for indemnity under workmen's compensation and employer's liability laws) applies only to actions under those laws, now Title II, Book IV of the Labor Code on employees' compensation. It **does not apply to disability claims based on contract, such as the POEA-SEC.**
- An award under the catch-all **Article 2208(11)** requires a factual, legal, or equitable justification.

On disability benefits (reiterated): the company-designated physician must issue a final assessment within 120 days, extendible to 240 days only with sufficient justification, which the employer must prove (Elburg Shipmanagement v. Quiogue). **An assessment is not final when the physician, on the same date, finds that the seafarer still needs treatment or re-evaluation** (Benhur Shipping v. Riego). Without a valid, final, and definite assessment within the period, the law deems the disability total and permanent, and the seafarer need not go through the third-doctor referral under the POEA-SEC.

### Facts
Pacific Ocean Manning, Inc. (POMI), the local agent of V. Ships UK Ltd., hired Nicolas Bobiles on October 17, 2016 as pumpman on the vessel Nordic Vega. His POEA-approved contract was covered by a CBA. On January 27, 2017, while lifting equipment for repair, he felt something snap in his back. He was disembarked in Vadinar, India on February 27, 2017, diagnosed there with L2-L3 instability, and repatriated on February 28, 2017. The company-designated physicians diagnosed L4-L5 disc herniation with radiculopathy and put him on physical therapy.

In a June 14, 2017 report, the company physician noted continuing low back pain and stiffness, told Bobiles to continue therapy and medication, and set a re-evaluation for June 30, 2017. On September 4, 2017, the company physician gave a Grade 11 disability assessment. A medical certificate of the same date, however, said the patient was "status quo," told him to continue his home exercises, and set a re-evaluation for October 11, 2017. Bobiles' own doctor, Dr. Magtira, declared him permanently unfit for sea duty on October 30, 2017. POMI offered USD 7,465.00 based on Grade 11. In grievance proceedings POMI was willing to refer him to a third doctor, but his representative moved to end the proceedings.

The Voluntary Arbitrator (NCMB) awarded USD 102,308.00 in total and permanent disability compensation under the CBA, plus 10% attorney's fees. The CA ruled that the CBA rates applied only to disability resulting from an accident, which this was not. It reduced the award to USD 60,000.00 under the POEA-SEC schedule but affirmed the attorney's fees, citing Article 111 of the Labor Code and Article 2208 of the Civil Code. In its Resolution denying reconsideration, the CA stressed that the September 4, 2017 assessment came 188 days after repatriation, with no explanation for missing the 120-day period. POMI filed a Rule 45 petition. It argued that Bobiles had refused a third-doctor referral, that the extension of the treatment period was justified, and that attorney's fees were not due because it had paid for all his treatment and his full sickness allowance.

### Issues
1. Whether respondent's failure to go through the third-doctor referral under the POEA-SEC bars his claim for total and permanent disability benefits.
2. Whether the extension of the treatment period to 240 days was justified, and whether the Grade 11 assessment of September 4, 2017 was a final assessment.
3. Whether respondent is entitled to attorney's fees under Article 111 of the Labor Code or Article 2208 of the Civil Code.

### Ruling
**1. No.** Under Marlow Navigation v. Osias and Paleracio v. Sealanes, referral to a third doctor is mandatory only when there is a valid and timely assessment by the company-designated physician and the seafarer's doctor disputes it. **Without a conclusive and definite assessment from the company-designated physician, compliance with the third-doctor provision is not needed, and the law steps in to treat the disability as total and permanent.**

**2. The extension was justified, but the September 4, 2017 assessment was not final.** The 120th day from repatriation (February 28, 2017) was June 28, 2017, and no final assessment was issued by then. Under Paleracio, the physician must perform a significant act to justify an extension. Here the June 14, 2017 report found continuing pain, referred Bobiles to a physiatrist, ordered more therapy and medication, and set a re-evaluation, which showed that he needed further treatment and justified the 240-day period. But the September 4, 2017 Grade 11 assessment was accompanied by a medical certificate of the same date setting a re-evaluation for October 11, 2017. Following Benhur Shipping v. Riego, **an assessment is not final when the physician contemporaneously finds that the seafarer still needs treatment or re-evaluation.** With no final assessment within the extended period, the law deems Bobiles' disability total and permanent. The CBA covered only "permanent disability as a result of an accident," which this was not, so the CA correctly applied the POEA-SEC schedule (USD 50,000.00 x 120% = USD 60,000.00), with 6% legal interest from finality.

**3. No attorney's fees.** The Court noted that it had been inconsistent on this issue in earlier POMI cases (Langam and Anuat denied fees; Balbarino granted them under Art. 2208(2); Castillo under Art. 2208(8)) and clarified:

(a) *Article 111 does not apply.* It speaks only of "unlawful withholding of wages" and fees on "the amount of wages recovered," and it falls under the chapter on "Payment of Wages." Heirs of Aniban, which said otherwise in a death benefits case, is "inaccurate"; G.J.T. Rebuilders and T&H Shopfitters correctly limit Article 111 to withheld wages. **This case involves disability compensation, not wages.**

(b) *Article 2208(2) does not apply.* The provision requires that the plaintiff be compelled "to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect [their] interest." Drawing on Vicente Francisco, American Jurisprudence, and the "wrongful act doctrine" (where A's tort involves B in litigation with C, B may recover counsel fees from A), the Court held that the doctrine requires litigation with a third party. That litigation may be in the same suit, but it must be the natural and proximate consequence of the wrongful act and be incurred necessarily and in good faith. In Borden Co. v. Doctors Pharmaceuticals, the Court en banc denied fees because the respondent was compelled to litigate only with the petitioner. **Expense, too, must be in relation to third persons, "[a] contrary rule would render Article 2208(2) applicable in virtually every case."** Here, petitioners compelled Bobiles to litigate only against them.

(c) *Article 2208(8) does not apply.* It covers actions for indemnity under workmen's compensation and employer's liability laws (formerly Act No. 3428 and Act No. 1874, now Title II, Book IV of the Labor Code). **Bobiles' claim rests on contract, the POEA-SEC**, not on those laws.

(d) *Article 2208(11) does not justify the award either.* Under Estate of Buan v. Camaganacan, a discretionary award needs a factual, legal, or equitable justification. Apart from the bare claim that he was forced to litigate, none was shown. Petitioners had paid all his treatment costs and full sickness allowances, so it was "only equitable" to delete the fees.

### Disposition
The Petition was PARTLY GRANTED. The July 15, 2021 Decision and March 22, 2022 Resolution of the CA in CA-G.R. SP No. 158388 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. The award of USD 60,000.00 (or its peso equivalent) for total and permanent disability earns 6% legal interest per annum from finality of the Decision until full payment, and the award of attorney's fees was DELETED.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Seafarer Dante won his claim for total and permanent disability benefits under the POEA-SEC against his manning agency, Blue Sea Manning. Blue Sea had paid for all of Dante's medical treatment and his full sickness allowance while the claim was pending. The Voluntary Arbitrator also awarded Dante 10% attorney's fees. The arbitrator cited Article 111 of the Labor Code and Article 2208(2) and (8) of the Civil Code, reasoning that Dante "was compelled to litigate to protect [their] interest." Is the award of attorney's fees proper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. None of the cited provisions supports the award, and it should be deleted.
- **Legal basis:** Article 111 of the Labor Code allows attorney's fees only in cases of unlawful withholding of wages, not claims involving only disability or death benefits. Article 2208(2) of the Civil Code applies only when the defendant's act compelled the plaintiff to litigate with, or incur expenses in relation to, third persons. Being compelled to sue the defendant itself is not enough. Article 2208(8) covers only actions for indemnity under workmen's compensation and employer's liability laws, not disability claims based on contract such as the POEA-SEC. An award under Article 2208(11) needs a factual, legal, or equitable justification. (Pacific Ocean Manning, Inc. v. Bobiles, G.R. No. 259982, October 28, 2024)
- **Application:** Dante's claim is for disability compensation, not withheld wages, so Article 111 does not apply. He was compelled to litigate only against Blue Sea, not any third person, so Article 2208(2) does not apply. His claim rests on the POEA-SEC, a contract, not on the employees' compensation provisions of the Labor Code, so Article 2208(8) does not apply. Nor is there any equitable reason under Article 2208(11): Blue Sea paid all of Dante's treatment and his full sickness allowance, and the bare claim that he was forced to litigate is not enough.
- **Conclusion:** The award of attorney's fees is improper and should be deleted.

**Q2.** Seaman Ernesto was medically repatriated on March 1, 2025 for a back injury. On day 110, the company-designated physician noted that he still needed physical therapy and set a re-evaluation date. On day 200, the physician issued a "final" Grade 10 disability assessment. A medical certificate the physician signed that same day, however, stated that Ernesto's condition was unchanged and directed him to return for re-evaluation a month later. Ernesto's own doctor declared him permanently unfit for sea duty. Ernesto then filed a claim for total and permanent disability benefits without asking for a third doctor. (a) Is his failure to seek a third-doctor referral fatal to his claim? (b) Is he entitled to total and permanent disability benefits?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The third-doctor referral is not required because there was no valid final assessment. (b) Yes. His disability is deemed total and permanent by operation of law.
- **Legal basis:** The company-designated physician must issue a final assessment within 120 days, extendible to 240 days with sufficient justification, such as the seafarer's need for further treatment, which the employer must prove. If no final assessment is issued within the applicable period, the disability becomes total and permanent. An assessment is not final when the physician contemporaneously finds that the seafarer still needs treatment or re-evaluation. Referral to a third doctor is mandatory only when there is a valid and timely assessment by the company-designated physician that the seafarer's doctor disputes. (Pacific Ocean Manning, Inc. v. Bobiles, G.R. No. 259982, October 28, 2024, applying Elburg Shipmanagement v. Quiogue and Benhur Shipping v. Riego)
- **Application:** The physician's day-110 finding that Ernesto still needed therapy justified extending the period to 240 days. The day-200 Grade 10 assessment fell within the extended period, but a certificate of the same date said his condition was unchanged and ordered a re-evaluation, so the assessment was not final or definite. With no valid final assessment within 240 days, the law deems Ernesto's disability total and permanent. Since there was no valid assessment to dispute, the third-doctor mechanism never came into play.
- **Conclusion:** Ernesto's claim is not barred by the lack of a third-doctor referral, and he is entitled to total and permanent disability benefits.

**Q3.** Victor sold a parcel of land to Ana. Unknown to Ana, Victor had earlier sold the same land to Carlos, who then sued Ana to recover it. Ana hired a lawyer and won against Carlos. Ana then sued Victor for damages for breach of warranty. She claimed attorney's fees for (i) defending the suit filed by Carlos and (ii) prosecuting her own suit against Victor, on the sole ground that she was compelled to litigate. Under Article 2208(2) of the Civil Code, which of these attorney's fees may Ana recover from Victor?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Ana may recover from Victor the attorney's fees she incurred in the suit with Carlos, but not, under Article 2208(2), the fees for her own suit against Victor.
- **Legal basis:** Article 2208(2) of the Civil Code allows attorney's fees when the defendant's act or omission has compelled the plaintiff "to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect [their] interest." Under the wrongful act doctrine adopted in Pacific Ocean Manning, Inc. v. Bobiles (G.R. No. 259982, October 28, 2024), the litigation or expense must be in relation to third persons, not the defendant itself. It must also be the natural and proximate consequence of the defendant's wrongful act and be incurred necessarily and in good faith. Being compelled to sue the wrongdoer directly does not justify fees under Article 2208(2); otherwise fees would be due in virtually every case and a premium would be placed on the right to litigate.
- **Application:** Victor's double sale is what drew Ana into the suit with Carlos, a third person. She defended it necessarily and in good faith, so those counsel fees are a recoverable consequence of Victor's wrongful act. Her suit against Victor, however, is litigation with the wrongdoer himself. The bare fact that she was compelled to sue him does not fall under Article 2208(2). She would have to show some other ground under Article 2208, such as gross and evident bad faith or a factual, legal, or equitable justification under paragraph (11).
- **Conclusion:** Under Article 2208(2), Ana recovers only the fees for the suit with Carlos, not the fees for suing Victor.

> Note: Hernando, J., was on official business. The decision says the dispositive portion of the NCMB (Voluntary Arbitrator) decision was copied from the CA Decision, because a copy of that decision was not attached to the Petition. The 2027 syllabus lists RA 12021 alongside the 2010 POEA-SEC under Seafarers. This decision applies only the POEA-SEC and the Elburg rules.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69730)

## Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao

**BOHOL WISDOM SCHOOL, DR. SIMPLICIO YAP, JR., AND RAUL H. DELOSO, PETITIONERS, VS. MIRAFLOR MABAO, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 252124 | 2024-07-23 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Labor Law and Social Legislation  
**Syllabus topic:** VI. Suspension and Termination of Employment > A. Termination or Suspension by Employer > 2. Just Causes (DO 147, s. 2015)  
**Specific topics:** Immorality as a ground for discipline is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality; Premarital sex and pregnancy out of wedlock between persons with no impediment to marry is not immoral; Suspension requires substantive and procedural due process; no substantial compliance when the penalty was decided before hearing the employee; Abandonment: unjustified absence plus overt act showing intent to sever the relationship
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45))

### Doctrine
**Whether an employee's conduct is disgraceful or immoral is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality.** Reiterating Leus v. St. Scholastica's College Westgrove and Inocente v. St. Vincent Foundation, the Court held that **sexual relations between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, even if they result in pregnancy out of wedlock, are not disgraceful or immoral.** No law proscribes them, and they contravene no fundamental state policy in the Constitution. A sectarian school therefore cannot validly suspend a teacher for "immorality" because she became pregnant by her boyfriend before marriage, even if the conduct violates the school's religious standards. Such a suspension is illegal.

A suspension must also satisfy due process. It must rest on a just or authorized cause under the Labor Code, and the employee must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the penalty is decided. There is no "substantial compliance" where no notice to explain was issued and the employer had decided the penalty before hearing the employee.

Abandonment requires (1) failure to report for work or absence without valid or justifiable reason, and (2) a clear intention to sever the employer-employee relationship shown by an overt act. An employee who refuses return-to-work notices after her suspension ends and writes that she "could no longer go back to work for the school" abandons her employment as of that letter, and her money claims accrue only up to that date.

### Facts
Miraflor Mabao had been a grade school teacher at Bohol Wisdom School (BWS) since June 7, 2007 and became regular in 2010. In September 2016 she told the principal and Raul Deloso, head of the Administrative Team, that she was two months pregnant by her boyfriend. Minutes of the Administrative Team meeting on September 21, 2016 showed that, before Mabao was brought into the meeting, the team had already decided to suspend her from September 22, 2016 until she was legally married. On September 22 she was verbally suspended. On September 27 she received a Disciplinary Form imposing "Indefinite suspension until legally married" and a Letter. The Letter cited RA 9710 ("The Magna Carta for Women") but held that premarital sex was immoral and that, as a grade school teacher, she was expected to have the highest moral standards. No written notice to explain was issued.

On October 5, 2016, Mabao married her boyfriend and filed a complaint for illegal suspension, illegal dismissal, separation pay, money claims, damages, and a certificate of employment. BWS sent three return-to-work notices, dated October 7, November 3, and November 22, 2016. Mabao refused to receive them, but she received the first by registered mail on October 24, 2016. In a letter dated November 9, 2016, she replied that the matter was already before the NLRC and that "I could no longer go back to work for the school." Her position paper prayed for separation pay in lieu of reinstatement because of strained relations.

The Labor Arbiter (January 31, 2017) found constructive dismissal and awarded backwages, separation pay, and benefits. The NLRC (May 31, 2017) reversed, finding no constructive dismissal. On certiorari, the CA (September 28, 2018 Decision; January 24, 2020 Resolution, CA-G.R. SP No. 11224) agreed that there was no constructive dismissal but held the suspension illegal. It awarded backwages from September 22 to October 7, 2016, 13th month pay and benefits until November 25, 2016, 10% attorney's fees, and a certificate of employment. BWS, Dr. Simplicio Yap, Jr. (Board Chairman), and Deloso filed a Rule 45 petition. They argued that the suspension was a valid exercise of management prerogative under the school's Christian standard of morality, and that due process was substantially complied with because Mabao was heard, admitted the violation, and agreed to the suspension.

### Issues
1. Whether the Court may review the factual findings in this Rule 45 petition.
2. Whether Mabao was illegally suspended.
3. Whether Mabao abandoned her employment, and when her employment ended.

### Ruling
**1. Yes.** Only questions of law may be raised under Rule 45, but the Court may review the facts when the findings of the lower tribunals are inconsistent on material points, as they were here among the LA, the NLRC, and the CA.

**2. Yes, the suspension was illegal, both substantively and procedurally.** The standard of morality the law applies is "public and secular, not religious," and refers to conduct proscribed because it is detrimental to the conditions on which the existence and progress of human society depend. If government relied on religious beliefs to set public morals, it would require conformity to a religious agenda. Following Leus and Inocente, **sexual intercourse between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, like Mabao and her boyfriend, is not immoral.** No law proscribes it, and it does not contravene any fundamental state policy. Mabao's premarital relations and resulting pregnancy were "not disgraceful or immoral within the contemplation of the law," so her suspension had no valid basis. The Court quoted with approval the CA's statement that "[o]n a secular level, premarital sex is not immoral per se."

The suspension also violated procedural due process. A suspension is reasonable only if it is based on just or authorized causes and the employee is given notice and an opportunity to be heard before judgment. BWS admittedly issued no notice to explain. The September 21, 2016 minutes showed that the Administrative Team decided the penalty before hearing Mabao, so **there was no substantial compliance.**

**3. Yes, Mabao abandoned her work, but as of November 9, 2016, not November 25, 2016.** There was no dismissal. BWS intended to take Mabao back once she married. Her suspension ended upon her marriage on October 5, 2016, and she was then obliged to return without need of a return-to-work order, but she never did. She ignored three return-to-work notices. Her November 9, 2016 letter, stating that she "could no longer go back to work for the school," was **the overt act showing a clear intention to sever the employment.** Her complaint and position paper praying for separation pay, and her statement at the mandatory conference that she was no longer interested in working at BWS, confirmed this. Her benefits therefore accrue only until November 9, 2016. Legal interest of 6% per annum applies from finality.

### Disposition
The petition was DENIED. The CA Decision dated September 28, 2018 and Resolution dated January 24, 2020 in CA-G.R. SP No. 11224 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Mabao was declared illegally suspended. BWS, Dr. Yap, and Deloso were ordered to jointly and solidarily pay her backwages from September 22, 2016 to October 7, 2016; 13th month pay, unpaid rice allowance, laundry allowance, midyear bonus, and proportionate vacation/sick leave accruing until November 9, 2016; and attorney's fees of 10% of the total award. They were also ordered to issue her a certificate of employment. All monetary awards earn 6% legal interest per annum from finality until full payment, and the records were remanded to the Labor Arbiter for computation.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Ana, a single teacher in a Catholic high school, became pregnant by her boyfriend, who is also single. The school suspended her without pay "until she is legally married," citing its policy that premarital sex is immoral and that teachers in a religious school must model Christian values. Ana questions the suspension. The school invokes its management prerogative. Is the suspension valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The suspension is illegal because Ana's conduct is not immoral under the applicable standard.
- **Legal basis:** Whether conduct is disgraceful or immoral is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality. Sexual relations between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, resulting in pregnancy out of wedlock, are not immoral. No law proscribes them, and they contravene no fundamental state policy. A suspension based on such conduct has no just cause and is illegal. (Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao, G.R. No. 252124, July 23, 2024, reiterating Leus v. St. Scholastica's College Westgrove)
- **Application:** Ana and her boyfriend are both single and have no legal impediment to marry. Their relationship and Ana's pregnancy may run against the school's Catholic teachings, but that alone does not make them immoral under public and secular standards. Management prerogative cannot justify a penalty that has no just cause, so the school cannot use its religious standard to suspend her.
- **Conclusion:** Ana's suspension is illegal, and she is entitled to backwages for the period of the suspension.

**Q2.** Assume instead that the school's handbook validly penalizes certain acts. When Bea, a teacher, disclosed a violation, the school's discipline committee met without her and decided to suspend her for 30 days. It then called her into the meeting, where she admitted the violation and said she would accept the suspension. The suspension was put in writing. No notice to explain was ever served. The school argues that it substantially complied with due process because Bea was heard, admitted the violation, and agreed to the penalty. Is the school correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. There was no substantial compliance with procedural due process.
- **Legal basis:** A suspension must be based on a just or authorized cause, and the employee must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the penalty is decided. Any disciplinary action affecting employment must pass due process scrutiny in both its substantive and procedural aspects. Where no notice to explain was issued and the employer decided the sanction before hearing the employee, the employer cannot claim substantial compliance. (Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao, G.R. No. 252124, July 23, 2024)
- **Application:** The committee fixed Bea's 30-day suspension before she was even brought into the meeting. Her later admission and acceptance came after the decision had been made, so she was not given a real chance to be heard before judgment. No notice to explain stated the charge and invited her written explanation. Putting the decision in writing does not cure the lack of prior notice and hearing.
- **Conclusion:** The school did not substantially comply with procedural due process in suspending Bea.

**Q3.** Carla was suspended by her employer until a stated condition happened. The condition happened on March 1, after which the employer sent her three return-to-work notices, which she refused to receive. On March 20, she wrote the employer that, because of the humiliation she suffered, she "could no longer go back to work" for it. Her position paper before the Labor Arbiter prayed for separation pay in lieu of reinstatement. The employer never issued a termination letter. The CA held that Carla's employment ended on April 5, the deadline in the last return-to-work notice. (a) Did Carla abandon her work? (b) Until what date do her 13th month pay and other benefits accrue?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, Carla abandoned her work. (b) Her benefits accrue only until March 20, the date of her letter, not April 5.
- **Legal basis:** Abandonment requires (1) failure to report for work or absence without valid or justifiable reason, and (2) a clear intention to sever the employer-employee relationship manifested by an overt act. An employee's letter stating that she could no longer go back to work, together with her refusal of return-to-work notices and her prayer for separation pay, shows that intention, and the employment ends on the date of that overt act. (Bohol Wisdom School v. Mabao, G.R. No. 252124, July 23, 2024)
- **Application:** Carla's suspension ended on March 1, after which she was obliged to return to work, yet she refused three return-to-work notices without valid reason. Her March 20 letter is the overt act showing her clear intention to end the relationship, and her prayer for separation pay confirms it. In Mabao, the Court rejected the CA's use of the deadline in the last notice and fixed the end of employment on the date of the employee's letter.
- **Conclusion:** Carla abandoned her work as of March 20, and her benefits accrue only up to that date.

> Note: The Court found abandonment even though the employee had filed a complaint for illegal suspension and illegal dismissal. It relied on her November 9, 2016 letter, her prayer for separation pay, her statement at the mandatory conference, and her refusal of three return-to-work notices. The LA's fallo gives the total award in words as ending "& 38/100" but in figures as PHP 320,678.19; the amount is omitted here because the LA decision was reversed. The fallo's "jointly and solidarity" is read as "jointly and solidarily."

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69612)
