## Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel

**HACIENDA SAN ISIDRO/SILOS FARMS AND REY SILOS LLAMADO, PETITIONERS, VS. LUCITO VILLARUEL AND HELEN VILLARUEL, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 220087 | 2023-11-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Labor Law and Social Legislation  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Employment Relationship > C. Kinds of Employment > 5. Seasonal  
**Specific topics:** Requisites for regular seasonal employment; Second-paragraph proviso of Art. 295 applies only to casual employees; Freedom to work for other farms; Mercado distinguished; Pakyaw workers and the control test; Set aside on reconsideration (2025)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45))

> **SET ASIDE — not the controlling rule.** Set aside on reconsideration by the Resolution of August 11, 2025. The two requisites for regular seasonal employment were kept, but the worker must still prove the employer's right of control by substantial evidence, and the result was reversed.

### Doctrine
**A seasonal employee becomes a regular employee when (1) the employee performs work or services that are seasonal in nature and (2) is employed to perform such work or services for more than one season.** The Court deduced these requisites from earlier cases and stated them "for the guidance of the bench and the bar." Under the first paragraph of Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code, the seasonal exception covers only employment "for the duration of the season," i.e., one season. A seasonal employee rehired for more than one season falls back under the general rule of regular employment. **The basis of regular seasonal status is this first paragraph, not the proviso of the second paragraph** (at least one year of service, continuous or broken). That proviso applies only to casual employees, i.e., those not covered by the first paragraph (*Paz v. Northern Tobacco Redrying Co.*; *Mercado*). The CA erred in treating the worker as a casual employee who became regular through the proviso.

Freedom to offer one's services to other farm owners does not negate regular status, as long as the worker is hired repeatedly for the same activities and not merely on and off for any single phase of agricultural work. *Mercado v. NLRC* was distinguished, as explained in *Hacienda Fatima*. Pakyaw is a method of paying wages, not the relationship itself. Pakyaw workers are regular employees if they are subject to the employer's control, and the control test requires only the existence of the right to control, not its actual exercise (reiterated from *Gapayao v. Fulo*).

**Caution:** In its Resolution of August 11, 2025, the Court granted the employer's motion for reconsideration, set aside this Decision, and reversed the CA. The Resolution kept the two requisites and the pakyaw rule. It held, however, that the worker failed to prove by substantial evidence that the employer had the right to control the manner and means of her work. It also rejected the inference that control exists simply because she worked on the employer's farm. See *Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel (Resolution)*.

### Facts
Spouses Lucito and Helen Villaruel worked in Hacienda San Isidro in Himamaylan, Negros Occidental. The hacienda was administered by Rey Silos Llamado and formed part of Silos Farms, owned by Fidel Silos. On December 18, 2009 and April 7, 2010, the spouses filed separate complaints against petitioners. They sought relief for illegal dismissal, underpayment of wages, service incentive leave pay, and attorney's fees, and the cases were consolidated.

On February 14, 2011, the Labor Arbiter found that Lucito was dismissed for just cause but without due process, and awarded him P5,000 nominal damages. The LA held that Helen was a regular employee who had been illegally dismissed, and awarded her backwages and separation pay. The NLRC first granted petitioners' partial appeal and held on September 30, 2011 that Helen was not an employee. On the spouses' MR, however, it reinstated the LA decision with modifications on January 27, 2012. It declared both dismissals illegal and awarded Helen P195,456.95.

Petitioners filed a petition for certiorari with the CA. On March 27, 2013, the CA held that Helen was not an employee because she failed to prove the element of control. On the spouses' MR, the CA issued an Amended Decision on January 9, 2015. It held that Helen was a regular employee who had been illegally dismissed, and awarded her backwages and separation pay. The CA reasoned that her sugar-farming work was necessary or desirable to petitioners' business. It added that, because she did not fit any category in the first paragraph of Art. 280, she was a casual employee under the second paragraph who became regular after at least one year of service. The CA denied petitioners' partial MR on July 20, 2015.

Petitioners filed a Rule 45 petition on the sole issue of whether Helen, a seasonal worker in a sugar plantation, should be considered a regular employee. The Court denied the petition on November 9, 2015, but on petitioners' MR it reinstated the petition on November 7, 2016. Petitioners did not dispute that Helen did seasonal work in a yearly cycle. They argued as follows:
- She worked only sparingly, on a pakyaw basis.
- She was not required to report daily or keep definite hours, and she ran her own sari-sari store.
- They did not control how she worked.
- Under *Gapayao*, citing *Mercado*, seasonal workers who are free to contract their services with other farm owners are not regular employees.

### Issues
1. Whether Helen, an admittedly seasonal worker, is a regular employee, and whether the CA correctly based that status on the proviso of the second paragraph of Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code.
2. Whether Helen's freedom to offer her services to other farm owners negates regular seasonal employment.
3. Whether Helen's engagement on a pakyaw basis, allegedly without petitioners' control, negates regular employment.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, Helen is a regular seasonal employee, but the CA's reasoning was wrong.** The LA, the NLRC and the CA had uniformly found her a regular employee. The Court said that factual findings of expert quasi-judicial agencies, when affirmed by the CA, are accorded respect and even finality, and it did not disturb this finding. It nevertheless corrected the CA's reasoning "for the guidance of the bench and the bar." A proviso qualifies only the clause immediately preceding it. The second paragraph of Art. 295 and its proviso apply only to employees not covered by the first paragraph, i.e., casual employees (*Paz v. Northern Tobacco Redrying Co.*, citing *Mercado*).

The correct basis is the general rule in the first paragraph. That paragraph excepts only seasonal work "for the duration of the season," i.e., one season. A seasonal employee employed for more than one season therefore falls under the general rule of regular employment. Regular seasonal employees are called to work from time to time, mostly during a season, and are temporarily laid off in the off-season. During the off-season they are not separated from service but are considered on leave until reemployed (*Abasolo*; *Gapayao*). Repeated hiring for the same tasks over several seasons is a badge of regular employment (*Universal Robina Sugar Milling Corp. v. Acibo*). From these cases the Court deduced two requisites: (1) the work or services are seasonal in nature; and (2) the employee is employed to perform them for more than one season. Both were present, and petitioners themselves admitted that Helen's seasonal work recurred every year.

**2. No, her freedom to work elsewhere is irrelevant.** Petitioners relied on *Mercado* as cited in *Gapayao*. *Hacienda Fatima* explained why *Mercado* does not apply here. In *Mercado*, the workers were hired "on and off for any single phase" of agricultural work, and the employer had the prerogative to take them in or not after each phase. Helen, by contrast, was hired repeatedly for the same activities: sugarcane cultivation, counting *patdan* (canepoints), and other sugar-farming work. Whether she was free to offer her services to others was therefore of no relevance. Her sari-sari store was likewise inconsequential and not incompatible with regular employment.

**3. No, pakyaw payment does not negate regular employment.** By raising this argument, petitioners were in effect asking the Court to re-examine the facts on whether an employer-employee relationship existed. That is not allowed in a Rule 45 review of a CA decision rendered under Rule 65. The inquiry is limited to whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC (*David v. Macasio*). Even if considered, the argument failed. A pakyaw or task basis arrangement "defines not the relationship between the parties but the manner of payment of wages" (*Abuda*). Pakyaw workers are regular employees if subject to the employer's control, and the control test "merely calls for the existence of the right to control, and not necessarily the exercise thereof" (*Gapayao*). Since Helen worked on petitioners' hacienda, they "could easily exercise control and supervision" over her, and whether they actually did so was immaterial. (This last inference was rejected in the August 11, 2025 Resolution.)

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The Court AFFIRMED the CA's Amended Decision dated January 9, 2015 and its Resolution dated July 20, 2015 in CA-G.R. SP No. 07025. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred.

The Court later SET ASIDE this Decision in its Resolution of August 11, 2025, which GRANTED the petition and REVERSED the CA.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Since 2015, Hacienda Esperanza, a sugarcane plantation, has hired Rosa every milling season to plant canepoints and weed the fields. She is laid off in the off-season and recalled at the start of the next season. It is undisputed that the hacienda's overseer prescribes how and when she does her tasks. In 2024 the hacienda stopped recalling her, saying that as a seasonal worker she was never a regular employee. In her illegal dismissal case, the Court of Appeals held Rosa a regular employee. It reasoned that she was a casual employee who became regular under the proviso of the second paragraph of Article 295 of the Labor Code, having rendered at least one year of service. (a) Is Rosa a regular employee? (b) Is the CA's reasoning correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, Rosa is a regular seasonal employee. (b) No. Her regular status rests on the first paragraph of Article 295, not on the proviso of the second paragraph.
- **Legal basis:** Under the first paragraph of Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code, the seasonal exception covers only employment "for the duration of the season." A seasonal employee becomes regular when (1) the employee performs work or services that are seasonal in nature and (2) is employed to perform such work for more than one season. The proviso of the second paragraph (one year of service, continuous or broken) applies only to casual employees, i.e., those not covered by the first paragraph. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023, citing Paz v. Northern Tobacco Redrying Co.)
- **Application:** (a) Rosa's planting and weeding work is seasonal, and the hacienda has hired her for the same tasks every season since 2015, which is more than one season. Both requisites are met. An employer-employee relationship is undisputed, since the overseer controls how she works. Rosa is therefore a regular seasonal employee who is merely on leave during the off-season, and the hacienda's failure to recall her is a dismissal. (b) Rosa is a seasonal employee covered by the first paragraph of Art. 295, so she is not a casual employee. The second-paragraph proviso does not apply to her. Her regular status comes from the general rule in the first paragraph, because her employment is no longer for the duration of a single season.
- **Conclusion:** Rosa is a regular seasonal employee, but under the first paragraph of Article 295, not the casual-employee proviso the CA used.

**Q2.** On a rice farm, the owner's foreman directs how all hired workers do their tasks. Ben has been hired every planting season for eight years to do the same work of plowing and transplanting. In the off-season he works on other farms and runs a small store. Carlo was hired for one harvest in 2023. Since then he has been taken in only on and off, for single phases of farm work, whenever the owner chooses to call him. The owner claims that neither is a regular employee because both are free to offer their services to other farm owners. Is the owner correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** The owner is wrong as to Ben, who is a regular seasonal employee, but correct as to Carlo, who is not.
- **Legal basis:** A seasonal employee is regular if the employee performs seasonal work and is employed for it for more than one season. Freedom to offer one's services to others does not negate regular status, as long as the worker is hired repeatedly for the same activities and not merely on and off for any single phase of agricultural work. Mercado v. NLRC, where workers were not regular, involved workers hired "on and off for any single phase" of agricultural work, whom the employer could take in or not after each phase (Hacienda Fatima). (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023.)
- **Application:** Ben is hired every season for the same tasks of plowing and transplanting, so his work is seasonal and his employment spans more than one season. His off-season work on other farms and his store do not matter, just as Helen's sari-sari store did not matter. Carlo's case is like Mercado. He is not rehired regularly and repeatedly for the same phase of work. He is called on and off for any single phase, at the owner's option. He therefore stays within the seasonal exception, and his freedom to work for others is simply the result of that on-and-off hiring.
- **Conclusion:** Ben is a regular seasonal employee, while Carlo, hired only on and off for single phases, is not.

**Q3.** Hacienda Luz pays Dina on a pakyaw basis per hectare weeded. The hacienda's written work rules prescribe the tools, the method, and the order of weeding. They also authorize the overseer to stop and correct any worker. In practice, the overseer seldom visits Dina's plots. (a) The hacienda argues that the pakyaw arrangement and the lack of actual supervision negate any employer-employee relationship. Is it correct? (b) The NLRC found that Dina was a regular employee, and the CA affirmed on certiorari. The hacienda then files a Rule 45 petition asking the Supreme Court to re-weigh the evidence on control. What is the scope of the Court's review?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Pakyaw is only a method of paying wages, and the control test requires only the right to control, which the hacienda has. (b) The Court reviews only whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC. It does not re-weigh the evidence, except in recognized exceptional cases.
- **Legal basis:** A pakyaw or task basis arrangement "defines not the relationship between the parties but the manner of payment of wages." Pakyaw workers are regular employees if subject to the employer's control, and the control test "merely calls for the existence of the right to control, and not necessarily the exercise thereof." In a Rule 45 review of a CA decision rendered under Rule 65 in a labor case, the narrow inquiry is whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023.) In the August 11, 2025 Resolution in the same case, the Court added two points. The right to control must cover the manner and means of the work and must be proven by substantial evidence. And the Court may review facts in exceptional cases, such as findings based on speculation or a misapprehension of facts.
- **Application:** (a) Paying Dina per hectare only fixes how her wages are computed. The written rules give the hacienda the right to dictate the tools, method and sequence of her work, and to correct her, which is control over the manner and means. That right exists whether or not the overseer actually uses it, so the infrequent visits are immaterial. (b) The hacienda's petition raises a question of fact. The Court will ask only whether the CA correctly found no grave abuse of discretion in the NLRC's ruling. Since documentary evidence supports the finding of control, none of the exceptions that would justify a factual review applies.
- **Conclusion:** Dina's pakyaw pay and the lack of actual supervision do not defeat her employment status, and the Court will not re-weigh the evidence under Rule 45.

> Note: SET ASIDE ON RECONSIDERATION. See Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel (Resolution), G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025 (case id gr-220087-20250811). That Resolution maintained this Decision's doctrine on the two requisites for regular seasonal employment and on pakyaw workers. It found, however, no substantial evidence that petitioners had the right to control the manner and means of Helen's work. It also said that Gapayao misappreciated Mercado and incompletely applied the control test. It granted the petition and reversed the CA, so Helen was ultimately not held a regular employee. This Decision's statement that petitioners "could easily exercise control" because Helen worked on their hacienda is no longer reliable, and the bar questions above therefore assume an established right of control. The Court's earlier minute resolutions (November 9, 2015 denying the petition; November 7, 2016 reinstating it) are known only from this Decision's recital. Lucito's case was not before the Court. The petition assailed the CA only as to Helen.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69220)

# Criminal Law

## People v. Sario

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. ANTONIO SARIO Y SERRANO AND MACARIO PEREZ, JR. Y MERCADO, ACCUSED; ANTONIO SARIO Y SERRANO, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 264409 | 2026-04-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Repealed. See instead Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640; See also AM 18-03-16-SC)  
**Specific topics:** Chain of custody: the four links (Kamad); Third link: non-presentation of the officer who received the drugs at the crime laboratory; Fourth link: stipulated chemist testimony silent on post-examination handling; Unsigned inventory and initials-only markings not fatal; Rule 122, Sec. 11(a): acquittal benefits a non-appealing co-accused who plea-bargained
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 1. Object or Real Evidence > c. Chain of Custody)

### Doctrine
In illegal sale and illegal possession of dangerous drugs (Secs. 5 and 11, RA 9165), the drug itself is the *corpus delicti*. The prosecution must prove its identity with moral certainty through an unbroken chain of custody covering the four links in *People v. Kamad*: (1) seizure and marking by the apprehending officer; (2) turnover to the investigating officer; (3) turnover to the forensic chemist; and (4) turnover by the forensic chemist to the court. Every person who handled the item must describe its condition and the precautions taken (*Mallillin v. People*). Reiterated.

**The third link is broken when the police officer who received the drugs at the crime laboratory is not presented**, leaving no evidence of the drugs' condition and safekeeping until the chemist retrieved them. **The fourth link is broken when the chemist's testimony is dispensed with by a stipulation covering only her qualifications, her receipt of the request and specimens, and the test results.** Such a stipulation says nothing on how the drugs were handled, stored and preserved after examination and before submission to the court (*People v. Supat*). These gaps create reasonable doubt and require acquittal. By contrast, the accused's failure to sign the inventory (when photographs show his presence) is inconsequential. So are markings that use only the accused's initials instead of the seizing officer's initials and the date, time and place required by the PNP Manual, as long as they segregate the items from other evidence.

**Under Rule 122, Section 11(a), a favorable judgment on appeal benefits a co-accused who did not appeal if it rests on a ground applicable to him. This holds even if he pleaded guilty to a lesser offense under a plea bargain and was convicted** (following *People v. Cordova*). A broken chain of custody that renders all the drugs presented in the cases unreliable, including those underlying the co-accused's charges, is such a ground.

### Facts
On July 22, 2017, police officers conducted a buy-bust operation in Barangay San Antonio, Los Baños, Laguna. Introduced by an informant, poseur-buyer PO1 Estrada handed a marked PHP 500 bill to Macario Perez, Jr., who passed it to accused-appellant Antonio Sario. Sario took a sachet of shabu from his pocket and handed it to Perez, who gave it to PO1 Estrada. After the arrest, Sario produced two more sachets and the marked money from his pockets, and Perez produced one sachet. At the scene, PO1 Estrada marked the sachets "AS-BB," "AS1," "AS2" and "MP1," and inventoried and photographed them. This was done in the presence of the accused, a media representative and a barangay kagawad. The accused did not sign the inventory receipts but were given copies.

PO1 Estrada kept the items and prepared the requests at the station. He then personally brought them to the Regional Crime Laboratory, where PO3 Villela received them at 4:30 a.m. Forensic chemist PCINSP Huelgas found the specimens positive for shabu: 0.07 g (AS-BB), 5.52 g and 5.95 g (AS1 and AS2), and 0.04 g (MP1). Her testimony was dispensed with by a stipulation covering only her qualification, the receipt of the requests and specimens, her examination and reports, and her lack of personal knowledge of the seizure. PO3 Villela was not presented.

Sario was charged with illegal sale of 0.07 gram of shabu together with Perez (Crim. Case No. 30023-17-C) and with illegal possession of 11.47 grams (Crim. Case No. 30024-17-C). Perez was separately charged with illegal possession (Crim. Case No. 30025-17-C). During trial, Perez entered into plea bargaining and pleaded guilty to two counts of illegal possession of drug paraphernalia, which the RTC approved in a May 9, 2018 Order. Sario claimed frame-up.

On September 19, 2018, the RTC of Calamba City (Branch 36) convicted Sario on both charges and imposed life imprisonment and a fine for each. The CA affirmed on June 29, 2020. On appeal, Sario argued improper markings, the non-presentation of PO3 Villela, the inadequate stipulation on the chemist's testimony, the absence of an elected official at the inventory, and his unsigned inventory receipt.

### Issues
1. Whether the alleged lapses in the marking and inventory of the seized drugs, including the accused's unsigned inventory receipt, compromised their integrity.
2. Whether the prosecution established the third and fourth links of the chain of custody.
3. Whether Sario's acquittal benefits his co-accused Perez, who did not appeal and had pleaded guilty to a lesser offense.

### Ruling
**1. No.** The Court held these arguments without merit, quoting with approval the CA's ruling. The inventory was made at the scene in the presence of Sario, a barangay kagawad and a media representative, and the photographs show their presence. It is not unusual for an accused to refuse to sign the inventory, and that refusal alone cannot exculpate him. The markings "AS-BB," "AS1" and "AS2," using Sario's initials, sufficiently separated the items from other evidence and prevented switching or contamination.

**2. No. The third and fourth links were not established, so Sario must be acquitted.** On the third link, PO1 Estrada delivered the drugs to the crime laboratory, where PO3 Villela received them, but PO3 Villela was never presented. As in *People v. Hernandez*, nothing on record shows the condition of the drugs or the precautions taken while they were in his custody until the chemist retrieved them. The Court "will not, as it cannot, speculate on such matters."

On the fourth link, the only evidence was PCINSP Huelgas's stipulated testimony. It covered only her qualification, the receipt of the requests and specimens, her positive findings, and her lack of personal knowledge of the seizure. It said nothing about the management, storage or preservation of the drugs after examination and before their submission to the court. As held in *People v. Supat*, such stipulations "do not prove how the drugs were handled." These gaps make it impossible to exclude contamination, substitution or alteration. **The *corpus delicti* was not proved with moral certainty.**

**3. Yes.** Rule 122, Section 11(a) allows a judgment on appeal by one accused to benefit those who did not appeal, if it is favorable and applicable to them. *People v. Cordova* applied this even to an accused who had pleaded guilty to, and been convicted of, a lesser offense. Sario's acquittal rests on gaps that render "defective and deficient all shabu presented by the prosecution in the cases a quo, including those related to the charges against Perez." Perez therefore benefits.

### Disposition
The appeal was GRANTED. The CA Decision of June 29, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 12743 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Sario was ACQUITTED in Criminal Case Nos. 30023-17-C and 30024-17-C and ordered released unless held for another lawful cause. The RTC's May 9, 2018 Order in Criminal Case Nos. 30023-17-C and 30025-17-C was SET ASIDE, and Perez was ACQUITTED in those cases on reasonable doubt and ordered released unless held for another lawful cause. The Director General of the Bureau of Corrections was directed to report the action taken within five days, and entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In a buy-bust operation, PO2 Cruz seized a sachet of shabu from Andres. He marked it at the scene and inventoried and photographed it in the presence of Andres, a barangay councilor and a media representative. PO2 Cruz personally delivered the sachet to the crime laboratory, where PO1 Dela Paz received it. Forensic chemist Reyes later examined it and found it positive for shabu. At trial, PO1 Dela Paz was not presented. The parties stipulated only that Reyes is an expert, that she received the request and the specimen, that the specimen tested positive as stated in her report, and that she has no personal knowledge of the seizure. Andres was convicted of illegal sale. On appeal, he argues that the chain of custody was broken. Is he correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. The third and fourth links of the chain of custody were not established, so Andres must be acquitted.
- **Legal basis:** In drug cases, the dangerous drug is the corpus delicti, and its identity must be proved with moral certainty through an unbroken chain of custody: seizure and marking, turnover to the investigating officer, turnover to the forensic chemist, and turnover by the chemist to the court (People v. Kamad). The non-presentation of the officer who received the drug at the laboratory breaks the third link. A stipulation on the chemist's testimony that does not cover how the drug was handled and preserved after examination breaks the fourth. (People v. Sario, G.R. No. 264409, April 13, 2026)
- **Application:** No one testified on the condition of the sachet while it was in PO1 Dela Paz's custody, from his receipt until Reyes retrieved it, or on the precautions he took. The stipulation on Reyes's testimony covers only her qualifications, her receipt of the specimen and her results. It is silent on how the sachet was stored and preserved after examination until it reached the court. The court cannot fill these gaps by assumption, so substitution or contamination cannot be ruled out.
- **Conclusion:** Andres must be acquitted because the identity of the corpus delicti was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

**Q2.** In another drug case, both the officer who received the specimen at the laboratory and the forensic chemist testified in detail on how it was received, sealed, examined, stored in the evidence vault and brought to court. Accused Bruno argues only that (a) he did not sign the inventory receipt, although photographs show that he and the required witnesses were present during the inventory; and (b) the sachet was marked only with his initials, "BV," instead of the seizing officer's initials and the date, time and place of seizure as the PNP drug manual requires. Should Bruno be acquitted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. These lapses do not affect the integrity of the seized drug.
- **Legal basis:** The accused's refusal or failure to sign the inventory cannot by itself exculpate him where photographs show his presence, and that of the required witnesses, during the inventory. Markings using the accused's initials suffice if they separate the seized item from all other similar evidence and prevent switching or contamination. In People v. Sario (G.R. No. 264409, April 13, 2026), the Court upheld the CA's rejection of these same arguments and acquitted only because the third and fourth links were missing.
- **Application:** Every link here is accounted for by testimony on custody and handling, including the laboratory receiving officer and the chemist. The photographs show Bruno's presence at the inventory, so his unsigned receipt is immaterial. The marking "BV" distinguished the sachet from other evidence; departing from the PNP manual's marking format does not by itself cast doubt on the drug's identity.
- **Conclusion:** Bruno's arguments do not warrant an acquittal.

**Q3.** Carlo and Dante were jointly charged with illegal sale of shabu, and Dante was separately charged with illegal possession, based on sachets seized in a single buy-bust operation. During trial, Dante entered into a plea bargain, pleaded guilty to illegal possession of drug paraphernalia, and was convicted. Carlo went to trial, was convicted, and appealed. The Supreme Court acquitted Carlo because the prosecution failed to prove the third and fourth links of the chain of custody for all the sachets seized. Dante did not appeal. Does Carlo's acquittal benefit Dante?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Dante should also be acquitted.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 122, Section 11(a) of the Rules of Court, a judgment on an appeal taken by one or more of several accused affects those who did not appeal insofar as it is favorable and applicable to them. The rule applies even to a co-accused who pleaded guilty to, and was convicted of, a lesser offense (People v. Cordova). (People v. Sario, G.R. No. 264409, April 13, 2026)
- **Application:** Carlo's acquittal rests on the broken chain of custody for all the sachets seized in the operation, including those underlying the charges against Dante. That ground applies equally to Dante. His plea bargain and conviction for a lesser offense do not bar him from benefiting.
- **Conclusion:** Dante's conviction should be set aside, and he should be acquitted on reasonable doubt.

> Note: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred. Promulgated April 13, 2026, within the June 30, 2026 cutoff. Footnote 8 states that the exact text of the Information in Criminal Case No. 30025-17-C could not be found in the records. The Court rejected the Section 21 arguments (no elected official at the inventory; unsigned receipt) by adopting the CA's ruling, which noted that a barangay kagawad and a media representative witnessed the inventory. It gave no separate discussion.

## People v. XXX258643

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. XXX258643, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 258643 | 2026-02-09 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > H. Title VIII – Crimes Against Persons  
**Specific topics:** Rape by force: refusing to heed the victim's resistance is force; Resistance need not be tenacious nor made before the act (Art. 266-D); Sweetheart theory; Acts of lasciviousness against a minor: RA 7610, Sec. 5(b) vs. Art. 336 RPC (Gramatica); Civil indemnity and damages for acts of lasciviousness against a minor

### Doctrine
**Refusing to heed the victim's expression of resistance constitutes force, whether the resistance is made prior to, at the beginning of, or in the middle of the sexual act.** Sexual congress with a person who expressed resistance by words (telling the accused to stop) or deeds (trying to stand up while being held down) is rape under Article 266-A of the RPC. Resistance need not be tenacious: Article 266-D accepts "[a]ny physical overt act manifesting resistance against the act of rape in any degree" as evidence, and the En Banc rule in *People v. Dulay* that tenacious resistance is not required was not overturned by *People v. Tionloc* and *People v. Cubay*. Force need not be irresistible, and the age gap between an adult offender and a minor victim may place the offender in a position to force his will. "It is the job of this Court to say what the law is; not how and when victims should resist sexual acts."

The **sweetheart theory** (reiterated) is an admission of carnal knowledge. The accused must prove by substantial evidence not only that he and the victim were lovers, but that she consented to the sexual act. A love affair does not justify rape.

Applying *Gramatica v. People* and *People v. XXX266039* (En Banc, 2025), lascivious conduct against a minor aged 12 to below 18 falls under **Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610 only if the child was "subjected to sexual abuse"**: the child indulged or engaged in the conduct (consented, though the consent is defective under the law), or was convinced, cajoled, or prevailed upon to take part because of the adult's "employment, use, persuasion, inducement, enticement or coercion." Without such proof, the crime is **acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC**. Because the resulting penalty was significantly lower than under RA No. 7610, the Court awarded PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages.

### Facts
Accused-appellant XXX, then 24 and a member of the Citizen Armed Force Geographical Unit (CAFGU) at a patrol base in Ligao City, Albay, was charged in four Informations involving AAA, then 14 (born January 21, 2003), whose father BBB was also assigned at the base. Criminal Case Nos. 8159, 8160, and 8161 charged rape through force, threat, and intimidation on December 16, 21, and 26, 2016. Criminal Case No. 8162 charged sexual abuse under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610, through influence and coercion, on December 28, 2016.

AAA testified that on December 16, XXX pushed her onto a bamboo bed and pulled down her shorts and underwear while she tried to pull them up. He then inserted his penis into her vagina while she tried to push him away; she told him to stop because her father was calling her, but he continued. On December 21, at an abandoned house, he made her bend over and had intercourse with her while holding her back as she tried to stand; she told him to stop, but he would not listen until he ejaculated. On December 26, he dragged her into a hut and, ignoring her pleas, had intercourse with her while pushing down on her back as she tried to stand. On December 28, he dragged and carried her to a hut, removed her shorts and underwear, and placed her legs on his shoulders. He tried to insert his penis but failed because she tried to stand up, and he stopped when they heard her father's motorcycle. The abuse came to light in January 2017. XXX claimed they were sweethearts and that they only talked during those meetings.

In its Joint Judgment dated August 2, 2018, the RTC convicted XXX of rape in Criminal Case No. 8159, with reclusion perpetua and PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages. Finding no similar allegation that the December 21, 26, and 28 incidents were attended by force, restraint, or intimidation, it convicted him of sexual abuse under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610 in Criminal Case Nos. 8160 to 8162. In its Decision dated July 17, 2020 (CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 11692), the CA affirmed but reduced the awards in Criminal Case Nos. 8160 to 8162 to PHP 20,000.00 civil indemnity, PHP 15,000.00 moral damages, and PHP 15,000.00 exemplary damages each. XXX appealed.

### Issues
1. Whether accused-appellant was correctly convicted of rape in Criminal Case No. 8159 despite his sweetheart theory and his claims about AAA's behavior after the incident.
2. Whether the CA correctly affirmed accused-appellant's conviction for sexual abuse under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610, instead of rape, in Criminal Case Nos. 8160 and 8161.
3. Whether accused-appellant was correctly convicted of sexual abuse under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610 in Criminal Case No. 8162, and what civil liability attaches.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the rape conviction in Criminal Case No. 8159 stands.** AAA's positive and categorical testimony established carnal knowledge through force: he pushed her onto the bed and forcibly pulled down her clothes, and she tried to push him away. The sweetheart theory effectively admits carnal knowledge and places on the accused the burden of proving the relationship by substantial evidence, and also that the victim consented to sexual relations. Apart from self-serving statements, he proved no relationship. In any case, "a 'love affair' does not justify rape, for the beloved cannot be sexually violated against her will." His theory that the charge was filed to save the family's honor was speculation; the gravamen of rape is sexual intercourse without consent. "Love is not a license for lust."

**2. No, he is guilty of rape, not sexual abuse, in Criminal Case Nos. 8160 and 8161.** The RTC's own findings showed that AAA told him to stop and tried to stand up while he held or pushed down her back. These are expressions of resistance. Citing *People v. Quintos*, sexual congress with a person who expressed resistance by words or deeds constitutes force; thus **"the mere act of refusing to heed the victim's expression of resistance already constitutes force."** Since *People v. Momo* (1931), force need not be irresistible. The old rule that resistance must be "manifested and tenacious" (*Cabading*, *Amogis*) was rejected by the Court En Banc in *People v. Dulay* (2002), consistent with Article 266-D, which accepts resistance "in any degree" and contemplates victims who could not resist at all. *Tionloc* and *Cubay* revived the old rule, and *Tionloc* even required resistance before consummation, but they "did not overturn the rule on resistance in Dulay," and *Nocido* reaffirmed that tenacious resistance is unnecessary. **"Whether the resistance is made prior to, at the beginning of, or in the middle of the sexual act, it is resistance just the same."** Citing *People v. Caballo*, the age disparity (24 vs. 14) placed him in a stronger position, and he had to drag and carry her on more than one occasion.

**3. No, the crime in Criminal Case No. 8162 is acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC.** On December 28 there was no sexual intercourse; he only removed AAA's underwear and placed her legs on his shoulders before they heard her father's motorcycle. Under *Gramatica v. People* and *People v. XXX266039*, RA No. 7610 applies only where the minor is subjected to sexual abuse, that is, she indulged or engaged in (consented, albeit defectively) or was convinced, cajoled, or prevailed upon to take part in the lascivious conduct due to the adult's "employment, use, persuasion, inducement, enticement or coercion." There was no such proof, so he is liable under Article 336. *People v. Tulagan* fixed PHP 20,000.00 each in damages for acts of lasciviousness against a victim of legal age. Following *XXX266039*, however, and **because the penalty for acts of lasciviousness is significantly lower than the penalty under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610, the Court found PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages justified.**

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED, and the CA Decision dated July 17, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 11692 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. In Criminal Case Nos. 8159, 8160, and 8161, accused-appellant was found GUILTY of three counts of rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua for each count, and ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages per count. In Criminal Case No. 8162, he was found GUILTY of acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six months of arresto mayor, as minimum, to four years and two months of prision correccional, as maximum, and ordered to pay PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages. All amounts earn 6% interest per annum from finality until fully paid.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Carla, 19, went with Bert into his room. She said nothing when Bert undressed her and began having sexual intercourse with her. Shortly after he started, Carla said, "Stop, I don't want this," and tried to get up, but Bert held her down by the shoulders and continued until he ejaculated. Charged with rape, Bert argues that Carla did not resist before the intercourse began and that her words and her attempt to get up in the middle of the act fall short of the tenacious resistance the law requires. Is Bert guilty of rape?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Bert is guilty of rape through force, because he refused to heed Carla's expression of resistance.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 266-A(1)(a) of the RPC, rape is committed by a man who has carnal knowledge of a woman through force, threat, or intimidation. Sexual congress with a person who expressed resistance by words or deeds constitutes force, and "the mere act of refusing to heed the victim's expression of resistance already constitutes force." Resistance need not be tenacious (People v. Dulay, En Banc), and Article 266-D accepts any physical overt act manifesting resistance "in any degree" as evidence. "Whether the resistance is made prior to, at the beginning of, or in the middle of the sexual act, it is resistance just the same." (People v. XXX258643, G.R. No. 258643, February 9, 2026)
- **Application:** Carla expressed resistance both by words ("Stop, I don't want this") and by deed (trying to get up). Bert disregarded both and held her down to continue the act. That refusal to heed her resistance is the force that makes the act rape. Her silence at the start does not matter: resistance offered in the middle of the act is still resistance. The law also does not require it to be tenacious. The contrary view in Tionloc, that resistance must come before consummation, did not overturn the En Banc rule in Dulay.
- **Conclusion:** Bert is guilty of rape.

**Q2.** Dindo, 22, is charged with raping Ella, 17. He admits having sexual intercourse with her but says they were sweethearts. He presents love letters and photographs of them together, which Ella admits are authentic. Ella testified that on the night in question she told Dindo she did not want to have sex and tried to push him away, but he was too strong and continued. Will Dindo's sweetheart defense prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Even if the relationship is proved, the sweetheart defense fails because there is no proof that Ella consented to the sexual act.
- **Legal basis:** The sweetheart theory is an admission of carnal knowledge and places on the accused the burden of proving the relationship by substantial evidence. Because it rests on the premise that the sexual act was consensual, it requires proof not only that the accused and the victim were lovers but also that the victim consented to the sexual relations. "[A] 'love affair' does not justify rape, for the beloved cannot be sexually violated against her will." The gravamen of rape is sexual intercourse without consent. (People v. XXX258643, G.R. No. 258643, February 9, 2026)
- **Application:** Dindo's letters and photographs prove only that he and Ella were sweethearts. They do not prove that she agreed to have sex that night. Her testimony that she said no and tried to push him away shows lack of consent. His refusal to heed that resistance is the force that makes it rape. His admission of intercourse, combined with proof of non-consent, supports conviction.
- **Conclusion:** The sweetheart defense will not prosper, and Dindo may be convicted of rape.

**Q3.** Fred, 25, dragged Gina, 15, into a hut, laid her on a bed, removed her shorts, and touched her private parts against her will until they were interrupted. There was no sexual intercourse. Fred was charged with lascivious conduct under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610. The evidence shows that Fred acted through force; nothing shows that Gina went along with the acts or that Fred persuaded, induced, enticed, or cajoled her into taking part. (a) Of what crime may Fred be held liable? (b) What civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages may be awarded?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Fred is liable for acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC, not under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610. (b) PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages may be awarded, with 6% interest per annum from finality.
- **Legal basis:** Not all acts of lasciviousness against minors aged 12 to below 18 are prosecuted under RA No. 7610. Section 5(b) applies only to minors "subjected to sexual abuse": those who indulge or engage in, that is, consent (albeit defectively) to, the lascivious conduct, or who are convinced, cajoled, or prevailed upon to take part due to the adult's "employment, use, persuasion, inducement, enticement or coercion" (Gramatica v. People, En Banc, 2025). Absent such proof, the crime is acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC. Applying this rule, the Court in People v. XXX258643 (G.R. No. 258643, February 9, 2026) convicted the accused of acts of lasciviousness. It awarded PHP 75,000.00 each in damages, more than the PHP 20,000.00 set in Tulagan for adult victims, because the penalty imposed was significantly lower than that under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610.
- **Application:** (a) Gina is 15, but there is no proof that she indulged or engaged in the conduct or was induced or cajoled into taking part; Fred simply forced himself on her. The case therefore does not fall under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610, and Fred is liable for acts of lasciviousness under Article 336. (b) As in People v. XXX258643, the victim is a minor and the penalty under Article 336 is much lower than what Section 5(b) would have carried, so PHP 75,000.00 each in civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages is justified.
- **Conclusion:** Fred is liable for acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC and may be ordered to pay PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages.

> Note: Only accused-appellant appealed, yet the Court convicted him of rape (instead of sexual abuse under Section 5(b) of RA No. 7610) in Criminal Case Nos. 8160 and 8161, where the Informations had charged rape; the main opinion does not separately discuss the rule that an appeal in a criminal case opens the whole case for review. On the December 28 incident (attempted insertion that failed), the Court ruled that the crime was acts of lasciviousness because there was no sexual intercourse; it did not discuss attempted rape. Apparent typographical errors in the text: the opening paragraph refers to sexual abuse under "Republic Act No. 7160" (should be 7610), and the CA's summary of the defense version dates one incident "December 28, 2017" (the other dates are in 2016). The caption anonymizes the accused as XXX258643; the body calls him XXX.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70301)

## People v. Olbato

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. JOSE OLBATO Y AURELLA, JAIME TOLEVA Y CAMPOSANO, ROMEO ARUTA Y FABIANO, RODRIGO ARUTA Y FABIANO, ALBERTO CULANAG Y FREJOLES, SPO4 ROMEO AYSON Y SEJIRA @ "ROMY," PO3 CLAYTON PATINGAN Y AMATIC @ "RICKY / BOBOT," EDWIN CASTILLO Y IGADA, LOLITA MONAREZ Y ESTRELLA, SEBASTIAN MAGAIPO Y ALIPANTE, MARY-ANN ANGCAHAN Y BUTILLA, JULLIEN MADRID Y ECHAVEZ @ "MARLOU," PEPE BIHAG Y BALTAZAR, YONG YONG MENTIS (AT LARGE), VINA ARGAYOZA (AT LARGE), AND FOUR JOHN DOES, ACCUSED; JOSE OLBATO Y AURELLA, JAIME TOLEVAS Y CAMPOSANO, ROMEO ARUTA Y FABIANO, RODRIGO ARUTA Y FABIANO, AND ALBERTO CULANAG Y FREJOLES, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.**  
G.R. No. 276833 | 2026-01-21 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > I. Title IX – Crimes Against Personal Liberty and Security  
**Specific topics:** Elements of kidnapping for ransom (Art. 267, RPC, as amended by RA 7659); Police officer who detains a person for ransom acts as a private individual (People v. Borja); Ransom money is not the corpus delicti; its loss or non-presentation is immaterial; Conspiracy inferred from concerted acts; denial and alibi vs. positive identification; Death of accused pending appeal extinguishes criminal and civil liability ex delicto (People v. Bayotas)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > C. Prosecution of Civil Action (Rule 111) > 4. Civil Liability Ex Delicto > b. When Accused Dies)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 4. Positive and Negative Evidence)

### Doctrine
The elements of **kidnapping for ransom under Art. 267 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 7659**, are: (1) the accused is a private person; (2) he or she kidnapped or detained, or in any manner deprived another of liberty; (3) the kidnapping or detention was illegal; and (4) the victim was kidnapped or detained for ransom. **A police officer who detains a person to extort ransom does not act in an official capacity**, so the first element is satisfied as to him (reiterating *People v. Borja*).

**Whether the ransom money was actually paid or received is of no moment, and the ransom money is not the corpus delicti** of kidnapping for ransom (reiterating *People v. Jatulan*). Its loss or non-presentation in court does not create reasonable doubt where the demand, negotiation and delivery are proved by testimonial and documentary evidence. Conspiracy may be inferred from the concerted acts of the accused before, during and after the crime; a conspirator need not take part in every detail, as the act of one is the act of all.

Denial and frame-up, like alibi, cannot prevail over positive identification; for alibi to prosper, the accused must prove that it was physically impossible for him to be at or near the crime scene, and an alibi corroborated only by acquaintances is viewed with suspicion (reiterated). **The death of an accused pending appeal extinguishes both his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto** (*People v. Bayotas*), without prejudice to a separate civil action against his estate based on a source of obligation other than delict.

### Facts
At about 9:00 a.m. on March 18, 2004, Genevieve Ong Sy was driving her Lancer along Severino Street, Sta. Cruz, Manila when two uniformed policemen, PO3 Clayton Patingan and SPO4 Romeo Ayson, flagged her down. PO3 Patingan dragged her to the back seat, where Romeo and Rodrigo Aruta sat beside her. Her jewelry, cash, cards and phone were taken. She was transferred to a Nissan Cefiro in North Fairview and brought, with Edwin Castillo among her escorts, to a house in Antipolo City, where Jose Olbato, Jaime Tolevas, Sebastian Magaipo and Alberto Culanag locked her in a room and guarded her in shifts.

That morning a caller, later identified as Magaipo, told her father Santos that she had been kidnapped and demanded PHP 50,000,000.00, later negotiated down to PHP 500,000.00. Santos sought help from the Police Anti-Crime Emergency Response (PACER). On instructions from a man calling himself "Major De Guzman," the family driver delivered PHP 500,000.00 in marked bills near McDonald's Quezon Avenue to SPO4 Ayson and Culanag, who left with PO3 Patingan in a pick-up that PACER operatives tailed. At about 5:30 a.m. of March 20, 2004, police rescued Genevieve from the Antipolo house and arrested several accused. Another team raided the North Fairview house, arrested Culanag, and recovered the ransom money, the victim's bag, and a police uniform bearing PO3 Patingan's name.

The accused raised denial, alibi and frame-up; PO3 Patingan claimed that he and Genevieve were lovers and that her father fabricated the kidnapping. The RTC convicted nine accused, including the five appellants, of kidnapping for ransom, imposed reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole, and ordered each to pay the victim PHP 100,000.00 as civil indemnity, PHP 100,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 as exemplary damages; it acquitted Monarez and Bihag. On January 31, 2024, the CA affirmed in toto.

The appellants jointly filed a notice of appeal. PO3 Patingan and Castillo then moved to withdraw their appeals to apply for executive clemency; the motion disclosed that SPO4 Ayson had died on November 16, 2023, yet still included him in the prayer to withdraw. The CA granted the withdrawal and gave due course to the appeal of Olbato, Tolevas, Romeo, Rodrigo and Culanag.

### Issues
1. Whether SPO4 Ayson's death pending appeal extinguished his criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto.
2. Whether the elements of kidnapping for ransom, including the first element as to a police officer co-accused, were proved beyond reasonable doubt.
3. Whether the loss and non-presentation of the ransom money creates reasonable doubt as to the ransom element.
4. Whether conspiracy was proved, and whether the defenses of denial, alibi, frame-up and an alleged romantic relationship prevail over the victim's positive identification.

### Ruling
**1. Yes.** SPO4 Ayson died on November 16, 2023, during the pendency of the appeal. Under *People v. Bayotas*, his death extinguished both his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto. The criminal case and the appeal were deemed dismissed as to him, without prejudice to a separate civil action against his estate, if warranted, based on a source of obligation other than delict.

**2. Yes.** Findings of fact of the trial court are accorded the highest respect absent a clear disregard of the evidence. (1) Genevieve positively identified her abductors, all private persons except PO3 Patingan; under *People v. Borja*, a police officer who detains a person to extort ransom cannot be said to act in an official capacity, so the first element was satisfied. (2) and (3) She was forcibly taken and detained under guard in Antipolo without lawful cause; she was held incommunicado, guarded in shifts and released only after the ransom was paid. (4) Santos testified to the demand for PHP 50,000,000.00 later reduced to PHP 500,000.00; the delivery to SPO4 Ayson and Culanag was made under PACER surveillance; and the officers testified to the recovery of the marked money, the rescue and the arrests.

**3. No.** Under *People v. Jatulan*, whether the ransom money was actually paid or received is of no moment, and the ransom money is not the corpus delicti of kidnapping for ransom. The testimonies of Genevieve and her father proved that ransom was demanded, negotiated and delivered; the non-presentation of the PHP 500,000.00 in court does not negate the demand and payment.

**4. Conspiracy was proved, and the defenses fail.** Conspiracy may be inferred from the concerted acts of the accused before, during and after the crime (*People v. Olidan*). The coordinated flagging down of the car, the transfer of the victim between vehicles, her guarded detention in Antipolo, and the ransom pickup showed unity of purpose and community of design, with each accused performing indispensable acts. Minor inconsistencies in Genevieve's testimony on trivial details are badges of truth, and she never wavered in identifying her abductors. Denial and frame-up, like alibi, are the weakest defenses and cannot prevail over positive identification. The appellants failed to prove physical impossibility of their presence at the crime scene, and Magaipo's alibi, corroborated only by his tricycle operator, was rightly viewed with suspicion. PO3 Patingan's claim of a romantic relationship was a bare allegation without proof.

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED and the CA Decision dated January 31, 2024 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 15854 was AFFIRMED in toto. Accused-appellants Jose Olbato, Jaime Tolevas, Romeo Aruta, Rodrigo Aruta and Alberto Culanag, and co-accused PO3 Clayton Patingan and Edwin Castillo, were declared GUILTY of kidnapping for ransom under Art. 267 of the RPC and sentenced to reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole. They were ORDERED to pay the victim PHP 100,000.00 as civil indemnity, PHP 100,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 as exemplary damages, with 6% interest per annum on all awards from finality until full payment. The criminal case against SPO4 Romeo Ayson was DISMISSED, his criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto having been extinguished by his death on November 16, 2023, without prejudice to a separate civil action against his estate based on sources of obligation other than delict.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** PO2 Lino and his civilian friend Marco flagged down Tessa's car at a fake checkpoint, forced her into another vehicle, and locked her in a room of a rented house. They called her mother and demanded PHP 2,000,000.00 for her release, later reduced to PHP 300,000.00, which the mother delivered. Tessa was rescued the next day. At trial, the ransom money could not be presented because it was lost while in police custody. PO2 Lino argues that (a) he cannot be convicted of kidnapping under Art. 267 because he is a public officer, not a private individual, and (b) the non-presentation of the ransom money creates reasonable doubt. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. PO2 Lino may be convicted of kidnapping for ransom.
- **Legal basis:** Kidnapping for ransom under Art. 267 of the RPC, as amended by RA 7659, requires that (1) the accused is a private person; (2) he kidnapped or detained, or in any manner deprived another of liberty; (3) the detention was illegal; and (4) it was for ransom. A police officer who detains a person to extort ransom does not act in an official capacity (People v. Borja). Whether the ransom was actually paid or received is of no moment, and the ransom money is not the corpus delicti; its loss or non-presentation does not create reasonable doubt where the demand and delivery are proved (People v. Jatulan). Both rules were applied in People v. Olbato (G.R. No. 276833, January 21, 2026).
- **Application:** (a) PO2 Lino seized and detained Tessa to extort money from her family. That is not the performance of any police function, so he acted outside his official capacity and the first element is satisfied as to him. (b) The demand for PHP 2,000,000.00, the negotiation down to PHP 300,000.00 and the delivery can be proved by the testimony of the mother and the rescuing officers. The money itself is not the corpus delicti, so its loss in police custody does not negate the ransom element.
- **Conclusion:** PO2 Lino is guilty of kidnapping for ransom despite being a police officer and despite the non-presentation of the ransom money.

**Q2.** Jun and three companions abducted Bea and held her in a farmhouse, then called her father and demanded PHP 1,000,000.00. Before any money was delivered, the police rescued Bea. At trial, Bea positively identified Jun as one of her guards at the farmhouse. Jun presented his employer, a tricycle operator, who testified that Jun was driving a tricycle that day in a town about 20 kilometers away, less than an hour's trip from the farmhouse. (a) Can Jun be convicted of kidnapping for ransom even though no ransom was paid? (b) Should his alibi be believed?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Payment of ransom is not required. (b) No. The alibi cannot prevail over Bea's positive identification.
- **Legal basis:** The fourth element of kidnapping for ransom under Art. 267 of the RPC is that the victim was kidnapped or detained for ransom; whether the ransom was actually paid or received is of no moment (People v. Jatulan, reiterated in People v. Olbato, G.R. No. 276833, January 21, 2026). In Olbato, the Court also held that denial and alibi are among the weakest defenses and cannot prevail over positive identification; for alibi to prosper, the accused must prove that it was physically impossible for him to be at or near the crime scene, considering the distance and facility of access; and an alibi corroborated only by acquaintances, such as the accused's tricycle operator, is viewed with suspicion.
- **Application:** (a) The demand for PHP 1,000,000.00 shows that Bea was detained for ransom; her rescue before payment does not erase that purpose. (b) Bea positively identified Jun as one of her guards. His employer's testimony places him only 20 kilometers away, less than an hour's trip, so it was not physically impossible for him to be at the farmhouse. The corroboration also comes from his employer, the kind of corroboration the Court views with suspicion.
- **Conclusion:** Jun may be convicted of kidnapping for ransom, as payment of ransom is unnecessary and his alibi fails.

**Q3.** Ramon was convicted by the RTC of kidnapping for ransom and ordered to pay the victim civil indemnity and moral and exemplary damages. While his appeal was pending before the Court of Appeals, Ramon died. (a) What is the effect of his death on his criminal and civil liability? (b) May the victim still recover from Ramon's estate?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) His death pending appeal extinguishes his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto, and the case is dismissed as to him. (b) Yes, but only through a separate civil action against his estate based on a source of obligation other than the crime.
- **Legal basis:** Under People v. Bayotas, as applied in People v. Olbato (G.R. No. 276833, January 21, 2026), the death of an accused pending appeal extinguishes both his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto; the criminal case and the appeal are deemed dismissed as to him, without prejudice to a separate civil action against his estate, if warranted, based on a source of obligation other than delict. Under Art. 89(1) of the RPC, criminal liability is totally extinguished by the death of the convict, and liability for pecuniary penalties is extinguished when death occurs before final judgment.
- **Application:** (a) Ramon died before his conviction became final, while his appeal was pending. His criminal liability, and the civil indemnity and damages awarded because of the crime, are extinguished, and the case must be dismissed as to him. (b) The victim may still sue Ramon's estate in a separate civil action, but the claim must rest on a source of obligation other than the crime, such as law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict (Art. 1157, Civil Code).
- **Conclusion:** Ramon's death pending appeal extinguishes his criminal and civil liability ex delicto, leaving the victim only a separate civil action against his estate on another source of obligation.

> Note: SPO4 Ayson died on November 16, 2023, before the CA promulgated its January 31, 2024 Decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the case as to him although a motion to withdraw appeal filed after his death, and granted by the CA, had included him; the Court did not discuss the effect of that motion. The fallo declares PO3 Patingan and Castillo guilty although they had withdrawn their appeals. Magaipo, convicted by the RTC, is not among the appellants before the CA and is not mentioned in the Supreme Court's fallo. The decision spells one appellant's surname both "Toleva" (caption) and "Tolevas" (body).

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70258)
