## Sedenio v. People

**JANITO M. SEDENIO, PETITIONER, VS. PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 276927 | 2026-01-19 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** IV. Special Penal Laws > Q. Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act (RA 9262, Secs. 3–6 and 24–27)  
**Specific topics:** Violence against women through harassment (Sec. 5(h)(5), RA 9262): elements; Present or past dating or sexual relationship; information need not allege the relationship had ended; Victim's credible testimony suffices to prove alarm or substantial emotional distress; Proof of text messages under the Rules on Electronic Evidence; judicial admission; Rule 45 defects: no proof of service on the lower court; incomplete material dates
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 2. Documentary Evidence > e. Electronic Evidence (AM 01-7-01-SC))

### Doctrine
Violence against women through harassment under **Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262** has three elements (reiterated, Ang v. CA). (1) The offender has or had a sexual or dating relationship with the offended woman. (2) The offender, personally or through another, commits an act or series of acts of harassment against her. (3) The harassment causes her alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress. The first element is met **as long as, at the time of the crime, the offender and the woman were or used to be in a sexual or dating relationship.** A clandestine affair between two people married to others qualifies. The Information need not allege that the relationship had already ended when the Information was filed; that fact is immaterial.

**Proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required. Whether she suffered alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress is personal to her, so her testimony, if found credible, is sufficient to prove the third element** (applying Araza v. People). No psychological report or expert testimony is needed.

Text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them (Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 11, Sec. 2). The recipient's testimony suffices. The accused's admission in open court that the sending number was his and that he sent the "humiliating [and] threatening" messages is a judicial admission. It binds him absent palpable mistake or proof that no such admission was made (Rule 129, Sec. 4). A Rule 45 petition that lacks proof of service on the lower court or omits material dates may be dismissed on that ground alone (Rule 45, Secs. 3-5).

### Facts
Petitioner Janito Sedenio was charged under Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262. The Information alleged that from February to August 2012, in Negros Oriental, he sent threatening and derogatory text messages to AAA, "with whom accused has a dating relationship," causing her alarm and substantial emotional or psychological distress.

Sedenio, a project engineer, met AAA in 2009 and they began a relationship. Both testified that it was a clandestine romantic relationship of about two years even though both were married to other people. Sedenio paid the amortization on AAA's housing unit. The relationship soured in 2011, after a dispute over a sugarcane harvest and after AAA told him about another man, YYY. Sedenio then sent her a series of text messages. On July 18, 2012, he threatened to humiliate her before her creditors and called her irresponsible and of ill repute. On July 20, 2012, he demanded payment of PHP 20,000.00 and wrote, "If you will ignore me, just wait for what I will do. I will include your consenting mother." On July 23, 2012, he accused her of embezzling money from the lending company where she worked. On August 2, 2012, he sent a vulgar message about YYY. On August 13, 2012, he forcibly entered her house using a kitchen knife. After that he sent mocking messages. In them he said she humiliated herself by calling the police, called her dumb, threatened to file a blotter against her, and threatened to show everyone a photo of the two of them in bed without clothes. AAA testified that she suffered mental anguish, sleepless nights for about six months, and a besmirched reputation, and that she could no longer look her neighbors in the eye.

Sedenio admitted the relationship. He also admitted on cross-examination that the sending number was his. He said that, hurt by AAA's relationship with YYY and sometimes drunk, he sent her "humiliating [and] threatening words."

The RTC (February 11, 2022) convicted him and imposed an indeterminate penalty of six months and one day of *prision correccional* to eight years and one day of *prision mayor*, a PHP 100,000.00 fine, mandatory psychological counseling, and PHP 3,000.00 moral damages. The CA affirmed on May 17, 2023 and denied reconsideration on July 15, 2024. In his Rule 45 petition, Sedenio argued the following. The text messages were never presented in court and authenticated under the Rules on Electronic Evidence. Intent to harass was not proved. The Information failed to state that their relationship had ended when it was filed. The victim's testimony alone, without a psychological expert or other witnesses, could not prove emotional distress.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition is dismissible for non-compliance with the requirements of Rule 45.
2. Whether the text messages were sufficiently proven.
3. Whether the Information was defective for not alleging that petitioner and AAA were no longer in a relationship when it was filed.
4. Whether the elements of violation of Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 were proven beyond reasonable doubt, including alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress without expert evidence.

### Ruling
**1. The petition was procedurally defective.** A petition for review must be accompanied by proof of service on the adverse party and on the lower court concerned (Rule 45, Sec. 3). It must also state the material dates: receipt of the assailed judgment, filing of the motion for reconsideration, and receipt of its denial (Sec. 4). Non-compliance is sufficient ground for dismissal (Sec. 5). Petitioner served the OSG but attached no proof of service on the CA. Although he attached the CA Decision and his motion for reconsideration, he did not state when he received the Decision or when he filed the motion. In any case, the Court found no reversible error on the merits.

**2. Yes, the text messages were sufficiently proven.** Under the Rules on Electronic Evidence, text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them. AAA, the intended recipient, testified on the messages. Petitioner himself admitted that the mobile number was his and that he sent AAA "humiliating [and] threatening words" because he felt hurt and was often drunk. **He cannot go back on this judicial admission, there being no showing of palpable mistake or that the admission was not made.**

**3. No, the Information was sufficient.** The first element is "either a present or past sexual or dating relationship." **"[A]s long as at the time the alleged crime was committed, the offender and the offended woman either were or used to be in a sexual or dating relationship, the foregoing element is present."** The Information alleged a dating relationship at the time of the offense and the sending of threatening and derogatory messages that caused AAA distress. Whether they were still in a relationship when the Information was filed is immaterial. Petitioner was sufficiently informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.

**4. Yes, all elements were proven.** (a) Both parties testified to a clandestine romantic relationship of about two years though both were married to others. (b) AAA's testimony and petitioner's judicial admission established a series of harassing text messages from July to August 2012. As the CA put it, what the law punishes is engaging in purposeful, knowing, or reckless conduct that causes psychological harm, and petitioner knowingly and purposefully sent the messages. (c) Harassment is a form of psychological violence (RA 9262, Sec. 3(a)(C)). Araza v. People held that proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required, and her testimony suffices to prove emotional anguish or mental suffering. **Likewise, whether a victim experienced alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress "is an experience that is particular to her. Hence, her testimony—if found credible by the court—is sufficient."** The messages threatened to humiliate AAA before creditors, threatened her and her mother, accused her of embezzlement, mocked her for calling the police, and threatened to show a nude photo of them in bed. AAA testified to mental anguish, about six months of sleepless nights, and a besmirched reputation.

On the penalty, Section 6 of RA 9262 punishes Section 5(h) acts with *prision mayor*. Applying the Indeterminate Sentence Law, with no modifying circumstance, the penalty imposed by the courts below was affirmed. The fine, moral damages, and mandatory counseling were also affirmed (Secs. 6 and 36), with 6% legal interest per annum on the moral damages from finality until full payment.

### Disposition
The Petition was DENIED. The CA Decision of May 17, 2023 and Resolution of July 15, 2024 in CA-G.R. CR No. 04105 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Sedenio was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six months and one day of *prision correccional*, as minimum, to eight years and one day of *prision mayor*, as maximum. He was ordered to pay a fine of PHP 100,000.00 and moral damages of PHP 3,000.00, the latter with 6% legal interest per annum from finality until full payment. He was directed to undergo mandatory psychological counseling or psychiatric treatment and to report compliance to the court of origin within 15 days from its completion.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** After Bea ended her two-year relationship with Carlo, he sent her dozens of text messages over three months. He called her a thief, threatened to post their intimate photos for her neighbors to see, and warned that she and her mother would "pay." Charged under Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262, Carlo argued that the prosecution presented no psychologist or medical report to prove that Bea suffered emotional distress, only Bea's own testimony that she could not sleep for months and was ashamed to face her neighbors. The trial court found Bea credible. Is Bea's testimony sufficient to prove the element of substantial emotional or psychological distress?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Bea's credible testimony is sufficient; no psychological report or expert testimony is required.
- **Legal basis:** The elements of Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 are: (1) the offender has or had a sexual or dating relationship with the woman; (2) he commits an act or series of acts of harassment against her; and (3) the harassment causes her alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress. Proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required. Whether she suffered alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress is particular to her, so her testimony, if credible, is sufficient (Sedenio v. People, G.R. No. 276927, January 19, 2026, applying Araza v. People).
- **Application:** Carlo and Bea had a past dating relationship. His repeated messages calling her a thief, threatening to expose intimate photos, and warning that she and her mother would "pay" are a series of acts of harassment. Bea testified to sleepless nights and shame before her neighbors, experiences personal to her, and the court found her credible. Nothing more is needed to prove the third element.
- **Conclusion:** Bea's testimony suffices, and Carlo may be convicted under Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262.

**Q2.** Dina and Edgar, both married to other people, carried on a secret affair for two years. Two months after Dina ended it, Edgar began sending her threatening and insulting text messages that caused her serious anxiety. The Information alleged that Edgar sent the messages to Dina, "with whom he had a dating relationship." Edgar moves to quash. He argues that (a) an adulterous affair cannot be a "dating relationship" under RA 9262, and (b) the Information is defective because it does not allege that the relationship had already ended when the Information was filed. Rule on both arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. (a) The affair is a sexual or dating relationship under RA 9262. (b) The Information need not allege that the relationship had ended when it was filed.
- **Legal basis:** The first element of Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 is that the offender "has or had" a sexual or dating relationship with the woman. It is present as long as, at the time of the crime, they were or used to be in such a relationship. Whether they were still in a relationship when the Information was filed is immaterial (Sedenio v. People, G.R. No. 276927, January 19, 2026). In Sedenio, the Court treated a clandestine two-year relationship between persons married to others as satisfying this element.
- **Application:** (a) Edgar and Dina had a two-year romantic relationship. That both were married to others does not take it outside RA 9262, as Sedenio shows. (b) The messages were sent after the relationship ended, but a past relationship suffices. The Information alleges a dating relationship and the harassing acts, which informs Edgar of the nature and cause of the accusation. The status of the relationship at the time of filing is not an element and need not be alleged.
- **Conclusion:** The motion to quash should be denied on both grounds.

**Q3.** In a prosecution under RA 9262, the private complainant testified on the contents of the threatening text messages she received and identified handwritten transcriptions of them, but the cellphone itself was not presented. On cross-examination, the accused admitted that the sending number was his and that he sent the complainant "insulting and threatening" messages because he was hurt. On appeal, he argues that the text messages are inadmissible because they were never presented and authenticated in court as ephemeral electronic communications. (a) How are text messages proved under the Rules on Electronic Evidence? (b) What is the effect of the accused's testimony?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or who has personal knowledge of them. (b) The accused's testimony is a judicial admission that binds him.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 11, Section 2, in relation to Rule 2, Section 1(k), of the Rules on Electronic Evidence, ephemeral electronic communications such as text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them. Under Rule 129, Section 4 of the Rules of Court, a judicial admission does not require proof. It may be contradicted only by showing that it was made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made (Sedenio v. People, G.R. No. 276927, January 19, 2026).
- **Application:** (a) The complainant was the recipient of the messages, a party to them with personal knowledge of their contents. Her testimony is the proof the Rules require; presentation of the phone itself is not indispensable. (b) The accused admitted in open court that the number was his and that he sent insulting and threatening messages. He shows no palpable mistake, so he cannot later deny authorship. Together, the complainant's testimony and his admission sufficiently prove the messages.
- **Conclusion:** The text messages were sufficiently proven, and the accused is bound by his judicial admission.

> Note: No separate opinions. The private offended party is anonymized as AAA (and third persons as YYY, KKK, etc.) per Amended Administrative Circular No. 83-2015; the digest keeps that anonymization. The facts portion of the E-Library text contains an apparent typographical error ("Negros Negros Occidental") while the Information and the RTC refer to Negros Oriental. The penalty computation is stated only as affirmed; per the exam rules, penalty periods are not tested.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70248)

## People v. Infortuno

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. RONALDO INFORTUNO, SR. Y CRUZ, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 269722 | 2026-01-06 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > H. Title VIII – Crimes Against Persons  
**Specific topics:** Rape through force, threat, or intimidation (Art. 266-A(1)(a), RPC); Out-of-court photographic identification: totality of circumstances test and "danger signals"; No standard reaction of rape victims; failure to call for help; "Lust is no respecter of time or place"; Deference to trial court findings on credibility
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 3. Competent and Credible Evidence)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (XII. Damages > C. Other Kinds of Damages)

### Doctrine
**Reiterated:** the reliability of an out-of-court identification is tested by the **totality of circumstances**: (1) the witness's opportunity to view the criminal at the time of the crime; (2) the witness's degree of attention at that time; (3) the accuracy of any prior description given by the witness; (4) the length of time between the crime and the identification; (5) the level of certainty demonstrated by the witness at the identification; and (6) the suggestiveness of the identification procedure. The Court also listed the twelve "danger signals" that tend to show an out-of-court identification may be erroneous (from *People v. Jimenez*). **A photographic identification is not suggestive where the victim was shown photographs of different men every day, the accused was not singled out, and the victim immediately recognized him when she saw his photograph.** A two-month gap does not defeat the identification where the victim saw the assailant's face up close, including by the light of his flashlight, and was not distracted.

There is no standard reaction of a rape victim; failure to shout or call for help does not impair her credibility. "Lust is no respecter of time or place": rape is not always committed in seclusion. The trial court's assessment of credibility is respected on appeal unless significant matters were overlooked, and it carries greater weight when affirmed by the CA (all reiterated).

Rape under **Article 266-A(1)(a) of the RPC**, as amended by RA 8353, requires (1) carnal knowledge of the victim, (2) accomplished through force, threat, or intimidation. A knife held to the victim's nape with a threat to hurt her if she screamed, followed by punches when she resisted, establishes force, threat, or intimidation. The penalty is reclusion perpetua (Art. 266-B), with PHP 75,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, plus 6% annual interest from finality until full payment.

### Facts
Accused-appellant Ronaldo Infortuno, Sr. was charged with forcible abduction with rape of 17-year-old AAA, a distant neighbor in San Ildefonso, Bulacan. According to the prosecution, at around 1:00 to 1:30 a.m. on July 22, 2017, a man entered the room where AAA was sleeping with her younger brother. He poked a knife at her nape and whispered, "Subukan mong sumigaw. Masasaktan ka." He tied her hands, gagged her, and brought her to a rice field. There he cut her shirt and bra with scissors and removed her pajama and panty. When she resisted his first attempt at penetration, he punched her stomach and right thigh. He moved her to another place and had carnal knowledge of her. Afterwards he made her lie down and, using a small flashlight, cut her pubic hair. AAA saw his face by the light of the flashlight. He then let her go.

AAA immediately told her grandmother, other relatives and her mother, MMM, and they reported the incident to the police. The assailant was a stranger to AAA, so his identity was unknown; she told her mother that she did not know his name but would recognize his face. Every day MMM showed AAA pictures of different people. Learning from neighbors that a drinking session had been held across the highway that night, MMM mentioned several names, which AAA did not recognize. One of them was the accused, who was working on the house next door. MMM found his photographs on Facebook. On October 2, 2017, about two months after the rape, MMM showed them to AAA, who immediately said, "Siya, siya ang naggahasa sa akin." A medico-legal officer found injuries and "clear evidence of recent blunt penetrating trauma to the hymen."

The accused denied the charge and said he was at a drinking session in another barangay from about 7:00 p.m. until about 6:00 a.m. The RTC of Malolos City (Branch 18, November 4, 2020) convicted him of forcible abduction with rape and imposed reclusion perpetua and damages. On appeal, he attacked AAA's credibility and identification. He argued that it was dark, the flashlight pointed at her private part and not at his face, she had never met him, she gave no prior description, and she identified him only two months later after her mother showed her his photograph. He also argued that a criminal would not use a flashlight, that force was not proved because she did not see the knife and did not shout, and that forcible abduction is absorbed in rape. The CA (March 27, 2023, CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 15216) affirmed with modification, convicting him of rape under Article 266-A(1) instead of forcible abduction with rape, with the same penalty and damages.

### Issues
1. Whether the CA erred in finding accused-appellant guilty beyond reasonable doubt of rape, including whether AAA was a credible witness and whether her out-of-court identification of accused-appellant was reliable.

### Ruling
**1. No. The conviction for rape was affirmed.**

*Credibility.* The Court held that not all rape victims react the same way: "some may shout, some may faint, and some may be shocked into insensibility." AAA's failure to call for help therefore did not affect her credibility. The argument that crimes are usually committed clandestinely also failed, because lust is no respecter of time or place. The trial court, affirmed by the CA, gave full credence to AAA, and no significant matter was overlooked.

*Identification.* Applying the totality of circumstances test and the danger signals, the Court found AAA's identification credible. Although there were no lights in the house or the rice field, AAA saw the accused's face when he placed the flashlight in her mouth. The light pointed toward her private part, but he was in the same direction, so she could see his face, and she was not distracted. AAA also testified that his face was "lapit na lapit" when he grabbed her and held the knife to her. **On the two-month gap, the Court found the photographic procedure "not at all suggestive": MMM showed AAA photographs of different men every day, nothing showed the accused was singled out, and AAA immediately recognized him only when she saw his photograph on October 2, 2017.**

*Elements.* AAA's testimony, corroborated by the medico-legal findings, proved carnal knowledge. Force, threat, or intimidation was clear: the accused held a knife to AAA's nape and threatened to hurt her if she screamed, cut her clothes with scissors, and punched her when she resisted. Reclusion perpetua was correctly imposed under Article 266-B, and the PHP 75,000 awards of civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages were affirmed, with 6% legal interest per annum from finality.

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA's March 27, 2023 Decision in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 15216 was AFFIRMED. Infortuno was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. He was ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 as civil indemnity, PHP 75,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 75,000.00 as exemplary damages, all with 6% legal interest per annum from finality of the Decision until full payment.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Past midnight, a stranger entered the room of BBB, 19, held a knife to her neck, dragged her to a vacant lot and raped her. The lot was dark, but the assailant's face was inches from hers, and he later switched on a penlight to look for his belongings, lighting up his face. BBB reported the rape that morning but said she did not know the man's name, only that she would know his face. For six weeks her brother showed her photographs of different men from social media every day; she recognized none. When she was shown the photographs of Dario, a worker at a nearby construction site, she immediately said, "Siya po iyon." At trial, Dario argues that the out-of-court identification is unreliable because of the darkness, the six-week delay, and the use of photographs. Is Dario correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. BBB's out-of-court identification passes the totality of circumstances test and is credible.
- **Legal basis:** The reliability of an out-of-court identification is determined by the totality of circumstances test: (1) the witness's opportunity to view the criminal at the time of the crime; (2) the witness's degree of attention; (3) the accuracy of any prior description; (4) the length of time between the crime and the identification; (5) the level of certainty at the identification; and (6) the suggestiveness of the procedure. In People v. Infortuno (G.R. No. 269722, January 6, 2026), the Court upheld a rape victim's identification of the accused from a Facebook photograph about two months after the crime. The victim saw his face by the light of his flashlight, she was shown photographs of different men daily, the accused was not singled out, and she immediately recognized him.
- **Application:** BBB had a close view of the assailant, whose face was inches from hers and later lit by the penlight, and nothing distracted her attention. From the start she said she would recognize his face. Six weeks is not so long as to make the identification doubtful. The procedure was not suggestive: she was shown many different men daily, recognized none of them, and immediately and positively identified Dario when she saw his photographs. Darkness alone does not defeat an identification made under these circumstances.
- **Conclusion:** Dario's objection fails because BBB's photographic identification of him is reliable under the totality of circumstances test.

**Q2.** CCC was raped at night by a man she had never seen before. At the police station that morning, she told the investigator that it was too dark and she could not identify her attacker. Five months later, a police officer showed her one photograph, that of Efren, saying, "This is the man the neighbors suspect. Is this him?" CCC said yes. No other photograph or lineup was shown to her. Would CCC's out-of-court identification satisfy the totality of circumstances test? Explain.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The identification is doubtful because the procedure was suggestive and several danger signals are present.
- **Legal basis:** Under the totality of circumstances test, the court considers, among others, the witness's opportunity to view the criminal, the length of time between the crime and the identification, and the suggestiveness of the identification procedure. Danger signals that an out-of-court identification may be erroneous include: the witness originally stated that she could not identify anyone; before the crime, the witness had limited opportunity to see the accused; and a considerable time elapsed between the witness's view of the criminal and the identification. (People v. Infortuno, G.R. No. 269722, January 6, 2026, citing People v. Jimenez)
- **Application:** In Infortuno, the Court upheld the identification because the victim saw the assailant's face by flashlight, said from the start that she would recognize him, and picked him out of photographs of different men shown to her daily, without his being singled out. Here, every one of those safeguards is missing. CCC said at the outset that she could not identify her attacker. She had never seen him before. Five months passed. She was shown a single photograph accompanied by a remark that he was the suspect, which singled Efren out and suggested the answer.
- **Conclusion:** CCC's out-of-court identification would not pass the totality of circumstances test and cannot by itself establish Efren's identity as the rapist beyond reasonable doubt.

**Q3.** Felix poked a knife at the nape of DDD while she slept and whispered that she would be hurt if she screamed. He tied her hands and brought her to a field, where he punched her when she resisted and then had carnal knowledge of her. DDD admitted on cross-examination that she never actually saw the knife and that she never shouted for help. (a) Was the element of force, threat, or intimidation proved, and does her failure to shout impair her credibility? (b) If Felix is convicted of rape, what civil liabilities should be imposed?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, force, threat, or intimidation was proved, and her failure to shout does not impair her credibility. (b) Felix should pay civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages of PHP 75,000.00 each, with 6% legal interest per annum from finality of the judgment until full payment.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 266-A(1)(a) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 8353, rape is committed by a man who has carnal knowledge of a woman through force, threat, or intimidation. There is no standard form of reaction for a victim of sexual assault; failure to call for help does not impair the credibility of a rape victim. In People v. Infortuno (G.R. No. 269722, January 6, 2026), the Court found force, threat, or intimidation where the accused held a knife to the victim's nape, threatened to hurt her if she screamed, and punched her when she resisted. It imposed reclusion perpetua and awarded PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, all with 6% interest per annum from finality.
- **Application:** (a) Felix's threat that DDD would be hurt if she screamed, made while pressing a knife to her nape, is intimidation whether or not she saw the blade. Tying her hands and punching her when she resisted is force. DDD's silence is consistent with fear and does not make her testimony less believable. (b) Following Infortuno, a conviction for simple rape carries civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages of PHP 75,000.00 each, earning 6% interest per annum from finality.
- **Conclusion:** Felix may be convicted of rape through force, threat, or intimidation and held liable for PHP 75,000.00 each in civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, with 6% annual interest from finality.

> Note: The Information charged forcible abduction with rape; the CA convicted for rape only, and the Supreme Court affirmed without separately discussing why forcible abduction was not imposed. The narration says AAA and her family reported the incident to the police on the day of the crime, while AAA testified that she lodged her complaint on October 2, 2017, when she saw the accused's photograph. The decision mentions an act of oral sex during the incident but does not treat it as a separate offense; it was not charged. Bar Q2 applies the Court's danger signals to facts the Court did not decide; its answer is derived from the test as the Court stated it.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70344)

## Solis v. People

**IAN SOLIS Y AQUINO, PETITIONER, VS. PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 255485 | 2025-11-26 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > A. Felonies > 4. Stages of Execution > c. Attempted, Frustrated, and Consummated Stages  
**Specific topics:** Frustrated vs. attempted homicide: the fatal character of the wound must be proven; Medico-legal certificate without the attending physician's testimony; Circumstantial evidence sufficient for conviction (Rule 133, Sec. 4); Voluntary surrender not appreciated when police are already at the accused's house; Treachery proven but not alleged: no qualification, but exemplary damages
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 2. Direct and Circumstantial Evidence)
  
**Also relevant to:** Criminal Law (II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > B. Criminal Liability > 8. Circumstances Affecting Criminal Liability > c. Mitigating Circumstances)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > B. Prosecution of Offenses (Rule 110) > 6. Complaint or Information > b. Sufficiency > ii. Designation of the Offense; Qualifying and Aggravating Circumstances)

### Doctrine
**Whether an injury is fatal is a question of fact. Absent testimony from the attending physician that the injury would have caused the victim's death without timely medical assistance, the Court cannot presume that it is fatal, even if the medico-legal certificate shows that vital organs were involved or that significant blood loss occurred, "since what may be fatal for one person may not be fatal for another."** In a prosecution for frustrated homicide, the victim's wounds must be proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the physician who attended to them. A medical certificate is merely the opinion of one who must first be established as an expert, and the defense must be able to cross-examine its author; a stipulation on the certificate's existence is not enough. The doubt on the character of the wounds is resolved in favor of the accused, so the crime is only **attempted homicide** (reiterating *Etino v. People* and *Oliveros v. People*).

Circumstantial evidence suffices to convict under **Rule 133, Section 4** when (a) there is more than one circumstance, (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven, and (c) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The circumstances must form an unbroken chain pointing to the accused, to the exclusion of all others, as the guilty person (reiterated).

Voluntary surrender is not appreciated when the accused gives himself up only after the police come to his house, tell his family he is a suspect, and ask his parents to surrender him; the surrender must be spontaneous. Treachery proven at trial but not alleged in the Information cannot qualify the crime to murder, but it supports an award of exemplary damages; the Court reiterated *People v. Solar*'s reminder to prosecutors to allege attendant circumstances with particularity.

### Facts
Ian Solis and the minors XXX (his brother), YYY and ZZZ were charged with frustrated homicide (Criminal Case No. 2017-0215-D) for stabbing Jun Ferriol around 1:30 a.m. of March 3, 2017 in Pangasinan, with intent to kill and in conspiracy, the victim surviving because of timely medical attendance. They were also charged with theft (Criminal Case No. 2017-0216-D). Ian, XXX and YYY were acquitted of theft. ZZZ escaped during the proceedings; when he surrendered, Jun executed an affidavit of desistance and the case against him was dismissed.

Ian, a friend of Jun for two years, came to Jun's house with his three companions around 10:30 p.m. of March 2, 2017. They drank brandy and watched a movie. Jun went to sleep and told them to lock the door when they left. He woke up to a pair of scissors in his right side; someone choked him while others covered his mouth and held his hands and feet. The room was dim, so he did not see his attackers. He played dead until they left, then went to his mother's house and was operated on at the Medical City Pangasinan. At the scene, the police found a blood-stained pair of scissors and a mobile phone bearing a picture of a man whom neighbors identified as Ian. Tricycle driver Noel Garcia said that around 2:30 a.m. he drove four teenagers who were rushing and seemed afraid of something; one carried a black bag, and another wore a blood-stained shirt. The police went to Ian's house, told his parents that Ian was a suspect, and asked them to surrender him; Ian then surrendered. Around 7:20 a.m., Garcia identified the four at the police station, naming Ian as the one still wearing the bloodied shirt. The accused claimed they left Jun's house at 11:00 p.m. and never returned.

The existence of the medico-legal certificate was stipulated; the attending physician did not testify. The certificate showed stab wounds that injured Jun's liver, colon and kidney, with about 400 ml of blood in the abdominal cavity. The hospital's total charges were PHP 288,993.65, but the final amount due after discounts was PHP 201,478.65.

The RTC convicted Ian, XXX and YYY of frustrated homicide, appreciated voluntary surrender for Ian, and awarded actual damages of PHP 282,993.65 and moral damages of PHP 20,000.00. The CA affirmed with modification, increasing the penalty and adding PHP 30,000.00 civil indemnity and PHP 10,000.00 more in moral damages. Ian's motion for reconsideration was denied. In his Rule 45 petition, Ian argued that the circumstantial evidence did not prove his identity as one of the assailants.

### Issues
1. Whether the prosecution proved, through circumstantial evidence, that Ian was one of the persons who stabbed Jun.
2. Whether the crime committed was frustrated homicide, when the fatal character of the wounds was shown only by a medico-legal certificate whose author did not testify.
3. Whether Ian is entitled to the mitigating circumstance of voluntary surrender.
4. Whether the civil liabilities were correctly awarded.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, Ian's identity was proven by circumstantial evidence.** The petition raised questions of fact beyond Rule 45, but even on review the lower courts were correct. Direct evidence is not required to convict, and its probative value is generally not superior to circumstantial evidence. The CA relied on eight circumstances: Ian and his companions were at the scene before the attack; they drank until Jun slept ahead of them; Jun woke to a stab from scissors; several persons held him while one stabbed him; contrary to their claim of leaving at 11:00 p.m., Garcia drove them at around 2:30 a.m., close to when the crime was reported; they were in a hurry; one passenger wore a bloodstained shirt; and Ian's phone was found at the scene. Each was proven by Ian's admission, Jun's testimony, Garcia's testimony or the police testimony, and together they were consistent with guilt and inconsistent with innocence. Garcia identified Ian about five hours later as the one in the bloodied shirt. As in *People v. Casitas*, where the accused was seen leaving the victim's house in blood-soaked clothes, **the fact that only Ian wore a bloodied shirt led to the conclusion that he was the one who stabbed Jun, to the exclusion of his companions or any other person.** Non-presentation of the shirt was not fatal, since it was merely corroborative. The RTC's credibility findings, affirmed by the CA, were binding.

**2. No, only attempted homicide was proven.** The elements of frustrated homicide are: (1) intent to kill, as shown by the use of a deadly weapon; (2) the victim sustained fatal wounds but did not die because of timely medical assistance; and (3) no qualifying circumstance for murder. Intent to kill was shown by the use of scissors and the number and location of the wounds. But the lower courts proved the second element only by the medico-legal certificate, whose existence was stipulated without the attending physician's testimony. Unlike in rape, where medical examination is not indispensable, in frustrated homicide the wounds must be "proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the physician who attended to said fatal wounds." Citing *Etino*, "where there is nothing in the evidence to show that the wound would be fatal if not medically attended to, the character of the wound is doubtful," and the doubt is resolved in favor of the accused. **Ian could be held liable only for attempted homicide; the Court "cannot presume" the wounds fatal even if vital organs were involved or significant blood loss occurred.**

**3. No.** Voluntary surrender requires that (1) the accused was not arrested, (2) he surrendered to a person in authority or an agent, and (3) the surrender was voluntary, showing spontaneity and an intent to surrender unconditionally. Ian surrendered only when the police were already at his house and had told him and his family that he was a suspect, and the police even had to implore his parents to surrender him. **Voluntary surrender is not appreciated when the authorities' presence in the accused's house has already precluded his escape.**

**4. Modified.** For attempted homicide, civil indemnity and moral damages are PHP 20,000.00 each (*People v. Jugueta*). Because an aggravating circumstance was proven at trial though not alleged in the Information, exemplary damages of PHP 20,000.00 were also awarded: Jun was stabbed while asleep and unable to defend himself, which was treachery and would have qualified the crime to attempted murder had the Information alleged the ultimate facts constituting it. Actual damages were reduced to PHP 201,478.65, the final hospital bill after discounts and subsidies, since a party may recover only the pecuniary loss duly proven. The Court reiterated *People v. Solar* in urging prosecutors to state in the Information, with sufficient particularity, the qualifying and aggravating circumstances.

### Disposition
Petition DENIED. The CA Decision of July 10, 2020 and Resolution of January 20, 2021 in CA-G.R. CR No. 41501 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Ian Solis y Aquino was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of attempted homicide and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six months of arresto mayor, as minimum, to four years and two months of prisión correccional, as maximum. He was ordered to pay Jun actual damages of PHP 201,478.65, and civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages of PHP 20,000.00 each, all with 6% interest per annum from finality of the Decision until fully paid.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Marco stabbed Paolo several times in the abdomen with a kitchen knife. Paolo was rushed to the hospital and survived after emergency surgery. Marco was charged with frustrated homicide. At pre-trial, the parties stipulated on the existence of the medico-legal certificate, which stated that Paolo suffered penetrating stab wounds that lacerated his liver, with about 500 ml of blood loss. The attending surgeon was never presented. The prosecution argues that a lacerated liver and heavy blood loss are obviously fatal. If Marco's identity and intent to kill are proven, of what crime should he be convicted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Marco should be convicted only of attempted homicide, not frustrated homicide.
- **Legal basis:** Frustrated homicide requires (1) intent to kill, (2) fatal wounds that did not cause death because of timely medical assistance, and (3) no qualifying circumstance for murder. Whether an injury is fatal is a question of fact. In a prosecution for frustrated homicide, the wounds must be proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the attending physician; absent such testimony, the Court cannot presume the wounds fatal even if the medico-legal certificate shows that vital organs were involved or that significant blood loss occurred, since what may be fatal for one person may not be fatal for another. Doubt on the character of the wounds is resolved in favor of the accused. (Solis v. People, G.R. No. 255485, November 26, 2025, reiterating Etino v. People)
- **Application:** Intent to kill is shown by the use of a knife and the location of the wounds. But the only proof that the wounds were fatal is the medico-legal certificate, whose existence alone was stipulated. Without the surgeon's testimony that Paolo would have died without timely medical help, and without the chance for the defense to cross-examine the author of the certificate, the fatal character of the wounds is doubtful. The involvement of the liver and the 500 ml blood loss do not allow the court to presume that the wounds were fatal.
- **Conclusion:** With the second element of frustrated homicide not proven, Marco is guilty only of attempted homicide.

**Q2.** Same facts as in the previous question, except that the attending surgeon testified in court. She explained her qualifications, identified the medico-legal certificate, and stated that Paolo's liver wounds would have caused his death from internal bleeding within hours had he not undergone emergency surgery. The defense cross-examined her but did not shake her testimony. Of what crime should Marco be convicted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Marco should be convicted of frustrated homicide.
- **Legal basis:** The second element of frustrated homicide, that the victim sustained fatal wounds but did not die because of timely medical assistance, must be proven beyond reasonable doubt through the testimony of the physician who attended to the wounds. A medical certificate gains weight when the doctor who issued it is presented to establish his or her qualifications and is subjected to cross-examination. (Solis v. People, G.R. No. 255485, November 26, 2025)
- **Application:** Unlike in Solis, the prosecution here presented the attending surgeon, who established her qualifications and testified that the wounds would have caused Paolo's death without the emergency surgery. Her testimony was tested by cross-examination. This proves that the wounds were fatal and that Paolo survived only because of timely medical assistance. Since intent to kill is shown by the use of a knife and the nature and location of the wounds, and no qualifying circumstance is alleged, all elements of frustrated homicide are present.
- **Conclusion:** With the fatal character of the wounds proven by the attending physician, Marco is guilty of frustrated homicide.

**Q3.** Lito stabbed Dino while Dino was fast asleep in his room. Dino survived. The Information charged Lito with attempted homicide and did not allege any qualifying or aggravating circumstance. At trial, the prosecution clearly proved that Dino was asleep and unable to defend himself when he was stabbed. (a) May Lito be convicted of attempted murder? (b) Does the proven circumstance have any effect on Lito's civil liability?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Lito may be convicted only of attempted homicide. (b) Yes. Exemplary damages may be awarded.
- **Legal basis:** Stabbing a sleeping victim who is not in a position to defend himself constitutes treachery, which qualifies homicide to murder. However, qualifying and aggravating circumstances must be alleged in the Information with the ultimate facts constituting them (Rule 110, Secs. 8 and 9); otherwise they cannot qualify the crime or raise the penalty. In Solis v. People (G.R. No. 255485, November 26, 2025), treachery was proven but not alleged, so it could not qualify the crime to attempted murder; but because an aggravating circumstance was proven at trial although not alleged in the Information, the Court awarded exemplary damages of PHP 20,000.00, in addition to civil indemnity and moral damages of PHP 20,000.00 each for attempted homicide (citing People v. Jugueta), and reiterated People v. Solar's reminder to prosecutors.
- **Application:** (a) Treachery was proven, but since the Information did not allege it, Lito cannot be convicted of attempted murder; doing so would violate his right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation. He is liable only for attempted homicide, the crime charged. (b) The proven treachery, though it cannot affect the crime or the penalty, justifies the award of exemplary damages, on top of civil indemnity and moral damages.
- **Conclusion:** Lito is guilty only of attempted homicide, but the proven treachery entitles Dino to exemplary damages.

> Note: XXX, YYY and ZZZ are minors whose names were replaced with fictitious initials under RA 9344; the victim's surname is also spelled "Ferreol" in parts of the record. The RTC also convicted XXX and YYY, but only Ian's petition was before the Court. The Decision says the RTC awarded actual damages of PHP 282,993.65 while the CA "arrived at PHP 288,993.65" (the total hospital charges) but upheld the RTC award; both were reduced to PHP 201,478.65. The Decision states that the medical findings showed "seven stab wounds"; the intraoperative findings it quotes also list non-penetrating wounds and abrasions. The penalty in the disposition is stated as the fallo reads; the 2027 Bar does not ask for computation of penalty periods.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70271)

## People v. Bautista

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. JERYL BAUTISTA Y MARTINEZ, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 255749 | 2025-10-15 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Repealed. See instead Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640)  
**Specific topics:** Chain of custody: marking, inventory and photography "immediately" after seizure; Waiting for the insulating witnesses is not a justifiable ground for delay; Nisperos guidelines on Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640; Plain view doctrine only supplements a valid warrantless search; Search incident to a lawful arrest (Ridon requisites)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > O. Search and Seizure (Rule 126) > 2. Warrantless Search > b. Plain View Doctrine)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 1. Object or Real Evidence > c. Chain of Custody)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > C. Right Against Unreasonable Searches and Seizures > 2. Warrantless Arrests and Searches)

### Doctrine
In illegal sale and illegal possession of dangerous drugs, the drug itself is the corpus delicti. The first link in the chain of custody requires compliance with Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, under the **Nisperos guidelines (reiterated)**. Marking must be done immediately upon confiscation, at the place of confiscation, and in the presence of the offender. Inventory and photography must be done immediately after seizure, in the presence of the accused and, for seizures from August 7, 2014, an elected public official and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media. "Immediately" carries a **time requirement** (no unreasonable delay or intervening period) and a **place requirement** (at the place of arrest). Any deviation must be acknowledged and justified by the prosecution, which must also show that the integrity of the items was preserved.

**Where the officers made the accused wait 10 to 15 minutes for the insulating witnesses to arrive before marking, inventorying and photographing the sachet sold, the marking was not "immediate." The witnesses' absence at the time of seizure is not a justifiable ground, because they should have been present or near the place of seizure from the start** (People v. Ramos). The seizure and custody of that item are void, its integrity is compromised, and the accused must be acquitted of illegal sale.

**The plain view doctrine only supplements an existing justification for a warrantless search** (People v. Musa). Compliance with it is not always required, especially when the search is limited to the person of the accused, where items are usually hidden. Drugs found in a frisk incident to a lawful arrest in flagrante delicto are admissible if the Ridon requisites are met: (a) a lawful arrest; (b) a warrantless search made after it; (c) limited to the person of the accused and the area within his immediate control; and (d) done at the place of arrest.

### Facts
Jeryl Bautista was charged in two Informations with illegal possession of dangerous drugs (three sachets of shabu weighing 0.673, 0.630 and 0.767 gram, or 2.07 grams in all) under Section 11 of RA 9165, and illegal sale (one sachet of 0.13 gram) under Section 5. Both offenses were allegedly committed on August 27, 2017 in San Carlos City, Pangasinan.

Acting on a tip that morning, PO2 De Guzman and an informant went to Bautista's house. The informant introduced De Guzman as a buyer, and they set a meeting for 4:00 to 5:00 p.m. At about 4:00 p.m., in Barangay San Pedro-Taloy, Bautista approached them, received the PHP 500.00 marked money from De Guzman, and handed over a sachet of shabu. On the pre-arranged signal, the team rushed in and PO1 Tuazon arrested Bautista. A DOJ representative and two barangay kagawads arrived shortly after. PO1 Tuazon then searched Bautista and found three more sachets inside a cellphone charger, together with a cellphone, a screwdriver, a weighing scale and the marked money. The items were marked, inventoried and photographed at the place of arrest in the presence of the witnesses, turned over to the investigators and the forensic chemist, and tested positive for methamphetamine hydrochloride. PO1 Tuazon admitted that after the arrest, "[w]e made the accused sit and waited for witnesses," for "[a]bout 10-15 minutes," before the marking.

Bautista claimed he had been framed. The RTC (January 11, 2019) convicted him on both charges. For possession it imposed 12 years and 1 day to 16 years and a fine of PHP 300,000.00; for sale, life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 500,000.00. The CA (October 6, 2020) affirmed in toto. On appeal Bautista argued that the buy-bust was not fully established, that Section 21 was not complied with, and that the three sachets were inadmissible because they were not in plain view.

### Issues
1. Whether Bautista is guilty of illegal sale of dangerous drugs, given that the sachet sold was marked, inventoried and photographed only after a 10- to 15-minute wait for the insulating witnesses.
2. Whether Bautista is guilty of illegal possession of dangerous drugs.
3. Whether the three sachets found on Bautista's person are inadmissible because they were not seized in plain view.

### Ruling
**1. No; he is acquitted of illegal sale.** PO2 De Guzman's positive testimony proved the identities of the buyer and seller and the consummated sale, but the prosecution failed to prove the third element: the existence and integrity of the corpus delicti. The Court applied Section 21 as amended by RA 10640, the Nisperos guidelines, and Tomawis's reading of "immediately after seizure and confiscation" as covering both time and place, and found the chain broken at the first link. The marking, inventory and photography were done at the place of seizure and before the accused and the witnesses. But PO1 Tuazon's admission that they waited 10 to 15 minutes for the witnesses "belies the prosecution's claim" that these steps were done immediately upon seizure. The officers gave no justifiable ground. The delay came from their own failure to have the witnesses at or near the place of the transaction, and under People v. Ramos, the witnesses' absence at the time of seizure "is not a justifiable ground for not immediately marking the items." The Court added that recent jurisprudence "veers towards marking immediately after seizure and confiscation or at the place of arrest and in the presence of the insulating witnesses." The seizure and custody of the sachet sold were therefore void, and its integrity and evidentiary value were compromised.

**2. Yes, he is guilty of illegal possession.** All the elements were proved: possession of a prohibited drug, without legal authority, held freely and consciously. PO1 Tuazon frisked Bautista in front of the DOJ representative and the barangay kagawads. The three sachets were marked, inventoried and photographed at the place of arrest in their presence, then passed to the investigators, the forensic chemist and the court, so every link was accounted for. Unexplained possession is prima facie evidence of animus possidendi, and hiding the sachets inside a cellphone charger showed an intent to possess them.

**3. No; the sachets are admissible as the fruit of a valid search incident to a lawful arrest.** A search incident to a lawful arrest and the seizure of evidence in plain view are separate exceptions to the warrant requirement. Under Ridon v. People, a search incident to a lawful arrest is valid when (a) the accused was lawfully arrested, (b) the officers then made a warrantless search, (c) the search was limited to the person and the area within his immediate control, and (d) it was performed at the place of arrest. Following People v. Musa (citing Coolidge v. New Hampshire), "the plain view doctrine only supplements the existing justification for a valid warrantless search." **Compliance with the plain view doctrine is not always required, which "is especially true if the search is limited to the person of the accused, where the seized items are usually hidden"; and plain view does not apply where officers are intentionally searching the person of the accused.** Bautista was lawfully arrested for selling drugs and frisked at the place of arrest, so the Ridon requisites were met. "His lawful arrest for selling dangerous drugs justifies the warrantless search, not the seizure of evidence in plain view."

The penalty for possession of less than five grams of shabu under Section 11 (12 years and 1 day to 20 years, and a fine of PHP 300,000.00 to PHP 400,000.00) was properly imposed.

### Disposition
The appeal was PARTIALLY GRANTED, and the CA Decision dated October 6, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 12591 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. In Criminal Case No. SCC-9606, Bautista was found GUILTY of illegal possession of dangerous drugs and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of 12 years and 1 day, as minimum, to 16 years, as maximum, and a fine of PHP 300,000.00. In Criminal Case No. SCC-9607, he was ACQUITTED of illegal sale of dangerous drugs on reasonable doubt, and entry of judgment in that case was ordered issued immediately.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In a buy-bust operation on March 3, 2025, PO1 Ramos bought a sachet of shabu from Jun for PHP 500.00 and arrested him on the spot. The team had not brought any witnesses with them. They made Jun sit by the roadside while they called a barangay kagawad and a media representative, who arrived 15 minutes later. Only then did the officers mark, inventory and photograph the sachet, at the place of arrest and in the presence of Jun and the two witnesses. The prosecution's only explanation for the delay was the witnesses' late arrival. Should Jun be convicted of illegal sale of dangerous drugs?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Jun should be acquitted because the chain of custody was broken at the first link.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, and the guidelines in People v. Nisperos, marking must be done immediately upon confiscation, at the place of confiscation, and in the presence of the offender. Inventory and photography must be done immediately after seizure, in the presence of the accused, an elected public official, and a National Prosecution Service or media representative. "Immediately" requires compliance with both the time and the place requirements, and any deviation must be acknowledged and justified. In People v. Bautista (G.R. No. 255749, October 15, 2025), the Court held that a 10- to 15-minute wait for the witnesses before marking was not immediate. The witnesses' absence at the time of seizure is not a justifiable ground, because they should have been present or near the place of seizure from the start (citing People v. Ramos).
- **Application:** The marking, inventory and photography took place at the place of arrest and before the required witnesses, but not immediately. For 15 minutes the sachet was in the officers' hands unmarked. The only reason was the team's own failure to bring the witnesses, which is not a justifiable ground. The identity and integrity of the corpus delicti are therefore in doubt.
- **Conclusion:** Jun must be acquitted of illegal sale of dangerous drugs on reasonable doubt.

**Q2.** Same buy-bust as in the previous problem, except that the barangay kagawad and the DOJ representative were waiting in the team's vehicle 20 meters away and came over as soon as the signal was given. Before the sachet could be marked, a crowd of Jun's relatives gathered and began throwing stones at the officers. The team brought Jun, the witnesses and the sachet straight to the nearest police station, where the sachet was marked, inventoried and photographed in the presence of Jun and the witnesses. The prosecution acknowledged the deviation, explained it, and accounted for every person who handled the sachet. Is the chain of custody broken?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The deviation from the place requirement is justified and the integrity of the sachet was preserved, so the seizure is not invalidated.
- **Legal basis:** For warrantless seizures, Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, allows the inventory and photography to be done at the nearest police station or office of the apprehending team, "whichever is practicable." Its saving clause provides that non-compliance on justifiable grounds does not void the seizure if the integrity and evidentiary value of the items are preserved. Under People v. Nisperos, the prosecution must acknowledge the deviation and prove both the justifiable ground and the preservation of integrity. People v. Bautista (G.R. No. 255749, October 15, 2025) reiterated that immediacy is judged case by case, and that where there is a practical reason, marking at the nearest police station falls within the concept of immediate marking (citing People v. Sahibil).
- **Application:** Unlike in Bautista, the witnesses were near the place of seizure from the start. The move to the police station was caused not by the officers' lack of preparation but by a hostile crowd that made marking at the scene impracticable. The prosecution acknowledged and explained the deviation and accounted for the sachet at every step until it was marked, inventoried and photographed at the nearest police station, in the presence of the accused and the witnesses.
- **Conclusion:** The chain of custody is not broken, and the sachet may support a conviction if the other elements are proved.

**Q3.** After arresting Lito in flagrante delicto for selling shabu, PO2 Diaz immediately frisked him at the place of arrest and found two sachets of shabu wrapped in tissue inside a coin purse in Lito's pocket. Charged with illegal possession, Lito moves to exclude the sachets. He argues that they were not in plain view and their discovery was not inadvertent, so the warrantless seizure violated his right against unreasonable searches and seizures. Should the motion be granted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The sachets were validly seized in a search incident to a lawful arrest, and compliance with the plain view doctrine was not required.
- **Legal basis:** A search incident to a lawful arrest is an exception to the warrant requirement under Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution and Rule 126 of the Rules of Court. It is valid when (a) the accused was lawfully arrested, (b) the officers then made a warrantless search, (c) the search was limited to the person and the area within his immediate control, and (d) it was performed at the place of arrest (Ridon v. People). In People v. Bautista (G.R. No. 255749, October 15, 2025), the Court held that the plain view doctrine only supplements an existing justification for a warrantless search. Compliance with it is not always required, especially where the search is limited to the person of the accused, and it does not apply where officers are intentionally searching the person.
- **Application:** Lito was lawfully arrested while selling drugs. PO2 Diaz then searched only Lito's person, at the place of arrest, so all four Ridon requisites are present. The sachets were hidden in a coin purse and were not in plain view, but that does not matter, because the lawful arrest itself justified the search.
- **Conclusion:** The motion should be denied because the sachets are admissible.

> Note: The decision does not expressly explain why the chain held for the possessed sachets but not for the sachet sold. The facts it adopts show that the frisk took place after the witnesses arrived and was done in front of them, so those sachets were marked in their presence immediately upon seizure. Zalameda, J. was on official leave.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70235)
