## People v. XXX

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. YYY, ZZZ (ACQUITTED), AND XXX, ACCUSED; XXX, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 264132 | 2025-08-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** IV. Special Penal Laws > P. Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act (RA 9208, Secs. 3–6 and 10–12, as amended by RA 10364, 11862, and 12312)  
**Specific topics:** Elements of trafficking in persons under Sec. 4(a), RA 9208, as amended; Mere receipt or hiring of a person for exploitation, with or without consent; Liability of a non-owner bar manager; registered ownership neither required nor sufficient; Means: taking advantage of the vulnerability of a minor; Qualified trafficking when the victim is a child (Sec. 6(a))

### Doctrine
Trafficking in persons under **Section 4(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended by RA No. 10364**, has three elements (reiterating *People v. Casio*): (1) the **act**: recruitment, obtaining, hiring, providing, offering, transportation, transfer, maintaining, harboring, or receipt of persons, "with or without the victim's consent or knowledge"; (2) the **means**: threat, force or other coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power or position, taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person, or giving or receiving payments or benefits to achieve the consent of one having control over another; and (3) the **purpose**: exploitation or prostitution of others, other forms of sexual exploitation, forced labor, slavery, servitude, or removal or sale of organs. The crime is **qualified under Section 6(a)** when the trafficked person is a child.

**The law punishes the mere receipt of persons for the purpose of trafficking, regardless of the victim's consent or knowledge.** A bar manager who hired and supervised a minor is liable even if she is not the owner of the bar and even if others brought the minor to her. Acts of trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of the establishment, and registered ownership by itself does not create criminal liability (*People v. Villanueva*). The means element is met by **taking advantage of the victim's vulnerability as a minor** (*People v. De Dios*), so the minor's admission that she was not forced to work and could have refused does not defeat the charge. Allowing customers to take the minor out for sex and collecting the "bar fine" establishes the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation.

### Facts
XXX, YYY, and ZZZ were charged with qualified trafficking in persons. The Information alleged that on or about July 1, 2014 and for some time after, in a municipality in Isabela, they conspired to recruit, transport, hire, receive, keep, and maintain AAA, a 17-year-old minor, for prostitution and sexual exploitation, under the pretext of employing her as a guest relations officer (GRO) at a bar.

The prosecution showed that on July 1, 2014, AAA's friends BJE and ZZZ brought her to the bar, where she was introduced to XXX, who hired her as a GRO. XXX made her sit and drink with male customers ("pa-table") for a PHP 50.00 commission per bottle. XXX also let customers take AAA to a hotel for sex after they paid XXX a "bar fine." AAA testified that a customer told XXX he would take her out, and XXX only told him to return her. The customer had sex with her at a hotel and handed PHP 1,500.00 to XXX. AAA received no salary because the manager kept her commissions. She identified XXX as the one who "employed" and "hired" her. XXX herself testified that YYY told her AAA would work with her at the bar. Police rescued AAA on July 7, 2014; SPO2 Rañeses testified that AAA pointed to XXX as the manager. On cross-examination, AAA agreed that she was not forced to work at the bar and could say no if she did not want to work there.

XXX denied being the owner, manager, or supervisor, claiming she was only a GRO and that AAA's decision to go out with customers was her own. In its Decision dated December 8, 2017 (Criminal Case No. 23-2530), the RTC convicted XXX and YYY of qualified trafficking. It sentenced each to life imprisonment and a PHP 2 million fine and ordered them to pay solidarily PHP 500,000.00 moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 exemplary damages with interest; ZZZ was acquitted. YYY's appeal was dismissed for failure to file a brief. In its Decision dated July 2, 2020 (CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 10297), the CA affirmed XXX's conviction, modifying the interest to 6% per annum from finality.

### Issues
1. Whether XXX performed the act of trafficking (hiring or receiving AAA) even though she was allegedly not the owner of the bar and others brought AAA to her.
2. Whether the element of means was proved despite AAA's admission that she was not forced to work at the bar.
3. Whether the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation was proved, so as to sustain XXX's conviction for qualified trafficking in persons.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, XXX hired or received AAA.** AAA testified that XXX "employed" and "hired" her. XXX herself admitted that YYY brought AAA and told her that AAA would work with her at the bar, and SPO2 Rañeses testified that AAA pointed to XXX as the manager. Even assuming XXX was not the registered owner, she is no less guilty. *People v. Villanueva* held that being the registered owner per se does not make one criminally liable, and the acts of trafficking "may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of establishments." **"The law punishes the mere receipt of persons, with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for purpose of trafficking."** XXX was responsible for hiring and supervising AAA.

**2. Yes, the means element was proved.** AAA agreed on cross-examination that she was not forced to work at the bar and could say no. But under *People v. De Dios*, trafficking may be committed by **taking advantage of the person's vulnerability as a minor**, as here. The element was further achieved through the financial gain from the illicit services AAA provided to customers.

**3. Yes, the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation was proved.** XXX made AAA sit with customers. A customer spoke to XXX before taking AAA to a hotel, and XXX told him to return her afterward. The customer handed the PHP 1,500.00 "bar fine" to XXX, who kept AAA's commissions. These facts belie XXX's claim that she never pimped AAA and had nothing to do with AAA's decision to go out with customers. **Since AAA was 17, the trafficking is qualified under Section 6(a).**

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED, and the CA Decision dated July 2, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 10297 was AFFIRMED. XXX was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of qualified trafficking in persons and sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 2 million. She was ordered to pay the victim PHP 500,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 as exemplary damages, both earning legal interest of 6% per annum from finality until fully paid.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Rina manages a videoke bar owned by her cousin. Two friends of Lea, a 16-year-old, brought Lea to the bar looking for work, and Rina took her in as a "waitress." Rina had Lea sit and drink with male customers, and allowed customers to take Lea to a motel for sex after they paid Rina a "bar fine," which Rina kept. Charged with qualified trafficking in persons, Rina argues that (1) she is not the owner of the bar, (2) she did not recruit Lea, since Lea's friends brought her, and (3) Lea agreed to work there. Decide.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Rina is guilty of qualified trafficking in persons. None of her defenses is valid.
- **Legal basis:** Section 4(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended by RA No. 10364, punishes the recruitment, hiring, maintaining, or receipt of a person, with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation. The means element includes taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person. Under Section 6(a), trafficking is qualified when the trafficked person is a child. "The law punishes the mere receipt of persons, with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for purpose of trafficking," and the acts of trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of the establishment. (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 264132, August 13, 2025)
- **Application:** (1) Ownership is not an element; Rina personally performed the acts of trafficking as the one who took in and supervised Lea. (2) Even if Lea's friends brought her, Rina hired and received her, and the mere receipt of a person for exploitation is punished. (3) Lea's consent is immaterial: the law punishes the act with or without the victim's consent. The means element is supplied by taking advantage of Lea's vulnerability as a minor and by the financial gain from her services. The purpose of prostitution is shown by Rina's practice of letting customers take Lea out for sex upon payment of a bar fine that Rina kept. Lea is 16, so the crime is qualified.
- **Conclusion:** Rina is liable for qualified trafficking in persons under Section 4(a) in relation to Section 6(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended.

**Q2.** Tony is the registered owner of a bar where a 17-year-old was found working as a GRO and being sent out with customers for sex. The evidence shows that Tony lives abroad, that the bar was run entirely by its manager, and that there is no proof that Tony hired, received, or dealt with the minor or knew of her exploitation. May Tony be convicted of qualified trafficking in persons solely because he is the registered owner of the bar?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Registered ownership of the establishment does not by itself make Tony criminally liable for trafficking.
- **Legal basis:** Being the registered owner of an establishment per se does not make one criminally liable for the acts of trafficking committed there; the acts constituting trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners. Liability attaches to whoever performs the punishable acts (recruitment, hiring, maintaining, receipt, and the like) for the purpose of exploitation. (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 264132, August 13, 2025, citing People v. Villanueva)
- **Application:** Liability for trafficking depends on performing the acts in Section 4(a) for an exploitative purpose, not on ownership. In People v. XXX, the manager was convicted though she was not the owner, because she hired and supervised the minor. The reverse also holds: Tony did not hire, receive, or maintain the minor, and nothing links him to her exploitation. The person liable is the manager who performed the acts.
- **Conclusion:** Tony cannot be convicted of qualified trafficking based solely on his registered ownership of the bar.

**Q3.** Mon hired Lito, 19, as a "helper" in his club and made him provide sexual services to customers, collecting the fees himself. Lito has a moderate intellectual disability that leaves him unable to fully protect himself from abuse or exploitation. On cross-examination, Lito said nobody forced him to work at the club. (a) Does Lito's statement that he was not forced defeat the charge of trafficking? (b) Is the trafficking qualified even though Lito is already 19?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The means element may be established by taking advantage of the victim's vulnerability, and the act of trafficking is punished with or without the victim's consent. (b) Yes. Under RA No. 9208, as amended, a "child" includes a person over 18 who cannot fully take care of or protect himself because of a physical or mental disability or condition, so the trafficking is qualified.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 4(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended by RA No. 10364, the act of trafficking is punished "with or without the victim's consent or knowledge." The means include "taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person." In People v. XXX (G.R. No. 264132, August 13, 2025), the minor's admission that she was not forced to work did not defeat the charge, because the means element was met by taking advantage of her vulnerability as a minor and by the financial gain from her services. Section 6(a) qualifies trafficking when the trafficked person is a child. Section 3(b), as amended, as quoted in the decision, defines a child as "a person below [18] years of age or one who is over [18] but is unable to fully take care of or protect himself/herself from abuse, neglect, cruelty, exploitation, or discrimination because of a physical or mental disability or condition."
- **Application:** (a) Lito's statement that nobody forced him addresses only force. Mon took advantage of Lito's vulnerability arising from his intellectual disability and profited from his sexual services, which satisfies the means element. Consent does not matter to the act element. (b) Lito is 19, but his disability leaves him unable to fully protect himself from exploitation, so he falls within the statutory definition of a child. The trafficking is therefore qualified under Section 6(a).
- **Conclusion:** Lito's lack of complaint about force is no defense, and Mon is liable for qualified trafficking in persons.

> Note: Many anonymized "People v. XXX" cases exist; cite this one with its G.R. No. 264132. Co-accused YYY's appeal before the CA was dismissed for failure to file a brief, and ZZZ was acquitted by the RTC; neither was before the Supreme Court. The RTC had imposed 12% interest from April 28, 2015; the CA changed it to 6% from finality, which the Court affirmed. The definition of "child" in Bar Question 3 is from footnote 15 of the decision (RA No. 9208, Sec. 3(b), as amended); the Court did not apply that clause in this case, since AAA was 17.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70082)

## People v. Williams

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. JAMES WILLIAMS Y FRANCIS AND JOY MONTECILLO Y BUTASLAC, ACCUSED, JOY MONTECILLO Y BUTASLAC, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 262644 | 2025-08-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Repealed. See instead Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640; See also AM 18-03-16-SC)  
**Specific topics:** Illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Sec. 5, RA 9165): elements and corpus delicti; Chain of custody; first link (marking, inventory, photographing); Three-witness rule for seizures before August 7, 2014 (pre-RA 10640); A growing crowd or a populated area is not a justifiable ground for deviation; Death of an accused before final conviction
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 1. Object or Real Evidence > c. Chain of Custody)

### Doctrine
In illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Sec. 5, RA 9165), the drug is the corpus delicti. The prosecution must account for every link in the chain of custody from seizure to presentation in court (reiterated). **For seizures before August 7, 2014 (before RA 10640), Section 21 of RA 9165 requires the inventory and photographing to be done immediately after seizure in the presence of the accused and three insulating witnesses: an elected public official, a DOJ representative, and a media representative.** Under the Nisperos v. People guidelines, any deviation must be positively acknowledged by the prosecution. The prosecution must then prove (1) justifiable grounds for non-compliance and (2) the preservation of the integrity and evidentiary value of the seized items.

**A growing crowd, a thickly populated place of arrest, or approaching darkness is not a justifiable ground** for skipping the inventory at the place of arrest when no actual threat to the team's safety is substantiated. This is especially so where the team was large and heavily armed (here, 15 agents). Failing to make earnest efforts to secure the witnesses, despite hours of waiting before the arrest, and **leaving out the DOJ representative with no explanation other than the team leader's instruction**, are unjustified deviations. They compromise the integrity of the seized drug and warrant acquittal, so the Court need not examine the other links.

The death of an accused before his conviction becomes final requires dismissal of the criminal case against him.

### Facts
James Williams and accused-appellant Joy Montecillo were charged with selling, in conspiracy, one heat-sealed sachet marked "JFW 05-02-12" containing 30.0476 grams of shabu to a poseur-buyer in Manila on or about May 2, 2012 (Sec. 5 in relation to Sec. 26, RA 9165). Both pleaded not guilty.

According to the prosecution, a PDEA confidential informant arranged a PHP 100,000.00 purchase of shabu from Williams. A buy-bust team of 15 agents plus the informant, in four cars, was formed with IO1 Tacloy as poseur-buyer. The 3:00 p.m. meeting was moved to a Ministop store near Kanumayan Hotel, where the team waited for more than three hours. At about 6:00 p.m., Williams arrived by taxi with a female companion, later identified as Montecillo. Williams took a sachet of shabu from her bag and exchanged it for boodle money. Both were arrested. At 7:30 p.m., IO1 Tacloy marked the sachet at the place of seizure, and photographs were taken. The ground commander then ordered the team to go to the PDEA office in Quezon City because it was getting dark and "unsafe because of the growing crowd." The team arrived at 9:00 p.m. and inventoried the items there in the presence of a barangay kagawad and a media representative. No DOJ representative was present. The specimen tested positive for shabu.

On cross-examination, IO1 Tacloy admitted the following. During the roughly four hours of waiting, the team did not coordinate with barangay officials, the DOJ, the city prosecutor, or the media. No elected official, media, or DOJ representative was present at the marking. The team "did no longer bother" to request a DOJ representative, despite passing by the DOJ and city halls, because that was the team leader's instruction. The 15 agents were armed with high-powered guns and pistols. Both accused denied the sale.

The RTC convicted both, imposing life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 500,000.00 each. The CA affirmed in toto on July 30, 2021. Williams had died on July 7, 2020, while his appeal was pending with the CA. Montecillo appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing non-compliance with Section 21 and a broken chain of custody.

### Issues
1. Whether the prosecution established the integrity and identity of the seized drug despite the buy-bust team's deviations from Section 21 of RA 9165 in the first link of the chain of custody.
2. Whether the criminal case against Williams should be dismissed by reason of his death pending appeal.

### Ruling
**1. No. The unjustified deviations broke the first link, and Montecillo must be acquitted.** The elements of illegal sale are (a) the identity of the buyer and the seller, the object, and the consideration, and (b) the delivery of the thing sold and the payment. Because the drug is the corpus delicti, each link in the chain must be accounted for. Since the seizure happened in 2012, Section 21 of RA 9165 before its amendment by RA 10640 applies, which requires three witnesses. The Court applied the Nisperos guidelines. It also listed the recognized justifiable reasons for not securing the witnesses: a remote place of arrest, threats to safety from retaliation, involvement of the elected official, earnest but futile efforts within the Article 125 RPC period, and time constraints and urgency of the operation.

The Court found three deviations. (a) *No witnesses at the place of arrest.* The CA treated the marking and photographing at the scene as enough. But IO1 Tacloy admitted that during the four-hour wait the team did not call any barangay official, DOJ representative, prosecutor, or media, and no witness was present when the drug was marked. The team "failed to exert earnest efforts." (b) *No immediate inventory at the place of arrest.* The prosecution never substantiated any threat to the team's safety. **"[T]he number of people at the place where the items were seized were already increasing, or the fact that the place of arrest was a thickly populated area, does not constitute a justification."** With 15 armed agents, the team could have ensured its own safety during an immediate inventory. (c) *Incomplete witnesses even at the PDEA office.* Only a kagawad and a media representative were present. The team gave no reason for the DOJ representative's absence beyond its team leader's instruction. These unjustified deviations compromised the integrity and evidentiary value of the seized items, so the other links need not be discussed.

**2. Yes.** Williams died on July 7, 2020, while his appeal was pending with the CA. **In view of his supervening death before his conviction became final, the case against him must be dismissed.**

### Disposition
The appeal was GRANTED. The CA Decision of July 30, 2021 in CA-G.R. CR HC No. 08903 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Joy Montecillo y Butaslac was ACQUITTED of illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Sec. 5 in relation to Sec. 26, RA 9165) for failure of the prosecution to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and ordered IMMEDIATELY RELEASED unless confined for another lawful cause. Criminal Case No. 12-291177 was DISMISSED as against James Williams y Francis by reason of his death before final conviction. The Director General of the Bureau of Corrections was directed to report the action taken within five days. Entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** On March 10, 2013, a PDEA team of 12 armed agents conducted a buy-bust operation outside a busy shopping mall after waiting there three hours for the seller, Dario. During the wait the team made no effort to contact any witness. After the sale, the poseur-buyer marked the sachet of shabu at the scene. The team leader then ordered everyone to the PDEA office 20 kilometers away because "a crowd was gathering." At the office, the items were inventoried and photographed in the presence of Dario, a barangay kagawad, and a media representative. No DOJ representative was present, and the team offered no explanation. Should Dario be convicted of illegal sale of dangerous drugs?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Dario should be acquitted because the integrity and evidentiary value of the seized drug were compromised by unjustified deviations from Section 21 of RA 9165.
- **Legal basis:** For seizures before August 7, 2014, Section 21 of RA 9165 (before its amendment by RA 10640) requires the inventory and photographing immediately after seizure, in the presence of the accused, an elected public official, a DOJ representative, and a media representative. Under the Nisperos guidelines, the prosecution must acknowledge any deviation and prove both a justifiable ground and the preservation of the integrity of the seized item. A growing crowd or a thickly populated place of arrest, without proof of an actual threat, is not a justifiable ground. Unexplained absence of the DOJ representative and failure to exert earnest efforts to secure the witnesses are unjustified deviations (People v. Williams, G.R. No. 262644, August 13, 2025).
- **Application:** The seizure was in 2013, so three witnesses were required. The team had three hours of waiting to arrange for witnesses but made no effort. It skipped the inventory at the scene because of a gathering crowd, without showing any actual threat, even though 12 armed agents could have secured the area. At the office, the DOJ representative was missing and the prosecution gave no reason. These deviations are unacknowledged and unjustified. Doubt is thus cast on the identity and integrity of the corpus delicti.
- **Conclusion:** Dario must be acquitted for failure of the prosecution to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

**Q2.** On October 5, 2015, police officers arrested Lina in a buy-bust operation in a quiet residential street. Immediately after the sale, at the place of arrest, the officers marked, inventoried, and photographed the sachet of shabu in the presence of Lina, a barangay councilor, and a television reporter, all of whom signed the inventory. No DOJ representative was present. On appeal, Lina argues that, as in People v. Williams, the absence of a DOJ representative is fatal. Is she correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The absence of a DOJ representative is not a deviation for a seizure made after August 7, 2014.
- **Legal basis:** Section 21 of RA 9165 was amended by RA 10640, effective August 7, 2014. For seizures from that date, only two insulating witnesses are required: an elected public official and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media. The three-witness rule (elected official, DOJ representative, and media representative) applies only to seizures from July 4, 2002 to August 6, 2014 (Nisperos v. People guidelines, applied in People v. Williams, G.R. No. 262644, August 13, 2025).
- **Application:** Williams involved a 2012 seizure governed by the original Section 21, so the missing DOJ representative was fatal there. Lina was arrested in 2015, after RA 10640 took effect. The inventory and photographing were done immediately and at the place of arrest, in the presence of Lina, an elected public official, and a media representative, who signed the inventory. That satisfies the amended law. There is no deviation to justify.
- **Conclusion:** Lina is not correct; the witness requirement was complied with.

**Q3.** Rene and Sonia were convicted by the RTC of illegal sale of dangerous drugs and sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 500,000.00 each. Both appealed to the Court of Appeals. While the appeal was pending, Rene died. The CA later affirmed the conviction of both, unaware of Rene's death. On further appeal by Sonia, the Supreme Court learns of Rene's death. (a) What should the Court do with the case against Rene? (b) Can the State still collect the PHP 500,000.00 fine from Rene's estate?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The Court should dismiss the criminal case as against Rene. (b) No, the fine can no longer be collected from his estate.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code, criminal liability is totally extinguished by the death of the convict as to personal penalties, and as to pecuniary penalties when death occurs before final judgment. In People v. Williams (G.R. No. 262644, August 13, 2025), the Court dismissed the criminal case against an accused who died while his appeal was pending with the CA, "by reason of his supervening death prior to his final conviction," even though the CA had affirmed his conviction.
- **Application:** Rene died while his appeal was pending, so his conviction never became final. The CA's affirmance, made without knowledge of his death, cannot revive a liability already extinguished. His criminal liability, including the fine, which is a pecuniary penalty, was extinguished because death came before final judgment. The case against him must be dismissed. Sonia's appeal proceeds independently on its merits.
- **Conclusion:** The case against Rene is dismissed, and no fine may be enforced against his estate.

> Note: No separate opinions. The decision does not expressly cite Article 89 of the Revised Penal Code for the dismissal as to Williams; Q3 applies that provision as basic law consistent with the Court's disposition. The record shows small time discrepancies (the CA narration says the suspects arrived at 6:00 p.m.; the poseur-buyer said 6:30 p.m. on cross).

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70117)

## People v. Paterno

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. ARISTON PATERNO, JR. Y SALES, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 256964 | 2025-08-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Repealed. See instead Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640; See also AM 18-03-16-SC)  
**Specific topics:** Penalty for illegal possession of 5 to less than 10 grams of shabu (RA 9165, Sec. 11[2]); Life imprisonment as maximum only when Sec. 13 circumstances are present; Indeterminate Sentence Law applied to a range penalty under a special law; Chain of custody: unruly accused and commotion do not justify marking and inventory at the police station; Inventory witnesses under RA 10640
  
**Also relevant to:** Criminal Law (II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > C. Penalties > 5. Determination of Imposable Penalty > a. Indeterminate Sentence Law (Act 4103, as amended))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 1. Object or Real Evidence > c. Chain of Custody)

### Doctrine
**While the imposable penalty for illegal possession of five grams or more but less than 10 grams of shabu under Section 11(2) of RA 9165 is 20 years and one day to life imprisonment, the maximum of life imprisonment may be imposed only when the circumstances in Section 13 are present**, i.e., the accused was found "possessing any dangerous drug during a party, or at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least [two] persons." Otherwise, a maximum term **below** life imprisonment must be imposed so the accused can avail of the Indeterminate Sentence Law, which by its Section 2 does not apply to persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. The Court followed *People v. Pis-an* and the reasoning in then Justice Peralta's concurring opinion in *People v. Obias*, which it quoted, and imposed 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum, where there was neither allegation nor proof of a Section 13 circumstance.

On chain of custody (reiterated): for offenses committed while RA 10640 was in effect, the inventory need only be witnessed by the accused or his representative or counsel, an elected public official, and a representative of the National Prosecution Service **or** the media; a DOJ representative is not required. Following *People v. Casa*, marking, inventory and photographing must be done at the place of seizure unless the safety of the officers, the witnesses or the items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger. **That the accused became unruly and his sister and friends caused a commotion is not a justifiable ground to do the marking and inventory at the police station**; the unjustified deviation renders the seizure and custody void, compromises the integrity of the drugs, and warrants acquittal. Drugs found in a later search at the police station, immediately marked and inventoried there before the required witnesses, and traced through an unbroken chain of custody, may still support a conviction for possession.

### Facts
Ariston Paterno, Jr. was charged in Legazpi City with illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Criminal Case No. 14279), for selling on or about February 1, 2015 one sachet containing 4.608 grams of shabu for PHP 12,000.00, and with illegal possession (Criminal Case No. 14280), for possessing two sachets marked NBG-2 (0.470 gram) and NBG-3 (4.732 grams) of shabu with a gross weight of 5.202 grams. He pleaded not guilty.

According to the prosecution, a confidential informant told PO2 Noel Grutas around 6:00 p.m. of February 1, 2015 that drug users and pushers were going to Paterno's house. A buy-bust was arranged with PO2 Grutas as poseur-buyer, using two marked PHP 500.00 bills and 11 pieces of PHP 1,000.00 boodle money. Around 10:30 p.m., Paterno handed PO2 Grutas a sachet from his shoulder bag in exchange for the money, and the team arrested him. While being apprised of his rights, Paterno became unruly and shouted, calling the neighbors' attention, so the officers brought him, the sachet and his bag to the police station. There, in the presence of barangay representatives and a media representative, PO2 Grutas inspected the bag and recovered the buy-bust money and two more sachets. The items were marked and inventoried at the station, the inventory was signed by the witnesses, and the sachets tested positive for methamphetamine hydrochloride.

Paterno claimed a frame-up: men in civilian clothes barged into his boarding house, mauled him, and found nothing on him at the scene, and drugs were "found" only after he was frisked several times at the station.

The RTC convicted him of both charges, imposing life imprisonment and a PHP 500,000.00 fine for the sale, and 20 years and one day to life imprisonment and a PHP 400,000.00 fine for the possession. The CA affirmed in toto, holding that marking at the nearest police station in the presence of the accused complied with the chain of custody rule. Paterno appealed, arguing that the items were not marked at the place of arrest and that no DOJ representative witnessed the inventory.

### Issues
1. Whether the absence of a DOJ representative at the inventory violated Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended.
2. Whether the failure to mark and inventory the sachet subject of the sale at the place of arrest, for the reasons given, warrants Paterno's acquittal of illegal sale.
3. Whether Paterno's conviction for illegal possession should be upheld.
4. Whether the penalty of 20 years and one day to life imprisonment for illegal possession was proper.

### Ruling
**1. No.** The crime was committed while RA 10640 was in effect, which requires only "the accused or the person/s from whom such items were confiscated and/or seized, or his/her representative or counsel, with an elected public official and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media" to witness the inventory. Barangay officials and a media representative witnessed it, so the witness requirement was met.

**2. Yes, Paterno must be acquitted of illegal sale.** The prosecution justified marking the sold sachet at the police station because Paterno became unruly and his sister and friends caused a commotion, forcing the officers to leave for security reasons. In *People v. Casa*, the Court En Banc collected cases rejecting similar excuses: a crowd of 200 people (*Dumanjug*) and a crowd that was "getting bigger" (*Salenga*). Under *Lim*, inventory and photographing at the nearest police station are excused only when the safety of the officers, witnesses or items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger, such as retaliatory action by those with the resources and capability to mount a counter-assault. **"The buy-bust team's excuses that accused-appellant became unruly and that his sister and friends caused a commotion at the place of arrest were not justifiable grounds to conduct the marking and inventory at the police station."** The seizure and custody of the sold sachet were rendered void and its integrity compromised.

**3. Yes.** The two other sachets were recovered from Paterno at the police station and immediately marked and inventoried there in the presence of the mandatory witnesses. The prosecution established their movement and custody from seizure until turnover to the trial court, so their integrity and evidentiary value remained intact.

**4. No.** Section 11(2) of RA 9165 prescribes 20 years and one day to life imprisonment, but under Section 13, the maximum penalties of Section 11 apply to one found possessing drugs during a party, at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least two persons. The Court quoted then Justice Peralta's concurring opinion in *People v. Obias*: although the Revised Penal Code rules on graduation do not apply to this special law, the Indeterminate Sentence Law applies when the penalty is a range; an indeterminate sentence with life imprisonment as the maximum would deny parole, and Section 2 of the ISL excludes persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. "It is only when the illegal possession under Section 11 . . . is committed in the presence of two or more persons or in a social gathering that the maximum penalty of life imprisonment may be imposed." Following *People v. Pis-an*, and **with neither allegation nor proof of a Section 13 circumstance, the sentence was modified to 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum.**

### Disposition
Appeal PARTIALLY GRANTED; the CA Decision of November 19, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 12805 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. In Criminal Case No. 14279, Paterno was ACQUITTED of illegal sale of dangerous drugs on reasonable doubt, with entry of judgment to issue immediately. In Criminal Case No. 14280, he was found GUILTY of illegal possession of dangerous drugs and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum, and a fine of PHP 400,000.00. Copies were ordered furnished to the Chief of the PNP and the Director General of the PDEA, and the RTC was directed to turn over the sachets to the Dangerous Drugs Board for destruction.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** During the lawful search of his house, police officers found Ramon alone in his bedroom with a sachet containing 6.2 grams of shabu. He was charged with illegal possession of dangerous drugs under Section 11 of RA 9165. The Information alleged no other circumstance, and the evidence showed that no one else was with Ramon. After trial, the court convicted him and sentenced him to an indeterminate penalty with life imprisonment as the maximum. Is life imprisonment a proper maximum term?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Life imprisonment may not be the maximum term because no Section 13 circumstance was alleged or proven.
- **Legal basis:** Section 11(2) of RA 9165 punishes possession of five grams or more but less than 10 grams of shabu with 20 years and one day to life imprisonment. The maximum of life imprisonment may be imposed only when the circumstances in Section 13 are present: possession during a party, at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least two persons. Otherwise, the maximum term must be below life imprisonment so that the accused may avail of the Indeterminate Sentence Law, which under its Section 2 does not apply to persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. (People v. Paterno, G.R. No. 256964, August 13, 2025, following People v. Pis-an)
- **Application:** Ramon possessed 6.2 grams of shabu, so Section 11(2) applies. But he was alone in his bedroom, and the Information alleged no party, gathering or company of at least two persons. Without a Section 13 circumstance, imposing life imprisonment as the maximum would deny him the benefits of the Indeterminate Sentence Law, such as parole. The court should impose an indeterminate sentence whose maximum is below life imprisonment, as the Court did in Paterno.
- **Conclusion:** The sentence is erroneous; the maximum term must be below life imprisonment.

**Q2.** Same facts as in the previous question, except that the police found Ramon holding the sachet of 6.2 grams of shabu during a drinking session in his house with four friends. The Information alleged, and the prosecution proved, that he possessed the drugs at a social gathering and in the proximate company of at least two persons. May the court impose life imprisonment, and does the Indeterminate Sentence Law apply?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes, the court may impose life imprisonment, and the Indeterminate Sentence Law does not apply.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 13 of RA 9165, any person found possessing any dangerous drug during a party, or at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least two persons, shall suffer the maximum penalties provided for in Section 11, regardless of the quantity and purity of the drugs. It is only when the possession is committed in these circumstances that the maximum penalty of life imprisonment may be imposed, and only then is the Indeterminate Sentence Law no longer applicable, since Section 2 of that law excludes persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. (People v. Paterno, G.R. No. 256964, August 13, 2025)
- **Application:** Unlike in Paterno, where there was neither allegation nor proof of a Section 13 circumstance, here the Information alleged and the evidence proved that Ramon possessed the shabu at a drinking session with four friends. Section 13 therefore requires the maximum penalty under Section 11(2), which is life imprisonment. Because the penalty imposed is life imprisonment, the Indeterminate Sentence Law cannot apply.
- **Conclusion:** Ramon may be sentenced to life imprisonment, and he cannot avail of the Indeterminate Sentence Law.

**Q3.** In 2016, police officers arrested Ben right after he sold a sachet of shabu to a poseur-buyer. Ben resisted and shouted, and his relatives and neighbors gathered and argued with the officers. Citing the commotion, the officers brought Ben and the sachet to the police station, where they marked and inventoried the sachet in the presence of a barangay kagawad and a media representative. Ben, charged with illegal sale, argues that (a) the inventory is invalid because no DOJ representative was present, and (b) the officers had no valid reason to do the marking and inventory at the station. Rule on each argument.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The first argument fails; no DOJ representative was required. (b) The second argument is correct; Ben should be acquitted of illegal sale.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, the inventory must be witnessed by the accused or his representative or counsel, an elected public official, and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media. Marking, inventory and photographing must be done at the place of seizure unless the safety of the officers, witnesses or items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger, such as retaliatory action by those with the resources to mount a counter-assault (People v. Casa). An accused becoming unruly and relatives or friends causing a commotion are not justifiable grounds to move the marking and inventory to the police station; the unjustified deviation renders the seizure and custody void and compromises the integrity of the drugs. (People v. Paterno, G.R. No. 256964, August 13, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The sale happened in 2016, after RA 10640 took effect, so the presence of an elected official (the barangay kagawad) and a media representative satisfied the witness requirement. (b) But the only reason for leaving the scene was Ben's resistance and a crowd of relatives and neighbors arguing with the officers. That is not the immediate or extreme danger that excuses marking and inventory away from the place of seizure. The deviation is unjustified, so the integrity and evidentiary value of the sachet are compromised.
- **Conclusion:** The witness requirement was met, but the unjustified marking and inventory at the police station creates reasonable doubt, so Ben should be acquitted of illegal sale.

> Note: The Decision's opening paragraph cites "Republic Act No. 9615," an evident typographical error for RA 9165. In the body, the sale case is referred to as "Criminal Case No. 14729" and the possession case as "Criminal Case No. 14780"; the Informations and the fallo use Nos. 14279 and 14280. The possession Information alleges "on or about February 2, 2015," while the narrated facts place the arrest on February 1, 2015 and the sachets bear the marking "02-01-15." The rule on the maximum term follows People v. Pis-an and the reasoning of Justice Peralta's concurring opinion in People v. Obias, which the main opinion quoted and adopted. Describing Pis-an, the Decision says the maximum imposable penalty "should be below life imprisonment which is pegged at 40 years and one day"; the phrase is ambiguous and is not relied on in this digest. The Court did not separately discuss the prayer to acquit on the ground of an invalid buy-bust operation beyond the chain of custody issues.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70105)

## People v. ZZZ

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. ZZZ, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 267815 | 2025-08-06 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > H. Title VIII – Crimes Against Persons > 1. All except Arts. 260–261  
**Specific topics:** Elements of statutory rape under Article 266-A(1)(d), as amended by RA 8353; RA 11648 raised the age to 16 but does not retroact against the accused (Art. 22, RPC); Victim's testimony consistent with medical findings suffices to prove penetration; Minor inconsistencies; denial versus positive identification; No "without eligibility for parole" qualifier; Jugueta damages
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 4. Positive and Negative Evidence)

### Doctrine
**Statutory rape** under Article 266-A(1)(d) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 8353, requires only that (1) the offended party is under 12 years of age and (2) the accused had carnal knowledge of her, whether or not there was force, threat, intimidation or grave abuse of authority. Consent is immaterial; the only questions are the victim's age and whether carnal knowledge took place (reiterated). A rape victim's straightforward testimony that conforms with the medico-legal findings is enough to prove penetration. Minor inconsistencies between witnesses do not destroy their credibility, and denial cannot prevail over positive identification.

RA 11648 (2022) raised the age for statutory rape to under 16. It added a close-in-age exemption (an age difference of not more than three years, with a sexual act proven consensual, non-abusive and non-exploitative), which does not apply if the victim is under 13, and it did not amend Article 266-B. **Because RA 11648 is not favorable to the accused, it does not retroact (Art. 22, RPC). A rape committed before it took effect is judged under Article 266-A as amended by RA 8353 alone.**

Statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua. Under A.M. No. 15-08-02-SC, the phrase "without eligibility for parole" is used only when the death penalty would have been imposed but for RA 9346; otherwise it must be deleted. Under People v. Jugueta, where the penalty is reclusion perpetua (and not death reduced by RA 9346), civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages are PHP 75,000.00 each, with 6% interest per annum from finality.

### Facts
ZZZ, who is deaf-mute, was charged with rape under Article 266-A(1)(d) in relation to Article 266-B of the RPC. The Information alleged that on June 17, 2020, in a town in Cotabato, he had carnal knowledge of AAA, a seven-year-old girl born on January 28, 2013.

At about 7:30 a.m. that day, AAA's mother was away getting a rice ration and her father, BBB, was tapping rubber. ZZZ took AAA by the hand and dragged her from the road into her house. He closed the door, pulled down her shorts, knelt behind her as she was made to bend forward, and inserted his penis into her vagina, causing her pain. BBB arrived and saw ZZZ kneeling behind AAA, both naked from the waist down, making push-and-pull movements. ZZZ threw a stone at BBB and fled, but the barangay captain apprehended him and turned him over to the police. The medico-legal examination found a "hymenal laceration on 5 o'clock position [secondary] to vaginal penetration of a blunt object." ZZZ, assisted in court by his mother, denied the charge and claimed he had only gone to the house to drink tuba.

The RTC (January 29, 2021) convicted ZZZ of "qualified rape," sentenced him to reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole, and awarded PHP 100,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages. The CA (February 22, 2023) treated "qualified rape" as a typographical slip, since the body of the RTC decision dealt only with statutory rape. It affirmed the conviction, deleted the parole qualifier, and reduced the awards to PHP 75,000.00 each with 6% interest. On appeal, ZZZ pointed to inconsistencies between AAA's and BBB's testimonies on whether he had undressed and whether he made push-and-pull movements, and argued that penile penetration was improbable.

### Issues
1. Whether the 2022 amendment of Article 266-A by RA 11648 applies to a rape committed on June 17, 2020.
2. Whether the prosecution proved the elements of statutory rape beyond reasonable doubt despite the alleged inconsistencies and the claimed absence of penetration.
3. Whether the penalty and damages imposed by the CA are correct.

### Ruling
**1. No, RA 11648 does not apply.** RA 11648 raised the age for statutory rape from under 12 to under 16 (People v. Dalaguet). Its close-in-age exemption does not apply if the victim is under 13, and it left Article 266-B unchanged. Under Article 22 of the RPC, penal laws retroact only insofar as they favor the accused. The crime was committed on June 17, 2020, and the amendment has "no favorable effect" on ZZZ, so the Court applied Article 266-A as amended by RA 8353, before its amendment by RA 11648.

**2. Yes, statutory rape was proved.** The elements are (1) an offended party under 12 years of age and (2) carnal knowledge, regardless of force or intimidation. Consent is immaterial because the law presumes that a child of tender years has no will of her own. AAA's birth certificate showed she was seven. Carnal knowledge was proved by her positive testimony, BBB's eyewitness account, and the medico-legal finding of hymenal laceration. The inconsistencies on whether ZZZ removed his clothes or made push-and-pull movements concern minor details. "[A]s long as the testimonies of the witnesses corroborate one another on material points, minor inconsistencies therein cannot destroy their credibility." Following People v. Gratela, "when a rape victim's straightforward and truthful testimony conforms with the medical findings of the examining doctor, the same is sufficient to support a conviction for rape." ZZZ's denial is self-serving negative evidence and could not prevail over the categorical identification by AAA and BBB.

**3. Yes, the CA's modifications are correct.** Under Article 266-B, as amended by RA 8353, statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua. Under A.M. No. 15-08-02-SC, "without eligibility for parole" qualifies reclusion perpetua only when the death penalty is warranted but not imposed because of RA 9346. Otherwise the phrase is unnecessary, since persons sentenced to an indivisible penalty are understood to be ineligible for parole. ZZZ's penalty is reclusion perpetua, not a death penalty reduced by RA 9346, so the phrase was properly deleted. For the same reason, under People v. Jugueta the damages are PHP 75,000.00 each for civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, with 6% interest per annum from finality.

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED, and the CA Decision dated February 22, 2023 in CA-G.R. CR HC No. 02764-MIN was AFFIRMED. ZZZ was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of statutory rape under Article 266-A, paragraph 1(d) of the RPC, as amended by RA 8353, and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. He was ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 as civil indemnity, PHP 75,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 75,000.00 as exemplary damages, with 6% interest per annum on all awards from finality until full payment.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** On May 10, 2021, Berto, 30, had sexual intercourse with Lia, his 10-year-old neighbor, inside her house. Lia testified that Berto pulled down her shorts and inserted his penis into her vagina. Her mother, who walked in on them, testified that Berto was fully naked, while Lia said Berto had only unzipped his pants. The medico-legal officer found a fresh hymenal laceration consistent with penetration by a blunt object. Berto argues that (a) the prosecution failed to prove force or intimidation, and (b) the conflicting accounts of how he was dressed destroy the witnesses' credibility. Should Berto be convicted of statutory rape?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Berto should be convicted of statutory rape.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 266-A(1)(d) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 8353, statutory rape requires only that the offended party is under 12 years of age and that the accused had carnal knowledge of her. Force, threat or intimidation is not necessary, and consent is immaterial. Minor inconsistencies do not destroy credibility when the testimonies agree on material points, and a victim's straightforward testimony that conforms with the medical findings is enough to prove penetration (People v. ZZZ, G.R. No. 267815, August 6, 2025, citing People v. Gratela).
- **Application:** Lia was 10 years old, so the first element is present and the absence of force does not matter. Her testimony that Berto inserted his penis is corroborated by the medico-legal finding of hymenal laceration and by her mother's eyewitness account. Whether Berto was fully naked or had only unzipped his pants is a minor detail that does not affect the material point, which is that he had carnal knowledge of Lia.
- **Conclusion:** Berto is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of statutory rape.

**Q2.** On June 1, 2020, Dodong, 19, had consensual sexual intercourse with Mia, who was then 13 years and 6 months old. No force, threat, intimidation or abuse of authority was involved. In 2023 the prosecutor charged Dodong with statutory rape, invoking RA 11648 (2022), which raised the age for statutory rape to under 16. (a) Can Dodong be convicted of statutory rape under Article 266-A(1)(d) for the 2020 act? (b) If the same act had been committed after RA 11648 took effect, would Dodong be exempt under its close-in-age proviso?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. RA 11648 cannot be applied retroactively against him, and under the law in force on June 1, 2020, Mia was not under 12. (b) No. The close-in-age exemption does not apply because their age difference is more than three years.
- **Legal basis:** Article 22 of the Revised Penal Code gives penal laws retroactive effect only insofar as they favor the accused. In People v. ZZZ (G.R. No. 267815, August 6, 2025), the Court held that RA 11648, which raised the statutory rape age from under 12 to under 16, has no favorable effect on the accused and therefore does not apply to a rape committed before it took effect; the Court applied Article 266-A as amended by RA 8353. As quoted in that decision, RA 11648 provides that there is no criminal liability for carnal knowledge of a person under 16 when the age difference is not more than three years and the act is proven consensual, non-abusive and non-exploitative, but the exception does not apply if the victim is under 13.
- **Application:** (a) The act was committed in June 2020, before RA 11648. Applying the amendment would make the act statutory rape when it was not statutory rape at the time it was done, which is unfavorable to Dodong and barred by Article 22. Under the RA 8353 version, statutory rape requires a victim under 12. Mia was 13, and none of the other circumstances in paragraph 1 was present, so Dodong cannot be convicted of statutory rape (without prejudice to liability under any other law whose elements are proved). (b) Had the act been committed after RA 11648, Mia, being under 16, would fall within the statutory rape age. The close-in-age proviso would not help Dodong, because their age difference of more than five years exceeds three years.
- **Conclusion:** Dodong cannot be convicted of statutory rape for the 2020 act, and he would not qualify for the close-in-age exemption had the act been committed after RA 11648.

**Q3.** The RTC convicted Pablo of the statutory rape of a nine-year-old girl, committed in 2019, and sentenced him to "reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole." It ordered him to pay PHP 100,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages. No qualifying circumstance was alleged or proved. On appeal, is the RTC's ruling on the penalty and damages correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The phrase "without eligibility for parole" should be deleted, and each award should be reduced to PHP 75,000.00, with 6% interest per annum from finality.
- **Legal basis:** Statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua under Article 266-B of the RPC, as amended by RA 8353. Under A.M. No. 15-08-02-SC, "without eligibility for parole" is used only when the circumstances warrant the death penalty but it is not imposed because of RA 9346. Otherwise the phrase is unnecessary, since persons sentenced to an indivisible penalty are understood to be ineligible for parole. Under People v. Jugueta, where the penalty imposed is reclusion perpetua other than death reduced by RA 9346, civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages are PHP 75,000.00 each (People v. ZZZ, G.R. No. 267815, August 6, 2025).
- **Application:** Pablo committed simple statutory rape with no qualifying circumstance, so the proper penalty is plain reclusion perpetua. Death was never warranted, so the parole qualifier must be deleted. For the same reason, the PHP 100,000.00 awards, which apply only when death is reduced to reclusion perpetua, must be reduced to PHP 75,000.00 each, with legal interest of 6% per annum from finality until paid.
- **Conclusion:** The judgment should be modified to plain reclusion perpetua, without the parole qualifier, and to PHP 75,000.00 each for civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages.

> Note: The fallo cites "Article 226-B," an evident slip for Article 266-B. The RTC's dispositive portion called the crime "qualified rape"; the CA and the Supreme Court treated the conviction as one for statutory rape. Only three Justices took part (Rosario, J., Gesmundo, C.J., and Hernando, J.); Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business. The relationship between ZZZ and AAA's family is redacted in the text.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70085)

## Evangelista v. People

**SILVINO C. EVANGELISTA, PETITIONER, VS. PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 241587 | 2025-08-06 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > G. Title VII – Crimes Committed by Public Officers  
**Specific topics:** Malversation through negligence requires inexcusable negligence approximating malice or fraud; Good-faith reliance on a tolerated practice and on the treasurer's advice; Negligence must be positively proven; post-taking remedial acts are irrelevant; Effect of dismissal of the administrative case on the criminal case; Civil liability despite acquittal
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > C. Prosecution of Civil Action (Rule 111) > 4. Civil Liability Ex Delicto > a. When Accused is Acquitted)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 1. Forms of Accountability)

### Doctrine
**For malversation through negligence under Art. 217 of the Revised Penal Code (as amended by R.A. No. 10951) to prosper, mere negligence is not enough. The negligence must be reckless, "positively and clearly shown to be inexcusable, approximating malice or fraud."** Simple negligence does not warrant conviction. The Court traced this rule to Art. 391 of the Spanish Código Penal ("abandono o negligencia inexcusables") and to *U.S. v. Catolico*. "Positive proof" means proof beyond reasonable doubt, not inferences, however logical. What counts is the act or omission that permitted another to take the funds. What the officer did after the taking is irrelevant.

A mayor is an accountable officer for municipal funds. Under P.D. No. 1445, Sec. 102(1) and R.A. No. 7160, Sec. 340, the head of the agency is responsible for its funds, and disbursements require the mayor's approval. A mayor who signed a fund-transfer check without supporting documents, in good-faith reliance on the treasurer's advice and on a practice tolerated even under his predecessor, was negligent. His negligence did not approximate malice or fraud, so he was acquitted (applying *Villacorta* and *Quizo*, subject to the *Cabello* caution that good faith is judged case by case).

The Court also reiterated two settled rules:
- **The dismissal of an administrative case for insufficiency of evidence does not bar the criminal case.** Only a finding that the act from which liability is anchored does not exist has that effect (*Constantino*; *Pahkiat*; *Paredes, Jr.*), because the two proceedings are independent.
- **Acquittal does not extinguish civil liability** unless a final judgment declares that the fact from which the civil liability might arise did not exist.

### Facts
Silvino C. Evangelista became municipal mayor of San Miguel, Bohol on July 1, 1998. During his term, six checks totaling P553,148.00 were issued without supporting documents:
- FCB-5644, September 11, 1998, P255,148;
- FCB-5655, October 26, 1998, P88,000;
- FCB-81203, April 8, 1999, P50,000;
- FCB-81284, November 24, 1999, P50,000;
- LBP-27405199, March 31, 2000, P60,000; and
- LBP-6593803, June 1, 2000, P50,000.

In 2002, the municipal accountant, Carcueva, discovered the checks while reconciling bank records on COA's directive. A COA Audit Observation Memorandum dated September 17, 2002, addressed to Evangelista, the treasurer Millare, and Carcueva, flagged unrecorded check disbursements. The 2005 Annual Audit Report noted that no action had been taken on a P733,148.00 cash shortage incurred by Millare from unrecorded checks issued from 1998 to 2001. A Notice of Disallowance dated February 12, 2007 followed. Afterwards, Evangelista approved a Sangguniang Bayan resolution asking Millare to settle her accountabilities, and he issued her a compliance memorandum on April 30, 2007. On March 12, 2009, Millare executed an affidavit acknowledging an obligation of P1,003,960.19 to the Municipality.

The practice of transferring funds between the Municipality's depository banks by checks without vouchers, supported only by a "Form 123," predated Evangelista's term. In its March 15, 2012 administrative decision, the Ombudsman found Millare guilty of dishonesty and dismissed her. It dismissed the complaint against Evangelista "for insufficiency of evidence," stating there was "no legal basis to drag [him] to the anomaly." On September 12, 2013, however, the Ombudsman found probable cause and charged him with six counts of malversation (Crim. Case Nos. SB-14-CRM-0232 to 0237). The Informations alleged that he consented to or permitted, through abandonment or negligence, Millare's taking of the funds by approving or causing the disbursements.

On June 29, 2018, the Sandiganbayan convicted him of malversation of public funds through negligence and imposed a fine of P553,148.00, among other penalties. It denied his motion for reconsideration on August 15, 2018. The evidence on the checks was as follows:
- *The four FCB checks.* The checks were not presented. FCB's Vice-President for Legal testified, based on bank records and ledgers that were also not presented, that Evangelista and Millare were the signatories. He said the signatures were genuine only because the checks had been encashed and cleared, and he admitted he had no personal knowledge.
- *The two LBP checks.* Neither was presented. The LBP branch manager identified the microfilm of LBP Check No. 27405199. The microfilm of LBP Check No. 6593803 was damaged.

Evangelista filed a Rule 45 petition.

### Issues
1. Whether the dismissal of the administrative case against petitioner bars his criminal liability for malversation arising from the same facts.
2. Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that petitioner, through negligence amounting to inexcusable negligence approximating malice or fraud, permitted the municipal treasurer to take public funds.
3. Whether petitioner remains civilly liable despite his acquittal.

### Ruling
Questions of fact are generally not reviewable under Rule 45. The Court reviewed the facts anyway because the Sandiganbayan had misapprehended them and drawn manifestly mistaken inferences.

**1. No, the administrative dismissal does not bar the criminal case.** Evangelista invoked *Constantino v. Sandiganbayan*. But his administrative case was dismissed "merely for insufficiency of evidence," which is different from a finding that the act from which liability is anchored does not exist. The Ombudsman's statement that there was "no legal basis to drag [him] to the anomaly" is consistent with a dismissal for insufficient evidence (*Pahkiat*; *Paredes, Jr.*). Administrative and criminal cases are independent. When the quantum of evidence was simply not met, the respondent is not absolved in other proceedings, and the prosecution may present additional evidence in the criminal case.

**2. No, inexcusable negligence approximating malice or fraud was not proven, so Evangelista is acquitted.** The first three elements of malversation were present. Evangelista was a public officer. As head of the Municipality, he was primarily responsible for its funds (P.D. No. 1445, Sec. 102(1)) and charged with their safekeeping (R.A. No. 7160, Sec. 340), and disbursements required his approval. The only question was the fourth element: whether he permitted another to take the funds through negligence. Malversation is punished with the same penalty whether committed by *dolo* or *culpa*, but negligence must be reckless, "positively and clearly shown to be inexcusable, approximating malice or fraud" (*U.S. v. Catolico*; Código Penal, Art. 391). Simple negligence will not do.

Evangelista's later acts did not count for or against him: the SB resolution, the memorandum to Millare, and her undertaking. "In malversation through negligence, what characterizes the negligence is not what the offender did after the public funds or property were taken by another person but what the offender did or omitted to do which permitted the taking thereof."

As to the four FCB checks, neither the checks nor the bank records were presented. The bank witness inferred genuine signatures only from clearing and had no personal knowledge. "Positive proof is not merely an inference drawn more or less logically from a hypothetical fact. It is proof beyond reasonable doubt." The auditor testified that Evangelista once admitted signing checks without vouchers, but that did not show he signed these particular checks. The prosecution thus failed to positively prove a recklessly negligent act. As to the LBP checks, Check No. 6593803 was not presented because its microfilm was damaged. The identified and unchallenged microfilm of Check No. 27405199, however, proved that Evangelista signed it without supporting documents, which enabled Millare to keep it off the books and take the funds.

Even so, Evangelista acted in good faith. The practice of transferring funds by checks supported only by a Form 123 was tolerated even under his predecessor, and he relied on the treasurer's advice that such checks needed no disbursement vouchers. Following *Villacorta* and *Quizo*, and heeding *Cabello*'s caution that each case turns on its facts, the Court held that this practice did not relieve him of his duty to safekeep the funds. His negligence, however, "did not approximate malice or fraud, thus warranting his acquittal."

**3. Yes, he remains civilly liable.** An acquittal does not extinguish civil liability unless the court declares in a final judgment that the fact from which the civil liability might arise did not exist. The Court made no such finding, so Evangelista was held civilly liable for P553,148.00.

### Disposition
The Petition was GRANTED. The Court REVERSED and SET ASIDE the Sandiganbayan's June 29, 2018 Decision and August 15, 2018 Resolution in Criminal Case Nos. SB-14-CRM-0232 to 0237. Evangelista was ACQUITTED of malversation of public funds for failure of the prosecution to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt. He was nonetheless ORDERED to pay the Government P553,148.00 as civil liability, with interest at 6% per annum from finality of the Decision until full payment. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson) and Hernando, J. concurred, while Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Mayor Ramon signed checks transferring municipal funds from one depository bank to another. The checks were not supported by disbursement vouchers, only by a form signed by the municipal treasurer. The treasurer assured him that fund transfers did not need vouchers, and the same practice had been followed under the previous mayor. The treasurer encashed the checks, never deposited the proceeds, and left the transactions out of the books. Mayor Ramon is charged with malversation of public funds through negligence. The prosecution proves that he signed the checks. Should he be convicted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Mayor Ramon should be acquitted, although he may still be held civilly liable for the amounts taken.
- **Legal basis:** Under Art. 217 of the Revised Penal Code, a public officer who, through abandonment or negligence, permits another to take public funds for which he is accountable commits malversation. Mere negligence is not enough. The negligence must be reckless, "positively and clearly shown to be inexcusable, approximating malice or fraud." Good-faith reliance on a practice tolerated even under one's predecessor, and on the advice of the municipal treasurer, may show negligence that does not approximate malice or fraud. An acquittal does not extinguish civil liability unless the court finds that the act from which it arises did not exist. (Evangelista v. People, G.R. No. 241587, August 6, 2025, applying Villacorta v. People and Quizo v. Sandiganbayan.)
- **Application:** The first three elements are present. As mayor, Ramon is a public officer accountable for municipal funds under P.D. No. 1445, Sec. 102(1) and the Local Government Code, Sec. 340, and he controls disbursements. Signing transfer checks without vouchers was negligent, because the long-standing practice did not relieve him of his duty to safeguard the funds. But he acted on the treasurer's assurance and followed a practice he inherited. Nothing shows he knew of or shared in the treasurer's scheme. His negligence is not of the inexcusable kind that approximates malice or fraud. Since there is no finding that the act giving rise to civil liability did not exist, he may still be ordered to pay the amounts lost.
- **Conclusion:** Mayor Ramon should be acquitted of malversation through negligence but may be held civilly liable.

**Q2.** In another malversation-through-negligence case against Mayor Lito, the checks were never presented in court. A bank officer testified that, according to the bank's ledgers, which were also not presented, the mayor was a signatory. He said the signatures were genuine because the checks had been cleared and encashed. On cross-examination he admitted he had no personal knowledge of the signatures. Separately, the prosecution proved that the mayor once told a COA auditor that "there were times" he signed checks without vouchers. The mayor's defense also points out that, once he learned of the shortage, he promptly ordered the treasurer to settle her accountabilities. (a) Is the prosecution's evidence enough to prove the negligent act? (b) Are the mayor's acts after learning of the shortage relevant to his liability?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The evidence does not positively prove that the mayor signed the checks in question. (b) No. Acts done after the funds were taken are irrelevant to whether his negligence permitted the taking.
- **Legal basis:** In malversation through negligence, the negligence must be positively and clearly shown. "Positive proof is not merely an inference drawn more or less logically from a hypothetical fact. It is proof beyond reasonable doubt." "[W]hat characterizes the negligence is not what the offender did after the public funds or property were taken by another person but what the offender did or omitted to do which permitted the taking thereof." (Evangelista v. People, G.R. No. 241587, August 6, 2025.)
- **Application:** (a) The checks and the ledgers were not presented. The bank officer's belief that the signatures were genuine rests only on the fact that the checks cleared, and he admitted he had no personal knowledge. This is an inference, not positive proof. The mayor's general admission that there were times he signed checks without vouchers does not show that these particular checks were among them. The negligent act charged is therefore not proven beyond reasonable doubt. (b) His later orders to the treasurer neither excuse nor aggravate the earlier conduct. The inquiry looks only at what he did or failed to do that allowed the taking.
- **Conclusion:** The prosecution failed to positively prove the negligent act, and the mayor's post-taking measures are beside the point.

**Q3.** The Ombudsman dismissed an administrative complaint for grave misconduct against Mayor Celia "for insufficiency of evidence." It observed that there was "no legal basis" to link her to the treasurer's cash shortage. Later, the Ombudsman filed malversation charges against her before the Sandiganbayan based on the same transactions. (a) Celia moves to dismiss the criminal cases, invoking the dismissal of the administrative case. Should the motion be granted? (b) If Celia is eventually acquitted because her negligence did not approximate malice or fraud, may she still be ordered to pay the amount lost?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. A dismissal for insufficiency of evidence does not bar the criminal case. (b) Yes. Her acquittal does not extinguish her civil liability, because the court made no finding that the act from which it arises did not exist.
- **Legal basis:** Administrative and criminal cases are independent of each other. The dismissal of an administrative case operates to dismiss the criminal case based on the same subject matter and evidence only when there is a finding that the act from which liability is anchored does not exist. A dismissal merely for insufficiency of evidence does not absolve the respondent in the other proceeding, because the prosecution may present additional evidence. An acquittal does not extinguish civil liability unless the court declares in a final judgment that the fact from which the civil liability might arise did not exist. (Evangelista v. People, G.R. No. 241587, August 6, 2025, citing Constantino v. Sandiganbayan, Pahkiat v. Office of the Ombudsman-Mindanao, and Paredes, Jr. v. Sandiganbayan.)
- **Application:** (a) The Ombudsman did not find that the acts imputed to Celia did not exist. It found only that the evidence before it was insufficient. Its remark that there was "no legal basis" to link her is consistent with that kind of dismissal. The criminal prosecution may proceed and may present more or different evidence. (b) An acquittal because her negligence fell short of malice or fraud rests on the lack of criminal negligence, not on the non-existence of the act that caused the loss. The court may therefore order her to pay the amount lost, with legal interest from finality.
- **Conclusion:** The criminal cases may proceed despite the administrative dismissal, and an acquittal of this kind still leaves Celia civilly liable.

> Note: Doubt on the civil liability amount: the Court ordered petitioner to pay P553,148.00, the total of all six checks. Yet it found that the prosecution failed to positively prove that he signed the four FCB checks, and that LBP Check No. 6593803 was never presented. Only the signing of LBP Check No. 27405199 (P60,000) was found proven. The decision does not explain why the civil liability covers all six checks beyond reciting the general rule. The Decision was rendered by a three-member First Division (Rosario, J., ponente; Gesmundo, C.J. and Hernando, J. concurring), with Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. on official business. The E-Library text begins the discussion at heading "II"; heading I is presumably the facts. The Sandiganbayan's penalty is mentioned only as background; the bar questions do not ask for penalty computation.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70008)
