## People v. Reyes

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. HERMINIO CASAL REYES, MUNICIPAL MAYOR, MA. MARLEY C. DADAY, LEO BAUSING GOMEZ, ARTURO ELUMBA ESTIL, JOEL DINGLE PLAZA, ROMEO O. MAGADAN (ALL) MEMBER, SANGGUNIANG BAYAN, VIRGILIO A. JULAO, MEMBER, SANGGUNIANG BAYAN/ACTING PRESIDING OFFICER, FILOMENO CASEÑAS SALISE, MUNICIPAL TREASURER, (ALL OF) LORETO, AGUSAN DEL SUR, ACCUSED; HERMINIO CASAL REYES, MA. MARLEY C. DADAY, LEO BAUSING GOMEZ, JOEL DINGLE PLAZA, ROMEO O. MAGADAN, AND VIRGILIO A. JULAO, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.**  
G.R. Nos. 246783-84 | 2025-07-29 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > G. Title VII – Crimes Committed by Public Officers  
**Specific topics:** Malversation: presumption under the last paragraph of Article 217, RPC; A stated public purpose does not rebut the presumption without proof of actual application; Section 3(e), RA 3019: "evident bad faith" vs. bad judgment or ignorance; Good-faith reliance on the resident COA auditor's opinion; Modalities of Section 3(e) must be alleged with particularity in the Information
  
**Also relevant to:** Criminal Law (IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910))
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > F. Burden of Proof and Presumptions (Rule 131) > 5. Presumption Against Accused in Criminal Cases)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > B. Prosecution of Offenses (Rule 110) > 6. Complaint or Information > b. Sufficiency > iii. Cause of the Accusation)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction)

### Doctrine
**Malversation (Art. 217, RPC).** Under the last paragraph of Article 217, an accountable public officer's failure to have public funds duly forthcoming upon demand by a duly authorized officer is prima facie evidence that the officer put them to personal use. This is a presumption of law that shifts the burden to the accused to rebut it with satisfactory evidence (reiterated, citing *Wa-acon v. People*). **Notwithstanding the stated purpose or intention for public funds to be applied for a public purpose, the presumption of malversation remains unrebutted absent proof that the funds were actually applied for that purpose.** A memorandum of agreement and sanggunian resolutions declaring that loans to local officials are for buying official service vehicles do not prove that the vehicles were bought and used for official purposes.

**Section 3(e), RA 3019.** Mere bad faith or partiality and negligence per se are not enough; the bad faith or partiality must be "evident" or "manifest" (reiterated, citing *Sistoza v. Desierto*). Evident bad faith connotes not only bad judgment but a "palpably and patently fraudulent and dishonest purpose to do moral obliquity or conscious wrongdoing for some perverse motive or ill will." **Local officials who, having no legal officer, acted on the opinion of the resident COA auditor that their fund realignment and loan scheme was legal did not act with evident bad faith.** They could presume the auditor performed his functions regularly and correctly, even though the opinion was verbal and given before audit. A finding that they "should have known better" shows ignorance, not evident bad faith.

Manifest partiality, evident bad faith, and gross inexcusable negligence **must be alleged with particularity in the Information**. The accused cannot be convicted on a modality that was not alleged (here, gross inexcusable negligence) or one the trial court made no finding on (here, manifest partiality).

### Facts
Herminio Casal Reyes was the municipal mayor of Loreto, Agusan del Sur; Daday, Gomez, Estil, Plaza, Magadan and Julao were members of the Sangguniang Bayan (SB). In early 2003, citing an urgent need for service vehicles, SB member Gomez and SB Secretary Irisari proposed that the municipality lend money to its officials to buy motorcycles for exclusively official use. The money would come from the idle budget for the municipal building, whose construction had been suspended. Irisari consulted the resident COA auditor, Lorete, who verbally opined that the realignment was legal as long as the required documents were complied with and it was supported by an SB resolution. The municipality had no legal officer.

In March 2003, the municipality and its officials signed a Memorandum of Agreement for loans totaling PHP 1.5 million (PHP 100,000 each for 15 officials) from the unexpended municipal building fund. The loans were "purposely to purchase service vehicle for official use," payable in three years by payroll deduction. The SB passed, and Reyes approved, two resolutions both numbered 38-2003 (one describing the loans as for buying motor vehicles, the other as "livelihood projects") and Resolution No. 126-2003 requesting the mayor and the treasurer to release PHP 1.6 million to Loreto Transport Services Association, Inc. (LOTSA). On July 1, 2003, Treasurer Salise wrote Land Bank, with Reyes's approval, to transfer PHP 1.6 million from the municipality's account to LOTSA's account, and the bank did so. All the accused except Julao obtained loans.

After complaints reached the Ombudsman for Mindanao, Lorete recommended terminating them. A COA Special Audit Team found instead that the municipality disbursed PHP 1.6 million to LOTSA, a private entity composed of municipal officials and employees, as loans for vehicles for personal use. It found the release was by debit advice without disbursement vouchers or LOTSA's receipt, was recorded in the books only in 2004, and that only PHP 735,811.10 had been repaid as of March 2007, leaving PHP 864,188.90 unpaid. Reyes and the SB members were charged with violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019 "through evident bad faith and manifest partiality" (SB-10-CRM-0127). Reyes and Salise were also charged with malversation (SB-10-CRM-0128). The cases against Salise were dismissed on his death.

The Sandiganbayan convicted all the accused of violating Section 3(e) and Reyes of malversation. It rejected the good-faith defense because the accused "should have known better than to rely on the verbal affirmation (albeit erroneous) of a COA auditor." Their motions for reconsideration were denied, and they appealed. Estil did not appeal.

### Issues
1. Whether accused-appellants are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019.
2. Whether Reyes is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of malversation of public funds.

### Ruling
**1. No. The accused-appellants were acquitted because evident bad faith was not proved.** The first element (public officers discharging official functions) was undisputed. On the second, the Court noted *Villanueva v. COA*: reliance on a COA representative's expertise is a matter of defense in the criminal case, although the COA is not estopped from questioning its officials' acts on post-audit, since estoppel does not lie against the government. The trial record showed that the accused "may have been misled" by Lorete's erroneous opinion; the Sandiganbayan justice himself told Lorete, "Probably you gave them a wrong advice." The Court asked: "If accused-appellants could not reasonably rely on the opinion of Lorete, who is presumed to possess expertise in auditing financial transactions of government entities, and considering that the Municipality had no legal officer at the time, on whose opinion could they rely?" That the opinion was verbal and given before audit did not matter, because Lorete affirmed he gave it as one of his functions. The accused "had every right to presume that he not only performed his functions regularly but also correctly." The prosecution's theory that the consultation was a "mere subterfuge" was speculative. Even if bad faith attended it, the law requires *evident* bad faith. **The Sandiganbayan's remark that the accused "should have known better" revealed "ignorance rather than bad faith," unlike a case where the accused knew better but deliberately chose otherwise.** The Sandiganbayan made no finding of manifest partiality, and the Information did not allege gross inexcusable negligence; these modalities must be alleged with particularity. Since the second element was absent, the Court did not reach the third.

**2. Yes. Reyes is guilty of malversation.** The elements are: (1) the offender is a public officer; (2) he had custody or control of the funds by reason of his office; (3) the funds were public funds for which he was accountable; and (4) he appropriated, took or misappropriated them, or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted another person to take them. As mayor, Reyes is by law immediately and primarily responsible for all government funds and property of his agency. Under Article 217, as amended by RA 1060, the State need not prove actual misappropriation: failure to have the funds forthcoming upon demand raises a presumption of law that shifts the burden to the accused. **Even assuming the loans were meant for a public use, Reyes, as the accountable officer, failed to account for the funds, and "no proof was adduced to show that said loans were indeed applied for said public purpose."** The Court refused to "simply rely on the MOA and SB Resolutions and presume that the recipients of the loans purchased motorcycles to be used exclusively as official service vehicles." It also found it "most irregular" that the municipality lent money to its officials to buy service vehicles instead of procuring the vehicles itself. Reyes "utterly failed to rebut the statutory presumption of malversation."

### Disposition
The appeal was PARTLY GRANTED. The Sandiganbayan's September 28, 2018 Decision and March 28, 2019 Resolution were AFFIRMED in Criminal Case No. SB-10-CRM-0128: Reyes was found GUILTY of malversation of public funds and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six years and one day of prision mayor, as minimum, to 10 years of prision mayor, as maximum, with perpetual special disqualification and a fine of PHP 1.6 million. They were MODIFIED in Criminal Case No. SB-10-CRM-0127: Reyes, Daday, Gomez, Plaza, Magadan and Julao were ACQUITTED of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019 on reasonable doubt, with entry of judgment to issue immediately as to them.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Mayor Ramon approved the transfer of PHP 2 million from the municipal general fund to a private association formed by municipal employees. The transfer was based on a sanggunian resolution and a memorandum of agreement stating that the money would be lent to municipal officials "exclusively to purchase service vehicles for official use," repayable through payroll deductions. Years later, a COA special audit found that a large balance remained unpaid. Charged with malversation, Ramon presented only the resolution and the agreement to show that the funds were intended for a public purpose. He presented no evidence that any vehicle was bought or used for official business. Has Ramon rebutted the presumption of malversation?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Ramon has not rebutted the presumption, and he may be convicted of malversation.
- **Legal basis:** Under the last paragraph of Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code, an accountable public officer's failure to have public funds duly forthcoming upon demand by a duly authorized officer is prima facie evidence that he put the funds to personal use. This presumption of law shifts the burden to the accused to rebut it with satisfactory evidence. A municipal mayor is immediately and primarily responsible for all government funds of his municipality. Notwithstanding the stated purpose or intention for public funds to be applied for a public purpose, the presumption remains unrebutted absent proof that the funds were actually applied for that purpose. (People v. Reyes, G.R. Nos. 246783-84, July 29, 2025)
- **Application:** Ramon is an accountable officer who approved the release of PHP 2 million in municipal funds, and the audit showed the funds were not fully accounted for. His only evidence is the resolution and the agreement, which state what the money was intended for, not what it was actually used for. As in Reyes, a court cannot simply presume from those documents that the borrowers bought vehicles and used them only for official business. He offered no proof of actual application to a public purpose, so the burden that shifted to him was not discharged.
- **Conclusion:** The statutory presumption of malversation stands unrebutted, and Ramon may be convicted of malversation of public funds.

**Q2.** Lacking a legal officer, the sanggunian members of a municipality asked the resident COA auditor whether they could realign the idle balance of a suspended infrastructure project into salary loans for officials. The auditor verbally opined that it was legal if supported by a sanggunian resolution. They passed the resolution and released the loans. Later audits found the scheme irregular. The Information for violation of Section 3(e) of RA 3019 alleged only "evident bad faith and manifest partiality." The Sandiganbayan convicted them, ruling that they "should have known better" than to rely on a verbal opinion, and made no finding of manifest partiality. (a) Did the accused act with evident bad faith? (b) May the Sandiganbayan instead convict them for gross inexcusable negligence?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No, evident bad faith was not established. (b) No, gross inexcusable negligence was not alleged in the Information.
- **Legal basis:** Section 3(e) of RA 3019 requires that the public officer acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. Mere bad faith or partiality and negligence per se are not enough. Evident bad faith connotes a palpably and patently fraudulent and dishonest purpose to do moral obliquity or conscious wrongdoing for some perverse motive or ill will, not mere bad judgment. These modalities must be alleged with particularity in the Information. In People v. Reyes (G.R. Nos. 246783-84, July 29, 2025), the Court acquitted local officials who relied on the resident COA auditor's verbal opinion, holding that the finding that they "should have known better" showed ignorance rather than bad faith.
- **Application:** (a) The officials had no legal officer and consulted the official presumed to have expertise in government financial transactions. They could presume that the auditor performed his functions regularly and correctly; that his opinion was verbal and given before audit does not matter. Saying they "should have known better" describes ignorance, not a conscious and deliberate wrongdoing driven by ill motive. (b) The Information alleged only evident bad faith and manifest partiality. Convicting them on gross inexcusable negligence, which was not alleged, would deprive them of their right to be informed of the charge. With no finding of manifest partiality, the second element of Section 3(e) is not proved.
- **Conclusion:** The accused must be acquitted of violating Section 3(e) because evident bad faith was not proved, manifest partiality was not found, and gross inexcusable negligence was not alleged.

**Q3.** A provincial government released funds after its resident COA auditor verbally assured the governor that the transaction was proper. On post-audit, a COA special audit team found the release irregular and recommended charges. The governor argues that the COA is estopped from questioning a transaction that its own auditor had cleared. Is the governor correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The COA is not estopped from questioning, on post-audit, a transaction that its own auditor earlier cleared.
- **Legal basis:** Estoppel does not lie against the government, more so when the acts of its officials are erroneous or irregular. The COA is therefore not estopped from questioning, in post-audit, the previous acts of its officials. Reliance on the expertise of a COA representative is instead a matter of defense in the criminal case. (Villanueva v. Commission on Audit, as applied in People v. Reyes, G.R. Nos. 246783-84, July 29, 2025)
- **Application:** The auditor's verbal clearance cannot bind the government or bar the COA's special audit team from finding the release irregular. At most, the governor may invoke his reliance on the auditor in a criminal prosecution, where good faith may negate evident bad faith under Section 3(e) of RA 3019, as in Reyes. That defense does not prevent the audit itself.
- **Conclusion:** The governor's estoppel argument fails, though his reliance on the auditor may be raised as a defense in any criminal case.

> Note: Accused Estil did not appeal; the Appellants' Brief alleges he died while the case was pending. He is not named in the acquittal, and the decision does not discuss whether the acquittal benefits him. The cases against Treasurer Salise were dismissed on August 22, 2017 on account of his death, although the decision's summary of the Sandiganbayan ruling says the Sandiganbayan "found Reyes and Salise guilty" of malversation. One sentence in that summary is garbled in the source ("It ruled that the failed to account for the funds"). The decision does not separately discuss the demand element; the Sandiganbayan found the accused failed to account after being presented with the COA audit observation.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70089)

## People v. Soriano

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. AMALIA SORIANO Y REALINGO A.K.A. "AMY", ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 257747 | 2025-02-05 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640)  
**Specific topics:** Chain of custody: failure to use an evidence bag is not automatically fatal; History of the evidence-bag requirement (PNP manuals, DDB and PDEA issuances, People v. Sanchez); Stricter scrutiny for minuscule quantities; heat-sealed packets; Illegal possession of shabu (Section 11, R.A. 9165): penalty for 10 to under 50 grams
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 1. Object or Real Evidence > c. Chain of Custody)

### Doctrine
**The failure to place seized drugs in an evidence bag or appropriate container is not automatically fatal** to a prosecution for illegal possession of dangerous drugs, because neither Section 21 of R.A. No. 9165 nor the chain of custody rule requires it. The evidence bag exists to prevent switching or contamination, so "it is not so much the type or designation of the container used to store the drug evidence that matters but the manner in which said evidence was handled and transferred from one officer to another in the chain of custody." **Where there is no proof that an evidence bag was used, courts look primarily at that handling and transfer, taking into account the type and amount of drugs involved and whether the circumstances warrant a different type of handling or container.** Conversely, if the evidence is improperly handled or transferred, using an evidence bag will not validate its custody.

The Court traced the evidence-bag requirement from the 1999 PNP Drug Enforcement Manual to the 2015 PDEA Guidelines and distinguished cases where unbagged or unsealed drugs led to acquittal (Tumabini, Alvarado, Ramos). It reiterated that a more exacting standard applies to minuscule amounts, which are more prone to tampering, while the chain of custody rule need not be applied as strictly to considerable amounts in heat-sealed packets (Ramos; Veloo).

Possession of 10 grams or more but less than 50 grams of shabu is punished under Section 11 of R.A. No. 9165 by **life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 400,000 to PHP 500,000**; an indeterminate penalty is erroneous.

### Facts
On June 30, 2014, the RTC of Daet, Camarines Norte issued a search warrant for shabu in Amalia Soriano's house. At about 6:10 a.m. on July 1, 2014, police officers served it, with PO1 Jesus Togores as the designated searcher. He found a matchbox containing three sachets of white crystalline substance on the bed. On a table near the bedroom door he found a multicolored coin purse with five sachets, a red pouch with eight sachets, and a gold wallet box with four sachets: 20 heat-sealed plastic sachets in all.

PO1 Togores laid the items on the floor, marked the containers and the sachets with his initials "JAT" and the date, and inventoried them in the presence of Soriano, a DOJ representative, a media representative and a barangay kagawad. He kept the items with him throughout: at the police station for the blotter entry, at the RTC when he made the return of the search warrant (where others only looked at the items), and until he personally delivered them, with the request for examination, to the forensic chemist, PCI Gorospe. She found that the markings matched the request and that the specimens were positive for methamphetamine hydrochloride, with a total net weight of 16.9618 grams. She added her own markings, sealed the specimens in a marked brown envelope, and kept them in a locked steel cabinet.

Soriano was charged under Sections 11 and 12 of R.A. No. 9165. The RTC acquitted her of possessing drug paraphernalia but convicted her of illegal possession of dangerous drugs, imposing an indeterminate penalty of 30 years to life imprisonment and a fine. The CA affirmed. Before the Supreme Court, Soriano argued that the chain of custody was broken because, among other things, nothing showed that the seized items were placed in a secured container or evidence bag.

### Issues
1. Whether the failure to place the seized drugs in an evidence bag or appropriate container is fatal to the prosecution for illegal possession of dangerous drugs.
2. Whether the penalty imposed by the RTC and affirmed by the CA was proper.

### Ruling
**1. No, it is not fatal.** The Court traced the history of the evidence bag:

- The 1999 PNP Manual required the evidence custodian to secure seized drugs in an evidence bag or appropriate container, including in the service of search warrants.
- DDB Board Regulation No. 1 (2002) required drug evidence to be stored in plastic heat-sealed envelopes in evidence vaults.
- People v. Sanchez (2008) stated that seized items "shall be placed in an envelope or an evidence bag unless the type and quantity of the seized items require a different type of handling and/or container."
- The 2010 PNP Manual placed the duty on the seizing officer, while the 2014 Revised PNP Manual dropped the term "evidence bag" for drug evidence.
- The 2015 PDEA Guidelines required sealing in a container or evidence bag, but were silent on the effect of failing to do so.

Tumabini, Alvarado and Ramos, where unbagged or unsealed drugs led to acquittal, were distinguished. Here the 20 heat-sealed sachets were already inside four containers (matchbox, red pouch, coin purse and wallet box), as alleged in the Information, and the containers were marked upon seizure, so there was "little point" in combining them in a single evidence bag. **Because neither Section 21 nor the chain of custody rule requires an evidence bag, what matters is how the drugs were handled and transferred** (People v. Magayon; People v. Habana). The testimonies of PO1 Togores and the forensic chemist, credited by the lower courts, established an unbroken chain from seizure to the trial court. Moreover, 16.9618 grams of shabu is "hardly miniscule," so the stricter scrutiny for minuscule amounts (Ramos; Veloo) did not apply, and the heat-sealed packets already minimized the risk of tampering.

**2. No, the penalty must be modified.** Under Section 11 of R.A. No. 9165, possession of 10 grams or more but less than 50 grams of shabu is punished by life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 400,000 to PHP 500,000. Possession of 16.9618 grams "no longer merits an indeterminate penalty, as erroneously imposed by the RTC," so the Court imposed life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 500,000.

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA Decision dated November 27, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 10190 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Soriano was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of violation of Section 11 of R.A. No. 9165 and sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 500,000.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Armed with a search warrant, PO2 Diaz searched Lito's house and found 12 heat-sealed sachets of shabu inside a cigarette case and a leather pouch. At the house, he immediately marked the sachets and both containers and inventoried and photographed them in the presence of Lito and the required witnesses. He kept the items in his personal possession at the police station and personally delivered them to the forensic chemist. The chemist found them positive for 14 grams of shabu, marked and sealed them, and kept them in a locked cabinet until trial. PO2 Diaz never placed the items in an evidence bag. Lito argues that the integrity of the corpus delicti was compromised because no evidence bag was used. Is he correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The failure to use an evidence bag is not fatal, because the prosecution established how the drugs were handled and transferred in an unbroken chain.
- **Legal basis:** Neither Section 21 of R.A. No. 9165 nor the chain of custody rule requires an evidence bag. Its purpose is to prevent switching or contamination, so where there is no proof that one was used, the primary consideration is how the evidence was handled and transferred from one officer to another, taking into account the type and amount of drugs and whether the circumstances call for a different kind of handling or container. (People v. Soriano, G.R. No. 257747, February 5, 2025)
- **Application:** The sachets were heat-sealed and already inside two containers, and both the sachets and the containers were marked at the place of seizure, so repacking them in an evidence bag would add little. More importantly, the handling is fully accounted for: PO2 Diaz alone held the items from seizure until he gave them to the chemist, who marked, sealed and secured them until trial. Fourteen grams of shabu is not a minuscule amount that calls for the strictest scrutiny.
- **Conclusion:** Lito is not correct; the integrity and evidentiary value of the drugs were preserved despite the absence of an evidence bag.

**Q2.** In a buy-bust operation, PO1 Lara seized from Mark one unsealed plastic sachet containing 0.03 gram of shabu. He marked it but did not seal it or place it in any envelope or evidence bag. He handed it to the investigator, who gave it to a desk officer, who later had a messenger deliver it to the crime laboratory. Only PO1 Lara and the forensic chemist testified; the investigator, the desk officer and the messenger did not. Citing People v. Soriano, the prosecution argues that the failure to use an evidence bag is not fatal. Will the argument save the prosecution's case?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Soriano does not help the prosecution, because the drug was unsealed and minuscule, and nothing accounts for how the intermediate custodians handled it.
- **Legal basis:** In People v. Soriano (G.R. No. 257747, February 5, 2025), the Court held that the absence of an evidence bag is not automatically fatal, because courts then look to how the drugs were handled and transferred, considering their type and amount. Quoting People v. Habana, it stressed that if the seized substance is not sealed, the prosecution must present every officer, messenger, laboratory technician and storage personnel in the chain to testify that it was not tampered with or substituted. Citing Ramos and Veloo, it reiterated that a more exacting standard applies to minuscule amounts, which are more prone to tampering, loss or mistake.
- **Application:** In Soriano, marked heat-sealed sachets stayed with one officer from seizure to the laboratory. Here, the sachet was unsealed and passed through three people who never testified on how they kept it. At 0.03 gram, the drug is minuscule and easily substituted, so the strictest scrutiny applies. What breaks the chain is not the mere absence of an evidence bag but these unexplained gaps in handling.
- **Conclusion:** The integrity of the corpus delicti was not established, so Mark should be acquitted.

**Q3.** (a) Police officers who seized 18 grams of shabu under a search warrant brought the drugs to the issuing judge when they made the return of the warrant, before taking them to the crime laboratory. The searching officer held the items the whole time, and the court staff only looked at them. Does the detour to the court break the chain of custody? (b) After trial, the RTC convicted the accused of illegal possession of the 18 grams and sentenced him to an indeterminate penalty of 30 years as minimum to life imprisonment as maximum, and a fine of PHP 500,000. Is the penalty correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The chain is unbroken because the searching officer kept the drugs in his possession throughout. (b) No. The proper penalty is life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 400,000 to PHP 500,000, not an indeterminate penalty.
- **Legal basis:** What matters in the chain of custody is how the seized drugs were handled and transferred. Testimony that the seizing officer kept the drugs with him from seizure, through the return of the search warrant to the issuing court, until he delivered them to the forensic chemist sufficiently establishes the links. Under Section 11 of R.A. No. 9165, possession of 10 grams or more but less than 50 grams of shabu is punished by life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 400,000 to PHP 500,000, and imposing an indeterminate penalty is error. (People v. Soriano, G.R. No. 257747, February 5, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Bringing the drugs to court for the return of the warrant did not change custody: the searching officer kept holding them, and no one else handled them before he delivered them to the chemist. (b) Eighteen grams falls within the bracket of 10 grams or more but less than 50 grams, for which the law prescribes life imprisonment and a fine. The RTC had no basis to impose an indeterminate penalty with a minimum of 30 years.
- **Conclusion:** The chain of custody remained intact, but the penalty must be corrected to life imprisonment and a fine within the statutory range.

> Note: The decision did not separately address Soriano's argument that the non-admission of the RTC's July 1, 2014 Order (on the return of the search warrant) meant non-compliance with Rule 126, Section 12. The amount of the RTC's fine is garbled in the source text ("[PHP 500,00.00]"). The marking and inventory were witnessed by a DOJ representative, a media representative and a barangay kagawad, but the decision did not discuss the witness requirement. Footnote 30 cites earlier unsigned (notice) resolutions holding that an evidence bag is not required by Section 21.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69897)

## People v. Estregan

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. JEORGE EJERCITO ESTREGAN, ARLYN LAZARO-TORRES, TERRYL GAMIT-TALABONG, KALAHI U. RABAGO, ERWIN P. SACLUTI, GENER C. DIMARANAN, AND MARILYN M. BRUEL, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.**  
G.R. No. 248699 | 2025-02-05 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910)  
**Specific topics:** Elements of Section 3(e), RA 3019: manifest partiality, evident bad faith, unwarranted benefits; Procurement violations do not per se establish Section 3(e); Sanggunian members who authorize and ratify a contract are not automatically liable; Accident protection agreement as a contract of insurance (PD 612, Sec. 2); Mode of appeal from Sandiganbayan judgments in original-jurisdiction criminal cases
  
**Also relevant to:** Commercial and Taxation Laws (II. Insurance Law > A. General Principles)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > N. Appeal (Rule 122))

### Doctrine
A violation of procurement laws, rules and regulations does **not per se** result in conviction under **Section 3(e) of RA 3019** (reiterated). The prosecution must still prove beyond reasonable doubt that:

- the accused is a public officer discharging administrative, judicial or official functions;
- the accused acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence; and
- the accused caused undue injury to any party, including the Government, or gave a private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference.

Under the second mode, the third element is met even without proof of damage. **A mayor who bypasses public bidding and contracts with an entity he knows lacks legal authority and any track record gives it unwarranted benefit with manifest partiality and evident bad faith.** The private party who conspires with him is equally liable. By contrast, **sanggunian members who merely pass an ordinance authorizing the mayor to contract with "any competent and qualified entity"** (even if it wrongly authorizes negotiated procurement) and later ratify the contract show no partiality toward a particular entity. This is especially so where the contract's validity did not depend on their resolution, which confers no rights.

An agreement by which one undertakes, for a consideration, to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability from an unknown or contingent event is a **contract of insurance** (PD 612, Sec. 2(1)). A memorandum of agreement under which a firm indemnifies tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and reimburses the municipality's medical expenses up to scheduled amounts, is accident insurance, because indemnity is its principal object. The absence of a separately labeled premium is not conclusive. As "goods" under RA 9184, such a contract must be procured by competitive bidding unless a ground for an alternative method exists. Procedurally, a Sandiganbayan judgment in a criminal case within its original jurisdiction is appealed to the Supreme Court by **notice of appeal** (2018 Revised Internal Rules of the Sandiganbayan, Rule IX, Sec. 1(a)).

### Facts
The Sangguniang Bayan (SB) of Pagsanjan, Laguna passed Municipal Ordinance No. 15-2008. It authorized Mayor Jeorge Ejercito Estregan to negotiate and contract with "any competent and qualified entity" for accident protection and assistance (APA) to tourists and boatmen on boat rides in the Pagsanjan Gorge Tourist Zone. On September 22, 2008, First Rapids Care Ventures (FRCV), owned by Marilyn Bruel, submitted a written proposal. Without public bidding, Estregan signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with FRCV on October 23, 2008. The SB ratified it the same day through Municipal Resolution No. 056-2008. Under the MOA, FRCV would indemnify tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and reimburse the municipality for actual treatment or confinement expenses up to the amounts in its tables of coverage. The APA fee of PHP 48.00 per tourist was part of a PHP 160.00 boat-ride ticket. The municipal treasurer collected the fee, and FRCV's share was remitted to it by check.

FRCV had no Certificate of Authority from the Insurance Commission. It was registered with the DTI only on March 19, 2008 and with the BIR only on September 17, 2008, five days before its offer, and its BIR-registered line of business was "Other Computer Related Activities." Bruel had been an insurance agent of Malayan Insurance before forming FRCV. Estregan said Philamlife and Oriental Insurance had made inquiries but could not meet all the program's requirements.

On a 2009 complaint by the United Boatmen Association of Pagsanjan, the Ombudsman found probable cause. On March 16, 2016, an Information for violation of Section 3(e) of RA 3019 was filed with the Sandiganbayan against the mayor, the vice mayor, six councilors and Bruel; the complaint against one councilor had been dismissed by reason of his death. The prosecution's sole witness identified the Insurance Commissioner's letter-opinion that the MOA is a contract of insurance. The councilors testified that the Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) refused to act because there was no approved budget for the contract. The Sandiganbayan found that the legal opinions they relied on were sought only after the MOA had been signed and ratified.

In its April 5, 2019 Decision in SB-16-CRM-0124, the Sandiganbayan acquitted Vice Mayor Vilar. It convicted Estregan, Councilors Torres, Talabong, Rabago, Sacluti and Dimaranan, and Bruel, and sentenced each to an indeterminate prison term with perpetual disqualification from public office. It denied reconsideration on July 5, 2019, and the convicted accused appealed. The OSP argued that they had used the wrong mode of appeal. Estregan's new counsel filed his brief more than three years after the Court granted him additional time.

### Issues
1. Whether accused-appellants used the correct mode of appeal from the Sandiganbayan.
2. Whether the MOA is a contract of insurance whose procurement required public bidding under RA 9184.
3. Whether Estregan and Bruel are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019.
4. Whether SB members Torres, Talabong, Rabago, Sacluti and Dimaranan are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, a notice of appeal was the correct mode.** The case was decided by the Sandiganbayan in its original jurisdiction. Under Rule IX, Sec. 1(a) of the 2018 Revised Internal Rules of the Sandiganbayan, which prevail over the procedure in PD 1606 (*People v. Talaue*), the appeal is by notice of appeal. The Court rejected the excuses of Estregan's counsel. Rule 7, Sec. 3 of the 2019 Amended Rules requires written submissions to be signed, and counsel's earlier motion was unsigned. Filing the brief more than three years after the extension "betrays his negligence, if not abandonment, of the appeal." In any case, the appeal failed on the merits.

**2. Yes, the MOA is an insurance contract that had to be bid out.** The MOA "unmistakably" shows that FRCV undertook to indemnify tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and the municipality for medical expenses up to stated limits. Bruel cited *Philippine Health Care Providers, Inc. v. CIR* (no insurance business where indemnity is merely incidental to service). That ruling does not apply, because indemnification was the MOA's principal object; training and assistance were incidental. Estregan's own testimony supported this: he had personally shouldered funeral and repatriation costs, and he first sought offers from insurance companies. An accident insurer, unlike a medical service provider, indemnifies only up to the scheduled rates, which is what FRCV did. As to the absence of a premium, PD 612, Sec. 2(2) states that the lack of profit or of a separate consideration is not conclusive. In any event, the "coverage outlay" of PHP 48.00 per tourist was the premium. Doing business "in substance equivalent" to insurance in a manner designed to evade the Code is still doing an insurance business.

An insurance contract is "goods" under Sec. 5(h) of RA 9184. Even if FRCV mainly trained boatmen, that would be consulting services, still within RA 9184. Competitive bidding is the default mode (Revised IRR, Rule IV, Sec. 10). Ordinance No. 15-2008 instead authorized negotiated procurement at once, although that method is allowed only in particular cases such as two failed biddings or emergencies (IRR, Sec. 53). None of those cases existed. Estregan claimed that the BAC and GPPB had said no bidding was needed, but that was a bare allegation. **The procurement law was violated.**

**3. Yes, Estregan and Bruel are guilty.** A procurement violation is not enough by itself, so the Court examined the elements. The first element (public officer) was undisputed. Section 3(e) may be committed by *dolo* (manifest partiality or evident bad faith) or *culpa* (gross inexcusable negligence). **Estregan acted with manifest partiality and evident bad faith.** He contracted with FRCV despite "glaringly questionable circumstances": its very recent DTI and BIR registrations and its lack of a Certificate of Authority. His claim that FRCV was the only qualified provider deserved scant consideration. The public consultations dealt only with increasing the boat-ride fee, not with FRCV's qualifications, which were the BAC's job "which Estregan arrogated upon himself." On the third element, "there is indeed no estimable proof of damage to any party." The element was nonetheless met under the second mode. **By sparing FRCV the procurement process and ignoring its irregularities, Estregan gave it unwarranted benefit, advantage or preference**, since FRCV had no legal authority to engage in insurance at all. **Bruel** fraudulently represented that FRCV was fully capable. It made no difference that she never called FRCV an insurer, because the MOA itself shows insurance business. FRCV's registrations showed it was created just for this contract. Even if FRCV performed under the MOA, that would not negate her fraud. She conspired with Estregan.

**4. No, the SB members are acquitted.** Ordinance No. 15-2008 referred to "any competent and qualified entity," which was yet to be determined. Even if the ordinance wrongly authorized negotiated procurement, it showed no partiality to any particular entity and did not prevent Estregan from holding a public bidding. Their ratification through Resolution No. 056-2008 did not make them liable either, because the MOA's validity did not depend on it. "No rights can be conferred by and be inferred from a resolution, which is but an embodiment of what the lawmaking body has to say in light of attendant circumstances."

### Disposition
The appeal was PARTLY GRANTED. The Sandiganbayan's April 5, 2019 Decision and July 5, 2019 Resolution in SB-16-CRM-0124 were AFFIRMED as to Jeorge Ejercito Estregan and Marilyn M. Bruel. Both were found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019 and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six years and one month, as minimum, to eight years, as maximum, with perpetual disqualification from holding public office. The Decision and Resolution were MODIFIED as to Arlyn Lazaro-Torres, Terryl Gamit-Talabong, Kalahi U. Rabago, Erwin P. Sacluti and Gener C. Dimaranan, who were ACQUITTED on reasonable doubt. Entry of judgment was ordered as to the acquitted accused-appellants.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** A municipal ordinance authorized Mayor Dante to contract with "any competent and qualified entity" for accident protection of tourists. Without public bidding, Dante signed an agreement with XYZ Ventures, a sole proprietorship that had registered with the BIR only five days before submitting its offer and held no certificate of authority from the Insurance Commission. Under the agreement, XYZ would indemnify tourists for accidental death and reimburse the town's medical expenses up to fixed amounts, in exchange for a fixed share of every boat-ride ticket. Charged with violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019, Dante argues that he cannot be convicted because the town suffered no actual damage: XYZ paid every claim during the life of the contract. Is Dante's defense tenable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Dante may be convicted even without proof of actual damage, because he gave XYZ unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference through manifest partiality and evident bad faith.
- **Legal basis:** Section 3(e) of RA 3019 punishes a public officer who, in the discharge of official functions and through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence, causes undue injury to any party or gives any private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference. The two modes are distinct; under the second, proof of damage is unnecessary. A procurement violation is not per se a Section 3(e) violation, but all the elements are present when a mayor bypasses the bidding process and contracts with an entity he knows lacks legal authority and a track record. (People v. Estregan, G.R. No. 248699, February 5, 2025)
- **Application:** Dante is a public officer who acted in the discharge of his functions. The agreement is a contract of insurance, which is "goods" requiring competitive bidding under RA 9184, yet he dispensed with bidding. He chose an entity registered only days before its offer and without a certificate of authority from the Insurance Commission. Those glaring circumstances show a clear inclination to favor XYZ and a conscious wrongdoing, which are manifest partiality and evident bad faith. By sparing XYZ the rigors of procurement and letting it do an insurance business it had no authority to do, Dante gave it unwarranted benefit. XYZ's payment of claims does not erase that benefit, since the second mode does not require damage.
- **Conclusion:** Dante's defense is untenable, and he may be convicted under the second mode of Section 3(e).

**Q2.** In the same case, Councilors Ella and Fe are also charged. Their only participation was (1) voting for the ordinance that authorized the mayor to negotiate and contract with "any competent and qualified entity" for accident protection, and (2) on the same day the mayor signed the agreement with XYZ, voting for a resolution ratifying it. The prosecution argues that the ordinance itself violated the procurement law by authorizing negotiated procurement when none of its grounds, such as two failed biddings or an emergency, existed. Are Ella and Fe liable under Section 3(e)?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Ella and Fe should be acquitted.
- **Legal basis:** A violation of procurement laws does not per se result in conviction under Section 3(e) of RA 3019; manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence and the resulting injury or unwarranted benefit must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. SB members who pass an ordinance authorizing the mayor to contract with "any competent and qualified entity" do not show partiality toward any particular entity, even if the ordinance wrongly authorizes negotiated procurement. A ratifying resolution does not make them liable where the contract's validity does not depend on it, because a resolution confers no rights. (People v. Estregan, G.R. No. 248699, February 5, 2025)
- **Application:** The ordinance did not name XYZ or any other entity, and it did not stop the mayor from holding a public bidding. Even assuming it erroneously authorized negotiated procurement, it shows no clear inclination to favor anyone. The choice of XYZ was the mayor's. The ratifying resolution was not needed for the agreement to be valid, so voting for it did not give XYZ the benefit. The prosecution has shown, at most, a procurement irregularity, not the elements of Section 3(e).
- **Conclusion:** Ella and Fe are not liable under Section 3(e) and must be acquitted on reasonable doubt.

**Q3.** Bea's firm is not licensed by the Insurance Commission. Under its agreement with a municipality, it indemnifies tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment and reimburses the municipality's medical expenses up to scheduled amounts. The firm also trains boatmen and deploys first-aid and rescue teams. Bea contends that the agreement is a "special services" contract, not insurance, because (i) her firm renders services, and (ii) the agreement does not require the municipality to pay any "premium," only a "coverage outlay" of PHP 48.00 per tourist taken from each ticket. (a) Is the agreement a contract of insurance? (b) Was public bidding required to award it?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, it is a contract of insurance. (b) Yes, public bidding was required.
- **Legal basis:** A contract of insurance is an agreement whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event (PD 612, Sec. 2(1)). The absence of profit or of a separate consideration is not conclusive. Doing business in substance equivalent to insurance in a manner designed to evade the Code is doing an insurance business (Sec. 2(2)). Where indemnification is the principal object and services are incidental, the contract is insurance. An insurance contract is "goods" under Sec. 5(h) of RA 9184, and procurement must be by competitive bidding unless an alternative method is justified by grounds such as two failed biddings or an emergency. Even training services would be consulting services covered by RA 9184. (People v. Estregan, G.R. No. 248699, February 5, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The firm's core undertaking is to pay for accidental death, dismemberment and medical expenses, all contingent events, up to scheduled limits. That is what an accident insurer does. The training and rescue teams are incidental to that indemnity. The "coverage outlay" of PHP 48.00 per tourist is the consideration for assuming the risk, so it is a premium in all but name. Calling the contract "special services" cannot avoid the Insurance Code. (b) As insurance, the contract is "goods" under RA 9184. If the services were the main object, they would be consulting services, also covered by RA 9184. Either way, competitive bidding was the required mode, and no ground for an alternative method appears.
- **Conclusion:** The agreement is an insurance contract, and it could be awarded only through public bidding.

> Note: The Sandiganbayan's summary of defense evidence refers to Ordinance No. 14-2008 (as amended by Ordinance No. 18-2008) for the fee schedule and also as the mayor's authority to contract. The stipulations and the Court's own discussion treat Ordinance No. 15-2008 as the authorizing ordinance, and this digest follows the Court. The Court criticized the late brief of Estregan's counsel but resolved Estregan's appeal on the merits; it did not expressly expunge the brief or dismiss his appeal for abandonment.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69812)

## People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr.

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PETITIONER, VS. DATU AKMAD "TATO" AMPATUAN, SR., RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 258710 | 2025-01-27 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > B. Criminal Liability > 7. Participation in Acts Giving Rise to Criminal Liability > b. Conspiracy and Proposal > i. As a Mode of Incurring Criminal Liability  
**Specific topics:** Overt act in furtherance of a conspiracy vs. mere approval or acquiescence; Liability of a conspirator absent from the crime scene; moral ascendancy must be proved; Finality-of-acquittal rule; certiorari against an acquittal only for grave abuse of discretion; Gross misapprehension of facts as grave abuse: must also be capricious or whimsical; Accessories exempt from liability (RPC, Art. 20)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VII. Criminal Procedure > I. Motion to Quash (Rule 117) > 2. Double Jeopardy)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > S. Right Against Double Jeopardy)

### Doctrine
**To be liable as a conspirator, the accused must have performed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy, that is, an act that promotes, advances, or facilitates the progress of the plan.** The overt act may be active participation in the crime itself, or moral assistance by being present at its commission or by exerting moral ascendancy over the co-conspirators. **Mere presence at the planning, and statements made in agreement with the plot, are approval or acquiescence, not acts in furtherance, and are not enough to convict**, unless the approval is so indispensable that without it the plan would not be set in motion or carried out. By contrast, offering one's guns for the killing is an overt act even if other guns were used: the act need only be done *in furtherance* of the conspiracy; it need not actually further it. A conspirator absent from the scene is liable only if it is proved that his moral ascendancy moved the others to carry out the plan. Moral ascendancy cannot be presumed from kinship or public position.

**A judgment of acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory** (finality-of-acquittal rule, which shares the purpose of the right against double jeopardy). It may be challenged only by certiorari for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, as where the prosecution was denied the opportunity to present its case or the trial was a sham. Gross misapprehension of facts is not by itself an exception to double jeopardy. It establishes grave abuse only if it is patent and gross and was exercised in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner, because "[w]himsicality, not accuracy, is the core of certiorari proceedings."

Under **Article 20 of the RPC**, one who would otherwise be an accessory is exempt when the principal is a relative within the degrees stated, including relatives by affinity within the same degrees (here, the son-in-law of a principal).

### Facts
Datu Akmad "Tato" Ampatuan, Sr., then OIC Vice Governor of Maguindanao and the nephew and son-in-law of clan patriarch Datu Andal Ampatuan, Sr., was charged with 58 counts of murder over the November 23, 2009 Maguindanao massacre. He attended the clan meetings where the plot to kill Datu Esmael "Toto" Mangudadatu was discussed: at Century Park Hotel on July 20, 2009, and on November 17 and 22, 2009. At one meeting he said "Pakinggan natin si Ama. Okay kami lahat na patayin sila" and "mabuti nga sa mga Mangudadatu na mahilig mag-ambisyon na patayin sila lahat." No eyewitness placed him at the crime site. He attended a medical mission the whole day of November 23, 2009.

In its December 19, 2019 Consolidated Partial Decision, the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 221, convicted several Ampatuans of 57 counts of murder. Among them was Datu Zaldy Ampatuan, who was absent from the scene but had pledged at a meeting: "Todo suporta ako diyan, kahit lahat ng baril ko gagamitin ko." The RTC acquitted Datu Akmad on reasonable doubt. It classed him among those who had prior knowledge of the plot but performed no overt act.

The State, through the OSG, filed a Rule 65 petition for certiorari with the CA. The CA dismissed it (Decision of May 24, 2021; Resolution of December 10, 2021), holding that the alleged errors went to the merits, that double jeopardy had attached, and that mere presence at meetings and acquiescence, without an overt act, did not make him a conspirator. The State then filed a Rule 45 petition. It argued that he expressed conformity with and encouraged the plan; that his situation was like that of Datu Zaldy and Datu Anwar, who were convicted though absent; that he lent his man Talembo "Tammy" Masukat, who joined the killing; that his absence was part of the plan, with absent clan members on standby to monitor and assist; and that at the least he was an accessory. Datu Akmad invoked the lack of an overt act, Article 20 of the RPC, and double jeopardy.

### Issues
1. Whether the CA correctly held that the RTC did not commit grave abuse of discretion in acquitting Datu Akmad, given the finality-of-acquittal rule and the right against double jeopardy.
2. Whether Datu Akmad's attendance at the planning meetings, his statements of approval, and his relationship with Talembo constitute overt acts in furtherance of the conspiracy.
3. Whether Datu Akmad may be held liable as an accessory.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the CA correctly found no grave abuse of discretion.** An acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory. It may be challenged without violating double jeopardy only for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, such as denial of the prosecution's chance to present its case or a sham trial. Gross misapprehension of facts may be used to show grave abuse but is not per se an exception. It must be patent and gross and also committed in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner. **Errors of judgment, misapplication of facts, and erroneous conclusions cannot be reviewed without trampling on the right against double jeopardy.** On a Rule 45 review of a CA ruling in a Rule 65 case, the Court asks only whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse, not whether the RTC decided the case correctly on the merits.

**2. No overt act was proved.** Quoting Bahilidad v. People, the Court held that a conspirator must have performed some overt act as a direct or indirect contribution to the crime, and that mere presence at the discussion of a conspiracy, "even approval of it, without any active participation," is not enough. Using Black's definitions, an overt act is an outward act done *in furtherance* of the conspiracy, and furtherance means facilitating the plan's progress or making it more likely to occur.

- *Datu Zaldy vs. Datu Akmad:* Datu Zaldy's offer of all his guns was an overt act, because the guns were the very tools needed for the killing. It counted even if other guns were used, since the act need only be "in furtherance of a conspiracy, not that it furthers the conspiracy." **Datu Akmad's statements, "debauched and depraved as they may be, are mere expressions of approval of or acquiescence to the plot."** Evidence of actual cooperation is required, not mere cognizance or approval. His approval was not indispensable, because the plan would have been carried out without it.
- *Moral ascendancy:* An absent conspirator may be liable if, through moral ascendancy, he moved the others to execute the plan. Apart from his being the patriarch's nephew and OIC Vice Governor, there was no proof that he exerted such ascendancy, and the RTC was silent on the effect of his words. **"Courts cannot rely on mere presumptions of moral ascendancy."**
- *Monitoring and standby:* The plan for others to monitor and help came from Datu Unsay. Datu Akmad's awareness of that statement was not agreement to it, much less an overt act.
- *Talembo:* There was no evidence that Datu Akmad offered Talembo's services. Talembo was a CVO commander who took directives from several bosses, including Datu Unsay, and the petition itself admitted only a "possibility." The Court would not rely on speculation.
- *Medical mission:* Even if the RTC erred in finding that he did not "cling" to the plot, "clinging" is not itself an overt act. It means only adherence or acquiescence, which is insufficient to convict.

**3. No accessory liability.** Even assuming he could be deemed an accessory, he is the son-in-law of principal accused Datu Andal, Sr. **Article 20 of the RPC exempts him**, because accessories are not penalized when the principal is their relative by affinity within the same degrees. The Court stressed that this "by no means signifies his innocence"; the law recognizes that family ties compel one to conceal crimes of near relatives.

### Disposition
The Petition was DENIED. The CA's May 24, 2021 Decision and December 10, 2021 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 164524, which dismissed the State's petition for certiorari, stand. Datu Akmad's acquittal was therefore left undisturbed.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Brothers Ariel and Benny met at their father's house with their cousin Cesar to plan the killing of a political rival. Ariel laid out the plan. Cesar, who sat through the whole meeting, said: "Tama, dapat lang siyang patayin." On the day of the killing, Ariel and Benny ambushed and killed the rival. Cesar was at a wedding in another town. No evidence showed that Cesar gave any money, weapon, men, or instructions, or that his words influenced the brothers. Is Cesar liable for murder as a conspirator?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Cesar is not liable as a conspirator because he performed no overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy.
- **Legal basis:** A conspirator must perform an overt act, an act that promotes, advances, or facilitates the progress of the conspiratorial plan, as a direct or indirect contribution to the crime. It may be active participation in the crime, or moral assistance through presence at its commission or moral ascendancy over the co-conspirators. Mere presence at the discussion of a conspiracy, and even approval of it, without active participation, is not enough to convict. Statements made in agreement with the plot must be distinguished from statements made in furtherance of it. (People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr., G.R. No. 258710, January 27, 2025, citing Bahilidad v. People)
- **Application:** Cesar's attendance at the meeting and his remark that the rival deserved to die are expressions of approval or acquiescence, like Datu Akmad's statements in Ampatuan. They did not promote or facilitate the plan. His approval was not indispensable, since Ariel and Benny carried out the killing on their own. He was not present at the crime, and there is no proof that he had moral ascendancy over the brothers or that his words moved them to act.
- **Conclusion:** Cesar must be acquitted because mere approval of the plot, without an overt act in furtherance of it, does not make him a conspirator.

**Q2.** Same facts as in the previous problem, except that at the planning meeting their uncle Dado, who was also absent from the ambush, declared: "Full support ako. Gamitin ninyo lahat ng baril ko para malinis ang trabaho." In the end, Ariel and Benny used their own guns. The prosecution also argues that Cesar, as the provincial vice governor and the eldest cousin, must have had moral ascendancy over the brothers. (a) Is Dado liable as a conspirator? (b) Does the prosecution's argument make Cesar liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Dado committed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy by offering his guns, even though they were not used. (b) No. Moral ascendancy must be proved and cannot be presumed from Cesar's position or relationship.
- **Legal basis:** An overt act need only be done in furtherance of the conspiracy; it need not actually further it. In People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr. (G.R. No. 258710, January 27, 2025), the Court held that Datu Zaldy's offer of "lahat ng baril ko" was an overt act showing unity of design, because guns are the very tools of the killing, even if other guns were later used. A conspirator remote from the scene may be liable if it is proved that his moral ascendancy moved the others to carry out the plan. But "[c]ourts cannot rely on mere presumptions of moral ascendancy," and being a relative and a vice governor is not proof of it.
- **Application:** (a) Dado did more than approve the plan: he offered the means to execute it. That offer advanced the plan and showed his unity of purpose with the brothers, so his absence from the scene and the brothers' use of other guns do not matter. (b) The prosecution offers only Cesar's office and his seniority in the family. Nothing shows that his words produced any reaction or that the brothers acted because of him. Moral ascendancy cannot be inferred from status alone.
- **Conclusion:** Dado is liable as a conspirator, but Cesar is not, because moral ascendancy over the brothers was not proved.

**Q3.** After trial, the RTC acquitted Ramon of murder, finding that the prosecution had failed to prove an overt act on his part. The prosecution, which had presented all its witnesses and evidence, filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the CA. It argued that the RTC misappreciated the testimony of its witnesses and drew wrong conclusions from them. The prosecution also argued that Ramon, who knew of the plan and later helped hide his father-in-law (a principal) from the police, should at least be convicted as an accessory. (a) Will the certiorari petition prosper? (b) Can Ramon be held liable as an accessory?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The petition will not prosper because it raises only errors of judgment, and reviewing them would violate the right against double jeopardy. (b) No. Ramon is exempt as an accessory under Article 20 of the RPC because the principal is his father-in-law.
- **Legal basis:** A judgment of acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory. It may be assailed through certiorari only for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, as where the prosecution was denied the opportunity to present its case or the trial was a sham. Misappreciation of evidence and erroneous conclusions are errors of judgment. Even gross misapprehension of facts amounts to grave abuse only if exercised in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner: "[w]himsicality, not accuracy, is the core of certiorari proceedings." Under Article 20 of the RPC, the penalties for accessories are not imposed on those who are such with respect to their spouses, ascendants, descendants, legitimate, natural, and adopted brothers and sisters, or relatives by affinity within the same degrees, except accessories under paragraph 1 of Article 19. (People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr., G.R. No. 258710, January 27, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The prosecution was fully heard, and it claims only that the RTC weighed the evidence wrongly. That is an error of judgment, not a capricious or whimsical exercise of discretion that ousted the RTC of jurisdiction. Reviewing the acquittal would place Ramon twice in jeopardy. (b) Helping conceal his father-in-law from the police falls under paragraph 3 of Article 19 (harboring or concealing the principal), not paragraph 1 (profiting from the crime). Since the principal is his relative by affinity in the direct line, Article 20 exempts him. As the Court noted, the exemption does not mean he is innocent; the law recognizes that family ties compel concealment of near relatives' crimes.
- **Conclusion:** The certiorari petition will be dismissed, and Ramon cannot be penalized as an accessory.

> Note: The Court cited an earlier ruling involving the same respondent, Datu Akmad "Tato" Ampatuan, Sr. v. Hon. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 200106, February 22, 2023, for the observation that his acquittal rested on the prosecution's failure to prove an overt act. Bar question 3(b) relies on the paragraph 1 exception quoted in Article 20 and on the basic text of Article 19 (paragraph 3 covers harboring or concealing the principal); the decision itself applied only Article 20.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69975)
