## People v. Asuncion

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. CARLOS RACADIO ASUNCION, MAMELFA R. AMONGOL, GENOVEVA R. RAGASA, ROSITA R. RAGUNJAN, AND VIRGINIA R. RAFANAN, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.**  
G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98 | 2022-04-06 | Second Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910)  
**Specific topics:** Sec. 3(e), RA 3019: evident bad faith, manifest partiality, gross inexcusable negligence; Erroneous interpretation of a law in good faith is not bad faith; Sec. 3(j), RA 3019: knowledge of the grantee's lack of qualification is essential; RA 3019 violations must be grounded on graft and corruption (Martel v. People); Malversation and conspiracy not proved; no presumption of bad faith
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (XIII. Local Governments > D. Powers and Administration of Local Government Units (LGU) > 1. Powers > g. Local Legislation)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 1. Standards > a. Proof Beyond Reasonable Doubt)

### Doctrine
To convict under **Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019**, the prosecution must prove that the public officer acted through manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. **An erroneous interpretation of a provision of law, absent any dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith** (reiterating *Ysidoro v. Leonardo-De Castro*); bad faith must be *evident*, partaking of fraud and showing a manifest deliberate intent to do wrong or cause damage. Manifest partiality requires a clear, notorious or plain inclination to favor one side over another, and gross inexcusable negligence is negated where the officer relied on Sanggunian accreditations, resolutions and appropriation ordinances. Repayment of the amounts upon COA disallowance is a badge of good faith.

**Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019 requires proof that the officer *knowingly* granted a privilege or benefit to one not qualified or not legally entitled to it.** Knowledge of the grantee's lack of qualification is essential because it is the basis for concluding that the officer acted with bias or partiality, and possibly corruption. **Violations of RA 3019 must be grounded on graft and corruption**: it is not enough that an official violated a law or rule, resulting in gain to a private person and damage to the government, if the root of the gain and damage is mere mistake (reiterating *Martel v. People*).

Malversation under Art. 217 of the RPC fails where the disbursement was supported by an appropriation ordinance, including one deemed reenacted under **Sec. 323 of the Local Government Code**. **Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt** by overt acts showing a conscious common design; the mayor's marriage to the president of the beneficiary federation is not enough. **There is no presumption of bad faith in cases involving violations of RA 3019.**

### Facts
Carlos R. Asuncion was mayor of Sta. Catalina, Ilocos Sur for three consecutive terms from 2007 to 2016. His wife Flora was the Federated President of the Bayanihan ng Kababaihan, an organization of women rural workers. Co-accused Amongol, Ragunjan, Rafanan and Ragasa were the presidents of its Cabittaogan, Subec, Paratong and Sinabaan chapters. The organization was accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan on September 20, 2010; the defense showed Sanggunian resolutions accrediting it as a community-based NGO and civil society organization since 2007.

On June 4, 2012, Asuncion approved four undated project proposals and signed four memoranda of agreement with the chapter presidents. Each chapter received PHP 100,000.00, released by checks dated June 15, 2012, as financial assistance for livelihood projects; the recipient members were to repay within six months with interest. The funds came from the municipality's 2010 share in the tobacco excise tax under RA 7171. The COA disallowed the disbursements, and the chapters returned the full amounts on February 22, 2016, before the criminal cases were filed.

On complaint of Jonathan Redoble, an opposition member and son of Asuncion's three-time rival, the Ombudsman charged all five with four counts each of violation of Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019, violation of Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019, and malversation of public funds. The prosecution claimed that the chapters lacked legal personality (not registered with the SEC, the CDA or DOLE), were not associations of tobacco farmers, and received the funds without Sanggunian authority or appropriation. The parties submitted a joint stipulation of facts in lieu of witnesses. The defense invoked the accreditations, Sangguniang Bayan Resolution No. 39, s. 2010 authorizing the mayor to sign contracts for the municipality, Appropriation Ordinance No. 01, s. 2010, reenacted in 2011 and 2012 under Sec. 323 of the LGC, and good faith.

The Sandiganbayan (Fourth Division) convicted all five on all counts, finding conspiracy, and denied reconsideration. They appealed. Rafanan filed her appellant's brief belatedly; the Court admitted it in the interest of substantial justice, noting that she and her counsel live in Ilocos Sur and the difficulty of filing during the pandemic lockdowns.

### Issues
1. Whether the Sandiganbayan erred in finding a conspiracy between Mayor Asuncion and the chapter presidents of the Bayanihan ng Kababaihan.
2. Whether the Sandiganbayan erred in holding that the guilt of the accused for violation of Sections 3(e) and 3(j) of RA 3019 and for malversation of public funds was proved beyond reasonable doubt.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, conspiracy was not proved.** The prosecution's only evidence of conspiracy was the Asuncions' marriage certificate and Flora's certification that she was the Federated President. Inferring a conspiracy in bad faith from the marriage alone "requires a big leap of the imagination." There is no presumption of bad faith in RA 3019 cases; conviction must rest on the strength of the prosecution's evidence. Conspiracy must be shown with the same degree of proof required for the crime, through overt acts showing a conscious common design (*Macairan v. People*; *Suba v. Sandiganbayan*). No nexus showed a unity of action and purpose to give unwarranted benefits to the chapter presidents. With no conspiracy, the mayor's acquittal carried with it the acquittal of the chapter presidents, absent other evidence of their guilt.

**2. Yes, guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt on any charge.**

*Sec. 3(e).* The first two elements (public officer acting in his official functions) were undisputed, but the third was absent. Sec. 2 of RA 7171 lists projects for the self-reliance of tobacco farmers but does not specifically exclude other farmers in the province, and Sec. 14 of RA 11346 later enlarged the use of the fund. The many circulars on the fund's use show how easily local executives err. Without an express exclusion, Asuncion could be excused for believing, albeit mistakenly, that the chapters could borrow from the fund, especially as tobacco farmers lived in their barangays. Under *Ysidoro v. Leonardo-De Castro*, an erroneous interpretation of law, absent a dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith, and bad faith must be evident. There was no manifest partiality, since the prosecution did not claim that other borrowers were unjustly set aside. There was no gross inexcusable negligence, since he relied on the Sanggunian accreditations, Resolution No. 39, s. 2010, and the reenacted Appropriation Ordinance No. 01, s. 2010. The repayment upon disallowance and before the filing of the cases is a badge of good faith.

*Sec. 3(j).* The element of knowledge was not proved. Given the Sanggunian's (and later DOLE's) accreditation, any lack of qualification of the chapters "would not have been apparent to anyone," including the mayor.

*Graft and corruption.* Under *Martel v. People*, a charge under RA 3019 must be grounded on graft and corruption. The loans rested on a mistaken belief in good faith; there was no evidence of a bribe or of personal gain by any accused. The Court should not interpret the law so as to punish "every minute mistake that incidentally caused a benefit to private parties."

*Malversation.* The decisive element, that the accused appropriated, took or misappropriated public funds or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted their taking, was not proved. No contract involving public funds may be entered into without a sufficient appropriation (PD 1445, Sec. 85), but here the disbursements were supported by Appropriation Ordinance No. 01, s. 2010, reenacted in 2011 and 2012 under Sec. 323 of the LGC.

### Disposition
The appeal was GRANTED. The Sandiganbayan (Fourth Division) Decision dated May 17, 2019 in Case Nos. SB-17-CRM-1393 to 1404 and its Resolution dated August 14, 2019 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Carlos R. Asuncion, Mamelfa R. Amongol, Genoveva R. Ragasa, Rosita Ragunjan and Virginia R. Rafanan were ACQUITTED for failure of the prosecution to prove their guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

### En Banc or Division?
Second Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Mayor Ana released PHP 500,000.00 from the municipality's share in the tobacco excise tax under RA 7171 as livelihood loans to a farmers' association accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan, whose members grow rice and vegetables in the tobacco-producing province. She relied on a Sangguniang Bayan resolution authorizing her to sign contracts for the municipality and on the reenacted annual appropriation ordinance. The COA disallowed the release on the ground that only tobacco farmers may benefit, and the association repaid the loans in full before any case was filed. There is no evidence that Mayor Ana received anything from the association or turned away other applicants. She is charged with violation of Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019. Is she liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Mayor Ana is not liable under Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019.
- **Legal basis:** Sec. 3(e) of RA 3019 requires, among others, that the public officer acted through manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. An erroneous interpretation of a provision of law, absent any dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith; bad faith must be evident and partake of fraud. Reliance on Sanggunian accreditations, resolutions and appropriation ordinances negates gross inexcusable negligence, and repayment upon COA disallowance is a badge of good faith. Violations of RA 3019 must be grounded on graft and corruption, not mere mistake (People v. Asuncion, G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98, April 6, 2022, citing Ysidoro v. Leonardo-De Castro and Martel v. People).
- **Application:** RA 7171 does not expressly exclude other farmers in a tobacco-producing province, so Mayor Ana's belief that the association qualified, even if mistaken, was an honest interpretation of the law. She relied on the Sangguniang Bayan's accreditation, its resolution authorizing her to contract, and the reenacted appropriation ordinance, so she did not act without even slight care. Nothing shows that she favored the association over other applicants, and the full repayment before any case was filed, with no evidence of personal gain, shows the absence of corrupt intent.
- **Conclusion:** Mayor Ana should be acquitted because the mode of commission required by Sec. 3(e) is absent.

**Q2.** Suppose instead that a municipal ordinance allowed livelihood loans from the fund only to organizations accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan, that the association had never been accredited, and that before approving the loans Mayor Ana received a written memorandum from the municipal accountant pointing this out. She approved the loans anyway because the association's president was her campaign leader. If she is charged under Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019, would the ruling in People v. Asuncion support her acquittal?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Unlike in Asuncion, the element of knowledge is present, so Mayor Ana may be held liable under Sec. 3(j).
- **Legal basis:** The elements of Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019 are: (1) knowingly approving or granting any license, permit, privilege or benefit; (2) in favor of any person not qualified for or not legally entitled to it, or a mere representative or dummy of one who is not so qualified or entitled. Knowledge of the grantee's lack of qualification is essential because it is the basis for concluding that the accused acted with bias or partiality, and possibly corruption. In People v. Asuncion (G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98, April 6, 2022), the mayor was acquitted because the prosecution did not prove he knew the grantees were unqualified; their accreditation by the Sanggunian made any lack of qualification not apparent to anyone.
- **Application:** Here the association was not qualified under the ordinance because it was never accredited, and Mayor Ana was told so in writing before she acted. Her knowledge is established, and her reason for proceeding (to favor her campaign leader) shows the bias and partiality that the knowledge element is meant to capture. This is favoritism, not an honest mistake of interpretation, so the good-faith reasoning in Asuncion does not apply.
- **Conclusion:** Mayor Ana may be convicted under Sec. 3(j) of RA 3019 because she knowingly granted a benefit to an unqualified grantee.

**Q3.** Mayor Carlo's wife heads a federation whose chapters received municipal loans that he approved. The disbursements were made under the previous year's annual appropriation ordinance, which was deemed reenacted because the Sangguniang Bayan failed to pass a new one within 90 days from the start of the fiscal year. The prosecution charges the mayor and the chapter presidents with malversation of public funds in conspiracy, relying solely on the mayor's marriage certificate and his wife's certification that she heads the federation. (a) Was malversation committed? (b) Was conspiracy established?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. (b) No.
- **Legal basis:** Malversation under Art. 217 of the RPC requires that the accountable public officer appropriated, took or misappropriated public funds, or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted another to take them. No contract involving the expenditure of public funds may be entered into without a sufficient appropriation (PD 1445, Sec. 85). Under Sec. 323 of the Local Government Code, if the sanggunian fails to enact the annual appropriations ordinance within 90 days from the beginning of the fiscal year, the preceding year's ordinance is deemed reenacted. In People v. Asuncion (G.R. Nos. 250366 and 250388-98, April 6, 2022), malversation failed because the loans were supported by an appropriation ordinance reenacted under Sec. 323, and conspiracy failed because the only evidence was the mayor's marriage to the federation's president; conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt by overt acts showing a conscious common design, and there is no presumption of bad faith in RA 3019 cases.
- **Application:** (a) The loans were disbursed under an appropriation ordinance deemed reenacted by operation of Sec. 323 of the LGC. The mayor therefore did not take, misappropriate, or permit the taking of public funds without authority. (b) The marriage certificate and the wife's certification show only a relationship. They show no overt act by which the mayor and the chapter presidents acted together toward a common unlawful purpose, and conspiracy cannot be presumed from kinship.
- **Conclusion:** The mayor and the chapter presidents should be acquitted, because neither misappropriation nor conspiracy was proved.

> Note: The Court did not discuss the last sentence of Sec. 323 of the LGC (quoted in its footnote 67), which limits the reenacted appropriations to salaries and wages of existing positions, statutory and contractual obligations, and essential operating expenses; it simply held that the disbursements were supported by the reenacted ordinance. The decision calls the disbursements both "financial assistance" (as in the Informations and the stipulation) and loans. The heading of the Sec. 3(j) charge appears in places as "Sec. (j)" in the decision.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68377)

## People v. Ricketts

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. RONALD N. RICKETTS, CYRUS PAUL S. VALENZUELA, MANUEL J. MANGUBAT, JOSEPH D. ARNALDO, AND GLENN S. PEREZ, ACCUSED, RONALD N. RICKETTS AND GLENN S. PEREZ, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.**  
G.R. No. 250867 | 2022-03-16 | Second Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910)  
**Specific topics:** Elements of Section 3(e), R.A. 3019; Independently relevant statements vs. hearsay; Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; No presumption of bad faith in R.A. 3019 cases; accused's silence does not shift the burden; Release of seized items held in custodia legis under the OMB Act (R.A. 9239)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 3. Testimonial Evidence > f. Hearsay Rule; Exceptions)

### Doctrine
**Under the doctrine of independently relevant statements, a witness's testimony that a third person told him something is admissible only to prove that the statement was made, not that it is true;** as to the truth of what was said, it remains hearsay. A security guard's report that the accused employee, caught removing seized items, said that the "Chairman" ordered the removal proves the employee's unauthorized act and that he made the statement. It does not prove that the Chairman gave the order (reiterated, citing XXX v. People and Gubaton v. Amador).

**Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt**, through overt acts showing a conscious common design; mere knowledge, acquiescence, or agreement to cooperate is not enough (Macairan v. People, reiterated). There is **no presumption of bad faith** in prosecutions under R.A. No. 3019. The accused's failure to testify does not shift the burden of proof, and a public officer enjoys the presumption of innocence like any other accused.

A public officer who, without written authority, takes out and returns to the owner items seized and held in preventive custody (custodia legis) under Section 10(e) of R.A. No. 9239 acts with manifest partiality and evident bad faith and **gives the owner unwarranted benefits under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019**. It is immaterial that some items remained in custody or that the seizure might later be questioned; whether the items were pirated or admissible is for the OMB and the courts to decide.

### Facts
Ronald Ricketts was Chairman and CEO of the Optical Media Board (OMB); Glenn Perez was an OMB Computer Operator. On May 27, 2010, OMB agents, Perez among them, raided a compound in Quiapo, Manila on a report that pirated optical discs were stored there. They seized 127 boxes and two sacks of DVDs and VCDs, a recording machine, and an Isuzu Elf van marked "Sky High Marketing." The seized items were brought to the OMB compound, turned over to the guard on duty, and recorded in the logbook.

At about 10:00 p.m. that day, guard Pedro Gazzingan found Perez reloading 121 boxes of the seized items onto the van. Asked for the gate pass required by OMB standard procedure, Perez had none and said that it was "Chairman" (Ricketts) who had told him to take the items out. Executive Director Valenzuela, the ranking officer on duty, reportedly told the guard, "kung utos ni Chairman, wala tayong magagawa." The next day only four boxes remained.

Ricketts, Perez, Valenzuela and two other OMB officers were charged with violating Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 for giving Sky High Marketing unwarranted benefits by releasing the seized discs. Valenzuela's demurrer to evidence was granted. Ricketts and Perez did not testify. Because the Sandiganbayan division could not reach a unanimous decision, a special division of five justices was formed. On March 15, 2019, it acquitted the two other officers but convicted Ricketts and Perez, sentencing each to imprisonment of six years and one day to eight years, with perpetual disqualification from public office.

On appeal, Ricketts argued that the guard's account of what Perez said was hearsay and that conspiracy was not proved. He also questioned the procedure of the special division. Perez argued that the government suffered no prejudice because the warrantless seizure made the discs inadmissible anyway, it was not certain that the discs were pirated, their ownership was not established, and some discs remained in OMB custody.

### Issues
1. Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Ricketts conspired with Perez, when the only evidence of his participation was the guard's account of what Perez told him.
2. Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt all the elements of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 against Perez.

### Ruling
**1. No; Ricketts must be acquitted.** The prosecution's theory of conspiracy rested solely on Gazzingan's report that Perez said Chairman Ricketts had ordered the pull-out, together with Ricketts' failure to deny it specifically at trial. Although Ricketts did not testify, he kept the presumption of innocence, and the prosecution kept the burden of proof: "there is no such thing as presumption of bad faith in cases involving violations of RA No. 3019." The report is an independently relevant statement only as to the fact that Perez made the statement. Gazzingan had no personal knowledge of who ordered the pull-out, so as to the truth of the statement the report is hearsay. **It proves Perez's unauthorized act but not that Ricketts ordered it, nor that a conspiracy existed.** Conspiracy requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of overt acts showing a conscious common design (Macairan v. People). The only overt acts proved were Perez's pull-out and the guard's act of allowing it, even though the guard had the power to stop a pull-out made without a gate pass. Ricketts' participation was "purely speculative and hearsay," and convicting him was a grievous error. Since Ricketts was acquitted, the Court found it unnecessary to discuss his procedural objections.

**2. Yes; Perez's conviction stands.** The elements of Section 3(e) are: (1) the accused is a public officer discharging administrative, judicial or official functions; (2) he acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence; and (3) his action caused undue injury to any party, including the government, or gave a private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference. Perez was a public officer and part of the raiding team, so he knew that the discs were in OMB's preventive custody under Section 10(e) of R.A. No. 9239. Such items may be returned only after 30 days unless a case is filed (Section 3, Rule 7 of the IRR) and must be destroyed if found to violate the law (Section 23). Yet he took them out after office hours without written authority and returned them. This was manifest partiality and evident bad faith, and it gave Sky High Marketing unwarranted benefits before the OMB could review the discs and file the proper case. **It is immaterial that he did not take all the discs; what matters is that he interfered with property in custodia legis before legal processes could run**, depriving the government of the right to have the discs destroyed if the owners were found liable. Whether the discs were pirated, whether Sky High violated R.A. No. 9239, and whether the discs would be admissible were matters for the OMB and the courts, not Perez, to decide. His arguments on these points amounted to admitting that he released the discs without authority.

### Disposition
Ricketts' appeal was GRANTED, and the Sandiganbayan Decision dated March 15, 2019 and Resolution dated November 15, 2019 in Case No. SB-15-CRM-0132 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Ricketts was ACQUITTED for failure of the prosecution to prove conspiracy and his guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the hold departure order against him was lifted and his cash bond released, and entry of judgment as to him was ordered issued immediately. Perez's conviction for violation of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019, with imprisonment of six years and one day as minimum to eight years as maximum and perpetual disqualification from holding public office, was AFFIRMED in toto.

### En Banc or Division?
Second Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Director Lim heads a government regulatory office. One night, security guard Tomas caught Officer Reyes loading confiscated goods into a private truck without the required gate pass. When challenged, Reyes told Tomas, "Director Lim ordered me to release these." Tomas let the truck go and wrote a report. Lim and Reyes were charged as conspirators with violating Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019. At trial, Tomas testified on what Reyes told him. No other evidence linked Lim to the release, and Lim did not testify. (a) Is Tomas's testimony on Reyes's statement admissible against Lim? (b) May Lim be convicted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) It is admissible only to prove that Reyes made the statement, not that Lim actually gave the order; on that point it is hearsay. (b) No. Lim must be acquitted because conspiracy was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
- **Legal basis:** Under the doctrine of independently relevant statements, only the fact that a statement was made is relevant; its truth or falsity is immaterial. Such a statement is admissible to prove that it was made, but it is hearsay as to the truth of what it asserts when the witness has no personal knowledge of it. Conspiracy must be proved by the same quantum as the crime, beyond reasonable doubt, through overt acts showing a conscious common design. (People v. Ricketts, G.R. No. 250867, March 16, 2022, citing XXX v. People and Macairan v. People)
- **Application:** Tomas personally saw Reyes loading the goods and personally heard Reyes say that Lim ordered it, so he may testify to those facts. He has no personal knowledge of whether Lim actually gave any order, so on that point his testimony is hearsay. With no other evidence of an overt act by Lim, his participation is speculative. Lim's silence at trial does not supply the missing proof. He keeps the presumption of innocence, and there is no presumption of bad faith under R.A. No. 3019.
- **Conclusion:** Tomas's testimony proves only that Reyes made the statement, and Lim must be acquitted.

**Q2.** Agent Bautista of the Optical Media Board took part in a raid that seized 100 boxes of suspected pirated DVDs, which were placed in OMB preventive custody. That night, without any written authority, he loaded 90 boxes back into the owner's van and let the owner drive away. Charged under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019, Bautista argues that (1) the government suffered no prejudice because ten boxes remained, which were enough to support a case; and (2) the raid was conducted without a search warrant, so the discs would have been inadmissible anyway, and no one has proved that they were pirated. Are his defenses tenable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. His defenses do not negate the elements of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019.
- **Legal basis:** Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 punishes a public officer who, through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence, causes undue injury to any party, including the government, or gives a private party unwarranted benefits. Optical media taken into preventive custody under Section 10(e) of R.A. No. 9239 are in custodia legis and may be returned only as the law and its implementing rules allow. If they are found to violate the law, they are to be destroyed (Section 23). In People v. Ricketts (G.R. No. 250867, March 16, 2022), the Court held that an OMB employee who took out and returned seized discs without written authority acted with manifest partiality and evident bad faith and gave unwarranted benefits. It was immaterial that he did not take all the discs, and whether the discs were pirated or admissible was for the OMB and the courts, not the accused, to decide.
- **Application:** Bautista knew the discs were in OMB custody because he took part in the seizure. Releasing 90 boxes at night without written authority favored the owner and shows a dishonest purpose, which is evident bad faith. The release gave the owner an unwarranted benefit and interfered with the OMB's processes before any case could be filed, depriving the government of the remedy of destruction. That ten boxes remained does not cure the interference. His arguments on the warrantless raid and the nature of the discs are questions for the OMB and the courts; raising them only confirms that he released the discs without authority.
- **Conclusion:** Bautista's defenses fail, and he may be convicted of violating Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019.

**Q3.** Mayor Cruz and his driver were charged as conspirators under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 for the release of impounded logs from the municipal compound. The only evidence linking the mayor was a guard's testimony that the driver, caught hauling the logs, said the mayor had authorized it. The trial court convicted the mayor, reasoning that (1) he chose not to take the witness stand to deny the driver's claim specifically; and (2) public officers are presumed to have acted in bad faith when government-held property is released irregularly. Is the trial court's reasoning correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Both premises are wrong, and the mayor's conviction cannot stand on this evidence.
- **Legal basis:** The constitutional presumption of innocence protects public officers like any other accused. The burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt stays with the prosecution even if the accused does not testify, and a conviction must rest on the strength of the prosecution's evidence, not on the weakness of the defense. There is no presumption of bad faith in prosecutions under R.A. No. 3019. A third person's out-of-court claim relayed by a witness without personal knowledge proves only that the claim was made. (People v. Ricketts, G.R. No. 250867, March 16, 2022, citing Suba v. Sandiganbayan and Martel v. People)
- **Application:** The mayor's decision not to testify cannot fill the gap in the prosecution's evidence. Unless the prosecution first proves his participation beyond reasonable doubt, he need not present evidence at all. The court also could not presume bad faith from the irregular release, because manifest partiality or evident bad faith is an element that must be proved. The guard's testimony shows only that the driver named the mayor, not that the mayor authorized anything, so no overt act of the mayor and no conspiracy was established.
- **Conclusion:** The trial court erred, and the mayor should be acquitted because his conviction rests on his silence and on a presumption of bad faith that the law does not recognize.

> Note: The Court did not resolve Ricketts' procedural objection that the Sandiganbayan special division of five was not dissolved as its internal rules required; it found the issue unnecessary after acquitting him on the merits. It also did not rule on whether the warrantless OMB raid was valid. It held only that this and the other questions about the discs were not for Perez to decide.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68327)

## DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman (Gomez)

**DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE-REVENUE INTEGRITY PROTECTION SERVICE (DOF-RIPS), REPRESENTED BY JOEL M. APOLONIO AND AGAPITO C. GUARIN, PETITIONER, VS. OFFICE OF THE OMBUDSMAN AND RAMIR SAUNDERS GOMEZ, SPECIAL AGENT I, BUREAU OF CUSTOMS, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 236956 | 2021-11-24 | Third Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Criminal Law  
**Syllabus topic:** II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > D. Extinction of Criminal Liability > 1. Total Extinction > e. Prescription > ii. Prescription under Special Laws (Act 3326)  
**Specific topics:** Section 8 of RA 6713 expressly amended Section 7 of RA 3019 on non-filing of SALN (Sec. 16, RA 6713); Non-filing of SALN prescribes in eight years under Act No. 3326; Perjury in a SALN prescribes in ten years, reckoned from filing of the SALN; Judicial non-interference with the Ombudsman's prosecutorial findings absent grave abuse of discretion
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 4. The Ombudsman and the Special Prosecutor (RA 6770) > d. Judicial Review)

### Doctrine
**Section 8 of RA 6713 amended Section 7 of RA 3019 on the non-filing of the SALN, through the express repealing clause in Section 16 of RA 6713.** Section 16 repeals or modifies inconsistent laws "unless the same provide for a heavier penalty." RA 6713 imposes the heavier penalty: imprisonment not exceeding five years, a fine not exceeding P5,000, or both, plus disqualification from public office. RA 3019 imposes only a fine of P100 to P1,000, imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. Because the repeal is express, the rule against implied repeals does not apply. **A public officer cannot be indicted for the same non-filing under both laws; he may be prosecuted only under RA 6713.**

RA 6713 sets no prescriptive period, so Act No. 3326 governs. **A violation of Section 8 of RA 6713 prescribes in eight years** (Act No. 3326, Sec. 1(c): imprisonment of two years or more but less than six years). The 15-year period for RA 3019 offenses under BP 195 does not apply. This reiterates Del Rosario v. People, DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman (Casayuran), and DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman (Germar).

**Perjury (Art. 183, RPC) committed through false statements in a SALN prescribes in ten years (Art. 90), reckoned from the filing of the SALN**, not from the complainant's later discovery of the falsity (reiterating Germar). Perjury is consummated upon filing, and the SALN is then open to review. This harmonizes Article 91 of the RPC with Section 8(C)(4) of RA 6713, which keeps SALNs available to the public for ten years. The Court applied the same reckoning to the falsification charges based on the same SALN entries. The Court also reiterated that it does not interfere with the Ombudsman's investigatory and prosecutorial findings unless grave abuse of discretion is shown; mere disagreement is not enough.

### Facts
On August 28, 2015, the DOF-Revenue Integrity Protection Service (DOF-RIPS) filed a complaint with the Office of the Ombudsman against Ramir Saunders Gomez, Special Agent I of the Bureau of Customs. The complaint charged violations of RA 3019, RA 6713, and Articles 171(4) and 183 of the RPC. It alleged that Gomez failed to file his 2003 SALN. It also alleged that he did not disclose six lots in Old Cabalan, Olongapo City in his SALNs for 1996 to 2009 (titles issued in his name in 1996 and 1998), a townhouse in Quezon City in his SALNs for 2004 to 2008, a Toyota Revo in his 2005 SALN, and a 9mm pistol in his SALNs for 2010 to 2013. Finally, it alleged that he filed inconsistent 2006 SALNs with false declarations. Gomez denied the charges, blamed his bookkeeper, and gave explanations for each item.

In a Resolution dated June 23, 2017, the Ombudsman found probable cause for three counts of perjury and three counts of falsification covering his 2007, 2008, and 2009 SALNs. It held that the non-filing of the 2003 SALN was punishable only under RA 6713, because RA 6713 has the heavier penalty and modified RA 3019, and that it had prescribed in eight years. Applying People v. Terrado, it held that the false statements in the 1996, 2004, 2005, and 2006 SALNs were punishable as perjury, which prescribes in ten years, and had prescribed. The Ombudsman reckoned prescription from the dates Gomez omitted the lots from his SALNs, because the titles were registered in his name and registration is notice to the whole world. In its Order dated October 20, 2017 denying both parties' motions for reconsideration, it added, by analogy to PCGG v. Carpio Morales, that prescription runs from the commission of the offense when the data needed to discover it is readily available to the public.

DOF-RIPS filed a Rule 65 petition. It sought additional charges for four counts of perjury, four counts of falsification, and one count of violating RA 3019. It argued that Section 7 of RA 3019 and Section 8 of RA 6713 are separate offenses, that RA 3019 offenses prescribe in 15 years under BP 195, that falsification prescribes in 15 years, and that prescription should run from its discovery of the falsity in 2014 and 2015, when it received the agencies' records. The Ombudsman manifested that it would not participate so as not to advocate for Gomez.

### Issues
1. Whether Gomez may be prosecuted for the non-filing of his 2003 SALN under both Section 7 of RA 3019 and Section 8 of RA 6713.
2. Whether the offense of non-filing of the 2003 SALN had prescribed.
3. Whether the Ombudsman gravely abused its discretion in ruling that the offenses arising from the false statements in the 1996, 2004, 2005, and 2006 SALNs had prescribed.
4. Whether prescription of those offenses runs from the filing of the SALNs or from DOF-RIPS's discovery of the falsity.

### Ruling
**1. No.** RA 3019 punishes non-filing of the SALN with a fine of P100 to P1,000, imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. RA 6713 punishes it with imprisonment not exceeding five years, a fine not exceeding P5,000, or both, plus disqualification. Section 16 of RA 6713 expressly repeals or modifies inconsistent laws unless they provide a heavier penalty. Since RA 6713's penalty is heavier, **Section 7 of RA 3019 was amended by Section 8 of RA 6713.** "[N]othing is implied in the repeal," so the rules on implied repeal do not apply. Gomez may not be indicted under both provisions, and the Ombudsman did not gravely abuse its discretion in limiting the charge to RA 6713.

**2. Yes.** Since Gomez can be prosecuted only under RA 6713, the 15-year period under RA 3019 as amended by BP 195 is beside the point. RA 6713 has no prescriptive period of its own, so Act No. 3326 applies. Under Section 1(c), **a violation of Section 8 of RA 6713 prescribes in eight years**, as held in Del Rosario v. People and applied in the Casayuran and Germar cases. The parties disagreed on whether 13 or 11 years had elapsed, but either way the eight-year period had lapsed.

**3. No grave abuse of discretion.** The Constitution and RA 6770 give the Ombudsman wide latitude to determine probable cause, and the Court generally does not interfere. Grave abuse means a capricious or whimsical exercise of judgment amounting to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of positive duty. "Disagreement with its findings is not enough." DOF-RIPS showed no specific act or omission of that kind.

**4. From the filing of the SALN.** Following DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman (Germar), perjury carries a correctional penalty and prescribes in ten years under Article 90. Prescription under Article 91 runs from discovery, but for a SALN, discovery is reckoned from filing. Perjury is consummated upon filing, and the SALN is then subject to review, and "[t]en (10) years is more than enough time to discover any such errors or inaccuracies." This harmonizes the RPC with Section 8(C)(4) of RA 6713, which makes SALNs available to the public for ten years and allows their destruction afterwards unless needed in an ongoing investigation. **Applying this, the discovery of the falsification and perjury is reckoned from the filing of each SALN**, so the false statements in SALNs filed more than ten years before the complaint were barred by prescription.

### Disposition
The petition was DENIED. The Ombudsman's Resolution dated June 23, 2017 and Order dated October 20, 2017 in OMB-C-C-15-0379 were AFFIRMED.

### En Banc or Division?
Third Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Rodel, a revenue officer, failed to file the SALN due from him in 2011. In 2021, a complaint was filed charging him with violating both Section 7 of RA 3019 and Section 8 of RA 6713 for this omission. The complainant argues that the two are distinct offenses and that RA 3019 offenses prescribe in 15 years. (a) May Rodel be charged under both laws? (b) Has the offense prescribed?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Rodel may be charged only under Section 8 of RA 6713. (b) Yes. The offense prescribed in eight years.
- **Legal basis:** Section 16 of RA 6713 expressly repeals or modifies inconsistent laws unless they provide a heavier penalty. Since RA 6713 punishes non-filing of the SALN more heavily than RA 3019, Section 7 of RA 3019 was amended by Section 8 of RA 6713, and an officer cannot be indicted under both. RA 6713 has no prescriptive period, so Act No. 3326 applies. Under Section 1(c), offenses punished by imprisonment of two years or more but less than six years prescribe in eight years. (DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. No. 236956, November 24, 2021, citing Del Rosario v. People)
- **Application:** RA 6713 provides imprisonment of up to five years, a fine of up to P5,000, and disqualification, which is heavier than RA 3019's penalty of up to one year and P1,000. RA 6713 therefore governs, and the express repeal leaves no room for the argument that repeals by implication are disfavored. Since Rodel can be prosecuted only under RA 6713, the 15-year period for RA 3019 offenses is irrelevant. About ten years passed between the 2011 omission and the 2021 complaint, beyond the eight-year period.
- **Conclusion:** Rodel can be charged only under RA 6713, and that charge has prescribed.

**Q2.** In April 2008, Lina, a customs examiner, filed a SALN that did not declare two lots titled in her name since 2005. In 2020, after a lifestyle check, the complainant obtained certified copies of the titles from the Land Registration Authority and filed a complaint for perjury. It argued that prescription should run only from its discovery of the titles in 2020. Has the crime of perjury prescribed?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. The perjury prescribed ten years after the SALN was filed.
- **Legal basis:** Perjury under Article 183 of the RPC carries a correctional penalty and prescribes in ten years (Art. 90). For false statements in a SALN, the period is reckoned from the filing of the SALN. Perjury is consummated upon filing, the SALN is then subject to review, and Section 8(C)(4) of RA 6713 keeps SALNs available to the public for only ten years. (DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. No. 236956, November 24, 2021, applying DOF-RIPS v. Ombudsman and Germar, G.R. No. 238660, February 3, 2021)
- **Application:** Lina's false SALN was filed in April 2008, so the ten-year period began then and ended in April 2018. The complainant's argument that discovery happened only in 2020 fails because discovery is reckoned from the filing of the SALN, not from when the complainant later gathered records. The complaint filed in 2020 came after the period had run.
- **Conclusion:** The perjury charge against Lina is barred by prescription.

**Q3.** The Ombudsman dismissed some counts of a complaint filed by a government agency against a public employee on the ground of prescription, explaining its computation in detail. The agency filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the Supreme Court, arguing only that the Ombudsman's computation was wrong and that the Court should substitute its own reading of the evidence. Will the petition prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Mere disagreement with the Ombudsman's findings is not grave abuse of discretion.
- **Legal basis:** The Constitution and RA 6770 give the Ombudsman wide latitude in its investigatory and prosecutorial powers, and the Court generally does not interfere with its determination of probable cause. Its acts are reviewable on certiorari only for grave abuse of discretion, meaning a capricious or whimsical exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of positive duty. Disagreement with its findings is not enough. (DOF-RIPS v. Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. No. 236956, November 24, 2021)
- **Application:** The agency points to no arbitrary, despotic, or whimsical act by the Ombudsman. It only says the Ombudsman reached a different conclusion on prescription. The Ombudsman's ruling was reasoned and followed the governing law and jurisprudence, so there is no basis for the extraordinary writ.
- **Conclusion:** The petition for certiorari should be dismissed for failure to show grave abuse of discretion.

> Note: The decision gives two filing dates for the DOF-RIPS complaint: August 28, 2015 in the facts and September 1, 2015 in the last part of the ruling. The Court did not squarely resolve DOF-RIPS's argument that falsification of public documents prescribes in 15 years. It held that the Ombudsman, which had treated the false SALN statements as perjury under People v. Terrado, committed no grave abuse of discretion, and it reckoned both the falsification and the perjury from the filing of the SALNs. The Ombudsman's charges for the 2007-2009 SALNs were not at issue. The index title contains a garbled character in "DOF-RIPS"; it is corrected in full_title.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68053)

# Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics

## Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo

**ANONYMOUS, COMPLAINANT, VS. JUDGE ELMER R. BERNARDO, MUNICIPAL TRIAL COURT IN CITIES, BATAC CITY, ILOCOS NORTE, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. MTJ-26-056 (Formerly JIB FPI No. 23-118-MTJ) | 2026-02-04 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 1. Standards of Ethical Conduct of Judges and Justices > e. Propriety (Canon IV)  
**Specific topics:** Propriety in a judge's private life (CJCA, Canon IV, Secs. 1-2); Prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service (CJCA, Canon VII, Sec. 18(k)); Retroactive application of the 2025 CJCA to pending cases; Substantial evidence; implausible defense and lack of remorse; Judge's liability as a lawyer (CPRA, Canon II, Sec. 2)

### Doctrine
Judges must be beyond reproach in both their public and private lives. Under **Canon IV (Propriety), Sections 1 and 2 of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA)**, a judge must freely and willingly accept personal restrictions that an ordinary citizen may find burdensome and must act consistently with the dignity of the judicial office. A judge must also refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to, or tend to tarnish, the judicial office. **A judge may be penalized even for conduct unrelated to official duties when it gravely tarnishes the public image of the Judiciary.**

**A judge who, at around 2:30 a.m., threw a piece of wood and a stone that damaged his neighbors' parked vehicles, then defended himself with an implausible story (that he was aiming at a rat), is guilty of "prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service," a serious offense under Canon VII, Section 18(k) of the CJCA.** This offense reformulates "conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service": acts that tarnish the image and integrity of public office without a direct relation to official duties. Even on the judge's own version, recklessly hurling objects where property could be damaged falls below the standard required of judges. An incredible defense, and "background facts" blaming the victims, show lack of remorse and worsen the judge's position.

The CJCA applies to cases pending when it took effect (transitory clause). The quantum of proof is substantial evidence; technical rules do not strictly apply, but the respondent must have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Under Canon VII, Section 22, a serious offense is punishable by dismissal, suspension, and/or a fine. Where there is a mitigating circumstance such as first offense (Sec. 24) and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum (Sec. 25). The Court imposed a fine of PHP 50,001.00. Because a judge is also a lawyer, the Court may separately remind him under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA (dignified conduct).

### Facts
On August 18, 2023, the Judiciary Public Assistance Section received an anonymous email complaint against Judge Elmer R. Bernardo, Presiding Judge of the MTCC of Batac City, Ilocos Norte. It alleged that while drunk he had hit a tricycle and injured its driver, had damaged about seven vehicles (throwing stones, smashing windshields, and pushing a jeep into a canal), had never paid compensation, and had made a police officer manipulate a blotter entry.

The OCA investigated in October 2023. The anonymous complainant did not answer the OCA's request for a meeting. The OCA obtained a police blotter entry of July 29, 2023: neighbors Allan Paul Paraoan and Richelle Joy Wronski reported that at about 2:30 a.m., Judge Bernardo, allegedly under the influence of liquor, threw a piece of wood and a stone at their parked Ford and Isuzu Crosswind, denting them and detaching their rain visors. They said he admitted the act while being recorded on a cellphone. Paraoan confirmed to the OCA that the blotter was accurate but would not execute an affidavit because he had already settled with the judge. The Batac PNP reported no record of the tricycle incident. The JIB's Office of the General Counsel filed a formal complaint on April 12, 2024 for prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service.

Judge Bernardo denied being drunk. He admitted throwing the wood and the stone but said he threw them from his veranda at a rodent "the size of a cat" and hit the vehicles by accident. He said he apologized, paid for the repairs, and that the owners later tried to pad the blotter with unrelated damage. He also added "background facts": his neighbors habitually parked on the narrow street and resented his requests to move their vehicles.

The JIB's Office of the Executive Director found his story hard to believe. In its May 21, 2025 Report, it recommended that he be found guilty, fined PHP 50,001.00, sternly reminded as a member of the Bar under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA, and sternly warned. The JIB adopted the report on June 27, 2025. The 2025 CJCA took effect while the case was pending.

### Issues
1. Whether the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability governs this case, which was pending when the Code took effect.
2. Whether Judge Bernardo is guilty of prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service for damaging his neighbors' vehicles.
3. What penalty should be imposed, and whether he should also answer as a member of the Bar.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the CJCA applies.** Its transitory clause makes it applicable to "all pending and future cases," except where retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice.

**2. Yes, he is guilty.** Under Canon IV, Sections 1 and 2, a judge must embrace personal restrictions, act consistently with the dignity of the office, and refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to the judicial office. Citing Obiedo v. Santos, the Court stressed that a judge, "[l]ike Caesar's wife," must be above suspicion, and that when a judge becomes a transgressor of the law he places his office in disrepute. **"The law penalizes judges even for conduct which does not relate to the performance of their duties, where their acts gravely tarnish the public image of the Judiciary."**

The quantum of proof is substantial evidence. The anonymous complaint and the police blotter alone did not prove that the judge acted deliberately or was intoxicated. But Paraoan's confirmation, together with the judge's own statements, painted "a vivid picture" of what happened. His story was implausible: he was on his veranda before dawn, a piece of wood and a stone were conveniently there, and he threw twice at a rodent near the very vehicles he had found illegally parked, causing a commotion that woke the neighbors. **Concocting "such a fantastic defense" worsened his position.** His unnecessary "background facts" about his neighbors' parking showed resentment and "utter lack of remorse." It was therefore reasonable to conclude that the incident "was not completely without malice." **Even assuming his version were true, his recklessness in throwing objects where property could be, and was, damaged still fell below the standard required of judges.** It created an appearance of impropriety and diminished public confidence in the Judiciary. The Court warned that when judges escape punishment through legal maneuvering, "it is the judicial institution itself that suffers."

Under Canon VII, Section 18(k), "conduct unbecoming of a judge or prejudicial, vulgar or scandalous conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service" is a serious offense. Its meaning is settled: the Rule 140 annotation (Rule 140 having been superseded by the CJCA) explains that the offense reformulates "conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service," which covers acts that tarnish the image of public office without direct relation to official duties, so that it would not remain a blanket offense.

**3. Fine of PHP 50,001.00; stern reminder as a lawyer.** Under Canon VII, Section 22, serious offenses are punishable by dismissal; suspension of one year and one day to three years; and/or a fine of more than PHP 101,000.00 up to PHP 500,000.00. First offense is a mitigating circumstance (Sec. 24). With a mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum (Sec. 25). This being his first offense, the Court adopted the JIB's recommended fine of PHP 50,001.00. As to his liability as a lawyer under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA (dignified conduct; no scandalous behavior in public or private life), a stern reminder sufficed: only one incident was established, he was already penalized as a judge, and he had expressed remorse and offered reparation.

### Disposition
Judge Elmer R. Bernardo was found GUILTY of prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service and FINED PHP 50,001.00, payable within three months from notice. He was STERNLY REMINDED, as a member of the Bar, to maintain dignified conduct and strictly observe Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA, and STERNLY WARNED that a repeat of the same or similar offense will be dealt with more severely.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Judge Ramos, an MTC judge, came home past midnight and found his neighbor's car parked across his gate, as it often was. In full view of other neighbors, he kicked and dented the car's door and shouted that the owner had no respect for a judge. The next day he paid for the repairs. In the administrative case that followed, Judge Ramos argued that the incident was a purely private quarrel unrelated to his judicial functions, so the Court has no basis to discipline him. Is he correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Judge Ramos may be disciplined for prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service, even though the act was unrelated to his official duties.
- **Legal basis:** Under Canon IV, Sections 1 and 2 of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability, a judge must accept personal restrictions an ordinary citizen may find burdensome, must act consistently with the dignity of the judicial office, and must refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to, or tend to tarnish, the judicial office. "Prejudicial, vulgar or scandalous conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service" is a serious offense under Canon VII, Section 18(k). It covers acts that tarnish the image of the Judiciary without direct relation to official duties. Judges may be penalized even for conduct unrelated to their duties when it gravely tarnishes the Judiciary's public image. (Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo, A.M. No. MTJ-26-056, February 4, 2026)
- **Application:** Kicking and denting a neighbor's car in front of other residents, out of resentment over parking, shows the lack of restraint that Canon IV forbids. That the quarrel was private does not matter: the offense covers acts with no direct relation to official functions, and a judge's private behavior must also be beyond reproach. Paying for the repairs may show remorse, but it does not erase the public spectacle that diminished respect for the judicial office.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Ramos is administratively liable despite the private nature of the incident.

**Q2.** Judge Velasco threw two stones from his balcony at night. The stones struck and dented two vehicles parked on the street. He claims he was trying to scare off a stray dog and never meant to hit the vehicles. He apologized and paid for the repairs that same week. Assume the investigating body believes his account that the damage was accidental. (a) Is Judge Velasco still administratively liable? (b) If this is his first offense and there is no aggravating circumstance, may the Court impose a penalty below the minimum fine prescribed for the offense?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Even if the damage was accidental, his reckless conduct falls below the standard required of judges. (b) Yes. With a mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum prescribed.
- **Legal basis:** In Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo (A.M. No. MTJ-26-056, February 4, 2026), the Court held that even assuming the judge's version (that he threw objects at a rodent and hit the vehicles by accident), "his recklessness in throwing items in an area where private property could be, and was in fact, damaged still constitutes conduct falling below the standard of behavior expected of members of the Judiciary," in violation of Canon IV of the 2025 CJCA. On penalty, Canon VII, Section 24 of the CJCA treats first offense as mitigating. Section 25 allows the Court, where there is one or more mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, to impose suspension or a fine not less than half the minimum prescribed. Applying these, the Court imposed a fine of PHP 50,001.00 on a first-time offender.
- **Application:** Judge Velasco threw stones toward a street where vehicles were parked. No prudent judge would hurl objects that could damage property nearby, so the lack of intent does not excuse him. The incident created an appearance of impropriety and exposed the judicial office to ridicule. His prompt apology and payment, and the fact that this is his first offense, bear on the penalty, not on liability. Since there is a mitigating circumstance (first offense) and no aggravating one, the Court may go below the minimum fine, down to half of it.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Velasco is liable, but as a first offender he may be fined an amount not less than half the minimum prescribed.

**Q3.** An anonymous email to the Supreme Court accused Judge Cruz of several drunken incidents: hitting a pedestrian, smashing car windshields, and pressuring police to alter blotter entries. The OCA's investigation found a police record of only one incident, in which Judge Cruz damaged a neighbor's car. The neighbor confirmed the blotter entry but refused to execute an affidavit because he had been paid. In his comment, Judge Cruz admitted causing the damage but gave an unbelievable explanation. (a) What quantum of proof is required, and may Judge Cruz be held liable on this record? (b) Being a lawyer, may he also be held to account under the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Substantial evidence is required. Judge Cruz may be held liable for the incident proved by the confirmed blotter entry and his own admissions, but not for the unproven allegations. (b) Yes. As a member of the Bar, he is bound by Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA, and the Court may also sanction or remind him under it.
- **Legal basis:** In administrative cases against judges, the quantum of proof is substantial evidence: relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion. Technical rules of procedure and evidence do not strictly apply, but the respondent must have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. In Anonymous v. Judge Bernardo (A.M. No. MTJ-26-056, February 4, 2026), the Court held that an anonymous complaint and a police blotter entry alone did not establish that the judge acted deliberately or was intoxicated. The owner's confirmation of the blotter, together with the judge's own statements, sufficed to hold him liable. Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA requires a lawyer to act with dignity and not to behave in a scandalous manner, in public or private life, to the discredit of the legal profession. In Bernardo, the Court sternly reminded the judge under this provision, finding that a stern reminder sufficed because only one incident was established, he was already penalized as a judge, and he had shown remorse and offered reparation.
- **Application:** The anonymous email, standing alone, does not prove the pedestrian incident or the blotter tampering; those charges fail for lack of substantial evidence. The car-damage incident, however, rests on the blotter entry confirmed by the owner and on Judge Cruz's own admission that he caused the damage. His unbelievable explanation does not help him and may show lack of remorse. That evidence is adequate for a reasonable mind, so he may be held liable for that incident. As a lawyer, his scandalous private conduct also falls under Canon II, Section 2 of the CPRA. The Court may impose a separate sanction or a reminder, depending on the circumstances.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Cruz may be held liable on substantial evidence for the proven incident only, and he may also be called to account as a member of the Bar under the CPRA.

> Note: Leonen, SAJ., dissented and would have dismissed the judge; the dissent is not examinable. Villanueva, J., took no part; the decision gives no reason, though footnote 7 shows he signed the November 15, 2023 OCA report as Court Administrator. The decision dates the Batac PNP letter to the JIB "February 23, 2023," which comes before the August 18, 2023 complaint; it is probably a typographical error in the source, so the date is left out. On the penalty, the decision quotes the CJCA fine for serious offenses as "more than PHP 101,000.00 but not exceeding PHP 500,000.00" and the half-of-the-minimum rule (Canon VII, Sec. 25). It then adopts the PHP 50,001.00 fine that the JIB had recommended in May 2025, before the CJCA took effect. Remember the amount as imposed and do not try to derive it. The anonymous complaint's other allegations (the tricycle driver, the seven vehicles, the blotter manipulation) were not established.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70386)
