## OCA v. Judge Dumayas

**OFFICE OF THE COURT ADMINISTRATOR, COMPLAINANT, VS. WINLOVE M. DUMAYAS, FORMER PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 59, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, MAKATI CITY, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570 | 2026-01-28 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Gross ignorance of the law vs. mere error of judgment; Retroactive application of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability to pending cases; Jurisdiction over a judge separated from service while the case is pending (Section 23, CJCA); Flip-flopping rulings; correction of an error on motion for reconsideration; Judgment on compromise; criminal liability cannot be compromised (Civil Code, Art. 2034)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (VIII. Obligations and Contracts > B. Contracts > 5. Interpretation of Contracts)

### Doctrine
**A judge is not administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law for an erroneous order issued in a judicial capacity, absent proof of bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or similar motive.** Gross ignorance of the law is the disregard of basic rules and settled jurisprudence. Where the law is straightforward and the facts evident, failing to know it or acting as if one does not know it is gross ignorance, without need to prove malice. Otherwise, the order must not only be erroneous; it must be shown that the judge was moved by bad faith, dishonesty, hatred, or some like motive (reiterating Cayabyab v. Judge Pangilinan, Jr.). Misreading a contractual provision that is not explicit, or issuing a wrong order that the judge later corrects on a motion for reconsideration, is an error of judgment, not gross ignorance. Reversing oneself, by itself, is not an infraction, and ill motive cannot be presumed.

**The 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA, A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC, effective December 21, 2025) applies to all pending and future cases** under its transitory clause (General Provisions, Section 1), unless the Court finds that retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. **Under Section 23 of the CJCA, a judge's separation from the service after the administrative case was instituted does not deprive the Court of jurisdiction.** If the judge is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal, the Court may impose, in lieu of dismissal, forfeiture of all or part of the benefits (never accrued leave credits) and disqualification from public office, and/or a fine.

Settled rules restated in the analysis: once a compromise agreement is approved by a final order, it becomes a judgment that the court has the ministerial duty to enforce and cannot modify; and under Article 2034 of the Civil Code, criminal liability cannot be the subject of a compromise.

### Facts
In a Decision dated September 13, 2017 in Team Image Entertainment, Inc. v. Solar Team Entertainment, Inc. (G.R. Nos. 191652 and 191658), the Court referred to the OCA, as a regular administrative matter, the May 19, 2008 Omnibus Order issued by Judge Winlove M. Dumayas of RTC Makati, Branch 59, in Civil Case No. 00-1122. It directed him to explain (1) why he ordered a PHP 2 million deposit with the Office of the Clerk of Court (OCC) and (2) why he reversed himself several times on whether Team Image could suspend payments and whether criminal cases could be dismissed under the parties' compromise agreement.

Solar Team and Team Image executed a Compromise Agreement on April 28, 2003, which Judge Dumayas approved on April 30, 2003. Item No. 24 provided that if a party breached the agreement, the aggrieved party was entitled to an immediate writ of execution and "the guilty party shall pay the innocent party" PHP 2 million as liquidated damages. It also said the innocent party could invoke the principle of reciprocity of obligations. Judge Dumayas then issued a string of conflicting orders. He allowed Team Image to suspend payments (April 29, 2004) and later set this aside (November 23, 2004). He granted a writ to enforce PHP 2 million in liquidated damages against Solar Team and again allowed suspension (November 3, 2005). On January 21, 2008, he allowed suspension, ordered Solar Team's William Tieng to cause the dismissal of criminal cases against Team Image's president, and imposed other liabilities.

In the May 19, 2008 Omnibus Order, Judge Dumayas set aside all his earlier orders allowing suspension of payments and declared Team Image in default. He also set aside the January 21, 2008 order, including the directive to dismiss the criminal cases. Without deciding whether Solar Team had actually breached the agreement, he granted Solar Team's motion to deposit the PHP 2 million with the OCC, to be released only after the parties' obligations and Solar Team's alleged breach were finally resolved. The CA reversed the deposit order, and the Supreme Court in 2017 also set it aside, applying legal compensation between the parties' equal PHP 2 million liabilities.

In his Comment, Judge Dumayas said he acted in the proper exercise of his judicial functions and his appreciation of the evidence, with no bad faith or corrupt motive. Meanwhile, in a separate case (A.M. No. RTJ-15-2435, Decision of March 6, 2018), he had been dismissed from the service for gross ignorance of the law or procedure and gross misconduct. The JIB (Report of November 15, 2023) recommended a finding of gross ignorance of the law for the deposit order and a PHP 200,000 fine. It recommended no liability for the flip-flopping, because his final rulings on those two points were upheld.

### Issues
1. Whether the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability applies to this case, which was pending when the Code took effect.
2. Whether respondent's dismissal from the service in another case deprived the Court of jurisdiction over this administrative case.
3. Whether respondent is guilty of gross ignorance of the law for issuing the May 19, 2008 Omnibus Order allowing Solar Team to deposit the PHP 2 million liquidated damages with the OCC instead of paying it to Team Image.
4. Whether respondent is administratively liable for repeatedly reversing himself on whether Team Image could suspend payments and whether the criminal cases could be dismissed under the compromise agreement.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the 2025 CJCA applies.** The CJCA, approved on November 11, 2025 and effective December 21, 2025, applies to all pending and future cases under its transitory clause, except where retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. The Court found no compelling reason why applying it to respondent would be unfeasible or unjust.

**2. No, the Court retained jurisdiction.** Under Section 23 of the CJCA, if a respondent is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal that can no longer be imposed because of a prior separation from the service (except death), the Court may impose forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) and disqualification, and/or a fine. This case was instituted on September 13, 2017, when the Court promulgated its Decision in G.R. Nos. 191652 and 191658. Respondent was dismissed in A.M. No. RTJ-15-2435 only on March 6, 2018. **His supervening separation during the pendency of the case does not prevent the Court from imposing sanctions if he is found liable.**

**3. No gross ignorance for the deposit order.** The Court restated the rule that a compromise agreement approved by final order becomes an enforceable judgment that the court cannot modify. It also noted that Item No. 24 required the guilty party to *pay* the innocent party and did not mention deposit in court. Still, there was "no indication or proof" that the order was attended by bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, or corruption. Nor was the Court convinced that respondent was unaware of the compromise terms or of the rule. He had earlier, on November 3, 2005, issued a writ to enforce direct payment of the PHP 2 million. In the May 19, 2008 Order he expressly tied the deposit to the unresolved question of whether Solar Team had breached the agreement. His "need to justify" the deposit "belies any suspicion of ignorance of the basic principles of law and the terms of the Compromise Agreement." **In the absence of fraud, dishonesty, or corruption, the order, done in his judicial capacity, is not subject to disciplinary action.**

**4. No liability for the reversals.** (a) *Suspension of payments.* Whether suspension was allowed required interpreting Item No. 24. Its first sentence speaks of a writ of execution, but its second gives the innocent party the right to invoke reciprocity of obligations. The CA read the agreement as allowing suspension. Under Article 1370 of the Civil Code, clear terms control, but Item No. 24 "is not explicit" on suspension, so the provision is not "so elementary" that misreading it makes a judge liable. An erroneous interpretation is an error of judgment. Reversing himself several times "does not warrant a finding that respondent committed an infraction," and the Court cannot speculate on ill motive without evidence. (b) *Dismissal of criminal cases.* Criminal liability cannot be compromised (Art. 2034, Civil Code), so the January 21, 2008 directive to cause the dismissal of the criminal cases was wrong. But **a motion for reconsideration exists precisely to let the court correct its errors, and respondent "rightly" reversed the order on Solar Team's motion. The earlier order was therefore a mere error of judgment, not gross ignorance.**

The Court added that respondent should have been more circumspect to avoid "flipflopping rulings," and that judges should avoid even the appearance of indecisiveness. Because he had already been dismissed from the service, however, a reminder or warning "no longer has practical value."

### Disposition
The administrative case against former Presiding Judge Winlove M. Dumayas, Branch 59, RTC, Makati City, was DISMISSED. The Court did not adopt the JIB's recommendation of a PHP 200,000 fine for gross ignorance of the law.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In a collection suit, Judge Reyes approved a compromise agreement providing that a party who breaches it "shall pay the innocent party" PHP 1 million as liquidated damages, enforceable by writ of execution. Years later, Debtor Corp. moved for execution, claiming Creditor Inc. had breached the agreement. Judge Reyes had earlier issued a writ for the direct payment of the PHP 1 million. In a later order, however, he allowed Creditor Inc. to deposit the PHP 1 million with the Office of the Clerk of Court instead, explaining that it would be released only after the question of Creditor Inc.'s breach was finally resolved. The Court of Appeals set aside the deposit order as contrary to the compromise judgment. Debtor Corp. then charged Judge Reyes with gross ignorance of the law. Nothing in the record shows bad faith, fraud, or corruption. Should Judge Reyes be held liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Judge Reyes is not liable for gross ignorance of the law. The deposit order, though erroneous, was an error of judgment made in his judicial capacity.
- **Legal basis:** Gross ignorance of the law is the disregard of basic rules and settled jurisprudence. Unless the law violated is so elementary that disregarding it shows ignorance in itself, a judge is liable only if the erroneous order was moved by bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or a similar motive. In the absence of these, acts of a judge in his judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action even if erroneous. In OCA v. Judge Dumayas (A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570, January 28, 2026), the Court applied this rule to a judge who allowed a deposit of liquidated damages with the clerk of court instead of payment to the innocent party under a compromise judgment.
- **Application:** A compromise judgment must be enforced as written, so the deposit order was wrong, as the CA held. But nothing shows bad faith, fraud, or corruption. Judge Reyes was plainly aware of the compromise terms and of the rule on compromise judgments: he had earlier ordered direct payment. He also explained why he required a deposit instead, pending resolution of Creditor Inc.'s alleged breach. As in Dumayas, the need to justify the departure belies ignorance of basic law. Debtor Corp.'s remedy against the error was judicial, and it already obtained relief from the CA.
- **Conclusion:** The administrative complaint for gross ignorance of the law should be dismissed.

**Q2.** A compromise agreement approved by Judge Lim in a civil case required each party to "cause the dismissal of all civil and criminal cases" filed against the other. On Mario's motion, Judge Lim ordered Nestor to cause the dismissal of an estafa case pending against Mario in another court. Nestor moved for reconsideration, and Judge Lim set aside that order, ruling that criminal liability cannot be compromised. Earlier, on the separate question of whether the compromise allowed a party to suspend payments, Judge Lim had also reversed himself twice. The provision on remedies was not explicit on this point. Mario charged Judge Lim with gross ignorance of the law and with "flip-flopping." Will the complaint prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Both the corrected order on the estafa case and the reversals on suspension of payments are errors of judgment, not gross ignorance of the law.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 2034 of the Civil Code, a compromise may cover the civil liability arising from an offense but does not extinguish the public action for the penalty; criminal liability cannot be compromised. A motion for reconsideration exists to give the court a chance to correct its errors. A judge who corrects an erroneous order on reconsideration commits a mere error of judgment. Reversing oneself, by itself, is not an infraction, and misreading a contractual provision that is not explicit (Art. 1370, Civil Code) is not gross ignorance. (OCA v. Judge Dumayas, A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570, January 28, 2026)
- **Application:** Judge Lim's first order directing Nestor to cause the dismissal of the estafa case was wrong, because criminal liability cannot be compromised. But he corrected it on Nestor's motion for reconsideration, which is exactly what that motion is for. On suspension of payments, the compromise was not explicit, so his changing readings were errors of interpretation. No evidence shows bad faith or ill motive, and the Court will not presume it from the reversals alone. At most, Judge Lim may be reminded to be more circumspect to avoid indecisive rulings.
- **Conclusion:** The complaint will not prosper because Judge Lim committed only errors of judgment, which are not administratively punishable absent bad faith.

**Q3.** In March 2024, the Supreme Court referred to the OCA, for docketing as an administrative matter, an order issued by Judge Santos. In 2025, while that matter was pending, Judge Santos was dismissed from the service in a different administrative case. In 2026 the Court is ready to decide the first matter. (a) Has the Court lost jurisdiction because Judge Santos is no longer in the service? (b) Which rules govern, and if Judge Santos is found guilty of an offense that merits dismissal, what penalties may still be imposed?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The Court retains jurisdiction. (b) The 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability governs. In lieu of dismissal, the Court may impose forfeiture of all or part of his benefits (except accrued leave credits) and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, and/or a fine.
- **Legal basis:** Under its transitory clause, the 2025 CJCA (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC, effective December 21, 2025) applies to all pending and future cases, unless the Court finds that retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. Under Section 23 of the CJCA, if a respondent is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal but dismissal can no longer be imposed because of prior resignation, retirement, or other separation (except death), the Court may impose (a) forfeiture of all or part of the benefits, never including accrued leave credits, and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, including GOCCs; and/or (b) a fine. A separation that occurs after the administrative case was instituted does not divest the Court of jurisdiction. (OCA v. Judge Dumayas, A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570, January 28, 2026)
- **Application:** The case against Judge Santos was instituted in March 2024, while he was still in the service. His dismissal in 2025 in another case came after the Court's jurisdiction had attached. Since the case was still pending when the CJCA took effect, the CJCA applies, and nothing suggests that applying it would be unfeasible or unjust. Dismissal can no longer be imposed on a judge already dismissed, but the Court may order forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits), disqualification from public office, and/or a fine.
- **Conclusion:** The Court keeps jurisdiction and, under the 2025 CJCA, may impose forfeiture, disqualification, and/or a fine in lieu of dismissal.

> Note: Not to be confused with the earlier OCA v. Judge Dumayas, A.M. No. RTJ-15-2435, March 6, 2018, where respondent was dismissed from the service; that earlier case is mentioned here only as background. The decision cites "Section 23 of the Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability" without naming the Canon; it is cited the same way here. The decision gives the date of the writ of execution implemented in 2008 as both January 10 and January 16, 2008, so that date is left out of the facts. Marquez, J., took no part; Singh, J., was on leave.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70380)

## People v. XXX (G.R. No. 260860)

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. XXX (G.R. No. 260860), ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 260860 | 2025-11-11 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Criminal Procedure > N. Appeal (Rule 122)  
**Specific topics:** Appeal by the accused waives double jeopardy, including the implied acquittal of the greater offense (absolute waiver); Appellate court may convict of the original, graver charge (Rule 124, Sec. 11); Defect in the date alleged in the Information is waived if not raised before arraignment; Consummated statutory rape of a child: pain and attempted penetration (People v. Agao)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > S. Right Against Double Jeopardy)
  
**Also relevant to:** Criminal Law (III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > H. Title VIII – Crimes Against Persons)

### Doctrine
**When the accused appeals a conviction for a lesser offense, he waives the constitutional safeguard against double jeopardy both as to that conviction and as to the implied acquittal of the original (greater) charge. The whole case is thrown open to review, and the appellate court may convict him of the original charge** (here, statutory rape instead of acts of lasciviousness). The Court reiterated the "absolute waiver" theory consistently applied in Philippine jurisprudence (Trono v. United States; Ko Bu Lin v. CA; People v. Carreon; People v. Rondero, all citing Lontoc v. People), which is reflected in Rule 124, Section 11 (the CA may "increase or reduce the penalty"). The rule that a "downgraded" conviction can no longer be reviewed applies only when the **State** appeals (Kepner; People v. Dela Torre) or, as in People v. Alarcon, in an automatic review in which the accused had no hand. The Court clarified that People v. Arcega (a State appeal) erred in relying on People v. Balunsat (an accused's appeal), and noted that the Balunsat doctrine had already been abandoned (People v. XXX262846, G.R. No. 262846, February 18, 2025, En Banc).

An Information alleging that rape was committed "on or about the year 2015" is defective: under People v. Ladrillo it covers the year and the years immediately before and after, so the accused must account for up to 36 months. The remedy is a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash because the Information does not conform substantially to the prescribed form (Rule 117, Sec. 3(e)). The Court clarified that **a defective information is not "cured" by evidence at trial. It is quashed, amended, or waived.** This ground is not among the non-waivable grounds in Rule 117, Section 9, so it is waived if not raised before arraignment and cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.

On consummation, the Court reiterated People v. Agao (En Banc, 2022). "Mere touching" means the penis penetrating the cleft of the labia majora, however slightly. With pre-pubescent victims, an attempt to penetrate likely indicates at least introduction into the vulval cleft. Where a child does not explicitly describe penetration, courts may find consummation from attendant circumstances, such as the victim's testimony that she felt pain in her genitals.

### Facts
AAA was born on March 7, 2006. Her mother cohabited with accused-appellant XXX and had a daughter with him. When the mother left to work in Qatar, XXX cared for AAA, who called him "Papa." XXX was charged with two counts of qualified rape (as AAA's stepfather) under two Informations. Criminal Case No. 17-0678 alleged rape "on or about the 5th day of July 2017," when AAA was 11. Criminal Case No. 17-0904 alleged rape "[on] or about the year 2015," when AAA was nine. XXX pleaded not guilty. He did not move to quash either Information or ask for a bill of particulars.

AAA testified about the first rape in June 2015 and the last on July 5, 2017. On cross-examination about 2015 she answered that he was not able to insert his penis ("Hindi po"). On redirect she said he was pushing it ("Tinutulak niya po") and that she was hurt. Elsewhere she testified "pinilit niya pong ipasok" and "nasaktan po" for both incidents. AAA reported the abuse to a teacher on July 7, 2017. The medico-legal officer found redness on the peri-hymenal region, clear evidence of blunt penetrating trauma to the hymen, and shallow healed lacerations. XXX raised denial and alibi.

The RTC's Joint Judgment convicted XXX of statutory rape for the July 5, 2017 incident. The qualifying circumstance of relationship was not proved because there was no proof that XXX was married to AAA's mother. He was sentenced to reclusion perpetua and ordered to pay PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages. For the 2015 incident, the RTC convicted him only of acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC in relation to Section 5(b) of RA 7610, because it found no penile penetration. It awarded PHP 50,000.00 for each kind of damages.

On XXX's appeal, the CA affirmed (June 23, 2021 Decision, CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 13804). The CA said that pain indicates penetration. However, relying on People v. Arcega, it held that XXX could no longer be convicted of rape for 2015 without violating double jeopardy, since the RTC's ruling was practically an acquittal of rape. XXX appealed to the Supreme Court. He invoked Ladrillo against the "year 2015" allegation and attacked AAA's competence and consistency.

### Issues
1. Whether the Information in Criminal Case No. 17-0904, alleging that the rape was committed "on or about the year 2015," violated accused-appellant's right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation, and whether he may raise the defect on appeal.
2. Whether the alleged inconsistencies in AAA's testimony impair her credibility.
3. Whether the 2015 incident was consummated rape rather than acts of lasciviousness.
4. Whether accused-appellant may be convicted of statutory rape for the 2015 incident, even though the RTC convicted him only of acts of lasciviousness, without violating his right against double jeopardy.

### Ruling
**1. The Information was defective, but the defect was waived.** AAA's sworn statement gave the date as June 2015, so the Court found it "inexcusable" that the State alleged "on or about the year 2015" and not "in or about June 2015." Under Ladrillo, such an allegation covers the year and the immediately prior and subsequent years. In United States v. Dichao, an interval of 22 months was already too indefinite, so 36 months is more so. The Court distinguished Magbanua, Santos, and Gianan. It rejected the statements in Cantomayor and Gianan that such a defect may be cured by the evidence: "an information's validity cannot be determined based on the evidence presented in a case"; "[s]trictly speaking, any defect in the information is not cured by evidence presented during trial. The defective information is only either quashed, directed to be amended, or waived." By going to arraignment without moving to quash or for a bill of particulars, accused-appellant waived the objection. Lack of conformity with the prescribed form is not among the four non-waivable grounds in Rule 117, Section 9, so **it was "too late in the day" to raise it on appeal.**

**2. No.** Inconsistencies on minor details that do not touch the central fact of the crime do not impair credibility. They bolster it by discounting the possibility of rehearsed testimony. Youth and immaturity are badges of truth and sincerity. The quoted portions of AAA's testimony cannot be taken in isolation from the rest of it.

**3. Yes, the 2015 incident was consummated rape.** Applying People v. Agao, the Court explained that "mere touching" means penetration of the cleft of the labia majora, however slight. Given the underdeveloped genitalia of a pre-pubescent child, an attempt to penetrate is likely indicative of introduction into the vulval cleft. Agao also directs courts to look at attendant circumstances, such as pain in the genitals, bleeding, redness, absent hymenal tags, or other injury, and to give due regard to a child's linguistic limitations. Viewed this way, AAA's statements "pinilit niya pong ipasok," "tinutulak niya po," and "nasaktan po" proved beyond reasonable doubt that rape was consummated in 2015 as well as in 2017, contrary to the RTC's finding.

**4. Yes. Double jeopardy is no bar because the accused himself appealed.** The CA relied on Arcega, which cited Balunsat, which cited Alarcon, which cited Dela Torre. Arcega was a State appeal and correctly barred the prosecution from assailing the acquittal, but it erred in citing Balunsat, where the accused appealed. The limitation in Balunsat applies only to prosecution appeals, and that doctrine has been abandoned. Alarcon was an automatic review and Dela Torre a prosecution appeal. Neither involved an accused's own appeal. Following Trono v. United States, when the accused appeals "the government had no voice in the matter of the appeal; it simply followed" him, and he "must take the burden with the benefit." The US Supreme Court rejected this "absolute waiver" theory in Green v. United States (1957). The Philippine Court, however, has consistently applied it (Ko Bu Lin, Carreon, Rondero, Lontoc), and Rule 124, Section 11 lets the CA increase the penalty. In cases such as San Andres, Solar, Ladra, and Perez, the Court convicted the accused of the graver original charge on appeal. The purpose of double jeopardy is to prevent government oppression, "not to frustrate justice"; the Court "could not claim to be dispensers of justice if Our power of review would be limited to 'downward' corrections of error." **Because accused-appellant's own appeal threw the whole case open, there was no bar to convicting him of statutory rape instead of acts of lasciviousness, whether by the CA or by the Supreme Court.**

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA's June 23, 2021 Decision in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 13804 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION: XXX was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of two counts of statutory rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua for each count. He was ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages for each count, all with legal interest of 6% per annum from finality of the Decision until fully paid.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Romeo was charged with statutory rape of his live-in partner's eight-year-old daughter. The child testified that Romeo "pinilit ipasok" his penis into her vagina and that she was hurt, but on cross-examination she answered "hindi po" when asked whether it went in. The RTC convicted Romeo only of acts of lasciviousness in relation to Section 5(b) of RA 7610, finding no penetration. Romeo alone appealed. The Court of Appeals found that rape was consummated and convicted him of statutory rape. Romeo argues that the RTC's judgment was an implied acquittal of rape and that convicting him of rape on his own appeal violates his right against double jeopardy. Is Romeo correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. By appealing, Romeo waived his right against double jeopardy, including as to the implied acquittal of rape. The CA could validly convict him of statutory rape.
- **Legal basis:** When an accused appeals a conviction for a lesser offense, he waives the constitutional safeguard against double jeopardy both as to that conviction and as to the implied acquittal of the original charge. The whole case is thrown open to review, and the appellate court may render the judgment that law and justice dictate, including conviction for the original charge (Rule 124, Sec. 11). The bar against reviewing a downgraded conviction applies only when the State appeals. On consummation, "mere touching" means penetration of the cleft of the labia majora, however slight, and a child's testimony of pain while the offender tried to penetrate supports a finding of consummated rape (People v. Agao). (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 260860, November 11, 2025, En Banc)
- **Application:** The appeal was taken by Romeo alone; the State merely followed him to the CA. Having asked the CA to review the judgment, Romeo cannot limit his waiver to the part he dislikes and use the implied acquittal as a shield. The child's testimony that Romeo forced his penis in and that she was hurt, read as a whole and with due regard to her limited vocabulary, shows at least penetration of the labial cleft. Her answer of "hindi po" on cross-examination does not negate this.
- **Conclusion:** Romeo's appeal opened the whole case to review, so his conviction for statutory rape by the CA does not violate double jeopardy.

**Q2.** Same facts as above, except that Romeo did not appeal his conviction for acts of lasciviousness. Instead, the People, through the OSG, appealed to the Court of Appeals, arguing that the evidence proved consummated statutory rape and that Romeo should be convicted of rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. Should the CA give due course to the People's appeal?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The People's appeal would place Romeo in double jeopardy and must be dismissed.
- **Legal basis:** The prosecution cannot appeal a judgment in a criminal case to reverse an acquittal or to increase the penalty imposed in a conviction. A conviction for a lesser offense is an implied acquittal of the greater offense charged, and an appeal by the State to review that downgrading violates the right against double jeopardy (People v. Dela Torre; Kepner v. United States). In People v. XXX (G.R. No. 260860, November 11, 2025, En Banc), the Court explained that this bar applies only when the State appeals. It does not apply when the accused himself appeals and thereby waives the protection.
- **Application:** Unlike in the previous problem, the appeal here is at the instance of the State, not Romeo. Romeo has not waived anything; he accepted the judgment. The People's appeal seeks to reverse Romeo's implied acquittal of rape and to increase his penalty, which is exactly what double jeopardy forbids. Whether or not the evidence actually showed penetration does not matter.
- **Conclusion:** The CA should dismiss the People's appeal because it seeks to review an implied acquittal and increase the penalty, in violation of double jeopardy.

**Q3.** Pablo was charged with rape in an Information alleging that the crime was committed "on or about the year 2019." The complainant's sworn statement, attached to the complaint, stated that the rape happened in March 2019. Pablo was arraigned and pleaded not guilty without filing any motion. After conviction, he argued on appeal for the first time that the Information violated his right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation, because it forced him to account for his whereabouts over several years. (a) Was the Information defective, and what remedies were available to Pablo before arraignment? (b) Will his argument on appeal prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes, the Information was defective for indefiniteness as to the date. Pablo could have moved for a bill of particulars or moved to quash because the Information did not conform substantially to the prescribed form. (b) No. He waived the defect by not raising it before arraignment.
- **Legal basis:** An allegation that a crime was committed "on or about" a given year covers the year and the immediately prior and subsequent years, which is too indefinite to let the accused prepare his defense (People v. Ladrillo). The remedy is a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash under Rule 117, Section 3(e). Under Rule 117, Section 9, failure to assert a ground before pleading is a waiver, except for the grounds in paragraphs (a), (b), (g), and (i) of Section 3. A defective information is not cured by evidence at trial; it is quashed, amended, or waived. (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 260860, November 11, 2025, En Banc)
- **Application:** Since the sworn statement said March 2019, the prosecution should have alleged "in or about March 2019." Alleging only the year exposed Pablo to a period of up to three years, so the Information was open to a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash under Rule 117, Section 3(e). But Pablo entered his plea without raising either. Non-conformity with the prescribed form is not one of the non-waivable grounds, so by pleading he in effect accepted that the Information sufficiently informed him of the charge.
- **Conclusion:** The Information was defective, but Pablo waived the defect by pleading without objection, so he can no longer raise it on appeal.

> Note: The abandonment of People v. Balunsat was not done in this case. The main opinion cites People v. XXX262846 (G.R. No. 262846, February 18, 2025, Per J. Kho, Jr., En Banc) for it. This case applied the abandonment and pointed out the error in People v. Arcega. Leonen, SAJ. filed a separate opinion and Kho, Jr., J. a concurring opinion; neither was used for the doctrine. The two Informations charged qualified rape by a stepfather, but the RTC found relationship unproved because there was no proof of marriage to AAA's mother; the qualifier was not revived on appeal. The E-Library text contains a stray string ("ycnaj") before a citation table; it does not affect the content.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70308)

## Francisco v. Judge Asuncion

**ATTY. PABLO B. FRANCISCO, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. MIGUEL S. ASUNCION, PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 99, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, ANTIPOLO CITY, RIZAL, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. RTJ-26-119 (formerly JIB FPI No. 21-076-RTJ) | 2025-11-05 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Undue delay in rendering a decision as simple neglect of duty (Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC); Three-month period to decide for lower courts (Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 15(1)) and the duty to ask for an extension; Excuses for delay: heavy caseload, pandemic, executive judge duties; Prior administrative liability as an aggravating circumstance; No separate liability as a lawyer absent corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of rules
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VI. Judicial Department > E. The Supreme Court > 1. Composition, Powers, and Functions > b. Administrative Supervision over Lower Courts)

### Doctrine
**Undue delay in rendering a decision is a form of negligence that may be gross neglect of duty (a serious charge) or simple neglect of duty (a less serious charge) under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC.** Lower courts must decide cases within three months from submission (Article VIII, Section 15(1), 1987 Constitution), and judges must deliver reserved decisions efficiently, fairly and with reasonable promptness (Canon 6, Section 5, New Code of Judicial Conduct). **A judge who cannot meet the period must ask the Court, through the OCA, for an extension** (OCA Circular No. 243-2022). Heavy caseload, the pandemic, duties as executive or assisting judge, and family health concerns do not excuse the delay when the judge never sought an extension and decided long after regular court operations resumed. Deciding the case later does not erase liability, and the judge cannot avoid the charge by saying the complainant should have appealed: the issue is the delay, not the merits (reiterated).

Simple neglect of duty is punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 but not exceeding PHP 100,000 (Rule 140, Section 15(b), in relation to Section 17(2)). A previous administrative liability for which a penalty was imposed is an aggravating circumstance (Section 19), allowing a penalty of up to double the maximum (Section 20). The complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence. The judge is not separately liable as a member of the Bar for the same delay without evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules.

### Facts
Atty. Pablo Francisco was the plaintiff in Civil Case No. 12-9697, an action to annul a TCT filed on June 14, 2012 in the RTC of Antipolo City, Branch 99, presided over by Judge Miguel Asuncion. The defendants and their counsel failed to attend mediation, JDR, pre-marking and pre-trial, so the Pre-Trial Order of June 21, 2018 deemed their right to participate waived and allowed Atty. Francisco to present evidence ex parte. He finished presenting evidence on November 8, 2018, filed his written offer of exhibits on November 19, 2018, and filed his memorandum on December 10, 2018. On April 11, 2019, the judge admitted all his exhibits except Exhibit "G."

Atty. Francisco filed a Motion for a Decision on January 7, 2020, a Motion to Transfer Case to Another Sala on February 21, 2020, and a Motion for Inhibition dated August 19, 2020. The judge acted on none of them. Atty. Francisco then filed an administrative complaint dated August 20, 2021 for neglect of duty. The Judicial Integrity Board (JIB) required the judge to comment on November 16, 2021, and again on April 20, 2023, when it also directed him to show cause why he should not be disciplined as a member of the Bar.

In his Comment dated April 20, 2023, Judge Asuncion apologized and blamed the delay on the "influx of equally important matters." He had served as executive judge from October 16, 2020 to November 3, 2022, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, acting on search warrant and bail applications and attending meetings and courtesy calls with local offices. He was also assigned in January 2021 as assisting judge to help decongest caseloads, including in a newly created branch; his court had a new branch clerk of court; and he had family health concerns. He reported that he had decided the case on March 24, 2023, dismissing it for lack of cause of action, and argued that an administrative complaint is not the remedy against an adverse decision. The records showed that he had previously been reprimanded for undue delay (RTJ-20-2592) and had four more pending complaints for delay.

The Office of the Executive Director of the JIB recommended a fine of PHP 50,000 for simple neglect of duty and a fine of PHP 18,000 for violating the CPRA. In its June 8, 2023 Report, the JIB recommended the PHP 50,000 fine with a stern warning, but the dismissal of the charge against him as a member of the Bar.

### Issues
1. Whether Judge Asuncion is administratively liable for undue delay in deciding Civil Case No. 12-9697, and for what offense.
2. What penalty should be imposed, considering his prior administrative liability.
3. Whether he is also liable as a member of the Bar under the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, he is guilty of simple neglect of duty.** In administrative cases the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence, meaning relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion, and the complainant did so. Simple neglect of duty is the failure to give proper attention to an expected task, signifying a disregard of duty resulting from carelessness or indifference. The complainant completed his evidence and memorandum in 2018, and his exhibits were ruled on by April 11, 2019, yet the decision came only on March 24, 2023, "three years and two months after the complainant filed the Motion for a Decision." "Even if a period of one year is removed in due consideration of the pandemic," the decision was rendered beyond the three-month period of Article VIII, Section 15(1). The judge did not deny the delay. His excuses may be valid reasons, but he never sought an extension, as OCA Circular No. 243-2022 allows, and regular court operations had long resumed when he decided the case. **His argument that the complainant should have used judicial remedies against the decision deserved "scant consideration": the crux of the case is the inordinate delay, not the merits.**

**2. A fine of PHP 50,000.** Simple neglect of duty is a less serious offense punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 but not exceeding PHP 100,000 (Rule 140, Section 15(b), in relation to Section 17(2)). His earlier reprimand for undue delay in RTJ-20-2592 is an aggravating circumstance under Section 19, and Section 20 allows a penalty of up to double the maximum when aggravating circumstances are present. The Court found a fine of PHP 50,000 appropriate and added a stern warning.

**3. No liability as a member of the Bar.** The Court agreed with the JIB that there was no evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rule that would make him liable under the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath.

### Disposition
The JIB's June 8, 2023 Report and Recommendation was ADOPTED in full. Judge Miguel S. Asuncion was found GUILTY of simple neglect of duty and FINED PHP 50,000, payable within three months from promulgation, and was STERNLY WARNED that a repetition of the same offense would be dealt with more severely. The complaint against him as a member of the Philippine Bar was DISMISSED for lack of merit.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** A civil case pending before RTC Judge Ramos was submitted for decision on February 1, 2022. The plaintiff filed motions for early decision in 2022 and 2023, but Judge Ramos decided the case only in September 2024. Charged administratively, he explained that he had a heavy caseload, served as executive judge, attended courtesy calls with local officials, and had a family member who was ill. He never asked the Supreme Court for an extension of time. Is he administratively liable? If so, for what offense?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. He is liable for simple neglect of duty for undue delay in rendering a decision.
- **Legal basis:** Lower courts must decide cases within three months from submission (Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 15(1)). Undue delay in rendering a decision is a form of negligence classified as gross or simple neglect of duty under Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. A judge who cannot decide within the period must ask for an extension through the OCA (OCA Circular No. 243-2022). Heavy caseload, duties as executive judge, courtesy calls and family health concerns do not excuse the delay where no extension was sought. Simple neglect of duty is a less serious charge punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 but not exceeding PHP 100,000. (Francisco v. Judge Asuncion, A.M. No. RTJ-26-119, November 5, 2025)
- **Application:** Judge Ramos had until about May 1, 2022 to decide, but he did so more than two years later. His reasons might have justified an extension, but he never asked for one, so they cannot excuse the delay after the fact. The delay shows a failure to give proper attention to a task expected of him, which is simple neglect of duty. Absent other circumstances, the penalty is suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 up to PHP 100,000.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Ramos is guilty of simple neglect of duty and may be suspended or fined within the range for a less serious charge.

**Q2.** Same facts as above, but (i) Judge Ramos argues that the complaint should be dismissed because he has already decided the case and the complainant's proper remedy is to appeal; and (ii) the records show that he was previously fined for a similar delay. (a) Rule on his argument. (b) How does the prior fine affect the penalty?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The argument fails because the charge concerns the delay, not the merits of the decision. (b) The prior fine is an aggravating circumstance that allows the Court to impose a suspension or fine of up to double the maximum.
- **Legal basis:** In an administrative case for undue delay, the crux is the inordinate delay, not the merits of the decision, so the availability of judicial remedies against the decision does not bar the complaint. Under Rule 140, Section 19, a previous administrative liability for which a penalty was imposed, whatever its nature or gravity, is an aggravating circumstance. Under Section 20, when aggravating circumstances are present, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not exceeding double the prescribed maximum. (Francisco v. Judge Asuncion, A.M. No. RTJ-26-119, November 5, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The complaint does not ask whether Judge Ramos decided correctly; it charges him with deciding years late. Rendering the decision afterward, and the complainant's right to appeal it, do not erase the delay. (b) Because he was previously fined, an aggravating circumstance is present, so the Court may go beyond the ordinary maximum for simple neglect of duty, up to double it. The Court still has discretion to impose a fine within the ordinary range; in Francisco it found PHP 50,000 appropriate despite a prior reprimand.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Ramos remains liable despite having decided the case, and his prior fine aggravates his liability.

**Q3.** In the same case, the complainant asks that Judge Ramos also be fined as a member of the Bar for violating the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, since every lawyer must be diligent. The only evidence offered is the delay itself. (a) Should the Court impose a separate penalty on him as a lawyer? (b) What quantum of proof does the complainant need in this administrative case?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. (b) Substantial evidence.
- **Legal basis:** A judge found liable for undue delay is not separately liable as a member of the Bar under the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath absent evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules. In administrative cases, the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence: relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion. The standard is met when there is reasonable ground to believe the respondent is responsible, even if the evidence is not overwhelming or preponderant. (Francisco v. Judge Asuncion, A.M. No. RTJ-26-119, November 5, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The only proof is the delay, which is already penalized as simple neglect of duty. Nothing shows corruption, an intent to violate the law, or a flagrant disregard of rules, so no separate penalty as a lawyer is warranted. (b) The complainant need only present substantial evidence of the delay, which the court records themselves supply.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Ramos should be penalized only for simple neglect of duty, which the complainant can establish by substantial evidence.

> Note: The decision applied Canon 6, Section 5 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct and Rule 140 as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. It did not cite the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC), on which the 2027 judicial ethics syllabus is based. The decision did not state the exact date the case was deemed submitted for decision; it measured the delay from the Motion for a Decision of January 7, 2020.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70338)

## Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva

**EDITHA M. BAYONA, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. AIDA THERESITA B. BASA-DIVIVA, PRESIDING JUDGE, MUNICIPAL CIRCUIT TRIAL COURT, STA. CRUZ-CANDELARIA, ZAMBALES, RESPONDENT.**  
OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ | 2025-11-03 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Judicial acts not subject to disciplinary action absent fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice; Administrative complaint is not a substitute for judicial remedies; Substantial evidence; presumption of regularity; bare allegations; Hold-departure orders are for RTCs only; first-level judges no longer conduct preliminary investigation; Arraignment without the private complainant (Rule 116, Sec. 1(f)); admonition for imprudent postponements
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > G. Liberty of Abode and Right to Travel > 2. Watchlist, Hold Departure Orders, and Precautionary Hold Departure Orders)

### Doctrine
**As a matter of policy, the acts of a judge in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action, however erroneous, as long as the judge acted in good faith. Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice are administratively sanctioned** (reiterating Pitney v. Judge Abrogar). Errors committed in the exercise of adjudicative functions must be corrected through judicial remedies, not administrative proceedings. Disciplinary proceedings do not complement, supplement, or substitute for judicial remedies, and an inquiry into administrative liability arising from judicial acts may be made only after the other available remedies have been settled. Bias and partiality require a showing of arbitrariness or prejudice.

**In administrative cases, the complainant bears the burden of proving the charges by substantial evidence.** Bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption that the judge regularly performed official duties. Requiring proof protects magistrates from flimsy and unsubstantiated charges.

Procedural rules reiterated and applied: (a) issuing a hold-departure order is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC (OCA Circular No. 39-97), so a first-level judge who issued one "would have reeked of ignorance of the law" (Re: Occiano); (b) under A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC, first-level court judges no longer conduct preliminary investigations, which are now with the provincial or city prosecutor, and unjust vexation, a light offense, does not require one; (c) the private complainant need not be present at the arraignment unless the court requires it (Rule 116, Sec. 1(f)). A judge whose postponements were not shown to be whimsical, but who was not cautious enough in granting them, may be admonished.

### Facts
On February 5, 2020, Editha M. Bayona filed a sworn complaint with the OCA charging Judge Aida Theresita B. Basa-Diviva of the MCTC of Sta. Cruz-Candelaria, Zambales, with dishonesty, violation of RA 3019, and gross ignorance of the law/procedure. Her complaint concerned three criminal cases: two against Josefina Medida-House (alarm and scandal, and violation of Section 48(3) of RA 9003), and one against Bayona herself (Criminal Case No. 5672, described as maltreatment/slight physical injuries by ill treatment). The complaint went to the JIB.

Bayona alleged the following. On September 13, 2018, the judge acted on House's handwritten, un-notarized manifestation asking permission to leave the country, which Bayona said should have complied with the rules on counter-affidavits. Bayona herself was not furnished the order setting her arraignment and was given no chance to file a counter-affidavit. The criminal complaint for unjust vexation against her had no preliminary investigation. She was arraigned on March 14, 2019 although private complainant House and her counsel were absent. The judge did not issue the warrant against House that she had warned of when House again failed to appear on July 11, 2019. Hearings were postponed many times without valid reason. She also accused the judge of bullying and harassing her, and she complained about her own counsel, Atty. Domingo A. Doctor, Jr.

The judge answered that allowing House to travel was just and lawful, and that issuing a hold-departure order was beyond an MCTC's authority. She said preliminary investigation belongs to the prosecutor under A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC, that the postponements were caused by the absence of the accused or the public prosecutor, and that the case against Bayona had in fact been dismissed. The OED-JIB recommended that the judge be fined PHP 1,000.00 for violating Section 5, Canon 6 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, that the other charges be dismissed, and that the charge against Atty. Doctor be referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant. In its March 9, 2022 Report, the JIB adopted these findings but recommended admonition instead of a fine. The judge compulsorily retired on December 28, 2021.

### Issues
1. Whether respondent judge is administratively liable for dishonesty, violation of RA 3019, or gross ignorance of the law for allowing an accused to travel abroad, for the lack of preliminary investigation, and for arraigning complainant without the private complainant.
2. Whether the charges of bullying, harassment, and denial of due process were proved by substantial evidence.
3. Whether respondent should be sanctioned for the repeated postponement of hearings.

### Ruling
**1. No.** There was "no iota of evidence" of dishonesty, graft, or gross ignorance, and the complainant did not even specify the acts constituting them.

- *Travel abroad:* Allowing House to travel was an exercise of judicial function. Under Pitney v. Judge Abrogar, a judge "cannot be subjected to liability... for any of [their] official acts, no matter how erroneous, as long as [they act] in good faith." Errors in adjudication must be corrected through judicial remedies, and disciplinary proceedings do not substitute for them. **Assuming the order was erroneous, it remained judicial in nature and, absent fraud, dishonesty, or corruption, was not subject to discipline.** Issuing a hold-departure order, an act within the RTC's exclusive jurisdiction under OCA Circular No. 39-97, "would have reeked of ignorance of the law." In Re: Occiano, a first-level judge who knowingly issued one despite the circular committed "disrespect for, and a willful violation of, a lawful circular."
- *Preliminary investigation:* A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC transferred the power to conduct preliminary investigations from first-level courts to the provincial or city prosecutor, so MCTC judges are no longer authorized to conduct them. Moreover, unjust vexation, a light offense, does not require preliminary investigation.
- *Arraignment:* "[T]here is nothing irregular with the arraignment of an accused in the absence of the private complainant," who need not be present unless the court requires it.

**2. No.** The bullying, harassment, and due process charges were "bare allegations unsupported by any evidence." **The complainant bears the burden of proving her charges by substantial evidence**: relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate, enough to give reasonable ground to believe the respondent is responsible, even if not overwhelming or preponderant. This requirement protects magistrates from flimsy charges. Without proof, the presumption of regularity in the performance of official functions prevails.

**3. Admonition only.** There was no clear showing that the postponements were whimsical or capricious, and one was caused by the absence of the complainant's own witness. Considering the judge's untarnished reputation over 38 years of service, the Court agreed with the JIB that she should merely be admonished for failing to exercise more caution in granting postponements. The complaint against Atty. Doctor was referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant.

### Disposition
The JIB's March 9, 2022 Report and Recommendation was ADOPTED in full. The complaint for dishonesty, violation of RA 3019, and gross ignorance of the law/procedure against Judge Aida Theresita B. Basa-Diviva was DISMISSED for being judicial in nature and for lack of merit. She was ADMONISHED for failing to exercise the necessary prudence in granting postponements of scheduled hearings. The complaint against Atty. Domingo A. Doctor, Jr. was referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant for appropriate action.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Lorna is the private complainant in a slight physical injuries case pending before MTC Judge Gomez. Over Lorna's objection, Judge Gomez granted the accused's motion for permission to travel abroad for two weeks. Lorna did not move for reconsideration or file any petition. Instead she filed an administrative complaint against Judge Gomez for gross ignorance of the law and dishonesty, alleging only that the order was wrong and favored the accused. Will the administrative complaint prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The complaint should be dismissed for being judicial in nature and for lack of merit.
- **Legal basis:** As a matter of policy, the acts of a judge in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action, no matter how erroneous, as long as the judge acted in good faith. Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice are administratively sanctioned. Errors in adjudication must be corrected through judicial remedies, and disciplinary proceedings do not complement, supplement, or substitute for them. The complainant must prove the charges by substantial evidence; bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption of regularity. (Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva, OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ, November 3, 2025, citing Pitney v. Judge Abrogar)
- **Application:** Granting the accused's motion to travel was an exercise of Judge Gomez's adjudicative function. Even if the ruling was wrong, Lorna's remedy was judicial: a motion for reconsideration or the proper petition, not an administrative case. Lorna alleges only that the order was wrong and favored the accused. She offers no evidence of fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or bad faith, and partiality requires a showing of arbitrariness or prejudice. Her bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption that Judge Gomez performed her duties regularly.
- **Conclusion:** The administrative complaint will be dismissed.

**Q2.** In a criminal case for estafa within the jurisdiction of his MCTC, Judge Tan issued a hold-departure order against the accused, on the private complainant's motion. Told that OCA Circular No. 39-97 limits hold-departure orders to cases within the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC, Judge Tan wrote in his comment that he "firmly believed" he had authority to issue one notwithstanding the circular. May Judge Tan invoke the rule that a judge's acts in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Judge Tan's knowing disregard of a clear circular is not a mere error of judgment, and he may be held administratively liable.
- **Legal basis:** The immunity of judicial acts from discipline does not cover errors tainted with gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice. Under OCA Circular No. 39-97, hold-departure orders may be issued only in criminal cases within the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC; issuing one in a first-level court case "would have reeked of ignorance of the law." In Re: Occiano, cited in Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva (OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ, November 3, 2025), the Court held that a judge who knew the circular yet insisted he had authority committed "not just grave abuse of authority amounting to a grave misconduct or a conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service" but "disrespect for, and a willful violation of, a lawful circular of the highest court of the land."
- **Application:** Unlike the judge in Bayona, who correctly refrained from issuing a hold-departure order and merely acted on a motion to travel, Judge Tan issued an order that the circular plainly reserves to RTCs. His own comment shows that he knew of the circular and chose to disregard it. That takes his act out of the protection given to good-faith judicial errors.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Tan cannot hide behind the judicial-function rule; he is administratively liable for willfully violating the circular.

**Q3.** Accused of unjust vexation before an MCTC, Nilda complained that (a) Judge Ruiz never conducted a preliminary investigation before the case proceeded, and (b) Judge Ruiz arraigned her even though the private complainant and her counsel were absent. Nilda claims both were violations of procedure amounting to gross ignorance of the law. Is she correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. (a) Judge Ruiz had no power to conduct a preliminary investigation, and none is required for unjust vexation. (b) Arraigning an accused without the private complainant is not irregular.
- **Legal basis:** Under A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC, the power of first-level court judges to conduct preliminary investigations was transferred to the provincial or city prosecutor, so MCTC judges are no longer authorized to conduct them. Unjust vexation, being a light offense, does not require preliminary investigation under Rule 112. Under Rule 116, Section 1(f), the private offended party need not be present at the arraignment unless the court requires it. (Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva, OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ, November 3, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Judge Ruiz could not have conducted a preliminary investigation even if one were required, and for a light offense like unjust vexation none is required at all. Proceeding without one is not error, much less gross ignorance. (b) The rules do not require the private complainant's presence at arraignment unless the court orders it, so arraigning Nilda in the complainant's absence was regular.
- **Conclusion:** Neither act is irregular, and the charge of gross ignorance of the law must be dismissed.

> Note: This Division decision was promulgated on November 3, 2025, after respondent's compulsory retirement on December 28, 2021 and before the 2025 CJCA took effect (December 21, 2025). The decision does not discuss the effect of her retirement on the case. The votes line shows Singh, J., on leave; he was designated additional member vice Marquez, J., per Raffle dated September 13, 2022. The decision is not consistent about the case against Bayona: Criminal Case No. 5672 is described as maltreatment/slight physical injuries by ill treatment, while the preliminary investigation discussion refers to an unjust vexation complaint against her. The digest follows each statement as written. The 2027 syllabus lists Rule 112 as partly repealed by A.M. No. 24-02-09-SC; check the current rules before relying on the preliminary investigation point beyond what this case holds.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70272)
