## Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc.

**ROXACO-ASIA HOSPITALITY CORPORATION [FORMERLY ROXACO-VANGUARD HOTEL CORP.], PETITIONER, VS. GULF CANARY CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT, INC. AND ASIA UNITED INSURANCE, INC., RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. Nos. 246250-51 | 2025-09-29 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > d. Issues Cognizable  
**Specific topics:** Finality of CIAC arbitral awards (EO 1008, Sec. 19); Question of law vs. question of fact in appeals from CIAC awards; Tribunal-centered (not fact-centered) grounds for factual review (Global Medical Center); Waiver must be clear and unequivocal; contractor's delay and extension of time; Attorney's fees and costs of arbitration require a showing of bad faith
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (VIII. Obligations and Contracts > A. Obligations > 2. Nature and Effects of Obligations > a. Breaches of Obligations; Remedies)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (XII. Damages > B. Actual and Compensatory Damages > 4. Attorney’s Fees and Expenses of Litigation)
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (IX. Special Contracts > D. Credit Transactions > 3. Guaranty and Suretyship > c. Extinguishment)

### Doctrine
Under **Section 19 of Executive Order No. 1008** (Construction Industry Arbitration Law), a CIAC arbitral award is **final and unappealable except on questions of law**. Reiterating *Global Medical Center of Laguna, Inc. v. Ross Systems International, Inc.*, the Court held that the CIAC's factual findings may be reviewed only on narrow, **"tribunal-centered" and not "fact-centered"** grounds: (1) a challenge to the integrity of the arbitral tribunal, i.e., (i) the award was procured by corruption, fraud or other undue means; (ii) evident partiality or corruption of the arbitrators; (iii) misconduct in refusing to postpone the hearing upon sufficient cause or in refusing to hear pertinent and material evidence; (iv) an arbitrator disqualified under Section 9 of RA 876 wilfully refrained from disclosing it, or other misbehavior materially prejudiced a party; or (v) the arbitrators exceeded their powers or so imperfectly executed them that no mutual, final and definite award was made; and (2) an allegation that the tribunal violated the Constitution or positive law. **Mere disagreement with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence, or perceived errors of fact, does not open the award to review.** A party invoking partiality or ground (v) must satisfactorily show that the arbitrators were compromised or that their integrity could not be relied upon.

The reviewing court asks two questions. First, is the issue one of law or of fact? If of law, the award may be appealed. Second, if of fact, is it only a disagreement with the tribunal's factual conclusions (not reviewable), or does it go into the integrity of the tribunal in a manner amounting to grave abuse of discretion (reviewable)? **Whether undisputed and authentic documents legally amount to an agreement to extend the completion date, or to a waiver of the contractual notice requirement for an extension, is a question of law.** Who caused the delay, whether the grounds for termination existed, and how much of the downpayment or rectification cost remains due are questions of fact. (The Court noted that *Global Medical Center*'s ruling on the modes of review, Rule 45 to the Supreme Court on questions of law and Rule 65 to the CA on factual issues involving grave abuse, applies prospectively and did not govern this case, but its exposition of reviewable factual issues applies squarely.)

On the merits: a **waiver must be clear and unequivocal**, and there is no implied waiver without a clear, unequivocal and decisive act. Letting the contractor continue working past the completion date, agreeing to acceleration measures, and extending the performance bond do not waive the contract's extension-of-time procedure, because a contractor's delay does not end the contract; it only makes the contractor liable for delay damages while its duty to finish remains, and an owner who keeps the project going is mitigating damages under **Article 2203 of the Civil Code**. Attorney's fees under **Article 2208** and costs of arbitration cannot be awarded without a finding that the losing party resisted the claim in bad faith (reiterated).

### Facts
On June 30, 2014, Roxaco (employer) and Gulf Canary (contractor) signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) for the construction of a 12-storey, 199-room hotel on Quirino Avenue, Parañaque City, for PHP 219,822,703.36. Roxaco paid a 20% downpayment of PHP 45,638,494.74 on September 3, 2014. On September 17, 2014, the parties executed a FIDIC Contract. Gulf Canary posted a Performance Bond of PHP 65,946,811.06 (30% of the price) issued by Asia United on July 4, 2014, which would expire on July 8, 2015. The MOA required completion by March 31, 2015 "unless an extension of time has been authorized and approved by the Employer in writing in accordance with the conditions stated in the FIDIC Contract." FIDIC Sub-Clause 20.1 required the contractor to give notice of a claim for extension within 28 days after it became aware of the event; otherwise "the Time for Completion shall not be extended."

The hotel was not finished by March 31, 2015. The parties agreed to augment Gulf Canary's resources, and Roxaco nominated Vision Properties as subcontractor. A March 16, 2015 letter from Pure Projects (Roxaco's project manager, acting as Engineer) recorded that Roxaco would not terminate Gulf Canary, and that Gulf Canary acknowledged it could not meet the completion date, which "will result in a claim for damages" for delay at 1/10 of 1% of the contract price per day. On July 7, 2015, Roxaco called on the Performance Bond, citing Gulf Canary's breach and its failure to deliver an extended bond, and stating that the extended work completion "would be until January 31, 2016." Asia United did not respond. On September 18, 2015, with only 34.92% of the works done, Roxaco terminated the contracts and engaged Vision to rectify and complete the works. Its demand on Gulf Canary dated September 22, 2017 went unanswered.

Roxaco sued Gulf Canary and Asia United before the CIAC. Gulf Canary claimed the completion date had been extended to January 31, 2016; Asia United claimed it was released because the contract was varied without its consent. The CIAC Tribunal's Final Award of September 24, 2018 found no valid extension, declared the termination valid and the bond subsisting, and ordered Gulf Canary to pay PHP 14,305,098.96 as liquidated damages, PHP 29,701,532.37 as recoupment of the downpayment, rectification costs, 6% interest from September 22, 2017, PHP 2,500,000.00 as attorney's fees, and the costs of arbitration. It denied the claim for cost of completion and held Asia United jointly and severally liable up to the amount of the bond.

On Rule 43 petitions, the CA reversed and dismissed Roxaco's complaint. It held that whether the completion date was extended is a question of law and, alternatively, that the arbitrators "exceeded their powers" by ignoring documents showing an extension. It ruled that the 28-day notice requirement was waived by the parties' acts: the March 13, 2015 meeting minutes on acceleration, the March 16, 2015 letter, Roxaco's July 7, 2015 letter, the extension of the bond to January 31, 2016, and Notices to Correct dated August 24, 2015. So there was no delay, the termination was premature, and the surety was not liable. Roxaco filed a Rule 45 petition.

### Issues
1. Whether the issue of whether the completion date was validly extended is a question of law that the CA could review, and whether the parties agreed to an extension or waived the contractual notice requirement.
2. Whether the CA could review the CIAC Tribunal's factual findings on Gulf Canary's delay and the validity of the termination on the ground that the arbitrators exceeded their powers or were partial.
3. Whether the CA erred in dismissing Roxaco's claims for recoupment of the downpayment and for rectification costs.
4. Whether Roxaco is entitled to attorney's fees and costs of arbitration.
5. Whether Asia United was released from its surety obligation by an alleged variation or novation of the construction contracts.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, it is a question of law, but there was no valid extension.** A question of law exists when the issue does not call for an examination of the probative value of the evidence, the truth of the facts being admitted; asking whether the evidence suffices to support a legal conclusion also raises a question of law (*New Rural Bank of Guimba v. Abad*; *Republic v. Vega*). The parties did not dispute that Gulf Canary sent no written notice under Sub-Clause 20.1, nor the existence and authenticity of the documents the CA relied on. The only question was their legal significance. The CA nonetheless drew the wrong conclusion. Under the MOA and Sub-Clause 20.1, Gulf Canary was not entitled to an extension. A waiver must be "clear and unequivocal," and none of the documents showed one. The CA wrongly assumed that Roxaco would have terminated the contract if Gulf Canary were in delay. Missing the completion date did not end the contract: under Sub-Clause 8.7, delay damages "shall not relieve the Contractor from his obligation to complete the Works," and the MOA imposed a daily penalty of 1/10 of 1% for delay. Continuing the works only meant Gulf Canary still had to finish, subject to its liability for delay; the March 16, 2015 letter itself said the delay "will result in a claim for damages." Extending the bond protected Roxaco while the works went on; agreeing to accelerate was consistent with the duty to mitigate under Article 2203; and the July 7, 2015 letter was a call on the bond precisely because of Gulf Canary's breach. The CIAC Tribunal's finding of no valid extension was affirmed.

**2. No, these are questions of fact that could not be reviewed.** Who caused the delay was determined by the CIAC Tribunal after examining the evidence. The CA's reason (the tribunal "gave a cold shoulder" to the documents) and Gulf Canary's charge of partiality were only disagreements with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence. **"That a party disagrees with the conclusions of an arbitral tribunal will not suffice to charge such a tribunal with partiality and warrant a judicial review of the arbitral award's factual findings."** Allowing such appeals would undermine the speed and expertise that make CIAC arbitration valuable and would relegate the CIAC to "a first level court." The finding that the termination grounds under Sub-Clause 15.2 (failure to comply with a Notice to Correct, abandonment, failure to proceed) were "well-documented" was likewise binding.

**3. Yes, the CA erred.** These claims did not depend on the extension issue. The downpayment was an advance payment, described by the tribunal as an "interest-free loan" repaid through percentage deductions in payment certificates (Sub-Clause 14.2). The unpaid balance of PHP 29,701,532.37 and the existence and cost of defects attributable to Gulf Canary were factual findings with no ground for review. Gulf Canary's liability for rectification costs rested on the MOA (defects corrected at the contractor's cost) and FIDIC Sub-Clauses 4.1, 11.1 and 11.2.

**4. No.** Attorney's fees are not recovered as a rule, because no premium is placed on the right to litigate. An award under Article 2208 "demands factual, legal, and equitable justification"; even a party compelled to litigate may be denied fees where the other side's persistence shows no bad faith beyond "an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of his [or her] cause" (*President of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints v. BTL Construction Corp.*). The tribunal made no finding of bad faith. For the same reason, the award of costs of arbitration was deleted.

**5. No.** Asia United relied on Article 1215 of the Civil Code (novation with a solidary debtor extinguishes the obligation) and the March 16, 2015 letter. But the tribunal found that Pure Projects had no authority to modify the MOA and that Roxaco never agreed to modify it, so no variation or novation was made. That factual finding was binding. **Asia United is solidarily liable with Gulf Canary up to the amount of the Performance Bond.**

### Disposition
Petition GRANTED. The CA Decision of March 27, 2019 in CA-G.R. SP Nos. 157863 and 157866 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The CIAC Final Award of September 24, 2018 in CIAC Case No. 45-2017 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION: Roxaco is not entitled to attorney's fees and costs of arbitration. The monetary award earns legal interest of 6% per annum from finality of the Decision until fully paid.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** BuildCo and Hotel Corp. arbitrated a construction dispute before the CIAC. After hearing both sides, the Arbitral Tribunal found that BuildCo caused the delay in the project and awarded Hotel Corp. liquidated damages. BuildCo seeks judicial review, arguing that the Tribunal gave too much weight to Hotel Corp.'s witnesses and "ignored" BuildCo's site reports, which shows that the arbitrators exceeded their powers and were partial to Hotel Corp. BuildCo offers no other proof of partiality. May the reviewing court re-examine and reverse the Tribunal's finding on who caused the delay?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The finding on who caused the delay is a factual finding that is final and not subject to review.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 19 of Executive Order No. 1008, a CIAC arbitral award is final and unappealable except on questions of law. Factual findings may be reviewed only on tribunal-centered grounds: a challenge to the integrity of the tribunal (corruption, fraud or undue means; evident partiality; misconduct in refusing to postpone or to hear material evidence; undisclosed disqualification; or the arbitrators exceeding their powers so that no mutual, final and definite award was made), or a violation of the Constitution or positive law. Mere disagreement with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence does not suffice, and a party claiming partiality must satisfactorily show that the arbitrators were compromised. (Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., G.R. Nos. 246250-51, September 29, 2025, reiterating Global Medical Center of Laguna, Inc. v. Ross Systems International, Inc.)
- **Application:** Who caused the delay requires weighing the evidence, so it is a question of fact. BuildCo's complaint is that the Tribunal believed Hotel Corp.'s witnesses over its own site reports. That is a disagreement with the Tribunal's appreciation of the evidence, not proof that the arbitrators were corrupt, partial or otherwise compromised. Calling it "exceeding their powers" does not change its nature. Allowing such a challenge would turn the CIAC into a first-level court and defeat the speed and expertise that justify construction arbitration.
- **Conclusion:** The reviewing court may not re-examine or reverse the Tribunal's finding that BuildCo caused the delay.

**Q2.** Under a construction contract, the completion date was June 30, 2025, and the contractor could get an extension only by giving the owner written notice of its claim within 28 days from the event causing delay; otherwise "the time for completion shall not be extended." The contractor never gave such notice. After June 30, 2025, the owner let the contractor keep working, agreed to measures to speed up the works, and required the contractor to extend its performance bond to March 31, 2026. The owner later terminated the contract and claimed delay damages. The contractor argues that the owner's acts waived the notice requirement and extended the completion date. The authenticity of all the documents is admitted. (a) Is the issue a question of law or of fact? (b) Did the owner waive the notice requirement and extend the completion date?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) It is a question of law. (b) No. The owner's acts do not amount to a waiver or an extension.
- **Legal basis:** A question of law exists when the issue does not call for an examination of the probative value of the evidence, the facts being admitted, and the only question is the legal significance of the evidence. A waiver must be clear and unequivocal, and there is no implied waiver without a clear, unequivocal and decisive act showing that purpose. A contractor's failure to meet the completion date does not end the contract; it only makes the contractor liable for delay damages while its obligation to finish remains. An owner who keeps the project going is mitigating its damages under Article 2203 of the Civil Code. (Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., G.R. Nos. 246250-51, September 29, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Since no one disputes that no notice was given or that the documents are genuine, the court need not weigh credibility. It only has to decide what these admitted acts mean in law, which is a question of law. (b) Allowing the contractor to continue simply meant the contractor still had to finish the works, subject to delay damages. Agreeing to accelerate the works was the owner's effort to minimize its loss. Requiring a longer performance bond protected the owner while the works continued. None of these acts clearly and unequivocally shows an intent to give up the 28-day notice requirement or to move the completion date.
- **Conclusion:** The question is one of law, and the completion date was not extended, so the contractor was in delay after June 30, 2025.

**Q3.** In the same CIAC case, the Arbitral Tribunal (a) awarded the owner attorney's fees solely because the owner "was compelled to obtain the services of counsel to protect its interest," with no finding of bad faith on the contractor's part; and (b) held the surety solidarily liable on the performance bond up to its face amount. The surety argues that it was released because a letter from the owner's project manager modified the contract without the surety's consent. The Tribunal had found that the project manager had no authority to modify the contract and that the owner never agreed to any modification. Rule on (a) and (b).

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The award of attorney's fees is improper. (b) The surety is not released and remains solidarily liable up to the amount of the bond.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, attorney's fees are not recoverable as a rule, since no premium is placed on the right to litigate; an award demands factual, legal and equitable justification, and is not proper where the losing party's resistance reflects no bad faith beyond an erroneous belief in the righteousness of its cause. Under Article 1215 of the Civil Code, novation with a solidary debtor extinguishes the obligation, but whether a novation or variation happened is a question of fact, and the CIAC's factual findings are binding absent a tribunal-centered ground for review. (Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., G.R. Nos. 246250-51, September 29, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The only basis for the fees was that the owner had to hire counsel. The Tribunal made no finding that the contractor resisted the claim in bad faith or refused to pay without justifiable cause. Losing on the merits is not bad faith, so the fees (and, for the same reason, an award of costs of arbitration) should be deleted. (b) The surety's defense depends on a modification of the contract, but the Tribunal found as a fact that the project manager had no authority to modify it and that the owner did not agree to any change. With no showing that the Tribunal's integrity was compromised, that finding stands, and there was no novation to release the surety.
- **Conclusion:** The attorney's fees must be deleted, but the surety stays solidarily liable with the contractor up to the amount of the performance bond.

> Note: The rectification cost is PHP 16,964,878.38 in the CIAC fallo as quoted, but PHP 16,964,858.38 in the Court's discussion; the Court affirmed the amount determined by the CIAC Tribunal. The CIAC fallo as quoted makes Asia United liable "in respect of items (i) and (vi)" up to the bond amount. The Court introduced the rule on costs of arbitration as "Section 15 of the CIAC Revised Rules of Procedure" but quoted "SECTION 16.5." One co-arbitrator (Atty. Julius A. Omilia) dissented from the Final Award. The case reached the CA by Rule 43 petitions; under Global Medical Center (applied prospectively), questions of law go to the Supreme Court under Rule 45 and factual issues involving grave abuse go to the CA under Rule 65.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70194)

## People v. Bazar

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. MARICRIS BAZAR Y BELLO, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.**  
G.R. No. 259037 | 2025-09-29 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 2. Direct and Circumstantial Evidence  
**Specific topics:** Requisites for conviction on circumstantial evidence; unbroken chain; test of moral certainty; Flight as evidence of guilt and its limits; Object evidence not linked to the accused or the victims; DNA results not formally offered; Court's power to order DNA testing motu proprio (Rule on DNA Evidence, Sec. 4); Robbery with homicide; acquittal on reasonable doubt
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > M. Rights of the Accused)

### Doctrine
**Circumstantial evidence suffices to convict only if (a) there is more than one circumstance; (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven; and (c) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt** (Rule 133, Rules of Court; reiterating People v. Modesto). The circumstances must form an unbroken chain leading to one fair and reasonable conclusion that points to the accused, to the exclusion of all others. **When the inculpatory facts can be explained in two or more ways, one of which is consistent with innocence, the evidence fails the test of moral certainty and cannot support a conviction.** Under People v. Monje, circumstantial evidence must be acted on with caution; all essential facts must be consistent with guilt; the facts must exclude every other theory; and they must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Because circumstantial evidence is only as strong as its weakest link, the prosecution must rely on the strength of its own case, not on the weakness of the defense.

**Flight per se does not establish guilt; it only tends to do so.** It must be coupled with other direct or circumstantial evidence, because it is inherently ambiguous and may have innocent explanations (fear of retribution, unwillingness to testify, fear of being wrongly apprehended). Flight that came only after the accused learned of a pursuit and a reward for her capture, after she had stayed beside the crime scene for hours, does not show a guilty conscience.

A blood-stained weapon and clothes found in a house occupied by about ten other people do not link the accused to the crime when no evidence traces the blood to the victims and nothing shows she wielded the weapon. DNA results that were not formally offered (and not recited in a stipulated testimony) cannot be considered. The Court observed that in a case resting purely on circumstantial evidence, the trial court could have ordered DNA testing **motu proprio** under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence, even if samples had already been tested at the police's request.

### Facts
On the early morning of July 26, 2015, spouses Alexander and Septy Jane Oliveros left their house in Barangay Balintawak, Lipa City, for their market stall, leaving three grandchildren at home: Princess Shane (9), Prince Andrei (6), and Joyce Ann (6). Later that morning a nephew found the door open, the jalousie window broken and blood-stained, and the children dead in bed. They had died of traumatic head injuries with skull fractures. Septy Jane's wallet with PHP 40,000.00 and a bracelet worth PHP 55,000.00 were missing.

Maricris Bazar and Abegail Jaingue, both bar waitresses, rented a house next to the victims' house. Landlady Balbina Pelagio testified that about ten people lived there. When the police inspected the rented house, they found blood traces on a wall, blood-stained towels, a t-shirt, a curtain, and a coco lumber with bloody handprints. A request for DNA examination was made. At trial, however, the prosecution formally offered only the request, not the results, and the RTC did not admit it. The parties stipulated only that a police officer could identify the laboratory documents.

Maricris was charged with robbery with multiple homicide. She testified that she slept at the house that night, went out when neighbors screamed that children had been killed, left at around 9:00 a.m. for church with friends, returned, and then went to a birthday party. She did not go back because Abegail texted her that police were at the house and that a PHP 300,000.00 reward was offered for her apprehension, and because the barangay captain advised her to stay away. She stayed in Banay-Banay and later at her sister's house in Nasugbu, Batangas, until her arrest on March 9, 2016. Abegail testified that Maricris left at about 10:00 a.m., came back in the afternoon, and left her clothes behind, not scattered. Abegail herself stayed in the house for three more days.

The RTC acquitted Abegail because she was at work when the children died (around 2:30 a.m.). It convicted Maricris on six circumstances: her presence next door; the occupants' departure and the disarray of the house; her hurried departure without notice to the landlady and without her belongings; her never returning; her hiding until arrest; and the blood-stained items recovered from the house. It sentenced her to reclusion perpetua "without the possibility of parole" and ordered her to pay PHP 95,000.00 for the stolen property, plus civil indemnity and moral, exemplary, and temperate damages. The CA affirmed and corrected the crime's designation to robbery with homicide.

### Issues
1. Whether accused-appellant's presence in the house adjacent to the victims' house, and her leaving it without notice and without her belongings, point to her guilt.
2. Whether her flight and hiding until her arrest is evidence of guilt.
3. Whether the blood-stained coco lumber, towels, and clothes recovered from the rented house link her to the crime, and whether all the circumstances together prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

### Ruling
**1. No.** The Court examined each circumstance and found that none excluded other explanations. *Presence next door:* both accused lived beside the victims, but so did about ten other occupants of the rented house. *Departure:* Septy Jane's own supplemental statement said that three unidentified men also left the house. Abegail's testimony, which the RTC found credible enough to acquit her, showed that Maricris left nearly eight hours after the killings, returned in the afternoon, and did not leave her clothes scattered. That testimony deserved more credence than Balbina's, since Balbina had no personal knowledge of when Maricris left.

**2. No.** Flight is "the evading of the course of justice by voluntarily withdrawing oneself in order to avoid arrest" (U.S. v. Alegado). Unexplained flight may tend to show guilt, but **"flight per se does not establish guilt but only tends to do so," cannot by itself overcome the presumption of innocence, and must be coupled with other evidence.** It is inherently ambiguous. As in People v. Bulawin, if the accused really meant to hide out of guilt, she would have fled at the first opportunity. Instead she stayed across from the crime scene for seven to eight hours and even returned. She fled only after learning of the reward for her capture and on the barangay captain's advice, so the adage that "the wicked man flees though no man pursueth" hardly applies.

**3. No, and the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.** The Information alleged that the children were killed with a coco lumber. But the prosecution offered only the requests for DNA examination, not the results, so the Court could not presume that the blood came from the victims. The exception to the formal-offer rule did not apply: although the documents were in the records and the parties stipulated that SPO4 Agustin could identify them, the stipulation did not recite their contents. The Court said the RTC "could have taken a more proactive role by ordering motu proprio the conduct of DNA testing" under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence. Earlier testing at the behest of the police did not preclude another test, since the information was relevant and would have dispelled doubts. Nothing showed that Maricris wielded the lumber, and with about ten other occupants, someone else could have used it, or used it against another person. Abegail did not notice any blood or blood-stained clothes during her three more days in the house, which leaves open the possibility that the items were placed there after Maricris left. It also "strains credulity" that a killer would bring the bloody weapon to her own room instead of leaving or disposing of it.

Citing U.S. v. Lim Sip (a crowbar found in a shared house did not prove guilt) and U.S. v. Villos (each link in the chain must be proven to the same certainty as the main fact), the Court held that **the inculpatory facts were capable of explanations consistent with innocence, so they did not meet the test of moral certainty.** "The accused is never called upon to disprove what the prosecution has not proved," and it is better to free a guilty person than to imprison one whose guilt has not been proved by the required quantum of evidence.

### Disposition
The appeal was GRANTED. The March 11, 2021 Decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 14046 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Maricris Bazar y Bello was ACQUITTED of robbery with homicide on reasonable doubt and ordered IMMEDIATELY RELEASED unless confined for another lawful cause. The Superintendent of the Correctional Institution for Women was directed to report the action taken within five days, and entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Rico rented a room in a boarding house shared by about a dozen tenants, directly beside the house of an elderly couple. One night the couple were bludgeoned to death and their cash box was taken. Two days later, police searched the boarding house and found a blood-stained steel pipe in a common hallway near Rico's room. Rico had moved out the morning after the killing without telling the landlord. No witness saw the crime, no forensic evidence tied the blood on the pipe to the victims, and nothing showed Rico ever held the pipe. The RTC convicted Rico of robbery with homicide on these circumstances. Is the conviction proper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The circumstantial evidence does not prove Rico's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and he should be acquitted.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 133 of the Rules of Court, circumstantial evidence suffices to convict only if there is more than one circumstance, the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven, and the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The circumstances must form an unbroken chain pointing to the accused to the exclusion of all others. Where the facts can be explained in two or more ways, one consistent with innocence, the test of moral certainty is not met. In People v. Bazar (G.R. No. 259037, September 29, 2025), the Court acquitted an accused convicted on her presence in a house next to the victims, her departure, her flight, and blood-stained items found in that house. About ten others lived there, and the blood was never traced to the victims.
- **Application:** Each circumstance against Rico has an innocent explanation. Many tenants lived beside the victims. The pipe was found in a common hallway that any of a dozen tenants could reach, and nothing showed that the blood came from the victims or that Rico held the pipe. Moving out without notice to the landlord, standing alone, does not exclude other reasons. The chain does not point to Rico to the exclusion of all others. The prosecution cannot rely on the weakness of Rico's defense to fill these gaps.
- **Conclusion:** The conviction is improper; Rico must be acquitted on reasonable doubt.

**Q2.** After a robbery-killing in their neighborhood, Lorna and Jun both left town. Lorna stayed in her house across the street from the crime scene for most of the day, talking with neighbors. She left only that evening, after a friend texted her that the police had named her a suspect and that a large reward was being offered for her capture. Jun, on the other hand, fled at dawn, minutes after the killing and before anyone knew of the crime, and gave no explanation. No other evidence links either of them to the crime. (a) May either be convicted on flight alone? (b) Does Lorna's flight have the same probative value as Jun's?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Neither may be convicted on flight alone. (b) No. Lorna's flight, which was explained and came only after she learned she was being pursued, has little or no value as evidence of guilt, unlike Jun's unexplained flight before the crime was even known.
- **Legal basis:** Flight is the evading of the course of justice by voluntarily withdrawing oneself to avoid arrest or prosecution. Unexplained flight may be considered as tending to establish guilt, but flight per se does not establish guilt. It is insufficient to overcome the presumption of innocence and must be coupled with other evidence, because it is inherently ambiguous and may stem from innocent reasons such as fear of being wrongly apprehended. In People v. Bazar (G.R. No. 259037, September 29, 2025), the Court held that an accused who stayed near the crime scene for seven to eight hours and fled only after learning of a reward for her capture did not show a guilty conscience. Had she intended to hide out of guilt, she would have fled at the first opportunity.
- **Application:** (a) Since no other evidence links Lorna or Jun to the crime, flight alone cannot support a conviction for either. (b) Lorna stayed for most of the day in plain view near the scene. She left only after learning she had been named a suspect and that a reward was offered, a situation in which fear of wrongful arrest is a natural explanation, as in Bazar. Jun's unexplained departure at the first opportunity, before the crime became known, is the kind of flight that may tend to show guilt. Even so, it would need corroborating evidence to convict.
- **Conclusion:** Flight alone convicts neither, and Lorna's explained, post-pursuit flight carries far less weight than Jun's unexplained flight.

**Q3.** In a murder case resting purely on circumstantial evidence, police sent a blood-stained knife found in the accused's room to the crime laboratory, which issued a DNA report. At trial the prosecution formally offered only the letter-request for DNA examination, not the report. The parties stipulated that the laboratory officer "could identify" the report, but the stipulation said nothing about its findings. (a) May the court consider the DNA report in deciding the case? (b) What could the trial court itself have done to resolve the doubt about the source of the blood?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The DNA report was not formally offered, and the exception to the formal-offer rule does not apply because its contents were never recited in the record. (b) The trial court could have ordered DNA testing motu proprio under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 132 of the Rules of Court, the court considers only evidence that has been formally offered. In People v. Bazar (G.R. No. 259037, September 29, 2025), the Court refused to consider DNA laboratory results that were incorporated in the records and that a witness was stipulated to be able to identify, because "there was no recital of their contents, particularly the forensic findings, in the stipulated testimony"; the exception to the formal-offer rule therefore did not apply. The Court added that where the prosecution rests entirely on circumstantial evidence, the trial court may order DNA testing motu proprio under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence (A.M. No. 06-11-5-SC). Prior testing at the behest of police does not preclude another test for good reason, especially when the information is relevant to the proper resolution of the case.
- **Application:** (a) Only the letter-request was offered. The stipulation that the officer could identify the report did not put its findings into evidence, so the court cannot presume that the blood on the knife came from the victim. (b) Because the case turned on circumstantial evidence and the source of the blood was decisive, the court could have ordered DNA testing on its own, even though the police had already had the knife tested. The results could have dispelled the doubt.
- **Conclusion:** The unoffered DNA report cannot be considered, but the trial court could have ordered DNA testing motu proprio.

> Note: Hernando, J., was Acting Chairperson (Special Order No. 3224, September 15, 2025); Gesmundo, C.J., was on official leave. The CA quote of Maricris's testimony gives the drinking spree as "July 25, 2016"; the year is evidently 2015 in context. The decision cites Sabay v. People for the exceptions to the formal-offer rule but does not state them. This digest states only what the decision says about why they did not apply.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70195)

## LABEARBCO v. Babao

**LAPUY BATTALION EMPLOYEES AGRARIAN REFORM BENEFICIARIES COOPERATIVE (LABEARBCO), REPRESENTED BY ITS CHAIRMAN, MARCOS ENDRINA, PETITIONER, VS. ENRICA O. BABAO, JULIUS ANTONIUS BABAO CO, MARIA ROSALIE BABAO CO, MARIA CONCEPTION BABAO CO, JOSEPHINE BABAO CO, MARIA ELENA BABAO CO, ANTHONY CRIS CO, ENRICO TAJANLANGIT, ANA RICA C. CACHO, MAR VINCE EMMANUEL C. REYES, AND JOHN LEE VINCENT C. REYES, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 215129 | 2025-09-29 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Civil Procedure > T. Execution, Satisfaction, and Effect of Judgments (Rule 39) > 7. Effect of Judgments or Final Orders  
**Specific topics:** A judgment binds only the parties; no execution against non-parties; Treating a new case as a mere motion to execute an old judgment; Collateral attack on a Torrens title (Sec. 48, PD 1529); Grave abuse of discretion by an agrarian adjudicator
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (VI. Land Titles and Deeds (PD 1529, as amended by RA 6732 and 11573) > F. Certificate of Title)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > A. Due Process > 2. Judicial and Administrative Due Process)

### Doctrine
**A person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a case to which he was not made a party. A writ of execution may be issued only against a party, not against one who did not have his day in court** (*Green Acres Holdings v. Cabral*). This principle conforms to the constitutional guarantee of due process. An adjudicator gravely abuses its discretion when it consolidates a new case against holders of derivative titles with an old, final case and orders the old judgment implemented against them, instead of deciding the new case on the merits. Doing so treats the new case as a mere motion for execution and binds the titleholders without a hearing.

**A Torrens title cannot be altered, modified or cancelled except in a direct proceeding (Sec. 48, PD 1529).** An attack is direct when the object of the action is to annul or set aside the title, and collateral when it is made as an incident in an action for a different relief (*Hortizuela v. Tagufa*). Cancelling the derivative titles of persons who were not impleaded, by implementing a judgment that only annulled an extrajudicial settlement of estate, is a prohibited collateral attack. The Court agreed with the CA that the agrarian adjudicator (RARAD) had no jurisdiction to entertain the action for cancellation of certificates of title issued to third persons. Reiterated.

### Facts
Manuel P. Babao was the registered owner of two parcels in Lapuy, Tigatto, Davao City: TCT No. T-1460 (413,439 sq m) and TCT No. T-561 (210,025 sq m). When he died on July 10, 1984, the lands passed to his wife, Rosa Ong Chua, and daughter, Enrica. In 1989 the DAR notified Chua that the lands would be covered by CARP, and she obtained a 10-year deferment that expired on June 15, 1998. Chua died on June 10, 1996, leaving Enrica as sole heir. After the deferment expired, the DAR issued new Notices of Coverage for both titles in 1998. On March 3, 1999, Enrica executed a Deed of Extrajudicial Settlement of Manuel's estate, adjudicating the lands to herself and her children.

The DAR sued before the Provincial Agrarian Reform Adjudicator (PARAD) to annul the extrajudicial settlement (DARAB Case No. XI-1783-DC-2003, the 2003 case). Enrica et al. questioned the DARAB's jurisdiction. On September 5, 2003, the PARAD declared the settlement void and directed the Register of Deeds to reinstate the two TCTs in Manuel's name and cancel all derivative titles. No appeal was taken, and the decision became final.

The Register of Deeds did not act on the writ of execution because it was uncertain which titles to cancel. On May 22, 2008, the PARAD denied the DAR's motion for an alias writ specifying the derivative titles. It held that titles issued to persons who were not parties could not be cancelled without a direct proceeding, and the RARAD denied reconsideration. The DAR then filed DARAB Case No. XI-2057-DC-2008 (the 2008 case) to cancel the derivative titles. It impleaded Enrica et al., several other titleholders (Jaime Babado, Gunie B. Cornelio, Gloriosa Vicera, Gerino Macrohon, Manuel Co, Jesus Enrie Co and Lorenzo T. Ng), and the Register of Deeds.

On January 12, 2011, the RARAD consolidated the 2003 and 2008 cases and directed the implementation of the September 5, 2003 decision. On February 14, 2011, it denied Enrica et al.'s notice of appeal because they had not furnished the DARAB a copy, and on March 22, 2011 it denied their omnibus motion. On certiorari, the CA (December 11, 2013) annulled the three Orders. It held that the RARAD had treated the 2008 case as a mere motion for execution and nullified the derivative titles without hearing respondents who were not impleaded in the 2003 case. It also held that the RARAD had no jurisdiction to annul those titles in what amounted to a collateral attack. The CA denied reconsideration on September 23, 2014. LABEARBCO, an agrarian reform beneficiaries' cooperative, filed a Rule 45 petition.

### Issues
1. Whether the RARAD gravely abused its discretion in consolidating the 2008 case with the 2003 case and ordering the 2003 PARAD Decision implemented against the derivative titles, without hearing titleholders who were not parties to the 2003 case.
2. Whether cancelling the derivative titles in this manner was a collateral attack on the titles, beyond the RARAD's jurisdiction.

### Ruling
**1. Yes.** Grave abuse of discretion is a capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty (*Pascual v. Burgos*). The RARAD consolidated the cases, ordered the 2003 decision implemented, and declared the derivative titles void, all without giving the respondents in the 2008 case who were not impleaded in the 2003 case a chance to be heard. It "treated the second case as a mere motion to implement" the 2003 decision. This violated the due process principle that a person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a proceeding to which he was not a party. Strangers to a case are not bound by the judgment, and a writ of execution may issue only against a party (*Green Acres*). The CA correctly found grave abuse of discretion.

**2. Yes.** Under *Hortizuela v. Tagufa*, a Torrens title may be cancelled only in a direct proceeding. The 2003 case sought only the annulment of the extrajudicial settlement. The PARAD itself had refused an alias writ because the derivative titles of non-parties could not be cancelled without a direct proceeding, which is why the DAR filed the 2008 case. Yet instead of deciding the 2008 case on the merits, the RARAD used the 2003 decision to annul the derivative titles of persons never impleaded in it. **This was a collateral attack, because the relief sought in the 2003 case was the annulment of the extrajudicial settlement, not the cancellation of those titles.** The RARAD thus gravely abused its discretion, and the Court agreed with the CA that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the action for cancellation of certificates of title issued to third persons.

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The CA's December 11, 2013 Decision and September 23, 2014 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 04191-MIN, which annulled and set aside the RARAD's Orders of January 12, February 14 and March 22, 2011, were AFFIRMED.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In a final judgment, the RTC annulled a deed of extrajudicial settlement executed by Ana and her children. It ordered the Register of Deeds to reinstate the mother title in the decedent's name and to cancel "all derivative titles." Before the suit, Ana's son had sold portions of the land to Ben and Carmen, who obtained their own TCTs. Ben and Carmen were never impleaded. The winning party now moves for an alias writ of execution directing the cancellation of Ben's and Carmen's titles. Should the motion be granted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The judgment cannot be executed against Ben and Carmen, and their titles cannot be cancelled this way.
- **Legal basis:** A person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in an action to which he was not made a party, and a writ of execution may issue only against a party, not against one who did not have his day in court. Under Section 48 of PD 1529, a certificate of title cannot be altered, modified or cancelled except in a direct proceeding; an attack made as an incident of an action for a different relief is collateral. (LABEARBCO v. Babao, G.R. No. 215129, September 29, 2025)
- **Application:** Ben and Carmen were strangers to the annulment case and were never heard, so the judgment does not bind them. The object of that case was to annul the extrajudicial settlement, not to cancel their titles, so cancelling their titles through an alias writ would be a collateral attack. The winning party must file a direct action to annul their titles, impleading them.
- **Conclusion:** The motion for an alias writ should be denied as to Ben's and Carmen's titles.

**Q2.** After the alias writ was denied, the winning party filed a separate complaint before the RTC to annul Ben's and Carmen's titles, impleading both. (a) Ben moves to dismiss, arguing that the complaint is a prohibited collateral attack on his Torrens title. Is he correct? (b) Suppose the court, instead of trying the new case, consolidates it with the old annulment case and, without hearing Ben and Carmen, orders the old judgment implemented to cancel their titles. Is that order valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The new complaint is a direct attack on the titles. (b) No. The order is a grave abuse of discretion because it binds non-parties without a hearing and cancels their titles collaterally.
- **Legal basis:** An attack on a title is direct when the object of the action is to annul or set it aside, and collateral when it is made as an incident of an action for a different relief (Sec. 48, PD 1529; Hortizuela v. Tagufa). A tribunal that consolidates a new case against titleholders with an old, final case and orders the old judgment implemented against them, treating the new case as a mere motion for execution without hearing them, gravely abuses its discretion. (LABEARBCO v. Babao, G.R. No. 215129, September 29, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The sole object of the new complaint is to annul Ben's and Carmen's titles, and both are impleaded, so it is the direct proceeding Section 48 requires. (b) Consolidating the new case with the old one and simply implementing the old judgment is exactly what the RARAD did in LABEARBCO. It denies Ben and Carmen their day in court and cancels their titles through a judgment that sought a different relief.
- **Conclusion:** Ben's motion to dismiss should be denied, but the court must decide the new case on the merits after hearing Ben and Carmen; an order simply implementing the old judgment against them is void for grave abuse of discretion.

**Q3.** An agrarian adjudicator ordered a final decision annulling a deed of extrajudicial settlement to be implemented by cancelling the titles of Dario, who bought part of the land and was never a party to that case. Dario was not given notice or a hearing. Dario filed a petition for certiorari with the Court of Appeals, invoking due process. The cooperative that benefits from the order argues that executing a final and executory decision is a ministerial duty, so there can be no grave abuse of discretion. Who is correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Dario is correct. The adjudicator gravely abused its discretion and violated his right to due process.
- **Legal basis:** Grave abuse of discretion is a capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty (Pascual v. Burgos). The principle that a person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a proceeding to which he was not a party conforms to the constitutional guarantee of due process (Const., Art. III, Sec. 1). Strangers to a case are not bound by the judgment, and a writ of execution may issue only against a party. (LABEARBCO v. Babao, G.R. No. 215129, September 29, 2025)
- **Application:** Whatever ministerial character execution has extends only to the parties bound by the judgment. Dario was a stranger to the annulment case, so the final decision cannot be enforced against him. Cancelling his title without notice or hearing deprives him of property without due process, and doing so through a decision that granted a different relief is a collateral attack on his title. That is an arbitrary exercise of power amounting to grave abuse of discretion.
- **Conclusion:** The adjudicator's order should be annulled on certiorari for grave abuse of discretion.

> Note: First Division. Hernando, J. (Acting Chairperson), Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred; Gesmundo, C.J. was on official leave. The Court did not separately address two of the petitioner's arguments. The first was that the notice of appeal was properly denied under Rule XIV, Section 1 of the 2003 DARAB Rules (failure to furnish the DARAB a copy). The second was that the CA should not have set aside the January 12, 2011 Order, which was not assailed. The affirmance rests on the grave abuse of discretion found.

The text has apparent typographical errors. It refers several times to a "September 5, 2023" decision; the PARAD Decision is dated September 5, 2003. The quoted *Hortizuela* passage cites "P.D. No. 1528" for PD 1529. The discussion ends by declaring "all proceedings rendered in DARAB Case No. XI-1783-DC-2003" void, although it concerns the RARAD's orders in the 2008 case (DARAB Case No. XI-2057-DC-2008); the fallo only affirms the CA. The decision does not explain how LABEARBCO became a party.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70190)

## People v. Peralta

**PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. RUDY PERALTA Y MABBONAG, CESAR LIBAN Y PERALTA, PHILIP SORIANO Y PASION, ADVIENTO SORIANO Y PASION, ROBERTO SORIANO Y PASION, FERDINAND SORIANO Y PASION ALIAS 'MAR,' AND NAPOLEON LIBAN (AT LARGE), ACCUSED; RUDY PERALTA Y MABBONAG AND CESAR LIBAN Y PERALTA, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.**  
G.R. No. 257105 | 2025-08-27 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Criminal Procedure > B. Prosecution of Offenses (Rule 110) > 6. Complaint or Information > d. Amendment and Substitution  
**Specific topics:** Amendment of an information before plea: a matter of right, with no leave and no order of admission needed; Amended information ipso facto supersedes the original; Frustrated murder to murder after the victim's death is a formal amendment (Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag); No re-arraignment needed for a formal amendment; Death of an accused pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto
  
**Also relevant to:** Criminal Law (II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > D. Extinction of Criminal Liability > 1. Total Extinction > a. Death of Convict)

### Doctrine
**Before the accused pleads, an information may be amended in form or in substance without leave of court, and the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original. No motion to admit it and no order admitting it are needed** (Rule 110, Section 14, Rules of Court). The exception is an amendment before plea that downgrades the nature of the offense or excludes an accused. That kind of amendment may be made only on the prosecutor's motion, with notice to the offended party and with leave of court. The Court likened the rule to a plaintiff's right to amend a complaint before a responsive pleading is served, where the amended pleading supersedes the original without an order of admission (Rule 10, Section 8). A later court order "admitting" such an amended information is "a superfluity."

**Changing an information from frustrated murder to murder after the victim dies is only a formal amendment.** Frustrated murder is a stage in the execution of murder and is necessarily included in it. The victim's death is a supervening fact that bears only on the penalty, and every defense available under the original information remains available (reiterating *Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag*). Such an amendment needs no new preliminary investigation and **no re-arraignment**. The purpose of arraignment, to inform the accused of the nature and cause of the accusation, was already served at the first arraignment.

When an accused-appellant dies before final judgment, his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto are totally extinguished (Article 89(1), Revised Penal Code; *People v. Bayotas*). Claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation are not affected.

### Facts
On or about June 11, 1994, in Baggao, Cagayan, an armed group that included Rudy Peralta and Cesar Liban went to the house of Virgilio Remigio. They ordered AAA to knock on the door and tell Virgilio that policemen were with her, and one of the group shot Virgilio and his son. An Information dated September 30, 1994 (Criminal Case No. 6621) charged Peralta, Liban and others with frustrated murder. It alleged conspiracy, intent to kill, evident premeditation, treachery and the aggravating circumstance of dwelling. Virgilio died on November 19, 1994. The prosecution then filed an Amended Information dated January 26, 1995 charging the same accused with murder, with the same allegations plus the fact of death.

Peralta's certificate of arraignment shows that he pleaded not guilty on January 30, 1995 to "the crime charged," without naming the crime. Liban, who had been at large, pleaded not guilty to murder on June 24, 1999. At trial, co-accused Lito Acierto was discharged as a state witness and testified to the events of that night.

After the prosecution rested, the defense filed a demurrer to evidence. Among other things, it argued that the RTC never admitted the Amended Information, so the accused could be tried only for frustrated murder. The RTC denied the demurrer on August 30, 2007. In an Order dated September 10, 2007, it then admitted the Amended Information and set a new arraignment. The PAO moved for reconsideration, invoking the right to speedy trial and double jeopardy; the records show no resolution of that motion. At trial, Peralta and Liban each testified that they were at home that night.

In its August 24, 2010 Judgment, the RTC convicted Peralta, Liban and Philip Soriano of murder in Criminal Case No. 6621. It imposed reclusion perpetua and awarded PHP 50,000.00 civil indemnity, PHP 50,000.00 moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 actual damages. On appeal, the accused argued that they had pleaded only to frustrated murder. The CA affirmed on March 19, 2014 (CA-G.R. CR-H.C. No. 04713) and added 6% legal interest. Peralta and Liban appealed to the Supreme Court; Philip did not. Peralta died on October 25, 2023, while the appeal was pending.

### Issues
1. Whether Peralta's death pending appeal extinguished his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto.
2. Whether the prosecution proved Liban's guilt for murder beyond reasonable doubt.
3. Whether Liban could be convicted of murder although the RTC issued an order admitting the Amended Information only in 2007, and the accused claimed they were arraigned only for frustrated murder.
4. Whether the penalty and damages imposed were correct.

### Ruling
**1. Yes.** Peralta died on October 25, 2023, before final judgment. Under Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code, his criminal liability is totally extinguished, and the dismissal of Criminal Case No. 6621 as to him follows as a matter of course. His civil liability ex delicto is also extinguished, but claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation, if any, remain unaffected (*People v. Bayotas*).

**2. Yes.** The Court found no reason to reverse the CA as to Liban. The elements of murder were proved. Only one malefactor shot Virgilio, but conspiracy was proved and may be inferred from the accused's concerted acts, since they arrived at the scene together and fully armed. Their alibi was inherently weak against their positive identification by credible witnesses, and the trial court's findings deserve the highest respect.

**3. Yes, the murder conviction stands, and no order admitting the Amended Information was needed.** Under Rule 110, Section 14, an information may be amended in form or substance without leave of court at any time before the accused pleads. "Without leave of court" means the prosecution need not ask the court's permission to amend before plea, as long as the amendment does not downgrade the offense or exclude an accused. This works like a civil complaint amended as a matter of right (Rule 10, Section 8): **the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original, without a motion to admit it and without further action from the court.** The RTC's 2007 Order admitting the Amended Information was therefore "a superfluity." It did not dismiss the original Information, which the 1995 amendment had already superseded. The accused also never moved to quash the Amended Information, and their own notice of appeal called the case one "for murder."

In any case, the amendment was merely formal. Quoting *Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag*, the Court explained that frustrated murder is a stage in the execution of murder and is necessarily included in it. The supervening fact of death only helps the court fix the penalty. The prosecution's theory, a felonious act done with intent to kill, stays the same, and any defense under the original information applies equally to the amended one. **Even if the accused had pleaded only to frustrated murder, re-arraignment was unnecessary, because a formal amendment does not require a second arraignment.** The purpose of arraignment was achieved at the first arraignment. The amendment could not have surprised the accused, since it charged no new offense and did not change the prosecution's theory.

**4. The penalty was affirmed, and the damages were modified.** Murder is punished by reclusion perpetua to death. The ordinary aggravating circumstance of dwelling would have warranted death, but Republic Act No. 9346 prohibits the death penalty, so the RTC correctly imposed reclusion perpetua. Under the Court's guidelines on non-eligibility for parole, the Court added the phrase "without eligibility for parole." It raised civil indemnity and moral damages to PHP 100,000.00 each and added PHP 100,000.00 exemplary damages (*People v. Jugueta*). Because no evidence of burial or funeral expenses was presented, it replaced the PHP 100,000.00 actual damages with PHP 50,000.00 temperate damages.

### Disposition
The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA Decision dated March 19, 2014 in CA-G.R. CR-H.C. No. 04713 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION as to Cesar Liban y Peralta. In Criminal Case No. 6621, he was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of murder and sentenced to reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole. He was ordered to pay the heirs of Virgilio Remigio PHP 100,000.00 civil indemnity, PHP 100,000.00 moral damages, PHP 100,000.00 exemplary damages and PHP 50,000.00 temperate damages, all earning 6% interest per annum from finality of the decision until fully paid. The award of actual damages was DELETED. Criminal Case No. 6621 was DISMISSED as to Rudy Peralta y Mabbonag because of his death.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Nestor was charged with frustrated murder for treacherously stabbing Oscar. Two weeks later, before Nestor's arraignment, Oscar died of his wounds. The prosecutor filed an Amended Information charging Nestor with murder, with the same allegations plus the fact of Oscar's death. The court never issued an order admitting the Amended Information. Nestor was arraigned and pleaded not guilty "to the crime charged." After the prosecution rested, Nestor argued that without an order admitting the Amended Information, the only charge pending against him is frustrated murder, so he cannot be convicted of murder. Is Nestor correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The Amended Information for murder superseded the original Information when it was filed. No order admitting it was necessary.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 110, Section 14 of the Rules of Court, a complaint or information may be amended, in form or in substance, without leave of court at any time before the accused enters his plea. The exception is an amendment that downgrades the offense or excludes an accused. Because an amendment before plea is a matter of right, the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original, without a motion to admit or an order admitting it; a later order of admission is a superfluity. (People v. Peralta, G.R. No. 257105, August 27, 2025)
- **Application:** The Amended Information was filed before Nestor pleaded. It neither downgraded the offense nor dropped any accused; it changed frustrated murder to murder because of Oscar's death. It therefore needed no leave and no order of admission, and it superseded the original Information as soon as it was filed. Nestor was arraigned after the amendment, so the charge he answered was murder.
- **Conclusion:** Nestor may be convicted of murder; the absence of an order admitting the Amended Information does not matter.

**Q2.** Paolo was charged with frustrated murder for shooting Quintin with treachery. Paolo was arraigned and pleaded not guilty. During trial, Quintin died of the gunshot wound. Over Paolo's objection, the court gave the prosecution leave to amend the Information to murder, alleging the same facts plus Quintin's death. Paolo argues that (a) the amendment is substantial and can no longer be made after his plea, and (b) in any event, he must be arraigned anew on the murder charge. Rule on both contentions.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The amendment is valid. It is only a formal amendment, which may be made after plea with leave of court. (b) Paolo need not be arraigned anew.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 110, Section 14, after the plea and during trial, a formal amendment may be made only with leave of court and when it can be done without prejudice to the rights of the accused. Amending frustrated murder to murder because the victim later died is merely formal. Frustrated murder is a stage of murder and is necessarily included in it, the death bears only on the penalty, and every defense under the original information remains available (Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag, reiterated in People v. Peralta, G.R. No. 257105, August 27, 2025). Unlike a substantial amendment, a formal amendment does not require a second arraignment, because the purpose of arraignment was already served at the first one (People v. Peralta).
- **Application:** (a) The Amended Information charges the same offense at a later stage of execution. The prosecution's theory, a shooting with intent to kill and treachery, is unchanged, and any defense Paolo had against frustrated murder applies equally to murder. The amendment is formal, and since the court gave leave and Paolo suffers no prejudice, it is allowed even during trial; his objection does not bar it. (b) Paolo was informed of the nature and cause of the accusation at his first arraignment. The amendment charges no new offense and cannot surprise him, so re-arraignment is unnecessary. A new preliminary investigation is likewise not required for a formal amendment.
- **Conclusion:** The amendment to murder is valid, and Paolo may be tried and convicted of murder without a new arraignment.

**Q3.** The RTC convicted Rico of murder and ordered him to pay the victim's heirs civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages. The CA affirmed. While Rico's appeal to the Supreme Court was pending, he died in prison. The victim's heirs asked the Supreme Court to affirm the judgment at least as to the damages, so they could collect from Rico's estate. (a) What is the effect of Rico's death on his criminal liability and on his civil liability arising from the crime? (b) Do the heirs have any remaining recourse?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Rico's criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto are both totally extinguished, and the case must be dismissed as to him. (b) The heirs may pursue only civil liability based on sources of obligation other than the crime, if any exist.
- **Legal basis:** Under Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code, the death of the convict totally extinguishes criminal liability as to personal penalties, and as to pecuniary penalties when death occurs before final judgment. Death before final judgment also extinguishes civil liability ex delicto, but claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation remain unaffected (People v. Bayotas). This was applied in People v. Peralta (G.R. No. 257105, August 27, 2025), where the case was dismissed as to an accused-appellant who died while his appeal was pending.
- **Application:** Rico died while his appeal was pending, before any final judgment. His criminal liability and the civil liability arising solely from the murder are extinguished. The Court must therefore dismiss the case as to him rather than affirm the award of damages. If the heirs have a claim against Rico based on another source of obligation, such as law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict, that claim survives his death and may still be pursued against his estate.
- **Conclusion:** Rico's death pending appeal extinguishes his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto, leaving the heirs only claims based on other sources of obligation.

> Note: The short title follows the first-named accused-appellant. Peralta died pending appeal, so the conviction stands only against Liban. Philip Soriano did not appeal to the Supreme Court, and a partial entry of judgment was issued as to him. The body quotes the older text of Rule 110, Section 14; footnote 38 quotes the current text, including the paragraph on amendments before plea that downgrade the offense or exclude an accused. Footnote 24 notes two versions of the RTC Judgment, one quoting the frustrated-murder Information and one quoting the Amended Information; both convict for murder. The E-Library text cites the parole guidelines as "A.M. No. 15-08-0-SC" (apparently truncated), so the digest refers to them by title. The victim AAA is anonymized in the decision.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70114)
