## Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te

**DEVELOPMENT BANK OF THE PHILIPPINES, REPRESENTED BY ITS GENERAL SANTOS CITY BRANCH HEAD, MARIELA LUZ T. CORTEZ, PETITIONER, VS. MANUEL TE, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 260664 | 2025-08-18 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Resolution

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Civil Procedure > T. Execution, Satisfaction, and Effect of Judgments (Rule 39) > 1. Immutability of Final Judgments; Exceptions  
**Specific topics:** Immutability of a final judgment of indirect contempt; Later (partial) compliance cannot undo a final contempt judgment; Civil vs. criminal contempt; direct vs. indirect contempt (Rule 71); An order modifying a final judgment is void; affirming it is grave abuse of discretion

### Doctrine
**A judgment finding a person guilty of indirect contempt, once final and executory, is immutable. The trial court cannot later lift it, or remove the penalties it imposed, because the contemnor has since (even partly) complied with the order he disobeyed.** Under the doctrine of finality or immutability of judgments, a final decision may no longer be modified in any respect, even to correct erroneous conclusions of fact or law. Any amendment that substantially affects it is null and void for lack of jurisdiction, as are the proceedings held for that purpose (Industrial Management International Development Corp. v. NLRC; Eusebio v. CSC, reiterated). An order that is worded as a recognition of compliance but in practice nullifies the final contempt judgment is an impermissible modification, and an appellate court that affirms it commits grave abuse of discretion.

Contempt is direct (committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct the administration of justice) or indirect (willful disobedience of the lawful process or order of the court). Contempt proceedings are sui generis. They are civil when the dominant purpose is remedial, to compel obedience to an order for the benefit of a party, and criminal when it is punitive, to vindicate the dignity and authority of the court (Lorenzo Shipping, reiterated). **Even when the contempt is civil in nature, the final judgment imposing it can no longer be disturbed.**

### Facts
In Civil Case No. 347 before the RTC of Polomolok, South Cotabato, Branch 39, Manuel Te, as attorney-in-fact of the Abedin group, sued DBP to recover 131 certificates of title and 34 other proofs of ownership that the group had surrendered as security for a loan. The RTC issued a writ of replevin; DBP surrendered the documents to the sheriff, who handed them to Te. Te then moved to dismiss the case because the Abedin group had lost interest in prosecuting it. On March 2, 2004, the RTC denied the motion and ordered Te, as the group's attorney-in-fact, to surrender to the court the titles and other proofs of ownership within 30 days. It denied his motion for partial reconsideration on October 11, 2004.

Te did not surrender all the documents, so DBP filed a petition for indirect contempt on December 1, 2010. On April 16, 2014, the RTC found Te guilty and sentenced him to a fine of PHP 30,000 and imprisonment of two months "or until he duly complies" with the court's order, under Rule 71, Sections 3(b) and (d) and 7. The CA affirmed. The Supreme Court denied Te's petition (G.R. No. 225250) on September 14, 2016 and his motion for reconsideration with finality on June 18, 2018, and entry of judgment issued.

Te later filed a Manifestation of Compliance with the RTC. He claimed that he had recovered 12 out of the 131 certificates of title and 34 proofs of ownership, and that the March 2, 2004 Order was directed to the Abedin group, not to him. On July 17, 2020, the RTC deemed its orders complied with and lifted the order of contempt. It found no willful disregard of its order because the titles had already been returned to the landowners, a matter beyond Te's control, and stated that despite the finality of its judgment it could still exercise discretion on whether to impose the penalty. DBP's motion for reconsideration was denied. On October 29, 2021, the CA dismissed DBP's petition for certiorari. It held that the RTC did not modify a final judgment but only gave effect to Te's compliance, and that DBP showed no grave abuse of discretion. The CA denied reconsideration on March 16, 2022.

### Issues
1. Whether the contempt proceedings against Te were civil or criminal in nature.
2. Whether a final and executory judgment of indirect contempt may be lifted because of the contemnor's later compliance with the order he disobeyed, and whether the CA gravely abused its discretion in affirming the RTC order that did so.

### Ruling
**1. The contempt was civil in nature.** Citing Lorenzo Shipping, the Court explained that contempt is direct or indirect, and that contempt proceedings, being sui generis, are criminal when their primary purpose is punishment (vindicating the dignity of the court) and civil when it is compensatory or remedial (enforcing compliance with an order for the benefit of a party). Te had been found guilty of indirect contempt for failing to obey the March 2, 2004 Order, and DBP filed the contempt case as a remedial measure to compel his compliance, so the proceedings were civil.

**2. No, the final judgment could not be lifted, and the CA gravely abused its discretion.** A final decision becomes immutable and may not be modified in any respect, even to correct errors of fact or law. An amendment that substantially affects it is void for lack of jurisdiction, as are the proceedings held for that purpose. In Eusebio v. CSC, the Court reversed the CA's reduction of a fine imposed in a final judgment of indirect contempt. The Court stressed that this principle is "especially vital in cases involving judgments for indirect contempt, which are punitive in nature and rendered after due process." Here, the Court itself had affirmed the contempt judgment in G.R. No. 225250. **Te's later attempt to comply "cannot operate to invalidate or undo a judgment that has long attained finality."** Although the RTC presented its order as a recognition of compliance, its practical effect was to nullify the final judgment and remove the penalties. That was an impermissible modification, and the proceedings for it were void ab initio for lack of jurisdiction; a lower court has no authority to alter a final ruling, least of all one upheld by the Supreme Court. **By affirming this patently void order, the CA acted capriciously and arbitrarily, amounting to grave abuse of discretion.**

### Disposition
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated October 29, 2021 and Resolution dated March 16, 2022 in CA-G.R. SP No. 10244-MIN, which affirmed the RTC's July 17, 2020 Order lifting the contempt, were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Te was directed to STRICTLY COMPLY with the Orders of the RTC of Polomolok, South Cotabato, Branch 39 dated March 2, 2004 and "October 11, 2014" (as written in the fallo; see notes).

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** The RTC found Gerry guilty of indirect contempt for refusing to deposit in court the original titles he had been ordered to surrender, and sentenced him to a fine of PHP 30,000 and imprisonment of two months or until he complies. The judgment was affirmed on appeal and became final and executory in 2022. In 2024, Gerry turned over a few of the titles and filed a manifestation of compliance, explaining that the rest were already with the landowners and beyond his control. The RTC deemed its order complied with and lifted the contempt judgment and its penalties. Was the RTC's order valid?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The order is void because it modified a final and executory judgment.
- **Legal basis:** Under the doctrine of finality or immutability of judgments, a final decision may no longer be modified in any respect, even to correct errors of fact or law, and any amendment that substantially affects it is void for lack of jurisdiction. A contemnor's later attempt to comply cannot invalidate or undo a final judgment of indirect contempt. An order that lifts the contempt and removes its penalties is an impermissible modification even if it is worded as a recognition of compliance. (Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te, G.R. No. 260664, August 18, 2025)
- **Application:** The contempt judgment against Gerry became final in 2022. The RTC's 2024 order speaks of compliance, but in practice it nullifies that judgment by removing the fine and the imprisonment. Whatever Gerry's reasons for delivering only some of the titles, they could not reopen a judgment that the RTC no longer had jurisdiction to alter.
- **Conclusion:** The RTC's order lifting the contempt is void because it violates the immutability of final judgments.

**Q2.** Same facts as above, but Gerry argues that the contempt was civil, not criminal, because the bank filed it to compel him to deliver the titles for the bank's benefit. Since the purpose of civil contempt is coercive, he says, that purpose is served once he complies, and the court may lift the penalty even after finality. (a) Is the contempt civil or criminal? (b) Does its civil character allow the court to lift the final judgment?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) It is civil contempt. (b) No. Even a civil contempt judgment, once final, cannot be lifted or modified because of later compliance.
- **Legal basis:** Contempt proceedings are sui generis. They are civil when the dominant purpose is to enforce compliance with an order for the benefit of a party, and criminal when the dominant purpose is to vindicate the dignity and authority of the court (Lorenzo Shipping Corp. v. Distribution Management Association of the Philippines). In Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te (G.R. No. 260664, August 18, 2025), the Court found the contempt civil because it was filed to ensure compliance with a court order, yet held that the final judgment could not be lifted upon the contemnor's later compliance, because doing so would violate the immutability of judgments.
- **Application:** The bank sued to compel Gerry to deliver the titles for its benefit, so the contempt is civil. But the nature of the contempt does not change the effect of finality. The judgment, including its penalties, became immutable, and the RTC lost jurisdiction to alter it. Gerry's partial delivery cannot reopen it.
- **Conclusion:** The contempt is civil, but the final judgment still cannot be lifted on account of Gerry's later compliance.

**Q3.** (a) Distinguish direct contempt from indirect contempt. (b) After the RTC lifted a final judgment of indirect contempt, the aggrieved party filed a petition for certiorari with the Court of Appeals. The CA dismissed it, reasoning that the petition merely questioned how the RTC appreciated the contemnor's compliance, which is at most an error of judgment, not grave abuse of discretion. Is the CA correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Direct contempt is committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct the administration of justice; indirect contempt is willful disobedience of a lawful process or order of the court. (b) No. The RTC order is void for lack of jurisdiction, and the CA gravely abused its discretion in upholding it.
- **Legal basis:** Direct contempt is committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct him in the administration of justice; indirect or constructive contempt consists of willful disobedience of the lawful process or order of the court. Proceedings to amend a final and executory judgment are void ab initio for lack of jurisdiction, and a court that affirms such a patently void order acts with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. (Development Bank of the Philippines v. Te, G.R. No. 260664, August 18, 2025, citing Lorenzo Shipping Corp. v. Distribution Management Association of the Philippines)
- **Application:** (a) Refusing to surrender documents as the court ordered is disobedience of a lawful order committed outside the court's presence, so it is indirect contempt. (b) The RTC's order is not a mere mistake in weighing compliance. By lifting a judgment that had become final, the RTC acted without jurisdiction, which is exactly the kind of defect that certiorari corrects. In refusing to annul the order and leaving it in force, the CA committed grave abuse of discretion, as the Supreme Court held in DBP v. Te.
- **Conclusion:** The CA is wrong; it should have annulled the RTC order that lifted the final contempt judgment.

> Note: Dates in the source text are inconsistent. The facts give the denial of Te's partial reconsideration as October 11, 2004, but the fallo directs compliance with the Orders dated March 2, 2004 and "October 11, 2014." The 2014 contempt decision refers to an "ORDER dated 4 March 2004," and the RTC's July 17, 2020 Order calls the Orders dated March 2, 2004 and "April 16, 2004" the "Contempt Order," although the contempt decision itself is dated April 16, 2014. The Court did not rule on whether Te actually had the remaining titles or whether the March 2, 2004 Order was directed to him personally; its holding rests only on the immutability of the final contempt judgment. The resolution calls the proceedings civil (remedial) in nature but also describes judgments for indirect contempt as "punitive in nature." Although a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, the case was decided on whether the CA committed grave abuse of discretion.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70080)

## Manongsong v. Atty. Reyes

**MARIFE C. MANONGSONG, COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. ARIEL M. REYES, RESPONDENT.**  
A.C. No. 13998 (Formerly CBD Case No. 22-6799) | 2025-08-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 9. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers (Canon VI) > c. Charges and Sanctions  
**Specific topics:** Worthless check and nonpayment of just debts as gross misconduct (Canon II); Mitigating circumstances under Canon VI, Section 38 (remorse, pandemic hardship, partial payment); Disobedience to IBP orders as a separate less serious offense (Canon III, Sec. 2; Canon VI, Sec. 34(c)); Penalties for serious and less serious offenses under the CPRA

### Doctrine
**A lawyer who issues a check that is later dishonored for having been drawn against a closed account, and who reneges on repeated promises to pay a just debt, commits gross misconduct** in violation of Canon II, Sections 1 (proper conduct) and 2 (dignified conduct) of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA). Such conduct shows "a lack of personal honesty and good moral character as to render him or her unworthy of public confidence" (reiterating *Wilkie v. Atty. Limos*, *Lao v. Atty. Medel* and *Tan v. Atty. Pangan*). Gross misconduct is a serious offense punishable by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, or a combination (Canon VI, Section 33 in relation to Section 37).

The Court may temper the penalty by appreciating mitigating circumstances under Canon VI, Section 38(a), including expression of remorse, humanitarian considerations and other analogous circumstances. **The lawyer's plea acknowledging a "wrong personal economic decision aggravated by the pandemic," the adverse impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on lawyers in private practice, and his partial payment (the first PHP 500,000.00 check cleared) justified a suspension of only six months**, consistent with *Egger v. Atty. Duran*, which reduced a one-year suspension to six months because of financial hardship caused by Typhoon Yolanda.

**A lawyer's unjustified failure to obey the IBP's orders in the disciplinary case** (to file a mandatory conference brief, appear at the mandatory conference, and file a position paper) **violates Canon III, Section 2 and is a less serious offense under Canon VI, Section 34(c)**, punishable by suspension of one to six months, a fine of PHP 35,000.00 to PHP 100,000.00, or both. It is **a separate and distinct offense**, unrelated to the mitigating circumstances appreciated on the main charge; following *Grand Pillar International Development, Inc. v. Atty. Cruz*, the Court imposed a PHP 50,000.00 fine. These are reiterated rules applied under the CPRA.

### Facts
Sometime in 2019, Atty. Ariel Reyes borrowed PHP 1 million from Marife Manongsong for the operational expenses of his law firm and law practice. As security, he issued two Metrobank checks of PHP 500,000.00 each. Manongsong encashed the first check as partial payment, but the second was dishonored for being drawn against a closed account.

When Manongsong demanded payment, Atty. Reyes promised to pay on a certain date, then proposed a new date, and the cycle continued. Manongsong hired a lawyer and served a demand letter at his law office, received by his secretary on September 22, 2022; a copy sent by LBC to his residence was received by his helper on September 9, 2022. He still did not settle, could no longer be reached by text, and could not be located at his residential and office addresses. Manongsong filed a complaint for gross misconduct with the IBP Commission on Bar Discipline.

In his Answer, Atty. Reyes pleaded for understanding and consideration, saying he had no malicious intent and was "financially devastated caused by wrong personal economic decision aggravated by the pandemic." He then failed, without explanation, to submit his mandatory conference brief, to appear at the mandatory conference, and to submit his position paper despite due notice.

The IBP Investigating Commissioner (Report and Recommendation dated May 2, 2023) found him guilty of gross misconduct for issuing a worthless check and recommended a one-year suspension. The IBP Board of Governors (Resolution dated June 2, 2023) modified the penalty to a six-month suspension.

### Issues
1. Whether respondent committed gross misconduct for issuing a check that was dishonored and for failing to pay his debt.
2. What penalty is proper for the gross misconduct, considering the mitigating circumstances.
3. Whether respondent is separately liable for disregarding the orders of the IBP in the disciplinary proceedings.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, he committed gross misconduct.** Lawyers must maintain a high standard of morality, honesty, integrity and fair dealing, and their duties to society include prompt payment of financial obligations. Under Canon II, Section 1 of the CPRA, a lawyer shall not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct; under Section 2, a lawyer shall not engage in conduct that adversely reflects on one's fitness to practice law, whether in public or private life. "A lawyer's issuance of checks which were later dishonored for having been drawn against a closed account indicates a lawyer's unfitness for the trust and confidence reposed on him or her." In *Tan v. Atty. Pangan*, reneging on a promise to return money despite repeated demands, issuing a bouncing check, and the substantial sum involved amounted to gross misconduct. Here, Atty. Reyes had an outstanding PHP 500,000.00 loan; his check was dishonored for being drawn against a closed account, in violation of BP 22; and he repeatedly reneged on his promises to pay, so that the complainant had to engage another lawyer to demand payment. **These acts constitute gross misconduct.**

**2. Six-month suspension, in view of mitigating circumstances.** Gross misconduct is a serious offense punishable by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, or a combination; in *Lao v. Atty. Medel*, deliberate failure to pay just debts and issuing worthless checks warranted a one-year suspension. But Canon VI, Section 38(a) allows the Court, in its discretion, to appreciate mitigating circumstances, including expression of remorse, humanitarian considerations and other analogous circumstances. The Court found that Atty. Reyes's plea and his acknowledgment of a "wrong personal economic decision aggravated by the pandemic" reflected "a measure of remorse," and that the COVID-19 pandemic had significantly affected the livelihood of many, including lawyers in private practice. Even before the CPRA, the Court had been lenient when mitigating factors were present, as in *Egger v. Atty. Duran* (2016). In addition, the clearing of the first PHP 500,000.00 check "manifests the respondent's intent and good faith to repay his loan." **A six-month suspension was therefore a sufficient penalty.**

**3. Yes, he is separately fined for defying the IBP.** Canon III, Section 2 requires a lawyer to promote respect for laws and legal processes and to conscientiously assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice. Without any justifiable reason, Atty. Reyes failed to submit a mandatory conference brief, to appear at the mandatory conference, and to submit his position paper despite due notice. Under Canon VI, Section 34(c), willful and deliberate disobedience of the orders of the Supreme Court and the IBP is a less serious offense, punishable by suspension of one to six months, a fine of PHP 35,000.00 to PHP 100,000.00, or both. In *Grand Pillar International Development, Inc. v. Atty. Cruz*, the Court described IBP-CBD orders as "not mere requests but directives which should be complied with promptly and completely" and imposed a PHP 50,000.00 fine for similar noncompliance. Given the striking similarity, the Court imposed the same fine.

The Court stressed that the power to discipline lawyers is exercised to protect the public, not to punish, and that sanctions affecting a lawyer's livelihood must be imposed with great caution. Its leniency, however, "should not be construed as a license for impunity": **the defiance of the IBP's orders is a separate and distinct offense, unrelated to the mitigating circumstances, and his financial difficulties "neither justify nor explain" it.**

### Disposition
Atty. Ariel M. Reyes was found GUILTY of violating Canons II and III of the CPRA and SUSPENDED from the practice of law for six months, effective immediately upon receipt of the Decision. He was also FINED PHP 50,000.00 for his repeated disobedience to the orders of the IBP, payable to the Court within 10 days from receipt, with proof of compliance to be submitted within 10 days from payment. He was directed to file a Manifestation that his suspension has started, stating the exact date of receipt of the Decision, copy furnished all courts and quasi-judicial bodies where he has appeared as counsel. Copies were ordered furnished to the Office of the Court Administrator (for dissemination to all courts), the IBP, and the Office of the Bar Confidant (to be appended to his personal record).

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Atty. Lito borrowed PHP 800,000.00 from his neighbor Mila to pay for his family's personal expenses and issued two checks of PHP 400,000.00 each. The first check was paid, but the second was dishonored because the account had been closed. For two years Atty. Lito kept promising to pay on new dates but never did, until Mila had to hire a lawyer to send him a demand letter, which he ignored. Mila filed an administrative complaint. Atty. Lito argues that the loan was a purely private transaction unrelated to his practice of law, so he cannot be disciplined. (a) Is Atty. Lito administratively liable, and for what offense? (b) What sanctions may be imposed for that offense under the CPRA?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Atty. Lito is liable for gross misconduct in violation of Canon II of the CPRA. (b) Being a serious offense, it is punishable by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, or a combination of these.
- **Legal basis:** Canon II, Section 1 of the CPRA bars a lawyer from engaging in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct, and Section 2 bars conduct that adversely reflects on one's fitness to practice law, whether in public or private life. A lawyer's issuance of a check later dishonored for being drawn against a closed account, together with reneging on repeated promises to pay a just debt, constitutes gross misconduct. Gross misconduct is a serious offense punishable under Canon VI, Section 33 in relation to Section 37 by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, or a combination. (Manongsong v. Atty. Reyes, A.C. No. 13998, August 13, 2025, citing Tan v. Atty. Pangan and Lao v. Atty. Medel)
- **Application:** Atty. Lito issued a check that bounced because the account was closed, and for two years he broke his promises to pay, forcing Mila to engage counsel. That the loan was personal is no defense: Canon II, Section 2 reaches conduct in private life that reflects on a lawyer's fitness, and prompt payment of financial obligations is part of a lawyer's duty to society. His acts show a lack of personal honesty and good moral character.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Lito is guilty of gross misconduct, a serious offense punishable by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, or a combination.

**Q2.** Atty. Nora borrowed PHP 600,000.00 from a businessman friend and issued two checks of PHP 300,000.00 each. The first check cleared; the second bounced because her account had been closed, and she failed to pay despite demands. Charged with gross misconduct, she admitted the debt in her Answer, apologized, and explained that her law practice collapsed during the COVID-19 lockdowns. The IBP Investigating Commissioner recommended a one-year suspension. (a) May the Supreme Court impose a lighter penalty? (b) Atty. Nora also points out that this is her first administrative case. Is that a mitigating circumstance?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. The Court may impose a lighter penalty, such as a six-month suspension, in view of mitigating circumstances. (b) No. Under the CPRA, first offense is not a mitigating circumstance in a charge of gross misconduct.
- **Legal basis:** Under Canon VI, Section 38(a) of the CPRA, the Court may, in its discretion, appreciate mitigating circumstances such as expression of remorse, humanitarian considerations and other analogous circumstances; but first offense is mitigating "except in charges of gross misconduct" and the other offenses listed in Section 38(a)(1). In Manongsong v. Atty. Reyes (A.C. No. 13998, August 13, 2025), the Court held that a lawyer's plea acknowledging a "wrong personal economic decision aggravated by the pandemic" reflected remorse, considered the pandemic's impact on lawyers in private practice, and treated the clearing of the first check as showing good faith to repay; it imposed only a six-month suspension for gross misconduct, consistent with Egger v. Atty. Duran.
- **Application:** (a) Atty. Nora admitted the debt and apologized, which shows remorse. The collapse of her practice during the pandemic is a humanitarian or analogous circumstance, and the clearing of her first check shows good faith in wanting to repay. As in Manongsong, these circumstances may justify reducing the recommended one-year suspension to six months. (b) Her clean record cannot be counted, because Section 38(a)(1) expressly excludes first offense as a mitigating circumstance in charges of gross misconduct.
- **Conclusion:** The Court may reduce Atty. Nora's suspension to six months on account of remorse, pandemic hardship and partial payment, but not on account of her being a first offender.

**Q3.** In a disciplinary case against Atty. Paolo for issuing a bouncing check to pay a debt, the IBP Commission on Bar Discipline ordered him to file a mandatory conference brief, attend the mandatory conference, and file a position paper. He ignored all three orders without explanation. Before the Supreme Court, he claims he was in deep financial distress after his law office closed. (a) Is Atty. Paolo administratively liable for ignoring the IBP's orders, and what penalty may be imposed? (b) May the financial distress that the Court considers in tempering his penalty for the bouncing check also excuse or mitigate his disobedience to the IBP?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. His unjustified disregard of the IBP's orders is a less serious offense punishable by suspension of one to six months, a fine of PHP 35,000.00 to PHP 100,000.00, or both. (b) No. It is a separate and distinct offense, and his financial difficulties neither justify nor explain it.
- **Legal basis:** Canon III, Section 2 of the CPRA requires a lawyer to promote respect for laws and legal processes and to assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice. Under Canon VI, Section 34(c), willful and deliberate disobedience of the orders of the Supreme Court and the IBP is a less serious offense, punishable by suspension of one to six months, a fine of PHP 35,000.00 to PHP 100,000.00, or both. In Manongsong v. Atty. Reyes (A.C. No. 13998, August 13, 2025), following Grand Pillar International Development, Inc. v. Atty. Cruz, the Court fined a lawyer PHP 50,000.00 for failing without justification to file his mandatory conference brief, attend the mandatory conference, and file his position paper, on top of a six-month suspension for gross misconduct, and held that this defiance is "a separate and distinct offense, unrelated to the mitigating circumstances considered in his favor."
- **Application:** (a) Orders of the IBP-CBD, the Court's investigating arm, are directives, not mere requests. Atty. Paolo ignored three of them without any explanation, which is willful disobedience of IBP orders and a less serious offense distinct from the bouncing-check charge. A fine such as the PHP 50,000.00 imposed in Manongsong is within the allowable range. (b) His financial distress may soften the penalty for the bouncing check, but it does not explain why he could not file a brief, attend a conference, file a position paper, or at least explain his noncompliance.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Paolo may be separately penalized, for example with a PHP 50,000.00 fine, for disobeying the IBP, and his financial distress does not excuse or mitigate that offense.

> Note: The Court adopted the IBP Board of Governors' findings and its six-month suspension, and added a PHP 50,000.00 fine for disobeying IBP orders. The CPRA (effective May 30, 2023, per the Decision's footnote) was applied. The Decision found six months a "sufficient penalty" for gross misconduct on the strength of Canon VI, Section 38(a) and Egger v. Atty. Duran; it does not cite any other CPRA provision on lowering a penalty below the range for serious offenses. The main opinion credits Associate Justice Hernando with pointing out the partial payment. The fallo does not order Atty. Reyes to pay the PHP 500,000.00 balance to the complainant.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70025)

## Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo

**HEIRS OF BENITA YANZON CIPRIANO, REPRESENTED BY MA. DOROTHY ARLENE CIPRIANO, PETITIONERS, VS. NATIONAL TRANSMISSION CORPORATION (TRANSCO), RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 255113 | 2025-08-06 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** V. Special Civil Actions > G. Expropriation (Rule 67; RA 10752, as amended by RA 12289) > 3. Just Compensation  
**Specific topics:** Inverse condemnation; reckoning point of just compensation (Rule 67, Sec. 4); Exceptions in Macabangkit Sangkay and Saludares; visible transmission lines; Present value formula (Nocom; Heirs of Mariano); Consequential damages as a component of just compensation; Exemplary damages, attorney's fees and costs against the expropriator
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (I. Basic Concepts > D. Fundamental Powers of the State > 2. Eminent Domain (See also RA 10752, as amended by RA 12289))
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (XII. Damages > C. Other Kinds of Damages > 5. Exemplary or Corrective Damages)

### Doctrine
**Just compensation is determined as of the date of the taking of the property or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first (Rule 67, Section 4).** This general rule applies even in inverse condemnation, where the government entered without filing expropriation proceedings. *NPC v. Heirs of Macabangkit Sangkay* and *NPC v. Saludares* reckoned value from the owner's filing of the inverse condemnation suit. Those rulings are exceptions justified only by special circumstances: stealth (underground tunnels the owners did not know of), or the expropriator's refusal to acknowledge the claim because it insisted it had already paid. They do not apply to **visible high-tension transmission lines**, whose existence the owners cannot claim to be unaware of. This is especially so where the expropriator invokes a right of way granted by the owner's predecessor. Reiterated (*NTC v. Oroville*; *NTC v. Religious of the Virgin Mary*).

The value at the time of taking must be computed with the **present value formula** of *Republic v. Spouses Nocom* and *Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga* (En Banc), which accounts for the owner's opportunity loss from non-payment. The total just compensation then earns 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment. **Consequential damages to the remaining portions are a component of just compensation.** They are likewise reckoned from the taking under the same formula.

The government's failure to file expropriation proceedings before taking the property ("construct first, expropriate later") warrants **exemplary damages and attorney's fees** (Civil Code, Arts. 2229 and 2208). The Court fixed them at PHP 1,000,000 and PHP 200,000. Rule 67, Section 12, which charges costs to the plaintiff, presupposes that the expropriator is the plaintiff. In an inverse condemnation suit filed by the owner, **the expropriator pays the costs**.

### Facts
On July 21, 2015, the heirs of Benita Yanzon Cipriano sued the National Transmission Corporation (TransCo) before the RTC of Legazpi City for inverse condemnation or just compensation, with damages. TransCo is the successor to the transmission functions of the National Power Corporation (NPC) under RA 9136. The heirs alleged that in 1977 NPC built high-tension transmission lines over their Lot Nos. 15870-B and 15939 in Villahermosa, Daraga, Albay, without their consent and without expropriation proceedings, and that their demands for payment went unheeded.

TransCo answered that NPC entered on the strength of a right of way granted by the heirs' predecessor, Trinidad P. Vda. De Yanzon, for PHP 1,074.71 (easement fee, pole and guy occupancy, and damaged improvements). It also argued that the claim was barred by prescription and laches, and that just compensation should be reckoned from the time of taking. The complaint was amended after TransCo admitted occupying a larger portion of Lot No. 15939.

The RTC found that the Daraga-Putiao 69kV lines, built in 1977, traversed 2,776 sq m of Lot No. 15870-B and 2,009 sq m of Lot No. 15939. The Daraga-Bacman 230kV lines, built in 1994, traversed another 1,709 sq m of Lot No. 15939, for a total of 6,494 sq m. Applying the *Macabangkit Sangkay* and *Saludares* exception, the RTC reckoned just compensation from the 2015 filing of the complaint. It adopted one commissioner's valuation with modification, pegging the fair market value at PHP 600 per sq m, and awarded PHP 100 per sq m as consequential damages for the remaining 39,688 sq m. Its September 6, 2019 decision fixed just compensation at PHP 700 per sq m (PHP 4,545,800) and awarded PHP 50,000 attorney's fees and PHP 200,000 exemplary damages. The interest was modified on reconsideration.

On November 16, 2020, the CA set aside the RTC ruling. Citing *Oroville*, it held that no special circumstance justified departing from the time-of-taking rule. It found that the appraisals, based on 2009 zonal values and 2012-2015 sales data, did not reflect values at the time of taking. It remanded the case for determination of just compensation, exemplary damages and attorney's fees, with 12% interest from taking until June 30, 2013 and 6% thereafter. The heirs filed a Rule 45 petition.

### Issues
1. Whether just compensation should be reckoned from the actual taking (1977 and 1994) rather than from the filing of the inverse condemnation complaint in 2015.
2. Whether consequential damages should be awarded.
3. Whether the heirs are entitled to increased exemplary damages and attorney's fees.
4. Whether TransCo should pay the costs of suit.

### Ruling
The Court found it unnecessary to rule on the credibility of TransCo's evidence of the right-of-way grant, since it was established that no expropriation proceedings were filed when NPC entered.

**1. Yes. Just compensation is reckoned from the actual taking, but it is computed under the present value formula.** Rule 67, Section 4 fixes the value "as of the date of the taking of the property or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first." *Macabangkit Sangkay* and *Saludares* are exceptions grounded more on equity than on Rule 67. In *Macabangkit Sangkay*, NPC secretly built underground tunnels that the owners discovered only when a buyer backed out. In *Saludares*, NPC refused to acknowledge the claim, insisting it had already paid. As held in *Oroville* and *Religious of the Virgin Mary*, transmission lines are visible, and their very nature precludes "the expropriator's stealth and the owner's utter cluelessness." Here, TransCo also claimed entry under a right of way granted by Trinidad for PHP 1,074.71, which is analogous to the prescription claim in *Religious of the Virgin Mary*.

Applying the general rule does not condone taking without expropriation. Under *Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga*, applying *Spouses Nocom*, the value at taking is brought to its present value to compensate the owner's opportunity loss; this is distinct from legal interest for delay. **The remand was proper** because the RTC's valuation relied on 2009 zonal values and 2012-2015 sales data, not values at the time of taking. The total just compensation shall earn 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment.

**2. Yes. The RTC must determine them on remand.** Consequential damages are a component of just compensation (*NPC v. Marasigan*): the court ascertains the market value, adds the consequential damages, and deducts the consequential benefits. The RTC's earlier award was made in relation to a valuation the CA correctly set aside, so the RTC must redetermine it. It is reckoned from the taking, subject to the present value formula, and earns 6% interest from the finality of the decision fixing just compensation.

**3. Partly.** Exemplary damages (Art. 2229) and attorney's fees (Art. 2208) are awarded when a government agency illegally occupies private property for a long time without expropriation proceedings, causing the owner pecuniary loss (*Heirs of Mariano*, citing *Tecson* and *Manalastas*). Following *Heirs of Mariano*, *Tecson* and *Oroville*, the Court fixed **exemplary damages at PHP 1,000,000**. Following *Tecson*, *Oroville* and *Manalastas*, which all involved owners who sued after a taking without expropriation, it fixed **attorney's fees at PHP 200,000**. Both earn legal interest from the finality of the Decision. The heirs' prayer for PHP 3,000,000 exemplary damages and PHP 1,000,000 attorney's fees was not granted.

**4. Yes.** Rule 67, Section 12 charges costs to the plaintiff unless the owner appeals and the judgment is affirmed. That rule presupposes that the expropriator is the plaintiff. **Since NPC entered without filing expropriation proceedings, it would be unjust to make the owners pay the costs**; NPC or TransCo should have filed the case before taking the property. The Constitution forbids taking private property for public use without just compensation (Art. III, Sec. 9). The government's failure to expropriate may be corrected by exemplary damages, attorney's fees and costs of litigation.

### Disposition
The Petition was PARTIALLY GRANTED. The CA Decision of November 16, 2020 in CA-G.R. CV No. 114206 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Just compensation shall be reckoned from the actual taking: 1977 for the Daraga-Putiao 69kV lines (2,776 sq m of Lot No. 15870-B and 2,009 sq m of Lot No. 15939), and 1994 for the Daraga-Bacman 230kV lines (1,709 sq m of Lot No. 15939). Just compensation, including consequential damages for the remaining unoccupied portions, shall be determined under the formula in *Republic v. Spouses Nocom* and *Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga*, and shall earn 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment. TransCo was ordered to pay PHP 1,000,000 exemplary damages and PHP 200,000 attorney's fees, with 6% interest from the finality of the Decision. The case was remanded to RTC Branch 1, Legazpi City, for the determination of just compensation, consequential damages and costs of suit, with utmost dispatch. Costs against TransCo.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In 1985, the National Power Corporation built steel towers and high-tension transmission lines across a portion of Mario's ranch without filing an expropriation case. The towers are several stories high and visible from the highway. In 2024, Mario filed a complaint for just compensation (inverse condemnation) against the government corporation that succeeded NPC. He argues that because the government never expropriated, his land should be valued as of 2024, when he sued. The corporation claims that Mario's father granted NPC a right of way in 1985. As of what time should just compensation be reckoned?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Just compensation should be reckoned from the time of taking in 1985, but the 1985 value must be brought to present value using the present value formula.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 67, Section 4, just compensation is determined as of the date of the taking or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first. Reckoning from the filing of an inverse condemnation suit is an exception reserved for special circumstances, such as stealth or the expropriator's refusal to acknowledge the claim (Macabangkit Sangkay; Saludares). Visible transmission lines do not qualify. The value at taking is computed under the present value formula of Republic v. Spouses Nocom and Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga, and the total earns 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing just compensation. (Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo, G.R. No. 255113, August 6, 2025)
- **Application:** The taking occurred in 1985, long before Mario sued in 2024. The towers are several stories high and visible, so there was no stealth, and Mario cannot claim he did not know of them. The corporation's claim of a right of way from Mario's father is a legal defense, not a refusal to acknowledge the facts of the taking. No special circumstance justifies the exception. Mario is still protected: the present value formula compensates for his lost opportunity to earn from the money since 1985, and he may also recover exemplary damages and attorney's fees for the failure to expropriate.
- **Conclusion:** Just compensation is reckoned from the 1985 taking and computed under the present value formula.

**Q2.** In the 1970s, a government corporation secretly bored an underground water tunnel beneath Lorna's farm without informing her and without filing an expropriation case. Nothing on the surface showed the tunnel. Lorna discovered it only in 2023, when a buyer backed out of a sale after learning of it. She filed an inverse condemnation suit in 2024. May just compensation be based on the value of her land in 2024?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. The case falls within the recognized exception, so just compensation may be reckoned from the filing of Lorna's complaint in 2024.
- **Legal basis:** The general rule under Rule 67, Section 4 reckons just compensation from the taking or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first. By way of exception, in NPC v. Heirs of Macabangkit Sangkay the Court reckoned it from the owners' filing of the inverse condemnation suit. There, NPC built underground tunnels without the owners' knowledge or consent, using stealth instead of expropriation, and the owners learned of them only when a buyer refused to proceed. Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo (G.R. No. 255113, August 6, 2025) reaffirmed that this exception rests on such special circumstances, which are absent when the structures are visible.
- **Application:** Unlike visible transmission lines, the tunnel was hidden underground, and Lorna was never informed of it. Like the owners in Macabangkit Sangkay, she learned of it only when a sale fell through. Valuing the land as of the 1970s would compound the unfairness caused by the corporation's stealth and let it profit from its denial of due process.
- **Conclusion:** Lorna's just compensation may be based on the value of her land when she filed her inverse condemnation complaint in 2024.

**Q3.** On the facts of the first question, the trial court ruled for Mario. (a) Rule 67, Section 12 states that costs shall be paid by the plaintiff unless the owner appeals and the judgment is affirmed. Since Mario is the plaintiff, must he pay the costs? (b) May the court also award Mario exemplary damages and attorney's fees, even though his just compensation will already be adjusted to present value and earn interest?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The government corporation, which should have filed the expropriation case, must pay the costs. (b) Yes. Exemplary damages and attorney's fees may be awarded for the government's failure to file expropriation proceedings before taking the land.
- **Legal basis:** Rule 67, Section 12 presupposes that the expropriator is the plaintiff. Where the owner had to sue because the government entered without expropriation, it would be unjust to charge the owner with the costs (see Const., Art. III, Sec. 9). Exemplary damages (Civil Code, Art. 2229) and attorney's fees (Art. 2208) may be awarded because of the government's long, illegal occupation of private property without expropriation proceedings, which causes the owner pecuniary loss. In Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo (G.R. No. 255113, August 6, 2025), the Court ordered TransCo to pay the costs and awarded PHP 1,000,000 exemplary damages and PHP 200,000 attorney's fees.
- **Application:** Mario is the plaintiff only because the government built its lines in 1985 without filing an expropriation case, so the costs fall on the government. The present value adjustment and legal interest compensate for the lost use of money and the delay in payment. Exemplary damages serve a different purpose: they correct the "construct first, expropriate later" practice for the public good. Attorney's fees are just and equitable because Mario was forced to litigate to be paid.
- **Conclusion:** The government corporation must pay the costs, and Mario may recover exemplary damages and attorney's fees in addition to just compensation.

> Note: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson) and Hernando, J. concurred; Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business. In the part on consequential damages, the text says the RTC's "prior award of PHP 600.00 per square meter" was tied to the PHP 600 valuation. It apparently means the PHP 100 per sq m consequential damages, so the digest states the point generally.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70027)

## Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano

**CAROLINA BAUTISTA-PANGILINAN, REPRESENTED BY MIRIAM B. BUSTAMANTE, COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. ENGRACIO M. ICASIANO, RESPONDENT.**  
A.C. No. 13752 (Formerly CBD Case No. 18-5596) | 2025-08-06 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 8. Duties and Responsibilities of Lawyers (CPRA) > c. Propriety (Canon II)  
**Specific topics:** Forum shopping by counsel (CPRA, Canon II, Sec. 23); Successive certiorari petitions against execution orders seeking the same reliefs; Abuse of court processes and unduly impeding execution (CPRA, Canon III, Sec. 7); Serious offense; aggravating circumstances allow doubling of the penalty (CPRA, Canon VI, Secs. 33, 37, 39)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 9. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers (Canon VI) > c. Charges and Sanctions)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (III. Civil Procedure > E. Pleadings > 2. Parts and Contents (Rule 7))

### Doctrine
**Forum shopping** is the repetitive availment of several judicial remedies in different courts, simultaneously or successively, all substantially founded on the same transactions and the same essential facts and circumstances, and all raising substantially the same issues either pending in or already resolved adversely by some other court. The ultimate test is the vexation caused to the courts and the parties by asking different fora to rule on the same or related causes or to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, creating the possibility of conflicting decisions (reiterated).

**A lawyer who, while a certiorari petition against an execution order is pending, files a second certiorari petition against a later execution order in the same case, seeking the same reliefs, commits forum shopping, even though the two petitions assail different orders and the client disclosed the first petition in the verification and certification.** The lawyer violates **Canon II, Section 23** of the CPRA (forum shopping), Canon I, Section 1, **Canon III, Sections 2 and 7** (prohibition against frivolous suits and abuse of court processes, including unduly impeding the execution of a warranted judgment), and the Revised Lawyer's Oath.

Willful and deliberate forum shopping is a **serious offense** under Canon VI, Section 33(n) of the CPRA, punishable under Section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law for more than six months, and/or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00. Under **Section 39**, when there are aggravating circumstances and no mitigating circumstances, the Court may impose suspension or a fine of up to double the maximum prescribed. A prior administrative sanction and lack of remorse were treated as two aggravating circumstances, and the Court imposed a one-year suspension instead of the three months recommended by the IBP Board of Governors.

### Facts
Complainant Carolina Bautista-Pangilinan, through her attorney-in-fact Miriam Bustamante, won an ejectment case before the MeTC of Quezon City, Branch 35, against Vivian Sanchez, who was assisted by respondent Atty. Engracio M. Icasiano. The property was covered by TCT No. 125621 in complainant's name. The MeTC Decision of May 8, 2013 ordered Sanchez to vacate, and a writ of execution was issued on November 21, 2013 under an Omnibus Order of the same date.

On February 14, 2014, through Atty. Icasiano, Sanchez filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition (First Petition) in the RTC, raffled to Branch 84. After Atty. Icasiano moved for the judge's inhibition, it was re-raffled to Branch 93, which dismissed it in a Decision dated July 15, 2015. Meanwhile, on January 28, 2015, complainant moved to implement the writ of execution, which the MeTC granted on May 5, 2015. On July 13, 2015, while the First Petition was still pending, Atty. Icasiano filed for Sanchez a petition for certiorari, prohibition and mandamus (Second Petition) assailing the May 5, 2015 Order. It was raffled to Branch 88 and, after the judge inhibited, re-raffled to Branch 105, which dismissed it on November 17, 2016 and declared the petitioners guilty of forum shopping. That Decision was not appealed.

Complainant filed a disbarment complaint charging Atty. Icasiano with forum shopping and land grabbing. He answered that the MeTC Decision was void because Bustamante's special power of attorney was invalid, that Bustamante also lacked authority to file the disbarment complaint, and that there was no forum shopping because the two petitions assailed different orders and he had even asked that the Second Petition be assigned to Branch 93.

The IBP Investigating Commissioner recommended dismissal, finding the land-grabbing charge unsupported, noting the absence of an SPA for the disbarment complaint, and finding no forum shopping because the MeTC Decision was void. The IBP Board of Governors (Resolution No. CBD-XXV-2022-04-24, April 23, 2022) reversed and recommended suspension for three months, finding that both petitions assailed the grant of execution, that the Second Petition was filed while the First was pending, and that the RTC's unappealed finding of forum shopping stood.

### Issues
1. Whether Atty. Icasiano committed forum shopping and violated the CPRA and the Lawyer's Oath by filing the two certiorari petitions.
2. What penalty should be imposed on him.

### Ruling
**1. Yes.** The Court agreed with the IBP Board of Governors. It was undisputed that Atty. Icasiano filed two separate but similar certiorari petitions against two orders of the MeTC, the November 21, 2013 Omnibus Order and the May 5, 2015 Order, both of which granted complainant's motions for execution. **"Although respondent questioned two separate orders and his client disclosed the filing of the First Petition in her Verification and Certification,"** he sought the same reliefs in the Second Petition: (1) to maintain the status quo of his client's possession of the property; (2) to prohibit the implementation of the writs of execution; and (3) to declare that the MeTC judge acted with grave abuse of discretion in granting the motions for execution. He was therefore guilty of forum shopping. RTC Branch 105 had also found forum shopping in its unappealed November 17, 2016 Decision, and that finding stands.

His conduct violated Canon II, Section 23 of the CPRA, under which a lawyer "shall not knowingly engage or through gross negligence in forum shopping" and "shall not institute or advise the client to institute multiple cases to gain leverage in a case, to harass a party, to delay the proceedings, or to increase the cost of litigation." It also violated Canon I, Section 1 (efficient and effective delivery of justice); Canon III, Section 2 (duty to promote respect for laws and legal processes and assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice) and Section 7 (a lawyer shall not unduly impede the execution of a warranted judgment or abuse court processes); and the Revised Lawyer's Oath.

**2. Suspension from the practice of law for one year.** Willful and deliberate forum shopping is a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(n), punishable by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, and/or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00 (Section 37[a]). Atty. Icasiano had previously been reprimanded with a stern warning in *Quilendrino v. Atty. Icasiano* (A.C. No. 9332, February 27, 2019) for violating Canon 8, Rule 8.01 and Canon 11, Rule 11.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, and he showed no remorse, insisting that he did not commit forum shopping. **With two aggravating and no mitigating circumstances, Section 39 allowed the Court to impose a suspension of up to double the maximum prescribed**, and it found a one-year suspension appropriate, rather than the three months recommended by the IBP.

### Disposition
Atty. Engracio M. Icasiano was found GUILTY of violating Canon II, Section 23; Canon I, Section 1; Canon III, Sections 2 and 7 of the CPRA; and the Revised Lawyer's Oath. He was SUSPENDED from the practice of law for one year, effective immediately upon receipt of the Decision, with a STERN WARNING that a repetition will be dealt with more severely. He was directed to file a manifestation that his suspension has started, copy furnished all courts and quasi-judicial bodies where he has appeared as counsel. Copies were ordered furnished the Office of the Bar Confidant, the Office of the Court Administrator, and the IBP.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Atty. Reyes represents Lina, who lost an ejectment case. When the MeTC granted the plaintiff's motion for execution, Atty. Reyes filed for Lina a petition for certiorari and prohibition with the RTC, asking that Lina's possession be maintained, that the writ of execution be enjoined, and that the MeTC judge be declared to have acted with grave abuse of discretion. While that petition was pending, the MeTC issued a second order directing implementation of the writ. Atty. Reyes then filed a second petition for certiorari, prohibition and mandamus with another RTC branch against the second order, seeking the same three reliefs. Lina disclosed the first petition in her verification and certification. Charged administratively, Atty. Reyes argues that there is no forum shopping because the two petitions assail different orders and the first petition was disclosed. Is Atty. Reyes administratively liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Atty. Reyes committed forum shopping and is administratively liable under the CPRA.
- **Legal basis:** Forum shopping is the repetitive availment of several judicial remedies in different courts, simultaneously or successively, all substantially founded on the same transactions and essential facts, and raising substantially the same issues; the ultimate test is the vexation caused by asking different fora to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, with the possibility of conflicting decisions. Under Canon II, Section 23 of the CPRA, a lawyer shall not knowingly or through gross negligence engage in forum shopping. Canon III, Section 7 prohibits a lawyer from unduly impeding the execution of a warranted judgment and from abusing court processes. Questioning two separate orders and disclosing the first petition do not negate forum shopping where the same reliefs are sought. (Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano, A.C. No. 13752, August 6, 2025)
- **Application:** Both petitions arise from the same ejectment judgment and attack the same thing: the execution of that judgment. Both seek the same reliefs, namely to keep Lina in possession, to stop the writ, and to declare the MeTC judge guilty of grave abuse. The second was filed while the first was pending in another branch, creating the risk of conflicting rulings. That the second petition targets a later implementing order, and that the first petition was disclosed, does not change the identity of the reliefs. Filing it also unduly impeded the execution of a final ejectment judgment.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Reyes is liable for forum shopping and abuse of court processes under Canon II, Section 23 and Canon III, Section 7 of the CPRA.

**Q2.** In an administrative case, Atty. Cruz was found to have committed willful and deliberate forum shopping. The records show that he had previously been reprimanded with a stern warning by the Supreme Court for another violation, and throughout the proceedings he insisted that he did nothing wrong. No mitigating circumstance was shown. The IBP Board of Governors recommended suspension from the practice of law for three months. Is the recommended penalty proper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Three months is too light; the Court may suspend him for more than six months, and up to double the maximum prescribed, as in Icasiano, where it imposed a one-year suspension.
- **Legal basis:** Willful and deliberate forum shopping is a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(n) of the CPRA, punishable under Section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law for a period exceeding six months, and/or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00. Under Section 39, if one or more aggravating circumstances and no mitigating circumstances are present, the Court may impose suspension or a fine not exceeding double the maximum prescribed, and may in its discretion impose disbarment. A prior administrative sanction and lack of remorse were treated as two aggravating circumstances. (Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano, A.C. No. 13752, August 6, 2025)
- **Application:** Since Atty. Cruz committed a serious offense, the minimum suspension is more than six months, so three months is below the prescribed range. His previous reprimand and his lack of remorse are aggravating circumstances, and no mitigating circumstance offsets them, so Section 39 allows the Court to go up to double the maximum. In Icasiano, on the same combination of circumstances, the Court rejected the IBP's three-month recommendation and imposed a one-year suspension with a stern warning.
- **Conclusion:** The IBP's three-month recommendation is improper; a suspension exceeding six months, such as one year, is warranted.

**Q3.** In the same situation as Atty. Reyes in the first question, the second RTC branch found that Lina and her counsel committed forum shopping. (a) What is the effect of willful and deliberate forum shopping on the second petition? (b) Lina argues that because she truthfully disclosed the first petition in her certification against forum shopping, she complied with the Rules and cannot be guilty of forum shopping. Is she correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) It is a ground for summary dismissal of the second petition with prejudice, and it also constitutes direct contempt and a cause for administrative sanctions. (b) No. Disclosure in the certification does not cure forum shopping.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 7, Section 5 of the Rules of Court, if the acts of the party or counsel clearly constitute willful and deliberate forum shopping, this is a ground for summary dismissal with prejudice and constitutes direct contempt, as well as a cause for administrative sanctions. Forum shopping is determined by whether the party seeks the same or substantially the same reliefs from different fora on the same facts, creating the possibility of conflicting decisions; in Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano (A.C. No. 13752, August 6, 2025), the Court held that counsel committed forum shopping although the client "disclosed the filing of the First Petition in her Verification and Certification," because the same reliefs were sought.
- **Application:** (a) Filing a second petition seeking the same reliefs while the first is pending is willful and deliberate forum shopping, so the second petition may be summarily dismissed with prejudice, and Lina and her counsel are exposed to contempt and, for counsel, disciplinary sanctions. (b) The certification requirement is a separate duty to inform the court; truthful disclosure avoids a false certification but does not make it proper to ask two courts for the same reliefs at the same time. The vexation and risk of conflicting rulings remain.
- **Conclusion:** The second petition is dismissible with prejudice, and Lina's disclosure of the first petition does not excuse the forum shopping.

> Note: The ejectment case number appears in the record as Civil Case No. 10-39977, 35-09-39977 and 35-39977. The Court agreed with the IBP Board of Governors except as to the penalty, and did not separately rule on respondent's defenses that the MeTC Decision was void and that Bustamante lacked an SPA, or on the land-grabbing charge (found unsupported by the Investigating Commissioner). The Court described willful and deliberate forum shopping as the serious offense under Section 33(n) without separately discussing intent. Rule 7, Section 5 in Bar question 3 is basic procedural law not discussed in the Decision. Only three Justices took part (Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business).

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70023)
