## Alzate v. Judge Alzate

**CORPUS B. ALZATE, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. RAPHIEL F. ALZATE, PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 1, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, BANGUED, ABRA, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. RTJ-25-099 [Formerly OCA IPI No. 18-4879-RTJ] | 2025-08-05 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 1. Standards of Ethical Conduct of Judges and Justices > d. Impartiality (Canon III) > i. Mandatory vs. Voluntary Inhibition (See also Rule 137)  
**Specific topics:** Compulsory inhibition where the judge's spouse acted as counsel in the case; Spouse-counsel's withdrawal does not remove the ground for inhibition; Violating the rule on compulsory disqualification is gross ignorance of the law or procedure; Substantial evidence in administrative cases against judges; gross misconduct and dishonesty not proved; Penalty when the respondent judge has already been dismissed; disbarment prayer
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII))

### Doctrine
**A judge must inhibit from a case in which his spouse acted as counsel. Under Rule 137, Section 1 of the Rules of Court and Canon III, Section 5 and Canon IV, Section 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, the inhibition is "not merely discretionary; it is compulsory."** Canon IV, Section 4 provides that judges "shall not participate in the determination of a case in which any member of their family represents a litigant or is associated in any manner with the case." **The spouse's withdrawal as counsel when the judge took over the case does not cure the disqualification.** She had actively participated before withdrawing (she prepared and filed the petition and presented the petitioner's evidence-in-chief), so a perception that the case was decided in her favor remains. A judge should not handle a case where there is a perception, rightly or wrongly, that he is susceptible to bias because of relationship.

**Disobeying the rule on compulsory self-disqualification is gross ignorance of the law or procedure** (following *Paderanga v. Judge Paderanga*), not simple misconduct as the JIB had recommended. It is a serious charge under Rule 140, as amended, punishable by dismissal, suspension of more than six months to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 up to PHP 200,000.00.

In administrative cases, the complainant must prove the allegations by **substantial evidence**. Mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions, such as a court's reputation as the "Annulment Capital of the North" or a "conjugal syndicate" offering "package deals," do not establish gross misconduct (which requires corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules) or dishonesty (reiterated).

### Facts
Complainant Judge Corpus Alzate charged respondent Judge Raphiel F. Alzate with misconduct and dishonesty in annulment cases in Branch 58, RTC, Bucay, Abra, which respondent presided over. He alleged that the branch was known as the "Annulment Capital of the North" and disregarded the residency requirement. He also alleged that respondent and his wife, Atty. Maria Saniata Liwliwa Gonzales-Alzate, were a "conjugal syndicate" offering "package deals": the wife would deal with the parties and assign the case to "accommodating" lawyers who did not take part in the proceedings, and respondent would decide in the parties' favor.

He cited two nullity cases. In *Villanueva v. Villanueva* (Civil Case No. 13-764), filed on June 24, 2013 when Judge Dojillo still presided, Atty. Gonzales-Alzate was counsel of record. She prepared the petition and presented the petitioner, Villanueva, to testify before Judge Dojillo. Complainant alleged that Villanueva, respondent's childhood best friend, actually lived in Bangued and not Bucay. Respondent was designated acting presiding judge on September 2, 2013. His wife then moved to withdraw as counsel, and respondent granted the motion at a November 7, 2013 hearing. He then tried and decided the case without inhibiting. Minutes of a March 2014 hearing bore the wife's name, which the court interpreter certified was his own inadvertence. In *Bermudez v. Bermudez* (Civil Case No. 14-804), complainant alleged that counsel of record Atty. Byrone Alzate merely lent his name, was never notified of hearings, and that the petition was granted without witnesses or a hearing. Atty. Byrone Alzate gave two contradictory affidavits. Respondent submitted affidavits and barangay certifications that both petitioners resided in Bucay.

Complainant asked that respondent be held liable and that the case also be treated as a disbarment proceeding. The Investigating Justice of the Court of Appeals found the evidence of gross misconduct and dishonesty insufficient. He treated non-inhibition in *Villanueva* as a matter of voluntary inhibition and recommended a judicial audit. The Office of the Executive Director of the Judicial Integrity Board (JIB) found that respondent violated Rule 137, Section 1 and the New Code of Judicial Conduct by not inhibiting, and recommended a PHP 5,000.00 fine. The JIB found him guilty of simple misconduct and, citing his prior administrative liabilities, recommended a PHP 100,000.00 fine.

### Issues
1. Whether respondent is guilty of gross misconduct and dishonesty in deciding the Villanueva and Bermudez nullity cases and through the alleged "package deals."
2. Whether respondent is administratively liable for not inhibiting from Villanueva, in which his wife had been counsel, and for what offense.
3. What penalty should be imposed, and whether the case should also be treated as a disbarment proceeding.

### Ruling
**1. No. Gross misconduct and dishonesty were not proved.** The complainant must prove the charges by substantial evidence; "mere allegation is not equivalent to proof." Gross misconduct is a serious transgression of an established rule that threatens the administration of justice, manifested in corruption or acts "done with the clear intent to violate the law or in flagrant disregard of established rules." The Court adopted the JIB's findings. No substantial evidence showed that respondent and his wife negotiated "package deals." The non-residency allegations were "sufficiently disputed" by affidavits and certifications. Neither the non-inhibition in *Villanueva* nor the claim that Atty. Byrone Alzate was never notified in *Bermudez* showed corruption. The Court noted that respondent's handling of nullity cases had already been examined in an audit case (*In re Alzate*), where he was found guilty of gross neglect of duty for proceeding without pre-trial and without awaiting collusion reports.

**2. Yes. Respondent is guilty of gross ignorance of the law or procedure for failing to inhibit in *Villanueva*.** Respondent did not deny that his wife filed the petition, and he admitted that she presented the petitioner to testify before Judge Dojillo. Under Rule 137, Section 1, Canon III, Section 5 and Canon IV, Section 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, "respondent's inhibition in Villanueva is not merely discretionary; it is compulsory. There is no excuse for respondent's failure to inhibit in said case." His defense that his wife had withdrawn failed: "such withdrawal does not change the fact that respondent's wife actively participated in the said case prior to her withdrawal," and a perception remains that the case was decided in her favor. A judge must not only be impartial but must also appear impartial. **Following *Paderanga*, the rules on compulsory self-disqualification are "as basic as a rule of thumb," so disobeying them is gross ignorance of the law or procedure, not the simple misconduct the JIB found.**

**3. A fine of PHP 200,000.00; no disbarment in this case.** Gross ignorance of the law or procedure is a serious charge under Rule 140, as amended, punishable by dismissal, suspension of more than six months to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 but not exceeding PHP 200,000.00. In *Sindon v. Alzate*, respondent had been reprimanded and warned for not inhibiting in his wife's application for a notarial commission. In the audit case he was suspended for five years for gross neglect of duty, and he was later dismissed from the service for failing to comply with the Court's directive there. This was his second violation of the rule on compulsory disqualification and his third administrative liability, and he had already been dismissed. The Court therefore imposed a fine of PHP 200,000.00. On the disbarment prayer, the Court found that "the offense respondent is guilty of in this case does not affect his qualification as a lawyer" and penalized him only as a member of the bench. It nonetheless directed the JIB to report on his fitness to remain a member of the Bar.

### Disposition
Judge Raphiel F. Alzate was found GUILTY of Gross Ignorance of the Law and ORDERED to pay a fine of PHP 200,000.00 within 30 days from finality, and to submit proof of payment within 10 days from payment. Failure to comply would lead to contempt proceedings under Rule 71, Section 3. Copies were ordered furnished to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the OCA's Office of Administrative Services (for his personal file), the OCA (for dissemination to all courts), and the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. The Judicial Integrity Board was directed to prepare a comprehensive report and recommendation on his fitness to remain a member of the Bar.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Atty. Lorna filed a petition for declaration of nullity of marriage for her client and presented him as a witness on direct examination before Judge Santos. Judge Santos was later transferred, and Judge Mario, Atty. Lorna's husband, was designated acting presiding judge of the branch. Atty. Lorna immediately moved to withdraw as counsel, and Judge Mario granted the motion. He then tried the rest of the case and granted the petition, reasoning that his wife was no longer counsel of record. (a) Was Judge Mario required to inhibit? (b) What is his administrative liability?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. His inhibition was compulsory, and his wife's withdrawal did not cure the disqualification. (b) He is liable for gross ignorance of the law or procedure, a serious charge.
- **Legal basis:** Rule 137, Section 1 of the Rules of Court and Canon III, Section 5 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct require judges to disqualify themselves where it may appear to a reasonable observer that they cannot decide impartially. Canon IV, Section 4 provides that judges shall not participate in the determination of a case in which any member of their family represents a litigant or is associated in any manner with the case. In Alzate v. Judge Alzate (A.M. No. RTJ-25-099, August 5, 2025, En Banc), the Court held that a judge's inhibition from a case in which his wife had been counsel was "not merely discretionary; it is compulsory." Her withdrawal did not change the fact that she actively participated before withdrawing. Disobeying the rule on compulsory self-disqualification is gross ignorance of the law or procedure, a serious charge under Rule 140, as amended.
- **Application:** Atty. Lorna prepared and filed the petition and presented the petitioner's testimony, so she was associated with the case. Her withdrawal when her husband took over left intact the perception that the case would be, and was, decided in her favor. Judge Mario's belief that he could sit because she was no longer counsel of record is exactly the defense the Court rejected in Alzate. Because the rules on compulsory disqualification are basic, his failure to observe them is gross ignorance of the law or procedure, not mere simple misconduct.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Mario should have inhibited, and he is administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law or procedure.

**Q2.** A complaint against Judge Ramos alleged that his branch had become known among lawyers as the "Annulment Capital" of the region, that he and his lawyer-wife offered "package deals" to couples, and that he granted nullity petitions of parties who did not reside in his territorial jurisdiction. The complainant offered only his own allegations and the reputation of the court. Judge Ramos submitted affidavits of the petitioners' relatives and barangay certifications showing that the petitioners resided within his territory. Should Judge Ramos be held liable for gross misconduct and dishonesty?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The charges of gross misconduct and dishonesty are not supported by substantial evidence.
- **Legal basis:** In administrative proceedings, the complainant has the burden of proving the allegations by substantial evidence, or such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion. Mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions cannot be given credence. Gross misconduct requires a serious transgression of an established rule, manifested in corruption or acts done with clear intent to violate the law or in flagrant disregard of established rules. Dishonesty is a disposition to lie, cheat, deceive or defraud. (Alzate v. Judge Alzate, A.M. No. RTJ-25-099, August 5, 2025, En Banc, citing Zara v. Joyas)
- **Application:** The complainant relied on reputation and his own assertions; he presented no competent evidence of any "package deal" or corrupt arrangement. The residency allegations were rebutted by affidavits and barangay certifications. As in Alzate, where identical charges were dismissed for lack of substantial evidence, nothing in the record shows corruption or a clear intent to violate the law.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Ramos cannot be held liable for gross misconduct and dishonesty on the basis of unproven allegations and reputation.

**Q3.** Judge Cruz was found to have violated the rule on compulsory inhibition. Years earlier, he had been reprimanded with a warning for the same kind of violation. In another case, he was suspended for gross neglect of duty and later dismissed from the service. (a) Given that he has already been dismissed, what penalty may still be imposed for his gross ignorance of the law or procedure? (b) The complainant asks the Court to disbar Judge Cruz in the same administrative case. Must the Court do so?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) A fine; the Court may impose the maximum fine of PHP 200,000.00 for a serious charge. (b) No. Where the offense does not affect his qualification as a lawyer, the Court may penalize him only as a member of the bench.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court, as amended, gross ignorance of the law or procedure is a serious charge punishable by dismissal from the service, suspension of more than six months but not exceeding one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 but not exceeding PHP 200,000.00. In Alzate v. Judge Alzate (A.M. No. RTJ-25-099, August 5, 2025, En Banc), the Court imposed a PHP 200,000.00 fine on a judge who had already been dismissed from the service. It considered that this was his second violation of the rule on compulsory disqualification and his third administrative liability. The Court declined to treat the case as a disbarment proceeding because the offense did not affect his qualification as a lawyer, but directed the JIB to report on his fitness to remain a member of the Bar.
- **Application:** (a) Dismissal and suspension are no longer possible because Judge Cruz is out of the service, but a fine can still be imposed. His prior reprimand for the same kind of violation and his other administrative liability justify the maximum fine of PHP 200,000.00, as in Alzate. (b) A judge's failure to inhibit is an offense committed as a member of the bench. If it does not affect his qualification as a lawyer, the Court may confine the penalty to his judicial accountability. It may separately look into his fitness as a lawyer, as it did in Alzate by directing a JIB report.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Cruz may be fined PHP 200,000.00, and the Court is not required to disbar him in the same case, though it may separately examine his fitness to remain a lawyer.

> Note: The decision applied Rule 137, the New Code of Judicial Conduct (A.M. No. 03-05-01-SC) and Rule 140, as amended. The 2027 syllabus is based on the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC), which the decision does not mention; the syllabus heading is the closest match. The complaint dates the wife's withdrawal to November 4, 2013, while respondent says the motion was granted at the November 7, 2013 hearing. The caption names respondent as Presiding Judge, Branch 1, RTC Bangued, Abra, but the acts complained of were in Branch 58, RTC Bucay, Abra, and the JIB called him a "former" presiding judge. The fallo says "Gross Ignorance of the Law," while the body says "gross ignorance of the law or procedure."

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70069)

## Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas

**ATTY. CARMEN CARMELA A. ARAULLO-ANTIPORTA, CLERK OF COURT VI, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, OFFICE OF THE CLERK OF COURT, MANDAUE CITY, CEBU, COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. DENIS L. PACAS, CLERK OF COURT V, BRANCH 54, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, LAPU-LAPU CITY, CEBU AND ANTHONY PACALDO, SHERIFF IV, BRANCH 84, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, MANDAUE CITY, CEBU [FORMERLY CLERK III, BRANCH 54, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, LAPU-LAPU CITY, CEBU], RESPONDENTS.**  
JIB FPI No. 21-006-P | 2025-08-04 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Resolution

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Gross neglect of duty: case records lost and untransmitted for over eight years; Gross insubordination: repeated disregard of superiors' directives; Branch clerk of court's liability for failure to supervise (simple neglect); Locally funded employees may not have custody of court records; Rule 140 penalties; admonition and warning are not aggravating circumstances
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline > a. Grounds)

### Doctrine
**A court employee directly charged with the custody and transmittal of case records who lets them go missing and untransmitted for more than eight years, without informing his superior or genuinely trying to locate them, is guilty of gross neglect of duty.** This is a serious charge under Rule 140, Section 14(d), as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. Such neglect threatens the public welfare, particularly the accused's right to a speedy disposition of his case. **Repeatedly ignoring superiors' directives without valid justification is gross insubordination** (Sec. 14(n)). Here the directives were to inventory cases, update the docket book, locate missing records, and turn over records before moving to a new post. A heavy workload is a "flimsy excuse."

**The branch clerk of court is liable for simple neglect of duty, a less serious charge (Sec. 15(b)), even if a subordinate was directly at fault.** As the official custodian of court records (Rule 136, Sec. 7) with general supervision over court personnel, his responsibility does not end when he delegates a task. He must ensure that his instruction is carried out and keep an effective record management system with periodic inventories. Clerks of court are chiefly responsible for the shortcomings of subordinates to whom their administrative functions are delegated (*Baring-Uy v. Salinas*). Locally funded employees detailed to lower courts may do only clerical work and may not be given custody of records (OCA Circular No. 42-2019), so blaming such an employee does not prosper.

On penalties (Rule 140, Secs. 17, 19 and 20, as amended): when there are one or more mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine of not less than half of the prescribed minimum. A first offense, and humanitarian considerations such as remorse, apology and prompt remedial action, are mitigating. **An earlier admonition or warning is not a penalty and cannot be treated as an aggravating circumstance.** Each offense was penalized separately.

### Facts
On June 29, 2012, Judge Victor A. Teves, Sr. directed the transmittal of the records of Criminal Case Nos. 018271-L, 018272-L and 018273-L (People v. Ceasar R. Baguio, for violation of Sections 5, 11 and 12 of RA 9165) to the Office of the Clerk of Court (OCC), RTC Mandaue City. The records reached the OCC only on November 24, 2020. Only the original records of Criminal Case No. 018271-L were delivered; machine copies of the other two had to be obtained from the Office of the Provincial Prosecutor. Complainant Atty. Araullo-Antiporta, Clerk of Court VI of the OCC, reported this in a December 7, 2020 letter, which was endorsed to the OCA and forwarded to the Judicial Integrity Board (JIB).

Branch Clerk of Court Atty. Denis L. Pacas's investigation report stated that the transmittal was the task of respondent Anthony Pacaldo, then clerk-in-charge of criminal cases. When confronted, Pacaldo said he could not find the records. The court interpreter later found the original records of Criminal Case No. 018271-L in a pile of folders under Pacaldo's table. Pacaldo denied receiving the instruction. He claimed it was given to Teofilo Bering, a locally funded employee detailed to Branch 54, who died in 2013. Atty. Pacas submitted affidavits of the accused's wife (who followed up with Pacaldo in 2012-2013) and of a jail records officer (who exchanged calls and texts with Pacaldo since 2019), and a sheriff's memorandum. All showed that Pacaldo had said the records could not be found. Pacaldo had also received memoranda since 2011 about inventories, the docket book, missing records and absences from his station. He did not comply with a 2020 directive to inventory and turn over his records before moving to his new post as sheriff, citing his workload. Atty. Pacas apologized and acted promptly, and the original records were eventually delivered on December 10, 2021.

The JIB's Office of the Executive Director recommended a finding of simple neglect against Pacaldo (fine of PHP 18,000) and dismissal of the case against Atty. Pacas with a stern warning. The JIB instead found both guilty of gross neglect of duty and Pacaldo also guilty of gross insubordination. It recommended a PHP 75,000 fine for Atty. Pacas, treating an earlier administrative matter as an aggravating circumstance, and a four-month suspension plus a PHP 55,000 fine for Pacaldo.

### Issues
1. Whether Pacaldo, the former clerk-in-charge of criminal cases, is guilty of gross neglect of duty and gross insubordination.
2. Whether Atty. Pacas, the branch clerk of court, is administratively liable even though Pacaldo was directly responsible for the delay.
3. What penalties are proper in light of the modifying circumstances.

### Ruling
The Court adopted the JIB's findings with modifications.

**1. Yes, Pacaldo is guilty of both.** The records were transmitted more than eight years after the judge's order. As clerk-in-charge of criminal cases, Pacaldo was directly responsible. The affidavits and memoranda of court staff, the jail records officer and the accused's wife showed that he knew of the task: they repeatedly followed up with him, and he told them the records could not be found. His claim that Bering received the instruction was an afterthought, since Bering had died in 2013 and could not refute it. It was also contrary to OCA Circular No. 42-2019, which bars locally funded employees from custody of records. Absent contrary proof, Atty. Pacas is presumed to have properly directed Pacaldo. Pacaldo made no genuine effort to locate the records or inform his superior, and his neglect threatened the accused's right to a speedy disposition of his case. That is **gross neglect of duty**. He also ignored his superiors' memoranda since 2011 and the 2020 directive to inventory and turn over his records, citing a heavy workload. This repeated, unjustified defiance is **gross insubordination**.

**2. Yes, Atty. Pacas is guilty of simple neglect of duty.** As branch clerk of court he exercises general supervision over court personnel and is the official custodian of court records. His responsibility "did not terminate when he delegated its transmittal" to Pacaldo; he had to make sure his instruction was complied with. He "blindly depended" on Pacaldo and failed to put in place an effective case management system and periodic inventory, which would have exposed the problem much earlier. Clerks of court are chiefly responsible for the shortcomings of subordinates to whom their functions are delegated (*Baring-Uy v. Salinas*). His lapse was carelessness, amounting to simple, not gross, neglect.

**3. The penalties were adjusted.** Gross neglect of duty and gross insubordination are serious charges, punishable by dismissal, suspension of more than six months up to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000 up to PHP 200,000 (Sec. 17(1)). Simple neglect is a less serious charge, punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 up to PHP 100,000 (Sec. 17(2)). Under Section 20, when there are mitigating and no aggravating circumstances, the penalty may be not less than half of the minimum.

This was Pacaldo's first administrative charge, a mitigating circumstance. For gross neglect, the Court adopted the JIB's recommended four-month suspension. For gross insubordination, "without the benefit of any mitigating circumstance," it suspended him for six months and one day. Atty. Pacas was credited with humanitarian considerations: he apologized, acted immediately, secured certified copies of the missing records, and kept searching until the originals were delivered. **The Court rejected the JIB's use of his earlier admonition and stern warning in a judicial audit as an aggravating circumstance, because admonition and warning are not penalties.** He was fined PHP 18,000, payable within 30 days from finality (*Ignacio v. Balading*).

### Disposition
Pacaldo was found GUILTY of gross neglect of duty in the performance of official functions and SUSPENDED for four months without salary or other benefits. He was also found GUILTY of gross insubordination and SUSPENDED for six months and one day without salary or other benefits. Atty. Pacas was found GUILTY of simple neglect of duty in the performance of official functions and FINED PHP 18,000, payable within 30 days from finality; if unpaid, contempt proceedings under Rule 71, Section 3 will be commenced. Both were STERNLY WARNED that a repetition will be dealt with more severely. A copy was furnished to the OCA.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In 2015, Judge Lim ordered the records of three criminal cases transmitted to the Office of the Clerk of Court. Branch Clerk of Court Atty. Rey assigned the task to Joel, the clerk-in-charge of criminal cases, and never followed up. Joel could not find the records. For years he told the accused's relatives that the records were "still being located," but he never informed Atty. Rey and never seriously searched. The records were transmitted only in 2023. What are the administrative liabilities of Joel and Atty. Rey?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Joel is liable for gross neglect of duty, a serious charge. Atty. Rey is liable for simple neglect of duty, a less serious charge.
- **Legal basis:** Gross neglect of duty is negligence marked by a glaring want of care, or a flagrant and culpable refusal or unwillingness to perform a duty; it is a serious charge under Rule 140, Section 14(d), as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. Simple neglect is the failure to give attention to an expected task through carelessness or indifference (Sec. 15(b)). The branch clerk of court is the official custodian of records (Rule 136, Sec. 7) and supervises court personnel. He remains responsible after delegating a task and is chiefly answerable for his subordinates' shortcomings. (Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas, JIB FPI No. 21-006-P, August 4, 2025)
- **Application:** Joel was directly in charge of the records and knew of the task, since he answered the relatives' follow-ups. Yet for about eight years he neither searched seriously nor told his superior, which delayed the cases and threatened the accused's right to a speedy disposition. That is gross neglect. Atty. Rey did not lose the records himself, but he delegated the task and never checked whether it was done, and he had no system or inventory that would have revealed the loss. His failure to supervise is carelessness, which is simple neglect.
- **Conclusion:** Joel should be held liable for gross neglect of duty and Atty. Rey for simple neglect of duty.

**Q2.** In the same case, Joel raises two defenses. (a) He says the judge's instruction was actually given to a job-order employee funded by the municipality and detailed to the branch, who has since died. (b) He admits ignoring the judge's memorandum to inventory his records and turn them over before transferring to his new post as sheriff, but blames his heavy workload in the new post. He has also received several earlier memoranda about his failure to update the docket book and locate missing records. Rule on his defenses.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both defenses fail. Joel remains liable for gross neglect of duty and is also liable for gross insubordination.
- **Legal basis:** Under OCA Circular No. 42-2019, locally funded employees detailed to lower courts may perform only clerical tasks and may not be given custody of court records. Absent contrary proof, the branch clerk is presumed to have regularly performed his duty of assigning the task to the proper employee. Gross insubordination is the inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey an order that a superior is entitled to give, importing a willful disregard of lawful and reasonable instructions; it is a serious charge under Rule 140, Section 14(n). (Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas, JIB FPI No. 21-006-P, August 4, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Blaming a deceased employee who cannot refute the claim is an afterthought. It is also implausible, since such an employee could not lawfully have been given custody of the records, and Joel offers no proof beyond his own word. (b) Joel repeatedly ignored lawful directives from the judge and the branch clerk, and a heavy workload is a flimsy excuse for not inventorying and turning over records in his custody. His persistent disregard of his superiors' orders is gross insubordination.
- **Conclusion:** Joel's defenses should be rejected; he is liable for both gross neglect of duty and gross insubordination.

**Q3.** In determining Atty. Rey's penalty for simple neglect of duty, the Judicial Integrity Board treated as an aggravating circumstance a ruling in an earlier judicial audit, where Atty. Rey was admonished and sternly warned for late docket inventories. Atty. Rey points out that he apologized, immediately secured certified copies of the missing records from the prosecutor's office, and kept searching until the originals were found. (a) Was the JIB correct in treating the earlier admonition as aggravating? (b) May the Court impose a penalty lower than the minimum for a less serious charge?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. An admonition and a warning are not penalties, so they cannot aggravate his liability. (b) Yes. With a mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a fine of not less than half of the minimum.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 140, Sections 19 and 20, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, humanitarian considerations are a mitigating circumstance. When one or more mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstance are present, the Court may impose a suspension or fine of not less than half of the minimum prescribed. Admonition and warning are not penalties and cannot be treated as an aggravating circumstance. (Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas, JIB FPI No. 21-006-P, August 4, 2025)
- **Application:** Because the earlier ruling merely admonished and warned Atty. Rey, it imposed no penalty, so there is no aggravating circumstance. His apology, his immediate remedial action, and his persistence until the originals were found are humanitarian considerations that mitigate his liability. With one mitigating and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may reduce his fine below the minimum for a less serious charge, as long as it is not less than half of that minimum.
- **Conclusion:** The prior admonition is not aggravating, and Atty. Rey may be fined below the minimum, but not less than half of it, because of the mitigating circumstance.

> Note: First Division Resolution. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson) and Hernando, J. concurred; Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business. The JIB acted on the endorsed letter on its own, as Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, allows.

The Resolution applied Rule 140 as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. The 2027 syllabus refers to the 2025 CJCA and the 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel (A.M. No. 25-06-11-SC), so check whether later rules changed the classification of these offenses or the sanctions. The syllabus has no separate heading for the discipline of court personnel; the closest heading is used. The Resolution does not explain why the first-offense mitigating circumstance was applied only to the gross neglect charge and not to gross insubordination.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70169)

## Fernando v. People

**CHARLON FERNANDO Y ESMA, PETITIONER, VS. PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 259589 (Formerly UDK-16849) | 2025-07-29 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Criminal Procedure > M. New Trial or Reconsideration (Rule 121)  
**Specific topics:** Three requisites for a witness's retraction to be a ground for new trial; Newly discovered evidence (Rule 121, Sec. 2(b)); Recantations are generally unreliable but may justify new trial when the sole identifying witness recants under special circumstances; CA may receive evidence on new trial (Rule 124, Sec. 12; CA Internal Rules); Relaxation of procedural rules when liberty is at stake

### Doctrine
**For the retraction of a witness to be a ground for new trial, it must be shown that: (1) the retracting witness's trial testimony is essential to the judgment of conviction, so that its elimination would lead the trial judge to a different conclusion; (2) special circumstances exist which, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the truth of the testimony given at trial; and (3) no other evidence sustains the judgment of conviction except that testimony.** The Court drew these requisites together from Reyes v. People (1941, En Banc) and People v. Manigbas (1960, En Banc). The ground is newly discovered evidence under Rule 121, Section 2(b): evidence discovered after trial, which could not have been discovered and produced at trial with reasonable diligence, and which is material and would probably change the judgment.

The general rule is reiterated: affidavits of recantation executed after conviction are "very unreliable," and merely impeaching evidence or retractions do not ordinarily justify a new trial. A new trial is warranted, however, where the sole eyewitness who identified the accused recants and the record shows special circumstances, such as suggestive identification, a complainant who suspected the accused beforehand, and a grudge between the families.

When a new trial on newly discovered evidence is granted in a criminal case on appeal, the CA may receive the evidence itself (Rule 124, Sec. 12; 2009 Internal Rules of the CA, Rule VI, Sec. 3(c)), so the Supreme Court remands to the CA. The Court may relax procedural rules in a Rule 45 petition when liberty is at stake and the petition has merit (Sanchez v. CA factors).

### Facts
Charlon Fernando was charged with carnapping under RA 6539 for taking, on October 28, 2013 in Olongapo City, a blue Honda XRM motorcycle owned by Francisco Combate and valued at PHP 102,816.00. The only eyewitness was Darius Santos. He testified that at about 8:42 p.m. he saw Charlon pushing the motorcycle, that he and his friends told Charlon to kick-start it, and that Charlon then sped away. Two days later Darius described the man to Francisco, who "immediately recognized" him as Charlon. Francisco brought Darius to where Charlon was with three others, and Darius pointed to Charlon. Francisco testified that he did not see the taking and that his basis was that Charlon's group "have bad intention." Charlon's uncle testified to a long-time grudge between the families, and Francisco's own December 13, 2013 affidavit before the prosecutor reflected hostility toward Charlon's family. Charlon's defense was alibi: he was at his cousin's birthday party.

The RTC (March 30, 2017, Criminal Case No. 319-14) convicted Charlon of carnapping on the strength of Darius's testimony. The CA affirmed in toto (January 30, 2020 Decision, CA-G.R. CR No. 40276). Charlon then moved for new trial before the CA. He presented Darius's Salaysay ng Pag-urong dated March 2, 2020, in which Darius stated the following: he did not see Charlon take the motorcycle; the taker was one "alyas Balong Camisera," a feared local figure; his aunt and uncle, Joan and Francisco Combate, coached him to point to Charlon and told him not to reveal they were relatives; he was a minor then and easily influenced; he did not know Charlon before seeing him in court, where Francisco told him to stare at Charlon so he could identify him; and he later saw the motorcycle at the Combates' house in 2018.

The CA denied the motion (January 14, 2021 Resolution), reasoning that a mere retraction does not necessarily vitiate the original testimony if credible. Charlon filed a Rule 45 petition. The OSG argued that the petition failed to attach material portions of the record, raised factual issues, and relied on an affidavit of retraction executed after conviction, which has no probative value.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition should be dismissed for non-compliance with Rule 45.
2. Whether Darius's retraction warrants a new trial.
3. Which court should receive the evidence on new trial.

### Ruling
**1. No; the rules were relaxed.** The Court may suspend its rules considering matters of life, liberty, honor, or property; special or compelling circumstances; the merits of the case; a cause not entirely attributable to the party's fault; the lack of any showing that the review is frivolous or dilatory; and the absence of unjust prejudice to the other party (Sanchez v. CA). Since petitioner stood to lose his liberty for a considerable time and the petition had merit, the Court relaxed the rules in the interest of substantial justice.

**2. Yes.** Under Rule 121, Section 2, a new trial may be granted for errors of law or irregularities, or for newly discovered evidence. Reyes v. People holds that retractions do not justify new trial "unless it is shown that there is no evidence sustaining the judgment of conviction except the testimony of the retracting witness." Manigbas warns that recantations after conviction are "very unreliable" and justify a new trial only if special circumstances, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the trial testimony and that testimony is essential to the conviction. Combining these, the Court laid out the three requisites, and all were present.

(a) **Darius's testimony was essential.** He alone identified petitioner; "[w]ithout it, the prosecution would have had no leg to stand on." (b) **No other evidence sustained the conviction.** Francisco proved only his ownership, did not witness the taking, and relied on what Darius told him. (c) **Special circumstances raised doubt.** First, the retraction itself explained that Darius was a coached minor who identified the wrong man. Second, Francisco's testimony showed he suspected petitioner beforehand and brought Darius to petitioner's location to pick him out of four people, which shows "the suggestiveness of the identification." Third, the uncle's testimony on a long-time grudge was consistent with Francisco's December 13, 2013 affidavit. Given the gravity of the penalty for carnapping, a new trial "would better serve the ends of justice since it is better to liberate a guilty man than to unjustly keep in prison one whose guilt has not been proved."

**3. The Court of Appeals.** Under Rule VI, Section 3(c) of the 2009 Internal Rules of the CA, the CA may receive evidence in criminal appeals where a new trial is granted on newly discovered evidence, pursuant to Rule 124, Section 12. The case was remanded to the CA.

### Disposition
The petition was GRANTED. The CA's January 30, 2020 Decision and January 14, 2021 Resolution in CA-G.R. CR No. 40276 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The CA was DIRECTED to receive evidence and render a new decision as warranted by the whole evidence of record, and the records were REMANDED to the CA for that purpose.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Jomar was convicted of carnapping solely on the testimony of Kiko, who identified him as the man he saw riding away on the stolen motorcycle. The owner did not witness the taking. While Jomar's appeal was pending in the Court of Appeals, Kiko executed an affidavit retracting his testimony. He stated that the owner, his uncle, had pointed Jomar out to him before the police lineup and coached him on what to say, and that the real thief was another person whom he feared. The owner had admitted on the stand that he suspected Jomar even before Kiko described the thief. Jomar moves for new trial. The prosecution argues that recantations are unreliable. Should a new trial be granted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Kiko's retraction, under these circumstances, is a valid ground for new trial on newly discovered evidence.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 121, Section 2(b), a new trial may be granted on newly discovered evidence. For the retraction of a witness to be a ground for new trial, three requisites must concur: (1) the retracting witness's testimony is essential to the conviction, so that its elimination would lead to a different conclusion; (2) special circumstances, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the truth of the trial testimony; and (3) no other evidence sustains the conviction except that testimony. (Fernando v. People, G.R. No. 259589, July 29, 2025, drawing on Reyes v. People and People v. Manigbas)
- **Application:** Kiko was the only witness who identified Jomar, so without his testimony the prosecution has no case, which satisfies the first and third requisites. The owner did not see the taking and only relayed suspicion. Special circumstances raise doubt about Kiko's trial testimony: the owner suspected Jomar beforehand and pointed him out to Kiko, which makes the identification suggestive, and Kiko explains he was coached by his own relative. Recantations are generally viewed with suspicion, but here they are coupled with circumstances already appearing in the record.
- **Conclusion:** A new trial should be granted so that Kiko's retraction can be tested and weighed with the whole evidence.

**Q2.** Same facts, except that the stolen motorcycle was found in Jomar's garage two days after the taking, a CCTV recording shows Jomar riding it out of the owner's compound, and Kiko's affidavit of retraction merely states that he "is no longer sure" of his identification, without explaining why. Should a new trial be granted?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The retraction does not meet the requisites for a new trial.
- **Legal basis:** Affidavits of recantation executed after conviction are "very unreliable," and evidence that merely impeaches or retracts trial testimony is not a ground for new trial unless (1) the retracting witness's testimony is essential to the conviction, (2) special circumstances coupled with the retraction raise doubt as to its truth, and (3) no other evidence sustains the conviction. (Fernando v. People, G.R. No. 259589, July 29, 2025; People v. Manigbas; Reyes v. People)
- **Application:** The conviction is supported by evidence independent of Kiko: the CCTV recording and the recovery of the motorcycle in Jomar's garage. Kiko's testimony is therefore not essential, and eliminating it would not lead to a different conclusion. His bare statement that he is "no longer sure," with no special circumstance casting doubt on his trial testimony, is the kind of retraction that would make a mockery of solemn trials if it were allowed to set aside a judgment.
- **Conclusion:** The motion for new trial should be denied because the retraction is neither essential nor coupled with special circumstances, and other evidence sustains the conviction.

**Q3.** The Supreme Court, on a Rule 45 petition, finds that an accused-appellant is entitled to a new trial on newly discovered evidence, consisting of the sole eyewitness's affidavit of recantation, which was first presented to the Court of Appeals after it affirmed the conviction. (a) Must the case be remanded to the RTC for the new trial, or may the CA receive the evidence? (b) Can the Supreme Court entertain the petition despite the petitioner's failure to attach material portions of the record?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The CA may receive the evidence, and the case may be remanded to the CA. (b) Yes. The Court may relax its procedural rules where the accused's liberty is at stake and the petition has merit.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule VI, Section 3(c) of the 2009 Internal Rules of the Court of Appeals, the CA may receive evidence in appeals of criminal cases where a new trial is granted on the ground of newly discovered evidence, pursuant to Rule 124, Section 12. The Court may suspend its rules considering matters of life, liberty, honor, or property; special or compelling circumstances; the merits of the case; a cause not entirely attributable to the party's fault; the lack of any showing that the review is frivolous or dilatory; and the absence of unjust prejudice to the other party. (Fernando v. People, G.R. No. 259589, July 29, 2025, citing Sanchez v. Court of Appeals)
- **Application:** Since the new trial is grounded on newly discovered evidence in a criminal appeal, the CA itself can take the recanting witness's testimony and render a new decision on the whole record, as the Supreme Court directed in Fernando. As to the procedural lapse, the accused faces long imprisonment and the petition shows merit, since the conviction rests on a single witness who has recanted under suspicious circumstances. These are the compelling reasons that justify relaxing the rules.
- **Conclusion:** The case may be remanded to the CA to receive evidence and render a new decision, and the procedural defect does not bar the petition.

> Note: The decision's summary of the CA Resolution reads that the CA "reluctantly finds [the recantation] to be sufficient ground for a new trial" but still denied the motion. This may be a typographical error for "insufficient." The digest describes only the CA's stated reason for denial. The petition also alleged grave abuse of discretion by the CA, but the Court resolved it as a Rule 45 petition on the merits of the new trial. The RTC imposed an indeterminate penalty under RA 6539; the Court did not rule on guilt or penalty, which are left to the CA after new trial.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/70090)

## Go v. Saint Jude Catholic School Manila

**ATTY. MELITA GO AND WAYNE GO, PETITIONERS, VS. SAINT JUDE CATHOLIC SCHOOL MANILA, INC., FR. MARCELINO NICASIO, SVD, FATIMA DE GUZMAN, AND SPOUSES EUGENE LEE AND JOANNE LEE, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 257761 | 2025-04-22 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** III. Civil Procedure > T. Execution, Satisfaction, and Effect of Judgments (Rule 39) > 4. How a Judgment is Executed  
**Specific topics:** Costs recoverable by the prevailing party are only those in Rule 142, Secs. 9-11; Attorney's fees as damages (Art. 2208) cannot also be taxed as costs; Taxation of costs by the clerk of court as a condition precedent to execution; Appealability of a ruling on taxation of costs vs. an order of execution
  
**Also relevant to:** Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds (XII. Damages > B. Actual and Compensatory Damages > 4. Attorney's Fees and Expenses of Litigation)

### Doctrine
**The only costs recoverable by the prevailing party are those fixed in Rule 142, Sections 9 to 11; any other item claimed as costs is properly a matter of damages. Reasonable attorney's fees may be recovered only as actual or compensatory damages under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, and may not also be taxed as costs.** Section 10 lists the costs recoverable in the RTC "and no other," including:
- PHP 15 for the complaint or answer (nothing for other pleadings or motions);
- a flat PHP 20 for the attendance of the party and counsel "down to and including final judgment," however many appearances there were;
- PHP 2 per day for each witness necessarily produced, plus lawful traveling fees;
- lawful fees paid for official copies of documents (nothing for original documents); and
- lawful docket, service and clerk's fees.

Under Section 6, no attorney's fees may be taxed as costs against the adverse party except as provided by civil law. A party already awarded attorney's fees as damages cannot also recover counsel's actual appearance fees as costs. In *Norsk Hydro*, the statement that costs are "not limited to" Sections 9 to 11 refers to costs the court may tax under other rules (e.g., Rule 23, Sec. 18; Rule 32, Sec. 13), not to costs recoverable by the prevailing party. Reiterating *Corpus v. Corpus*.

**In the RTC, a superior court, costs must first be taxed by the clerk of court.** The prevailing party gives five days' written notice with a verified statement of the items; objections are made in writing; and either party may appeal the clerk's taxation to the court (Rule 142, Sec. 8). Taxation is a condition precedent to the obligation to pay costs, to the court's power to pass on disputed items, and to the inclusion of costs in an execution (*Romulo v. Dasalla*). A judge errs in ruling on the bill of costs outright instead of directing the clerk to assess it. An order granting execution is not appealable (Rule 41, Sec. 1), but **a ruling on the taxation of costs is final, not interlocutory, and may be appealed**. A Rule 45 petition on a pure question of law regarding costs is proper (*Del Rosario v. Bayona*).

### Facts
In a complaint for damages, the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 97, rendered a Decision on October 7, 2019. It ordered Saint Jude Catholic School Manila, Inc., Fr. Marcelino Nicasio and Fatima de Guzman to pay petitioners Atty. Melita Go and Wayne Go, principally and solidarily, PHP 21,128 actual damages, PHP 100,000 exemplary damages, PHP 100,000 attorney's fees, and "cost of suit." Spouses Eugene and Joanne Lee were held subsidiarily liable.

Petitioners moved for execution with a verified bill of costs totaling PHP 348,014: PHP 30,000 for pleadings and motions from 2011 to 2019; PHP 264,000 for 88 appearances of Atty. Go and her counsel at 41 hearings; PHP 5,000 for the traveling fees of five witnesses; PHP 24,014 for filing and docket fees; PHP 5,000 for photocopying, notarization and certification; and PHP 20,000 for transcripts. The RTC denied the motion on February 23, 2021 because respondents had not yet received the resolution on their motion for reconsideration.

After the decision became final, petitioners filed a second motion. In its July 21, 2021 Resolution, the RTC granted the writ of execution but denied the PHP 348,014 "additional cost of suit." It reasoned that the amount was not passed upon at trial and that allowing it would modify a final judgment. Partial reconsideration was denied on September 10, 2021.

Petitioners filed a Rule 45 petition. Respondents argued that orders of execution are not appealable and that the items were really additional attorney's fees not proven at trial. Petitioners replied that counsel's appearance fees are necessary expenses recoverable as costs, separate from the attorney's fees awarded as damages.

### Issues
1. Whether a Rule 45 petition may be taken from the RTC resolutions, which granted execution but denied the items of costs.
2. Whether petitioners, already awarded attorney's fees as damages, may also recover their counsel's appearance fees and the other items in their bill as costs of suit.
3. Whether the RTC judge correctly ruled on the bill of costs instead of having it taxed by the clerk of court.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, insofar as costs are concerned.** The resolutions are unappealable insofar as they granted execution (Rule 41, Sec. 1). But the denial of the items of costs is a ruling on the taxation of costs, even if it was erroneously made by the judge rather than the clerk. Following *Del Rosario v. Bayona*, such a ruling is final, not merely interlocutory, and may be appealed. Petitioners correctly availed of Rule 45 on that point.

**2. No. Attorney's fees cannot be recovered both as damages and as costs.** Costs have a fixed, technical meaning: allowances authorized by statute to reimburse the successful party for its expenses in the action. The only costs recoverable are those in Rule 142, Sections 9 to 11, and Section 10 allows the prevailing party in the RTC the listed items "and no other." Before the Civil Code took effect, attorney's fees could be recovered only as costs. Article 2208 now allows reasonable attorney's fees as actual or compensatory damages, but only by stipulation or in the 11 instances it lists. Nothing allows their simultaneous recovery as costs beyond Rule 142. "[I]t would be absurd to award a reasonable amount of attorney's fees as damages, only to later award the actual appearance fees of the prevailing party's counsel as costs."

Section 10(b) provides a flat PHP 20 for all appearances down to final judgment. Though small today, "unless amended, that amount remains the only amount of lawyer's fees that can properly be awarded as costs." Only PHP 15 is allowed for the complaint or answer, nothing for other pleadings, and nothing for original documents. *Norsk Hydro* does not help petitioners: its statement that costs are "not limited to" Sections 9 to 11 refers to costs taxable under other rules, such as Rule 23, Section 18 and Rule 32, Section 13. **Petitioners are entitled only to the attorney's fees awarded as damages, PHP 20 for their counsel's attendance, and the other items exclusively enumerated in Section 10.**

**3. No.** Denying attorney's fees as costs was correct in principle, but the judge erred in performing a duty that belongs in the first instance to the clerk of court. In superior courts, costs are taxed by the clerk on five days' written notice with a verified statement of the items. Objections are made in writing, and either party may appeal the clerk's taxation to the court (*Romulo v. Dasalla*, under the former Rule 131, Sec. 8). Taxation is "a condition precedent to the obligation to pay them, to the power of the court to pass on disputed items, or to the inclusion of costs in an execution." The court takes part only on appeal from the clerk's taxation. Instead of denying the PHP 348,014 outright as "additional cost of suit," the judge should have directed the clerk to assess the costs at the rates in the Rules.

### Disposition
The Petition was DENIED. The case was REMANDED to Branch 97, RTC, Quezon City, which was ORDERED to direct its clerk of court to assess the costs of suit in accordance with the Decision and Rule 142 of the Rules of Court.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** After trial, the RTC awarded Liza PHP 150,000 as attorney's fees under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, plus costs of suit. The judgment became final. Liza then submitted a verified bill of costs that included PHP 180,000 for her lawyer's appearance fees at 60 hearings and PHP 25,000 for the preparation of pleadings and motions. May these items be recovered as costs of suit?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Liza may recover her lawyer's fees only through the attorney's fees awarded as damages. As costs, she may recover only the amounts fixed in Rule 142, Section 10, such as PHP 20 for attendance and PHP 15 for the complaint.
- **Legal basis:** The only costs recoverable by the prevailing party are those fixed in Rule 142, Sections 9 to 11; any other item is a matter of damages. Under Section 6, no attorney's fees are taxed as costs except as provided by civil law. Section 10 allows, "and no other," PHP 15 for the complaint or answer and a flat PHP 20 for the attendance of the party and counsel down to final judgment. Reasonable attorney's fees are recoverable only as actual or compensatory damages under Article 2208 and cannot also be taxed as costs. (Go v. Saint Jude Catholic School Manila, G.R. No. 257761, April 22, 2025)
- **Application:** Liza has already been awarded PHP 150,000 as attorney's fees by way of damages. Allowing her lawyer's actual appearance fees as costs would let her recover attorney's fees twice. The number of hearings does not matter because Section 10(b) fixes one flat amount for all appearances. As for pleadings, only the complaint or answer earns PHP 15; other pleadings and motions earn nothing.
- **Conclusion:** The PHP 180,000 and PHP 25,000 items cannot be taxed as costs; Liza's costs are limited to those enumerated in Rule 142, Section 10.

**Q2.** Same facts. Liza filed a motion for execution with her bill of costs attached. The RTC judge granted the writ but struck out all the items of costs himself, reasoning that they were "additional costs" that would modify a final judgment. The clerk of court never taxed the costs. (a) Did the judge follow the proper procedure? (b) May Liza bring the ruling on costs to a higher court even though an order of execution is not appealable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The judge should have directed the clerk of court to tax the costs first. (b) Yes. A ruling on the taxation of costs is final and may be appealed.
- **Legal basis:** In superior courts, costs are taxed by the clerk of court on five days' written notice with a verified statement of the items. Objections are made in writing, and either party may appeal the clerk's taxation to the court (Rule 142, Sec. 8). Taxation is a condition precedent to the obligation to pay costs, to the court's power to pass on disputed items, and to their inclusion in an execution. An order granting execution is not appealable (Rule 41, Sec. 1), but a ruling on the taxation of costs is final, not interlocutory, and may be appealed. (Go v. Saint Jude Catholic School Manila, G.R. No. 257761, April 22, 2025, relying on Romulo v. Dasalla and Del Rosario v. Bayona)
- **Application:** The judgment itself awarded "costs of suit." Which items are recoverable, and in what amounts, is a matter for taxation, which must first be done by the clerk of court. The judge may pass on disputed items only on appeal from the clerk's taxation, and no taxation was ever made. Liza is not questioning the grant of execution but the ruling on costs, which finally disposes of that matter, so it may be elevated (by Rule 45 if it raises a pure question of law).
- **Conclusion:** The judge erred by ruling on the costs in the first instance, and Liza may appeal that ruling; the clerk must then tax the costs under Rule 142.

**Q3.** Nina sued Omar to collect a sum of money. Omar defended the suit in the honest belief that he owed nothing. There was no stipulation on attorney's fees. The court ruled for Nina but found that Omar had not acted in bad faith, and it found no other ground under Article 2208 of the Civil Code to award attorney's fees. Nina argues that she should at least recover, as costs, the PHP 120,000 she paid her lawyer. Is she correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Nina cannot recover her lawyer's fees as damages or as costs. She may recover only the costs fixed in Rule 142, Section 10.
- **Legal basis:** Attorney's fees and expenses of litigation may be recovered as damages only if there is a stipulation or if one of the 11 instances in Article 2208 applies, and the award requires factual, legal and equitable justification. Even when a party is compelled to litigate, attorney's fees may not be awarded without a sufficient showing of bad faith, beyond an erroneous conviction in the righteousness of one's cause. Otherwise, only the costs under Rule 142 may be recovered, and Rule 142, Section 6 bars taxing attorney's fees as costs except as provided by civil law. (Go v. Saint Jude Catholic School Manila, G.R. No. 257761, April 22, 2025)
- **Application:** There is no stipulation, no Article 2208 ground was found, and Omar litigated in good faith, so attorney's fees cannot be awarded as damages. Nina cannot get around this by claiming her lawyer's fees as costs, because the only lawyer-related amount recoverable as costs is the flat PHP 20 for attendance under Section 10(b).
- **Conclusion:** Nina is limited to the costs enumerated in Rule 142, Section 10 and cannot recover the PHP 120,000 she paid her lawyer.

> Note: En Banc. Thirteen Justices concurred; Singh, J. was on leave. The 2027 syllabus has no specific heading for costs (Rule 142). The case is mapped to execution because taxation of costs is a condition precedent to their execution. The bill of costs in the source text is garbled. A stray "PHP 3,000.00" appears to be the per-appearance rate (PHP 264,000 for 88 appearances), and the pleadings item is PHP 30,000, which matches the PHP 348,014 total.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69952)
