## Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr.

**MANUEL H. REYES, COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. DIOSDADO C. SEBRIO, JR., RESPONDENT.**  
A.C. No. 14062 (Formerly CBD Case No. 08-2188) | 2025-04-02 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 9. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers (Canon VI) > c. Charges and Sanctions  
**Specific topics:** Improper claim of influence or familiarity (Canon I, Sec. 2; Canon II, Sec. 15); Duty to account for and return client funds (Canon III, Sec. 49); Failure to pay a just debt as dishonest conduct (Canon II, Sec. 1); Penalties on a lawyer already disbarred; aggravating circumstances; Return of money linked to the lawyer-client relationship vs. personal loans

### Doctrine
A lawyer who tells a client that he has friends in government offices who "will definitely offer a hand" in the client's transaction violates **Canon I, Section 2 and Canon II, Section 15 of the CPRA** (merit-based practice; improper claim of influence or familiarity). **Whether the boast is true, or whether the connections are actually used, is irrelevant; the mere claim of influence consummates the offense** (reiterating *Rodco Consultancy v. Concepcion*, decided under Rule 15.06 of the CPR).

A lawyer who receives money for a specific purpose must account for it and, if it is not used for that purpose, return it promptly; failure to return it upon demand gives rise to a presumption of misappropriation (**Canon III, Section 49**, the successor of Rule 16.01 of the CPR). Accepting payment without rendering the service violates Canon II, Section 1, Canon III, Section 6, and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6. Failure to pay a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct under Canon II, Section 1. Each of these may amount to **gross misconduct, a serious offense** under Canon VI, Section 33(a), punishable under Section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00.

When the respondent has already been disbarred, **the Court keeps its jurisdiction over offenses he committed while still a lawyer.** It can no longer impose a second disbarment, but it may still declare the penalty, to be recorded in his file with the Office of the Bar Confidant for consideration if he later petitions to lift the disbarment or seeks judicial clemency. It may also impose fines, which may be increased under Canon VI, Section 39 when aggravating circumstances are present (here, prior administrative liability and lack of remorse). Under Canon VI, Section 37, **the lawyer must return money "intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship," but the Court will not order payment of a personal loan from the complainant**, because a disciplinary case is not a civil action for collection (reiterating *Sosa v. Mendoza* and *Heenan v. Espejo*). The complainant may file a separate civil or criminal action.

### Facts
Complainant Manuel Reyes agreed to finance the clearance of a Quezon City property that his friend Danilo Zialcita had bought under a Deed of Absolute Sale dated November 24, 1997. Zialcita introduced respondent Atty. Diosdado Sebrio, Jr., who was to work out clearances with government agencies to facilitate the transfer and registration of the property in Zialcita's name, with fees on a contingency basis once the property was sold. Reyes alleged that Atty. Sebrio claimed to know personally the LRA Administrator and the Register of Deeds of Quezon City and promised to deliver the title within six months.

As shown by handwritten receipts signed by Atty. Sebrio, Reyes paid him PHP 400,000.00 (January 19, 2007), PHP 100,000.00 (January 29, 2007), PHP 70,000.00 (February 2, 2007), PHP 128,000.00 (March 2007), and PHP 72,000.00 in cash plus a PHP 100,000.00 check (April 9, 2007) for LRA expenses and representation. After six months Reyes stopped giving money. Atty. Sebrio then avoided him, and the LRA and the Registry of Deeds did not know him. On June 7, 2007, Atty. Sebrio also borrowed PHP 200,000.00 under a promissory note, promising to deliver a check by June 13, 2007. He never paid or issued the check, despite a final demand letter he received on November 19, 2007.

In his Answer, Atty. Sebrio admitted receiving the amounts (totaling PHP 870,000.00), but called them part of Reyes's commitment to finance PHP 10 million in exchange for a 40% return. He denied claiming to know the LRA Administrator personally, saying instead that he had told Reyes he had friends in the LRA, the Registry of Deeds, the Quezon City Assessor's Office, and the Land Management Bureau "who will definitely offer a hand [in] this transaction." He admitted the loan but blamed a 20% monthly interest that Reyes allegedly demanded, and he denied receiving the demand letter.

The IBP-CBD (Report dated May 13, 2023) found him liable under Rules 1.01, 15.06, and 16.01 of the CPR and recommended a five-year suspension. Because Atty. Sebrio had already been disbarred, the IBP Board of Governors (Resolution dated June 21, 2023) applied the CPRA and recommended instead a fine of PHP 100,000.00 and the return of PHP 870,000.00 and PHP 200,000.00 with legal interest.

### Issues
1. Whether respondent is liable for claiming influence or connections in government offices.
2. Whether respondent is liable for failing to render the services paid for and to account for the money he received.
3. Whether respondent's failure to pay his loan from complainant is a ground for discipline.
4. What penalties may be imposed on respondent, who was already disbarred, and whether he may be ordered to return both the advances and the loan.

### Ruling
The Court adopted the IBP's findings, applied the CPRA (A.M. No. 22-09-01-SC), and modified the penalty.

**1. Yes, he violated Canon I, Section 2 and Canon II, Section 15 of the CPRA.** He boasted that he had friends in the LRA, the Registry of Deeds, the Assessor's Office, and the LMB "who will definitely offer a hand [in] this transaction." Under *Rodco Consultancy and Maritime Services Corp. v. Concepcion*, whether such boasts are true or whether the lawyer actually uses the connections "is irrelevant"; the offense is consummated by the mere claim of influence, which "inflicts damage to the image of the judiciary." Under *Lim v. Bautista*, lawyers guilty of influence-peddling are unworthy of the title of attorney and may be disbarred.

**2. Yes, he violated Canon II, Section 1; Canon III, Sections 6 and 49; and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6.** He admitted receiving the money but showed no steps taken and no proof of any legal service performed. As in *Reddi v. Sebrio, Jr.*, he failed to credibly account for the funds. Citing *Professional Services, Inc. v. Rivera*: a lawyer who receives money for a particular purpose must account for how it was spent and, if it was not used for that purpose, return it immediately; failure to return it upon demand creates a presumption of misappropriation. Failure to account or return violates Rule 16.01 of the CPR, now Canon III, Section 49.

**3. Yes, his non-payment of the loan violates Canon II, Section 1.** Prompt payment of financial obligations is a lawyer's duty. Under *Sosa v. Mendoza*, failure to honor a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct, and flimsy excuses only confirm the refusal. His excuse (the alleged 20% monthly interest) was unsubstantiated, and bare denials do not overcome the evidence against a lawyer (*Reddi*).

**4. Penalties.** The influence-peddling, the failure to render services, and the failure to account together amount to **gross misconduct, a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(a)**, punishable under Section 37(a). Since the Court has disbarred lawyers both for failing to account for money received for unrendered services and for influence-peddling, disbarment is the penalty for this first count. The failure to pay the PHP 200,000.00 loan is a second count of gross misconduct. Because he was already disbarred, a fine of PHP 101,000.00 was deemed appropriate, increased to PHP 150,000.00 under Canon VI, Section 39 because of two aggravating circumstances: his previous administrative liability (disbarment) and his lack of remorse. **A second disbarment can no longer be imposed, but it is recorded in his personal file with the Office of the Bar Confidant** for consideration in any petition to lift the disbarment or for judicial clemency. **The Court may still impose fines because it does not lose jurisdiction over offenses committed by a disbarred lawyer while still a member of the Bar**, so it fined him PHP 150,000.00 for each count.

On restitution, the Court ordered the return of the **PHP 870,000.00** in unutilized advances with 6% interest, since Canon VI, Section 37 requires the return of money "intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship." It **declined to order payment of the PHP 200,000.00 loan**. Following *Sosa v. Mendoza* and *Heenan v. Espejo*, a disciplinary proceeding is not a civil action for collection: it involves no private interest and only determines the lawyer's fitness to remain a member of the Bar. The ruling is without prejudice to any civil or criminal action the complainant may file.

### Disposition
Respondent was found GUILTY of two counts of Gross Misconduct for violating Canon I, Section 2; Canon II, Sections 1 and 15; Canon III, Sections 6 and 49; and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6 of the CPRA. The Court imposed DISBARMENT for the first count (with an order striking his name from the Roll of Attorneys) and a FINE of PHP 150,000.00 for the second count. Because he had been previously disbarred, the disbarment may no longer be imposed but should be considered, and the Court instead imposed fines of PHP 150,000.00 for each count, a total of PHP 300,000.00, payable within 10 days from receipt, with proof of payment due within 10 days after paying. He was ORDERED TO RETURN PHP 870,000.00 to complainant with legal interest of 6% per annum from receipt of the Decision until full payment.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Mario hired Atty. Lim to have a lost land title reconstituted. Atty. Lim told Mario that he had "close friends" at the Land Registration Authority and the Registry of Deeds who would "definitely help" speed up the process. Mario paid Atty. Lim PHP 500,000.00 for "LRA expenses and representation." A year later nothing had been filed, and Atty. Lim could not explain where the money went. In the disbarment case, Atty. Lim argues that his statement about his friends was harmless puffery because he never actually talked to any LRA official. (a) Is Atty. Lim liable for his statement about his friends? (b) What other violations did he commit, and what may the Court order regarding the PHP 500,000.00?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. The mere claim of influence or connections violates the CPRA, whether or not he actually used them. (b) He also violated the CPRA rules on propriety, fidelity to the client, competence and diligence, and accounting for client funds. Taken together, these acts are gross misconduct warranting disbarment, and the Court may order him to return the unutilized PHP 500,000.00 with legal interest.
- **Legal basis:** Canon I, Section 2 and Canon II, Section 15 of the CPRA prohibit a lawyer from making claims of power, influence, or relationship with any officer of a court, tribunal, or government agency. Whether the boasts are true or the connections actually used is irrelevant; the mere claim consummates the offense. A lawyer who receives money for a specific purpose must account for it and return any unused amount (Canon III, Section 49). Accepting payment without rendering the service also violates Canon II, Section 1, Canon III, Section 6, and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6. These acts together constitute gross misconduct, a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(a), for which disbarment may be imposed under Section 37(a). Money intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship must be returned (Canon VI, Section 37). (Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr., A.C. No. 14062, April 2, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Atty. Lim's statement that his friends at the LRA and the Registry of Deeds would "definitely help" is a claim of influence. That he never talked to any official is no defense, because the offense is complete upon the claim; it damages public confidence in the integrity of government processes. (b) He received PHP 500,000.00 for a specific purpose, did nothing, and could not account for it, which violates his duties of fidelity, diligence, and accounting. Combined with the influence-peddling, his acts amount to gross misconduct, and the Court has disbarred lawyers for both kinds of acts. Because the money was given for his legal services and related expenses, it is intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship, so the Court may order its return with legal interest.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Lim is liable for gross misconduct and may be disbarred and ordered to return the PHP 500,000.00 with legal interest.

**Q2.** Atty. Cruz borrowed PHP 300,000.00 from his client Nena and signed a promissory note in which he promised to deliver a check in payment within a week. He never paid or issued the check despite demand. His only excuse, which he did not prove, was that Nena had demanded usurious interest. Nena filed a disbarment complaint and asked the Supreme Court to order Atty. Cruz to pay her the PHP 300,000.00 with interest. (a) Is Atty. Cruz administratively liable? (b) May the Court order him to pay the loan in the disciplinary case?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. His willful failure to pay a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct that may amount to gross misconduct. (b) No. The Court will not order payment of the loan in a disciplinary proceeding, without prejudice to a separate civil or criminal action.
- **Legal basis:** A lawyer shall not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct (Canon II, Section 1, CPRA). Prompt payment of financial obligations is a lawyer's duty, and failure to honor a just debt, especially when coupled with flimsy excuses, is dishonest and deceitful conduct. In Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr. (A.C. No. 14062, April 2, 2025), reneging on a promise to issue a check for a loan and failing to pay it despite demand was gross misconduct under Canon VI, Section 33(a). Under Canon VI, Section 37, the Court orders the return only of money or property intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship. A disciplinary case is not a civil action for collection: it involves no private interest and determines only the lawyer's fitness to remain a member of the Bar (Sosa v. Mendoza, applied in Reyes).
- **Application:** (a) Atty. Cruz signed a promissory note, promised a check, and paid nothing despite demand. His excuse about usurious interest is unsubstantiated, so it only confirms his refusal to pay a valid debt. This is dishonest and deceitful conduct that may be treated as gross misconduct. (b) The PHP 300,000.00 is a personal loan, not money received for legal services or client funds entrusted to him for a purpose. The Court will therefore not order its payment in the disbarment case. Nena must file a separate civil action (or a criminal action, if warranted) to collect.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Cruz may be disciplined for failing to pay his debt, but the Court will not order him to pay the loan in the disbarment case.

**Q3.** Atty. Dela Paz was disbarred in 2020 in an unrelated case. In 2024, a former client filed a complaint against him for misappropriating client funds in 2018, while he was still a member of the Bar. The Court finds him guilty of gross misconduct, and notes that his pleadings show no remorse. Atty. Dela Paz argues that the Court can no longer discipline him because he is no longer a lawyer. (a) Is he correct? (b) What penalty may the Court impose?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The Court keeps its jurisdiction over offenses a disbarred lawyer committed while still a member of the Bar. (b) The Court cannot disbar him again, but it may declare the penalty of disbarment for recording in his file with the Office of the Bar Confidant. It may also impose a fine, increased because of aggravating circumstances, and order the return of the misappropriated funds.
- **Legal basis:** The Court does not lose its exclusive jurisdiction over other offenses committed by a disbarred lawyer while still a member of the profession. A second disbarment can no longer be imposed, but the penalty is recorded in the lawyer's personal file with the Office of the Bar Confidant for consideration if he petitions to lift the disbarment or seeks judicial clemency, and the Court may impose fines. Gross misconduct is a serious offense (Canon VI, Section 33(a), CPRA) punishable under Section 37(a) by, among others, a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00. Under Sections 38 and 39, a finding of previous administrative liability and lack of remorse are aggravating circumstances, and when aggravating circumstances are present with no mitigating ones, the fine may be up to double the maximum. Money intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship must be returned (Section 37). (Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr., A.C. No. 14062, April 2, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) The misappropriation happened in 2018, while Atty. Dela Paz was still a lawyer, so his later disbarment does not remove the Court's power to discipline him for it. (b) His gross misconduct would ordinarily merit disbarment, but he has already been disbarred, so the Court will only declare that penalty and record it for future petitions for reinstatement or clemency. It may also impose a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, increased because of two aggravating circumstances: his prior disbarment and his lack of remorse. Because the misappropriated money was client funds, the Court may also order him to return it with legal interest.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Dela Paz may still be held liable: the Court will record a disbarment, impose an increased fine, and order restitution of the client's funds.

> Note: Respondent's earlier disbarment was in Reddi v. Sebrio, Jr., 597 Phil. 168 (2009), as cited in the decision. The fallo is internally layered: it first imposes disbarment for the first count and a PHP 150,000.00 fine for the second, then states that the disbarment may no longer be imposed but should be considered, and imposes fines of PHP 150,000.00 for each count (total PHP 300,000.00). For the second count, the body first sets a PHP 101,000.00 fine and then increases it to PHP 150,000.00 because of the aggravating circumstances; it does not explain how the same PHP 150,000.00 figure was reached for the first count beyond stating that a fine of PHP 150,000.00 is proper "for each count of gross misconduct, considering the presence of aggravating circumstances." Interest on the PHP 870,000.00 runs from respondent's receipt of the Decision.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69953)

## Anonymous v. Judge Bajan

**ANONYMOUS, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. JULIETO N. BAJAN, PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 2, MUNICIPAL TRIAL COURT IN CITIES, SURIGAO CITY, SURIGAO DEL NORTE, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. MTJ-25-035 [Formerly JIB FPI No. 21-053-MTJ] | 2025-03-04 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Retirement does not oust the Court of administrative jurisdiction; Habitual tardiness, smoking in court, hearing other courts' cases, sleeping during trial (Revised Rule 140); Ignoring OCA and JIB directives to comment is gross insubordination; Rule 140, Section 4 does not automatically make a judge's offense a ground for discipline as a lawyer; Penalties for multiple offenses; second offense; fine in lieu of suspension for a retired judge
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VI. Judicial Department > E. The Supreme Court > 1. Composition, Powers, and Functions > b. Administrative Supervision over Lower Courts)

### Doctrine
Once administrative jurisdiction attaches (the complaint was filed while the respondent was in office), the judge's later **retirement does not oust the Court of jurisdiction or make the case moot** (reiterated, OCA v. Fuensalida). Under Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC): smoking in court and in chambers against the Court's anti-smoking issuances, and hearing cases of other courts without authority against OCA Circular No. 90-2004 (only the Supreme Court may change the venue or place of trial, Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 5(4)), are each a **violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars** (less serious, Sec. 15(e)). Starting sessions at 11:00 to 11:30 a.m. is **habitual tardiness** (less serious, Sec. 15(c)); "a judge's work is 24/7" is no excuse. Sleeping during trial is **simple misconduct** violating Canon 4, Section 1 (propriety) of the New Code of Judicial Conduct (Sec. 15(a)). **Repeatedly ignoring OCA and JIB directives to comment is gross insubordination**, a serious charge. Only gross insubordination, not simple insubordination, is an offense under Revised Rule 140.

The Court **clarified** that Section 4 of Revised Rule 140 **does not automatically make a judge liable as a lawyer** for every improper act that has a matching provision in the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath. The Court must first ask whether the misconduct casts serious doubt on the judge's moral fitness and integrity as a member of the Bar. Added sanctions as a lawyer are confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character. Acts that pertain to the performance of official functions (tardiness, smoking, hearing cases outside the proper court, sleeping in trial) do not qualify.

On penalties: a separate penalty is imposed for each offense (Sec. 21). A retired judge who can no longer be suspended is fined. Length of service is not mitigating if the judge has a prior disciplinary record. A repeat offense after a warning may justify a fine up to double the maximum (Sec. 20). The Court may, in its discretion, decline to order forfeiture of retirement benefits even for a serious charge.

### Facts
Two undated anonymous letter-complaints from litigants, who hid their identities for fear of reprisal, were sent to the Office of the Chief Justice and to the Executive Judge of the MTCC of Surigao City. They accused Judge Julieto N. Bajan, Presiding Judge of Branch 2, MTCC Surigao City, of starting trial at 11:30 a.m. instead of 8:30 a.m. and keeping parties waiting more than two hours only to postpone, of smoking and sleeping during trial, and of hearing in Surigao City cases raffled to another court (MTCC Placer-Bacuag). Judge Bajan also held designations as acting presiding judge of other stations.

The OCA referred the complaints to the RTC and MTCC Executive Judges of Surigao City for discreet investigation. Both confirmed that Judge Bajan held hearings only from about 11:00 or 11:30 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., smoked in open court until November 2012 and still smoked in chambers, did not report daily to his regular court, and slept during trial so that lawyers had to leave. They also confirmed that he heard at MTCC Branch 2 one case from Placer-Bacuag and one from Sison-Tagana-an. No apparent or serious delay in acting on cases was found.

In a letter-comment dated February 28, 2014, Judge Bajan asked for dismissal of the second complaint as harassment. He attacked its lack of verification and supporting records, not its substance. The OCA's May 2, 2014 directive to file a more comprehensive comment went unheeded despite a tracer (July 24, 2015) and a reiteration (February 1, 2021). The OCA referred the matter to the JIB, whose Office of the General Counsel filed a formal complaint. The JIB twice directed him to file a verified comment (May 10, 2022 and March 9, 2023). The second directive also required him to show cause why he should not be disciplined as a member of the Bar and warned that non-compliance would be a waiver. He did not comply. He retired on May 23, 2023.

The JIB recommended that the matter be re-docketed and that he be fined PHP 50,000.00 for each of six offenses. These were habitual absenteeism or tardiness, smoking, sleeping during hearings (simple misconduct), hearing cases not raffled to him, simple neglect of duty for delay, and simple misconduct as a member of the Bar.

### Issues
1. Whether the Court retains jurisdiction over the administrative case despite Judge Bajan's retirement.
2. Whether Judge Bajan is liable for violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars for smoking within court premises and for hearing cases of other courts.
3. Whether he is liable for habitual tardiness, and for simple neglect of duty for delay in resolving cases.
4. Whether sleeping during trial is simple misconduct constituting a violation of the New Code of Judicial Conduct.
5. Whether his failure to comply with the OCA's and the JIB's directives to comment is gross insubordination.
6. Whether he should also be disciplined as a member of the Philippine Bar for the same acts.
7. What penalties should be imposed.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the Court retains jurisdiction.** Jurisdiction attaches when the complaint is filed during the respondent's incumbency and is "not lost by the mere fact that the public official or employee was no longer in office during the pendency of the case." Retirement is not a ground to dismiss the case or render it moot (OCA v. Fuensalida).

**2. Yes, two counts of violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars (less serious, Sec. 15(e), Revised Rule 140).** (a) *Smoking:* Memorandum Circular No. 01-2008 and Office Order No. 06-2009 prohibit smoking inside court buildings and adjacent areas; smoking is allowed only in designated places. Judge Bajan smoked openly during trial and in chambers, despite complaints from court staff. (b) *Hearing other courts' cases:* Under the Constitution only the Supreme Court can order a change of venue or place of trial. OCA Circular No. 90-2004 requires that cases remain in the branch to which they were raffled. By hearing and bringing cases of other courts to his sala, he inconvenienced litigants, jeopardized the safekeeping of records and evidence, and "arrogated upon himself authority no less than only the High Court possesses."

**3. Liable for habitual tardiness (less serious, Sec. 15(c)), but not for simple neglect of duty.** OCA Circular No. 63-2001 (then in force) and OCA Circular No. 250-15 require session hours of 8:30 a.m. to 12 noon and 2:00 to 4:30 p.m. He began sessions between 11:00 and 11:30 a.m. while the public arrived as early as 8:30 a.m. His excuse that a judge's mental work is "24/7" was unacceptable. Circulars on session hours "are not just empty pronouncements." However, neither investigating judge confirmed any delay in his cases, so there was no factual basis for the JIB's recommended finding of simple neglect of duty.

**4. Yes, simple misconduct (Sec. 15(a)).** Misconduct is an intentional wrongdoing or deliberate violation of a rule or standard of behavior connected with official functions. Gross misconduct requires corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules. Scandalous behavior that erodes public esteem for the Judiciary is simple misconduct. Falling asleep during trial, so that lawyers had to step out, violated Canon 4, Section 1 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, which requires judges to avoid impropriety and its appearance.

**5. Yes, gross insubordination, a serious charge.** Directives of the OCA, issued in the exercise of the Court's administrative supervision, and of the JIB, to which the Court delegated the processing of complaints, "are not mere requests" and must be obeyed promptly and completely. Insubordination is the "inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey some order that a superior is entitled to give and have obeyed." Unlike the 2017 RACCS, Revised Rule 140 retains only gross insubordination as an offense. For more than 10 years Judge Bajan ignored the OCA's directive to file a comprehensive comment and the JIB's two directives to file a verified comment. Compliance cannot be partial or selective (Judge Santiago v. Fernando; Beltran v. Pabica). His indifference showed defiance of the Court itself.

**6. No, he is not separately disciplined as a lawyer.** The OGC complaint did not seek his liability as a lawyer, though the JIB recommended it under the CPRA. **Section 4 of Revised Rule 140 "does not contemplate automatically holding judges liable for all improper acts that have a corresponding provision under the CPRA or the Revised Lawyer's Oath."** The CPRA and the Oath are broad, so nearly every act of a judge could otherwise be a ground for discipline as a lawyer. The Court must assess whether the judge's transgressions "cast serious doubt on his or her moral fitness." Added discipline is confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character or fitness to practice law. Smoking in court, ignoring session hours, hearing cases outside the proper court, and sleeping during trial pertain to his official functions. They do not rise to a level of moral delinquency warranting bar discipline.

**7. Penalties.** Separate penalties are imposed for each offense (Sec. 21). Being retired, he can no longer be suspended, so fines are imposed. His more than 10 years of service is not mitigating because he had prior administrative liabilities: A.M. No. MTJ-20-1941 (including PHP 20,000.00 for habitual tardiness, with a stern warning), A.M. No. MTJ-16-1868, and A.M. No. P-17-3707. The Court fined him PHP 50,000.00 each for the two circular violations and for simple misconduct. Habitual tardiness drew PHP 100,000.00, the maximum for a less serious charge, as his second offense after a warning. Gross insubordination drew **PHP 300,000.00, above the PHP 200,000.00 ceiling for serious charges**, because it was a second offense and to stress strict compliance with directives to comment. The Court chose not to forfeit his retirement benefits out of compassion, though not as a mitigating circumstance. It considered his multiple designations (Executive Judge and acting judge of two other stations), that gross insubordination was his only serious charge, and the absence of evidence that he neglected his judicial duties.

### Disposition
Retired Judge Julieto N. Bajan was found GUILTY under A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC of: (1) two counts of violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars (Sec. 15(e)) for smoking during trial and within court premises and for hearing cases from other courts, fined PHP 50,000.00 each; (2) habitual tardiness (Sec. 15(c) in relation to Sec. 20), fined PHP 100,000.00; (3) simple misconduct constituting a violation of the New Code of Judicial Conduct (Sec. 15(a)), fined PHP 50,000.00; and (4) gross insubordination, fined PHP 300,000.00. The aggregate fine of PHP 550,000.00 is payable within 30 days from finality; if unpaid, contempt proceedings under Rule 71, Section 3 shall be commenced. Copies were furnished to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the IBP, and the OCA.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Judge Cruz of a Municipal Trial Court in Cities was the subject of an anonymous complaint. The OCA directed him to comment. He sent a one-page letter calling the complaint harassment and pointing out that it was unverified, without addressing the charges. The OCA twice directed him to submit a comprehensive comment, and the Judicial Integrity Board later twice directed him to file a verified comment. He ignored all four directives. While the case was pending, Judge Cruz compulsorily retired. (a) Should the case be dismissed because of his retirement? (b) What is his administrative liability for ignoring the directives?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The Court retains jurisdiction despite his retirement. (b) He is liable for gross insubordination, a serious charge under Revised Rule 140.
- **Legal basis:** Once jurisdiction attaches because the complaint was filed during the respondent's incumbency, it is not lost by his later retirement, which neither warrants dismissal nor renders the case moot (OCA v. Fuensalida, as applied in Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, A.M. No. MTJ-25-035, March 4, 2025). Directives of the OCA and the JIB to comment are issued in the exercise of the Court's administrative supervision over lower courts and are not mere requests. Under Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), which retains only gross insubordination as an offense, a judge's repeated and unjustified failure to comply with them is gross insubordination, a serious charge (Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, supra).
- **Application:** (a) The complaint was filed and acted upon while Judge Cruz was still in office, so the Court's jurisdiction had attached; his compulsory retirement does not end the case. (b) His one-page letter dodged the substance of the charges, and compliance with a directive to comment cannot be partial or selective. He then ignored two OCA directives and two JIB directives without explanation. That is a willful disregard of lawful orders from offices acting for the Supreme Court. Because he can no longer be suspended or dismissed, the Court may impose a fine or, in lieu of dismissal, forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) under Revised Rule 140.
- **Conclusion:** The case proceeds despite retirement, and Judge Cruz is liable for gross insubordination.

**Q2.** In an administrative case against Judge Reyes, the Judicial Integrity Board found him guilty of habitual tardiness, smoking inside his courtroom, and sleeping during trial. After requiring him to show cause, the JIB also recommended that he be fined as a member of the Bar for violating Canon II (Propriety) of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, relying on Section 4 of Rule 140, as amended. Should the Supreme Court also discipline Judge Reyes as a lawyer?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The Court should not impose an additional sanction on Judge Reyes as a member of the Bar for these acts.
- **Legal basis:** Section 4 of Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, allows an administrative case against a judge to be considered a disciplinary case against him as a lawyer. However, it does not automatically hold judges liable as lawyers for every improper act that has a counterpart in the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath. The Court first determines whether the misconduct casts serious doubt on the judge's moral fitness as a member of the Bar. Additional sanctions are confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character (Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, A.M. No. MTJ-25-035, March 4, 2025).
- **Application:** Habitual tardiness, smoking in court, and sleeping during trial are improper and are punishable under Rule 140 as offenses of a judge. But they pertain to the performance of his official functions. They do not involve dishonesty, deceit, immorality, or abuse of power that would put in question his fitness to remain a lawyer. That the JIB issued a show-cause order satisfies due process, but it does not by itself justify a second sanction. The result could differ if the acts showed moral delinquency, such as dishonest or deceitful conduct.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Reyes should be penalized only as a judge, not additionally as a member of the Bar.

**Q3.** Judge Lim presides over an MCTC in Municipality A and was designated acting presiding judge of an MTCC in City B, 40 kilometers away. To save travel time, he ordered several cases pending in the MCTC of Municipality A, which were still at the trial stage, brought to City B and heard there, without authority from the Supreme Court. (a) Did Judge Lim act within his authority? (b) What administrative offense, if any, did he commit?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Only the Supreme Court may order a change of venue or place of trial. (b) He committed a violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars, a less serious charge under Revised Rule 140.
- **Legal basis:** Article VIII, Section 5(4) of the Constitution vests in the Supreme Court the power to order a change of venue or place of trial to avoid a miscarriage of justice. Section 6 gives it administrative supervision over all courts. To implement these, OCA Circular No. 90-2004 provides that, except as stated in the guidelines, all cases shall remain in the branch to which they were raffled or assigned. A judge who hears and transfers cases of other courts to his station without authority commits a violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars under Section 15(e) of Revised Rule 140 (Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, A.M. No. MTJ-25-035, March 4, 2025).
- **Application:** The cases were raffled to the MCTC of Municipality A and were still at the trial stage, so they had to remain and be heard there. By moving them to City B on his own, Judge Lim exercised a power that belongs only to the Supreme Court. He also inconvenienced the litigants and witnesses, for whose convenience venue exists, and exposed the court records and evidence to risk. His convenience is not a justification.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Lim overstepped his authority and is administratively liable for violating Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars.

> Note: Leonen, SAJ. wrote a separate concurring and dissenting opinion (he would have dismissed the respondent); Caguioa, J. concurred; Marquez, J. took no part (prior action as Court Administrator). Only the main opinion is digested. The body cites gross insubordination under "section 14(11)" while the fallo cites "section 14(n)" of Revised Rule 140; this appears to be a text or OCR inconsistency, so the digest refers only to Section 14 (serious charges). The decision applied Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), the New Code of Judicial Conduct, and the CPRA as in force at the time. The 2027 syllabus frames judicial ethics under the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC); this decision does not discuss that Code, so check the corresponding CJCA provisions separately.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69912)

## Tallado v. Judges Racoma and Dating

**HON. JOSEFINA B. TALLADO, COMPLAINANT, VS. PRESIDING JUDGE WINSTON S. RACOMA, BRANCH 39, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, DAET, CAMARINES NORTE, AND PRESIDING JUDGE ARNIEL A. DATING, BRANCH 41, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, DAET, CAMARINES NORTE, RESPONDENTS.**  
A.M. No. RTJ-25-084 [Formerly JIB FPI No. 21-086-RTJ] | 2025-02-18 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Errors in adjudicative functions must be corrected through judicial remedies, not administrative complaints; When judicial errors become administratively sanctionable; Guidelines for identifying harassment suits against judges (Tallado v. Judge Racoma, 2022); Request for a judicial audit used to harass judges; show cause for indirect contempt; Belated compliance with A.O. No. 63-2020 on submission of TROs
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (IV. Provisional Remedies > C. Preliminary Injunction (Rule 58) > 1. Preliminary Injunction vs. Temporary Restraining Order vs. Status Quo Ante Order)
  
**Also relevant to:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics (V. Special Civil Actions > K. Contempt (Rule 71) > 1. Direct vs. Indirect Contempt)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VI. Judicial Department > E. The Supreme Court > 1. Composition, Powers, and Functions > b. Administrative Supervision over Lower Courts)

### Doctrine
**Errors attributed to judges in the exercise of their adjudicative functions must be assailed in judicial proceedings, not in an administrative case.** Examples are issuing 20-day TROs without a prior summary hearing; the proper remedies are a motion for reconsideration and, if warranted, certiorari. A judge cannot be held civilly, criminally or administratively liable for official acts, however erroneous, done in good faith. **Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, corruption, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do an injustice are administratively sanctioned** (*Mahinay v. Judge Daomilas, Jr.*, reiterated).

The Court applied the guidelines laid down in *Tallado v. Judge Racoma* (2022) for determining whether a disciplinary case against a justice, judge or court personnel is a **harassment suit**:

- the existence of other cases filed against the respondent by the same or related complainants;
- the complainant's position and influence, particularly in the locality where the respondent is stationed;
- the number of times the respondent has been charged administratively, and how those cases ended;
- any decisions or judicial actions the respondent previously rendered for or against the complainant;
- the complainant's propensity for filing administrative cases against members and personnel of the Judiciary; and
- any other factor indicating improper pressure or influence.

Applying these guidelines to a **request for a judicial audit**, the Court found the request a ploy to harass the judges. It ordered the complainant to show cause why she should not be held in **indirect contempt** for requesting a judicial audit for unfounded reasons.

### Facts
In a January 5, 2021 letter, Representative Josefina B. Tallado of the 1st District of Camarines Norte asked the Court for a judicial audit of the courts of Judge Winston S. Racoma (RTC Branch 39, Daet) and Judge Arniel A. Dating (RTC Branch 41, Daet). She cited reports of anomalous issuances of TROs and of cases heard regardless of jurisdiction, while admitting she was not privy to the specifics. Her husband, Governor Edgardo A. Tallado, was a respondent in SP Civil Case Nos. 8484 and 8513.

The OCA audit found two things. First, Judge Racoma had issued 20-day TROs in those two cases without the summary hearing required by Administrative Circular No. 20-95. Second, both judges had failed to submit copies of their TROs to the Office of the Chief Justice within five days of issuance, as required by Administrative Order No. 63-2020 (issued February 18, 2020). The OCA recommended that Judge Racoma be held liable for gross ignorance of the law. Judge Racoma answered that his TROs were issued under Rule 58, Sec. 5 and stated their factual and legal bases. He said the complainants were the same parties aggrieved by his orders, who filed administrative cases instead of using judicial remedies. Both judges attributed their delay under A.O. No. 63-2020 to inadvertence during the pandemic. Judge Dating added that the order reached their court only on May 12, 2020, and was distributed only after the court reopened on June 1, 2020.

The Office of the Executive Director (OED) of the Judicial Integrity Board recommended dismissal. It found that the TRO issue was judicial in nature: Judge Racoma had cited Rule 58, Sec. 5, which allows an ex parte 20-day TRO if great or irreparable injury would result before the matter can be heard on notice, together with supporting jurisprudence. It also found the belated compliance with A.O. No. 63-2020 not serious enough to warrant sanction. The JIB agreed and recommended dismissal for being judicial in nature and for lack of merit. It found no evidence of malice or bad faith, and it found the audit request to be a ploy to intimidate and harass the judges. The request was connected with other administrative cases filed against them by Camarines Norte officials led by Governor Tallado.

### Issues
1. Whether Judges Racoma and Dating are administratively liable for issuing the questioned TROs and for their belated compliance with A.O. No. 63-2020.
2. Whether the request for a judicial audit was a harassment suit warranting action against the complainant.

### Ruling
**1. No, the judges are not administratively liable.** The complainant attributed errors to the judges' adjudicative functions, "which are not the proper subject of an administrative case." Citing *Mahinay v. Judge Daomilas, Jr.*, the Court held that such errors should be assailed in judicial proceedings. **"Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty and corruption, gross ignorance, bad faith[,] or deliberate intent to do an injustice will be administratively sanctioned."** The questioned orders "were issued with factual and legal bases, following relevant procedural rules." Even assuming error, there was no evidence of fraud, dishonesty, corruption, gross ignorance, bad faith or deliberate intent to do injustice. The Court adopted the JIB's findings. Those findings included its agreement with the OED that the belated compliance with A.O. No. 63-2020 was not serious enough to warrant sanction: it was explained as inadvertence during the public health emergency, and the judges undertook to comply.

**2. Yes, the audit request was a harassment suit.** The Court took judicial notice of earlier cases. In *Tallado v. Judge Racoma* (2022), the complaint against Judge Racoma was dismissed, and the complainants were ordered to show cause why they should not be held in indirect contempt for a premature complaint meant to harass him. In *Venida v. Judge Dating*, a complaint filed by an appointee of the Governor was dismissed. In *Tallado v. Judge Dating* (2022), the Court noted the complainants' propensity for filing administrative complaints against judges. "[U]nfounded criticisms against members of the Judiciary degrade the judicial office and greatly interfere with the due performance of their functions in the Judiciary." Applying the *Tallado v. Judge Racoma* guidelines:

- **First**, the complainant is the wife of the Governor, a respondent in SP Civil Case Nos. 8484 and 8513, and therefore an interested party.
- **Second**, as district representative she holds a highly influential position in the province where the judges are stationed.
- **Third**, persons related to her and her husband had filed earlier administrative cases against the same judges. Most were dismissed, with the complainants ordered to show cause for indirect contempt.

**The request was a ploy to intimidate, harass, demoralize and influence the judges.** The complainant was directed to explain why she should not be cited in contempt for requesting a judicial audit for unfounded reasons. Such an audit "does not only interfere with the due performance of judicial functions, but also undermines and degrades or impairs the respect due the judicial office."

### Disposition
The Court ADOPTED and APPROVED the findings of fact, conclusions of law and recommendations of the Judicial Integrity Board. The administrative complaint against former Presiding Judge Winston S. Racoma (RTC Branch 39, Daet) and Presiding Judge Arniel A. Dating (RTC Branch 41, Daet) was DISMISSED for being judicial in nature and for lack of merit. Complainant Hon. Josefina B. Tallado was ORDERED to SHOW CAUSE within 10 days from notice why she should not be held in indirect contempt of court for requesting a judicial audit for unfounded reasons, intended to harass or vex the respondent judges.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Governor Gil is a respondent in a petition for prohibition pending before Judge Hana of the RTC. Judge Hana issued ex parte a 20-day TRO against Gil. Her order stated the facts showing that great or irreparable injury would result to the petitioner before the matter could be heard on notice, and it cited Rule 58, Section 5. Without moving for reconsideration or filing a petition for certiorari, Gil filed an administrative complaint for gross ignorance of the law against Judge Hana. He claims that a summary hearing was required before any TRO could issue. Nothing shows fraud, corruption or bad faith on the judge's part. Will the complaint prosper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The complaint should be dismissed for being judicial in nature.
- **Legal basis:** Errors attributed to judges in the exercise of their adjudicative functions should be assailed through judicial remedies, such as a motion for reconsideration and, if warranted, a petition for certiorari, and not through an administrative case. A judge is not liable for official acts, however erroneous, done in good faith. Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, corruption, gross ignorance, bad faith or deliberate intent to do an injustice are administratively sanctioned. (Tallado v. Judges Racoma and Dating, A.M. No. RTJ-25-084, February 18, 2025, reiterating Mahinay v. Judge Daomilas, Jr.)
- **Application:** Whether a summary hearing should have preceded the TRO is a question about how Judge Hana exercised her judgment in a pending case. Her order stated its factual basis and cited Rule 58, Section 5, so it was not issued arbitrarily. If Gil believed it was wrong, his remedy was a motion for reconsideration and then certiorari, which he never used. Nothing shows fraud, corruption, bad faith or deliberate intent to do injustice that would make the alleged error administratively punishable.
- **Conclusion:** Gil's administrative complaint will not prosper; his remedy lies in the judicial process.

**Q2.** Suppose instead that, in the same case, evidence shows that Judge Hana met privately with the petitioner the day before issuing the TRO and received PHP 200,000 from him. Gil files an administrative complaint. Judge Hana argues that issuing a TRO is an adjudicative act that may be questioned only through judicial remedies. Is she correct?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The rule that adjudicative errors must be corrected judicially does not shield a judge whose act is tainted with corruption or bad faith.
- **Legal basis:** A judge is immune from administrative liability for official acts, however erroneous, only if they are done in good faith. Judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, corruption, gross ignorance, bad faith or deliberate intent to do an injustice will be administratively sanctioned. (Tallado v. Judges Racoma and Dating, A.M. No. RTJ-25-084, February 18, 2025, reiterating Mahinay v. Judge Daomilas, Jr.)
- **Application:** Unlike the first situation, the TRO here was preceded by a private meeting and the receipt of money from the party who benefited from it. The complaint does not merely question the judge's legal reasoning; it charges corruption and bad faith in the issuance itself. That falls within the exception, and it is a proper subject of administrative discipline regardless of the judicial remedies against the TRO.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Hana may be held administratively liable, because her act is alleged and shown to be tainted with corruption.

**Q3.** Congresswoman Rita's husband, the provincial governor, is a party in several cases before Judges Kiko and Lito, two of the few RTC judges in the province. Rita wrote the Supreme Court asking for a judicial audit of their salas, citing "reports" of anomalous TROs while admitting she knew no specifics. Relatives and political allies of the governor had previously filed administrative complaints against both judges. Most were dismissed, and the complainants were ordered to show cause why they should not be cited in contempt. The audit and the investigation that followed found no basis to hold the judges liable. (a) What factors will the Court consider in determining whether Rita's request is a harassment suit? (b) What action may the Court take against Rita?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) The Court considers the harassment-suit factors in Tallado v. Judge Racoma, and they show that Rita's request is harassment. (b) The Court may order Rita to show cause why she should not be held in indirect contempt of court.
- **Legal basis:** In determining whether a disciplinary case against a judge is a harassment suit, the Court considers: (1) other cases filed against the respondent by the same or related complainants; (2) the complainant's position and influence in the locality where the respondent is stationed; (3) the number of times the respondent has been charged and how those cases ended; (4) the respondent's previous decisions or actions for or against the complainant; (5) the complainant's propensity for filing administrative cases against members and personnel of the Judiciary; and (6) any other sign of improper pressure or influence. A request for a judicial audit for unfounded reasons interferes with judicial functions and degrades the respect due the judicial office, and the Court may order the requester to show cause why she should not be held in indirect contempt (Rule 71). (Tallado v. Judges Racoma and Dating, A.M. No. RTJ-25-084, February 18, 2025)
- **Application:** (a) Rita is an interested party because her husband is a litigant before the two judges. As a congresswoman she wields great influence in the province. Persons related to her and the governor have repeatedly charged the same judges, mostly without success and with show-cause orders for contempt. Her request rested on unspecified "reports" and was ultimately unfounded. These factors show the audit request was meant to intimidate and pressure the judges. (b) Because the unfounded request interfered with the judges' functions and impaired respect for the judicial office, the Court may direct Rita to explain why she should not be cited for indirect contempt.
- **Conclusion:** Rita's request is a harassment suit, and the Court may order her to show cause why she should not be held in indirect contempt.

> Note: Not to be confused with Tallado v. Judge Racoma, 929 Phil. 40 (2022) (Singh, J.), which laid down the harassment-suit guidelines applied here. Marquez, J. took no part, having signed the OCA memorandum as Court Administrator. Singh, J. was on leave. The decision quotes the OCA as citing "Administrative Complaint No. 20-95," apparently meaning Administrative Circular No. 20-95, and the OED as recommending compliance with "Administrative Order No. 62-2020," apparently meaning A.O. No. 63-2020. The text is kept as written. The OCA said a summary hearing must precede a TRO except for a 72-hour ex parte TRO by the Executive Judge; the OED read Rule 58, Sec. 5 as allowing an ex parte 20-day TRO. The Court did not resolve that conflict; it held only that the orders had factual and legal bases and that any error was judicial. The case was decided under Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, before the 2025 CJCA. The syllabus heading is by subject matter. The bar question on corruption (Q2) applies the exception the Court quoted, not facts of this case.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69902)

## Re: Resolution Dated August 30, 2017 in OMB-C-C-13-0357 v. Atty. Talaboc

**RE: RESOLUTION DATED AUGUST 30, 2017 IN OMB-C-C-13-0357, ETC., COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. EDITHA P. TALABOC, ATTY. DELFIN R. AGCAOILI, JR., AND ATTY. MARK S. OLIVEROS, RESPONDENTS.**  
A.C. No. 11889 [Formerly CBD Case No. 18-5671] | 2024-11-13 | First Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 9. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers (Canon VI) > e. Burden of Proof and Quantum of Evidence  
**Specific topics:** Substantial evidence and the lawyer's presumption of innocence in disciplinary cases; Notary not liable where signatures and seals were forged (Rigon v. Subia distinguished); Failure to answer is not an admission; Disregard of IBP-CBD directives as a less serious offense under the CPRA; Mitigating and aggravating circumstances (CPRA Canon VI, Secs. 38-39)

### Doctrine
**In disciplinary proceedings, the lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed his or her duties in accordance with the oath; the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence** (Rule 133, Sec. 6 of the Rules on Evidence). Mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions are not proof, and the respondent's failure to answer the complaint is not an admission of its allegations (reiterated).

A notary public is **not liable** for notarizations made in his or her name where there is substantial evidence that the signatures were forged and the notarial certificates themselves are irregular (missing the commission serial number, office address, IBP chapter or place of issue of the PTR; commission periods and IBP/PTR receipts that do not match official records), casting doubt on the validity of the seals and stamps used. Negligence in safekeeping the notarial paraphernalia cannot then be inferred: "Notaries are not immune from identity theft." The Court distinguished *Rigon v. Atty. Subia* (notary accountable for his seal where he did not deny its authenticity) and cases where negligence was shown by giving secretaries full access to the notarial paraphernalia or by entries in the notarial books. Given the proliferation of fake notaries, liability for alleged violations of the Notarial Rules is determined **case by case**.

Separately, **failing to comply with the IBP-CBD's directives** (to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper) **violates Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA** and is a **less serious offense under Canon VI, Sec. 34(c)**, sanctioned under Sec. 37(b). A first offense is mitigating (Sec. 38(a)(1)), allowing a fine of not less than half the minimum (PHP 17,500.00) under Sec. 39; previous administrative liability is aggravating, allowing a penalty up to double the maximum.

### Facts
Criminal complaints for plunder, graft, malversation through falsification and other offenses were filed with the Office of the Ombudsman (OMB) in OMB-C-C-13-0357 over the release and liquidation of PHP 900 million of the Malampaya Fund. The complainants there alleged that the memoranda of agreement used were "notarized" by Ben Hur Luy, who forged the signatures of respondents Attys. Editha P. Talaboc, Delfin R. Agcaoili, Jr. and Mark S. Oliveros and used their registers, stamps and seals; that Atty. Oliveros, Janet Lim Napoles's wedding godson, knew of the use of his name and was paid; and that the notarial details of the two others were supplied by one Tess Rodino. The OMB found that respondents did not notarize the documents and that there was insufficient proof they knew of or were part of the scheme, but recommended disciplinary action for allowing the use of their signatures, seals and registers for a fee. The matter was forwarded to the Court and referred to the IBP.

Only Atty. Agcaoili answered. He denied notarizing the documents, said he kept his notarial paraphernalia in a locked drawer, and pointed out that in the NBI investigation Luy admitted signing above his name. Atty. Talaboc filed several motions for extension but never filed an answer or position paper. Atty. Oliveros filed nothing; notices sent to the address supplied by the OMB were returned unserved, so the IBP sent its March 4, 2019 Order (requiring position papers) to his residence as shown in IBP records. Neither Atty. Talaboc nor Atty. Oliveros attended the mandatory conference.

The Investigating Commissioner counted 95 documents in Atty. Oliveros's name, 132 in Atty. Talaboc's and 104 in Atty. Agcaoili's, all showing only community tax certificates (or nothing) as proof of identity. He found that Atty. Oliveros knew his notarial details were being used and that the two others were negligent in safekeeping theirs, and recommended that each be suspended for six months, have any notarial commission revoked, and be disqualified from being commissioned for two years. The IBP Board of Governors adopted this on March 17, 2022.

### Issues
1. Whether respondents are administratively liable for violating the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice for the documents notarized in their names.
2. Whether Attys. Talaboc and Oliveros are liable for failing to comply with the IBP-CBD's directives, and what penalties apply.

### Ruling
**1. No. The OMB failed to prove the notarial charges by substantial evidence.** A lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed his or her duties in accordance with the oath; the complainant bears the burden of proof by substantial evidence, and mere allegations are not proof. Failure to answer is not an admission. The parts of the OMB Joint Resolution relied on by the Investigating Commissioner were whistleblowers' statements that were "merely the allegations of the complainants" in the OMB case. No notarial register was presented, and there was no proof that respondents consented to the use of their signatures, seals and registers or received money for it.

The documents themselves cast doubt on the commissions used. Certificates in Atty. Talaboc's name lacked her commission serial number, office address, IBP chapter and the place of issue of her PTR (contrary to Rule VIII, Sec. 2 of the Notarial Rules); those in Atty. Agcaoili's name also lacked his Roll of Attorneys number; those in Atty. Oliveros's name lacked the commission serial number and office address. Atty. Agcaoili's certificates claimed a commission valid until December 31, 2009, but the Quezon City RTC certified that he was commissioned only from August 7, 2007 to December 31, 2008 and not since 2009; a one-year commission would violate the two-year term under Rule III, Sec. 11. Certificates in Atty. Oliveros's name stated a commission valid until December 31, 2010, which did not match the Pasig RTC certifications, and his supposed 2010 notarizations bore 2008 IBP and PTR numbers although he had 2010 receipts. The seals and stamps were thus themselves doubtful, and negligence in safekeeping could not be concluded, since others could have had stamps and seals made in respondents' names. "Notaries are not immune from identity theft."

The Court distinguished its rulings penalizing notaries who blamed others, where negligence was shown by giving secretaries full access to notarial paraphernalia or by entries in the notarial books, and *Rigon v. Atty. Subia*, where the notary did not deny the authenticity of his seal. Here there was substantial evidence that respondents' signatures were forged. Atty. Agcaoili's earlier sanctions (*Triol v. Atty. Agcaoili*; *Dionisio, Jr. v. Padernal*) did not involve established forgery.

**2. Yes, as to Attys. Talaboc and Oliveros.** Neither filed an answer or a defense, and neither attended the mandatory conference. Atty. Oliveros is presumed to have received the March 4, 2019 Order under the disputable presumption that a letter duly directed and mailed was received in the regular course of mail (Rule 131, Sec. 3(v)). Following *Kelley v. Atty. Robielos III*, their disregard of the IBP-CBD's directives violated **Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA** and is a less serious offense under Canon VI, Sec. 34(c). For Atty. Oliveros, a first offense (mitigating under Sec. 38(a)(1)) with no aggravating circumstance allowed a fine of not less than half the minimum under Sec. 39: **PHP 17,500.00**. Atty. Talaboc had twice before been sanctioned for ignoring directives to file pleadings (*Completo v. Talaboc*, fine of PHP 10,000.00; *Sia Su v. Talaboc*, three-month suspension); with this aggravating circumstance, she was **suspended for six months**.

The Court added that notarization is not an empty, routinary act but is invested with substantive public interest; still, with the proliferation of fake notaries public, liability for alleged violations of the Notarial Rules must be determined case by case. It reminded Executive Judges of their duty to monitor notaries public, directed the IBP to be more proactive in pursuing fake notaries, and ordered compliance with OCA Circular No. 291-2023 (Task Force Honesto Notario).

### Disposition
The complaint against Atty. Delfin R. Agcaoili, Jr. was DISMISSED for lack of merit. Atty. Editha P. Talaboc was found GUILTY of violating Canon III of the CPRA and SUSPENDED from the practice of law for six months from receipt of the Decision, with a stern warning, and DIRECTED to file a manifestation that her suspension has started, copy furnished to all courts and quasi-judicial bodies where she has appeared as counsel. Atty. Mark S. Oliveros was found GUILTY of violating Canon III of the CPRA and ORDERED to pay a fine of PHP 17,500.00 within 10 days from receipt, with a stern warning, and to submit proof of payment within 10 days from payment. The OCA was ordered to remind all concerned judges to comply with OCA Circular No. 291-2023, and the Executive Judges of the RTCs of Manila, Quezon City and Pasig, with the OCA and the IBP, were ordered to investigate the notarial services rendered in respondents' names.

### En Banc or Division?
First Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** In a graft investigation, the Ombudsman found that dozens of contracts used to release public funds bore the notarial seal and signature of Atty. Dina, but that she did not actually notarize them. Relying on whistleblowers' statements that she had allowed her seal to be used for a fee, the Ombudsman referred her to the Supreme Court for discipline. Before the IBP, Atty. Dina answered, denying any participation. The notarial certificates on the contracts omit her commission number and office address and state a commission period that conflicts with the certification of the Executive Judge. No notarial register or proof of payment to her was presented. Should Atty. Dina be held liable for violating the Notarial Rules?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The charge was not proved by substantial evidence, and the irregularities point to forgery rather than negligence on her part.
- **Legal basis:** In disciplinary proceedings the lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed her duties in accordance with her oath; the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence, or such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion (Rule 133, Sec. 6, Rules on Evidence). Mere allegations are not proof. Where the notarial certificates lack details required by Rule VIII, Sec. 2 of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice and state commission periods contradicted by official records, the validity of the seals used is doubtful and negligence in safekeeping cannot be presumed, because "[n]otaries are not immune from identity theft" (Re: Resolution Dated August 30, 2017 in OMB-C-C-13-0357 v. Atty. Talaboc, A.C. No. 11889, November 13, 2024).
- **Application:** The only evidence that Atty. Dina allowed the use of her seal for a fee is the whistleblowers' statements, which are mere allegations. No notarial register or proof of payment was presented. Meanwhile, the certificates omit her commission number and office address and state a commission period that conflicts with the Executive Judge's certification, which suggests that someone else had a seal and stamp made in her name. Negligence cannot be inferred from these facts.
- **Conclusion:** The charge against Atty. Dina for violating the Notarial Rules should be dismissed.

**Q2.** Suppose that in the same case Atty. Dina's notarial register, presented before the IBP, contains entries for the questioned contracts, and Atty. Dina admits that the seal on them is genuinely hers. She claims only that her office clerk, who had free access to her seal and register, forged her signature without her knowledge. Would your answer be different?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Atty. Dina may be held liable for negligence in the handling of her notarial seal and register.
- **Legal basis:** In the Talaboc case (A.C. No. 11889, November 13, 2024), the Court acknowledged its earlier rulings penalizing lawyers who claim that someone else notarized documents in their name, where factors proved the lawyer's negligence, such as allowing secretaries full access to the notarial paraphernalia and the appearance of the notarized documents in the notarial books. It also cited Rigon v. Atty. Subia: where the notary's seal appears on the document and he fails to deny its authenticity, he bears accountability for its use even if done without his consent and knowledge. The Talaboc respondents were exonerated only because these factors were absent and there was substantial evidence that their signatures, and even the commissions stated, were not genuine.
- **Application:** Unlike the Talaboc respondents, Atty. Dina admits that the seal is hers, the contracts appear in her own notarial register, and she gave her clerk free access to both. These are the very factors the Court identified as proof of negligence. Even if the clerk forged her signature, the misuse was made possible by her failure to safeguard her notarial paraphernalia.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Dina may be held administratively liable for negligence as a notary public.

**Q3.** Atty. Ernie was charged before the IBP Commission on Bar Discipline. He did not file an answer, did not attend the mandatory conference, and did not file a position paper. The IBP order requiring position papers was mailed to his residence as shown in IBP records; he later claimed he never received it. The charge on the merits was eventually dismissed for lack of evidence. (a) May Atty. Ernie still be penalized? (b) If this is his first offense and there is no aggravating circumstance, what is the lowest fine the Court may impose?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. His disregard of the IBP-CBD's directives is a separate violation of Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA, even if the main charge fails. (b) PHP 17,500.00, which is half of the PHP 35,000.00 minimum fine for a less serious offense.
- **Legal basis:** Failing to comply with the IBP-CBD's directives to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper violates Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA and is a less serious offense under Canon VI, Sec. 34(c), punishable under Sec. 37(b) by suspension of one to six months (or revocation of notarial commission and disqualification of less than two years) or a fine of PHP 35,000.00 to PHP 100,000.00. A first offense is mitigating under Sec. 38(a)(1), and under Sec. 39, if there are mitigating and no aggravating circumstances, the Court may impose a fine not less than half the minimum. A letter duly directed and mailed is presumed received in the regular course of mail (Rule 131, Sec. 3(v)). In Re: Resolution Dated August 30, 2017 in OMB-C-C-13-0357 v. Atty. Talaboc (A.C. No. 11889, November 13, 2024), the notarial charge was dismissed, but Atty. Oliveros was fined PHP 17,500.00 for ignoring the IBP's order.
- **Application:** (a) The order was mailed to Atty. Ernie's residence on IBP records, so he is presumed to have received it, and his bare denial does not overcome the presumption. His total non-participation is an infraction against the disciplinary process itself, independent of the merits of the complaint, so the dismissal of the main charge does not absolve him. (b) As a first offender with no aggravating circumstance, he may be fined as low as half of PHP 35,000.00, or PHP 17,500.00.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Ernie may be penalized for violating Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA, with a fine that may go as low as PHP 17,500.00.

> Note: Per the decision's own footnote, the "Resolution" in the caption should read "Joint Order." The decision's narration of the IBP mandatory conference dates is internally inconsistent (a conference on December 3, 2019 said to have been reset to January 28, 2019), so those dates are left out. Although the Court said the aggravating circumstance allowed a penalty up to double the maximum, the six-month suspension it imposed on Atty. Talaboc is within the ordinary range for a less serious offense.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69740)
