## Usama v. Judge Tomarong

**MARILOU CASAS USAMA, COMPLAINANT, VS. (RET.) HON. OSCAR D. TOMARONG, BRANCH 28, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, LILOY, ZAMBOANGA DEL NORTE, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. RTJ-21-017 [Formerly OCA IPI No. 19-4935-RTJ] | 2023-03-08 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Granting bail without notice to the prosecutor and without hearing: gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct; Habeas corpus is not the vehicle for granting bail; no relief for non-parties; Tallado v. Racoma outright-dismissal rule inapplicable when the complainant has no judicial remedy; Revised Rule 140: retroactivity, penalties for multiple offenses, and fine in lieu of suspension for a retired judge
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > M. Rights of the Accused)

### Doctrine
**In all cases, whether bail is a matter of right or of discretion, the judge must notify the prosecutor of the bail application or require his recommendation. Where bail is discretionary (offenses punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment), the judge must hold a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong** (Const., Art. III, Sec. 13; Rule 114, Secs. 7, 8, and 18; OCA v. Judge Flor, Jr.; Villanueva v. Judge Buaya, which requires notice and hearing even when bail is a matter of right, to apply the Section 9 guidelines in fixing the amount). The judge's own view that the killing was "only homicide," and the fact that no Information had yet been filed, do not excuse notice and hearing. A judge who grants bail on the day it is filed without either commits **gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct**. A petition for habeas corpus is not the proper vehicle to assert a right to bail (Galvez v. CA), and ordering the release on bail of persons who are not parties to the habeas corpus case is a separate act of gross ignorance and gross misconduct.

The rule in Tallado v. Racoma (an administrative complaint is dismissed outright if a judicial remedy is still available) does not apply where the complainant had no judicial remedy. A private offended party, whose interest is limited to the civil aspect, has no legal personality to question a grant of bail.

The Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, effective April 4, 2022) applies to all pending and future cases even if prejudicial to the respondent (Sec. 24), and Dela Rama v. De Leon is abandoned. Under Section 21, separate acts are penalized separately, while a single act constituting several offenses gets only the penalty for the most serious. **When a respondent who deserves suspension can no longer serve it because of retirement, the Court applies Section 18(b) by analogy and imposes a fine under Section 17(1)(c).** The Court will no longer impose "forfeiture of salary" equivalent to the suspension period, a practice derived from the civil service rules.

### Facts
On May 4, 2016, days before the May 9, 2016 elections, police officers on patrol in Tampilisan, Zamboanga del Norte exchanged gunfire with mayoral candidate Alson Chan and his campaign volunteers. PO1 Mirdan Usama, complainant's husband, was killed. Chan and his volunteers were arrested on the morning of May 5, 2016.

At 2:00 p.m. on May 5, 2016, a Muslim holiday, Chan filed with respondent Judge Tomarong's court (RTC Branch 28, Liloy) an "Application to Post Bail and to Release the Detained Person Pending Filing of Proper Information" (Misc. Sp. Proc. No. MSP-328). The application stated that an Information would be filed on May 6. The same day, respondent granted bail at P200,000.00. He did not notify the prosecutor and held no hearing. The police refused to release Chan. On May 6, after inquest, the provincial prosecutor prepared Informations against Chan and three volunteers for murder, two counts of attempted murder, illegal possession of firearms (RA 10591), and illegal possession of explosives (RA 9616).

On May 7, Chan's wife filed a petition for habeas corpus for Chan only (Sp. Proc. No. SR-763). Respondent issued the writ, and after a hearing on May 10 he ordered "the release of accused Alson Chan and the released (sic) of the three other accused ... after posting a bail of ... (P200,000.00) each in all cases that will be filed against them." Complainant moved for his inhibition the same day, and respondent inhibited on July 26, 2016.

Complainant filed her Complaint-Affidavit dated February 19, 2019. Respondent optionally retired effective April 1, 2019. In his Comment, he invoked SC Circular No. 95-96 on acting on bail during weekends and holidays. He said he had "analyzed" that the crime was only homicide, a bailable offense, so no hearing was needed, and that his acts were judicial in nature. The JIB found him liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct. It recommended forfeiture of one year's salary and benefits, in lieu of one year's suspension, with a stern warning.

### Issues
1. Whether the administrative complaint should be dismissed outright under Tallado v. Racoma because a judicial remedy was available to the complainant.
2. Whether respondent is administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct.
3. What penalty should be imposed on respondent, considering his retirement.

### Ruling
**1. No.** Tallado laid down guidelines against abuse of the administrative disciplinary mechanism, including outright dismissal when a judicial remedy is still available. That rule does not apply here because complainant had no judicial remedy against the grant of bail. In criminal cases the State is the real party in interest, and the private offended party's interest is limited to civil liability. **As the victim's widow, complainant had no legal personality to question the grant of bail**, so the Court proceeded to the merits.

**2. Yes, on two separate acts.** The Court applied the Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC). Section 24 makes it retroactive to all pending cases even if prejudicial, so it is "uniformly applicable to all cases, regardless of when the infractions are committed." Chan was charged with murder, punishable by reclusion perpetua to death, so bail was discretionary and required a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt was strong (Rule 114, Secs. 7 and 8). Notice to the prosecutor is required in all cases (Rule 114, Sec. 18; OCA v. Judge Flor, Jr.). The absence of an Information on May 5 did not excuse notice and hearing, especially since Chan's own application said one would be filed the next day and respondent knew the detention involved a killing. His "appreciation" that the crime was only homicide "cannot do away with the requirement of conducting a hearing." **Granting bail on the same day without notice and hearing was gross ignorance of the law, and his flagrant disregard of the rules on bail was gross misconduct.**

Second, in the habeas corpus case he ordered the release on bail of the three volunteers, who were not parties to it, which was a separate act of gross ignorance. He also disregarded the scope of habeas corpus under Rule 102, Section 1: "a petition for habeas corpus is not the appropriate vehicle for asserting a right to bail or vindicating its denial" (Galvez v. CA). That flagrant disregard was also gross misconduct.

**3. A fine of P110,000.00 per act, or P220,000.00 in total.** Gross ignorance and gross misconduct are serious charges (Sec. 17(1)). Under Section 21, each act constituting both offenses gets one penalty, and the two separate acts get separate penalties. The Court found one year's suspension commensurate for each act (Sec. 17(1)(b)), but respondent had retired. The JIB's recommended forfeiture of one year's salary is a civil-service practice that the Court "should no longer perpetuate." Section 18 covers only respondents who deserve dismissal, but **the Court applied Section 18(b) by analogy and imposed a fine within the range of Section 17(1)(c) (more than P100,000.00 up to P200,000.00) in lieu of suspension.** A stern warning is no longer viable for a retired judge.

### Disposition
Retired Judge Oscar D. Tomarong was found GUILTY of two counts of gross ignorance of the law and two counts of gross misconduct arising from two separate acts. He would have been suspended for one year without salary and benefits for each act had he not retired on April 1, 2019. He was ordered to pay a FINE of P110,000.00 for each act, or P220,000.00 in total, within three months from promulgation. If unpaid, the amount will be deducted from his retirement benefits, including his accrued leave credits.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Diego was arrested without a warrant for shooting a barangay tanod to death. That same afternoon, before any Information was filed, Diego applied for bail with the RTC, stating that an Information would be filed the next day. Judge Rivera granted bail of P150,000.00 within an hour. He did not notify the prosecutor and held no hearing because, in his view, the killing was only homicide. The next day, an Information for murder was filed. (a) Is Judge Rivera administratively liable? (b) If Judge Rivera has since retired and the Court finds that his offense merits one year's suspension, what penalty may be imposed?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. Judge Rivera is liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct. (b) A fine under Section 17(1)(c) of the Revised Rule 140, applying Section 18(b) by analogy, not forfeiture of one year's salary.
- **Legal basis:** Whether bail is a matter of right or discretion, the judge must notify the prosecutor or require his recommendation. Where the offense is punishable by reclusion perpetua, he must hold a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong (Rule 114, Secs. 7, 8, and 18). Patent disregard of these elementary rules is gross ignorance of the law, and flagrant disregard of them is gross misconduct. When a respondent who deserves suspension can no longer serve it because of retirement, the Court imposes a fine under Section 17(1)(c), applying Section 18(b) by analogy. (Usama v. Judge Tomarong, A.M. No. RTJ-21-017, March 8, 2023, En Banc)
- **Application:** Diego was detained for a killing and was about to be charged, so a bail hearing and notice to the prosecutor were necessary. That no Information had yet been filed did not excuse them. The judge's private estimate that the crime was only homicide cannot replace the hearing, whose necessity depends on the gravity of the offense charged, here murder. Granting bail within an hour without notice and hearing shows a disregard of basic rules. Since Judge Rivera has retired, suspension can no longer be served. Following Usama, the Court imposes a fine of more than P100,000.00 up to P200,000.00, not the civil-service practice of forfeiting salary equivalent to the suspension period.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Rivera is liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct, and being retired, he may be fined under Section 17(1)(c) of the Revised Rule 140 in lieu of suspension.

**Q2.** The widow of the slain tanod filed an administrative complaint against Judge Rivera for granting bail to Diego without notice and hearing. Judge Rivera moves to dismiss the complaint outright under Tallado v. Racoma, arguing that the widow should first have questioned the bail order in a judicial action, such as certiorari. Should the complaint be dismissed outright?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The outright-dismissal rule in Tallado does not apply because the widow had no judicial remedy against the grant of bail.
- **Legal basis:** Under Tallado v. Racoma, an administrative complaint is dismissed outright if a judicial remedy is still available to the complainant. In criminal cases, however, the State is the real party in interest, and the private offended party's interest is limited to the civil liability. A private offended party therefore has no legal personality to question the grant of bail, so Tallado's rule does not apply. (Usama v. Judge Tomarong, A.M. No. RTJ-21-017, March 8, 2023, En Banc)
- **Application:** The widow is only a private offended party in the criminal case against Diego. She cannot assail the bail order on her own because only the State, through the prosecutor, may do so. Since no judicial remedy was available to her, there is nothing she must first exhaust, and her administrative complaint may proceed on the merits.
- **Conclusion:** The motion to dismiss should be denied, and the administrative complaint resolved on the merits.

**Q3.** Lorna filed a petition for habeas corpus for her husband Andres, who had been detained since his warrantless arrest for a stabbing. At the hearing, the prosecutor manifested that an Information would be filed that day. Judge Cruz then ordered the release of Andres and of two co-detainees, Ben and Carlo, "upon posting bail of P100,000.00 each in all cases that will be filed against them." Ben and Carlo were not named in the petition. Did Judge Cruz act properly?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Judge Cruz misused the habeas corpus proceeding to grant bail and granted relief to non-parties. This is gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct.
- **Legal basis:** Under Rule 102, Section 1, the writ of habeas corpus extends to cases of illegal confinement or detention; its purpose is to inquire into involuntary restraint and to relieve a person from it if illegal. A petition for habeas corpus is not the appropriate vehicle for asserting a right to bail or vindicating its denial (Galvez v. CA). Ordering in a habeas corpus case the release on bail of persons who are not parties to it is gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct. (Usama v. Judge Tomarong, A.M. No. RTJ-21-017, March 8, 2023, En Banc)
- **Application:** The only question in Lorna's petition was whether Andres's detention was illegal. Instead of resolving that question, Judge Cruz fixed bail, which belongs to the bail rules under Rule 114 with notice to the prosecutor and a hearing where required. He also extended the relief to Ben and Carlo, who had not sought any relief from the court and were not parties. Both acts show a flagrant disregard of the rules on habeas corpus and bail.
- **Conclusion:** Judge Cruz acted improperly and may be held administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct.

> Note: Decided under the Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, 2022). The 2027 syllabus bases Judicial Ethics on the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC); check whether that Code changed the sanctions and section numbers cited here. The complaint was filed on February 19, 2019, before respondent's optional retirement took effect on April 1, 2019; the decision did not separately discuss jurisdiction over a retired judge. Marquez, J. took no part because of prior action as Court Administrator.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68944)

## Judge Santiago v. Fernando

**JUDGE JAIME B. SANTIAGO, COMPLAINANT, VS. ROMELITO G. FERNANDO, UTILITY WORKER I, BRANCH 18, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, [RTC], TAGAYTAY CITY, CAVITE, RESPONDENT.**  
A.M. No. P-22-053 (Formerly OCA IPI No. 15-4466-P) | 2023-01-17 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Resolution

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)  
**Specific topics:** Revised Rule 140 applies to all pending cases regardless of when the infraction was committed; Jurisdiction not lost by separation from service (AWOL, dropping from the rolls) during pendency; Gross insubordination: defying the presiding judge, and failing to comment despite OCA directives; Court employee receiving money from a litigant is grave (gross) misconduct; Separate penalties for multiple offenses; penalties in lieu of dismissal (Revised Rule 140, Secs. 18 and 21)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline)

### Doctrine
**Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, effective April 4, 2022) governs all pending and future administrative cases against Judiciary personnel, regardless of when the infractions were committed** (Section 24). It is a disciplinary framework wholly independent of the Civil Service rules.

**Once the Court acquires jurisdiction over an administrative case, it is not lost because the respondent leaves the service while the case is pending** (here, by going on AWOL and being dropped from the rolls). What matters is that the case was instituted while the respondent was still in the service. A respondent's failure to comment does not prevent the Court from imposing sanctions; under Section 3(3) it is a waiver of participation, and the case proceeds on the available evidence. Silence in the face of serious accusations may be taken as an implied admission (*qui tacet consentire videtur*).

**Gross insubordination**, the "inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey some order that a superior is entitled to give and have obeyed," covers (a) a court employee's repeated disregard of the presiding judge's directives to transmit pleadings and case records promptly, and (b) willful failure to file a comment despite the OCA's directives, which is defiance of the Court itself. **A court employee's receipt of money from a litigant, whatever the reason and even if the litigant approached him, is grave misconduct**, now termed gross misconduct constituting a violation of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel (Canon I, Sec. 2). Both are serious charges under Section 14(a) and (n). Under **Section 21, a separate penalty is imposed for each offense** arising from separate acts in one proceeding. Where dismissal can no longer be imposed because of a supervening separation, **Section 18** allows forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) and disqualification **"and/or"** a fine, so either or both may be imposed.

### Facts
Romelito G. Fernando was a Utility Worker I at RTC Branch 18, Tagaytay City. In December 2014 the Acting Presiding Judge, Jaime B. Santiago, appointed him Clerk III in charge of civil cases. In an August 11, 2015 complaint, Judge Santiago charged him with insubordination, irregularity in the performance of duty, and gross neglect of duty. Despite repeated admonitions and written warnings, Fernando had failed to refer to the judge the formal offers of evidence in two land registration cases (filed October 10, 2014 and February 17, 2015), giving them to him only on August 11, 2015. In his comment, Fernando blamed his workload and his co-employees.

In an October 5, 2015 supplemental complaint, Judge Santiago charged him with continued irregularities, gross incompetence, and gross misconduct. On September 18, 2015, Mrs. Lolita Borja came to court looking for Fernando. She said he had asked for PHP 40,000.00 to facilitate the bail of her son, detained for violation of Section 11 of RA 9165, but her son remained in jail. A handwritten note signed "Rommel Fernando" acknowledged receipt of PHP 35,000.00 "for safekeeping" on May 12, 2015, plus PHP 5,000.00 on May 22, 2015. During a January 2014 inventory, 51 criminal case folders and one Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court case folder were found in his work area. Three more criminal case folders were later found in his custody, and the missing records of two land registration cases turned up in his steel drawer.

The OCA directed Fernando to comment on the supplemental complaint. He asked for and was granted an extension until March 29, 2016, citing health reasons, but he never filed a comment, even after a January 16, 2017 tracer with a final warning. He last logged in on January 22, 2016 and went on AWOL. On November 29, 2017, his name was dropped from the rolls. The OCA recommended that he be found guilty of gross insubordination and grave misconduct and, since dismissal could no longer be imposed, that he suffer forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) and perpetual disqualification from re-employment in government.

### Issues
1. Whether Revised Rule 140 governs the case, and whether respondent may still be held liable despite being dropped from the rolls and despite his failure to file a comment.
2. Whether respondent is guilty of gross insubordination and grave (gross) misconduct.
3. What penalties should be imposed.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, Revised Rule 140 applies, and the Court retains jurisdiction.** Revised Rule 140, effective April 4, 2022, was meant to be a disciplinary framework for the entire Judiciary, independent of the Civil Service rules and applicable to all pending and future cases regardless of when the infractions were committed (Section 24). **Respondent's absence without leave during the pendency of the case does not prevent the Court from determining his liability:** jurisdiction, once attached, is not lost because the employee is no longer in office, and what is essential is that the case was instituted while he was still in the service. His failure to comment does not prevent sanctions either (Section 3(3): waiver of participation, with the investigation proceeding on the evidence).

**2. Yes, two counts of gross insubordination and one count of gross misconduct.** *First count:* judges must supervise their personnel and stamp out irregularities. Judge Santiago acted within his authority in requiring prompt transmittal of pleadings and records. Even without proof of corruption, respondent's repeated disobedience delayed the disposition of cases ("justice delayed is justice denied"). *Second count:* respondents in administrative cases must comment on the accusations, as part of their duty to preserve the integrity of the Judiciary. Respondent ignored the OCA's 1st Indorsement even after asking for and getting an extension, then went on AWOL. This was willful disrespect for the OCA, through which the Court supervised lower court personnel, and so **defiance of the lawful orders of the Court itself.** Given the gravity of the accusations, his silence was contrary to human experience. Citing Yoshimura v. Panagsagan, the Court deduced "his implicit admission of the charges," so the withholding of records and the receipt of money stood undisputed.

*Gross misconduct:* grave misconduct is a serious transgression of an established rule that threatens the administration of justice, and it may manifest as corruption. Canon I, Section 2 of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel bars court employees from soliciting or accepting any gift, favor, or benefit on the understanding that it will influence their official actions. Respondent had no authority to collect PHP 40,000.00 from Mrs. Borja. His liability did not rest on silence alone: the signed handwritten receipt stood uncontroverted, and the spouses Borja's statements in the judge's investigation detailed how he promised, for PHP 40,000.00, to take care of their son's bail. **That the Borjas approached him first is no excuse; "the sole act of receiving money from litigants, whatever the reason may be, is antithesis to being a court employee."** Grave misconduct is the same as gross misconduct, which is a serious charge under Section 14(a).

**3. Separate penalties for each offense.** All three offenses are serious charges, punishable under Section 17(1) by dismissal, suspension of more than six months up to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 up to PHP 200,000.00. Under Section 21, separate penalties are imposed for separate offenses. Because respondent had been dropped from the rolls, dismissal could no longer be imposed, so Section 18 applied. **Its "and/or" authorizes either or both of its penalties.** The Court modified the OCA's recommendation as follows: the first count of gross insubordination was penalized under Section 18(a) (forfeiture and disqualification), and the second count of gross insubordination and the gross misconduct were each penalized with a PHP 150,000.00 fine. Under Section 22, the fine is payable within three months. If unpaid, it may be deducted from his salaries and benefits, including accrued leave credits.

### Disposition
Respondent Romelito G. Fernando was found GUILTY of two counts of GROSS INSUBORDINATION and one count of GROSS MISCONDUCT constituting a violation of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel. Under Section 18(a) of Revised Rule 140, he was meted forfeiture of all benefits, except accrued leave credits, and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, including GOCCs. He was ordered to pay an aggregate FINE of PHP 300,000.00 within three months from promulgation; if unpaid, it is to be deducted from his salaries and benefits, including accrued leave credits. He was also ordered to RETURN PHP 40,000.00 to Mrs. Lolita Borja, with 6% interest per annum from finality of the Resolution until full payment.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Lito, a court stenographer, received PHP 30,000.00 from Mrs. Dela Cruz, whose son was detained for a drug offense, after promising to "fix" the son's bail papers. The son was never released. Charged administratively, Lito admitted signing a receipt for the money. He argued that (1) Mrs. Dela Cruz approached him first and begged for help, and (2) he only held the money "for safekeeping" and never promised to influence any judge. Is Lito administratively liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Lito is liable for grave misconduct, now designated gross misconduct constituting a violation of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel.
- **Legal basis:** Grave misconduct is a serious transgression of an established rule of action that tends to threaten the administration of justice, and it may manifest as corruption. Canon I, Section 2 of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel prohibits court employees from soliciting or accepting any gift, favor, or benefit on the understanding that it will influence their official actions. A court employee's act of soliciting or receiving money from litigants is grave misconduct. "[T]he sole act of receiving money from litigants, whatever the reason may be, is antithesis to being a court employee," and it is no defense that the litigant approached the employee first. Gross misconduct is a serious charge under Section 14(a) of Revised Rule 140. (Judge Santiago v. Fernando, A.M. No. P-22-053, January 17, 2023)
- **Application:** Lito, a court employee, admittedly received PHP 30,000.00 from the mother of a detained accused after promising to facilitate bail. He had no authority or legal basis to collect that money. Calling it "safekeeping" changes nothing, since the mere receipt of money from a litigant is the offense. That Mrs. Dela Cruz sought him out does not exculpate him either.
- **Conclusion:** Lito is guilty of gross misconduct and may be dismissed from the service.

**Q2.** Rosa, a clerk at an RTC branch, was administratively charged in 2024 with withholding case records. Before filing her comment, she stopped reporting for work, and the Court dropped her from the rolls for being absent without official leave. She never filed a comment. (a) Has the Court lost jurisdiction to decide the administrative case? (b) If Rosa is found guilty of serious offenses warranting dismissal, may the Court impose both forfeiture of benefits with disqualification and a fine?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. The Court retains jurisdiction. (b) Yes. In lieu of dismissal, the Court may impose either or both of the alternative penalties.
- **Legal basis:** Jurisdiction over an administrative case, once acquired, is not lost because the respondent is no longer in office while the case is pending; what is essential is that the case was instituted while the respondent was still in the service. Failure to file a comment results in waiver of participation, and the case proceeds on the available evidence (Revised Rule 140, Sec. 3(3)). Under Section 18 of Revised Rule 140, if dismissal can no longer be imposed because of a supervening separation (except death), the respondent may be meted (a) forfeiture of all or part of the benefits (never accrued leave credits) and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, "and/or" (b) a fine. The "and/or" authorizes either or both. (Judge Santiago v. Fernando, A.M. No. P-22-053, January 17, 2023)
- **Application:** The complaint was filed in 2024 while Rosa was still a court employee, so the Court's jurisdiction had attached. Her later AWOL and dropping from the rolls do not divest it, and her failure to comment simply waives her participation. Because dismissal can no longer be carried out, Section 18 applies. As in Santiago, where the Court imposed forfeiture and disqualification for one count and fines for two other counts, the Court may combine both penalties. Under Section 21, it imposes a separate penalty for each offense.
- **Conclusion:** The Court may still decide the case and may impose forfeiture, disqualification, and a fine against Rosa.

**Q3.** The OCA directed Ben, a court process server, to comment on a complaint accusing him of extorting money from litigants. Ben asked for a 15-day extension, which was granted, but he never filed a comment, even after a tracer with a final warning. (a) Is Ben's failure to comment an administrative offense separate from the charge of extortion? (b) What is the effect of his silence on the extortion charge, and how will the penalties be imposed if he is found liable on both?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) Yes. His willful failure to comment despite the OCA's directives is a separate offense of gross insubordination. (b) His silence may be taken as an implied admission of the extortion charge, and the Court will impose a separate penalty for each offense.
- **Legal basis:** Gross insubordination is the "inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey some order that a superior is entitled to give and have obeyed." A respondent's willful refusal to comply with the OCA's directive to comment is disrespect of the OCA, through which the Court supervises lower court personnel, and so defiance of the Court's own lawful orders. When a respondent stays silent despite serious accusations, the Court may deduce an implied admission (qui tacet consentire videtur). Under Section 21 of Revised Rule 140, when a respondent is liable for more than one offense arising from separate acts in a single proceeding, a separate penalty is imposed for each. (Judge Santiago v. Fernando, A.M. No. P-22-053, January 17, 2023, citing Yoshimura v. Panagsagan)
- **Application:** Ben acknowledged the OCA's directive by asking for, and getting, an extension. He then ignored both the directive and the final warning. That is willful defiance, a separate act from the alleged extortion, and so a separate count of gross insubordination. Faced with an accusation as serious as extortion, an innocent employee would naturally deny it. His silence lets the Court treat the charge as admitted, especially if other evidence such as receipts or witness statements supports it. If found liable for both, he receives one penalty for the insubordination and another for the misconduct.
- **Conclusion:** Ben's failure to comment is a separate offense of gross insubordination, his silence may be taken as an admission, and separate penalties will be imposed for each offense.

> Note: The caption describes respondent as Utility Worker I, but the Resolution says Judge Santiago appointed him Clerk III in December 2014, and the dropping-from-the-rolls matter (A.M. No. 17-10-252-RTC) refers to him as Clerk III. Marquez, J., took no part because of prior action as Court Administrator. This Resolution applied Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), and the peso ranges quoted are those of Revised Rule 140. The later 2026 decisions in this topic say that the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability superseded Rule 140 as to judges. The 2027 syllabus also lists a 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel (A.M. No. 25-06-11-SC). Check that code's current penalty provisions before relying on these amounts for court personnel.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68861)

## Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi

**MONICA M. PONTIANO, ROSALYN M. MATANDAG, ELSIE R. BALINGASA, CRISELDA J. ESPINOZA, MIGUEL R. PANGLILINGAN, MARLON A. VILLA, AND LOUIE T. DELA CRUZ, COMPLAINANTS VS. ATTY. FABIAN A. GAPPI, RESPONDENT.**  
A.C. No. 13118 | 2022-06-28 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 8. Duties and Responsibilities of Lawyers (CPRA) > e. Competence and Diligence (Canon IV)  
**Specific topics:** Gross negligence: missing every hearing and failing to file the position paper; Dishonesty toward clients (Rule 1.01, Canon 1, CPR); Disregard of the Labor Arbiter's processes (Canon 11, CPR); Three-year suspension for gross negligence plus dishonesty (Olvida v. Gonzales); Separate fine for ignoring IBP-CBD directives

### Doctrine
A lawyer who **fails to attend any of the scheduled hearings and fails to file his clients' position paper despite their reminders**, causing the dismissal of their illegal dismissal complaint, is guilty of gross negligence under **Rule 18.03, Canon 18 of the Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR)**. Once a lawyer takes up a client's cause, he must attend to it with competence, diligence, care and devotion, whether he accepts it for a fee or for free; neglect of a legal matter entrusted to him is inexcusable negligence for which he is administratively liable. Deliberately failing to attend hearings ordered by the Labor Arbiter also shows willful disregard of lawful orders, contrary to **Canon 11**.

A lawyer who hands his clients, for signature, a document that would withdraw their complaint while representing that it merely formalizes his withdrawal as counsel commits **dishonesty and deceit in violation of Rule 1.01, Canon 1** of the CPR and of the lawyer's oath to "do no falsehood."

On the penalty, the Court reiterated *Olvida v. Gonzales*: gross negligence in failing to file a position paper, coupled with dishonesty toward the client, warrants **suspension from the practice of law for three years**. A respondent's failure to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper before the IBP-CBD shows willful disregard of its authority (Canons 11 and 12, CPR) and is separately penalized with a **fine (here P15,000.00)**.

### Facts
Complainants were among the 16 complainants in an illegal dismissal case (NLRC NCR Case No. 12-16403-13 and 01-00057-14) before the Labor Arbiter (LA). Respondent Atty. Fabian A. Gappi was their counsel. He did not attend a single scheduled hearing.

Before March 11, 2014, the deadline for their position paper, complainants went to respondent's office to ask about it, and he told them, "Ako na ang bahala." He filed no position paper. On March 11, 2014, complainants returned and asked him to withdraw as their counsel. Respondent prepared a document that supposedly formalized his withdrawal, but on reading it complainants found that it was a withdrawal of their illegal dismissal complaint. They refused to sign it. In a Decision dated April 7, 2014, the LA dismissed the complaint because no position paper had been filed.

Complainants filed an administrative complaint with the IBP. Respondent filed no answer, did not appear at the mandatory conference set on April 6, 2018 (which complainants also missed) or at the reset conference on June 1, 2018, and filed no position paper. The IBP-CBD found him liable under Rule 1.01 of Canon 1, Canon 11, and Rule 18.03 of Canon 18 of the CPR and recommended a two-year suspension. On February 15, 2019, the IBP Board of Governors (IBP-BOG) adopted the findings but increased the suspension to three years and added a P15,000.00 fine for his failure to attend the mandatory conference and file the required pleadings.

In his motion for reconsideration, respondent blamed complainants' indecision over whether to replace him as counsel and the long process of reading and evaluating the evidence of all 16 complainants. The IBP-BOG denied the motion on August 22, 2020.

### Issues
1. Whether respondent is administratively liable under Rule 18.03 of Canon 18, Canon 11, and Rule 1.01 of Canon 1 of the CPR for his handling of complainants' illegal dismissal case.
2. Whether the IBP-BOG's recommended penalty of three years' suspension and a P15,000.00 fine is proper.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, respondent is liable.** The Court adopted the findings of the IBP-CBD as modified by the IBP-BOG. Respondent failed to appear at any scheduled hearing, failed to file the position paper despite his own clients' reminders, and tried to deceive them with a document that would have withdrawn their complaint. The complaint was dismissed to their prejudice. Respondent never repudiated these facts and "even implicitly admitted them" through the explanations in his motion for reconsideration.

These facts showed gross negligence and gross inefficiency, a "propensity to disobey lawful processes of the LA," and dishonesty. Adopting the IBP-CBD's discussion: under Canon 18 and Rule 18.03, a lawyer must serve his client with competence and diligence, for a fee or for free, and neglect of an entrusted legal matter is inexcusable negligence; deliberately failing to attend hearings ordered by the LA shows willful disregard of orders, contrary to Canon 11; and deliberately misrepresenting the document he gave his clients to sign violated Rule 1.01 of Canon 1 and his oath, revealing "basic moral flaws that make him unfit to practice law."

**2. Yes, the penalty is proper.** In *Olvida v. Gonzales*, the Court imposed a three-year suspension on a lawyer who was grossly negligent (he failed to file a position paper) and dishonest with his client (he concealed the resulting adverse decision), even raising the IBP's four-month recommendation despite the absence of a motion for reconsideration. Like the lawyer in *Olvida*, respondent was grossly negligent and dishonest, so the three-year suspension was applied. The Court also adopted the P15,000.00 fine: respondent's failure to attend the mandatory conference and file the required pleadings reflected "willful disregard of the IBP-CBD's authority and disrespect of the board's proceedings," which are clear infractions of Canons 11 and 12 of the CPR.

### Disposition
Respondent Atty. Fabian A. Gappi was found GUILTY of violating Rule 1.01 of Canon 1, Canon 11, and Rule 18.03 of Canon 18 of the CPR and SUSPENDED from the practice of law for three years, effective upon receipt of the Decision, with a WARNING that a repetition would be dealt with more severely. He was also ORDERED to pay a fine of P15,000.00 for failing to comply with the directives of the IBP-CBD. Copies of the Decision were ordered entered in his personal record and furnished to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the IBP, and the Office of the Court Administrator for circulation to all courts.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Atty. Lara represented ten workers in an illegal dismissal case before the Labor Arbiter. She did not appear at any of the scheduled hearings. A week before the deadline for the position paper, the workers asked her about it, and she assured them she would take care of it. She filed nothing, and the Labor Arbiter dismissed the complaint for failure to file a position paper. The workers filed a disbarment complaint. Atty. Lara argues that a lawyer cannot be disciplined for a lapse in handling a case because the clients' remedy is to sue her for damages. Is Atty. Lara administratively liable?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Yes. Atty. Lara is administratively liable for gross negligence in handling her clients' case.
- **Legal basis:** Under Canon 18 and Rule 18.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, a lawyer shall serve the client with competence and diligence and shall not neglect a legal matter entrusted to him, and his negligence in connection therewith renders him liable. Once a lawyer takes up a client's cause, she must attend to it with diligence, care and devotion, and neglect of an entrusted legal matter is inexcusable negligence for which she is administratively liable. A lawyer who missed every hearing and failed to file the position paper despite his clients' reminders, causing the dismissal of their illegal dismissal complaint, was held grossly negligent (Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi, A.C. No. 13118, June 28, 2022). The duty now appears under Canon IV (Competence and Diligence) of the CPRA.
- **Application:** Atty. Lara missed every hearing and let the deadline for the position paper pass even after her clients specifically asked about it and she assured them she would handle it. Her inaction directly caused the dismissal of the complaint, to her clients' prejudice. This is not a mere lapse but the neglect of an entrusted legal matter, which the Code makes a ground for discipline regardless of any civil action the clients may bring against her.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Lara is administratively liable for gross negligence and may be suspended from the practice of law.

**Q2.** Atty. Bert agreed, without charging a fee, to represent a group of farm workers in a labor case. When the workers could not decide whether to keep him or hire another lawyer, Atty. Bert stopped attending hearings and did not file their position paper. He later explained that he was waiting for them to decide and that the evidence of all the workers took long to evaluate. When the workers asked him to withdraw as their counsel, he handed them a paper that he said would formalize his withdrawal; it was in fact a withdrawal of their complaint. The workers noticed and refused to sign. (a) Do the facts that he worked for free and that his clients were undecided excuse his failure to act? (b) What is his liability for the paper he asked them to sign?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Neither the absence of a fee nor the clients' indecision excuses his neglect. (b) He is liable for dishonesty and deceit under Rule 1.01, Canon 1 of the CPR, which, together with his gross negligence, warrants a suspension (three years in the controlling case).
- **Legal basis:** A lawyer who takes up a client's cause must serve it with competence and diligence, attending to it with diligence, care and devotion "whether he accepts it for a fee or for free" (Canon 18 and Rule 18.03, CPR). Rule 1.01, Canon 1 forbids dishonest and deceitful conduct, and the lawyer's oath binds him to "do no falsehood." In Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi (A.C. No. 13118, June 28, 2022), the Court held liable a lawyer who offered the same excuses (his clients' indecision about replacing him and the long evaluation of the evidence of 16 complainants) and who presented a withdrawal of the clients' complaint as a mere withdrawal of counsel. Following Olvida v. Gonzales, it suspended him for three years.
- **Application:** (a) Atty. Bert's duty of diligence attached when he accepted the case, fee or no fee. While he remained their counsel, the workers' indecision did not suspend his duty to attend hearings and meet deadlines; in Pontiano the same excuses did not prevent a finding of gross negligence. (b) Passing off a withdrawal of the complaint as a withdrawal of counsel is deceit practiced on clients who trusted him. Had they signed, they would have lost their case. This is dishonesty under Rule 1.01, on top of his gross negligence.
- **Conclusion:** Atty. Bert is liable for both gross negligence and dishonesty, warranting suspension from the practice of law.

**Q3.** In disciplinary proceedings before the IBP Commission on Bar Discipline, Atty. Carlo filed no answer, did not appear at two mandatory conferences, and filed no position paper. The Investigating Commissioner found that he had neglected his client's case and lied to the client about its status, and recommended a two-year suspension. The IBP Board of Governors increased the suspension to three years and added a P15,000.00 fine for his non-compliance with the IBP-CBD's directives. Before the Supreme Court, Atty. Carlo argues that (a) his non-participation in the IBP proceedings cannot be separately penalized because it is not the act complained of, and (b) the penalty cannot be raised above the Investigating Commissioner's recommendation. Rule on his arguments.

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** Both arguments fail. (a) His disregard of the IBP-CBD's directives may be separately penalized with a fine. (b) The Supreme Court determines the penalty on the facts and may adopt the IBP Board's heavier penalty.
- **Legal basis:** In Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi (A.C. No. 13118, June 28, 2022), the Court adopted the IBP Board of Governors' modification that raised the suspension from two to three years and added a P15,000.00 fine. It held that the respondent's failure to attend the mandatory conference and file the required pleadings reflected "willful disregard of the IBP-CBD's authority and disrespect of the board's proceedings," which are clear infractions of Canons 11 and 12 of the CPR. Quoting Olvida v. Gonzales, the Court explained that it exercises its discretion on the penalty on the basis of the facts of the case, and in Olvida it imposed a three-year suspension in place of the IBP's four-month recommendation.
- **Application:** (a) Atty. Carlo's failure to answer, attend the mandatory conferences, and file a position paper is a distinct infraction against the disciplinary process, separate from the neglect and dishonesty charged. A separate fine is proper. (b) The IBP's recommendation does not bind the Supreme Court, which fixes the penalty based on the facts. Since Atty. Carlo was both grossly negligent and dishonest toward his client, a three-year suspension is consistent with the penalty imposed in Pontiano and Olvida.
- **Conclusion:** The Court may suspend Atty. Carlo for three years and fine him P15,000.00 for ignoring the IBP-CBD's directives.

> Note: The decision applied the 1988 Code of Professional Responsibility. It predates the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (A.M. No. 22-09-01-SC, dated April 11, 2023 per the Court's citation in A.C. No. 11889), on which the 2027 syllabus is based. The CPRA cross-reference in the suggested answers (Canon IV, Competence and Diligence) points to the syllabus heading and is not part of the ruling. One quoted IBP passage cites "Rule 18.03 of Canon 8"; this is a typographical error for Canon 18.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68396)

## Cruz v. Cervantes

**ANTONIO R. CRUZ AND LORETO TERESITA CRUZ-DIMAYACYAC, AS HEIRS OF THE LATE SPOUSES DR. PROGEDIO R. CRUZ AND TERESA REYES, PETITIONERS, VS. CARLING CERVANTES AND CELIA CERVANTES SANTOS AND ALL PERSONS CLAIMING RIGHTS UNDER THEM, RESPONDENTS.**  
G.R. No. 244433 | 2022-04-19 | En Banc | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** V. Special Civil Actions > J. Forcible Entry and Unlawful Detainer (Rule 70)  
**Specific topics:** Ejectment vs. agrarian dispute: jurisdiction of the MTC; Mandatory referral to the DAR under Section 50-A of RA 6657 (as added by RA 9700); Kind of proof needed to show that a party is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant; Courts not bound by a DAR/PARO certification that states no findings of fact; Proof of agricultural tenancy (consent and sharing of harvest)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (X. Administrative Law > D. Judicial Review of Administrative Action > 1. Doctrine of Primary Jurisdiction)

### Doctrine
Under **Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as added by Section 19 of RA No. 9700**, the judge or prosecutor must automatically refer a case to the DAR when two requisites concur: (1) an allegation from any one or both parties that the case is agrarian in nature; and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. A mere allegation suffices for the first requisite, but the second must be proved (reiterating *Chailese Development Co. v. Dizon* and *Dayrit v. Norquillas*). The Court **clarified** that the proof required for the second requisite is **any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant**; a facial assessment is enough, so that the referral mechanism is not defeated by protracted proceedings in the referring court.

Courts must comply with the referral mechanism, but they are **not bound to accept the DAR's recommendation** where it clearly violates the procedure in DAR Administrative Order No. 03-11, which requires a summary investigation and a PARO certification that states the findings of fact on which it is based. Under Section 54 of RA No. 6657, DAR findings are final only if based on substantial evidence. **A PARO certification that states no factual basis does not bind the referring court, which must independently assess the evidence and determine its own jurisdiction.**

Reiterated: occupancy and cultivation of agricultural land, no matter how long, do not make one a de jure tenant. There must be independent and concrete evidence of personal cultivation, sharing of harvest, and the landowner's consent, and receipt of produce without an agreed system of sharing does not create tenancy. Absent a tenancy relationship, the ejectment case remains within the MTC's jurisdiction.

### Facts
Petitioners, heirs of the spouses Progedio and Teresa Cruz, filed a complaint for unlawful detainer dated February 22, 2016 with the MTC of Plaridel, Bulacan against respondents Carling Cervantes and Celia Cervantes Santos. They alleged that in 1960 Teresa allowed respondents' father Isidro to temporarily occupy a portion of their 2,702.10-square-meter lot in Bintog, Plaridel and build a house, on condition that his family would vacate upon demand. After the spouses died (1966 and 1999) and Isidro died (2005), respondents continued to occupy the property by tolerance. Petitioners revoked their tolerance by demand letter dated October 20, 2015, giving respondents 15 days to vacate; respondents refused. Petitioners also asked for PHP 5,000.00 monthly rentals.

In their Answer dated March 11, 2016, respondents claimed the land was agricultural and that they had succeeded to the tenancy rights of Isidro, who cultivated the land from 1965 to 2005 and planted camote, palay, vegetables, and fruit trees. They attached a rice mill tally sheet with the entry "Name: Mrs. Teresa Reyes Vda de Cruz; Kasama: Isidro Cervante[s]" and a handwritten receipt dated March 31, 1992 reading "Buwis sa Bakuran x x x ni Sidro Cervantes." Petitioners denied any tenancy: respondents occupied only about 300 square meters, and no crops were planted on the land.

In an Order dated March 29, 2016, the MTC referred the case to the Provincial Agrarian Reform Office (PARO) under RA No. 6657, as amended by RA No. 9700, and OCA Circular No. 62-10. On October 28, 2016, the PARO certified that the case was agrarian in nature "for it involves an agricultural land and the cause of action is ejectment of a farmer, farmworker or tenant," and recommended dismissal. The MTC dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction on February 9, 2017. The RTC of Malolos (Branch 15) affirmed on February 28, 2018, and the CA affirmed on September 27, 2018 (CA-G.R. SP No. 155023), denying reconsideration on January 21, 2019. Petitioners filed a Rule 45 petition, arguing among others that the dismissal relied merely on the PARO certification without affording them a hearing.

### Issues
1. Whether the MTC correctly referred the unlawful detainer case to the DAR (through the PARO) under Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as amended.
2. Whether the MTC correctly dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction by relying on the PARO certification that the case is agrarian in nature.
3. Whether respondents proved an agricultural tenancy relationship that would place the case within the DAR's jurisdiction.

### Ruling
**1. Yes, the referral was proper.** Section 50-A requires automatic referral when (1) a party alleges that the case is agrarian in nature, and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. Following *Chailese* and *Dayrit*, a simple allegation suffices for the first requisite, but adequate proof is needed for the second. The law is silent on the kind of proof, so the Court held that it "shall pertain to any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant". A higher standard would prolong proceedings in the referring court and defeat the purpose of letting the DAR, with its expertise, determine the nature of the dispute. Respondents' answer and its annexes (the tally sheet and the receipt) supported, on their face, the claim that Isidro was a tenant, so the MTC did not err in referring the case.

**2. No, the MTC erred in adopting the PARO certification.** DAR AO No. 03-11 requires the PARO to conduct a summary investigation, receive the parties' evidence and position papers, and issue a certification that "shall state the findings of fact upon which the determination by the PARO was based." The PARO certification here only stated its conclusion and gave no findings of fact, leaving the courts "with no basis to ascertain the evidence from which its findings were drawn." **While courts must comply with the referral mechanism, "they are not bound to accept the recommendation where such determination clearly violated the procedures and requirements set forth by DAR AO 03-11."** The referring court must independently assess the DAR's recommendation in light of the evidence. Administrative findings of fact deserve respect, but under Section 54 of RA No. 6657 they are final only when based on substantial evidence. Where the administrative body fails to state the basis of its findings or misappreciates the evidence, courts may disregard them.

**3. No tenancy was proved, so the MTC has jurisdiction.** The tally sheet naming Isidro as "Kasama" and the receipt for "Buwis sa Bakuran" did not show that the spouses Cruz consented to a tenancy relationship or agreed to share the harvest. "[O]ccupancy and cultivation of an agricultural land, no matter how long, will not ipso facto make one a de jure tenant"; independent and concrete evidence of personal cultivation, sharing of harvest, or the landowner's consent is necessary, and the tenant must show that he delivered the landowner's share. Citing *Rivera v. Santiago*, mere receipt of produce without an agreed sharing system does not create tenancy. Respondents failed to discharge their burden, so **the complaint remains an ordinary ejectment case within the MTC's jurisdiction.**

### Disposition
The petition was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated September 27, 2018 and Resolution dated January 21, 2019 in CA-G.R. SP No. 155023 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE, and the case was REMANDED to the MTC of Plaridel, Bulacan for further proceedings.

### En Banc or Division?
En Banc

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** The spouses Abad own a 2,000-square-meter lot in Bulacan. In 1990 they allowed Celso to build a house on a portion of it, on condition that he would leave upon demand. In 2024 they demanded that he vacate, and when he refused, they filed an unlawful detainer complaint with the MTC. In his answer, Celso alleged that the case is agrarian because he is their tenant, and attached a rice mill tally sheet listing him as "kasama" of Mrs. Abad. The MTC referred the case to the PARO. The PARO issued a one-paragraph certification that the case is agrarian in nature because it involves agricultural land and the ejectment of a tenant, and it recommended dismissal. The certification states no findings of fact. Relying on it, the MTC dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction. Was the dismissal proper?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The referral was proper, but the MTC erred in dismissing the complaint on the strength of a PARO certification that states no findings of fact.
- **Legal basis:** Under Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as added by Section 19 of RA No. 9700, a court must refer a case to the DAR when a party alleges that it is agrarian in nature and one party is shown to be a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. DAR AO No. 03-11 requires the PARO to conduct a summary investigation and to state in its certification the findings of fact on which it is based. Courts must comply with the referral mechanism but are not bound to accept a recommendation that clearly violates DAR AO No. 03-11; they must independently assess it in light of the evidence. Under Section 54 of RA No. 6657, DAR findings are final only if based on substantial evidence. (Cruz v. Cervantes, G.R. No. 244433, April 19, 2022)
- **Application:** Celso alleged that the case is agrarian and attached a tally sheet that, on its face, tends to show he is a tenant, so the MTC correctly referred the case. But the PARO certification states only a conclusion. It gives no findings of fact, so the court has no way to tell what evidence supports it. The MTC could not simply adopt it. It had to assess the evidence itself and determine whether a tenancy relationship exists and, therefore, whether it has jurisdiction.
- **Conclusion:** The dismissal was improper; the MTC must make its own determination of jurisdiction instead of relying on a certification without factual basis.

**Q2.** In an unlawful detainer case before the MTC, defendant Dario states in his answer, without attaching any document, that "this case is agrarian in nature and I am the agricultural tenant of the plaintiff." (a) Is the MTC required to refer the case to the DAR? (b) Would your answer be the same if Dario had attached a handwritten receipt signed by the plaintiff acknowledging delivery of the landowner's share of the palay harvest?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. A bare allegation that he is a tenant does not satisfy the second requisite for mandatory referral. (b) No, the answer would be different: the receipt is evidence which on its face shows that Dario is a tenant, so the MTC must refer the case.
- **Legal basis:** Referral to the DAR under Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as amended by RA No. 9700, is mandatory when two requisites concur: (1) an allegation that the case is agrarian in nature, and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. A simple allegation suffices for the first requisite, but adequate proof is necessary for the second. The proof required is any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. (Cruz v. Cervantes, G.R. No. 244433, April 19, 2022, reiterating Chailese Development Co. v. Dizon)
- **Application:** (a) Dario's statement that the case is agrarian satisfies the first requisite. But his claim that he is a tenant is only an allegation with no supporting proof, so the second requisite is not met and the MTC may proceed with the ejectment case. (b) A receipt signed by the landowner acknowledging delivery of her share of the harvest is evidence that, on a facial assessment, a reasonable mind would accept as showing that Dario is a tenant. The MTC need not and should not try the tenancy issue in full before referring. Both requisites are then present, and the MTC must refer the case.
- **Conclusion:** Referral is not required on a bare allegation of tenancy, but it becomes mandatory once Dario presents evidence that on its face shows he is a tenant.

**Q3.** Ramon has occupied and cultivated a portion of Lourdes's agricultural land for 30 years, planting vegetables and fruit trees. When Lourdes sued to eject him, Ramon claimed to be her agricultural tenant. His only evidence is (1) a rice mill tally sheet naming him as "kasama" of Lourdes's late mother and (2) a 1995 receipt for "buwis sa bakuran." (a) Has Ramon proved a tenancy relationship? (b) If the MTC had referred the case to the DAR and the PARO had certified that it is agrarian, what judicial recourse would Lourdes have against that determination, and in which court?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** (a) No. Long occupancy and cultivation, a tally sheet, and a receipt for "buwis sa bakuran" do not prove the landowner's consent to a tenancy or an agreed sharing of the harvest. (b) Lourdes may seek judicial recourse from the DAR's determination; since the case was referred by the MTC, the appeal lies with the proper RTC.
- **Legal basis:** Occupancy and cultivation of agricultural land, no matter how long, do not make one a de jure tenant. Independent and concrete evidence is needed to prove personal cultivation, sharing of harvest, or consent of the landowner, and the tenant must show that he delivered the landowner's share. Receipt of produce without an agreed system of sharing does not create tenancy. (Cruz v. Cervantes, G.R. No. 244433, April 19, 2022, citing Rivera v. Santiago) Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as amended by RA No. 9700, provides that from the DAR's determination "an aggrieved party shall have judicial recourse," and that in cases referred by the MTC "the appeal shall be with the proper regional trial court."
- **Application:** (a) Ramon's 30 years of occupancy and cultivation do not by themselves make him a tenant. The tally sheet and the 1995 receipt, as in Cruz, do not show that Lourdes or her mother consented to a tenancy relationship or agreed to share the harvest, and nothing shows he delivered a landowner's share. Ramon has not discharged his burden, so the case remains an ejectment case for the MTC. (b) If the PARO certifies that the case is agrarian, Lourdes is not without remedy. Since the MTC was the referring court, she may appeal the DAR's determination to the proper RTC. And the MTC itself is not bound by a determination that lacks factual basis or is unsupported by substantial evidence.
- **Conclusion:** Ramon has not proved tenancy, and Lourdes may elevate an adverse DAR determination to the proper RTC.

> Note: Petitioners also argued that Section 19 of RA No. 9700 and OCA Circular No. 62-10 are unconstitutional; the main opinion did not rule on that argument and decided the case on the grounds above. The "facial evidence" standard for the second requisite was drawn from Justice Caguioa's concurring opinion but was expressly adopted by the Court in the main opinion ("As such, We hold that the proof required shall pertain to any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows..."). The concurring opinions of Perlas-Bernabe, Leonen, Caguioa, and Lazaro-Javier, JJ. were not used for the doctrine.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68390)

## Go v. People

**ENCARNACION GO, PETITIONER, VS. THE PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.**  
G.R. No. 249563 | 2022-03-09 | Second Division | Rosario, J. | Decision

**Bar subject:** Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics  
**Syllabus topic:** VII. Criminal Procedure > B. Prosecution of Offenses (Rule 110) > 6. Complaint or Information > b. Sufficiency > iii. Cause of the Accusation  
**Specific topics:** Accused charged as a direct participant cannot be convicted in a capacity (corporate officer, owner, operator) not alleged in the Information; Defect in the Information is not cured by documents attached to it; Rule 45 bar on questions of fact is relaxed in criminal cases; Muro-ami versus pa-aling fishing (RA 8550, Sec. 92)
  
**Also relevant to:** Political and Public International Law (VIII. Constitutional Rights > M. Rights of the Accused)

### Doctrine
**An accused who is charged in the Information as a direct participant in the offense cannot be convicted on the theory that she is liable as an officer, director, treasurer, owner, or operator of the corporation or vessel that committed it, if the Information does not allege that capacity.** Such a conviction violates the constitutional right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation. Every element of the offense must be alleged in the information so the accused can prepare her defense, and the nature of the charge is determined by the facts recited in it (Canceran v. People; Domingo v. Rayala). The rule that corporate officers who participate in a corporate violation are criminally liable (People v. Tan Boon Kong; Sia v. People) applies only where the information charged them in that capacity.

The defect is not cured by documents attached to the Information, such as affidavits, a boarding certificate, or receipts, that identify the accused as owner or officer. That the attachments point to different capacities only highlights the defect in the charge.

Reiterated: Rule 45 allows only questions of law, but this is not strictly applied in criminal cases. An appeal in a criminal case throws the whole case open for review, so the Court may review the facts (Constantino v. People).

### Facts
In an Information dated January 12, 2006, Encarnacion Go and ASB Fishing Development Corporation (ASB) were charged with violating Section 92 of RA 8550 (Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998). The Information alleged that on November 20, 1999, at Brooke's Point, Palawan, the accused, "while on board Fishing Vessel Prince Arnold, fished ... using the method of 'Muro-Ami'" to pound and destroy coral reefs. At pre-trial the parties stipulated that ASB was engaged in pa-aling fishing in 1999 and that F/V Prince Arnold was owned, managed, and operated by ASB and was licensed.

Prosecution witness Joegie Baldado, recruited at 16 or 17, testified that about 400 people, some of them minors, worked the operation. Surface swimmers pounded the seabed with hoses weighted with about five kilos to drive fish into a waiting net, using a net with a mesh the size of a ten-centavo coin. The Philippine Navy chased and accosted the vessel. The Navy's joint affidavit named ASB as owner, while its Boarding Certificate and receipts for seized articles listed Go as owner. Go admitted being an ASB stockholder and nominal treasurer, denied muro-ami, and testified that she was not on board.

The RTC of Puerto Princesa (September 9, 2015) convicted both accused. It fined ASB P500,000.00 and sentenced Go to three to five years of imprisonment. Relying on Tan Boon Kong and Sia, it held Go liable as treasurer/director who knew of the business, could have prevented the violation, and benefited from it. The CA (March 14, 2019 Decision; September 20, 2019 Resolution, CA-G.R. CR No. 39682) affirmed. It held that the attachments to the Information showed Go was the vessel's owner, and that her presence on board was irrelevant because a "fishery operator" under Section 4(35) of RA 8550 does not personally engage in fishery. Go filed a Rule 45 petition, invoking her right to be informed. The OSG argued that the petition raised questions of fact.

### Issues
1. Whether the petition should be dismissed for raising questions of fact under Rule 45.
2. Whether F/V Prince Arnold engaged in muro-ami fishing.
3. Whether Go's conviction as an officer or owner, under an Information charging her as a direct participant on board the vessel, violated her right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.

### Ruling
**1. No.** The prohibition against questions of fact in Rule 45 "is not religiously followed in penal cases." Because criminal cases involve the right to liberty and the presumption of innocence, an appeal throws the whole case open for review, and the Court may review the trial court's factual findings (Constantino v. People).

**2. Yes.** Section 4 of the "Fishery Administrative Code, No. 90, Series of 1994" (as the Court cited it) limits pa-aling to a maximum of 250 fisherfolk, requires a mesh size of not less than 3.38 centimeters, and bars persons below 18 from engaging as fisherfolk. Baldado's testimony showed about 400 workers, minors among them, a net with a smaller mesh, and pounding of the seabed with weighted hoses to drive fish into a net. That is "essentially the essence of muro-ami and not pa-aling fishing, a matter that this Court can take judicial notice of."

**3. Yes. Go must be acquitted.** The Information charged Go with "taking a direct part in the commission of muro-ami fishing by allegedly being on board the vessel." She "was not indicted as an officer or a director of ASB nor as the owner of the said vessel." Her defense therefore centered on her physical role, and she established that she had no direct hand in the offense and was not on board. **"This should thus suffice to acquit her of the charges."** Tan Boon Kong and Sia cannot be applied because the informations there charged the accused in their capacity as corporate officers. "Nowhere in the Information was she charged as treasurer, director, operator, or owner of F/V Prince Arnold, and thus she could not be convicted in such capacity."

**The CA erred in holding that the attachments cured the defect.** The joint affidavit named ASB as owner, while the Boarding Certificate and receipts named Go as owner. Read with the Information, the attachments would make Go appear charged as a direct participant, as a director and treasurer, and as owner and operator all at once. That "even highlighted the defect in the charge" and made matters "all the more offensive to the defense of petitioner."

### Disposition
The petition was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated March 14, 2019 and Resolution dated September 20, 2019 in CA-G.R. CR No. 39682 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Encarnacion Go was ACQUITTED of violation of Section 92 of RA 8550, and entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

### En Banc or Division?
Second Division

### Bar Exam Questions (ALAC)

**Q1.** Marites is the treasurer of Isla Fishing Corp., which owns the fishing vessel F/B Maya. An Information charged Marites and the corporation with violating the Fisheries Code. It alleged that the accused, "while on board F/B Maya," fished using a method that pounded and destroyed coral reefs. Attached to the Information was a boarding certificate listing Marites as owner of the vessel. At trial it was proved that the crew used the prohibited method, but also that Marites was not on board. The RTC convicted her as treasurer who knew of and benefited from the operations, and as owner of the vessel per the boarding certificate. Should her conviction be sustained?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Marites must be acquitted because her conviction violates her right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.
- **Legal basis:** Every element of the offense must be alleged in the Information, and the nature of the charge is determined by the facts recited in it. An accused charged as a direct participant cannot be convicted as an officer, director, owner, or operator of the corporation or vessel when that capacity is not alleged. The rule holding participating corporate officers liable applies only when the information charges them in that capacity. Attachments to the Information identifying the accused as owner or officer do not cure the defect. (Go v. People, G.R. No. 249563, March 9, 2022; Const., Art. III, Sec. 14(2))
- **Application:** The Information charged Marites only with personally fishing while on board F/B Maya. She proved she was not on board, which defeats the only charge alleged. The RTC convicted her on different theories, as treasurer and as owner, which the Information never alleged and against which she had no reason to prepare a defense. The boarding certificate attached to the Information cannot supply the missing allegation. If anything, it shows the confusion over the capacity in which she was charged.
- **Conclusion:** Marites's conviction should be reversed and she should be acquitted.

**Q2.** Suppose instead that the Information alleged that Marites, "as treasurer and director of Isla Fishing Corp. and as operator of F/B Maya, who directed, financed, and permitted" its crew to fish using a method that pounded the coral reefs, violated Section 92 of RA 8550. Marites argues that she cannot be convicted because it is undisputed that she was not on board the vessel. Is her absence from the vessel a valid defense?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. Her absence from the vessel is not by itself a defense, because she is charged in her capacity as corporate officer and operator, not as a person who was physically on board.
- **Legal basis:** In Go v. People (G.R. No. 249563, March 9, 2022), the acquittal rested on the fact that the Information charged the accused only as a direct participant on board, and the Court distinguished People v. Tan Boon Kong and Sia v. People, where the informations charged the accused in their capacity as corporate officers. Section 92 of RA 8550 penalizes, among others, the "operator," and Section 4(35) defines a fishery operator as one who owns and provides the means, including vessels and gear, "but does not personally engage in fishery."
- **Application:** Here, the Information alleges Marites's capacity as treasurer, director, and operator, and her acts of directing, financing, and permitting the prohibited fishing. She is therefore informed of the charge she must meet, unlike the accused in Go. Since an operator by definition does not personally fish, her physical absence from the vessel does not negate the offense charged. The prosecution must still prove her participation in that capacity beyond reasonable doubt.
- **Conclusion:** Marites's absence from the vessel will not defeat a charge that properly alleges her capacity as officer and operator. Conviction depends on proof of her participation in that capacity.

**Q3.** Convicted by the RTC and the CA of a violation of a special penal law, Noel filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court. He argued that the evidence did not prove the prohibited act and that he was convicted on a theory not alleged in the Information. The OSG moves to dismiss the petition outright because it raises questions of fact, which are not allowed under Rule 45. Should the petition be dismissed outright?

**Suggested answer:**

- **Answer:** No. The Rule 45 limitation to questions of law is not strictly applied in criminal cases.
- **Legal basis:** Rule 45 provides that only questions of law may be raised in a petition for review on certiorari. However, because criminal cases involve the constitutional right to liberty and the presumption of innocence, the rule "is not religiously followed in penal cases." An appeal in a criminal case throws the whole case open for review, and the Court may review the factual findings if it is not convinced they conform to the evidence. (Go v. People, G.R. No. 249563, March 9, 2022, citing Constantino v. People)
- **Application:** Noel's petition questions the sufficiency of the evidence, which is a factual matter, and invokes his right to be informed of the accusation, which is a constitutional issue. Since his liberty is at stake, the Court may examine the records to see whether significant facts were overlooked and whether he was convicted of something not charged. The OSG's procedural objection does not bar this review.
- **Conclusion:** The petition should not be dismissed outright, and the Court may review the facts of Noel's criminal case.

> Note: The decision cites the pa-aling restrictions as "Section 4 of the Fishery Administrative Code, No. 90, Series of 1994." The issuance's exact designation is reproduced as written and was not verified. The CA had treated the minimum mesh size as a maximum ("should not exceed 3.38 centimeters"), while the Supreme Court stated it as "not be less than 3.38 centimeters"; the Court's version is used here. The decision did not discuss the conviction of co-accused ASB Fishing Development Corporation, which was not a petitioner. Q2's answer extends the Court's distinction of Tan Boon Kong and Sia and uses Section 4(35), which the CA quoted; the Supreme Court did not decide a case charged in that form.

Sources: [SC E-Library](https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68319)
